Whether it’s nostalgia or a sense that technology has gotten a bit too pervasive, there’s no denying that Slate Auto appears to be tuned into the particular moment. The startup has a simple pitch: an affordable electric truck with just the basics, leaving owners to DIY and BYOD for everything else, all for a sub-$25,000 starting price.
Among the things Slate does without is an embedded infotainment system. The small digital display on the dashboard that shows your speed and range is also where the backup camera appears if you engage reverse, and there are two USB-C ports that provide power but not connectivity, and that’s that. But there is a solution to getting lost, and it’s called “Screenless GPS.” Even though we don’t have a Slate truck to test it with, the OEM sent us a unit to review.
That’s right, it’s a good old spiral-bound road atlas! “We believe you should use the devices you know and love,” Slate says, and it reckons that maps worked just fine for past generations, so they should still work now.
Upside: a bored child can stare at the maps in the back seat endlessly on long drives. Not me, obviously.
Downside: wait, this Slate doesn't have a back seat! Where's little Joey!?

The U.S. must respect India's right to defend itself and should maintain a zero-tolerance policy towards terrorism, former U.S. Secretary of State Antony Blinken said on Saturday (November 14, 2026), while describing Washington’s ties with New Delhi and Islamabad as “fundamentally different".
“India is a global force,” Mr. Blinken said, adding that the relationship and shared interests between Washington and New Delhi were “really global in nature”.
In contrast, the U.S. relationship with Pakistan is “regional," he said during a conversation with Jawed Ashraf, chairman of the India Trade Promotion Organisation, at a summit in New Delhi.
“The relations with Pakistan are regional, and there are still going to be important areas where we need to do things with them, particularly, for example, when it comes to counter-terrorism, but these are fundamentally different relationships,” he said.
“We have to have a zero-tolerance policy for terrorism. Period. And that means that we have to have respect for India's right to defend itself,” he added.
Mr. Blinken said the U.S. approach must include support for India’s efforts to respond to attacks as well as diplomatic efforts to prevent an escalation between New Delhi and Islamabad, the two nuclear-armed neighbours.
He added that efforts to prevent escalation were important given the destructive potential of the weapons both countries possess.
Reflecting on Washington's past engagement with Islamabad, Mr. Blinken said U.S. strategic interests during the Cold War and the war in Afghanistan may have led successive administrations to be less critical of Pakistan's civil-military establishment.
“And there's certainly an opportunity for the United States to do more,” he added.
On India-U.S. relations, Mr. Blinken described the transformation in ties over the past few decades as a shift from estrangement to a strategic partnership, underpinned by shared interests and people-to-people connections.
“We moved from estrangement to a genuine and, in some ways, unique partnership, built on a convergence of strategic interests. Of course, it is also underpinned by the profound people-to-people connections between our societies,” he said.
He identified cooperation in emerging technologies as an important area for the two countries, pointing to collaboration in space, quantum technology and artificial intelligence.
“The next step is tech cooperation, our ability to work in space, tech, quantum, and artificial intelligence,” he said.
On India’s relations with Russia, Mr. Blinken acknowledged the partnership's historical depth and said Washington did not expect New Delhi to sever those ties.
“There will be places where we don't have the same perspectives. For Russia, we understand there is deep history between India and Russia. So, we don't want them to end it,” he said.
Mr. Blinken, who served as the 71st Secretary of State from 2021 to 2025 under then-President Joe Biden, said the world was at a profound inflection point, citing rapid technological change, inequality and shifting power.
“The speed and profundity of change is beyond anything we've seen, certainly in my lifetime,” he said, noting that ChatGPT, an Artificial Intelligence (AI) chatbot, took one month to reach 50 million users, compared with 75 years for the telephone.
He said the private sector increasingly drove technological change, while governments struggled to keep pace. Growing inequalities had fuelled a sense among younger people that they were being “left out, left behind", he said.
Mr. Blinken warned that the U.S. risked weakening its strength by damaging cooperation between the government, universities and research institutions, and by becoming less welcoming to skilled people from abroad.
“The biggest danger I think we face is a huge self-inflicted wound,” he said.
On U.S. domestic politics, Mr. Blinken said the recent midterm results went beyond the usual setback for the party of a sitting President. He attributed the outcome partly to frustration over the cost of living and concerns about corruption.
In the November 3 midterm elections, the Democratic Party won majorities in both the House of Representatives and the Senate, shifting control of the US Congress away from Republicans.
Mr. Blinken described the U.S.-Israeli military campaign against Iran, launched in February by President Donald Trump, as “a war of choice" and said the first Trump administration’s withdrawal from the 2015 nuclear agreement with Tehran had contributed to the crisis.
He said the agreement, signed in 2015 and formally known as the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA), required Iran to ship out 97% of its enriched uranium and placed limits on its centrifuges, while allowing extensive inspections.
After the U.S. withdrawal from JCPOA in 2018, Iran accelerated its nuclear programme, Blinken added, saying the ongoing military action would not resolve the issue.
“It is very hard to try to force this Iranian regime to capitulate; it is possible to get it to negotiate. And these are very different things,” he said.
He called for an “off-ramp” to the conflict, warning that escalation could involve attacks on regional infrastructure, US bases and partner countries.
The Strait of Hormuz, he said, had become a major challenge for global energy supplies after not being a problem before the war. Since February, Iran has repeatedly restricted access to the narrow chokepoint, one of the world's busiest oil shipping channels.
On the wider West Asia conflict, Mr. Blinken said a lasting settlement required resolving the Palestinian question and establishing a sovereign Palestinian state alongside a secure Israel.
“There are seven million Jews in Israel. There are seven million Arabs and Palestinians between Israel proper, the West Bank and Gaza. No one is going anywhere despite what extremists on both sides would like to see happen," he said.
"The solution remains, I fully believe, even though this is not a popular view, a secure Israel and a sovereign state of Palestine," he added.

In Brazil, they rallied online by the millions, sharing videos and spreading memes. In Serbia, they cycled across Europe and ran ultramarathons to make their voices heard.
Both movements burst into international public view last month as they became central during election campaigns to the pushback against authoritarianism. What they also offered, however, was a window into a wider phenomenon playing out across the globe, as youth-led movements reshape political landscapes.
“Gen Z is rising,” said Erica Chenoweth, a political scientist at Harvard Kennedy School. “It is abundantly clear that a significant proportion of gen Z is tired of sitting on the sidelines while their political systems fail them.”
Researchers have documented at least 25 protests around the world in which this age group – roughly those between the ages of 14 and 29 – has played a role.
From Bangladesh to Belgium and Italy to India, it seems gen Z, who account for about a third of the world’s population, have found their voice. “Gen Z may be experiencing a global political awakening,” Chenoweth wrote in a recent essay.
Their reasons for taking to the streets have varied widely, from protesting against corruption and an unequal playing field to calling for more investment in education, affordable housing and action on the climate crisis.
Many of the first protests to make waves were in Asia and Africa. In 2024, students in Dhaka, Bangladesh, made global headlines after they pulled off what was described as the world’s first successful gen Z-led revolution.
The protests began over a quota law but swiftly snowballed into a wider show of discontent against the increasingly autocratic rule of the prime minister, Sheikh Hasina. Two months later, Hasina resigned and fled the country by helicopter after being, as the Associated Press reported, “chased out by young protesters”.
Two years later and 4,000 miles away, students were at the helm of another revolution in Serbia, pushing back against a government that had steadily tightened its grip on the media and stuffed institutions with party loyalists.
Late last month, Serbia’s students’ movement was catapulted from the streets to the halls of power as they ousted Aleksandar Vučić in elections, bringing an end to his party’s 14 years in power.
Students and young people have long been at the forefront of the push for change, the analysts Cait Dallaire and Sebastian Dittgen wrote recently, citing the US civil rights movement and the 2011 Arab spring.
“What is unique about the current movement is the infrastructure of mobilisation: TikTok and X amplify and accelerate grievances; Discord servers and group chats enable decentralised planning; virtual private networks and mirrored content help organisers circumvent internet shutdowns,” they said.
It was this potent combination – young people in the streets and social media – that helped drive Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s comeback to win Brazil’s presidential election last month. After a bruising loss in the first round to the rightwing senator Flávio Bolsonaro, there was dismay in the country’s political left.
That was until students from the Fluminense Federal University mobilised in a pro-Lula march, setting off a wave of similar actions across the country. Soon after, the congressman and Lula ally André Janones, 42, created a WhatsApp channel called “Lula’s Army” that attracted millions of people looking to help boost pro-Lula content on social media.
On the night of his victory, Lula recognised their power. “I want to thank the generosity of Brazil’s young people who took to the streets to defend democracy,” he said.
Some politicians have sought to engage gen Z from the start. In the US, Zohran Mamdani’s campaign for New York mayor combined a canny use of social media with a legion of about 50,000 volunteers that had young people at its heart. The New York Times wrote that “volunteering for Mr Mamdani’s campaign became a salve” for young New Yorkers as the campaign became not just about “mobilising, but socialising”.
It was a nod to the global context in which many gen Zers have come of age; one riven by conflicts such as the Israel-Gaza war, the escalating climate crisis and the rise of nationalism, while the rules that have shaped the international order since the second world war are fraying.
In recent weeks, youth-led protests have begun to sweep Europe, from school students in France demanding better conditions in which to work to those in Spain who pitched tents to rally for affordable housing. In Germany, thousands of people took to the streets to protest against the cost of living and call for more investment in education, health and climate action in a movement organised by a group calling itself Gen Z regelt!, or Gen Z will sort this.
Analysts have been swift to point to the link between the protests. “The reasons are different, but they share the same spark: the breakdown of the social contract,” Arancha González, the dean of the Paris School of International Affairs, told the Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera. “In Europe, the idea that economies generate wellbeing and social equality has been shattered.”
A similar note of disillusionment threads through India’s Cockroach movement, which began as an online satire and has since swelled into a show of force against the strongman government of Narendra Modi. Fuelled by social media and rooted in democratic ideals, the power of the movement was laid bare this summer after Cockroach-led protests forced the resignation of the country’s education minister.
Equally visible is the pushback by India’s security forces against the movement, detaining thousands, unleashing teargas and beating people with lathis, or wooden clubs. Authorities went to extreme lengths in October to keep them from gathering in central Delhi, barricading roads and shutting down the internet and public transport.
It was a window into another facet that has defined youth-led protests, as research suggests they tend to be met with higher levels of repression, despite the fact that they are no more likely to use violence than others.
In France, lawyers and rights groups say several teenagers have suffered war-like injuries from police weapons. After the 2024 protests in Bangladesh, UN human rights experts said as many as 1,400 people had been killed, mostly by security forces, while thousands more suffered severe, often life-altering injuries.
In a recent analysis, Civicus, a non-profit that monitors global civic freedoms, said: “Because they question the distribution of economic and political power, gen Z-led protests have invariably been met with state violence,” linking the violence meted out to young protesters with their focus on systems and institutions that have long been generally accepted.
In Morocco, more than 2,000 people were charged and many received harsh prison sentences after a 2025 movement known as Gen Z 212 targeted officials over corruption, neglected public services and the lack of opportunities. Weeks later, in Mexico, youth-led protests over corruption and crime led to clashes with police in which dozens of people were arrested.
The outcomes of both of these movements show the varying success of gen Z protests. But at times, the foundations laid in one protest have given rise to others. In the US, much of today’s youth organising was shaped by the pro-Palestine student movement, in which there were thousands of arrests, expulsions and suspensions. Many schools instated anti-protest policies amid a broader rollback of educational freedom on campus.
Students, however, have continued to push for change. Last month hundreds in North Carolina marched in the heat to the polls after their historically Black university was denied a polling site, while thousands across the country have responded to the Cornell 7 case by skipping class, protesting and launching occupations.
As Chenoweth of the Harvard Kennedy School noted, the wave of recent youth-led protests may mark the beginning of a “profound generational transformation in world affairs” – one that could be capable of countering the global trend of democratic backsliding.
Ultimately, however, as Bilal Narjissi, a 17-year-old high school student in a suburb north of Paris recently told the Associated Press, the explosion of youth movements across Europe hints at a wider truth that has long been overlooked across the globe.
“We all agree on one point,” he said. “That young people are treated like children, far too much, and that they aren’t listened to enough.”

“There is no established playbook for making wearables in India. If you have the capital, you can set up a team, hire a bunch of researchers and scientists and come up with a product and even start selling it,” a California-based Indian founder of a wearable startup told us this week. The heated and contentious battle on X over Temple has brought out a lot into the open. A lot has been said and written about Temple this month, and who’s right and who’s wrong. What has gone unanswered in the cacophony is what it takes to actually launch a health or fitness tracking wearable that’s made in India. Where do founders turn when they need their hypothesis tested? Which agencies are the most approachable and how much red tape can one expect? These questions are not just about Temple. It’s about any new device that’s being launched in India, whether it is looking to track blood flow to the brain or it is just a heart rate or fitness monitor. The distinction matters in a market where wearable manufacturers can build and sell products that track physiological parameters without necessarily undergoing the clinical validation expected of medical devices. For India’s wearable industry, the debate has exposed gaps in how companies develop, validate and market products that make health-related claims or even basic activity tracking. But first, let’s see where Temple stands before diving deeper into the ecosystem of health wearables. Temple’s Bet On Something New Deepinder Goyal launched Temple with a core proposition of tracking blood flow to the brain and entropy. The company set out to create two new metrics that give users something their smartwatches could never. Firstly, BrainFlow is said to track relative changes in the blood flow to the brain during everyday activity. On the other hand, Goyal has described Entropy as a measure of how hard the body works to shed heat. The company’s website says the metric captures the body’s load across thermal, immune, digestive, cognitive, emotional, pharmacological, postural, reproductive and recovery systems. However, research papers uploaded on its website clearly state that Temple cannot directly measure cerebral blood flow. In response to Inc42’s questions about how these are measured, Temple said the Brain Flow Index is a relative index derived from optical signals collected at the temple. The company said the index rose and fell alongside blood-flow velocity in the middle cerebral artery, a major artery in the brain, as measured through transcranial Doppler ultrasound. Temple said the metric currently has two applications in its fitness app. It helps users compare the intensity of their cardio sessions and sends prompts to move when their Brain Flow Index drops during long periods of sitting. Unlike heart rate or sleep tracking, which have been part of consumer wearables for years, Entropy is being positioned as a new physiological metric. Its scientific validity will depend on whether the underlying signals can reliably measure what the company claims. The fact that Temple is broaching new territory with these metrics is what has set alarm bells ringing. Founders we spoke to say most wearables already have algorithms available for the heart rate and sleep tracking that have been improved and enhanced over the years since the first such devices came about. “The real work comes when you develop a new tracker or establish a new biomarker or a new benchmark for measuring something new,” the founder quoted at the beginning said, adding that specialised algorithms need research papers and validation. This is why there’s so much scepticism around Temple in the medical fraternity, with many doctors accusing the company of pushing a product without adequate backing. Temple’s research page lists multiple studies examining its BrainFlow technology, including a study involving 23 healthy adults that compared its reading with transcranial Doppler (TCD), a clinical technique used to measure blood-flow velocity in major brain arteries. Another study compared Temple’s BrainFlow readings with near infrared spectroscopy (NIRS), a technique that can distinguish blood volume changes in the brain from those in the scalp. The company says it has partnered with academic institutions across the world to study additional and more diverse groups of people, with further validation studies underway. Both studies are listed as being under peer review. A Temple spokesperson told Inc42 that validation work on Entropy is in its final stages and that it plans to publish the findings soon. Of Preprints And Peer Reviews After much criticism, on November 8, Goyal acknowledged the gap between the peer reviews, the studies and the launch of the devices, adding that the research on Entropy would be published soon. He also said BrainFlow was not the primary proposition behind Temple, but the starting point for its research. In an earlier November 5 post, Goyal said preprints would precede peer-reviewed publication and that further validation would continue as the product reached users. The distinction between publishing a white paper, uploading a preprint and completing peer review matters. But what do these words mean for founders who are entering the space fresh? Simply put, a white paper and a preprint make research available for public scrutiny, while peer review brings an independent assessment of the methodology, findings and conclusions. A second founder, an early stage entrepreneur building neuro-centric wearables, said credible validation requires controlled trials. “Generally, you need a double-blind test, a control group and a placebo group. The bare minimum that is respectable enough is 90 people.” However, there is no fixed requirement on the number of participants, they said when we asked whether 23 people is a large enough sample size for Temple’s study. “You can do it for 10 people. Nothing is a mandate. But is it respectable to have a big test group? Maybe,” the founder added. We were also told that publishing research papers is not compulsory either, but it helps establish credibility. At the moment, no regulations govern the release of such papers along with a product. “It’s not necessary to put out your research papers, but it is something that people demand for credibility,” the second founder added. Plus, getting a study peer-reviewed is not easy. Founders need to find the right testing bodies to conduct reviews. This comes along with a growing demand for independent validation from investors and others who want to partner with the startup. “Third-party trials are what most wearables get asked for, by investors and consumers. Even doctors are asking for them,” the founder added. For early stage startups, the cost of conducting larger studies can be a huge constraint. In their case, a study comprising just 100 subjects cost the startup around ₹15 Lakh, which the company claims is a lot at the early stage especially when the product has already been built. Most of the funds raised are depleted by the time the startup reaches the testing stage. Is Temple A Medical Device? The debate also raises questions about how India’s regulatory framework applies to wearable devices. Under the Medical Devices Rules, 2017, a product’s classification depends on its intended purpose and the function it is designed to perform. The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) regulates devices intended for purposes such as diagnosing, preventing, monitoring or treating diseases, as well as investigating or modifying physiological processes. Simply calling a product a fitness or wellness tracker does not settle its regulatory classification. Its intended use, advertised claims and actual functionality matter when it comes to clearances. Some well-known doctors in the country, who are sceptical of Temple claims, said the device's capabilities are not backed by peer-reviewed research. Hence, they have called for the device to come under the purview of medical regulators. However, Goyal has repeatedly maintained that Temple is not a medical device and is not intended to diagnose or prevent any diseases. He has also said that the company will obtain regulatory clearance wherever required before making claims that need it. Responding to Inc42, a Temple spokesperson said the device does not diagnose, treat, cure, mitigate or prevent any disease, and makes no claims about any medical condition. The company argued that under Indian law, a product is classified as a medical device based on its manufacturer's intended purpose. It also cited CDSCO's 2026 guidance on medical-device software, which says software intended for general wellness, without any reference to disease, does not fall under the purview of the Medical Devices Rules, 2017. Temple said that if it ever intends to introduce a feature for a medical purpose, it will seek CDSCO approval before making it available to users. The Regulatory Road Uncertainty extends beyond how companies position their products into what regulatory clearances are needed. The second founder, who had earlier spoken about the importance of clinical trials and third-party validation, said their company obtained CDSCO approval despite not making any medical claims. The founder said the company pursued approval because it was developing a brain-focused wearable device. “In India, any brain wearable device needs CDSCO approval. Whether it is tracking blood flow or not,” the second founder claimed, adding that wearables targeting the brain face additional requirements compared with other wearable devices. “Even though I am not making a medical device, I have a CDSCO clearance. Because it is mandatory in India.” The approval process in this case stretched around 16 months from November 2024 to March 2026. We were told that before receiving approval, companies can test only a limited number of units in India, with CDSCO determining the permitted number. This also makes it harder for companies to continuously iterate and test. The founder was describing their company’s regulatory experience. However, CDSCO’s 2026 guidance on medical device software does not establish a blanket approval requirement for all brain wearables. The founder acknowledged that rules remain unclear for products positioned as wellness devices. They also pointed to gaps in enforcement, saying regulatory scrutiny is not always consistent. “The CDSCO is not very active in looking into such companies, unfortunately. This is a loophole in India that many exploit,” the founder said. A third founder said navigating regulatory requirements can be difficult for early stage startups, leading some companies to be over-cautious. “Here you need to play around with the regulatory parts. Because in India the regulations are very hard. The only reason we never say that it is a medical device is that compliance becomes very hard. Especially for a new startup.” The founder said companies need to be particularly careful about making claims related to detecting or predicting medical conditions. “So if we say we can detect, then it would be a medical device. So you have to play very carefully with the words.” The question, therefore, is whether wearable manufacturers are making claims that bring their products within the scope of medical-device regulation, regardless of how they choose to market them. Beyond medical device approvals, the founder also highlighted other certifications such as Wireless Planning and Coordination (WPC) approval for relevant equipment that allows wireless connectivity, and Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) certification that are mandatory for electronic devices. Similarly, the US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) framework applies to relevant products marketed in the US and should not be confused with Indian regulatory clearance. Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) certification, meanwhile, relates to an ultra-low-power short-range data transmission over Bluetooth. The Temple spokesperson told Inc42 that it holds all the certifications required to sell the device in the countries where it is currently available. However, the company did not specify the individual certifications. Does The Wearable Industry Trust Temple? Temple’s development also needs to be viewed in the context of Goyal’s earlier work through Continue research and the Gravity Aging Hypothesis. The hypothesis explores whether gravity’s long term influence on blood circulation could contribute to aging, particularly through changes in cerebral blood flow. Goyal has previously argued that understanding brain circulation could help researchers investigate longevity and aging. Temple emerged from this broader research effort. The device was developed to monitor brain-flow-related signals continuously, giving researchers a way to study physiological changes outside conventional laboratory settings. However, a hypothesis, a measurable physiological signal and a validated biomarker are all different things. Establishing a relationship between a wearable’s readings and an existing clinical measurement does not automatically demonstrate that the device can predict aging or provide meaningful insights into longevity. One of the founders we spoke to said Temple’s placement near the temporal artery was a considered engineering decision, as the location offers a relatively accessible site for optical sensing. However, the founder cautioned that measuring blood flow at the temple does not necessarily establish that a device can measure blood flow within the brain. The second founder suggested the strength of Temple’s existing athlete study as a basis for broader performance claims arguing that larger studies involving control groups and independent validation would provide greater confidence. For Goyal, the next task is to establish that Temple’s proprietary measurements offer meaningful information beyond existing wearable metrics. In his November 8 post, he said consumers were free to wait for peer-reviewed evidence before purchasing the device. He also promised a detailed explanation of how BrainFlow is calculated, its potential application and its limitations. The wearable industry does not necessarily need every product to become a medical device; some can remain lifestyle devices. But as manufacturers move beyond counting steps, measuring sleep and tracking heart rates to developing new physiological benchmarks, they will have to show what those numbers actually mean, and how they actually derived it. Breakthrough products often begin with a hypothesis. Innovation lies in testing it, learning from the evidence and iterating, while being clear about the outcomes achieved and what remains under study. Many senior founders and investors have shown faith in Goyal’s ability to build Temple, pointing to his record of building and scaling Zomato and Blinkit (Eternal). Temple is an opportunity for him to bring that experience to a far less proven field: establishing a new category of wearable technology. Most importantly, Goyal has shown conviction by committing substantial personal capital to Temple. However, its scientific claims will need to withstand independent scrutiny before consumers can judge what the device can deliver. If Temple can successfully demonstrate that, through continued testing and iteration, it could help create the wearable playbook India lacks. Edited By Nikhil Subramaniam Creatives: Abhyam Gusai

Is this the end of the Electoral College?
The Democratic takeover in states like Michigan and Pennsylvania means a controversial reform could be back on the table.
I don’t know how much time you spend in the more feverish right-wing corners of the internet, but some conservative commentators are growing very alarmed about a specific Democratic policy proposal that could be nearing fruition.
It’s not abolishing ICE. It’s not nationalizing grocery stores. It’s not even investigating President Donald Trump over his reported failure to act on intelligence about his newly jobless/disgraced pal, Nvidia ex-CEO Jensen Huang.
Instead, they’re concerned about a wonky electoral workaround called the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, which would essentially sidestep the Electoral College. (And in the words of one right-wing commentator, “effectively [rig] the system so Democrats could never lose again.”)
NPV isn’t quite as nefarious as that (Trump won the popular vote just two years ago!), though it would revolutionize how the United States conducts presidential elections. The compact is basically an agreement between states to award their electors to the winner of the national popular vote, regardless of how their own state voted. Once enough states sign on, their combined electoral votes would guarantee the presidency to whoever wins the national popular vote.
The compact has laid dormant for two decades, however, while its backers lobby to sign on more states and their electoral votes. Eighteen states and Washington, DC, have signed on thus far, representing 222 votes.
But with Democrats soon controlling state governments in Arizona, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin, NPV could finally gain the critical mass to become reality. Politico reported on Tuesday that lawmakers in several states, including Pennsylvania, are already discussing the possibility.
There’s just one problem: Conservative influencers aren’t the only ones worried about the plan. In fact, even one of its architects has come to regard NPV as a “doomsday machine” that could trigger gigantic constitutional problems.
Go a little deeper
My colleague Andrew Prokop called up this conflicted architect, the Yale University professor Akhil Amar, earlier this week. Andrew has been writing and thinking about NPV for years. But Amar has been thinking about it even longer — since the aftermath of the 2000 election that made George W. Bush president.
Famously, Bush was elected even though he lost the popular vote, which Al Gore won by roughly half a percentage point. Amar thought the Electoral College was historically and inherently flawed, but only a constitutional amendment could abolish it.
Recognizing the long odds there, Amar and his brother instead sketched out a quick thought experiment — the broad strokes of what is now the NPV compact. The concept was later picked up and championed by the computer scientist John Koza and his group National Popular Vote Inc.
Koza has had quite a lot of success getting states to sign on to this workaround. But all the signees so far have leaned Democratic, which concerns Amar. The institution of the Electoral College doesn’t inherently favor one party over the other (in fact, both parties nearly got rid of it after the 1968 election), and the NPV wasn’t designed to tilt the scales, either. But as the discourse on right-wing social media suggests, Trump’s 2016 victory with a popular vote minority has only further hardened views on each side, and all the Democratic signatories have made it look like a partisan proposition.
There’s another problem too, Amar says. The compact leaves each participating state to calculate the national total, without a centralized body to oversee a nationwide count or recount. A very close election could leave states disagreeing over who won. But in the current environment, it’s actually hard to imagine a centralized body that both parties would find credible: People just don’t trust institutions the way they did in, say, 2000.
That puts NPV advocates in a tricky spot: The political process may finally favor the compact, but it faces significant cultural problems that could undermine its legitimacy.
Amar, for his part, thinks that even the small risk of electoral disruption outweighs the benefits of NPV. Especially since the Electoral College does actually work, whatever its shortcomings.
“The one thing we really do need to avoid as the stabilizing superpower in the world is constitutional chaos,” he told Vox. “And because this is sort of a new plan, even if it’s in principle likely to be better in all sorts of scenarios, if in a certain small percentage of cases it would lead to chaos, that’s something we need [to] seriously consider.”
One link for later
➨ Stop subway scrolling. If social media feels exhausting and overwhelming to you — which it does to me, often — try to stop logging on from public places. “People feel more lonely when they use social media while in transit, around people they have close relationships with, and when they are in nature,” says Vox contributor Shayla Love. “In contrast, when people use social media for shorter periods when they are alone at home or in study locations, it doesn’t have as much of a negative effect.”

Rosemary Nyirumbe became a nun when she was just in her mid-teens – and she felt her true vocation lay in rehabilitating children who had been through some of the worst trauma imaginable. So that’s what she did. In this episode Mike Wooldridge hears Sr Rosemary’s astonishing story. The feared rebel group, the Lord’s Resistance Army, started to terrorise the north of Uganda in the 1980s. Many children, girls as well as boys, were abducted and forced to become child soldiers. In many cases, the LRA forced them to commit atrocities, leaving them deeply traumatised. Many of the girls also bore the children of rebel leaders. As they started to return home, these children were often rejected by their families and communities, says Sr Rosemary. So she set about giving them a future and a hope: through enabling them to acquire skills like sewing, and by helping them see that God had not rejected them for the atrocities they had been forced to commit. A massive scientific collaboration meant to unravel the mysteries of the human brain has produced the most detailed map yet of the basal ganglia, a region closely associated with a wide array of psychiatric and neurologic disorders.
Researchers profiled more than 25 million cells, generating a deluge of data that allowed them to generate a “parts list” of what cells are present in the basal ganglia and how they’re arranged. In the process scientists discovered a new type of neuron that appears to play a role in schizophrenia. They also identified cell types linked to depression, bipolar disorder, and post-traumatic stress disorder.
Demonstrating the value of the work, the scientists produced preliminary evidence that they can use their more detailed understanding of brain cell types to deliver therapies with increased precision. Authors working in mouse models of Parkinson’s disease showed that a gene therapy designed to work in a subset of basal ganglia cells was as effective as a blanket approach; it was also safer.

US has floated Ukraine ceding Donbas for Nato membership, Zelensky says
- Published
US negotiators have touted the idea of Ukraine withdrawing its remaining forces from the eastern Donbas region in exchange for Nato membership, Volodymyr Zelensky has said.
The Ukrainian president's comments on Saturday come after US envoys visited Moscow and an EU summit in Dublin as part of ongoing efforts to end the war between Russia and Ukraine.
Kyiv has long sought membership of the military alliance as a condition of any peace deal to deter future threats, while Russia has said another Nato member on its border was unacceptable.
Zelensky has also consistently said Ukraine was unwilling to give up sovereign territory, despite Moscow's demands for it to cede the Donbas.
"The Americans raised a question: 'What if Ukraine joins Nato? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?' This was the first time this had been raised," Zelensky told reporters on Saturday.
He went on to say that if he received a proposal that contained security guarantees, no constraints on Ukraine's military and funds to rebuild the country, he would put it to a referendum.
US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff travelled to the Irish capital on Thursday to meet Zelensky, after a round of talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow the day prior.
Comments by both Putin and Kremlin officials suggest that Russia's position on the war has not shifted, and that Moscow's demands for territory and neutrality continue to far exceed what Ukraine is prepared to consider.
Moscow has previously proposed limits on the size of Ukraine's military, territorial concessions and Kyiv's guaranteed neutrality as conditions of a peace deal.
Ukraine has rejected these, arguing that such constraints would hamper its ability to stave off any future invasion.
There have, however, been recent signs the two can find common ground: last month, US First Lady Melania Trump was able to broker a temporary ceasefire in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky to allow for evacuations and aid deliveries.
US officials had previously said that Ukrainian Nato membership was off the table.
Zelensky said on Saturday that the US proposal made him believe that "Nato is back on the agenda".
But he cautioned: "You have also heard Putin's signals, and this is an extremely difficult conversation."
Russia currently occupies roughly a fifth of Ukrainian territory, including most of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions that compose the Donbas.
Ceding the small portions of land Ukraine still controls there would be a small concession in practical terms, but would be symbolically significant for Kyiv because it would constitute an acceptance of the Donbas being Russian.
Zelensky has previously spoken of retaking Russian-controlled territory in four of Ukraine's regions, as well as the Crimean peninsula, which Moscow annexed in 2014.

India should prioritise meeting its growing energy requirements and strengthening climate resilience rather than pursuing rapid decarbonisation at the cost of economic development, Steven E. Koonin, Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution, Stanford University, said at the Hindustan Times Leadership Summit. India’s immediate energy needs must take precedence over emission-reduction targets as the country continues to develop, the professor said, noting that access to reliable and affordable power is essential for raising living standards, boosting industrial activity and building resilience against climate-related risks. “India’s overwhelming priority must be to get the energy that it needs to develop. Secondarily, you can worry about emissions,” he said in an interview, adding that countries must balance three essential pillars of energy policy: affordability, reliability and decarbonisation. His remarks come amid India's continued reliance on coal to meet electricity demand, even as the country expands renewable energy capacity and pursues long-term decarbonisation goals. Developing economies require more power as they grow, Koonin said, pointing to the low penetration of air conditioning in India as a sign of unmet energy demand. Only 15% of Indian households own an air conditioner, the professor noted, stressing that expanding electricity access must remain a priority as incomes rise. "Energy needs are immediate; they are soluble, whereas the climate threat is distant, vague and uncertain," he said. While acknowledging that human activities influence the climate, Koonin questioned the scale of projected impacts, arguing that climate debates often overstate future risks while paying too little attention to the economic and technological constraints of cutting emissions. Widely seen as a climate sceptic, Koonin worked as chief scientist before serving in the US Department of Energy, or DoE, in the first Barack Obama administration. He shot to prominence with his 2021 book Unsettled: What Climate Science Tells Us, What It Doesn’t, and Why It Matters. The professor identified nuclear power as a vital part of India's future energy mix, saying the country needs dependable electricity sources to sustain economic expansion. “I think nuclear energy has got to be a big part of India's future,” he said, adding that greater investment in climate science, improved forecasting models and adaptation measures should also remain priorities. Economic growth will itself help India build resilience against climate challenges, Koonin said, as better infrastructure, stronger public services and wider energy access improve its capacity to handle extreme weather. Countries should also focus on developing lower-emission technologies that cost no more than conventional coal-based power, he added. Renewable energy expansion has not yet substantially reduced fossil-fuel dependence, the professor noted. Coal, oil and natural gas still account for around 80% of global primary energy consumption, with renewables largely adding to overall energy supply rather than replacing conventional fuels. Citing India Meteorological Department (IMD) data, Koonin said India's average temperature has risen by about 0.68 degrees Celsius over the past century—considerably less than the average warming recorded across global land areas. On the monsoon, the professor noted that long-term rainfall data shows no significant downward trend, despite wide variations across decades. He also pointed to changes in northwest India's Thar Desert, noting that the region has grown wetter and greener over the past two decades alongside gains in agricultural productivity. On extreme weather, Koonin said tropical cyclones have not become more frequent over the long term, nor is there a clear upward trend in deaths linked to extreme temperatures in India. Referring to IMD figures, the professor noted 35 heatwave-related deaths in the previous year, while acknowledging that some observers believe official tallies undercount such fatalities. India's farm output has also climbed over the past two decades despite higher temperatures, he said, arguing that climate change has had no detectable impact on the country's overall economic growth. According to Press Information Bureau releases, India’s total foodgrain production reached an estimated 376.56 million tonnes in 2025–26 (Third Advance Estimates), up from 265.05 million tonnes in 2013–14. While human activities have influenced the climate, Koonin said current data does not reflect the dramatic shifts often reported. In 2025, under the second presidency of Donald Trump, Koonin was one of the authors of a DoE report, A Critical Review of Impacts of Greenhouse Gas Emissions on the U.S. Climate, which questioned the scientific conclusions of greenhouse gas emissions driving climate change. “The question is how climate responds to human influences—are we gonna see more storms, sea level rising more rapidly? The data does not show that,” the professor said, noting that the globe has warmed by 1.3 degrees Celsius and is projected to warm by a similar amount over the next century. “What gives me hope for the future is that since 1900, the globe has warmed 1.3 degrees Celsius, and it is projected to warm up the same amount over the next century. In the last 120 years, as global temperature rose, population rose, lifespan rose to 70 years, GDP per capita has gone up by a factor of 7, literacy increased, and the death rate from extreme weather also went down,” he said. Reaffirming his point on India's monsoon, Koonin added: "You can see ups and downs that happen over many decades, but long term it’s hard to see a trend." Addressing Delhi's persistent air pollution crisis, the professor said local pollution and carbon dioxide emissions are distinct problems requiring different policy responses. Local air quality can be tackled through regulation and cleaner technology, he said, citing Los Angeles as a city that cleaned up its air despite population growth. On climate science, Koonin called for stronger monitoring systems, better forecasting models and deeper research into regional climate patterns. The professor also touched upon geoengineering—specifically solar radiation management, which involves reflecting a fraction of sunlight back into space to lower global temperatures—cautioning that the method carries high risks and could disrupt rainfall patterns. Ultimately, India should focus on economic growth, wider energy access and climate adaptation while exploring affordable low-emission technologies, rather than letting decarbonisation targets hold back its immediate development needs, Koonin concluded. India has had decades of unchanged high anaemia prevalence in women and children that has historically been thought to be due to iron deficiency. This has led firstly to an iron and folic acid (IFA) tablet supplementation targeted at women and children, and secondly to fitful implementation of mandatory fortification of staple foods. IFA is a ‘precision’ strategy, applying as it does to the vulnerable population it is intended for, while fortification is a broad strategy that applies to the entire population. The latter works in controlled settings such as clinical trials, but has not worked in real-world settings, and might have adverse effects when given to those it is unintended for.
The reason for pivoting: anaemia is mistakenly conflated with iron deficiency In India. The evidence is otherwise: in national Indian surveys, it has been shown that iron deficiency is not the major cause of anaemia. Indeed, fully one-third of anaemia cases demonstrate no micronutrient deficiency or obvious cause. Even so, giving iron should have sorted out those who did have iron deficiency anaemia, and reduced the general anaemia prevalence. While this could be a problem with inefficient programme implementation, two important questions arise: is there is really a deficiency in dietary iron intake in India? And is the administered iron being adequately absorbed and utilised for haemoglobin formation?

Question: Which two men's club sides have won three successive competition finals at the new Wembley?
You probably knew Pep Guardiola's Manchester City won three League Cups on the bounce between 2018 and 2020 before adding a fourth in 2021 – but another side did the silverware hat-trick first.
Whitley Bay, who play in the ninth-tier Northern Football League, won three successive FA Vase finals between 2009 and 2011 – an unprecedented achievement in non-league football.
The FA Vase, a national competition for amateur teams, was established in 1974; and in more than half a century The Seahorses are the only ones to win it four times – including those three on the trot.
And they did so under the eye of an unassuming IT manager from Sunderland, who used "quiet moments in the day" to plan historic cup success.
Ian Chandler, who had three spells at Whitley Bay as a player, became manager in 2004 and spent 10 years in charge.
It was no mean feat, as any non-league manager will tell you. Instead of focusing on work meetings, Chandler says he spent more time sorting hotel bookings or discussing scouting reports.
His team were inspired by missing out on Wembley in 2007-08, when Whitley Bay reached the FA Vase semi-finals. They lost 4-0 to Lowestoft Town in the first leg, and despite going 3-0 up inside 20 minutes of the return fixture at Bay's Hillheads Park stadium they were unable to overturn the deficit.
After that elimination, Chandler developed a superstition of never again giving pre-match interviews - as the last time he did so was before the 4-0 defeat.
Whether because of his renewed focus, or because of a desire among players to make amends, it steeled the group to make history.
"It's the hardest thing to keep a team together - as soon as players get noticed, they get picked up at higher level," Chandler tells BBC Sport.
"But after we got to the Vase semis, players wanted to stay and prove what they could do.
"Then the lads wanted to do it again."
And again.
Despite being a lifelong Sunderland fan, Chandler admits basing his team on Kevin Keegan's Newcastle - with entertainment even placed above winning.
"There was a standing joke in the team, two or three at the back? One time we chased a game with two at the back," he says.
"The Premier League can be so boring; fans want to be entertained, that's what we promised."
Chandler was already a Whitley Bay hero when he was appointed manager by chairman Paul McIlduff, having scored the winner in the 2002 FA Vase final against Tiptree United at Villa Park.
After a slow start as the then-35-year-old with no prior managerial experience found his bearings, Chandler built a talented team which became the envy of non-league football nationwide.
"We played good football. We had pace on the wing, fantastic midfielders, and strikers who were deadly," says McIlduff, who has been Whitley Bay chairman since 2001.
"When we brought them in, it was about fitting the psychology of the dressing room. No-one thought they were better than anyone else, they played for each other."
A growing influence in the side was the 'Whitley Bay Maradona'.
Paul Robinson came through Newcastle United's academy before a career spent across various non-league clubs in the north-east – including Whitley Bay from 2007 to 2013.
Like several other players and staff, he worked with Chandler both in his day job at software company Sage and at Hillheads Park.
"He was my manager at work and football, I was sick of him," he tells BBC Sport. "But it helped get time off for matches."
And it meant he also had an understanding boss if his mind drifted at work.
"Zoning out happened regularly, picturing scoring and winning, what the opposition would be like - hoping they were rubbish so we could have an easy stroll," he says.
Perhaps Robinson's greatest Whitley Bay moment came in the 2010 FA Vase semi-final second leg, when his last-minute diving header in the driving rain secured a 6-5 aggregate victory over Barwell, sparking a pitch invasion.
"Everyone goes to the finals, you were there, you could enjoy it," says Robinson, who is now academy head at South Shields.
"But the rounds before were the bigger games. At home, we would get 2,000 or 3,000 at every game. You felt like a real player. You associate those memories with 90s FA Cup you never think it will happen in non-league."
Chandler played in a 2-0 win over Preston in round two as they reached the FA Cup third round for the first and only time in the 1989-90 season, and they also progressed to round two the following campaign.
Those seasons of success - made The Bay a feared side for non-league clubs across England, and meant they were ready for the big games in a way most amateur sides are not.
"One quarter-final against Biggleswade [in 2009], they turned up in suits and ties," says Robinson. "We thought, this is their day out, their cup final. We won 5-2.
"By the end, teams were turning up afraid of us. We had it won beforehand."
Off the pitch, the team's success had an influence on the whole of Whitley Bay. A working-class town near Newcastle, which had its heyday as a Victorian-era holiday destination, sporting success brought local pride to the north-east coast.
And like any lower league club, that success could only be supported by dedicated volunteers, who went into overdrive before the Vase finals.
They would go door to door across shops in Tynemouth, North Shields and Whitley Bay to raise support. A van selling tickets was parked outside Woolworths on the high street.
"There was such excitement around the whole of Whitley Bay - every shop had things in the windows, the blue and white stripes," says one of the volunteers, Jenn Robinson.
She got involved because her late husband Mike was a club board member and if she wanted to see him she "had to go around there".
"Everyone wanted to come and watch, we got so many local sponsors," adds Jenn.
"I still do buffets and things for players and long-standing fans. We have a game tonight, and I'm making the sandwiches now."
Newcastle United helped out with selling tickets for the finals, while North Tyneside Council provided security services as thousands flocked to Hillheads Park for big cup games.
But even the best laid plans can go awry.
"We organised a train down to London, the guarantee was that it would go straight to Wembley," says McIlduff. "The first time it worked, second time they were taken to Kings Cross - we had to organise taxis up to Wembley."
By hook or by crook, The Seahorses army made it three times to the national stadium. Some even got royal treatment.
"It was absolutely surreal, and a delight," Jenn says. "The first Wembley final we played at, it had just opened. My husband being on the board, we sat in the royal box, which was fabulous.
"One of the security guys showing me to our seats said, 'Miss Robinson, this is Prince William's seat'. He hadn't even sat in it at that point."
Chandler, whose son Benjamin was a mascot at all three finals, said it was an overwhelming experience at times for the players too.
"The first year was crazy, everything was brand new," he says. "The first year the bus driver scraped the side up of the bus driving into the ground.
"The second year we tried to take everything in, all the lads had their mobiles. Then the third year, it was just a case of can we do it, win three in a row."
And three times, Whitley Bay rose to the occasion.
After beating Glossop North End 2-0 in 2009 in front of 12,200 supporters, Whitley Bay returned a year later to thrash Wroxham 6-1.
The opening goal was scored by prolific striker Paul Chow after only 21 seconds. At the time this was the quickest goal in a Wembley final and was only surpassed 13 years later when Ilkay Gundogan scored for Manchester City inside 13 seconds in the FA Cup final.
The hat-trick was completed in 2011 with a frantic 3-2 win over Coalville Town, who equalised twice before Chow was again the hero with an 86th-minute winner.
In total, nearly 30,000 fans were in the stands across the three finals.
After each final, Whitley Bay celebrated in The Green Man pub just 15 minutes' walk from the famous Wembley arch.
"In the first year we just went back to the bar and it was an anti-climax," Robinson says. "The second and third years the club got their act together and we rented a room; families, friends and fans were invited, they were brilliant nights.
"In 2010, we actually spent 10 days together - the week of the final we spent as a squad preparing, then we went to Marbella for five nights. Best 10 days of my life!"
The 2010 trophy lift was perhaps the most emotional though, as the players were joined by former team-mate Mark Taylor. He had played in the previous year's final, before being diagnosed with motor neurone disease, forcing an early retirement.
"Mark used to come on the away trips after he got diagnosed, he just wanted to be Mark - we had a good laugh everywhere we went," says Chandler. "He's still knocking about, abusing me on Facebook. He was the core of our second and third year."
Success ensured the lives of Chandler and his team were never quite the same again. Reporters turned up to Sage to speak with the manager and his players; even Chandler's mum was interviewed by BBC Radio Newcastle legend Paul Dixon.
Chandler - and his wife - even got up close and personal with managerial icons.
"I was invited to the annual sports awards in Manchester. There were people there like Sven Goran Eriksson and Sir Alex Ferguson [and] numerous others," he says.
"I had my wife with me and Sven came over gave her a peck on the cheek - she wasn't aware of who it was until I told her later that evening."
Robinson admitted that going back to work at an IT company after Wembley glory was a "massive comedown".
"One year I got a standing ovation when I walked into the office, but after that it was just back to normal," he says.
"People wind you up about it - 'are you talking about Wembley again? Give it a rest Robbo!"
Like all good things, Whitley Bay's golden era came to an end. Chandler departed in 2014 after a dip in form; the club have not won a major honour since the 2011 FA Vase and remain in the ninth tier.
But the memories in the football-mad north-east remain.
"Me and my wife went out on a Sunday at a pub in Durham just a few weeks back, and this guy came up out the blue and asked, 'Are you Ian Chandler?'" he laughs.
"Then he started talking about that team; in the north-east, everyone follows football. It was so lovely."

Medicine is AI’s real test, and India has a historic opportunity: Siddhartha Mukherjee
The oncologist said AI will have failed if it does not make medicines faster, cheaper and better
Artificial intelligence (AI) should be judged by whether it makes medicines faster, cheaper and better, oncologist and author Siddhartha Mukherjee said on Saturday, warning that if it does not, "we have failed the AI revolution".
Mukherjee, co-founder and chief executive of the drug-discovery company Manas AI, opened his talk at the Hindustan Times Leadership Summit by noting the widespread concern over AI’s rapid rise. Its capacity to produce transformative medicine, he said, was the one feature that could offset that concern, and if AI failed there, doubts about its value would return. He returned to the point at the end of his talk: “If it’s not true that medicines become faster, cheaper, better, then we have failed the AI revolution."
Medicine has been moving the wrong way, he said. “The number of medicines approved over time has actually been decreasing… and the cost of each medicine has been increasing."
Drug researchers call this pattern Eroom's Law, Moore's Law spelt backwards.
If AI can reverse it, Mukherjee said, "we will truly have mastered the capacity of bringing medicines to vast numbers of people".
He said India could help lead that change, and called it the main message of his talk. "Of all countries in the world, China and I truly believe India, with appropriate regulatory and technological reform, can reverse the trend," he said. "We have a historic opportunity in this country."
Mukherjee explained that every medicine binds to a protein in the body the way a key fits a lock. He said aspirin, Lipitor and Tylenol all work this way.
Mukherjee said trying every possible key is out of the question. He added that small-molecule drugs number 10 to the power of 24. Mukherjee said that no amount of power in the current system can possibly test 10 to the 24th keys against one single target protein.
Mukherjee said modern drug design instead identifies the target, finds its "keyhole," and builds a chemical from scratch to fit it.
He added that Manas does this with a combination of artificial intelligence, which is a neural system, and what they started calling medicinal intelligence, meaning the rules of physics and chemistry.
Mukherjee said that for daraxonrasib, a pancreatic cancer drug, a human researcher took about 10 years to find the keyhole, but their algorithm took two hours to find it. "That is the kind of speed that we get, the kind of compression of speed that we get just from this module, just from the keyhole finding."
Mukherjee said Manas sends 50 to 100 proposed compounds every three weeks to Chinese chemical companies, which test them and return data in about three weeks. He added that the model learns from each batch before the next is made until it reaches a medicine. Mukherjee called this the design-make-test cycle, and one of the fastest they have ever been able to achieve.
He gave an Indian example of what AI could deliver. About three years ago, he said, he launched Immuneel, a cell-therapy company in Bengaluru, in collaboration with Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw. In cell therapy, doctors extract a patient’s T cells, “weaponise” them in a laboratory to kill the cancer, grow them for 10 to 12 days and infuse them back. Mukherjee said the treatment, used against leukaemia and lymphoma and now being extended to myeloma, is potentially curative and was not available anywhere in India before.

Manipur CM chairs security review meeting after killings in Kangpokpi, Ukhrul
The meeting also discussed measures to further strengthen security arrangements in vulnerable areas of the state
Manipur chief minister Yumnam Khemchand chaired a security review meeting on Saturday at the Cabinet Hall of the Chief Minister’s Secretariat in Babupara, Imphal, to review the current law and order situation in the state.
The meeting was convened following incidents at Taphou Kuki village in Kangpokpi district and the ambush at New Heaven in Ukhrul district on Friday.
During the meeting, the attendees decided that combing operations would continue to apprehend those involved in various crimes. It was also decided that security personnel deployed at posts in different areas would strengthen security arrangements in their respective jurisdictions.
The meeting also discussed measures to further strengthen security arrangements in vulnerable areas of the state.
Home minister Govindas Konthoujam; chief secretary Rajeev Singh Thakur; security advisor Kuldiep Singh; DGP Mukesh Singh; ADGP (law and order); senior officers of the Assam Rifles, CRPF and BSF; other senior officers of central security agencies; and officials from the home department attended the meeting.
Five people have been killed in two separate incidents in the state over the past two days. On Thursday, a woman from the Kuki community was killed while working in a paddy field during an armed attack at Taphou Kuki village. The following day, suspected Kuki militants ambushed and killed four civilians from the Naga community at New Heaven village in Ukhrul district, along National Highway 202 (Imphal-Nagaland via Ukhrul).
Meanwhile, the Tangkhul Naga Long (TNL), a Naga body, issued a “public ultimatum” to the state and central governments, giving them three days to drive out all “Kuki terrorist” from Naga areas. The organisation also demanded that the case be handed over to the National Investigation Agency (NIA) within the deadline.
In a statement, the TNL said: “This is the 4th such incident at the same location. The entire responsibility for failing to protect the lives of innocent civilians is solely fixed upon the State Government and the Central Government. We have lost complete faith in the central security forces. Therefore, all the central security forces deployed therein must be immediately withdrawn.”
The Naga body warned that failure to resolve the issue would lead to an indefinite agitation until justice was delivered.
Separately, the Kuki Inpi Manipur (KIM), a Kuki organisation, issued a 72-hour ultimatum to the Manipur Police over what it described as “selective reporting and ethnic bias”.
According to the KIM, the police described the killing of Kimneineng Chongloi, a 40-year-old Kuki woman, as a mere “firing incident” without identifying the perpetrators. However, in a separate statement about an injured Tangkhul Naga civilian, the police explicitly identified the attackers as “suspected Kuki armed miscreants”.
The KIM has demanded an internal investigation, a public explanation and corrective action from the police. It warned that failure to comply within 72 hours would lead it to pursue legal remedies and suspend cooperation with the Manipur Police in Kuki areas.

Sorry, Margaret, your email is working again.
After a widespread outage shut down Microsoft 365 services for businesses, governments, and tens of millions of other users around the world, the essential cloud services are now (mostly) back online, according to the company’s status page.
The outage debacle began around lunchtime on the East Coast on Thursday, with users reporting Outlook outages to the service-tracking website Downdetector just after 12 pm ET. Within the hour, Microsoft said it was investigating reports of an outage that at the time was limited to North America. It quickly spread to impact more than 70 countries around the world.
The full cause of Microsoft’s unprecedented outage remains unknown, but the company repeatedly ruled out a cyberattack as the cause in statements to its status page. It is also ruling out AI or AI agents playing a role in the debacle.
“We are seeing broad recovery and stability across our services,” a Microsoft spokesperson says in a statement. “This was a technical issue not related to cyber or AI/agents. The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change. We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions.”
The company has promised a “full post-incident report” after it has fully reviewed what went wrong.
As Outlook, Teams, Copilot, and other Microsoft 365 systems come back online, users will likely see their inboxes turn into a mess. “You're probably going to get a lot of notifications when things come back,” says Jonathan Leitschuh, an independent researcher.
Microsoft said it had increased the queue time for emails to 48 hours in an attempt to ensure that every message that people tried to send while its systems were down gets delivered. Leitschuh points out that, even with the bulk of systems restored, users may receive “a flood of notifications a few hours down the pike” as subsystems come back online.
The total impact of the Microsoft outage may never be fully known, but it’s safe to say it’s already significant. Governments from Japan to the United States reported disruptions to a bevy of functions. Airlines reported problems with their ability to communicate with customers. Many law enforcement and emergency services ground to a halt. And hospitals reported widespread interruptions to their operations.
Ultimately, the episode serves as a reminder of the risks involved when the whole world relies on a single company for a critical service. “We're very interdependent on these systems in modern life,” says Leitschuh. Next time, delayed emails may be the least of our worries.

At least 24 killed after bus collides with truck in north-east India
- Published
At least 24 people have died and 11 others injured after a bus collided with a truck in Assam, north-east India.
The accident happened near Kaziranga National Park, a Unesco World Heritage site, and the injured have been admitted to Jorhat Medical College and Hospital.
Several of the deceased are college students, according to Assam's rural development minister Atul Bora, but they have not yet been publicly identified.
Bora added that witnesses reported one of the vehicles may have been speeding when the crash took place, but "the exact reason will be known after [an investigation]".
Assam chief minister Himanta Biswa Sarma wrote in a post on X that "the scale of this loss has shaken all of us".
He adds: "Our foremost priority now is to make sure the injured receive the best possible medical care without delay."
The bus was carrying passengers from Bokakhat and was headed towards Nagaon.
Bokakhat is best known as the gateway to Kaziranga National Park, famous for its one-horned rhinoceroses.
Nagaon is an important agricultural and commercial centre in central Assam, about 120km (74.5 miles) west of Bokakhat by road.
Lurinjyoti Gogoi, chief of a regional opposition party, said road safety has long been a major concern in the state.
"The government must take it up seriously," he said.
Road accidents are responsible for thousands of deaths in India every year.
In 2023, 172,000 people lost their lives on Indian roads, or 474 a day – roughly one every three minutes.
The count increased to 183,382 deaths in 2025.
Experts say the crisis is rooted not just in infrastructure but in human behaviour, enforcement gaps and systemic neglect.

New Delhi: Artificial intelligence (AI) is compressing early-stage cancer drug discovery from nearly eight years down to three or four months, according to Dr. Siddhartha Mukherjee, an oncologist and co-founder and CEO of Manas AI, an American drug discovery startup. Speaking at the Hindustan Times Leadership Summit 2026 in New Delhi on Saturday, Dr. Mukherjee said healthcare is the single most critical proving ground for AI. For decades, the pharmaceutical sector has faced rising development costs alongside fewer new drug approvals—a trend known as Eroom's Law. To reverse rising drug costs, Manas AI combines machine learning with basic rules of physics and chemistry. Instead of testing billions of existing chemicals one by one to see if they work, the software finds weak spots on disease-causing proteins—much like identifying a keyhole on a lock—and builds new drug molecules from scratch out of atoms to block them, said Dr. Mukherjee, also an associate professor of medicine at Columbia University. Finding a target spot on a pancreatic cancer protein, a task that previously took human researchers a decade, now takes Manas AI’s algorithms just two hours. By pairing AI molecular design with automated robotic lab testing, the company completes each design-and-test cycle in three weeks, yielding experimental cancer candidates up to 200 times stronger than existing competitor drugs on the market. Despite these breakthroughs, Dr. Mukherjee cautioned that cancer cannot be cured in one fell swoop because every cancer is biologically distinct. While remarkable progress has been achieved against specific cancers such as breast cancer, leukemia, and lymphoma, complex diseases like pancreatic and stomach cancers remain formidable challenges, he said. Dr. Mukherjee also emphasized that speeding up early lab discovery at Manas AI is only half the battle, noting that human clinical trials, manufacturing, and government approvals still take years and drive up costs. "AI buys time and cost in the front end, but what it does not change yet is the cost of running a trial and the regulatory clock," he said, urging India and China to streamline testing rules without compromising safety checks. "Of all countries in the world, China and—I truly believe—India, with appropriate regulatory and technological reform, can reverse Eroom’s Law." Highlighting real-world impact, Dr. Mukherjee pointed to Immuneel Therapeutics, the Bengaluru-based cell therapy company he co-founded with Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw. By placing an automated, hospital-adjacent manufacturing facility right next to doctors and using AI-designed binders, the team developed customized blood cancer treatments costing roughly $35,000 in India compared to $500,000 in the United States, successfully curing patients like a young boy from Kolkata who had exhausted all standard leukemia therapies. According to the World Health Organization (WHO) and its cancer research agency (IARC) 2026, the world sees an estimated 20.6 million new cancer cases and nearly 10 million deaths every year. In India, the same global report estimates 1.56 million new cases and over 900,000 deaths annually, with 3.32 million people living with the disease over a five-year period. Separate data from the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) projected 1.57 million cases for 2025, noting that one in nine Indians faces a lifetime cancer risk. Priyanka Sharma is a journalist at Mint, where she covers the Union Ministry of Health and the pharmaceutical industry. Her work focuses on explaining government policies and how they impact healthcare and the medicine market in India. With 12 years of experience in journalism, she has built a reputation for providing clear and honest news on important health topics that affect the entire country.

Her educational background includes a journalism degree from the prestigious Indian Institute of Mass Communication (IIMC) and specialized training in public health from the Public Health Foundation of India. Before her current role at Mint, Priyanka worked with India Today, The Pioneer, and ANI. She also served as a lead consultant for the National Health Authority, which gave her firsthand knowledge of how the government manages large-scale health programmes.
