A Mexican Singer Gives Old Ballads New Heroines
Grammy-nominated songwriter Vivir Quintana is known throughout Latin America for giving voice to women who fought back against domestic violence.
Against the backdrop of a centuries-old stone church in the Mexican city of Oaxaca, the singer Vivir Quintana raised her deep, husky voice above the blare of trumpets, trombones and the booming pulse of a tuba.
Behind her stood a brass band of young Indigenous girls in embroidered white blouses and brightly colored skirts. Hat in hand and fist raised, Ms. Quintana sang a corrido, a traditional Mexican folk ballad usually used to recount tales of revolutionaries, outlaws, folk heroes, and more recently, drug traffickers.
Corridos are typically sung by men, about men. Ms. Quintana sang a corrido she wrote based on the true story of a woman who fought back when her abusive partner tried to gouge out her eyes with a knife.
“I used to think that what united us women was our pain. Now I have realized it is love and resistance,” Ms. Quintana told the crowd in October during a women’s conference in Oaxaca called Decididas, drawing a roar of applause. “We must keep defending ourselves!”
On Thursday, Ms. Quintana will take the stage at the Latin Grammy Awards in Las Vegas alongside the Colombian pop superstar Juanes, with whom she is nominated for song of the year for “Humano.” It is her second Latin Grammy nomination.

FAA ground stop: Sport stars scramble as flight chaos and major travel disruption hits America
Sporting events across the country are slowly returning to normal after the Federal Aviation Administration grounded all flights nationwide for several hours

Major sporting events across the United States slowly returned to normal on Saturday, following a nationwide grounding of all flights by the Federal Aviation Administration a day prior that disrupted travel plans for professional and college teams.
Most college football programs playing on Saturday travel the day before kickoff, and several matches were delayed by hours to give visiting squads extra time to land and prepare.
Second-ranked Utah’s fixture at 22nd-ranked Arizona was pushed back by three hours, as was Arizona State’s game at Central Florida. Other teams, including Auburn, chose charter buses. One way or another, most programs secured a solution.
There was, of course, a single major exception: 19th-ranked Mississippi’s game at Oklahoma will now compete directly with the NFL, with kickoff scheduled for 1 p.m. EST on Sunday.
The NFL benefited from its Sunday schedule, as teams usually travel the day before their matches. Friday's travel pause ultimately had the greatest impact on official Don Willard, who is set to referee two games on the same day.
Willard will officiate the Dolphins-Colts fixture at 1 p.m. EST before travelling 112 miles east for a Steelers-Bengals Sunday Night Football contest.
JuJu Watkins and her third-ranked Southern California teammates had just boarded their flight to face top-ranked South Carolina when the ground stop was issued. The Trojans women's basketball team stayed in Los Angeles for the night after being deplaned, and their departure for Greenville was pushed to Saturday.
In women's soccer, the Utah Royals already were in the Washington, D.C., area ahead of their National Women’s Soccer League semifinal against the Washington Spirit on Saturday. The Kansas City Current were supposed to depart Friday for their semifinal against Gotham FC on Sunday in New York.
The Current told ESPN they were “collaborating with key stakeholders, including the NWSL and our charter partner, to identify next steps in order to arrive safely ahead of our match against Gotham FC on Sunday.”
There were 14 scheduled NHL games on Saturday, and the majority made it to their destinations before the flight stoppage began. The San Jose Sharks, who were left waiting to see whether they would be able to travel, arrived late Friday in Utah.
In the NBA, most teams were, at worst, mildly affected by Friday’s events. Cleveland was the outlier.
The Cavaliers started their Saturday much earlier than usual, leaving Miami at 8:54 a.m. on a plane taking them to Cleveland — where they were set to play the Dallas Mavericks on Saturday night.
The Cavs couldn’t get out of Miami on Friday night as planned after a game against the Heat that capped a three-game road trip, then scrambled to re-book some hotel rooms. NBA teams typically don’t fly on the morning of a game, but there have been exceptions made for unusual situations.
Cavaliers guard Donovan Mitchell said he would have preferred Saturday’s game to get rescheduled, but noted the team will “make adjustments, figure it out and go from there.”
“Back-to-back, three-hour flight, it was already a tough one,” Mitchell said. “But hey, they say we’ve got to play, we’ve got to play.”
Rescheduling the game against the Mavericks wasn’t an ideal option. Cleveland has a busy arena with a minor league hockey team, college games and other events scheduled; Saturday’s game falls in a stretch where the arena is playing host to events on 11 consecutive days.
“It’s part of it," Cleveland coach Kenny Atkinson said. "You just adapt.”

Pope laments violence enveloping Peru as he ministers in his former diocese
Pope Leo XIV prayed for an end to the violence ravaging Peru, addressing one of his adopted homeland’s most pressing concerns from his former cathedral
CHICLAYO, Peru -- CHICLAYO, Peru (AP) — Pope Leo XIV prayed Saturday for an end to the violence ravaging Peru, addressing one of his adopted homeland’s most pressing concerns during visits to his former cathedral and a remote community in his onetime diocese.
At Chiclayo’s cathedral, Leo entrusted his pontificate to the Virgin Mary in a special ceremony before traveling to Santa Cruz de Succhabamba, nestled in lush green mountains near the diocese’s outer reaches.
He traveled by helicopter to the city, 150 kilometers (93 miles) from central Chiclayo and 2,035 meters (6,675 feet) above sea level. The journey reflected his belief that shepherds must reach the peripheries to minister to their flocks.
Leo, formerly Robert Prevost, is beloved in the region for venturing beyond the sacristy to serve poor, outlying communities. As bishop, he would make the difficult drive to Santa Cruz de Succhabamba himself in his pickup truck.
“We all know the pope’s love of cars,” the Rev. Kevin Noriega, who oversees pastoral services, said before Mass. “He would drive everywhere.”
Before leaving, Leo led a special prayer at the Cathedral of St. Mary in Chiclayo, where he served as bishop from 2014 to 2023. He spoke of the “darkness” enveloping Peru, referring to rising crime amid political instability.
The homicide rate has nearly doubled over the past five years, from 5.8 to 10.7 per 100,000 people. Reports of extortion increased from 2,421 in 2019 to 26,734 in 2025, according to official data.
“We feel threatened by the uncertainty of widespread violence and by the unspeakable suffering that continues to afflict so many of our brothers and sisters,” Leo said in the cathedral. “Yet, despite this darkness, which so often dims our hope and weakens our trust, God’s gift continues to shine before our eyes.”
Conservative Keiko Fujimori took office in July after pledging to tackle crime, which has become a top concern for Peruvians. She has since declared states of emergency, including in Lima in August and in prisons holding inmates linked to criminal organizations in September.
Fujimori has also moved to strengthen ties with Washington by bringing Peru into the “Shield of the Americas,” a U.S.-led regional coalition formed to conduct joint military operations against drug cartels.
In Santa Cruz de Succhabamba, Leo acknowledged the temptation to respond to injustice with violence but urged a different response.
“Selfishness, injustice and evil are not overcome by brutality, but by prayer, patience and perseverance in denouncing what is wrong, by making our pleas with determination and working diligently to bring about the necessary changes,” he said.
The country also faces widespread illegal gold mining and is the world’s second-largest producer of coca leaves, the raw material for cocaine, after Colombia, according to the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime.
Leo, who received a joyous welcome in Chiclayo on Friday, is expected to address those issues when he meets with Amazonian and Indigenous peoples on Sunday.
Indigenous community representatives sought a meeting with Leo in Chiclayo to raise another pressing concern: the loss of ancestral lands to companies linked to the influential Peruvian Catholic movement Sodalitium Christianae Vitae.
Members of the San Juan Bautista de Catacaos community are demanding justice and reparations from the church. They allege that companies linked to the Sodalitium used lawsuits and opaque land-titling arrangements to try to evict them.
Pope Francis, who supported the villagers’ campaign, suppressed the Sodalitium last year, shortly before his death. But community members say the group retains economic influence in Peru and want the Vatican to do more.
“We recognize the importance of suppressing the Sodalitium Christianae Vitae. However, we believe that this decision — significant as it may be — cannot mark the end of a process that still has outstanding obligations toward the victims,” community representative Fiorella Martínez told a news conference Saturday, reading from a letter addressed to Leo.
The disputes stretch back at least a decade, when Sodalitium-linked companies began legal proceedings to evict farmers from thousands of hectares in Catacaos after a series of property transfers the farmers did not recognize. Dozens were prosecuted for alleged “usurpation,” and two community leaders were shot dead during clashes linked to the eviction efforts.
Leo is familiar with the dispute. As bishop of Chiclayo, he served as the Peruvian bishops’ point person for dealing with Sodalitium victims.
In May, Peru’s Catholic hierarchy held a symbolic reparation ceremony for Indigenous people who had lost their land.
Tania Pariona, secretary of Peru’s National Human Rights Commission, called it a “historic gesture,” saying the church “is taking the lead over the state, which has failed to protect rural communities.”
On Saturday, she called for further action.
“They demand the restitution of their lands, the right to their territory, and protection for those who defend that territory; for our brothers who also suffered sexual abuse by the Sodalicio, we demand that same justice — that same reparation,” she said.

త్రిపురలోని సెపాహిజాలా జిల్లాలో భారత్-బంగ్లాదేశ్ సరిహద్దు సమీపంలో బీఎస్ఎఫ్ సిబ్బందిపై కొందరు దాడి చేయడంతో ముగ్గురు అధికారులు గాయపడ్డారు. ఈ ఘటనకు సంబంధించి తొమ్మిది మందిని పోలీసులు అరెస్ట్ చేశారు. ఈ నేపథ్యంలో, పోలీసులు ఒక వ్యక్తిని బలవంతంగా తీసుకెళ్లి వాహనంలో ఎక్కిస్తున్న వీడియోను, బీఎస్ఎఫ్ సిబ్బందిపై దాడి చేసిన వారిని పోలీసులు అరెస్ట్ చేస్తున్న దృశ్యాలంటూ షేర్ చేస్తున్నారు (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ). దీని వెనుక ఎంత నిజముందో ఇప్పుడు చూద్దాం. 
క్లెయిమ్: త్రిపురలో బీఎస్ఎఫ్ సిబ్బందిపై దాడికి పాల్పడిన నిందితులను పోలీసులు అరెస్ట్ చేస్తున్న వీడియో.
ఫాక్ట్: వైరల్ వీడియో త్రిపురకు చెందినది కాదు. నేపాల్లోని సప్తరి జిల్లాలో, సప్తకోశి మున్సిపాలిటీ-5లోని గంగాజలిలో నిర్వహించిన ‘Indigenous and Tribal Literature Festival’ సందర్భంగా మద్యం మత్తులో ఉన్న ఒక వ్యక్తి దుకాణం వద్ద గొడవ సృష్టించడంతో పోలీసులు అతడిని అదుపులోకి తీసుకున్న దృశ్యాలు ఇవి. కాబట్టి, ఈ పోస్టులో చేసిన క్లెయిమ్ తప్పుదోవ పట్టిస్తుంది.
వైరల్ వీడియోను జాగ్రత్తగా పరిశీలించగా అందులో ఉన్న పోలీసు వాహనంపై “Nepal Police” అని రాసి ఉండటాన్ని గుర్తించాము. దీంతో ఈ వీడియో త్రిపురకు చెందినది కాదనే అనుమానం కలిగింది.
తదుపరి, దీని గురించి మరింత తెలుసుకోడానికి వైరల్ వీడియోలోని కీ ఫ్రేములను ఉపయోగిస్తూ రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చైయగా, ఇదే వీడియో 31 అక్టోబర్ 2026న నేపాల్కు చెందిన వార్తా సంస్థ ‘జన చర్చా టైమ్స్’ ఫేస్బుక్ పేజీలో షేర్ చేయటాన్ని గమనించాము. ఆ పోస్టులో తెలిపిన వివరాల ప్రకారం, నేపాల్లోని సప్తరి జిల్లాలో, సప్తకోశి మున్సిపాలిటీ-5లోని గంగాజలిలో నిర్వహించిన ‘Indigenous and Tribal Literature Festival’ సందర్భంగా మద్యం మత్తులో ఉన్న ఒక వ్యక్తి దుకాణం వద్ద గొడవ సృష్టించాడు. దీంతో పోలీసులు అతడిని అదుపులోకి తీసుకున్నారు.
అదే వీడియోను మరో నేపాలీ వార్తా సంస్థకు చెందిన ఫేస్బుక్, ఇన్స్టాగ్రామ్ పేజీలలో కూడా 31 అక్టోబర్ 2026న షేర్ చేసినట్లు గుర్తించాము. అక్కడ కూడా ఇదే ఘటనకు సంబంధించిన వివరాలను పేర్కొన్నారు.
వీడియోలో కనిపిస్తున్న ప్రదేశాన్ని జియోలొకేషన్ ద్వారా ఇది నేపాల్లోని సప్తరి జిల్లాలో గంగాజలి కమ్యూనిటీ హాల్ సమీపంలోని ప్రాంతమని గుర్తించాము.
చివరిగా, త్రిపురలో బీఎస్ఎఫ్ సిబ్బందిపై దాడి చేసిన నిందితుల అరెస్టు వీడియో అంటూ నేపాల్కు చెందిన పాత వీడియోను షేర్ చేస్తున్నారు.

In Moscow, Witkoff and Kushner Ask Putin to Include Europe in Peace Talks
The Kremlin, taking a hard line, is pushing to widen negotiations to overhaul European security structures.
President Trump’s envoys went to Moscow on Thursday to seek agreement from President Vladimir V. Putin to bring Europe into talks on the war in Ukraine, as the Kremlin pushes to widen the negotiations to overhaul European security arrangements.
The envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, arrived in Russia one day after mediating peace talks in Abu Dhabi between Russian and Ukrainian representatives, who spoke directly for the first time in nine months. After meeting with Mr. Putin in the Kremlin, the envoys were scheduled to travel to Dublin to meet with President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine.
Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner are pressing to involve Europe in the talks as Russia makes clear that it will not consider a cease-fire until its broader demands to redraw the European security architecture are addressed.
The Trump administration, seeking a foreign policy win after Republicans’ drubbing in the midterm elections, is making another push for peace even as Russia gives no indication that it will stop the war anytime soon, and in fact appears to be hardening some of its positions.
Russia has intensified attacks on Ukrainian cities ahead of a winter bombing campaign, taking advantage of Ukraine’s lack of air defenses. On Thursday, Mr. Zelensky said that the Ukrainian armed forces were again facing restrictions on Starshield, the military version of the satellite internet network Starlink, and had asked the United States for information.

As Kolkata choked on toxic air following Diwali and Kali Puja celebrations, West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari accused those raising concerns over firecracker pollution of being communists opposed to Hindu traditions. His remarks were consistent with the concerted push by a section of the Right wing to portray criticism of firecrackers as an attack on Hindu religious practices. However, among those complaining about noise levels and pollution in Kolkata were members of Adhikari’s own party and cabinet.
The Bengal CM made the remarks while addressing the media during a visit to the coastal town of Digha on Monday, where he had gone to attend an administrative meeting and visit the Kali Puja organised by the Shyama Prasad Mukherjee Traders Association.
Speaking to reporters, Adhikari said, “There has been an awakening of Sanatan in this state, and some people have a problem with that. The people making these allegations (about firecrackers) had turned Hindu religious festivals into cultural fests… These people do not apply ‘tika’ or religious markings on their foreheads, they do not wear ‘dors’ or religious threads on their wrists, nor do they wear tulsi beads around their necks.”
Adhikari further said, “The communists are raising this issue of firecrackers. We have controlled it in accordance with the Supreme Court’s directives. Firecrackers were burst in some places even after 10 pm, and the police took necessary action. We have stopped DJs, and we do not want environmental pollution. But people will have fun during Diwali. They will celebrate with lights and burst firecrackers. Where is the problem with that?”
While acknowledging that firecrackers had been burst beyond the time limit prescribed by the Supreme Court, Adhikari sought to deflect criticism by pointing to action taken by the administration.
“Those complaining that sound crackers were burst for a few hours longer than the time stipulated by the Supreme Court should know that the Pollution Control Board and the police are taking action against such violations. I would request those complaining about firecrackers to also congratulate the state government for stopping DJs. I will not say that DJ incidents did not happen in remote corners, but I did not hear them blaring, at least near the roads,” he said.
Firecrackers can Cure Diseases, Says Bengal Minister, then Apologises
According to the Supreme Court’s directives, only green firecrackers were allowed to be burst between 8 pm and 10 pm on Diwali. However, statements by ministers, the West Bengal Police’s deletion of a post urging responsible Diwali celebrations, and the general perception that a BJP government would not impose restrictions on Hindu festivals had collectively sent out a clear message: When it came to celebrating a majoritarian festival, the rules could be bent, if not ignored altogether.
BJP leader and Tollygunge MLA Papia Adhikary said on Monday, “Our honourable chief minister has said that people will definitely burst firecrackers. How can we celebrate Kali Puja without firecrackers? But we will burst them in accordance with the instructions of the local police station. Also, many diseases can be prevented simply by lighting firecrackers.”
Although Adhikary later apologised and backtracked on her statement, claiming that the media had misinterpreted her remarks, the message had already got across.
A section of social media users also began targeting dissenting voices who tried to reason with their fellow citizens. A user named Partha Pratim Kundu, who describes himself as a wildlife photographer, asked in a post how elderlies, children and birds and animals survived in earlier times when there was no curb on firecrackers.
Another Facebook user, Chayan Mukherjee, who hailed the chief minister’s indulgence on firecrackers, claimed in a post that “most of the Indian environmentalists and human rights activists, as well as professors at various institutions, receive funding from outside to oppose the country’s development.”
Domkal’s CPI(M) MLA Mostafijur Rahaman Rana had urged people to celebrate Diwali as a festival of lights, without noise and loud firecrackers. BJP MLA Tarunjyoti Tiwari gave the issue a communal twist by asking whether the legislator would also call for a ‘bloodless Eid’.
State BJP leader Keya Ghosh also criticised Mostafijur Rahaman for advocating a noise-free and smoke-free Diwali.
The lone CPIM MLA of West Bengal had wished smokeless, soundless Diwali.

The political messaging was accompanied by widespread violations on the ground. A large section of the public openly flouted firecracker regulations. Almost all media outlets reported that loud firecrackers were burst throughout the night severely inconveniencing elderlies, children and also pets, birds and stray animals.
Kolkata’s AQI reached 623 around 11 pm on Sunday night, reported The telegraph. At 12.51 am on Monday, IQAir classified the city’s air quality as hazardous, recording an AQI of 532, with PM2.5 at 342 and PM10 at 405. Both particulate matter concentrations were several times higher than the WHO’s recommended limits.
Left with no other option, residents in several localities took matters into their own hands, protesting against the rampant bursting of firecrackers and intervening to stop it. Facebook user Anitesh Chakraborty narrated his experience in a post.
Chakraborty went up to a neighbouring apartment’s rooftop around 1.45 am to ask people bursting firecrackers to stop. While some residents supported his objection, others on nearby rooftops mocked him with gestures and taunts. Nevertheless, the intervention succeeded in stopping the firecrackers. He observed that the rooftops of apartment buildings had become spaces where people felt free to flout restrictions, and argued people to raise their voices against such violations.
According to a report by the Times of India, by 1 am, the West Bengal Pollution Control Board had received 84 noise-related complaints, while Kolkata Police had recorded 434 complaints.
Police rounded up 371 people for bursting illegal firecrackers, arresting 205 of them. Another 387 people were arrested for disorderly conduct. Several commentators pointed out that the most effective way to curb the use of illegal firecrackers was to stop their manufacture and sale. This year, only 238.6 kg of such products were seized, compared to 853 kg last year.
Kolkata’s high-rise buildings were particular hotspots for violations of firecracker and noise restrictions. Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari himself acknowledged that the rules could not be enforced in every high-rise apartment building, as the state did not have enough police personnel.
Even hospitals located in silence zones were not spared. According to a report by The Telegraph, areas near hospitals such as B C Roy, R G Kar, M R Bangur and Sishumangal also faced onslaught of loud firecrackers.
To Celebrate Responsibly or Not? Bengal Police in a Fix
Signs of this situation had emerged earlier, when the West Bengal Police deleted a firecracker awareness post within hours of publishing it, as previously reported by Alt News.
Published on the morning of November 5 with the caption, “Please celebrate responsibly. It’s our Diwali too!”, the AI-generated poster featured two stray cats and a dog shivering due to the loud noise of firecrackers. However, it was deleted within three hours.
The post’s comment section was flooded with threatening messages directed at police and familiar Right-wing arguments, including questions about whether the police would also call for a ‘bloodless Eid’ and why the police and administration interfered only in Hindu festivals.
Similarly, Delhi Police, too, deleted a firecracker awareness post, while the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC) removed a video featuring actor Dia Mirza advocating for a pollution-free Diwali from its social media accounts. Both decisions followed social media outrage from BJP-RSS supporters who claimed that the posts hurt Hindu religious sentiments.
A similar message by AISA leader Neha Bora also faced backlash from the far-right social media ecosystem.

BJP MLAs Complain about Noise Levels
Although a section of the Right wing encouraged unrestrained celebrations during Diwali and Kali Puja in the name of upholding Hindu traditions, some voices within the BJP struck a different note.
BJP leader and Sonarpur Dakshin MLA Roopa Ganguly tagged Kolkata Police in a post on Facebook stating she was unable to sleep because of the noise of firecrackers. However, the post is no longer available now.
State urban development minister Agnimitra Paul was seen roaming around the city in a police vehicle, attempting to curb the firecracker menace.
Paul said, “Please think about other people. Consider the condition of the elderly and the sick. The firecrackers are bursting so loudly that my heart is trembling.”
However, these interventions came too little, too late. The ruling dispensation had, through its rhetoric and its reluctance to enforce restrictions, effectively given people a free hand to flout the law, with the environment and public health bearing the consequences.

This is an updated version of an article first published in August 2026
Kimi Antonelli was 10 when his father Marco first realised the boy sitting on his lap, operating the steering and gears, might have an exceptional talent as a racing driver.
The pair were at the Adria circuit in north-east Italy, Marco with his Lamborghini sports car team, Kimi competing in a karting race.
It was the end of the day and Marco, a former driver himself, asked his son: "Do you want to try the Lamborghini?"
Of course he did.
Marco strapped himself and Kimi into the car, belts extended around both. Dad was in charge of the throttle and brake, his son would control the rest.
"I couldn't see the track because he was in front of me with a helmet on," Marco tells BBC Sport. "I could only see beside me the marker panels before each corner - 100m, 50m.
"We started to drive, step by step, faster, faster, faster. In the end, I pushed like I was alone and I arrived at the braking point at the end of the straight, 320km/h, braked very hard and at the limit.
"The car had a lot of oversteer. Kimi controlled the oversteer perfectly, then I went on the throttle, Kimi finished the oversteer, changed gear, and went.
"I said: 'OK, stop, because it has now become dangerous.' But when I saw the video, 10 years old, on my leg, oversteer, everything perfect, I said: 'Maybe he has something special.'"
And now Kimi, who turned 20 only in August, has dominated F1 in only his second season, and become the youngest world champion in the sport's history.
This is the story of a boy his dad says was "born in a garage".
"Kimi from 15 days old was in the garage and heard the sound of the engine and the smell of the exhaust," says Marco, who worked with his wife Veronica on their racing team business.
It was the Christmas holidays when Kimi was about three, and Marco had brought home a simulator he had bought for his guests to try out at the Bologna Motor Show.
"Each evening, Kimi wanted to drive," Marco remembers.
Just like seven years later in the Lamborghini, Kimi would sit on Marco's leg, the controls divided in the same way.
"I remember one night I started to fall asleep because I had been at work very early and we had a crash because I didn't brake when we arrived at the end of the straight," Marco says.
"And Kimi said: 'Dad, dad, no sleep, no sleep. I have to drive.'"
Marco Antonelli did not originally want his son to become a racing driver, because of his own struggles during his career.
"Sometimes you are fast but not in the right position to become a professional driver," he says.
In the 1990s, Marco Antonelli was on the cusp of becoming a works driver in the DTM touring car series, then a huge hit with audiences across Europe.
He tested for Alfa Romeo, but then the team boss left and the opportunity evaporated. Another chance came up with BMW, alongside Roberto Ravaglia and Steve Soper - stars at the time. Again, the same thing happened.
"I suffered a lot for it," Marco says. "And, of course, I was scared that my son [would] relive the same situation. At the beginning, I was very stressed about the passion my son had for motorsport."
Kimi tried a go-kart for the first time when he was five, and immediately showed an awareness of racing lines, braking points and car control.
The Antonellis were what Marco describes as "a normal family". They could not possibly afford to pay for Kimi to take part in all the categories on the way to Formula 1.
Marco decided he could fund Kimi through karting and a year of the basic single-seater category, Formula 4. After that, he figured he might be able to put him in one of his GT cars and become professional that way.
But Kimi immediately started to impress. Whatever category he entered, he was quick, and won.
By the time Kimi was 11, his name was buzzing around motor racing circles. Mercedes heard about him, and their driver academy scout Gwen Lagrue flew to Italy to check him out.
It was a season in which Antonelli had ended up driving a kart with less power than those of his rivals. Marco had told Kimi this would be good for him - he should think not about the result, but about how to improve, always push hard.
"Gwen was impressed about this condition of power and driving in this category that Kimi did," Marco says. "And maybe they understood that Kimi was a different child."
Now Kimi was a member of the Mercedes driver academy, Marco could stop worrying about money, and start focusing on helping his son achieve his full potential.
Mercedes were not the only big names in F1 who had noticed Antonelli's promise.
"When he was in karting, you could already see he was one of the stand-out talents," says four-time world champion Max Verstappen, the only other teenager to win an F1 race.
At 15, Antonelli was ready to move up to cars, and, as a final preparation, did a couple of races in a karting category with gears. On his debut, with minimal pre-event testing, he took pole position. After that, he went to the world final, and stuck it on pole again.
This was the end of 2021, after which Antonelli moved full-time into cars. Through 2022, he swept the board in various championships in Formula 4, and the same happened in Formula Regional in 2023.
1 of 4
By now, Mercedes team boss Toto Wolff was already thinking that Antonelli would be his next F1 driver, potentially a replacement for Lewis Hamilton. With the seven-time champion approaching 40, Wolff was planning on taking control of that generational transition.
So when it came time to negotiate a new contract with Hamilton in 2023, Wolff played hardball. Hamilton wanted to sign for at least two firm years, Wolff only one. In the end, they compromised on a contract for 2024 with an option for 2025.
Hamilton, unimpressed, decided to look at his options, and signed to join Ferrari in 2025, telling Wolff in late January 2024, before the start of that season.
Wolff immediately phoned Marco Antonelli, to tell him the "very big news".
"'We put Kimi in Formula 1,'" Marco remembers Wolff saying. "'What do you think?'
"I said: 'Oh, [it] is a difficult question you ask me. Of course I'm happy that you think about Kimi but are you sure he's ready?'"
Mercedes were at a management away day. Wolff called his senior engineers together to tell them about Hamilton's decision.
"We were reviewing options and trying to come to a fairly rapid conclusion," says trackside engineering director Andrew Shovlin.
"We were all keen to just go with Kimi, which we knew was a bit of a risk. But it was quite exciting and we thought, based on his career to date, he had a good chance of being very good. It seemed like a good challenge."
Antonelli had not even driven an F1 car when Wolff made the call. Mercedes put together a testing programme for him, 20-odd days in cars a couple of years old at tracks all over the world to prepare him for his F1 debut in 2025.
Shovlin and the engineers were immediately impressed.
"It was how rapidly he would get up to speed," Shovlin says. "What you normally see with drivers is they're just incrementally going a little bit quicker, braking a bit later.
"If you compare with other drivers we've seen in an F1 car for the first time, the best I'd ever seen until then was George [Russell]. You suddenly saw someone who was quite similar.
"With Kimi, he took a couple of runs to work out how the car behaved and then he'd be more or less on the limit.
"The other thing you can see is the fidelity of the car control, how they can sit with it right on the edge of breaking away from them on entry to a corner, but they can just control it in that condition.
"Equally, when you looked at the mistakes he was making, they were often errors of judgement or lack of experience. They weren't run-out-of-talent mistakes."
Antonelli made one of these at the 2024 Italian Grand Prix. Wolff decided to give him his first experience of an F1 weekend in first practice at his home race at Monza.
It was a spectacular debut - for both good and bad reasons.
Antonelli set the fastest time on his first lap. Then he went for another. He was flying, miles quicker than anyone up to that point, but then he crashed heavily at the final corner, Parabolica.
"No-one on earth could have got the car around the corner at the speed he was attempting," Shovlin says. "He clearly got into his head that he would try and do something special and it was an error of judgment."
Wolff took Antonelli aside, told him it was OK, and not to worry about it. But the crash had a significant impact on Antonelli.
Wolff was very clear in public about managing expectations of Antonelli going into his debut season.
"I conditioned myself so strong that I said: 'There's going to be moments of brilliance and moments where you want to tear your hair out'," Wolff says.
There were stand-out moments, including pole for the sprint in Miami.
But the middle part of the season, through Europe, was a disappointment. A change to the rear suspension design made the car nervous and rocked his confidence. His pace was not impressive, and he made too many mistakes.
"We expected more highlights from him," Shovlin says.
Marco Antonelli explains: "Mercedes needed to have a good result after a period that was not like the Hamilton era. And, of course, needed two cars that always take points.
"Kimi felt this necessity. The crash in Monza was very tough for him to forget. It created on him a big pressure."
Wolff said the "moments of brilliance were there" but then there was "a spell of nine races that was really not good".
"Me, personally, I never doubted," says Wolff. "Other people doubted. In the team and externally."
A year on from his practice debut, Antonelli crashed again in Monza practice.
"This was the point where I said: 'Kimi, you've got to turn this around. This is just not good enough'," says Wolff. "He said: 'I know.'"
Marco Antonelli says he and his son talked a lot during this period and that Kimi "understood that everything can change".
"The period was bad but you can see light at the end of the tunnel," he says. "And step by step he started to take confidence."
Once F1 had left Europe in the autumn of last year, there was a shift.
"Suddenly, we felt like we were making really good progress," says Shovlin.
"There were signs towards the end of the year. I'm not saying any of us thought we'd see what we've seen so far this year, but that we had a decent F1 driver."
Antonelli has been rather more than that this year. He took the season by storm, and established a consistent supremacy over Russell.
In the best car in the field, Antonelli took six poles and six wins in the first 11 races, establishing a 50-point lead in the championship.
Mercedes lost their dominant form in the second half of the season in the face of challenges from first McLaren and then Red Bull.
But Antonelli remained a consistent threat at the front, and he killed off his Monza ghosts in the Italian Grand Prix with a stunning victory after an engine penalty led to him starting 19th on the grid.
He put in a drive of clinical excellence and, with help from a safety car, chased down and caught Russell in the final laps to take a win that will go down in folklore.
The extent of his turnaround in form has shocked almost everyone.
"We were all surprised," Wolff says. "My thoughts were always that he needed to make the experience of knowing all the tracks, the pressure of performing on such a high level under the spotlight of the media, the constant public feedback, whether you're doing well or not, the situations everyone wanted to be close to him.
"There wasn't one single defining factor where I would have said that made it difficult for him, but this year, he knew exactly what to expect. What was really nice to see is that the self-confidence, without feeling any entitlement, has shone."
Marco points to his son's "very strong" mentality.
"In F4 and Freca, he started with not good results, and he was able to remake everything and, at the end, work hard and win the championship," he says.
"We talk about F1. I don't know what the spark is in his brain, but Kimi in the past did the same."
Verstappen says: "For me, there was never any doubt that he would make the jump the year after and already be a lot more consistently competitive.
"It's normal in the progression of a driver. In your rookie season, it can be quite tough, but at the moment, of course, he's doing an amazing job."
Kimi pays tribute to his father, describing him as his "rock", while Wolff also praises the driver's "typical Italian family".
"They are caring, they are loving," Wolff says. "Kimi's character, he's gentle, he has empathy, he has charisma, he has the right amount of intelligence for being a racing driver."
Mercedes have been talking to Antonelli about managing his emotions, which have flared at times this season, such as in the sprint in Canada, when the racing between the two Mercedes drivers came close to boiling over.
Shovlin says: "He just says: 'I'm young, I'm Italian, what do you expect?'"
The remark reveals Antonelli's sense of humour, but also a maturity and self-awareness that might not always be expected in someone so young.
Wolff says: "He has all that. He's actually not [fitting the stereotype of] a typical emotional Italian. He's so clear [in] what he needs to do in a car. I don't see lots of emotion. I see full focus, full concentration. I see, 'OK, this is a problem, let's analyse it, and move on.'
"You see him in a debrief afterwards. You couldn't really say whether there was a bad or a good session. It's all very balanced and stable."
Antonelli took advice on this when he met tennis legend Roger Federer at Wimbledon this summer.
"We chatted about my races," Antonelli says. "About when he used to play, and about life in general.
"About pressure, he just told me to focus on one race at a time, just focus on what you can control, and also to control the emotions, especially the ones that can make you do mistakes."
Federer's words echoed something Marco has always impressed on his son.
"In our family, we use this concept in normal life as well," he says.
"We have to live every day our best day. You work hard every day to arrive at the end of the project you have."
Back in February 2024, Wolff followed up his phone call to Marco with a meeting in Milan.
"Toto said 'Of course it will be difficult, but I think after one year of experience, we can do very well with Kimi in F1'," Marco says.
"The project was 2025 experience, 2026 start to achieve results. I think we overachieved."

The Mundka monitoring station of the Delhi Pollution Control Board recorded a PM2.5 concentration of 3,744 µg/m³ at 2 am on the Diwali night, which is 60 times the standard measure. Yes, you read it right. 60 times. Reports emerged the next day that 93 of the top 100 cities with worst AQI were from India following Diwali celebrations on November 8. AIIMS pulmonologist Vijay Hadda told ANI on November 9, “I am honestly surprised that we are still alive. I do not think this kind of air is suitable for human survival.”
In any country with a functional government, this would warrant the environment minister to at least make a statement, even if not take direct accountability. Not in India.
Union minister of environment, forest and climate change, Bhupender Yadav, has remained conspicuously silent on the country’s deteriorating air quality before or after Diwali.
From the days preceding Diwali to four days after the festival when this article is being written, Yadav neither issued a single public appeal urging citizens to responsibly engage in celebrations, nor used his social media handles to spread awareness about the environmental consequences of bursting firecrackers or to address the mounting pollution crisis affecting major parts of the country.
Did Bhupender Yadav go Missing from Public Platforms?
Far from it. Yadav remained active on social media throughout this period. Between November 1 and November 12, he made 29 posts on his X account. Not one of them addressed the worsening air pollution, deteriorating air quality across Indian cities, or the need for public awareness and precautionary measures.
The days before Diwali are also crucial because pollution levels skyrocketing on the day of the festival and immediately after has become an annual phenomenon. It is reasonable to expect the minister holding the environment and climate change portfolio to make a public appeal ahead of Diwali, more so because firecracker pollution has been a matter of contention and has reached the Supreme Court in recent years.
Clearly, the Alwar MP thinks otherwise.
Modi Reigns Supreme on Yadav’s X Timeline
On November 7, observed as Chhoti Diwali, and November 8, the main day of Diwali, Yadav shared nine posts. These included amplification of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Diwali greetings to citizens, Modi’s Diwali celebrations and interactions with jawans at the CoBRA (Commando Battalion for Resolute Action) Operations Base in Karanpur, in Chhattisgarh’s Bastar district, as well as Yadav’s own festive greetings.
On November 7, Yadav shared a video of Narendra Modi greeting fellow citizens with wishes for Diwali and shared that, like every year, he would celebrate Diwali with the “veer jawans” of the country.

Updates on Political Assignments etc
A review of Yadav’s remaining social media activity during this period shows that he continued to document his political engagements, meetings with public representatives, participation in political programmes and official engagements.
On November 1, Yadav attended the “Save democracy, remove anarchy” rally alongside the Maharashtra chief minister and deputy chief minister. The following day, he met the Governor of Uttarakhand. On November 3, he met Uttarakhand chief minister Pushkar Singh Dhami and Bihar Chief Minister Samrat Choudhary in Delhi.
On November 5, he shared another post about his participation in the ‘Save Democracy, Remove Anarchy’ protest in Darbhanga, Bihar. He also posted about his visit to the residence of senior BJP leader and Rajya Sabha MP Dr Ravindra Kishore Sinha, where he met Sinha’s son, Rituraj Sinha, and other family members and paid his respects.

On November 9, he attended the funeral of Dr Jaswant Yadav, the MLA from Bahror and former Member of Parliament, alongside the Rajasthan Chief Minister Bhajanlal Sharma.
His latest post, on November 12, documented an interaction chaired by him with Indian LeadIT (Leadership Group for Industry Transition) member companies and project partners in New Delhi.
In addition to these engagements, five of Yadav’s posts during the November 1–12 period were dedicated to sharing decisions taken by the Union Cabinet on various policy matters.
Despite maintaining a steady stream of updates on his political engagements, official meetings and public appearances, the environment Mminister’s X account offered no indication of concern over the environmental consequences of the widespread bursting of firecrackers during Diwali. Neither before it. Nor after.
Incidentally, on October 30, Yadav posted about an integrated command and control centre in Delhi to review and monitor air pollution real-time across Delhi-NCR.
The Firecracker Pollution Debate was Raging Since October 25
As early as October 25, Delhi Police had shared a video on its X handle urging citizens not to burst crackers this Diwali. The post said: “This festive season, let tails wag, not tuck. Say NO to crackers, YES to a greener Diwali.” Soon after it was posted, social media users predicted that it would be taken down. Delhi Police proved them right, deleting the post within hours.
The episode sparked a debate, with a section of the Right-wing putting forward what has become its usual pre-Diwali stance on firecracker pollution: that any call to shun firecrackers or celebrate with restraint is an affront to Hindu faith. The debate intensified when Bengal Police did much the same thing, posting about “responsible celebrations” before deleting the post, and the Mumbai civic body took down a similar post featuring actor Dia Mirza.
Yadav, it appears, has been blissfully unaware of all this.
There were no cautionary appeals ahead of the festivities urging citizens to celebrate responsibly or remain mindful of the deteriorating air quality and the environmental and health hazards associated with firecrackers. Nor did Yadav acknowledge the worsening situation in the aftermath of the celebrations, when several Indian cities were engulfed in thick layers of smog, and the country dominated global rankings of the most polluted cities.

Odisha is bracing for a potential third cyclone in just three weeks as a well-marked low-pressure system over the Bay of Bengal threatens to intensify into a severe cyclonic storm.
The India Meteorological Department (IMD) said the low-pressure area over the Bay of Bengal had intensified into a well-marked low-pressure system and was likely to become a depression by Sunday, before further intensifying into a cyclonic storm on November 16.
The system could further intensify into a severe cyclonic storm over the sea by November 18. While the storm's exact landfall trajectory remains uncertain, its extensive cloud bands and strong winds will trigger extreme weather across multiple regions.
Alongside Odisha, neighbouring coastal states are bracing for the system's impact.
The weather agency, in its latest bulletin, said that North Coastal Andhra Pradesh is expected to face isolated heavy rainfall on November 18 and 20, escalating to isolated very heavy rainfall on November 19.
The region will also be battered by intense thundersqualls, with wind speeds reaching 50-60 kmph and gusting up to 70 kmph on November 19.
Gangetic West Bengal will experience isolated heavy rainfall and gusty winds (40-50 kmph, gusting to 60 kmph) on November 19 and 20, the Met Dept said.
The IMD has forecast isolated heavy rainfall over the Andaman & Nicobar Islands on November 15 and November 16.
The region will simultaneously face isolated thunderstorms, lightning, and squally winds reaching 40-50 kmph (gusting to 60 kmph) through November 17.
Odisha Disaster Management Minister Suresh Pujari emphasised the need for extreme vigilance, explaining that even if the storm does not make direct landfall in Odisha, the state will receive substantial rainfall (12-20 cm in some districts) and squally winds.
“We do not know whether the impending cyclone will hit the Odisha coast. But we need to remain prepared, keeping in view the impact of Cyclone Arnab,” Pujari said, according to PTI.
The state government has put all collectors on alert, following the severe impact of Cyclone Arnab, which caused devastating floods in Odisha's southern districts late last month.
The Meteorological Centre, Bhubaneswar, has forecast heavy rainfall of 7-11 cm at isolated places on November 18, while very heavy rainfall of 12-20 cm is likely in some districts on November 19 and 20 across Andhra Pradesh, Odisha and West Bengal.
The IMD said squally weather, with wind speeds of 45-55 kmph gusting to 65 kmph, was likely to begin along and off the south Odisha coast from the morning of November 17.
Fishermen have been strongly advised to return to the coasts by November 15 and are strictly instructed not to venture into the Andaman Sea, Southeast Bay of Bengal, Southwest Bay of Bengal, or Central Bay of Bengal until the cyclonic system has safely passed.
While the coasts battle a cyclonic system, Northern India is being impacted by a fresh Western Disturbance. The IMD said that this system is likely to cause light to moderate rainfall and snowfall over the Western Himalayan Region—including Jammu, Kashmir, Ladakh, Himachal Pradesh, and Uttarakhand—on November 15.
The plains of Northwest India, including Punjab, Haryana, Chandigarh, and Rajasthan, are also expected to see isolated light rainfall.
Additionally, the weather agency has issued a dense fog warning for Uttar Pradesh, predicting low visibility conditions in West UP from November 15 to 17, and in East UP on November 16 and 17.
For the national capital, the IMD has forecast a generally cloudy sky for November 15, with mist or shallow fog at most places and moderate fog in isolated areas during the morning hours.
Delhiites might also experience a spell of very light rain or drizzle from the morning into the forenoon.
The maximum temperature is expected to settle between 25°C and 27°C (below normal), while the minimum temperature will hover around 16°C to 18°C, remaining appreciably above normal for this time of year.

In 1976, at the dawn of the modern Alzheimer’s era, the neurologist Robert Katzman, champion of efforts to extract Alzheimer’s from senility and “normal aging,” concluded his short essay “The prevalence and malignancy of Alzheimer disease” with this notably qualified call to action:
“In focusing attention on the mortality associated with Alzheimer disease, our goal is not to find a way to prolong the life of severely demented persons, but rather to call attention to our belief that senile as well as presenile forms of Alzheimer are a single disease, a disease whose etiology must be determined, whose course must be aborted, and ultimately a disease to be prevented.”

Hajra Begum rolls a potato in her hands, checking its skin for cuts, soft spots and signs of rot. After a day harvesting in her family’s field in Chorwan, a remote mountain village in Gurez, Indian-administered Kashmir, she is sorting the crop for winter storage. Some of the potatoes will feed her family through the cold months; others will be saved for planting in spring.
“It should be perfect for planting,” she says. “If you keep a bad potato, you will waste the whole next year.”
Begum, 40, is preparing to lower the potatoes into a khraw, a traditional underground storage pit lined with straw and sealed against the cold. For generations, khraws have kept potatoes, turnips and cabbages through Himalayan winters, when heavy snowfall cuts villages off from the Kashmir valley and temperatures fall below -20C (-4F) – cold enough to crack pipes and freeze diesel.
But the practice is slowly dying out. As roads have improved and young people have left for work and education, fewer families maintain the pits. Their decline threatens not only a traditional way of storing food but also the local potato varieties themselves and the knowledge of which ones store well, resist rot and produce reliable harvests.
“When I was young, almost every family had three or four pits,” Begum says. “Now, down in the main valley, they have abandoned the practice altogether. Only a handful of families still use them. The rest buy from the market or subsidised ones from the government.”
Begum learned from her mother how to tell potatoes that store well from those that rot or sprout too quickly. She is passing this on to her daughter, but is unsure whether the skill will survive into another generation.
Gurez is a high-altitude Himalayan valley perched near the Line of Control, the heavily militarised boundary separating Indian- and Pakistani-administered Kashmir. About 80 miles (125km) from Srinagar, the valley remains cut off each winter when snow closes Razdan pass, its main road link, which sits at roughly 3,600 metres.
It is home to the Dard-Shin people, an Indigenous community who speak Shina and have a culture that is distinct from Kashmiri, with community links across the border in Gilgit-Baltistan, administered by Pakistan.
Potatoes account for about 45% of Gurez’s cultivated area, according to a 2019 study by the Indian Council of Agricultural Research’s National Bureau of Plant Genetic Resources (ICAR-NBPGR), a government body that studies and conserves India’s crop diversity. Yet the genetic diversity of the valley’s potatoes has not been systematically documented.
Dr Sheikh M Sultan, a senior scientist based at ICAR-NBPGR’s Srinagar station, surveyed the valley and later struggled to find some of the varieties he had once encountered. “When I first visited, I saw many varieties,” he says. “Later, I could hardly locate even one sample of some. The loss of genetic diversity is tremendous.”
Sultan says migration, improved roads and changing lifestyles have contributed to the decline. As traditional farming disappears, so does knowledge about selecting, cultivating and preserving local varieties.
“When people stop producing their own seeds and start relying entirely on commercial varieties, the loss can be irreparable,” he says.
He warns that research institutions often prioritise introduced varieties over indigenous crops whose characteristics remain poorly understood. “Our indigenous varieties may possess valuable characteristics, including tolerance to cold and resistance to certain pests and diseases,” he says.
“These are resources we should be studying and improving, rather than neglecting.”
Climate breakdown is adding to the pressures on farmers across the Himalayas. People in Gurez report drier springs, reduced snowfall and water shortages, which they say have affected potato production.
Abdul Jabbar Mapnoo, 70, a farmer in Chorwan, remembers winters when deep snow covered the valley. “Every house used to have two or three khraw, each holding about five quintals – 500kg – of potatoes,” he says. “The springs are drying up, and there is less snow in winter. Potato production has fallen. I remember winters when six feet of snow would cover the valley in January or February.”
As farming becomes more difficult and markets easier to access, households have less incentive to grow their own potatoes. Varieties adapted to local conditions over generations could disappear from cultivation before researchers establish what makes them distinctive.
Dr Parveen Kumar, a scientist at the Sher-e-Kashmir University of Agricultural Sciences and Technology of Kashmir, says locally adapted varieties should not be overlooked. “Climate change is a reality, and farmers need to be aware of adaptation strategies,” he says.
Pressure on farmland poses another risk. In Gurez, where cultivable land is scarce, the Kishanganga hydroelectric project has affected land in the valley through acquisition and submergence. Among the areas affected is Badwan, a village known for its potatoes.
One potential route for preserving the varieties could be through using geographical indications – a designation granted by the UN’s Food and Agriculture Organization, and is similar to the French appellation d’origine contrôlée. It can be used on goods that have a specific origin and possess qualities or a reputation linked to this – which can help increase the market value and give them greater recognition. This, and the globally important agricultural heritage systems programme have helped areas such as the saffron-growing landscape of Pampore in Kashmir.
However, recognition alone will not preserve the varieties. They must be identified and documented before they disappear from cultivation, along with farmers’ knowledge of how to select, store and replant them.
In Chorwan, Begum unloads the last sack of potatoes into the pit and covers it, ready for another winter. Some will feed her family; the rest will be replanted in spring. Knowing which potatoes to eat and which to save as seed relies on knowledge passed down through generations.
If these varieties are not documented while they are still being cultivated, Kashmir may lose a living agricultural treasure trove before scientists can fully understand what it contains.

Damascus, Nov 14: An explosive device placed inside a car in a suburb of Syria's capital exploded Saturday evening, killing two people and wounding at least one, state TV and the Interior Ministry said.
The explosion took place in the southern Damascus suburb of Jaramana near a factory where batteries are produced, state TV said. It said two people were killed and two were wounded, without giving further details.
The Interior Ministry said the dead included a child, adding that one person was wounded. It said security forces cordoned off the area and started an investigation.
Several explosions have taken place in Damascus and its suburbs in recent months as the country's security remains fragile nearly two years after five decades of Assad family rule ended in December 2024. Militants stormed the capital and removed then-President Bashar Assad from power.
Jaramana is home to a large community of the Druze religious minority. The suburb has faced tensions between some members of the community and Sunni Muslim Syrians supportive of the country's current Islamist-led government.

The Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza has been cleared of using AI to write a prize-winning short story, after the prestigious Caine prize for African writers concluded that his entry was “human-written” after a month-long investigation.
Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter, which charts the declining fortunes of a family after the father invests in fish tanks, was announced as the winner of the £10,000 prize on 6 October.
Five days later, the Atlantic published an article titled “Yet another literary prize winner seems to be AI”, in which the author and journalist Vauhini Vara said the AI-detection software Pangram, which itself uses AI, had deemed the story to be almost completely artificially generated.
The Caine prize chair, Ellah Wakatama, said in a statement: “From our detailed investigation, we feel the evidence is clear: The Blue Fighter was human-written. We now look forward to awarding and celebrating Simbarashe Steyn Kundizeza … before the end of the year.”
She said: “When concerns were raised, we have a duty as an organisation to look at them carefully and fairly,” adding that the prize had taken a “human-centred” approach to its investigation.
“Our review included interviews with the author, the 2026 judging panel and The Shallow Tales Review, where the story was first published,” Wakatama said. “It also included independent and expert-led metadata analysis of drafts written by the author.”
Kundizeza, who had strongly denied using generative AI to write the story, said he was “relieved” that the allegations had been dismissed after the investigation. “It was not necessary in the first place, I am happy to put all this behind me and continue with my writing journey,” he said.
Vara’s article prompted outrage online, with many claiming that Black writers, and Africans in particular, were being unfairly singled out by allegations of the use of AI.

A former Louisiana police officer and volunteer firefighter has been sentenced to three life terms in prison and chemical castration for raping multiple children.
Kedreyon K. Williams, 31, of New Roads, was sentenced Thursday after being convicted of three counts of first-degree rape, indecent behavior with a juvenile and possessing child pornography, according to the 18th Judicial District Attorney's Office.
Williams sexually abused multiple children, ages 8 to 11, forcing them to perform sex acts on him at several locations, including fire stations where he volunteered, his workplace and his home, prosecutors said.
“If a man takes sexual advantage of a child, then we will take his manhood!” District Attorney Tony Clayton said Friday. He added that he hoped the sentence would bring the victims' families comfort.
Chemical castration uses prescription medication to lower testosterone and suppress sexual urges, rather than surgical removal of the testicles, according to the Cleveland Clinic. It is a reversible procedure.
Louisiana is the only state that allows surgical castration as a sentence for sex offenders convicted of crimes involving victims younger than 15. However, in September, the state Department of Corrections confirmed it has never carried out the procedure, the Louisiana Illuminator reported.
Williams was also convicted of possessing a video on his cellphone showing a child performing a sex act on him, prosecutors said.
The investigation into his case began after the mother of one of the children contacted police with information her child had shared with her. That investigation led to the discovery of other child victims.
Williams previously served as a part-time officer with the New Roads Police Department from October 2017 to May 2019. He was arrested in July 2024, according to local news reports.
Williams' conviction followed a four-day jury trial. The 12-member jury deliberated for just 39 minutes before finding him guilty. District Judge Kimball said this was the “worst case” of child sexual abuse he had seen when handing down the sentence.
Each first-degree rape conviction carries a mandatory sentence of life in prison. However, Clayton sought an additional punishment, filing a motion to have Williams castrated because of the severity of the crimes.
“He performed disgusting acts on children who could not defend themselves. He is a child predator and he deserves exactly what he is getting and more,” Clayton said in a statement.

In French Election, Centrists Eye a Judo Star and a Central Banker
Centrists want alternatives to a matchup between the far right and far left in the 2027 presidential election. Teddy Riner, the judo champion, is in, while Christine Lagarde is less likely.
When Teddy Riner, a judo champion and one of France’s most popular athletes, announced this week that he would run for president, it was less a game changer than a welcome diversion. For all of his appeal, Mr. Riner, 37, is unlikely to win the race to replace President Emmanuel Macron next spring.
Yet his quixotic candidacy reveals a hard truth about France’s presidential campaign. Five months before voters go to the polls, many are eager, even desperate, for a fresh face to upend a race that looks increasingly as if it’s on a glide path to the election of France’s first far-right government since World War II.
The main far-right candidate, Marine Le Pen, has held a commanding lead over all her rivals for months — a lead that has only been reinforced by weeks of protests, marred by violence, that have shaken France. The most prominent center-right candidate, Édouard Philippe, has faded in the polls as the unrest has sharpened the appeal of far-right calls for law and order and left-wing calls for social justice.
Another beneficiary of the upheaval is a far-left firebrand, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who now appears to be the likeliest candidate to advance into a second round against Ms. Le Pen in France’s two-round system. As things currently stand, French voters would be confronted with a choice between two poles of the political spectrum.
Centrist voters are “afraid of being confronted with a duel between Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon,” said Jean-Daniel Lévy, deputy director of Toluna France, a polling firm. These voters, he said, are an “orphan electorate,” lacking an inspiring candidate, and are “still looking for someone.”
Raphaël LLorca, an analyst at the Jean-Jaurès Foundation, a left-leaning research group in Paris, said the search for a white knight showed “the panic of the centrist bloc.” He added, “It is clear that the election is slipping away from them.”

WASHINGTON — Two senators are introducing a bill Friday to rein in conflicts of interest on an influential federal panel that evaluates preventive medical services.
The bill, from Sens. Angus King (I-Maine) and Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), follows reports that a number of members picked by health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. could profit from the decisions they make on the panel, known as the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force. It would codify standards for membership on the panel and for avoiding conflicts of interest.
The bill comes after STAT reported that members of the panel hold stock in pharmaceutical and medical device companies and that two of them own private medical practices that could profit should the panel recommend particular types of care. The New York Times reported on the financial investments as well. Federal officials granted all members blanket waivers, allowing them to remain on the panel, though they could still be required to recuse themselves from particular matters. The panel has not met in more than a year.

Families of slain Special Police Officers seek CBI probe, accountability for security lapses in J&K's Kishtwar
SPOs Babi Chand and Rashpal Kumar, both residents of Kiyar village, were found dead in the Dachhan forest early Thursday, a day after they went missing.
The last of the killings had been reported in 2004; now, after more than two decades, terror has returned to Kiyar village in Jammu and Kashmir's Kishtwar district. The recovery of bullet-riddled bodies of two special police officers (SPOs) on Thursday has rekindled memories of past attacks and renewed fear among locals.
The affected families are demanding a Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) probe into the killings, accountability for alleged security lapses and immediate strengthening of security arrangements in the area to neutralise the terror threat.
Locals say at least 10 people from the village -- located in the remote Dachhan tehsil -- lost their lives in the killings between 2000 and 2004.
Also Read | SPOs and their role in J&K’s security operations in focus after 2 found dead in Kishtwar
The latest killings have reopened wounds dating back to August 2000, when eight residents of Kiyar village were gunned down by terrorists, followed by two more murders in 2004.
SPOs Babi Chand (57) and Rashpal Kumar (45), both residents of Kiyar village, were found dead in the Dachhan forest early Thursday, a day after they went missing.
The two SPOs were on their way to a security post at Basnand in adjoining Marwah tehsil when they were allegedly killed between Deharna and Kiyar villages, at an altitude of nearly 8,860 feet.
Their service weapons -- an INSAS rifle and a .303 rifle -- along with magazines and ammunition were found missing and are suspected to have been taken away by the attackers.
Empty cartridges of Pakistan-origin armour-piercing ammunition were recovered from the scene, adding to security concerns.
Kiyar is a predominantly Hindu hamlet at an average elevation of 9,460 feet, where even mobile network is very poor.
Deharna, situated at an elevation of 6,560 to 7,220 feet, is about 14 km from the Marwah tehsil headquarters and 30-50 km from Kishtwar town. The region lacks direct all-weather road connectivity, making access difficult, particularly during adverse weather conditions.
For Ramesh Kumar, brother of slain SPO Babi Chand, the latest killings are not isolated incidents but part of a painful history of violence that, he believes, was never properly investigated.
"One (of the victims) was my brother, the other was my nephew. We have lost loved ones, but nobody is listening to us. Two of our people were assigned duty in a far-flung area. We believe something is amiss. Why were they assigned duty outside their jurisdiction when security posts already exist in that area?" Kumar said.
He said the killings have left the families without a sense of security or justice. He demanded a CBI investigation to establish the circumstances surrounding the latest killings, as well as the previous attacks.
Questioning the security grid, Kumar claimed that the number of security personnel and posts in the area has drastically declined over the years. He said while around 45 security posts had been set up in the region following the August 2000 massacre, only four personnel were presently guarding their hamlet, leaving the population vulnerable.
Pawan Kumar, grandson of Ramesh Kumar, also called for an urgent review of the security deployment in Dachhan and adjoining areas.
"Why were our men sent away from here when security posts already exist in Marwah? This is Dachhan, and the security of our villages should have been the priority. We want Lt Governor Manoj Sinha to intervene and order a CBI probe into the killings. A thorough investigation is necessary to establish what happened and why," he said.
Apart from seeking a CBI investigation, the bereaved families expressed anguish over what they described as negligence by senior police officials following the killings.
They claimed that no senior officer has visited them and the victims have not been accorded due honour.
They urged the Lt Governor to intervene and ensure restoration of security infrastructure, adequate deployment of personnel, effective intelligence gathering and regular security reviews to prevent further attacks on vulnerable villages.
Kishtwar Deputy Commissioner Pankaj Kumar Sharma, who camped in the village, attended the last rites of the deceased along with senior BJP leaders, including Leader of Opposition in Jammu and Kashmir Assembly Sunil Sharma and Kishtwar MLA Shagun Parihar, on Friday evening.
The deputy commissioner has assured the bereaved families of all possible assistance.
He said cases for compassionate appointment of eligible dependent family members under the Jammu and Kashmir Rehabilitation Assistance Scheme, along with compensation admissible under applicable rules, would be taken up and processed, based on recommendations from police and competent authorities.
He also assured villagers that issues relating to road connectivity, mobile network coverage and other developmental requirements of Kiyar would be assessed by the concerned departments and taken up on priority.
BJP MLA Shagun Parihar raised concerns over the security situation, claiming threats had been issued to the deceased.
She questioned the pattern of selective killings and called for a thorough investigation into the incident, besides action against those providing support to terrorists.

The Keralam government will take steps to implement ‘Family Sustainability Mapping’ across the State to identify, at an early stage, children living in high-risk environments, Minister for Women and Child Development Bindhu Krishna has said.
Speaking at a press conference to announce the Ujjwala Balyam Awards on Wednesday (November 11, 2026), she said a decision regarding the mapping was reached during a meeting convened following the death of a two-year-old child in Alappuzha recently due to suspected malnutrition.
The circumstances of families and children will be assessed with the cooperation of schools, Anganwadis, local self-government institutions, District Child Protection Units, healthcare workers and the police. Children facing risks such as malnutrition, neglect, domestic abuse, child labour, begging, school dropouts, substance abuse-related issues or various forms of exploitation will be identified and necessary protection and rehabilitation will be ensured.
“Child protection efforts should not be limited to intervening only after abuse or exploitation has already occurred. The government’s objective is to proactively identify high risk situations and ensure timely protection for children. Coordinated action among various departments and institutions will be strengthened to prevent issues such as sexual abuse, physical and mental abuse, neglect, child labour, child begging, human trafficking and online exploitation,” she said.
Activities will be jointly coordinated by departments including the Department of Women and Child Development, the Health Department, the Police, and the Local Self Government Department. This will enable the strengthening of existing child protection systems as well as the proactive identification of risks and the implementation of preventive measures. The Minister stated that the active participation of society is essential to ensure a safe childhood and equal opportunities for every child and to create an environment in which they can grow up with self confidence.
Ms .Krishna said that a total of 52 children from 14 districts have been chosen for the Ujjwala Balyam Awards for showcasing exemplary talent in arts, sports, literature, science, social work, environmental protection, information technology, agriculture, waste management, humanitarian activities, crafts, sculpture and acts involving extraordinary courage.
The winners were selected by a committee chaired by the District Collector in each district. The award consists of a cash prize of ₹25,000, a citation and a plaque. The awards will be presented at the State-level Children’s Day celebration to be held in Thiruvananthapuram on November 14.
The award recipients are children who have demonstrated excellence in various fields, including social work, environmental protection, information technology, agriculture, waste management, humanitarian activities, crafts, sculpture, and acts involving extraordinary courage.
