Two skulls, including that of a man believed to have taken part in Brazil’s greatest slave revolt but whose remains were taken to the United States and used in racist eugenics studies at Harvard University, were repatriated on Wednesday.
The remains had been outside Brazil since the 19th century. One was taken about 190 years ago from Salvador, the capital of the state of Bahia; the other, about 160 years ago, from Rio de Janeiro – and were welcomed back in moving, subdued ceremonies in both cities.
The skulls are believed to have belonged to Africans or Afro-Brazilians in the country that received more enslaved Africans than any other during the transatlantic slave trade.
Each was brought back in a padded box inside a reinforced suitcase, carried on flights by Brazilian diplomats after a four-year campaign to recover the remains from Harvard’s Peabody Museum of Archaeology and Ethnology in the US.
Brazilian researchers from local universities will now try to learn more about who the two individuals were.
The skulls will not be displayed in museums or have their images released, and the Brazilian government has pledged that they will be buried with funeral rites as soon as the identification process is complete.
“It’s very important to restore the dignity of these people, which was taken from them in life and in death,” said Carolina Dias dos Reis, a government official who travelled to Boston to sign the agreement with Harvard.
The existence of the skulls was revealed in 2022, and Brazilian researchers sought their repatriation from Harvard, but said they faced a drawn-out process that only moved forward after the Brazilian government became involved in late 2024.
In recent months, concerns grew that Donald Trump’s sometimes hostile behaviour towards his Brazilian counterpart, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, could derail the repatriation. But everything worked out.
“We need to recover our past as a country, however difficult and violent it was, so that we can understand what we are living through in the present: the consequences and scars of structural racism,” added Reis.
Slavery was abolished in 1888, but nearly a century and a half later, Afro-Brazilians make up the majority of the population while occupying the bottom of every socioeconomic indicator, dominating the statistics on hunger, poverty, gender-based violence and victims of homicides committed by criminals or the police.
During the repatriation ceremony in Rio de Janeiro, Ivanir dos Santos, a history professor and a cleric of the Afro-Brazilian religion Candomblé, poured a glass of water on to the ground as researchers received the suitcase.
“It was a ritual act because you cannot deal with the remains of our ancestors without paying reverence to them. This is not a research object … for us, that person is still alive in memory and as our ancestor,” he said.
It is not precisely known who the skulls belonged to. The one taken to Salvador is believed to have belonged to a man who took part in the most significant urban slave revolt in Brazilian history, in 1835, when about 600 African Muslims attempted to seize control of what was then the country’s second most important city. They were ultimately defeated by police, who killed 70 rebels.
The man died at a hospital, and a US diplomat, Gideon T Snow, is believed to have sent the skull to Boston.
The Bahia Islamic Cultural Centre, one of the most active campaigners for its repatriation, has named the man Arakunrin, meaning brother in Yoruba.
Even less is known about the other person: initially, only that they were “an individual … exhumed from the ‘streets of Rio de Janeiro’” in the 1860s. Brazilian government officials, however, said on Wednesday that Harvard researchers had told them that some features – including that the skull was smaller than that of an adult man but larger than that of a child – suggested it may have belonged to a woman.
Bruno Veras, a historian who was part of the group that closely followed the repatriation, cross-referenced diaries, letters and maps of the city and believes the skull may have been taken from a cemetery for newly arrived Africans who either did not survive the long Atlantic crossing or died soon after disembarking.
The person believed to have taken it to the US was Walter Hunnewell, a student from a wealthy Boston family. He was part of an expedition led by the Harvard professor Louis Agassiz, who was in Brazil trying to document physical types to support his racist theories.
“To steal a skull and take it to another country was violent even in the context of racist research,” said Veras.
Researchers in forensic anthropology will now try to confirm the sex of the individuals and other information through measurements of the skulls – the one in Salvador is complete, while the one in Rio is missing its jaw – and microscopic analyses. If necessary, they will seek authorisation to carry out genetic or dating tests.
“This history of slavery cannot be undone,” said Irina Feisthauer Silveira, a diplomat who carried one of the skulls. “But acknowledging the mistakes of the past with transparency is a first step towards building a more equal, just and less violent future.”

As much as I appreciate the ingenious design of the Nintendo Switch’s Joy-Con, my family and I can’t stand using them as standalone gamepads. So when we travel with the Switch 2, we always bring at least one full-size gamepad, plus a couple of 8BitDo’s Zero 2 controllers for games that don’t use analog thumbsticks. I’ve spent years hunting for an alternative that pairs the size of the Zero 2 with as much of the functionality of a larger controller as I can get, and CRKD’s new Atom Plus is nearly exactly that. But if you have larger hands like I do, you may find the gamepad’s focus on portability a struggle.
This tiny gamepad with dual analog thumbsticks pushes the limits of portable controllers
Larger hands may struggle with the Atom Plus, but it squeezes a lot of functionality into an extremely tiny controller.
Measuring around 3.5 inches wide, the $29.99 Atom Plus is about a half-inch smaller than the 8BitDo Zero 2 but squeezes in considerably more features and functionality. The most obvious is a pair of symmetrical analog thumbsticks with anti-drift tunneling magnetoresistance technology. You also get shoulder buttons and triggers, rumble feedback, a dedicated home button, motion controls, and customization through a mobile app.
Like many third-party controllers, the Atom Plus works with multiple platforms, including the Switch and Switch 2, PCs, Android, iOS, and various smart TVs. And just like other gamepads, pairing to different devices requires putting the Atom Plus into one of several Bluetooth modes by holding down a combination of buttons at power-up, which in this case is the home button plus a specific direction on the D-pad. It’s easy to do, but never easy to remember: I frequently needed to grab the manual or quickly Google which direction I need to press when switching devices. The Atom Plus already features a bunch of technical info etched into the back of the controller, so I’d love to see these important pairing instructions included there, too. (And that goes for all multiplatform gamepads.)
I primarily tested the Atom Plus with the Nintendo Switch 2 since I mostly plan to use the controller as a travel accessory. The thumbsticks are about the same size as those on the original Switch Joy-Con, which means they’re smaller than the Switch 2’s. And while I prefer an asymmetrical layout, the Atom Plus’ sticks are very good, with a little more tension than Nintendo’s that I find actually helps with precision movements given their limited travel.
While the overall build quality feels excellent, the Atom Plus’ tiny footprint creates some compromises and challenges. The front action buttons and D-pad feel nice and squishy, but the gamepad’s controls are a little crowded. When pressing down or right on the D-pad, my thumb regularly bumps the left thumbstick. It doesn’t hinder gameplay, but I do find it an annoying distraction.
The shoulder buttons use digital microswitches, as do the triggers, which means the latter can’t be used for racing games that support analog acceleration controls. I like that the two sets of buttons on the top edge sit at slightly different heights, but I would have preferred a little more differentiation since I’ve occasionally accidentally pressed the triggers when I meant to hit the shoulder buttons.
I was impressed with the Atom Plus’ customizability, however. When paired to an accompanying mobile app, you can check the controller’s remaining charge, turn off rumble feedback, see its unique product number (by tapping your phone to an NFC chip inside the controller), and remap any of its controls. That includes the pair of dual-function shortcut levers that replicate the Switch’s plus and minus buttons and screenshot shortcut.
Those levers move up and down and cleverly reduce the number of buttons crowding the front of the Atom Plus, but they feel a little too small, which is more or less the general theme. It’s a tiny gamepad that’s great for travel or stashing in your everyday carry. But, unsurprisingly, it probably won’t find its way into your regular gaming rotation. It’s assumed that players will be willing to settle for the compromise of occasionally contorting their fingers in weird, new ways for one of the smallest fully featured controllers on the market.
I don’t think a dual-stick controller could get any smaller than the Atom Plus without making too many ergonomic compromises. So while I applaud CRKD for the careful balancing act behind the Atom Plus’ design, and would certainly recommend it for those wanting a very capable controller that’s also cheap and portable, I’m now curious how it compares to Microsoft’s recently announced Xbox Nano controller that’s “surprisingly comfortable,” according to The Verge’s Tom Warren. It’s $20 more expensive than CRKD’s and noticeably larger, but it adds analog triggers, a more spacious design, and stubby grips making it easier to hold for those of us with beefy mitts.

'Very inconvenient': Residents, shop owners frustrated by indiscriminately parked bicycles despite stepped-up enforcement
The Land Transport Authority has removed 489 bicycles in the first 10 months of 2026 as it ramps up efforts to tackle the issue.
SINGAPORE: For 55-year-old postal worker Mdm Kua, delivering mail at a Housing and Development Board (HDB) estate in Admiralty Drive often starts with heavy lifting before she can even reach the letterbox.
Almost every day, bicycles and personal mobility devices are left directly in front of letterboxes, forcing her to physically move them aside in order to carry out her job.
The SingPost worker of 15 years said: "When the bicycles are parked at the letterbox, I cannot work… so I have to carry (them away). It's a difficulty for me.
"There's no way for me to do my job. I have to open the (letterbox) door."
Elsewhere, a 69-year-old Sembawang resident told CNA about the daily obstacle course she faces in order to get home. Mrs Tan, who wanted to be known only by her surname, said bicycles parked near the entrance of the block she walks through to get to her estate sometimes leave barely enough room for people to pass.
"(It's) horrible. Sometimes, there's maybe only a metre for you to pass through," she said.
Their frustrations reflect a perennial issue of indiscriminate bicycle parking across Singapore’s heartlands and transport hubs, even as the Land Transport Authority (LTA) has stepped up efforts to tackle the problem.
In response to CNA's queries, a spokesperson on Saturday (Nov 14) said LTA has been "stepping up efforts to address indiscriminate bicycle parking and remove derelict bicycles", particularly at high-traffic locations such as MRT stations and other key transport nodes, to keep public passageways clear and free up parking spaces for other cyclists.
Bicycles obstructing public passageways may be relocated to designated parking areas or impounded and subsequently disposed of if unclaimed.
LTA said it removed 186 bicycles from bicycle parking areas at key transport nodes and other locations in the first half of 2026, followed by another 303 between July and October.
A bicycle may be considered derelict if it has been abandoned or left in a state of disrepair. This means the bicycle is heavily rusted, missing key components like wheels or a saddle, or left unused at the same location for an extended period.
Bicycles that have not been moved for more than seven days and show signs of disuse may be tagged for removal, and notices are issued to owners who park indiscriminately, said the LTA spokesperson.
Pointing to recent amendments to the Land Transport and Related Matters Act passed last month, LTA said the period for owners to reclaim impounded bicycles will be cut from 30 days to seven days, with a further seven days' notice before they are disposed of.
This will facilitate the timely disposal of unclaimed bicycles and free up capacity at holding yards to support ongoing enforcement efforts, said the spokesperson.
INCONVENIENCE CAUSED
Despite the authorities’ efforts, indiscriminate bicycle parking continues to hinder residents, workers as well as other cyclists in some hotspots near transport nodes.
On Saturday, CNA visited nine locations, including MRT stations and residential areas across Singapore.
At most MRT stations visited, bicycles were parked neatly without obstructing pedestrian access, but there were still some bicycles that were inappropriately chained to pillars or railings along sheltered walkways.
The problem appeared more acute at Paya Lebar and Admiralty MRT stations, where several rows of bicycles could be seen parked outside designated lots.
Postal worker Mdm Kua, who did not want to be identified by her full name, said she frequently encounters bicycles obstructing walkways at HDB blocks along Admiralty Drive.
With many elderly residents in the estate, including wheelchair users, she has seen some struggle to get past the parked bicycles.
"Sometimes the owner has to think about the others' needs," she said.
Town councils are responsible for managing and maintaining common areas in HDB estates and may remove and detain any object obstructing the lawful use of any common property.
At Admiralty MRT station, CNA observed cyclists parking their bicycles in non-designated areas despite multiple signs warning against it. Most declined to speak when approached.
A group of three cyclists who parked their bicycles inappropriately claimed they were unaware that parking was prohibited there, adding that they stopped there only for a short while to withdraw cash from the MRT station. They left about five minutes later.
At a nearby bus stop, Admiralty resident, 52-year-old Mdm Zaripah, said she frequently saw bicycles parked outside designated areas but felt there was "nothing that can be done".
Confronting cyclists for their actions could invite hostile responses and risk being accused of being a "kaypoh" (Hokkien for “busybody”), she said.
Mdm Kua, the postal worker, said she too encounters hostility when urging cyclists not to park at letterboxes.
Her requests are also sometimes met with irritation as well as half-hearted attempts to move the bicycles.
"(If) I still cannot fit in, then 'bo pian' (Hokkien for "no choice"), I have to carry (the bikes). Sometimes we try to keep quiet and do our job, (but it's) very inconvenient for us," she said.
Mr Bryan Lee, who works at homeware store Good Price Hub in Bukit Batok, said customers occasionally leave their bicycles near the shop, obstructing the walkway.
Some react unhappily when asked to move their bicycles, he said.
LIMITED PARKING, LACK OF SHELTER IN DESIGNATED SPOTS
Sembawang resident Mrs Tan suggested installing shelters over bicycle parking areas to discourage indiscriminate parking.
"Cyclists don't want to park their bicycles under the sun, rain so they park their bikes under HDB blocks," she said, adding that this leaves open-air parking spaces going to "waste".
Computer engineer Greg Tan, 45, said he faces occasional difficulties finding bicycle parking at MRT stations.
He cycles every morning before work and often makes a quick stop at Admiralty MRT station for breakfast, parking his bicycle at the designated lots before heading home.
"There's usually a lot of bicycles parked even in the morning so finding a slot might be a bit challenging," he said. But this had not happened frequently enough to become a major inconvenience for him, he added.
The problem also affects other cyclists like Ms Cheng too, as finding a suitable parking spot can also be a challenge.
The 34-year-old, who works in the hardware industry and wanted to be known only by her surname, cycles to work daily and usually parks outside West Mall or near Bukit Batok MRT station.
But bicycles parked haphazardly sometimes leave little room for her to secure her own. "On Saturday, Sunday, it’s usually a bit difficult to park," she said.
Despite this, she continues using the same parking areas because of their convenience for her daily commute.
LTA EXPLORING HOW TO OPTIMISE SPACE
In its reply to CNA, LTA said indiscriminate bicycle parking is more commonly seen at key transport nodes, where demand for bicycle parking tends to be higher during peak commuting hours.
"This may result in temporary pressure on available parking spaces, rather than necessarily indicating a shortage of parking facilities or a mismatch in their locations.
"The presence of derelict bicycles at designated parking areas can also reduce the number of spaces available to active cyclists," the authority said.
Signage and banners have also been put up to remind cyclists to park responsibly, particularly at locations with higher incidences of indiscriminate parking.
LTA added that it is exploring ways to optimise available space for additional bicycle parking where feasible, as well as working with development and building owners to identify alternative parking locations nearby.
As Singapore's cycling path network continues to grow, the authority said it will continue to review and expand bicycle parking facilities at key transport nodes to better meet cyclists' needs.
"We encourage all cyclists to park responsibly and make use of designated bicycle parking facilities where available."

“It’s really happening. I promise. For real.” Those are the first words from Roy Graham, Head of Story at Magic: The Gathering, in a video posted yesterday announcing Planeswalker, the animated series heading to Netflix in 2027.
Magic: The Gathering is getting a Netflix animated series. For real this time.
Magic The Gathering: Planeswalker is set to debut on Netflix in 2027.
An animated Magic: The Gathering series was first teased back in 2019 with Joe and Anthony Russo at the helm. But that fell apart. In 2024, Netflix announced it still planned to make a series based on the game, but it decided to rework it from the ground up.
Now fans are finally getting their first glimpse of the show, which will be called Planeswalker. According to the sneak peek, because each plane exists in its own pocket universe, it will have a unique design, animation, and filmmaking style.
According to a synopsis of the show shared with IGN, Planeswalker will focus on Chandra Nalaar, a “volatile pyromancer hunted for her gifts, and haunted by her past.” Storyline details beyond that are vague, other than mentioning an “insidious force” that Chandra and other Planeswalkers will team up to confront “to prevent a cataclysmic war that threatens to consume their very existence.”

Global powers converge on Manila as ASEAN summit kicks off
Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos (second from left) attends a bilateral meeting with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney in Manila on Saturday ahead of an Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit.
| POOL / VIA AFP-JIJI
Manila – A key regional summit opens on Sunday in Manila, with Southeast Asian heads of state facing questions on trade, security and an ongoing energy crisis while playing host to a who’s who of global leaders.
U.S. President Donald Trump is scheduled to arrive on Tuesday near the summit’s conclusion, a visit expected to include a sideline meeting with fellow “Quad” countries India, Japan and Australia — the first of his second term.
The meeting of the Quad — a grouping broadly aimed at counterbalancing China’s regional influence — would come days before a historic sit-down with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russia’s Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen.

Parents who devote their lives to securing a better future for their children, including helping them move abroad or attain prestigious positions, often find themselves spending their twilight years in old-age homes, Kannada novelist and writer Kumbar Veerabhadrappa was quoted as saying by The Hindu.
He made the remarks while inaugurating a district-level Children's Day programme for 2026-27 at the Zilla Panchayat Conference Hall in Ballari on Thursday.
Raising concerns over the increasing number of old age homes across the country, Veerabhadrappa said the education system was becoming increasingly driven by financial considerations, with human values and respect for elders taking a back seat.
He emphasised the importance of safeguarding rural traditions, folk arts and cultural practices and ensuring that they are passed down to future generations. He also lauded the practice of donating the bodies of deceased elderly parents to medical colleges, describing it as a worthy initiative that more people should follow.
Acknowledging the Karnataka government's efforts towards child welfare, nutrition and improving the quality of food served at anganwadis, Veerabhadrappa said the state was approaching these matters with scientific reasoning and a rational outlook.
He also flagged concerns over the semester-based education system and the heavy homework burden placed on children, saying these were reducing the time available for outdoor activities and the development of communication skills.
The growing use of mobile phones was another major challenge, he said, warning that it was coming in the way of children's overall development.
Calling on government officials to look beyond routine meetings and administrative responsibilities, Veerabhadrappa urged them to prioritise the health, safety and holistic development of the younger generation.
Senior Civil Judge and District Legal Services Authority Member-Secretary Rajesh N. Hosamane, who also addressed the gathering, underlined the need to instil moral values, discipline, cultural traditions and respect for heritage among children, according to The Hindu.
Expressing concern over minors increasingly riding motorcycles, he urged parents to ensure that underage children do not drive vehicles.
He said following the law was a responsibility shared by every citizen and stressed that wearing helmets and complying with traffic regulations were compulsory.
Parents, he added, must educate their children about the importance of obeying the law and ensure they do not disregard traffic rules.
The programme featured several competitions and activities for children aged between nine and 16. These included events related to creative arts, writing, performing arts and scientific innovations.
Winners were felicitated and prizes were presented at the event.

India’s tuberculosis (TB) burden remains substantial despite progress. The country has the largest TB burden in the world, accounting for approximately one-quarter of all TB cases globally. The number of new cases fell 21% between 2015 and 2024, while treatment coverage rose to 92%, according to World Health Organization data cited by the government. The Central government recently started the JOSH campaign -- launched in 11 States and 55 districts to promote screening, early diagnosis and treatment adherence. JOSH stands for Joint Squad for Health. It is a youth-led community mobilisation initiative to strengthen India’s campaign to eliminate TB.
Dhun Davar, deputy CEO & chief of programmes, Asian Venture Philanthropy Network (AVPN) spoke to The Hindu about the challenges in the TB elimination programme. AVPN is a pan-Asian network of social investors, philanthropists, foundations, corporations and other organisations that work to direct funding and expertise towards social and environmental challenges. Its work includes health equity, gender equality, climate action and economic inclusion.

For motorists navigating the Ranigunj rail underpass during peak hours, the familiar sight is a long queue of vehicles inching towards the narrow passage from Tank Bund, with buses, trucks, cars and two-wheelers jostling for space. What should be a short passage into a frustrating bottleneck. The proposed widening promises relief, but commuters will have to negotiate six months of traffic diversions before the work is completed.
Work on widening the Ranigunj Road Under Bridge (RuB) is expected to begin within a week. The existing carriageway, which is around 13 metres wide and currently accommodates two-way traffic, will be expanded to 22 metres to facilitate four-way movement. Officials expect the additional width to ease congestion and improve traffic flow along the busy stretch.
Traffic will be diverted through alternative routes. Under the proposed plan, vehicles travelling from MG Road towards Paradise and Ranigunj will be asked to take a left towards Distillery Road, pass through another road underbridge and proceed towards Karbala before joining MG Road.
Buses and trucks will be diverted from Old Ambedkar towards Liberty, Kavadiguda and Musheerabad, while smaller vehicles will be routed through Karbala and Ranigunj. To facilitate smoother movement at Karbala, the concerned agency has been asked to provide an additional three metres of road space to enable one-way traffic.
Officials said that if congestion builds up near Karbala Maidan, a portion of the traffic will be diverted through Minister Road and Rasoolpura. Flexi boards and signboards have been put up along the stretch to alert motorists about the upcoming work and diversions.
A. Chandra Shekar, who works at the Nampally court, commutes every day from Bolarum to reach work by 9 a.m., travelling through the stretch during the morning rush hour. He said the diversions would mean a longer commute for the next six months, but felt the eventual improvement would justify the inconvenience. “Although it will be a struggle to make the extra ride to dodge the stretch for six months, I speak for everyone when I say that this will bring much relief to a lot of commuters,” he said.
For Kalpana C, the congestion is not restricted to peak hours. She travels along Hussain Sagar Road from Himayatnagar towards her home in Rasoolpura and said the stretch frequently gets choked. “I take the Hussain Sagar Road to come home in Rasoolpura from Himayatnagar and it chokes up at any given time. Check the maps and it will be red constantly, especially the road towards Paradise from Tank Bund,” she said.
An official traffic advisory detailing the vehicle-wise diversion routes and restrictions will be issued by the Hyderabad Traffic Police before construction begins. Commuters will be advised to follow the notified routes and plan their journeys accordingly.

A video showing smoke and flames gushing from a multi-storey building is being widely shared on social media (here, here, here) with the claim that it shows a massive fire at Aranya Society in Sector 119, Noida, caused by an AC blast in a flat on the 21st floor. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Visuals show a massive fire at Aranya Society in Sector 119, Noida, caused by an AC blast in a flat on the 21st floor in November 2026.
Fact: While a fire accident took place at Aranya Society in Sector 119, Noida, after an AC unit exploded in June 2026, the viral visuals are AI-generated. Gautam Buddha Nagar Police Commissionerate clarified in a post on X that the information being circulated was misleading and baseless. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
Upon conducting a relevant keyword search using the details mentioned in the viral claim, we found reports from June 2026 stating that a fire broke out in a flat on the 21st floor of Aranya Society in Sector 119, Noida, at around 8 AM, following an AC unit explosion. According to reports, six fire engines rushed to the spot after receiving information about the incident, and firefighters brought the fire under control after about 30 minutes (here, here, here).
However, we also found reports dated 10 November 2026 stating that an AI-generated video of a fire sparked panic; 20 fire brigade teams arrived, but found nothing (here, here). According to these reports, a video claiming to show a fire caused by an AC blast in a flat on the 21st floor of Aranya Society in Sector 119, Noida, went viral on social media. Following this, the police and fire brigade teams were alerted and rushed to the location. However, they found no fire at the site.
Moreover, the Gautam Buddha Nagar Police Commissionerate clarified in a post on X that the information being circulated was misleading and baseless. It also stated that a case had been registered under relevant sections against the person responsible for creating and sharing the misleading information, and that strict legal action was being taken.
We also verified the viral video by running it through AI detection tools, HIVE AI and SynthID.
To sum up, an AI-Generated fire accident video is falsely linked to AC Blast at Noida’s Aranya society.

On 11 November 2026, terrorists reportedly opened fire on a CRPF checkpoint near Mir Bazar in the Kulgam district of Jammu and Kashmir, injuring three personnel. The attackers fled after the firing, and security forces launched a search operation to track them down.
In this context, a video (here & here) is being shared on social media claiming that former Army officer Pravin Sawhney referred to the Kulgam terrorist attack as another “false flag” operation, similar to the Pulwama and Pahalgam attacks. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: The video depicts genuine footage of former Army officer Pravin Sawhney describing the November 2026 Kulgam terrorist attack as a “false flag” operation.
Fact: The video is an AI-generated deepfake and does not feature Pravin Sawhney. The original footage actually stems from a March 2025 interview on The Wire, where journalist Sushant Singh discusses the 2019 Balakot air strikes. Furthermore, Singh has made no such statements regarding the recent Kulgam attack. Hence, the claim made in the post is False.
First, we observed that the interviewee in the video is not ex-Army officer Pravin Sawhney but rather journalist and author Sushant Singh. Next, a reverse image search of keyframes extracted from the viral video led us to the original, full-length video uploaded on The Wire’s YouTube channel in March 2025. This video was published 20 months before the Kulgam attack and features journalist Ashutosh Bhardwaj interviewing Sushant Singh to critically assess the February 2019 Balakot air strikes, six years after the event. Singh made no such statements as those heard in the viral video.
Further, we ran the video through AI detection tools and found that the audio has been manipulated using artificial intelligence.
Furthermore, both Sushant Singh and the host, Ashutosh Bhardwaj, have publicly stated that the video is AI-manipulated and completely fabricates their past conversation.
To sum it up, an AI-manipulated video is being falsely shared to claim that an ex-Army officer called Kulgam attack a false flag operation.

The 2030 World Cup final will be in Spain, Spanish Football Federation (RFEF) head Rafael Louzan reiterated on Saturday, adding that he is not considering “withdrawing” should he be wrong.
Spain is organising the next World Cup with Portugal and Morocco. The decision on the venue for the final will be made in 2028, Louzan said.
Spain favours Real Madrid’s Santiago Bernabeu Stadium for the final. Portugal does not have a suitable stadium but Morocco has suggested the 115,000-capacity Hassan II Stadium being built in Benslimane near Casablanca.
“There is no other plan than for the final to be held in Spain,” said Louzan at a conference at the RFEF’s Ciudad del Futbol on the outskirts of Madrid.
“I am not currently considering the possibility of withdrawing from Spain, as the prospect of Spain not hosting the final is not on the table,” he said.
READ | Scaloni to stay on as Argentina coach until 2030 World Cup
Louzan was responding to Alberto Nunez Feijoo, the leader of the right-wing People’s Party.
In a television interview on November 5, Feijoo said that were he to become prime minister in the general election on November 29, he would advocate withdrawing Spain’s bid to host the World Cup should Morocco be awarded the final.
Luzon said the question was entirely hypothetical.
“That notion simply doesn’t exist,” he said, adding that under FIFA’s tradition of rotating the World Cup, the staging of the final “belongs to the European continent”.
A delegation of FIFA technical experts spent last week visiting Spanish stadiums that are hoping to host matches during the tournament, Louzan said.

Dangerous and severe “supercell” thunderstorms with the potential for giant hail and destructive winds were forecast for parts of New South Wales on Sunday, as volatile weather continued in the eastern states over the weekend.
Storms dumped heavy rain across large parts of northern and eastern NSW and much of Queensland on Saturday, with strong winds recorded up to 98km/h in Goulburn and rainfall totals of between 30mm and 50mm in the Coffs Harbour area.
A man in his 20s was struck by lightning while swimming at Ettalong beach on NSW’s Central Coast on Saturday afternoon. He was pulled from the water by fellow swimmers and given CPR by first responders until NSW Ambulance paramedics arrived. He was taken to Gosford hospital in a serious condition, and later transferred to Royal North Shore hospital.
The young man was in a critical but stable condition on Sunday morning, a hospital spokesperson said.
Witnesses said while there was storm activity visible in the distance towards Gosford, the area around the beach was clear and sunny and that the lightning bolt appeared to come “out of nowhere”.
Lightning can strike up to 30km from the centre of a storm cell.
Sunday was expected to be “another big storm day”, with “very dangerous and severe thunderstorms” likely for north-eastern NSW, said Sarah Scully, senior meteorologist at the Bureau of Meteorology.
Those storms could bring hail with a diameter greater than 5cm, and winds in excess of 120km/h.
“That’s being driven by a southerly change that’s pushing up the New South Wales coast,” Scully said. “It’s a potential trigger for these supercell high-end thunderstorms.”
Severe thunderstorms with 2cm hail, wind gusts in excess of 90km/h, heavy rainfall and flash flooding was possible on Sunday through a broader area of NSW extending down towards inland parts of the ranges to the east of Sydney, and pushing up into south-east and central parts of Queensland.
Storms were expected in Sydney on Sunday, but were likely to be less severe than further north, though rain was likely. The forecast temperature was 23C. Showers and thunderstorms were expected in Brisbane with a top of 31C.
The BoM expected to release more severe weather warnings throughout Sunday as the storms develop.
On Monday, the risk of high-end severe thunderstorms would move into the NSW northern rivers and south-eastern parts of Queensland, including Brisbane, the Gold Coast and the Sunshine Coast, again with the potential to bring giant hail, destructive winds, and intense rain that could lead to life-threatening flash flooding.
“That again is being driven by that trough that’s pushing up the coast combined with the very humid conditions that eastern Australia has been experiencing the last few days,” Scully said.
A coastal trough with a low-pressure system appeared to be developing off the north coast of NSW near the Queensland border, which had the potential to bring even more rain onto the coast.
“How much rainfall accumulates is highly dependent on how close that trough sits to the coast, and also how long it lingers there,” Scully said.
“At this state we’re only expecting moderate rainfall totals during tomorrow from that coastal trough, between 30mm to 70mm, easing into Tuesday morning. But we are watching it very closely as rainfall totals associated with these coastal troughs are notoriously challenging to predict. If they just move that little bit closer to the coast they can sometimes dump a whole lot of rain.”
Elsewhere, there were showers developing in Melbourne on Sunday with a forecast top of 17C. There was a high chance of showers in Hobart, with 13C expected, and cloudy in Adelaide with a mild 20C forecast. It was partly cloudy in Canberra, where they were expecting 24C, and in Perth, with an expected top of 28C. Darwin was expecting 34C and an afternoon storm.

Italy fines Meta €805m over accessing users' photos
- Published
Italian regulators have fined social media giant Meta €805m (£670; $887m) for accessing Android users' photos without their specific consent.
Italy's Data Protection Authority said Meta did not properly inform about 20 million smartphone users that it had access to their photos and videos via a feature of the Facebook app.
It has given Meta 60 days to disable the feature by default and seek users' consent separately.
The fine is among the largest an Italian authority has ever imposed on a tech giant.
A Meta spokesperson told the BBC that it planned to appeal.
The charge is related to a feature which suggests photos and videos from a user's phone gallery as ideas for posts.
Facebook requested access to users' photo galleries through a single app-wide authorisation. According to the Italian regulator, a preceding notice did not make clear that this would also allow Facebook to generate suggestions based on photos in their gallery.
The regulator said it took into account "the high number of people affected" and the fact it is "still ongoing for those who have not updated the app and for those who have already given their consent to the system".
It also cited "Meta's lack of co-operation".
Meta told the BBC: "We strongly disagree with the [regulator's] assessment of the facts, its application of the law, and the disproportionate level of the fine.
"This is a straightforward feature which helps people post photos and videos to Facebook. People must give permission on their device before it can operate, and they can change this permission at any time via their settings."
Last month, Meta, which is also behind Instagram and WhatsApp, was hit with its largest fine ever for its business practices.
A US judge in New Mexico ordered the company to pay $25bn (£18.6bn) after it found that found it had spent years lying to the public about how it handled Facebook user data.

Indian security personnel carrying batons and shields and accompanied by riot control vehicles surrounded the site of a planned opposition protest in Delhi on Sunday that is set to demand the resignation of the country’s election chief over a controversial revision of voter lists.
Authorities warned of traffic diversions ahead of the protest march and rally that will be led by Congress party leader Rahul Gandhi. The opposition says it expects hundreds of thousands of people to participate in what it says will be a major challenge to the prime minister, Narendra Modi, and his Bharatiya Janata party (BJP).
Opposition parties, student organisations and the youth-led Cockroach Janta party have held near-daily demonstrations since last month demanding that the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, step down over the voter list revision that critics say favours the BJP.
The Election Commission has denied favouring any party and said wrongly deleted voters can re-enrol, while the BJP has accused rivals of trying to undermine democracy by wrongly questioning legitimate electoral processes.
Analysts say the youth protests, and growing support for the opposition, form the worst crisis for Modi since he came to power in 2014. But his government remains stable and the next general election is not due until 2029.
The opposition parties have announced they will hold a nearly 1.5km march on Sunday from central Delhi to the Ramlila Maidan, a ground that is the designated site for their protest rally.
Visuals from news agency ANI showed riot control vehicles and dozens of security personnel armed with batons and shields outside the rally venue, where announcements were being made urging people to ensure smooth traffic movement and cooperate with police officials.
Delhi traffic police said a “large gathering” was expected at the venue, and traffic regulations and diversions would be implemented “as required”.
“People have started coming to participate in this rally ... we have ensured proper arrangements at the venue, and arrangements are also planned on the route of the march that will happen in a few hours from now,” senior police officer Rohit Rajbir told ANI.
The protests demanding Kumar’s resignation erupted after the Indian Express newspaper reported in September that his two deputies had raised several concerns internally about voter list revisions, registration procedures and digital systems.
The change, which began last year, removed over 130 million names from voter lists, including 28 million who died, 63 million who relocated and 30 million who could not be traced.
Opposition parties allege the deletions disproportionately affect Muslim voters and other minorities, who are unlikely to support the Hindu nationalist ruling party – allegations the poll panel and BJP reject.

Red gold from purple flowers: saffron harvest in Kashmir – in pictures

Kashmir’s saffron industry is facing challenges, with farmers reporting declining yields due to climate change and inadequate irrigation. Photograph: Firdous Nazir/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

Beta Pictoris is a young star, roughly 20 million years old, and located about 64 light-years away from Earth. It is surrounded by a vast disk of dust and rubble where planets are still forming—astronomers have already found three. In a new Science study, a team led by Sarah Betti, an astronomer at the Space Telescope Science Institute in Baltimore, used the James Webb Space Telescope to look for ice in this disk. Researchers found both water and carbon dioxide ice.
The water ice is glassy rather than crystalline, and it is mixed with carbon dioxide in roughly the same proportions we see in comets of our own Solar System. This suggests ingredients necessary to form water-rich worlds might be common around young stars.
The missing ice
Beta Pictoris is one of the best studied stars in the sky. Its disk was among the first ever imaged, back in 1984, and we see it almost exactly edge-on, which makes it a natural laboratory for studying how planetary systems grow. It’s what astronomers call a debris disk, where the dust is constantly replenished by collisions among comets and planetesimals, small bodies that are the building blocks of planets.
The outer parts of the disk are far enough from the star that water and other volatile molecules should freeze into solid ice. The disk holds a large reservoir of carbon monoxide gas, which ultraviolet light from the star should destroy within 50 to 300 years. For that gas to still be there, something must keep replenishing it—most likely it’s released from ice when volatile-rich comets collide. The properties of the planet Beta Pictoris b also suggest it formed from ice-rich material.
Yet despite plenty of reasons to suspect the system is full of ice, earlier searches have failed to find it. Attempts to detect water vapor found nothing, and a search for the telltale dip that water ice leaves in starlight at a wavelength of 3 micrometers also failed.

The leader of a Kenyan doomsday sect has been sentenced to 200 years in prison for the murders of 190 children and one adult in one of the world’s worst cult disasters in recent history.
The sentence, comprising 100 years for murder by starvation and 100 years by direct homicide, came two weeks after the court in Kenya’s coastal city of Mombasa found the cult leader guilty of the crimes.
Prosecutors said Paul Mackenzie and his Good News International church ran a Christian doomsday sect whose members were ordered to starve themselves and their children to death to go to heaven before the world ended.
His accomplices threatened and beat victims to ensure they followed his orders. The emaciated bodies were found scattered in shallow graves and dumped in latrines. Some had been buried alive.
Mackenzie was arrested in 2023 after police received a tipoff, and weeks later authorities began uncovering bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola forest near the coast in south-eastern Kenya.
In total, more than 400 bodies have been recovered. Many were severely decomposed and only 26 could be identified.
Mackenzie denied murder charges, saying he did not force the victims to starve, but the court rejected that argument.
The Shakahola tragedy has gripped Kenya since the discovery of mass graves in the forest more than three years ago.
It raised questions about how Mackenzie was able to continue operating despite being on the radar of the authorities since 2017, when police searched his premises.
In 2019, authorities shut down Mackenzie’s church and he relocated to the Shakahola forest, police said.
The case has also led to calls for tougher oversight of churches and other religious organisations in a country where religious faith plays a prominent role in public life.
Mackenzie, a former taxi driver, forbade cult members from sending their children to school and from going to hospital when they were ill, describing such institutions as satanic.
Cult members lived in makeshift homes of polythene sheeting and thatch that Mackenzie divided into areas with biblical names such as Jerusalem and Judea.
The plight of his followers began to emerge in March 2023, when a man told police his brother and wife had starved their children to death in the forest on Mackenzie’s orders.
Mackenzie was arrested but released on bail, after which relatives said he brought forward the date on which he told his followers the world would end. Police rearrested him and started combing through the forest more systematically and began exhuming mass graves.
Last month’s judgment covered 191 deaths while investigations into more than 200 other deaths are continuing.
Justice Diana Kavedza-Mochache said in a hearing lasting more than eight hours that in some cases children were isolated and denied food while their parents watched.
Mackenzie faces other charges over the forest deaths, including those of terrorism, which he has denied.
Prosecutors said that while he was in detention he also directed the deaths of 52 people in Kwa Binzaro village, about 18 miles from Shakahola. Mackenzie has pleaded not guilty in that case.
Reuters contributed reporting

Australia has endorsed this week’s historic summit between Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in China, even as European leaders warn that the US president must not make major concessions over the war in Ukraine.
The three-way summit is planned to take place in Shenzhen, where the leaders will gather for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) meeting. Likened to the 1945 summit at Yalta, the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has warned the talks must not lead to a redistribution of influence among world powers or the abandonment of his country, more than four years into the war sparked by Putin’s full-scale invasion.
Speaking in Manila on Sunday, the Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, welcomed the talks taking place but insisted the clear message to Putin was that the war should end.
Albanese, in the Philippines before a meeting of Quad leaders and talks with south-east Asian leaders at the Asean summit, left open the possibility of joining an Apec group photo with Putin if China wished for it to go ahead.
“We think that dialogue is a good thing and we await the outcome of that dialogue,” he said.
“It’s obviously quite significant, the fact that President Trump will be at Asean as well as at Apec, and that we’ll have a Quad leaders meeting as well.
“We want to see something constructive come out of that, including we want to see a de-escalation in the conflicts around the world.”
German’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, expressed hesitation about the talks at a meeting of EU leaders on Friday.
“I want to state our message to the US very clearly once again: please, no surprises,” he said. “Stay on Team Europe and Team Ukraine, and let us work together for a genuine peace in Ukraine.”
France’s president, Emmanuel Macron, warned against forcing “an unjust peace” on Ukraine and, by extension, all of Europe.
“That is the spirit of defeat,” Macron said. “That is a recipe for another war.”
Zelensky has warned that the meeting must not turn into “Yalta 2, 3, 4”, invoking the conference in Crimea when the then US president, Franklin D Roosevelt, Britain’s Winston Churchill and the Soviet leader Joseph Stalin carved up influence across war-ravaged Europe.
The historian Timothy Garton Ash has called the trilateral summit, organised after a proposal by Putin last month, “a sort of parody” of Yalta, even as analysts say decisions on the future of Ukraine or China’s ambitions to take control of Taiwan without their involvement is unlikely.
Albanese said the summit would not undercut a growing push by countries including Australia and Canada for middle powers to have greater influence in world affairs.
“We’ll continue to engage with like-minded countries,” he said. “There are two super powers in the world.
“What’s important about the struggle of the people of Ukraine is that they’re not just standing up for their own sovereignty; they’re standing up for the international rule of law.”
Asked if he would join the so-called “family photo” of Apec leaders if Putin took part, Albanese said he would consider the wishes of China as the host nation. But he said the Russian president should know Australia’s opposition to the invasion.
“If he’s in a room where I am, I’m sure they’ll hear my contribution,” Albanese said.
After the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting, Australia’s Penny Wong joined with European and Canadian counterparts to avoid a group photo. It was cancelled by US officials when a third of participants declined to stand alongside the Russian foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov.
Albanese signed a new defence agreement with the Philippines on Sunday, visiting the supply ship HMAS Stalwart in the Port of Manila. Australia is helping to strengthen the Philippines’ defensive capability against Chinese aggression.
More freedom-of-navigation naval exercises are planned in an attempt to counter Beijing’s efforts to influence the South and East China seas.

Judge temporarily blocks Trump from moving ahead on Washington public golf course redevelopment
WASHINGTON — A federal judge on Saturday ordered a two-week delay to any work at a historic Washington public golf course not far from the White House, blocking for now President Donald Trump's push to redevelop the site along the Potomac River into a championship-level venue.
U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes issued the temporary restraining order before the East Potomac Golf Links was due to close Sunday for 15 months. Trump had announced work would begin that day despite the legal challenge initiated against the project in February by the DC Preservation League and two local golfers.
The plaintiffs argue that Trump's plan would change the character of the accessible golf course and make it unaffordable, something the Republican president denies. They had sought the stop-work order, saying that closing the course and launching work on the project would "irreparably injure plaintiffs and the public interest."
The president's public announcements on social media last month outlining the date of the closure of East Potomac Park and linking it to the renovation of the golf course weighed heavily in the decision. Trump said on Oct. 26 that "We are closing the East Potomac Golf Course Site as scheduled on November 15th in order to renovate and rebuild for Competitive (with other such projects!), Safety, Modernization, and Aesthetic reasons." He added that the goal was to renovate and rebuild "a World Championship Public Facility."
Reyes in her ruling Saturday noted that Trump's posts presented a problem for the government. "They indicate that the Washington National Plan is final and that NPS will close the Park to implement it," she wrote. "Both points favor granting Plaintiffs' motion for another temporary restraining order."
Reyes said her order "ENJOINS the government from closing East Potomac Park and the East Potomac Golf Course during the daily hours in which they were open as of November 14, 2026. It does not order the Government to undertake any active management of either. Further, for the avoidance of any doubt, the Government remains free, as it has since the onset of this litigation, to conduct repairs on any part of the Park and Course with any notice required by the existing Preliminary Injunction."
The judge said the order is in effect "through November 28, 2026, or further order from the Court, whichever comes first."
The Justice Department said in a statement Saturday that the judge acknowledged that the National Park Service can limit access to its facilities where the public is at risk of harm. "Nothing in the Court's order precludes planning for the development of a world class golf course to continue," it said. "The Department of Justice will always vociferously defend the Trump Administration's agenda in court."
Catherine Carroll, a senior legal adviser at Democracy Forward, which is representing the plaintiffs, praised the ruling. "We are grateful that once again, a court has intervened to prevent irreparable harm caused by the Trump-Vance administration's pursuit of another one of the president's vanity projects," she said. "The administration's inexplicable drive to destroy East Potomac Park would have taken away a treasured park that could never be replaced."
The park's redevelopment is one of multiple projects in the nation's capital that Trump has championed to remake the city. They include a large memorial arch, a White House ballroom and the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, among others.
Reyes had signaled throughout a five-hour court hearing Friday that she was likely to issue some stoppage for the park closure. The only issue was how expansive it might be. Justice Department lawyer Adam Gustafson argued that the entire East Potomac Park, which includes three golf courses, a miniature course, bike riding lanes and other recreational areas, was being closed because of safety factors. He also noted that the lease between the government and the current operator, National Links Trust, was ending Sunday.
Reyes pointed out that safety had not been part of the discussion over the closure for months and that ending the lease felt more like an action that provided a premise for the closure rather than an action that led to the closure of the course about 2 miles from the White House.
Even before the order, Trump lashed out in a social media post Saturday, contending that Reyes "doesn't want us to quickly and inexpensively fix up the Course which is, also, very dangerous." He said people who live in the Washington area would get a 50% discount on "any and all Rates charged" and that the redevelopment would "evolve into something very special, something which the Judge will be able to take great pride in seeing!"
Reyes' order was the latest in a series of rulings in lawsuits challenging Trump's projects that were issued just hours before construction was expected to begin. A different judge recently ordered a 14-day delay on work for the arch, a decision that came shortly after a key planning commission stacked with Trump appointees approved plans for the project.
Reyes, who was nominated to the court by Democratic President Joe Biden, had for months been reticent about approving the plaintiffs' requests for work stoppages. The plaintiffs had argued the administration was moving ahead with work related to the project despite the pending lawsuit.
Her reluctance to issue orders ended in October, spurred in part by a tree-cutting spree by the administration over a holiday weekend with little notification to the judge or plaintiffs.
Officials and government lawyers said the tree work was part of a 2019 plan that recommended the cutting. In response, the judge confronted the administration over what she portrayed as deceitful actions over its intentions for the project.
Reyes has repeatedly expressed frustration over the minute planning details she has been asked to adjudicate, including over the trees being cut down at the 106-year-old park. The Justice Department filed a request that Reyes be removed from the case because of what it called her "egregious behavior" and questioned her impartiality. Reyes has not recused herself.
The restraining order was one of two issues Reyes took up during Friday's hearing.
She announced plans last week to name Jessie Liu, a former U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, to examine whether officials with the Interior Department and the National Park Service and attorneys with the Justice Department had violated ethics or misled her during the course of the case.

A family photo, a hand to hold: An occupational therapist learnt what matters most to dying patients
Some patients worry less about dying than about the loved ones they will leave behind. For St Luke’s Hospital occupational therapist Esther Lim, caring for people nearing the end of life has revealed their regrets, surprisingly simple wishes and moments of joy.
After working with terminally ill patients at St Luke’s Hospital for the past three years, occupational therapist Esther Lim has observed how patients’ priorities shift as they approach the end of life. In the face of death, many think about loved ones they will leave behind.
One elderly patient wanted a makeover and photo shoot with his loved ones. Another asked to return home and spend his remaining time with family.
Other patients wrote letters, made cards or recorded messages for their loved ones, while some wanted to reconcile with an estranged family member.
“When time is limited, the priorities often become much clearer,” said the 40-year-old. “A fair share of our patients are concerned not so much for themselves, but whether their loved ones can cope emotionally or financially after they are gone.”
Some patients also reflect on their lives, expressing regret that they spent so much time on work and had less time for the people they loved, she added.
HELPING END-OF-LIFE PATIENTS FIND MEANING AND COMFORT
Working in the palliative care ward, Lim is part of a multidisciplinary team that helps patients navigate the last days of their lives.
Patients admitted to the ward generally have a prognosis of three months or less, said Lim. They may have conditions such as advanced cancer, end-stage organ failure or neurological conditions, including late-stage dementia.
Lim joined the community hospital in Bukit Batok in 2014, rotating through several wards before working with palliative care patients in 2023. Her patients range in age from their 30s to over 100.
While occupational therapy (OT) is typically associated with recovery and regaining independence, the goals are different for patients with advanced and life-limiting illnesses.
“In palliative care, the goals of OT are not so much of restoring function or independence, but about bringing comfort, exploring meaning and having closure,” explained Lim.
This includes managing symptoms such as pain, fatigue and breathlessness through energy conservation techniques, as well as modifying tasks and patients’ environments.
THE PATIENT ENCOUNTER THAT LED HER TO PALLIATIVE CARE
Sometimes, what a patient needs may be much simpler. This became clear to Lim after encountering an elderly patient in a wound care ward who had only months to live.
At the time, Lim was accustomed to helping patients recover and regain independence. But recovery was no longer possible for that patient.
During a therapy session, she asked him if he needed anything and expected a practical request, perhaps help getting his favourite food or drink.
Instead, the patient, who did not have family other than an elderly sister, asked if he could hold her hand. “I just held his hand and assured him that he’s not alone in that journey, and that the healthcare team will continue to walk alongside him,” she said.
The encounter prompted Lim to think differently about how OT could continue to support patients nearing the end of life.
It is also the reason why a significant part of Lim’s work in palliative care now involves fulfilling patients’ last wishes and helping them create something meaningful to leave behind for people they love.
HOW TO RECONNECT WITH SOMEONE APPROACHING THE END OF LIFE
For those hoping to reconnect with someone who is at the end of life, there is “no perfect moment” or “perfect script”, said Leong Si Jie, a senior medical social worker at St Luke’s Hospital. She suggested ways to approach them:
Don’t force reconciliation: When approaching an estranged family member, first explore whether they are open to reconnecting. Reconciliation should never be assumed or forced.
Begin gently and calmly: Start with a simple check-in. Ask open-ended questions, for example, “What do you think about what the doctor has shared regarding your medical condition?” or “How are you feeling about it?”.
Let them set the pace: Pay attention to both verbal and non-verbal cues. For example, if they turn their head away or keep answers brief, change the subject or remain quiet.
Listen and acknowledge their feelings: Simple statements such as, “I imagine this news must be difficult for you” or “I’m here to listen if you feel like talking” can help the patient feel heard and supported.
Avoid dismissing feelings and giving false reassurances: Responses such as “You will recover” or “Why are you giving up?” may shut down the conversation.
If the person dies before reconciliation is possible, Leong said the first step is to acknowledge the loss and allow yourself to experience the emotions that come with it. If it helps, talk to a trusted friend or family member.
“Sometimes, it is about finding your own sense of resolution after the loss,” she said.
If unresolved grief or feelings about the relationship continue to significantly affect your daily life, seek support from a counsellor or psychologist, said Leong.
PRESERVING MEMORIES AND FULFILLING LAST WISHES
Legacy projects give patients an opportunity to reflect on their lives and share what matters most with their loved ones, said Lim. This could involve creating photographs, cards, fingerprint art or voice recordings for loved ones.
These projects, she explained, provide comfort and connection for the patients and their loved ones, and offer a tangible reminder of the person after they are gone.
For patients who have difficulty writing, Lim adapts by adjusting their sitting position or propping them up in bed and providing a modified table to make writing easier. For those who are no longer able to write, Lim explores other options, such as audio recordings and photographs.
Lim said not every patient wants their messages handed over immediately. Some have told her: “Pass it to them when I pass away”.
Lim also helps some patients fulfil their last wishes. Going home is a common request. When families cannot manage care at home, the team may search for a middle ground, such as a trip home for a few hours, said Lim.
Other common requests involve satisfying a craving for a favourite food, such as a simple bowl of mee rebus, some fried carrot cake, chicken rice or char kway teow.
Lim has facilitated outings to coffeeshops near St Luke’s Hospital. “We need a lot of manpower for these trips because at the end of life, patients generally do not have much strength,” she said.
With the help of staff, volunteers and family members, Lim has wheeled patients out in reclining wheelchairs, with portable oxygen cylinders and painkiller drips in tow, to have their favourite hawker meal.
MAKING ROOM FOR JOY AND JOKES
When Lim first started working with palliative care patients, she worried about how she would cope emotionally. She soon realised that the end-of-life journey is not always filled with sadness and tears.
“There are also moments of laughter, joy and connection,” she said.
There was a seriously ill patient who made her laugh during a photo shoot because he knew she was camera-shy. Then, there was the octogenarian who, after a makeover, appeared in a blazer, vest and hat, and had photos taken with around 20 family members by the hospital’s fishpond.
“I could see how happy he was. He shared with me: ‘I come alive now’,” she said. “It’s not always just sadness. Many patients can also be quite humorous and share jokes.”
Working with palliative patients has also reminded Lim that “no one will truly know how much time we have”.
A patient once asked her: “If you only had seven days left on Earth, what would you do?”
“It prompted me to reflect on my priorities and what gives my life meaning. It reminds me to be present, to nurture the relationships that are important to me, and to make time for what truly matters,” she said.
Lim has come to see death as a part of life. “Life is full of transitions. Death and dying are also one of them – the final transition,” she said.
That’s why she believes conversations about end-of-life care and death should begin early and openly.
Having these conversations early, Lim said, can reduce fear and uncertainty, and help patients and families navigate this final stage of life “with love”.

Lutnick Took a Softer Line on Nvidia as Calls for Tougher Controls Grew
Critics say Howard Lutnick, the commerce secretary, and his department have shielded Nvidia as concerns have grown over A.I. chip sales to firms like Megaspeed.
There is broad agreement among most senior Trump administration officials that the United States should more aggressively tighten controls on Nvidia’s advanced chips to keep China from using them to catch up in the race to dominate artificial intelligence.
Then there is Howard Lutnick, who runs the Commerce Department.
Over the past year, Mr. Lutnick has frequently clashed with top officials over how to regulate sales of advanced technology, particularly Nvidia’s chip sales to Asia. That has drawn accusations from others in the administration and in Congress that the Commerce Department has become too cozy with Nvidia and its co-founder, Jensen Huang, and failed to adequately police the firm’s chip sales to China, in particular.
The issue has exploded into public view in recent weeks with the revelations from The New York Times that Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, was in a relationship with a woman believed by U.S. intelligence agencies to be a Chinese spy. The woman, Alice Huang, was a top executive at a Singapore-based company, Megaspeed, that is suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China. On Thursday, Mr. Huang announced that he was stepping down from the company, sending the company’s shares tumbling.
The astonishing developments have thrust Mr. Lutnick into an uncomfortable spotlight and raised questions about whether he went too far in protecting Nvidia’s interests. And it has focused attention on whether the influence of Mr. Huang, an ally of President Trump’s and among the most high-profile and successful of American business leaders, kept the United States from moving faster to clamp down on sales of Nvidia chips to companies like Megaspeed.
The stakes in the A.I. race between the United States and China are high. China hawks warn that allowing sales of advanced chips to that country is speeding its A.I. development and giving it an economic and military edge. Those who support the sales say they help U.S. technology maintain global leadership, while deterring China from developing rival products. As the head of a sprawling department that has control over enforcing restrictions on technology sales, Mr. Lutnick is best positioned to single-handedly shape whether China has access to American technology, including Nvidia’s.
Within the Commerce Department, Nvidia is treated differently than other firms, current and former officials say, with its issues given high priority and sent through specific channels.

Burger King said it believed the video was fake, writing, "We do not use, nor are we aware of any Franchisee across the U.S. or Canada using a tool like this." The video was originally posted by a creator who regularly shares similar humorous AI job interview videos.
In November, social media users shared a video supposedly showing a artificial intelligence job interview for the fast-food chain Burger King. In the clip, a virtual interviewer named Karen appears to be increasingly frustrated with an applicant who is shirtless, has a shoe on his head and gives unusual answers to her questions.
"Sending AI bots to interview for a $4 per hour job … that's about the respect they deserve. People need to push back on this dehumanizing practice. This can literally be an email," one X post (archived) captioned the video.
"This is Burger King! Burger King uses this weird ai lady to interview people," the same user wrote (archived) in another post.
The video also circulated on other social media platforms, including Reddit, Facebook and LinkedIn.
In short, the video doesn't show an authentic interview for a job at Burger King. The company denied using the AI interviewer featured in the recording, which was originally posted by a content creator who regularly shares similar humorous videos. We have therefore rated the claim as miscaptioned.
It is unclear how the video was created, including whether the AI interviewer responded in real time or whether parts of the conversation were scripted. We have reached out to the creator of the video and will update this report if we receive a response.
What we know about the video
We traced the video to content creator Nick Reid, who uses the handle @itsnickreid on TikTok and @nickreidx on X.
"I'm Karen from Burger King, and I'm here to chat with you about the team member position to get us started. What should I call you?" the AI interviewer said at the beginning of the video, with the candidate responding, "You can call me Cranjis McBasketball."
A series of unusual exchanges follows. For instance, the AI interviewer questions why the applicant is shirtless and has a shoe on his head, while he gives absurd answers, including saying he can get to work because he "has feet." Later in the video, the applicant asks for a salary of $725,000, while the AI interviewer says the position pays only $4 per hour.
AI INTERVIEWER: Since you are still here, let's talk money. What are your salary expectations for this role?
APPLICANT: $725,000 a year. No negotiations whatsoever.
AI INTERVIEWER: $725,000 a year? You have to be absolutely delusional to think that is a realistic number for a team member position. The pay for this location is $4 per hour and it is non-negotiable. Now do you have any questions for me about the role or the process?
APPLICANT: Yeah, how does it feel to scam employees by paying them only $4 an hour? Jacka**.
AI INTERVIEWER: I have already told you that the pay is $4 an hour. I will not be called names, especially not by someone who thinks throwing sandwiches at people is an acceptable way to handle a customer.
Reid's accounts posted several similar videos showing supposed job interviews for different companies, featuring the same AI interviewer, with captions such as "Bathing during an AI interview" or "Golfing During an AI Job Interview." This suggests the videos were created as comedy content and weren't showing real job interviews.
(TikTok account @itsnickreid)
On Nov. 11, business media outlet Fast Company described Reid's video as a comedy skit in an article about "comedy videos online highlight the awkward shortcomings of AI avatars that could screen job applicants."
However, some social media users appeared to believe the interview was real, expressing shock at the AI interviewer's behavior and the $4 hourly wage mentioned in the video.
(TikTok account @itsnickreid)
Burger King addressed the video on X, writing, "We are aware of this video and we want to be clear: we believe it's fake, and we do not use, nor are we aware of any Franchisee across the U.S. or Canada using a tool like this."
(X account @BurgerKing)
After the company's response, the creator wrote on X, "@BurgerKing wanna collab?"
When we reached out to Burger King for comment, the company said it had "nothing further to add" to its previous statement, which was also published on its official website.
Has Burger King used AI in recruitment?
While Burger King denied using the AI interviewer shown in the video, some of its franchisees have used AI tools in their hiring processes in the past.
For instance, recruitment company AMS published a case study about its work with Starboard Investments, a Burger King franchise operator. According to AMS, its "conversational AI technology has significantly expedited the candidate screening and interview scheduling process." According to the case study, the AI tool was used for "screening candidates and coordinating interview schedules."
Emi, another recruitment company, also described working with Burger King. According to the company, its AI-powered recruitment platform helped automate tasks such as "candidate screening and interview scheduling."
Neither company mentioned AI avatars conducting job interviews with applicants. Therefore, while there is evidence that AI tools have been used in recruitment at Burger King restaurants, we found no evidence that they were used to conduct live interviews like the one shown in the in-question video.
The AI interviewer in the video also claimed that the position paid $4 per hour. However, this seems unlikely, as the federal minimum wage in the U.S. is $7.25 per hour, according to the U.S. Department of Labor. A similarly low rate is the youth minimum wage of $4.25 per hour, but it applies only to workers under 20 during their first 90 days of employment. We found no evidence Burger King actually offers jobs at the $4 hourly rate mentioned in the video.
All in all, while some AI tools have been used in recruitment at Burger King restaurants, there was no evidence that the video spreading on social media in November showed a real job interview for the company.
