If you were living in Colorado in May and bet on sports online, you’d statistically have been most likely to bet on professional basketball. Next on the list was baseball. The third-most wagered sport?
Why online gamblers are obsessed with table tennis
Competitive ping-pong has been engineered into a kind of slot machine. What could this do to sports?
Table tennis.
Colorado is almost certainly not an outlier. Table tennis occupies a similarly high ranking in Oregon, the only other state to provide sport-by-sport breakdowns of gambling revenue. And it’s likely true in every other state that allows sports gambling. This is a strange fact, one that’s been reported by a few local and national outlets. And beyond the bets involved, it’s also a window into where sports gambling is going, and how sports betting is morphing into something stranger and more destructive than dropping $100 on the New York Yankees to cover the spread on Saturday.
There’s the old quip that the Holy Roman Empire was neither holy, nor Roman, nor an empire. In some sense, this is sports betting that involves neither sports nor betting. The gambling on table tennis isn’t really on the game of table tennis. It’s on a strange simulacrum of table tennis created solely for the purpose of creating more ways to gamble on it. For many of the people involved, it’s a kind of mindless, by-the-second slot machine rather than an informed wager on a player they might think can win. Ping-pong, in other words, has been reengineered into an addictive technology.
The story of how table tennis came to occupy this outsized role in sports betting — and what it really looks like now — offers an unsettling peek at how fast all of this is moving, and how much the business of gambling can distort the real world around it.
First, there’s a recent historical quirk. When most professional sports leagues shut down during the early stages of the Covid-19 pandemic, low-level, peculiar table tennis leagues in Eastern Europe popped up and were often the only game in town when it came to being able to place bets on sports. In May 2020 in Colorado, $6.5 million was wagered on table tennis, more than 25 percent of the statewide total — making it the most popular sport to bet on, simply because it was available.
But even after other sports came back, table tennis stuck around. In Colorado this past May, with every other sport back and operating, table tennis was bringing in $33.9 million, five times what it had been. The same pattern held in Oregon: In May 2020, table tennis was the most bet sport in Oregon, with $3.7 million wagered. By this past February, it was still the second-most bet sport, but now with $9.5 million wagered.
LSports, a company that collects and provides the real-time data that sportsbooks use to take and pay out bets, has a report intended for gambling operators that provides some of the starkest information on this. Its advice: “Table tennis is no longer sports betting’s dark horse; it has become an essential asset for sportsbooks seeking 24/7 bettor engagement.” And a main reason for the appeal is the intense, constant flow of matches, so betting companies have “minimal gaps in their live offerings.”
How is table tennis producing this much betting content? Sports aren’t on 24/7, and they have leagues, tournaments, offseasons, and training camps. But table tennis is different. The matches being bet on are not real leagues.
They have players that true fans of the sport would not recognize. They are played in strange, unmarked basements in Eastern Europe, with players whose names, if searched, reveal nothing beyond profiles on sports betting websites. The players’ abilities are clearly not at a professional level. Real, professional table tennis like World Table Tennis has packed arenas, high production value, professional announcers, and trophies for winners. Top athletes are elite physical specimens, able to hit small plastic balls 50 miles an hour at 150 rotations a second, with unfathomable hand-eye coordination. Players are national celebrities in their home countries.
When I logged on to DraftKings in Maryland and saw the “TT Elite” league available to bet on, the livestream of the match showed a single table in a bare, windowless, dark-gray room with no evident spectators, coaches, or even windows.
It is the gambling tail wagging the sports dog; the sports exist solely to provide fodder to be bet on.
How sports betting became an addictive product
For those who don’t gamble on sports, there may still be a misunderstanding that what people are doing on DraftKings or FanDuel is dropping a basically simple bet or two a week, gambling on this or that team to cover the spread, or maybe betting a favorite player will win an end-of-season award. It isn’t.
These apps, however, are now a labyrinth of parlays (combining multiple bets into one, all of which must win to pay out), prop bets (bets on some individual event, like a single point), and invitations to bet on the next quarter, the next point, the next five seconds. The betting dashboard gives an impression of nothing so much as a casino floor: overwhelming and constantly changing, giving the impression that skilled play is possible, whether or not that’s the case. Most of all, there are hundreds upon hundreds of ways to bet, a salami that can be sliced infinitely thin.
This is very much how these companies intended it. Simple sports bets, like who will win a game, are actually not terribly profitable for bookmakers, who in fact can lose if betting lines are set incorrectly. This made companies actively seek to reengineer sports betting into slot machines, where bets come close to becoming totally abstracted button pushing. With prediction markets entering every nook and cranny of culture and politics, and casinos pushing states extraordinarily hard to get their products on our phones, it’s difficult to see where this stops.
“Betting on ping-pong…is not a product built for recreation. It’s a product built to deliver constant action.”
— Harry Levant, Public Health Advocacy Institute
The Public Health Advocacy Institute (PHAI) filed a lawsuit against FanDuel, DraftKings, and the NFL, among others, for selling a “known addictive product.” The organization’s complaint filed on March 24 specifically notes of one of their client’s betting behavior that “if there were no U.S. games happening at a certain time, he would bet on international table tennis, again wagering repeatedly on every single point.” FanDuel did not respond to a request for comment on the allegations in the suit. DraftKings referred Vox to its trade group, the Sports Betting Alliance.
I reached out to Harry Levant, PHAI’s director of gambling policy, and while he declined to expand on the facts in the complaint, he spoke generally about how someone might end up betting hundreds of times on table tennis a day. “By the time a person reaches pathological betting on ping-pong, they have often experienced many other forms of gambling, but more importantly, betting on ping-pong…is not a product built for recreation,” Levant said. “It’s a product built to deliver constant action.”
Joe Maloney, the president of the Sports Betting Alliance, a trade advocacy organization representing online sportsbooks, told me on the question of addictiveness that “the existence of any market doesn’t make it more or less addictive.” He went on to say that “the vast majority of people that enjoy these products, that walk into casinos, that download legal apps…overwhelmingly these are people that are able to enjoy these products responsibly, but there are some people that demonstrate problematic behavior, and those people need all the support.”
One reason for the rise in table tennis betting is, frankly, its fakeness allows it to provide that action during otherwise barren hours. These are not prexisting and longstanding sports leagues that an interested consumer can decide they enjoy and place a bet on — they are ad hoc “leagues” created solely for the purpose of allowing sports betting for consumers at hours and during dates when more “normal” bets are not available, like PHAI’s client.
So, availability is one reason for table tennis’s continued success on sportsbooks — the fact that one can find a bet at almost any time, any day of the year.
The second is the betting itself. By now, the concept of a proposition (prop) bet has become well-known: Will the first touchdown be from a pass or a run? Will the first pitch be a ball or a strike?
Prop bets have come under fire from critics who say they push sports betting into dangerous territory. Two MLB pitchers were indicted for altering pitches in order to rig specific prop bets they could then profit on. Similarly, two NBA players pled guilty to federal charges after manipulating their performances to ensure certain prop-bet outcomes. One of them, according to a story in the New Yorker, was an avid table-tennis bettor. (In October, the NBA directed sportsbooks it has partnerships with to remove certain kinds of prop bets.)
But those scandals aside, online, mobile technology that allows live, in-game betting has fundamentally warped how sports gambling now takes place. In those TT Elite games and many other sports, you have the ability to make individual bets point by single point, which means many gamblers end up with dozens, even hundreds of bets laid an hour, with a constant stream of wins and losses. This is what led one gambling researcher to refer to it as “the crack cocaine of sports gambling.”
Tennis is a sport I play poorly but follow reasonably seriously. On DraftKings, betting on tennis is completely inscrutable to me. I can barely interpret the odds it offers for point-by-point betting, or the numbers and statistics flashing and disappearing on the screen constantly. But there’s a reason it’s all there: As with ping-pong, tennis has a reasonably fast pace of point play, which fits the need for a gambler who wants the ability to push a button incessantly to gamble.
It isn’t about winning and losing bets
You may ask: Why? What does a gambler get out of this? It seems to defeat the purpose of sports betting as one sees it in pop culture, even degenerate gambling like in Uncut Gems: the immense bet on an outcome that will either make you a zillionaire or bankrupt you. What satisfaction is someone getting out of a steady stream of $30 bets on individual points of table tennis, which doesn’t even dangle the prospect of making you rich?
The answer brings us to slot-machine design, which is what in-game betting has in essence devolved into.
Natasha Dow Schull, who wrote Addiction by Design on casino gambling and specifically slot machines, explained why players end up searching for this experience. She interviewed many users of slot machines, who explicitly stated they were not searching for excitement or a prospective “big win” but a kind of flow state or sedating “zone” through high-speed action.
Dow Schull writes, “Speed is a critical element of the zone experience,” and gives several stark quotes from her interviewees.
“The speed is relaxing. It’s not exactly excitement; it’s calm, like a tranquilizer. It gets me into the zone,” says one. “In a very paradoxical way, the speed of it slows me down,” says another. Schull expands, “As he [the interviewee] recognizes, a mechanically mediated tempo functions as a form of predictability that structures and regulates his play, transforming risk into rhythm. As long as gamblers hold their speed steady, it suspends them into the holding pattern of the zone.”
As a matter of fact, problem gamblers sometimes even actively dislike winning a jackpot. Schull describes gamblers telling her, “It’s so weird, but when I win a jackpot, I get really frustrated and angry and irritated. … I think it’s because it interrupted the zone, and really why I’m sitting there is to stay in the zone. And when I win a jackpot, the lights start flashing, the machine freezes up. … Suddenly I’m back in the world where I don’t want to be.” Levant echoed this to me. He said, noting that winning money is not the point, really, “Gambling disorder has nothing to do with money, full stop. … It’s being in action, and that is what all of these products, including every serve in a ping-pong [match] that you can’t even see, is delivering.”
This is how one can mindlessly bet on two men playing mediocre table tennis in an empty gymnasium. No, there’s no inherent meaning — but does a slot machine have any inherent meaning?
This was discovered by casino management consultants decades ago, long before the same phenomenon started infecting sports betting. Schull cites one consultant as writing, they designed the machinery of slot machines to “harness technology for continuous gaming productivity.” Long play durations and a slow bleed definitively take more money than single, high-stakes bets. (As a side point, this is actually why traditional slot machine arms were replaced with digital buttons: They were easier and faster to push, and fatigued users less to allow for longer play durations. Phones have the same benefits versus, say, traveling to a physical sportsbook.)
This language is echoed in that LSports report on table tennis, where they note specifically that the game’s strength is that its “extraordinary fixture volume enables fast cycles, encouraging bettors to reinvest their winnings quickly and fueling repeat engagement.”
I was struck listening to Schull in an interview describe modern slot machines as fundamentally inscrutable in a way similar to what I experienced looking at tennis bets. Unlike an old-fashioned one-armed bandit, that you pulled once and hoped you won by a single line of three cherries, modern slot machines have hundreds of possible ways to win, with diagonal lines, criss-crossing lines, and so on.
A player might “bet 100 pennies on 100 lines,” which “creates more of a sense of flow. Instead of losing everything, winning everything, which can be very jarring…today, people are lounging back with glazed-over eyes in these ergonomic chairs spending a huge amount of time…slowly chipping away at their money…if you put in $100 and you win back $20, that’s a loss…it feels the same as a win. Lights flash, ding ding ding ding, and you kind of relax into the flow of the machine.”
This is remarkably similar to the kinds of same-day parlays, bet hedging, and in-game live point-by-point betting that saturates modern sports gambling. In the same way it sounds a bit off to say you’re “betting” on a slot machine, this is the second part of that fork: The sports aren’t real, and neither is the betting.
If you were asked to look at two players you’d never heard of, in a sport you neither watched nor played, and decide who would win this point, then the next, then the next, you would have created a certain kind of slot machine. A button is being pushed and a result is coming back. A single DraftKings page might have rows of bets, “Game 3 – Point 9,” “Game 3 – Point 10,” “Game 3 – Point 11,” each a spin of the proverbial slots.
What you’re gambling on becomes rapidly irrelevant to someone deep into problem gambling; there simply has to be something available and preferably fast. In the podcast Nothing Off the Table, a recovering problem gambler explained simply: “When you don’t have anything to gamble, you find a way, no matter what.” Which is why he also states at night he’d gamble on “Chinese ping-pong, Japanese tennis, anything I could get my hands on.”
The bleak future of sports betting
Companies are well aware of this phenomenon, which is why even legitimate niche sports are quickly taking sponsorship deals to collate and provide their data to betting platforms hoping that they can be the next table tennis.
In many states you can now bet on the Disc Golf Pro Tour, the World Surf League, and the Grand Slam of Curling. For those not deep into the weeds of this kind of gambling, seeing maps of where gambling on “Street League Skateboarding” is legal, FAQs answering: “Why can’t I bet on BKB Bareknuckle Boxing in my area?” and headlines like “How to Get Started with Power Slap Betting?” might be jarring.
If the legitimate version of these sports are not available, they can simply be created ex nihilo, like the basement table tennis leagues. A reporting collaboration between Bellingcat and Josimar found similar “leagues” of school gymnasium soccer, sometimes with actual children as the players being bet on, along with glorified lawn games and literal arcade games, all taking place in gymnasiums and warehouses in Russia, Ukraine, and Belarus solely to provide something to bet on.
The scale is breathtaking: Bellingcat’s reporter, Ross Higgins, estimated that they “played” and streamed 1,000 games in a 24-hour period: “It’s like watching sport with all the fun and competitive element taken out. You’re watching it to gamble on. … There’s no commentary…there’s no referee, there’s nothing that you’d enjoy from sports.”
Because these are filmed with cheap webcams, they have the appearance of “watching Squid Game through a camcorder.” The images are frankly difficult to fathom.
While this may seem like a seedy underbelly of the sports betting industry, it has to be emphasized that there are only a couple jumps between these sham competitions and the most successful multinational sports betting companies, along with professional sports.
These fake school gym matches were being streamed and bet on 1xBet, which is an official sponsor of FC Barcelona, one of the top soccer clubs in the world, and sponsors many legitimate sports, like the ATP Challenger Tour, professional tennis’s “minor league.” LSports lists “TT Elite,” the warehouse table tennis I watched on Draftkings, as the second-most popular table tennis league to bet on. The seedy underbelly is just the creature itself. (I also contacted 1xBet and TT Elite for their comments on steps they take to ensure match integrity, but they didn’t respond.)
It’s unsurprising that many of these matches have turned out to be rigged. This was a serious enough problem in the early days of Covid that New Jersey, Colorado, and Indiana suspended betting on these kinds of leagues, that is, those “not sanctioned by the sport’s top governing bodies.” And in 2023, an Australian table tennis player pleaded guilty of having inside information and placing over a thousand bets on matches he knew were rigged.
As real sports leagues like the NBA and MLB desperately try to control the damage to their brands by having platforms like DraftKings and FanDuel limit prop bets, problem gamblers will simply flow downstream to platforms and sports that allow the behavior they’re now in thrall to. Table tennis, for the time being, has a unique and powerful alchemy of speed of play and constant availability, but the devolution will likely continue.
Indeed, by the time you read this, this piece of writing may itself be out of date. Companies from multiple sectors are pushing extraordinarily hard to open up new venues to exploit potential profit centers. Eight states have already legalized so-called iGaming, which allows casino games and slot machines themselves to be played on one’s phone, removing the need for a fake sport to be played at all.
Prediction markets, widely talked about as they enter into sports, politics, and current events also have bets on things like “Lowest temperature in Denver on November 5” and “# of views of next MrBeast video on day 4.” States have resisted legalization and in some cases sued prediction markets as being de facto gambling operators. But when they are legalized, the evolutionary process here escalates rapidly.
As The Upshot found, Pennsylvania allowed mobile casino gambling in 2017, and within seven years, it was generating more than five times the revenue than all of sports betting. (They also rocketed up as the reason for calls to problem gambling hotlines.)
A moderate’s commonsense position might be to decide that if sports betting is to be legal, then the activity should consist of, well, betting on the sport. Not betting on whether a first pitch of a game is a strike, or the 14th point of the third game of a table tennis league in a warehouse basement will be won by player A or B, but a bet about an event at least one hour into the future, on the final outcome of a sport overseen by a top governing body. What’s wrong with “$100 on the Yankees to cover the spread tomorrow”?
Various countries have versions of these kinds of limits. Australia prohibits betting on live games online. Germany has intervals between live bets to prevent compulsive by-the-second bets. Norway has monthly limits on losses imposed on every resident. Nebraska voters on Election Day rejected a referendum supported by DraftKings and FanDuel to allow mobile gaming, in what Nate Grasz, the executive director of the Nebraska Family Alliance, a conservative organization, told me was “an effort by out-of-state gambling companies to make money off addiction.” That result means that residents will continue to need to go to a physical racetrack casino to bet.
Each of these restrictions share the same goal of increasing friction on betting. Meanwhile, we’ve let companies do the opposite — remove every last form of friction, whether physical, financial, or psychological. Even if we can’t return to the days of $100 on the Yankees, we don’t need to allow $5,000 to be spent in seconds on the 27th, 28th, 29th, and 30th point of YouTube gymnasium table tennis.

UP set for ‘new rule, new reality’ after polls: Akhilesh at HT Leadership Summit
Uttar Pradesh is slated for assembly polls early next year, alongside Punjab, Manipur, Goa and Uttarakhand.
The electorate in Uttar Pradesh is set to vote out the BJP government and usher in a new political reality in the upcoming assembly elections, Samajwadi Party (SP) chief Akhilesh Yadav said on Saturday.
Addressing the 24th Hindustan Times Leadership Summit, the former Uttar Pradesh chief minister targeted the chief minister Yogi Adityanath-led government and hinted at the seats sought by ally Congress.
Alluding to the summit’s theme of “New Rules. New Realties”, Akhilesh, during a conversation with HT’s National Political Editor Sunetra Choudhury, said: “Rule and reality will change in UP.” Uttar Pradesh is slated for polls early next year, alongside Punjab, Manipur, Goa and Uttarakhand. Track LIVE updates from Hindustan Times Leadership Summit here.
The SP chief said the law-and-order situation had deteriorated in the state, rejecting the notion that frequent police encounters were a sign of swift justice.
“If law and order is better, what is the proof of that? The government says it is ‘tough on crime’, but data shows crime against Dalits, women and minorities has increased,” he said.
Akhilesh also criticised the Uttar Pradesh government’s “bulldozer policy”, alleging that the homes of marginalised sections were disproportionately targeted.
“You talk about the bulldozer as a symbol of law and order. But law and order cannot be maintained through bulldozers. Whose houses have you demolished? Whose homes have you destroyed? Those who were poor and vulnerable, those who had nowhere else to go. There are records of these actions,” he said.
Asked about the Congress’s seat-sharing demands for the upcoming assembly elections, Yadav said the party had sought “one more than 180 seats.”
According to Akhilesh, the theft of donations at the Ram temple will be a major poll issue, with the BJP set to face voters' anger over the issue.
“The devotees are hurt, their vote will show anger,” he said, questioning how the chief minister was unaware of the scale of the alleged misappropriation.
The controversy surfaced on June 7 when SP leader Tej Narayan ‘Pawan’ Pandey alleged that donations worth ₹5 crore to ₹7.5 crore had been siphoned off from the temple offerings. The state government constituted an SIT on June 13, following which eight employees associated with the handling and counting of donations were arrested on June 26.
The Supreme Court had intervened in the matter in July and constituted a second SIT. Investigators have identified 105 instances of alleged unauthorised removal or concealment of cash during the counting of donations inside the temple premises, according to the state’s submissions in the top court.

TORONTO — When a company is building technology that could totally transform the world — technology so high-stakes and secretive that it may underpin the future of geopolitics — you might expect its leaders to have a handle on the basics of security.
America’s AI secrets are leaking — and not just because of the Nvidia spy scandal
Who needs Chinese espionage when you’ve got security as bad as OpenAI or Anthropic?
Basics like, say, not having an extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Basics like not selling the tech to someone who may help smuggle it to a top foreign adversary.
Instead America got Jensen Huang, the CEO of AI chipmaker Nvidia, who resigned Thursday after admitting that he’d had just such an affair. The woman in question, Alice Huang, worked for a company called Megaspeed, which was buying billions of dollars’ worth of chips from Nvidia. Megaspeed is under investigation for allegedly smuggling chips into China.
The spy scandal raises serious questions about security in the AI corporate world. How is it possible that an alleged Chinese spy so easily embedded into Nvidia, one of the world’s most valuable companies and a huge strategic asset to America in the global AI race?
What’s even more disturbing, however, is that Nvidia is just the tip of the iceberg.
In fact, just as the Huang story was breaking, some of the world’s top AI researchers were gathered in Toronto for the Hinton Lectures, where “godfather of AI” Geoffrey Hinton was hosting AI alignment pioneer Paul Christiano for a series of talks. I was in attendance and, strikingly, I didn’t hear Huang’s scandal mentioned once. The focus was on how the frontier AI companies are racing ahead on building this incredibly powerful technology even though they can’t keep it safe or secure it. For months now, OpenAI and Anthropic have been having their own embarrassing security problems, including corporate espionage and cyber breaches.
“We are not able to adequately secure AI developments,” Christiano, who recently joined the OpenAI nonprofit board, bluntly acknowledged at the event. “We need to be able to defend models and algorithms from theft.”
Ironically, national security is a big part of the large AI companies’ rationale for how they operate in the first place. OpenAI and Anthropic, backed by White House policy, both justify their blistering speed in the AI race by saying that the US can’t afford to let China win. And Anthropic recently justified heavily redacting a key independent report on its AI progress by claiming that it can’t afford to let China glean its secrets.
But that may be the equivalent of worrying that you’ve left the window open a crack when your front door is swinging wide open.
“I’m frustrated with a lot of the companies because they simultaneously use security as an all-purpose cudgel with which to withhold information — even information that’s very much in the public interest to know — and yet they have terrible security,” Daniel Kokotajlo, a former researcher at OpenAI who became a prominent whistleblower, told me. (Disclosure: Vox Media is one of several publishers that have signed partnership agreements with OpenAI. Our reporting remains editorially independent.)
While the story of Huang’s affair has fired up imaginations, the real lesson to be taken from his spectacular downfall is not that he was uniquely weak on security, but that he was remarkably similar to the other big players in AI. They are asking the world to trust them as they claim to be building a machine god — and, in the case of Anthropic, chasing a $1.4 trillion IPO on that basis — yet they haven’t gotten ahold of basic security.
Are OpenAI and Anthropic practically giving away their secrets due to bad security?
OpenAI revealed last month that it had found a recording device in a conference room where sensitive discussions take place. Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi national working as an engineer at OpenAI, is alleged to have plugged the recorder into the USB port of a television and simply wrapped it in toilet paper. Another recorder was found in a bag in another room. Questions about how to build a device that records continuously and encrypt data also showed up on his spouse’s chatbot account.
“At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data,” OpenAI said last month, adding, “Our security program is designed to protect against a wide range of threat actors, from insider risks to cybercriminals to nation states.”
But the incident was worrisome. Alfozan had been working at OpenAI since June 2025. The recording device was sitting in that conference room for a couple of days before OpenAI discovered it. Maybe Alfozan wasn’t sophisticated enough to steal model weights — the billions of numbers that shape how an AI system turns input into output — but what if he’d been just slightly more careful or clever?
OpenAI has also had security weaknesses of a different kind — and no, it’s not just this summer’s notorious Hugging Face incident. Of the ones we know about (sometimes these are only revealed later), a recent example stands out: A group of “white-hat” hackers, who aim to find vulnerabilities but not to do a company harm, discovered a way to access OpenAI employees’ ChatGPT accounts, where sensitive research is potentially being done. The whole operation took just 72 hours.
Over at Anthropic, a group of ex-DOGE staffers who founded an AI startup called Cathedral managed to breach Anthropic’s internal systems in under 12 hours. They reportedly accessed the company’s Slack, where employees trade messages discussing the company’s state-of-the-art models, as well as meeting transcripts.
“My guess would be that the Slack would contain enough information to get a good sense of what the company is doing and how they’re training their AIs — basically, the juicy secrets would be there,” Kokotajlo told me. “And I would say getting the algorithmic secrets is like 80 percent as good as getting everything, including the model weights.”
Alleged spies (like Alice Huang or Abdulrahman Alfozan) and cyber breaches (like those targeting OpenAI and Anthropic) are obviously different types of security issues that demand very different types of internal controls. But for Kokotajlo and others, it makes sense to think of them all under the same umbrella — weak security. And it all points to a trend that seems common among the most powerful AI companies: They’re prioritizing rapid technological advancement over the perhaps more boring and slower process of ensuring their work is secure.
“They show that the companies are very far from having security adequate to protect themselves from a well-resourced state actor,” Kokotajlo said, adding: “If China wants to get the stuff, China will get the stuff.”
This is all happening against the backdrop of China’s aggressive distillation of US models, which involves training a new model on the output of a more advanced one. It’s a way to gain powerful capabilities without having to incur the real cost — a bit like cheating on a test by copying off a better student. For example, Anthropic found that the Chinese lab DeepSeek has been using Claude to improve its models, which is not a breach per se but illustrates how vigorously China is taking advantage of American companies’ research.
Kokotajlo also emphasized that there’s another bucket of security incidents we should be worried about: the hacks perpetrated against companies by their own misaligned AI models. Many people forget that in the Hugging Face incident, OpenAI agents didn’t only hack into Hugging Face — OpenAI’s own systems were breached, too. The sandbox meant to contain the agents was far from airtight, and they broke out.
“You should consider the AIs as an insider threat,” Kokotajlo said. “And it doesn’t feel like these companies have that locked down very well either.”
The top AI companies can’t keep using the security practices of a startup
There are three main reasons why security at the frontier AI companies hasn’t been up to snuff, according to David Robinson, who led transparency work for OpenAI’s safety team until he left in September.
One is the fact that the companies are building AI agents so capable that it can be genuinely hard — even for their creators — to keep them from doing damage. “We’re training systems to be good at conducting attacks of the kind that the labs internally are now also trying to defend against,” Robinson told me. “That is a challenging situation.”
There’s also a cultural problem. “If you look back with 20/20 hindsight at the Hugging Face incident, it’s clear that at the time OpenAI had underinvested in cybersecurity controls, and I think part of the reason for this was that there’s a [higher] level of cachet associated with working on alignment,” or the problem of how to get AIs to do what humans want them to do, Robinson said. “Some of the day-to-day practical questions about our cybersecurity posture — even though the people working on those questions are extremely good — I think it was not the same kind of organizational priority as it needed to be.”
Finally, there’s the fact that market incentives push AI companies to race ahead on developing the tech as fast as they can.
“Time pressure on the company,” Robinson said, “made it very difficult to be sufficiently careful.” And although researchers still at OpenAI now say the company has gotten dramatically better on security, Robinson noted that those competitive pressures “continue to exist.”
This is a well-documented trend at the company. “OpenAI’s security seems to be about what you’d expect from a research lab that scaled at a blistering pace over four years and focused more on beating its competitors than securing its infrastructure,” Joshua Saxe, the chief technology officer of the AI security firm Abundant Security, told the New York Times after the Hugging Face incident.
OpenAI itself has implicitly acknowledged that improving security measures sometimes comes “at the cost of research velocity,” as it wrote in a public memo after the incident.
But if a company cuts corners on security, it can’t ultimately protect its lead over others. If anything, it just ends up helping its adversaries race against it even faster.
As Kokotajlo and his colleagues at the AI Futures Project recently warned when writing about the companies’ quest to build a superhuman AI researcher (SAR), an AI that’s as good as the top human researcher: “If we train SAR in the immediate future, the algorithms will probably leak to China, and maybe the model weights too. AI companies have very poor security right now, and so we are on track for SAR leaking to China.”
And it’s not just that poor security can make it self-defeating for American companies to keep racing forward. Their security weakness could also make it harder for them to slow down even if they themselves want to.
In his lecture this week in Toronto, Christiano asked all of us in the audience to imagine a scenario that he said currently looks likely: We arrive at a point when further progress on AI seems risky. There’s a demand in the US to slow down. But there’s also a high probability that the AI models or algorithms have already leaked to an adversary like China.
“We now face a dilemma between either proceeding with a technology we believe to be unsafe — or risking competition from an adversary who has the same resources, who has taken those algorithms, and perhaps is willing to tolerate higher risk,” Christiano said, as the hundreds of people seated around me seemed to visibly tense up. “I think that is one of the most likely ways that we end up in an extremely bad situation.”

Affluent LA residents living by the iconic Hollywood sign are fed up with tourists. Now they’re suing
Residents blame a viewing platform, along with social media and mapping apps, for drawing more tourists to the area

It’s lights, camera, frustration for Los Angeles residents living near the iconic Hollywood sign who say selfie-taking tourists have taken over their neighborhood.
About 100 homeowners are suing the city, claiming officials have failed to stop tourists from clogging narrow roads, trespassing and leaving trash, including cigarette butts that could spark wildfires.
Filed October 26, the lawsuit does not seek monetary damages. Instead, residents want a court order forcing the city to address crowds that block driveways, create safety hazards and disrupt their neighborhood. The suit also names LA Mayor Karen Bass and Councilmember Nithya Rama as defendants.
Traffic camera data showed more than 48,200 vehicles passed through the area over 13 days this summer, up 15 percent from the same period in 2025, according to CBS News.
Emergency vehicles have also struggled to navigate the narrow roads, CBS News reported, with residents citing delays for police, ambulances and fire engines.
“It's like there's a festival every day, especially in the summer,” Rose Ware, a 74-year-old estate agent who has lived in her home for 32 years, told The Times Friday. “Bumper-to-bumper traffic. Emergency vehicles can't get through. Lots of tourists smoke cigarettes and they get very belligerent when you ask them to stop.”
Residents blame a viewing platform built about 15 years ago, along with social media and mapping apps, for drawing more tourists to the area.
Visitors now crowd the winding roads day and night, leaving behind trash, discarded cigarettes and even bottles of urine and soiled diapers, residents said.
Ware said she understands the sign's appeal but believes the city has failed to accommodate the crowds.
“But it's not the tourists' fault. They come here expecting a world-class site to experience the sign, but it's not here. The parking's terrible,” she told the newspaper.
The Independent has contacted an attorney representing the homeowners and representatives for the City of Los Angeles for comment.
The sign was originally built in 1923 to promote a real estate development called Hollywoodland. The final four letters were later removed, turning it into one of the world's most recognizable symbols of the entertainment industry.
Millions of visitors flock to the landmark each year for photos. Fences, security cameras and motion sensors surround it to prevent trespassing and vandalism, but residents say tourists still wander onto their lawns and try to park in their driveways.
“It's like a pilgrimage for them,” Ware said. “They take a million pictures, trampling on people's lawns and yards for the best shot.”
David Smalley, a 46-year-old comedian and restaurant owner, told The Times that his doorbell camera caught a woman letting her child urinate in his yard. But his biggest concern is wildfire risk, with tourists continuing to ignore no-smoking signs.
Residents have collected hundreds of cigarette butts as evidence for their lawsuit, the outlet reports.
City officials say they have taken steps to address the congestion, including increasing traffic enforcement and towing vehicles during busy periods.
In a statement to CBS News, Bass' office said the LA Police Department has dedicated additional units to traffic and parking enforcement and worked with transportation officials on a neighborhood traffic plan.
“The Mayor's office will continue working to address this issue with our public safety partners,” the statement read.
Ilan Wurman, the attorney representing the homeowners, said the city should adopt crowd controls similar to those around the Eiffel Tower in Paris, including ticketing, access restrictions and alternative viewing spots.
“We're not telling the city how to do it, but we're telling them that they're legally obligated to do something,” Wurman told The Times.
The lawsuit has received little sympathy from some tourists, who argue that homeowners should have expected crowds when moving next to one of LA’s most famous landmarks.

The COVID-19 pandemic is having a devastating impact across the world. Efforts to contain the coronavirus are vital to the health of the world’s population, but they are also exposing children to increased risk of violence – including maltreatment, gender-based violence and sexual exploitation.
As leaders of organisations committed to ending violence against children, we come together in solidarity to share our deep concern, call for action and pledge our support to protect children from violence and reduce the impact of COVID-19 on children in every country and community.
A third of the global population is on COVID-19 lockdown, and school closures have impacted more than 1.5 billion children. Movement restrictions, loss of income, isolation, overcrowding and high levels of stress and anxiety are increasing the likelihood that children experience and observe physical, psychological and sexual abuse at home – particularly those children already living in violent or dysfunctional family situations. And while online communities have become central to maintain many children’s learning, support and play, it is also increasing their exposure to cyberbullying, risky online behavior and sexual exploitation.
The situation is aggravated by children’s lack of access to schoolfriends, teachers, social workers and the safe space and services that schools provide. The most vulnerable children – including refugees, migrants, and children who are internally displaced, deprived of liberty, living without parental care, living on the street and in urban slums, with disabilities, and living in conflict-affected areas – are a particular concern. For many, growing economic vulnerability will increase the threat of child labour, child marriage and child trafficking.
We must act now. Together, we call on governments, the international community and leaders in every sector to urgently respond with a united effort to protect children from the heightened risk of violence, exploitation and abuse as part of the broader response to COVID-19.
Governments have a central role to play. They must ensure that COVID-19 prevention and response plans integrate age appropriate and gender sensitive measures to protect all children from violence, neglect and abuse. Child protection services and workers must be designated as essential and resourced accordingly.
Working with and supporting governments, our collective response must include: maintaining essential health and social welfare services, including mental health and psychosocial support; providing child protection case management and emergency alternative care arrangements; ensuring social protection for the most vulnerable children and households; continuing care and protection for children in institutions; and communicating with and engaging parents, caregivers and children themselves with evidence-based information and advice. National helplines, school counsellors and other child-friendly reporting mechanisms enable children in distress to reach out for help, and must be adapted to the challenges of COVID-19.
Given the heightened risks of online harms, technology companies and telecoms providers must do everything they can to keep children safe online. This includes providing access to cost-free child helplines, age-appropriate services and safe e-education platforms - and using their platforms to share child online safety advice. They must also do more to detect and stop harmful activity against children online, including grooming and the creation and distribution of child sexual abuse images and videos.
As global organisations working to end violence against children, we will continue to advocate for and invest in effective child protection solutions. We will collectively develop and share technical resources and guidance for policymakers, practitioners, parents, caregivers and children themselves. And we will support the courageous health, child protection and humanitarian professionals working around the clock to keep children safe during these unprecedented times.
In recent years, the global community has made significant gains in protecting children from violence. We must not allow those gains to be lost during the current turmoil. We must do all we can to keep children safe now. And we must plan ahead together, so that once the immediate health crisis is over, we can get back on track towards the goal of ending all forms of violence, abuse and neglect of children

New Orleans port sues for control of China-linked tanker that crashed into cruise ship
Move comes hours after tanker lost its steering, slammed into docked river cruise boat
Just hours after a tanker in New Orleans lost its steering and slammed into a docked river cruise boat, the city's port sued to make sure federal investigators can seize the vessel that is owned by a subsidiary of a Chinese company.
All 197 passengers and crew on the American Heritage cruise ship survived Friday as well as the crew on the tanker.
Officials said 32 people were brought to the hospital, including two police officers thrown into the Mississippi River when the boat rolled. But none of the injuries were critical and eight remained hospitalized Saturday.
The lawsuit, filed by the Board of Commissioners of the Port of New Orleans, said the Atlantic Asphalt tanker caused at least $1 million US in damage to its terminal. A judge issued a warrant Friday giving federal officials control of the ship for now.
The tanker has been towed away from the site, but it could take weeks to move the cruise ship, which remains turned on its side against a terminal in the Mississippi River, Coast Guard Capt. Melanie Burnham told reporters Saturday.
It could take weeks to move the cruise ship, which remains turned on its side against a terminal in the Mississippi River. (Matthew Hinton/The Associated Press)
The first step is to make sure the 60,500 litres of fuel on the boat are removed safely, she said. Traffic has been limited on the Mississippi River, but Burnham said boats should be able to move both upstream and downstream soon.
The tanker appeared to lose steering, but the exact cause of the crash is not known, Burnham said. The U.S. National Transportation Safety Board was sending investigators to New Orleans.
'I thought I was drowning'
The first warning people on board the American Heritage had was the tanker blasting its horn several times as it floated toward the cruise ship, passenger Joe Knab told local news outlet WDSU-TV.
The hit was hard, and the ship immediately started leaning. The crew gathered everyone on the third deck to put on life vests and start getting them off the boat, but it suddenly rolled and sent Knab and about 100 other passengers and crew into the muddy Mississippi River, where the water was 19 C.
Tugboat operators, other cruise ship captains, nearby workers, police and other rescuers rushed to help.
People are helped out of the water by responders on Friday. Dozens were hospitalized but none of the injuries were deemed critical. (Devon Flanagan/The Associated Press)
"It's fine now, but it was a little scary there at the time. I thought I was drowning because I kept bobbing underneath — and the water doesn't taste very good," Knab told the television station, still in the jeans he was wearing on the boat, now covered in mud.
Knab said he thinks he was in the water about 15 minutes. He laughed and said his 20 years in the Navy likely helped him.
"They taught us not to drown," Knab said.
Knab was wearing a shirt from a Hilton hotel where the passengers gathered. The rest of his belongings were in the river. Somehow his cellphone still worked. He hoped to get on a plane soon back to Wichita, Kansas, but he was not sure how Friday's nationwide ground stop was going to throw another problem at him.
Putting the life vests on the passengers as they waited to get off the boat likely saved a number of lives when the boat suddenly turned into the water, New Orleans Harbor Police Chief Melanie Montroll said.
"Whether it's 10 feet of water or 200 feet, having those vests, having that population put those vests on and kind of float upriver while we retrieve them — I think was the best factor of success," Montroll said.
The American Heritage was finishing an eight-day cruise to several Mississippi River destinations.
Tanker owner a subsidiary of Chinese company
The Atlantic Asphalt is a 160-metre-long vessel. It had a final destination in New Orleans, according to MarineTraffic, and was sailing under a flag for the Marshall Islands.
The ship is owned by a company called Nave Shipping SA, which is registered in Monrovia, Liberia, according to the International Maritime Organization and was one of the defendants in the lawsuit filed Friday.
Nave Shipping is a subsidiary of the China State Shipbuilding Corporation, a sprawling Chinese state-owned conglomerate, according to the live shipping tracker MarineTraffic.
China State Shipbuilding Corp. didn't respond to an emailed request for comment.
The tanker involved in the crash specializes in carrying large quantities of asphalt and bitumen, a semi-solid substance that is often used for road construction and roofing, according to MarineTraffic.

Representative Lauren Boebert of Colorado, who lost her seat to a Democratic challenger in one of the biggest upsets of the midterm elections, posted a farewell video on social media declaring that “God’s got this.”

The race was called Friday for Democratic challenger Eileen Laubacher, a retired U.S. Navy rear admiral and former National Security Council member. It is a major upset in a heavily Republican district that President Donald Trump won by 18 points in 2024.
Following the loss, Boebert shared a video on X reflecting on her political rise from her former gun-themed restaurant, Shooters Grill, in Rifle, Colorado.
“Years ago, while in fervent prayer inside my restaurant in Rifle, Colorado, I cried out ‘Here I am, Lord! Send me!’” Boebert wrote in the post. “I did not know at that time where He would send me. He sent me to 53 Colorado counties and to our Nation’s Capitol. He sent me to serve.”
She added: “My time to be sent to another unknown place is now. God’s got this. He’s got US! Jesus is Lord and I am proud to live in the greatest country on earth! Stay Tuned!”
Her post, which had racked up more than 1 million views Saturday, was swiftly mocked in the comments.
“He sent you to the Beetlejuice play,” one person replied, referring to when Boebert was escorted out of a 2023 performance of “Beetlejuice” in Denver — clips of which featured prominently in Democratic attack ads this cycle.
“Trying to convince us that you are a real Christian is easily the most ridiculous part of your tweet,” another user replied.
“LOL you lost,” another said. “God answered our prayers,” someone else posted.
“If God really sent Lauren Boebert to Congress, I think it's time we seriously question His recruitment process,” another user quipped.
Her defeat followed her decision in 2024 to switch to the more conservative 4th District after narrowly surviving her re-election campaign in the 3rd District two years earlier.
Earlier in the week, as Laubacher attended new-member orientation on Capitol Hill, Boebert blamed her trailing vote count on campaign spending. She told reporters outside the Capitol that “there was a lot of money dumped on my head,” calling the spending “gross.”

Laubacher, a former Republican who switched parties after retiring from the Navy in 2024, campaigned as a moderate focused on constituent service rather than partisanship.
“It was about people who felt that they were not being heard and not being served,” Laubacher told the Post earlier in the week.
Colorado-based Republican strategist Dennis Lennox told the Post that Boebert’s tenure was defined by “six years of largely unforced errors and scandals and endless controversies.”
First elected in 2020 after gaining national attention for confronting Beto O’Rourke over gun control, Boebert quickly became a prominent figure in the MAGA movement.
However, her time in Washington was repeatedly overshadowed by public incidents and controversy.
Boebert had also strained her relationship with Trump in 2025 after joining three other House Republicans to force a vote on releasing additional files related to Jeffrey Epstein, and later campaigning for Representative Thomas Massie of Kentucky.
Although Trump criticized her earlier in the year, he ultimately endorsed her in late October.

BOUGAINVILLE DISPATCH
A Sweaty, Muddy Jungle Trek to a Famed World War II Wreck
Seven Chinese tourists, a dozen villagers and a couple of journalists forded streams and bushwhacked to the downed plane of Isoroku Yamamoto, the Japanese admiral. Machetes proved handy.
Halfway through the morning, I’m being tossed around like a popcorn kernel in the back of a troop carrier playing an eclectic medley of Backstreet Boys and Papua New Guinean jams.
We’re traveling along what feels more like a collection of loose rocks, arranged to be roughly vehicle width, than a road. I’ve lost count of the number of river crossings, including one where the water lapped a few inches from the car’s windows. And this is during a dry spell.
Our caravan is headed for an unlikely tourist destination deep in the jungle on Bougainville Island, an autonomous region of Papua New Guinea in the Solomon Sea.
The piecemeal remnants of a Mitsubishi G4M1 — Betty, as the planes were code-named by the Allies in World War II — have remained for some 80 years at the crash site of Japanese Navy Adm. Isoroku Yamamoto. This is the spot where Admiral Yamamoto, mastermind of the Pearl Harbor attack, archvillain to Americans in the war, a respected and memorialized figure to the Japanese, met his end in 1943.
Bougainville was occupied by the Japanese in early 1942, in the months after Pearl Harbor, as the Imperial Navy pushed into the South Pacific, with Admiral Yamamoto at the helm. In April 1943, Allied forces intercepted and deciphered Japanese communication on the admiral’s travels, and American P-38 Lightning fighters gunned down his plane over southern Bougainville, a feat the Americans triumphantly dubbed Operation Vengeance.

4 decades ago, Robert Munsch attended Moira Green's birthday. Her story became a children's classic
The author visited the Northwest Territories in 1983 to tell stories and find inspiration
On Moira Green’s 10th birthday, she put on a giant paper bag and a homemade crown and headed down to Hay River’s public library, where a surprising number of residents from the remote Northwest Territories town were waiting.
There were 200 pizzas and 200 little cakes. She ran into a dragon, Prince Ronald and other valiant attempts by her Grade 5 classmates to bring the beloved characters from Robert Munsch’s earliest works to life.
Technically, Green could have come dressed as herself: the inspiration behind Moira’s Birthday.
“After we did our little performances and stuff, they got Robert Munsch on the line,” Green said in a recent interview. “I don't know how they did it back in the day, but everyone in the library could hear him. And then, he read the story [to] all of us."
It was November 1987.
Six months earlier, Toronto-based Annick Press had published Moira’s Birthday. And exactly four years previous, the Guelph, Ont., children’s author had visited the Northwest Territories for the first time, leaving behind a trail of memories for many in the community of roughly 3,500 people living there at the time, and, as Green recalls, whenever anyone new turned up, her parents insisted they come for supper.
That small-town friendliness was how Munsch, known for billeting with families during his tours, came to stay with Bruce and Marilyn Green and their five children, all of whom would make an appearance in the first of three books he would dream up during the trip.
Green, shown wearing the Paper Bag Princess costume, is seen here at her 10th birthday party in Hay River, N.W.T., in November 1987. She and other kids performed skits based on Munsch's books. (Submitted by Moira Green)
Those connections Munsch forged with kids, living in big cities and tiny hamlets, became the fabric of the nearly 100 books he has written in his career. In an interview with CBC News last year, his “last hurrah,” the author revealed that another 50 books will likely be published after his death.
As first reported in the New York Times in September 2025, Munsch has been approved for medical assistance in dying (MAID), when he chooses. He has been living with Parkinson’s disease and dementia.
“Nobody lives forever," he told CBC in December. “But I will at least have a couple of years, as many years as I’ve already had [after I’m gone], and that will be nice," he said, of his hope to publish a book per year after his death.
Munsch and his wife, Ann, who have been married for more than five decades, are shown here at their home in November 2025. (Turgut Yeter/CBC)
The breadth of his travels helped him capture what it was like to be a kid in a country as vast as Canada.
Even in a place as remote as Hay River.
Moira’s 6th birthday
On the morning of her sixth birthday party in November 1983, Green and her siblings went to see Munsch perform at the library. He captivated his audience, she said, despite having just flown in hours before from Yellowknife.
Her party had already been planned for that afternoon before news of Munsch’s visit came out.
It was not quite as raucous as the story suggests — a handful of friends, not the whole school, showed up. And during a quiet moment, her dad walked over.
“He said ‘You should ask Mr. Munsch if he could tell you a story.’ And I was like, ‘Mmmm, I'm not going to do that. I'm way too shy.’”
Green, left, shown in her Grade 1 photo, which helped artist Michael Martchenko illustrate the book, shown right. (Submitted by Moira Green/Annick Press)
But a friend did it for her, she said. The author recalls that he couldn’t refuse.
“Sometimes when a kid asks me to make up a story, I get this strange feeling that something is going to happen,” Munsch wrote of the experience. “I look out at a group of kids and get this firm conviction that I can tell a new story about a particular kid.
“Usually, it’s not true, but I do always try a new story when I get the feeling.”
- 'The stories will be the last thing to go': Robert Munsch on his legacy as one of Canada's great storytellers
- Exclusive Beloved children's author Robert Munsch promising dozens of books to come after his death
Green was just as surprised, as she had assumed he would retell a previous story.
“But he came over … sat down and then he just sort of started telling — making up — the story on the spot: Moira’s Birthday.
Anyone who has heard Munsch perform knows how he revs up a crowd, along with his own volume, asking questions and weaving the answers into his words.
“Lots of interactions, stopping to talk about the local bakery and, you know, other things from around town and kind of integrate that into the story."
Even before he finished, Munsch said, he knew he had a winner.
He added Green to his “Story Kids file" and asked if he could stay in touch, both recalled. Illustrator Michael Martchenko followed up, looking for pictures of the family, their green house and even the dog.
The Green family's home, shown here in the 1980s, in Hay River, N.W.T. It became part of the iconic story. (Submitted by Moira Green)
“We heard later that he had continued to tell that story,” Green said, “kind of fine-tuning it and shaping it as he does by telling it to the kids and gauging their reaction."
When Munsch sent her an early draft, Green saw the story had evolved.
In the first rendition, she had received money in all of her presents. And she said she used the money to either pay for the massive order of pizza and cake — or paid her guests to help clean up.
"There was a little bit of a difference in how the story kind of tied up.”
In the published version, Moira’s beleaguered parents look at the destruction of their home. Then, the birthday girl announces that anyone who helps clean up will get one of her (many, many) presents. Within minutes, the house is spotless.
Reconnecting as an adult
Green and the author stayed in touch, exchanging Christmas cards, letters and signed copies of new books.
“Sometimes, he would even send manuscripts of a potential story, asking for feedback,” she said. “It was kind of a neat world to be a part of at that point — you sort of joined the Robert Munsch family."
Each of Munsch’s books — which have sold more than 90 million copies in North America alone — is dedicated to the child who inspired it. Several feature his own children: Tyya, Andrew and Julie. In fact, Julie’s decision to invite far more kids than she was allowed to contributed to the narrative behind Moira’s Birthday, the author writes.
Others, like Green, continued corresponding with Munsch — like Gah-Ning Tang, the protagonist in Where is Gah-Ning, whose letters spanned more than 30 years, leading her to eventually refer to the author and his wife as uncle and aunt, she told CBC’s Day 6 in a 2025 interview.
Green lost touch shortly after university, she said.
Then, as a young mother in Saskatoon, she saw that Munsch was coming into town for a performance. She brought her daughter and reconnected with him afterward.
“He spent some time with us and was thrilled,” Green said. They exchanged contact information and he got in touch before his next trip to the city.
Green loved reading her copies of Munsch’s books to her four children, though “mine wasn’t necessarily their favourite,” she said, laughing.
As she celebrates her 49th birthday this month, she recalls being a shy kid who didn’t always appreciate the attention.
Now, though, she said she “can recognize the cool factor” in all of it.
“It’s my go-to icebreaker.”

The catastrophic floods in Nepal which resulted in the deaths of thousands of people in August 2026, is overwhelmingly attributed to climate change. This is yet another worst-case climate change scenario from South Asia, after the floods in Pakistan in 2022.
A debate that has not drawn much attention so far in this part of the world is that there is scope to explore and establish the flood victims as victims of climate wrongs. The case for the Nepalese people needs to be analysed from the prism of climate litigations used by plaintiffs in many jurisdictions of Europe and the U.S. in the last two decades.
