Although I'm happy living in Ireland, I sometimes long for warmer weather and a slower pace of life.
So when I travel, I'm always wondering if my destination could become more than a vacation spot — maybe a place to retire to someday.
In 2023, I spent a month seeing if Malta could be a potential forever home. Unfortunately, it wasn't a match for me, but it had so much going for it that I decided to try its charming sister island, Gozo.
Gozo lies a few miles northwest of Malta and belongs to the same archipelago. It's just 26 square miles (roughly the size of Manhattan) and home to around 40,000 people.
I first visited Gozo in 2012 and have returned a handful of times since then. On my most recent trip this September, I stayed in a gorgeous little villa in Xagħra, a small, historic town with a population of about 5,400.
As much as I adore the Maltese island, my most recent trip there made me realize it might not be the perfect spot for me to retire.
Gozo has great Mediterranean vibes and feels ideal for slow exploring
Gozo seemed to have many of the same draws as Malta, but with slightly fewer crowds and a slower pace of life.
For one, English is widely spoken in both Malta and Gozo, which I appreciate. Gozo has lovely weather with about 300 days of sunshine a year and mostly mild temperatures.
The island really does feel Mediterranean, with limestone buildings, beautiful churches, and endless sea views.
It had a nice balance of rural beauty and bustling shops and eateries. People were friendly, the villages I've explored so far have all felt safe, and life seemed to move at an unhurried pace. The Visit Gozo website describes the island as "developed just enough but not too much," which I think defines its charm.
There are many things to see and do in Gozo, but the island didn't feel super aimed at tourists with a massive list of must-see attractions.
Gozo has world-class diving, swimming at Ramla Bay, and leisurely boat rides along the coastline. There's also the ancient Ġgantija Temples and the Rotunda Church in Xewkija.
I loved exploring the Citadel in Victoria, and I spent happy days taking lovely long lunches, some with waterfront views.
While staying in my small villa in Xagħra, there was something idyllic about having so many restaurants and shops within walking distance and taking a five-minute stroll into the village square for groceries or dinner.
I was especially impressed by the small island's impressive dining scene, which consists of well over 100 restaurants and dozens of snack bars and coffee shops.
I enjoyed alfresco dining, local wine and seafood, Gozitan cheese, Maltese specialties like rabbit, and a superb range of delicious pasta dishes.
On this past trip, I also attended the annual Fontana Wine Festival, where I got real community vibes. There were a handful of local wineries, live music, and a food truck. There were no pulsing crowds, no huge lines, and plenty of room to wander.
It felt intimate and local rather than a huge event aimed at tourists.
Sadly, I found there were some downsides …
Despite being a small island, it didn't feel as easy to get around Gozo as I expected.
There aren't sidewalks everywhere, so walking between villages isn't always possible. There are buses, but I found they didn't run very frequently — sometimes just once an hour in each direction. (Thankfully, ride-hailing services such as Bolt and Uber were relatively affordable.)
Then there were the bugs. Mosquitoes are to be expected in the Mediterranean, but the Asian tiger mosquito is especially aggressive and bites during the daytime as well as around dawn and dusk.
They're very present in the Maltese islands, and insect repellent only went so far. I'd sometimes find five new bites a day.
I also found the relentless presence of Oriental hornets, a large native species that becomes particularly active in late summer and early autumn, to be off-putting. Their stings are notoriously painful.
When looking closer at long-term considerations, I also didn't love that Gozo doesn't have its own airport.
The nearest international airport is in Valletta, Malta's capital, and can be reached by a 45-minute ferry that runs several times a day. However, this meant each time I wanted to fly, I'd need to take a taxi to a ferry terminal, then a ferry, then another taxi to the airport.
As someone who loves to travel and would need to fly home to visit family, I could see that becoming a frustrating hurdle and grind over time.
In addition, I enjoyed the two commercial centers and dozens of shops along the main streets in Gozo's capital, Victoria. They sold just about all of the basics and essentials I could want, plus some lovely local handmade jewelry and ceramics.
However, if I were to live here for an extended period, I think I'd start to miss having access to more big-name retailers, high-end brands, and even luxury department stores, like Brown Thomas in Dublin.
Gozo may not be a perfect retirement spot for me, but I can see why it may be for others
I can genuinely understand why people would want to retire in Gozo. It's gorgeous, and I could picture having a wonderful life there — however, it would come with trade-offs.
Although I sometimes fantasize about a slower-paced life, this trip also made me realize it might not suit me in reality. I worry the peace and quiet that makes it a perfect holiday destination would end up feeling limiting over time.
I personally need a bit more buzz and glamour day-to-day — lively bars, glitzy restaurants, and high-end shopping. Although Gozo has outstanding food, too, I love Dublin's ever-evolving dining scene and its vibrant bars.
With all that in mind, I think I need to look into a larger European city next, definitely one with its own international airport.
I'd definitely return to Gozo for vacation, but not for forever. In the meantime, the search for my retirement location continues …

On January 6th, 2025, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang got his rockstar moment at last. He strode triumphantly onstage, hand raised in the air, to the claps and cheers of a 14,000-person arena absolutely packed with influencers and fans, their faces awash in blue glow, as he made his entrance in a black leather jacket that shimmered in the stadium’s lights.
Jensen Huang and the decline of the visionary showman founder CEO
The Steve Jobs of GPUs has been shown the door.
Few are cheering for Jensen Huang now. He has left Nvidia after seemingly enabling two chip smuggling scandals and allegedly having three extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy at the same time he was mingling with President Donald Trump.
The world is watching to see if this scandal might disrupt the entire US AI industry and perhaps destabilize the stock market along with it. That’s because Huang wasn’t merely running the first $5 trillion company, he was the visionary leader in control of the must-have GPUs powering the worldwide AI boom, part of a company that represents around 6 percent of the S&P 500 stock market index all by itself. And he didn’t plan for succession if he ever stepped down.
The 63-year-old once said he preferred to die on the job; he once suggested he’d work until he was 90 or 100, then carry on leading the company as a robot.
It’s not easy to replace Huang, partly because he had no deputies. Around 60 employees reported directly to the CEO. “He built the company around himself, and everything that happened there flowed through him,” says IDC analyst and former computing journalist Tom Mainelli.
“Jensen is Nvidia, and Nvidia is Jensen,” Jon Peddie, a computer industry analyst who’s been tracking Nvidia since its inception, tells me.
But Nvidia isn’t Jensen anymore. He has left the company he cofounded 33 years ago. It’s the end of an era, and not just for Nvidia — because Jensen Huang was Big Tech’s last true example of a visionary showman founder CEO.
“He was both the visionary and the tactical leader, the closest thing tech has had to Steve Jobs,” Moor Insights & Strategy chief analyst Pat Moorhead tells me.
Elon Musk didn’t exactly found Tesla and has quite the track record of broken promises, and Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg has proven to be neither visionary nor showman so far. Google’s Larry Page and Sergey Brin stepped away in 2019 as their company dealt with growing employee turmoil, leaving the company in the hands of Sundar Pichai, and both Microsoft and Apple have each passed the torch twice since the days of Bill Gates and Steve Jobs.
Some say Apple’s Steve Jobs broke the CEO mold, but he created a mold of his own. Huang was one of countless tech leaders who followed his example by introducing their products in keynote speeches, adopting a single recognizable piece of clothing like Jobs’ trademark black turtleneck, and even occasionally teasing “one more thing” for the surprise at the end of their presentations. In the newsroom, we’d sometimes joke about the Jobs wannabes; many were stiff suits who didn’t have the credibility to pull it off.
I thought Huang might be a Jobs wannabe, too, the first time I saw that he’d adopted a black jacket as his uniform. (It was not always a leather jacket; an earlier version was a Nvidia-branded softshell.) Huang later insisted on wearing a jacket even when the temperature was hot — more than once, I saw him sweat profusely rather than take it off. Unlike Jobs, he also held quite a few keynotes when he didn’t have much news to share; he liked to repeat the company’s previous accomplishments as if they were brand-new.
But even if Huang didn’t have the same gravitas as Jobs, he did have exciting tech up his sleeves and loved to demo it onstage. He knew how to get people excited about the future of visual computing with eye-opening gaming graphics, physics and lighting demos, and eventually image recognition, AI weather simulations, digital copies of real-world factories, and the robots that can virtually train in them.
His Nvidia tried to educate people about the how and why of GPUs, too; I still remember in 2008 when Nvidia invited the Mythbusters to demo the difference between serial processing and parallel processing by firing a 1,100-nozzle paintball gun to “paint” the Mona Lisa in one shot.
What I didn’t know back then: Huang was a visionary founder. He took Nvidia to fame and fortune through a series of tremendous bets.
In 1996, three years after he cofounded the company at a Denny’s diner, Nvidia nearly went out of business while working on a failed graphics chip for the Sega Dreamcast game console. But even though he didn’t deliver that chip, Huang personally convinced Sega to invest $5 million afterward, The Wall Street Journal reported in 2024.
He then turned around and bet the company again on the Riva 128 PC graphics accelerator, an effort so ambitious he had to lay off over half of Nvidia’s roughly 100 staffers, skip the prototyping stage, and rush it straight to production, and he still only had one month of payroll left by the time it shipped, The New Yorker wrote in 2023. Thankfully, it was a success, selling a million units in just four months and paving the way for both the GeForce GPU and a long-term relationship with chip fabricator TSMC.
Roughly eight years later, Huang decided it wasn’t enough to be the leader in PC gaming graphics alone. He bet the company’s entire gross profit, he told podcaster Lex Fridman, on shipping a new feature inside those graphics cards that no one had asked for: CUDA. It was the ability to use a GPU for other kinds of computing tasks beyond graphics, and Huang said it increased the cost of every GeForce graphics card by 50 percent.
“Originally there was no market or market demand for it. It was almost as if they built it because they could,” says Peddie. “Jensen had the vision for what it could be and the courage to pursue it in spite of the opinions of others.”
“NVIDIA was effectively investing in a computing platform that extended far beyond graphics, with no guarantee of a near-term return,” says HotTech analyst Dave Altavilla.
“Huang saw that a GPU was really a parallel computer that happened to render graphics. CUDA turned that insight into a platform, and it’s why NVIDIA was ready when AI arrived,” Mainelli tells me.
It was a bad time for graphics cards to suddenly cost more. When the Great Recession hit in 2007–2009, and Nvidia laptop graphics chips also started failing due to design defects, the company lost 80 percent of its market value.
But Huang believed in CUDA enough to invest even more. “He literally handed out high-end NVIDIA GPUs to researchers at industry conferences, while the company seeded universities like Stanford with hardware to encourage development on its platform,” says Altavilla. And by 2012, Nvidia’s potential for AI had started to emerge.
That’s when University of Toronto researchers used Nvidia GPUs to train a prize-winning image-recognition neural network called AlexNet, which is widely credited for sparking the AI revolution.
Not all of Huang’s visions panned out the way he publicly expected. That AlexNet demo directly led to Huang’s bets on chips for self-driving cars, he said, but he didn’t exactly predict AI — CUDA was instead thought of as better and more affordable supercomputing for researchers and scientists. In 2013, I also wrote about how his grand plan for the future of the company relied heavily on putting Nvidia chips in your phone, which didn’t pan out.
But that bet on ARM-based phone chips did put Nvidia inside every Nintendo Switch and may have helped make future “AI superchips” possible — the latest Nvidia AI server chips have ARM CPU cores. And in 2022, the leaders of the AI revolution launched the most groundbreaking AI tech yet on Nvidia hardware: ChatGPT. Six years earlier, Huang hand-delivered Nvidia’s first purpose-built AI workstation to OpenAI, and by 2022 Microsoft had strung together tens of thousands of Nvidia A100 GPUs to handle the load.
“Every time competitors got close, he moved the fight up a level: the chip, then the server, then networking with the $6.9 billion Mellanox deal, then the full rack, all tied together by CUDA,” says Moorhead. “The speed came from how he ran the company,” he adds. “Decisions that took other companies four weeks took Nvidia four days.”
“Decisions that took other companies four weeks took Nvidia four days.”
As Nvidia’s fortunes and profit ballooned — thousands of dollars in pure profit every single second! — and as it became clearer that AI would reshape the world in one way or another, something strange happened. Huang became a celebrity. In summer 2024, The Wall Street Journal and social media chronicled that he received a hero’s welcome in his birthplace of Taiwan. He stopped over and over to sign autographs, including one on a woman’s chest.
In person, at presentations, and in the company’s investor Q&As, I saw the tone shift. People began treating the leather-jacketed man like an actual rockstar instead of a wannabe rockstar, asking for photos and autographs and complimenting him rather than asking tough questions.
It felt like he’d attained Steve Jobs’ infamous “reality distortion field” at last — until he popped that bubble himself with his infidelity.
But one fewer reality distortion field in the world isn’t necessarily a bad thing, and as Apple has shown, a company doesn’t go bust just because its charismatic founder is gone. Tim Cook made Apple the most profitable company in the world. The question now is: who for Nvidia?
“He was the king,” says Peddie. “Make no mistake – it was the Jensen Huang company. He called all the shots, took all the glory, and shouldered all the blame.”
Does Nvidia work without Huang?
Even without a named successor, analysts don’t think Nvidia is in big trouble yet.
“This is a stock shock, not a business shock, for the next year. The roadmap and manufacturing are locked in through 2027,” says Pat Moorhead, Moor Insights & Strategy. “The question is whether Nvidia keeps inventing at Jensen’s pace once those plans run out. The bigger risk than any rival chip is customers hedging during a vacuum. That is why the next CEO needs technical credibility, an operating model that doesn’t depend on one person, and a plan to protect CUDA.”
“Founder visionary, culture setter, leader, AI industry spokesperson etc., is the real loss. We don’t think anything changes strategically,” says Creative Strategies analyst Ben Bajarin.” The product roadmap is set and remains strong, and the next several generations are already in design, in tape-out or on order. NVIDIA is still the company best placed to ship its roadmap at scale, because it has spent years locking up the supply chain behind it, from leading-edge wafers and CoWoS-class packaging to HBM and the rack-level partners. That supply position does not walk out the door with one person.”
“He was the consummate showman, salesman, and visionary for NVIDIA, so he will be hard to replace,” says IDC analyst Tom Mainelli. “But the company’s technology road map is sound, and the team behind him is still there. Choosing the right person to replace him will be key, and there will undoubtedly be bumps along the way. But the company will survive.”
“Jensen built an exceptionally talented organization with a deep engineering bench, a mature, heavily-resourced software ecosystem, and strong customer relationships,” says Dave Altavilla, HotTech Vision and Analysis. “His departure undoubtedly leaves a leadership and strategic vision gap, but the technology, talent, and execution capabilities he helped establish aren’t going away. The real question is whether his successor can sustain that same long-term vision and willingness to invest ahead of the market.”
“No one in the company really wants to step into his shoes, so an outsider is going to have to be found,” says Jon Peddie of Jon Peddie Research. “Whoever that is will not be Jensen, won’t have the same ambitions, the same contacts and relationships, the same vision, or the same courage to make big, long-term bets. We’ve seen this in Apple, AMD, Intel, and other companies. So the stock will probably get battered around a bit until investors see some stability and fewer ‘what if’ questions.”

Video games rarely take over the entire entertainment world at once, yet Rockstar Games has pulled off a marketing blitz that breaks every traditional boundary. Instead of sticking to standard gaming conventions, the studio turned the launch of GTA 6 into an unavoidable pop-culture event spanning music, fashion, sports, and street art.
Even my friends who have never touched a controller are suddenly talking about it because their favorite niche creators, fashion influencers, and indie artists won’t stop posting about Vice City. Let’s talk about how Rockstar Games is making the GTA 6 countdown something as iconic as a pop-cultural phenomenon.
GTA 6 Crashing Netflix and Fashion Magazines
The GTA 6 momentum kicked off with two record-breaking trailers that turned every frame into an internet event. The first trailer pulled 93 million YouTube views in a single day for the debut look at Jason and Lucia. Then, after year-long silence, Rockstar dropped 70 detailed screenshots with the second trailer.
Rockstar then skipped gaming outlets entirely by dropping Grand Theft Auto VI: An Extended Look straight onto Netflix, where it racked up 31.1 million views in four days and hit number one across 87 countries. By taking over the world’s biggest streaming platform, GTA 6 instantly became must-watch living-room entertainment that rivals blockbuster movies and prestige TV.
That is where Rockstar took it up a notch. Print magazines and adult animation quickly joined the wave as GTA 6 crept into every corner of daily media.
Dazed put Jason and Lucia on the cover of its “New Idols” issue wearing custom digital outfits designed by Rockstar alongside rare developer interviews. High-end fashion and culture outlet LOVE Magazine also made GTA 6 the centerpiece of Issue 27 with a collectible cover and exclusive screenshots exploring the duo’s modern “American Dream.”
Even French film magazine Trois Couleurs asked if GTA 6 was the “best film of the year” ahead of a 30-year franchise documentary on French TV.
But what is a Rockstar-made game if it is not filled with some good music, right? Well, GTA 6 doesn’t miss out on that frontier at all.
Chart-Topping Music, Vinyls, and a Live Miami GTA 6 Festival
Music drives the heart of this cultural takeover, starting with a cryptic September social media tease where global superstars dropped Vice City-styled artwork alongside nationwide Spotify billboards. That rollout launched Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album with Atlantic Records.
The 34-track powerhouse of original songs features Travis Scott, Guy-Manuel de Homem-Christo, Future, Metro Boomin, Yung Lean, Cardi B, Morgan Wallen, Keith Richards, Rauw Alejandro, Fuerza Regida, CA7RIEL & Paco Amoroso, PinkPantheress, Fred again.., Étienne de Crécy, and a wild Justice collab with Tame Impala, SZA, and King Gizzard & the Lizard Wizard.
Beyond the album, French electronic duo Justice produced a 30-track adaptive GTA 6 score dropping in December, while the in-game radio dial packs stations hosted by Bad Bunny on Cocoteo FM, Lana Del Rey and Morgan Wallen on Back Country Radio, and Slayer’s Kerry King and Tom Araya on The Chamber 106.6.
To bring those tracks to life, Rockstar announced Grand Theft Auto 6: The Festival, an exclusive real-world concert takeover at Miami’s Mana Wynwood on November 21. Fans who book GTA 6 festival tickets through the lottery will catch live sets from album artists like Travis Scott, Cardi B, Justice, Metro Boomin, Don Toliver, Kodak Black, Paco Amoroso, Nick León B2B DJ Python, Prospa B2B Skream, Rauw & Friends, and Suero.
Putting these mainstream pop artists on a real festival stage bridges the gap between hardcore gamers and everyday music fans whose playlists are already dominated by the soundtrack. But Rockstar is not just remodeling Miami for a day.
Turning Real-World Miami into Living Leonida
Nowhere is this cultural crossover more obvious than in South Florida, where Rockstar practically rebuilt Miami into a real-life version of Leonida of GTA 6. Six massive $1.2 million downtown banners and free Vice City commuter shuttles are running through January 2027. If that sounds like not enough, a $4 million South Beach deal supplying branded umbrellas and beach chairs has completely made over the coastline.
Rockstar even brewed up a real-world caffeine fix by teaming up with Miami’s Vice City Bean for a limited-edition $23 “Leonida” coffee blend. It features Colombian and Ethiopian beans with notes of cacao, apricot, and Brazil nut. Turning a local specialty roast into an official GTA 6 collectible means even your morning cup of coffee is now part of the GTA 6 release.
Moreover, planes fly banners for the fictional “NINE1NINE” club over the sand, recreating a shot from Trailer 1. Thanks to another collab, the real E11EVEN nightclub parodied in the game actually rebranded itself as NINE1NINE for a grand opening with Flo Rida, right alongside Halloween club takeovers at Wynwood’s Dirty Rabbit and Mad Club and a Scarface-style Cadillac display on Ocean Drive.
Even the NBA court got a neon makeover through the “A Night in Vice City” collab with the Miami Heat. After slapping a $975,000 logo onto the Kaseya Center roof, the Heat will play their November 18 televised game against the Milwaukee Bucks.
Miami Heat will don the limited-edition jerseys designed by Rockstar, Nike, and Travis Scott’s Cactus Jack brand. The match will also take place on a custom Vice City court.
At the same time, Rockstar teamed up with the Wynwood Walls museum to cover free admission for Miami-Dade locals through 2028. Through this collab, they unveiled ten real-world murals by street-art legends like Tristan Eaton, Ron English, Lady AIKO, FAILE, DENIAL, and Gons and Audet, all of which also show up inside the virtual streets of GTA 6.
From El Clasico Pitchsides to Your Favorite Creator Feeds
Rockstar also made sure the most anticipated video game of all time, GTA 6, was displayed on the grandest non-gaming pop-culture event stages across the globe. During football’s biggest club clash, La Liga’s El Clasico between Barcelona and Real Madrid at Spotify Camp Nou, pitchside LED boards flashed the game’s launch promos. The GTA 6 ads in El Clasico were shown to an estimated 650 million live viewers worldwide.
On the flip side, Rockstar snuck hilarious, exclusive gameplay straight into a new episode of South Park. In a funny clip, we see Jason throwing dog poop at an NPC, which even makes it to the news. It shows how this pop-cultural juggernaut can jump from gritty athletic energy to prime-time comedy overnight.
That same crossover energy flooded YouTube, where Rockstar bypassed traditional Twitch streamers to sponsor massive lifestyle, comedy, and culinary creators. Comedian Druski teamed up with Sacha Baron Cohen’s iconic Ali G character for a Coulda Been Records “OLD HEADS” audition special officially presented by GTA 6.
Celebrity chef Nick DiGiovanni, on the other hand, brought Leonida’s fast-food lore into the real kitchen with a sponsored video recreating the game’s infamous Prairie Chicken sandwich. Tapping into comedy and food channels explains why casual viewers who don’t follow gaming news at all are suddenly hyped for launch day.
Merch, Streetwear, and Sold-Out GTA 6 Collectibles
We all know GTA 6 launches without a physical disc. Rockstar still kept collectors happy with a smart lineup of streetwear and physical merch. Music lovers instantly sold out the $124.98 limited-edition magenta-and-blue liquid-filled vinyl of the soundtrack. Splatter-wax records and jewel-case CDs hit stores like Urban Outfitters and Blood Records.
For die-hard fans, the $399.99 The Goodtime State – Vice City Collection box delivered high-end physical gear. It was led by a “Macca the Gator” statue and a custom Zippo lighter. Alongside that, Rockstar also revealed an 88-piece “Art of Vice City” Wynwood museum clothing line and a 14-piece Miami Heat merch drop.
By blending GTA 6 into global football, viral creator culture, chart-topping music, and fashion, Rockstar has written a brand-new playbook for entertainment marketing. When rival movie studios actively move release dates to avoid a video game, NBA players like Steven Adams joke at media day about league-wide performance drops in November, and non-gamer friends bring up Leonida over dinner, the cultural hierarchy has officially flipped.
GTA 6 is no longer just a game launch; it is the biggest global pop-culture milestone event of the decade. And it is putting the entire gaming industry at the center of the world’s conversation.

Clinicians first noticed medetomidine in the Philadelphia drug supply during the spring of 2024. There was a cluster of overdoses one weekend, leaving patients more sedated and with lower heart rates than normal after receiving the reversal medication naloxone.
It raised some red flags, but amid a constantly changing drug supply, not many. None of the patients died, and most went home from the hospital the same day. It wasn’t until autumn, when patients started coming in with excruciating withdrawal symptoms, that doctors knew something had dangerously shifted.
“It took a while for our patients to consistently have a supply that was exposing them to this enough so that when they stopped, they would rapidly develop withdrawal,” said Jeanmarie Perrone, an emergency medicine physician and director of the Penn Medicine Center for Addiction Medicine and Policy. “It’s the withdrawal that has caused so many problems.”
While clinicians in Pennsylvania and other hotspots are now familiar with the signs of medetomidine withdrawal, the American Society of Addiction Medicine this week released the first national guidance for recognizing and treating patients who have taken the sedative. Technically, the document consists of “considerations,” not guidelines, since researchers have not yet conducted larger studies that could validate the inferences clinicians are making on the ground.
If people are using medetomidine, it’s nearly always in combination with illicit opioids, experts say. That means naloxone should still be the first step if somebody appears to be overdosing. But it also means the patient may not be responsive even after they start breathing again. When it comes to acute medetomidine intoxication, low heart rate and low blood pressure can be treated with IV fluids and other basic care, the guidance notes.
The first symptoms of medetomidine withdrawal tend to be nausea and vomiting, without the diarrhea that accompanies opioid withdrawal, said Perrone, one of the co-authors. That’s when they recommend clonidine, a medication that, like medetomidine and xylazine before it, acts as an alpha-2 agonist. If that doesn’t help or patients can’t keep it down, they could develop very high blood pressure and a fast heart rate within a few hours. That may signal the need for the related IV medication dexmedetomidine, or Precedex.
“It’s scary. We thought we were already living in unprecedented times with the adulteration of fentanyl with xylazine,” said Kory London, an emergency physician and addiction specialist at Thomas Jefferson University. (He didn’t contribute to the considerations, but he works with many people who did.) Unlike withdrawal from other illicit drugs, coming off of medetomidine may require a stay in the intensive care unit.
“We are giving doses [of clonidine and dexmedetomidine] that, as an experienced addiction provider, I would not have given five years ago when dealing with the initial xylazine adulteration,” London said. “Unless you’re experienced with this, giving enough medications to avoid getting somebody to the ICU is really challenging.”
Before medetomidine started taking over, xylazine was the dominant adulterant in much of the American drug supply. It leaves users with horrific wounds and is such a powerful sedative that it could knock people out for hours, often leaving them vulnerable in public.
Medetomidine doesn’t seem to cause the same wounds. But as a sedative, it’s far more potent.
By the end of 2025, medetomidine had been detected in at least 18 states. It’s important for physicians to know whether medetomidine is present in the local drug supply, experts emphasize, as the symptoms may resemble other conditions, including sepsis. In general, it’s critical to stay familiar with the local supply and to consider what effects different adulterants could have on users, said Michael Lynch, a co-author of the considerations and an emergency medicine doctor specializing in medical toxicology at the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center.
“The next thing, and then the next thing, and then the thing after that are coming,” Lynch said. “We can try to predict what they’re going to be, but we can’t always.”
Not every community has the resources to do rigorous, regular drug checking. But “if we do a good job at describing our experience in places where we do have resources and have that early experience, hopefully other places can see the clinical manifestation,” Lynch said. There are drug testing strips for medetomidine.
While the clinical considerations offer doctors a blueprint for treating medetomidine withdrawal, experts say that more research is needed to understand the drug’s long-term effects and to develop better treatments.
Some patients who make it through withdrawal and begin to take medications for opioid use disorder can still experience cravings, experts said. They might think that the cravings are for opioids and begin to use again, but really, the cravings are for medetomidine.
“We’re going to have to recognize that there are now patients who are developing a sort of novel substance use disorder of alpha-2 agonist sedative addiction,” said London. “We urgently need both ways to understand that and ways potentially to help treat patients.”

Elephants live in some of the most complex and resilient societies in the animal kingdom. Individuals die or move away, calves grow up, and newcomers join, but the local communities as a whole usually hold together. Long-term studies of African savanna elephants have shown that, even after poaching or other spikes in deaths, survivors tend to rebuild their lost connections over time. But a new study suggests that resilience may not keep the community intact when steady losses accumulate over time.
Anastasia Madsen, a behavioral ecologist at the University of California, San Diego, and her colleagues analyzed 12 years of observations of wild Asian elephants in Sri Lanka. They found that, once losses began to outpace newcomers, the elephants’ society didn’t just get smaller. It fractured.
Accidental savanna
Udawalawe National Park in southern Sri Lanka was created in the 1970s around a reservoir on one of the country’s four major rivers. “Before that, it was basically a tropical deciduous forest,” said Shermin de Silva, an ecologist at UC San Diego and senior author of the study (de Silva started the Udawalawe Elephant Research Project in 2006).
The reservoir had brought farming and settlers, some of whom lived inside what later became the park. When they were moved out, the land they had cleared for their crops turned into grassland that, according to de Silva, looks very much like an African savanna. With far more food than the original forest offered, the park became famous for its big elephant herds.
But the savanna was only a stage in the forest’s comeback. Without fires and clearing, invasive plants like lantana took over. “In some places, they’re like an impenetrable thicket. Not even elephants really like to go there because there’s no food for them,” de Silva said. This is a problem because elephants tend to move where the grass is. A park with less forage, the team says, stops attracting elephants from outside while, due to limited food, fewer calves reach adulthood.

Violence erupts in Bangladesh as ousted PM's supporters stage protest
- Published
Police in Bangladesh have fired tear gas and rubber bullets to disperse supporters of the deposed Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, who are demanding her return to the country.
A police vehicle was set on fire in Gopalganj district, where the banned student wing of Hasina's Awami League party clashed with security forces.
Nationwide protests by pro-Hasina activists started a day after the former leader said she had requested a passport to return to Bangladesh from exile in India.
The demonstrations by the student wing, called Bangladesh Chhatra League (BCL), are seen as the first organised show of force by Hasina's supporters since she was ousted in August 2024 following a huge uprising against her rule.
Traffic was disrupted in some parts of the country as protesters tried to set up roadblocks using burning tyres.
Several passenger vehicles were also set on fire in various parts of Bangladesh in the run up to the protest.
A 60-year-old driver of a passenger bus was killed by smoke inhalation after people set fire to the vehicle in the city of Faridpur early on Tuesday.
Elsewhere, about 200 protesters briefly blocked traffic on the 6.2km (4 mile)-long Padma bridge across the Ganges, that connects the capital Dhaka with the south-western region.
Bangladeshi local media said dozens of crude bombs exploded in the past few days in Dhaka and elsewhere.
"Any attempt to worsen the law-and-order situation or create instability through any conspiracy within the country from across the border (India) will not be allowed to succeed," Bangladesh Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed said.
"Our supporters were not responsible for the violent incidents. They were carried out by unknown miscreants. We believe in peaceful protests," a senior leader of the BCL, who is now in exile in a foreign country, said.
Hasina fled to neighbouring India two years ago following a massive uprising, bringing an end to her 15-year reign.
Opposition parties accused Hasina of jailing political rivals, supressing dissent and overseeing widespread human rights abuses. She always denied the charges.
The United Nations has estimated up to 1,400 people were killed, most by gunfire from security forces, during the anti-government protests in 2024.
The activities of the Awami League were banned soon after she fled the country and it was not allowed to contest the February general election.
A special Bangladeshi tribunal last year sentenced her to death in absentia after being found guilty of crimes against humanity.
She has denied all the charges, calling the trial "biased and politically motivated".
Despite the death penalty threat, Hasina said she wanted to return to Bangladesh in December and requesteded the Bangladesh High Commission in New Delhi to issue her with a passport.
But the Bangladeshi government said the country would not provide a passport to her and called her "a terrorist".
"She is a fugitive criminal. We have an active extradition treaty with India. We want her handed over," Humaiun Kobir, Bangladesh's junior foreign affairs minister, said.
"Should we treat her like an ordinary commercial traveller and tell her to come and visit her in-laws' residence?" Kobir asked.
A state prosecutor in Bangladesh on Tuesday said the verdict would be executed if she came back, saying she had missed the opportunity to appeal.
Awami League leaders allege that in the past two years hundreds of supporters have been killed in mob violence and dozens have died in the custody of security forces.
Dhaka officials reject accusations that Awami League supporters are being systematically targeted.

U.S. air travel should be fully recovered from the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years by the end of Sunday, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said on Saturday (November 14, 2026).
Mr. Bedford said the flights “will still have delays and cancellations” on Saturday (November 14) but promised that the “worst is behind us.”
His comments came as airlines across the U.S. worked to recover from a ground stoppage that lasted four hours, stranding hundreds of thousands of passengers.
New technology being added to the nation's air traffic control system overloaded antiquated equipment and caused “intermittent” communications and radar gaps, leading to the flight shutdown of more than four hours, Trump administration officials said.
Planes were taking flight and landing on Saturday (November 14), Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said. But the effects could be felt for days. Officials say the system will likely return to normal in time to handle the Thanksgiving travel rush.
The nationwide stop was the first since January 2023, when another key Federal Aviation Administration computer system that sends notices to pilots malfunctioned, and the second since the September 11, 2001, attacks.
Andrew Charlton, an aviation consultant, said Friday's (November 13) stoppage affected about a quarter of the 45,000 flights in the U.S. each day.
“The knock-on effect of that is incredible,” said Mr. Charlton, managing director of Aviation Advocacy. “The aircraft doesn't just fly from A to B and back to B and then stop. It then moves onto C and then over to E and around and around and around. It is, of course, exacerbated if you're talking about long-haul flights, international flights over the Atlantic or over the Pacific.”
Thousands of flights delayed and cancelled
At airports, passengers stared at screens showing delays or rushed to find buses or trains to their destinations.
Emily Brown and her 14-year-old daughter waited more than four hours on Friday (November 13) at the Dallas airport for their flight to Columbus, Ohio, before giving up. They were travelling to surprise her daughter's best friend. Instead, she had to settle for phoning the friend through tears in the airport, Ms. Brown said.
“She saved up her money to buy her own ticket, and she's planned this whole weekend,” Ms. Brown said. “Now we're not sure when we're gonna be able to go.”
A cheerful Southwest Airlines gate agent greeted passengers at Dallas Love Field at dawn on Saturday (November 14) with, “Good morning, good morning,” then repeatedly said all flights were full and asked passengers to have boarding passes ready to expedite the process and help keep flights moving.
Sports teams scheduled to play this weekend adjusted game start times, searched for hotel rooms, rescheduled flights and chartered buses. No. 19 Mississippi's game at Oklahoma was delayed a full day to Sunday (November 15). Start times for some other games were pushed back hours.
FlightAware, a website that tracks flights, said more than 4,100 flights had been cancelled. Cirium, a similar site, put that number above 3,200 flights.
Corbyn Wascher's flight was on the tarmac at the Charlotte, N.C., airport for four hours on Friday (November 13) on his way home to Moline, Illinois, from a conference in Miami. The 37-year-old high school teacher paid $100 to take an Uber to a hotel 25 minutes from the airport after he was unable to find a flight until Saturday (November 14) afternoon to Chicago.
At London's Heathrow Airport, several flights to and from the U.S. were listed as delayed or cancelled on Saturday (November 14).
“While U.S. flights have resumed, there may be some follow-on disruption as airlines work to rebook affected passengers and get all services back to normal,” said Tim Johnson, consumer director at the U.K. Civil Aviation Authority.
‘No one in danger during ground stop’
Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin told reporters at the White House that no one was in any danger as more than 3,000 flights in the air at the time of the grounding order landed safely.
Mr. Duffy blamed Congress for failing to approve more funding for new technology, while downplaying the fact that trying to implement new fixes overtaxed the system. He suggested more disruptions might occur.
“We didn't think we would have this kind of outage. We did,” he said. “We were able to review what went wrong, and then reboot the system and go. But, you will have more of these.”
Mr. Duffy said the failure involved old equipment and was not linked to the FAA's new AI-powered system, which the agency is rolling out to help predict problems in the sky.
The problem was due to updating a system that can never shut down, Mr. Charlton said.
“What you're watching here is trying to change the tires of your car when the car's going at 80 miles an hour down the expressway, because nothing stops in aviation,” Mr. Charlton said. “It's a 24/7 operation. And to make changes on the fly, if you'll pardon that pun, is incredibly complex and dangerous.”
The FAA already replaced thousands of old copper wires with fibre optic lines and upgraded hundreds of radio systems as part of the overhaul that began last year after Congress approved $12.5 billion in funding. Mr. Duffy and the White House are pushing for $30 billion more to complete the work.
Past problem linked to equipment failures
The problem appeared similar to a regional air traffic control communication outage in September that snarled hundreds of flights across the Northeast, although that disruption was linked to a construction crew cutting a fibre optic line. Ageing equipment was also blamed for brief radar outages last year that disrupted Newark airport.
Aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said the difference this time was the nationwide scale of the disruption, which left controllers unable to reliably talk to pilots.
“If you don't have that ability, whether it's because the old wires that they have are just run down or for whatever reason, you've got to stop airplanes on the ground and not put them in the air, where you're going to risk not being able to communicate with them,” said Mr. Arroyo, a former United Airlines pilot.
It differed from the one after 9/11 because planes were not being told to land immediately and pilots likely were able to communicate with ground controllers at airports, Mr. Arroyo said.

Teenage sensation Vaibhav Sooryavanshi has become the youngest captain in top-level men's Twenty20 cricket after taking charge of his state side Bihar on Saturday.

Sooryavanshi played in two of India's five T20 internationals in New Zealand earlier this month, with a top score of 45 in the third match in Wellington.
He is also due to be part of India's side at the Rising Stars Asia Cup, a development 50-over tournament which takes place in Doha later this month.

The failed federal Liberal candidate Katherine Deves, who campaigned to exclude transgender women from women’s sport, will stand for One Nation at next year’s New South Wales election.
Deves was among four NSW Legislative Council candidates announced by One Nation’s NSW leader, Mike Newman, on Sunday.
The other candidates were Arnon Wither, a construction worker from the Hunter region who works as an electorate officer for Senator Sean Bell; Manti Steele, a farmer, teacher and mother of eight from Dubbo; and Daniel Hill, a surf lifesaver from the state’s south coast.
The NSW election will be held on 13 March.
Newman said on Sunday the upper house candidates were “authentic”, “people from the real world” and not “career politicians”.
One Nation has only announced a single lower house candidate – Newman, in the electorate of Cessnock – but he said the party would run candidates in all 93 lower house seats.
“We want to make sure that these people bleed orange, and like I said, they’re all from the real world,” he said.
“That’s the that’s the type of person we’re aiming at … people from the real world who understand business, who understand their pinch points and pain points, understand the cost of living, understand cashflow.”
Deves was handpicked by the former prime minister Scott Morrison to run in the federal NSW seat of Warringah in 2022. Her candidacy was marred by controversy, including when she likened anti-trans activism to standing up against the Holocaust.

“Where we can restore clear and accurate language around biological sex, men and women, and ensure that women and girls are safe and have spaces for services, sports, etc, where it’s inappropriate for males to be there.”
One Nation has required candidates at state elections to sign non-disclosure agreements preventing them from discussing their potential candidacy with the media.

Have you heard of the names Kadambini Ganguly and Anandibai Joshi? Considered India’s first female doctors, these names have often been looked past in the pages of history and even medical textbooks. Today, let’s talk about the story of Kadambini Ganguly — India’s first practising lady doctor.
It was in 1861 that Brahmo reformer and headmaster Braja Kishore Basu had a daughter. She was named Kadambini Basu. Young Kadambini, despite hailing from a community that did not necessarily support women’s education like many others at the time did, received an education at the Brahmo Eden Female School and later at the Hindu Mahila Vidyalaya.
As the daughter of someone who organised and fought for women’s emancipation, Kadambini went on to study in college and became the first woman to pass the University of Calcutta entrance examination. In 1882, she passed the examination for the Bachelor of Arts (BA) degree along with Chandramukhi Basu from the University of Calcutta, making her and Chandramukhi the first female graduates in the country.
Entry into medicine
Wanting to study medicine, Kadambini decided to enrol at the Calcutta Medical College after graduation. She was, however, believed to have been unable to receive the BMC certificate due to a shortage of a couple of marks. She did receive the GBMC (Graduate of Bengal Medical College) degree, though, in 1886. Thus, she became the first Indian woman to be allowed to practice Western medicine.
Around 1888, Kadambini started working at the Lady Dufferin Hospital for a monthly salary of 300 rupees. She had even gone to Nepal to treat British royalty. Along with pursuing medicine, she was also politically quite vocal and active. Around 1899, Kadambini was one of the first women delegates elected to the Fifth Session of the Congress in Bombay and the next year, she won to become the first women speaker at the Congress.
She also served as the president of the Transvaal Indian Association, founded by Gandhiji’s colleague Henry Pollock. She was a member of the Women’s Conference held in Calcutta and even presided over the General Brahmo Samaj session in Calcutta.
A doctor, wife and mother
Around 1883, Kadambini married Dwarakanath Ganguly (thus the change in name from Kadambini Bose to Kadambini Ganguly in many documents). Dwarakanath Ganguly was a Bengali Brahmo reformer, educator, journalist, and pioneer of women’s rights in British India.
She was a mother to eight children and is often said to have been deft in needlework. She became a practising doctor while equally devoting herself to family and household affairs, an action which was deemed impossible by many in the era.
Despite having being burdened with domestic chores, like most women of that time, Kadambini still managed to smash the glass ceilings and societal stereotypes in both her professional and personal life.
A name which should not be forgotten in the course of time, Dr Kadambini is a reason many of us are able to pursue our passion — in medicine and in life.

An organ transplant controversy tests 'the dead donor rule'
The U.S. organ transplant system has approved the first national policy for a controversial procedure used to remove organs from hospital patients. The guidelines are designed to protect potential donors. But critics say they do little to improve safety and fail to address deeply troubling ethical concerns.
The procedure is called normothermic regional perfusion, known as NRP. It can be used after a family has decided to withdraw care because there's no hope of meaningful recovery for the person. To perform NRP, doctors attach an external pump to a donor minutes after their circulation has ended and they've been declared dead. The pump restores blood flow to their hearts, lungs, kidneys, liver and other organs to keep them from deteriorating.
"The hope with NRP is that it increases the supply of organs and it increases the quality of the organs," says Dr. Raymond Lynch, the director of transplantation at the Health Resources & Services Administration, the federal agency that oversees the organ transplant system.
NRP could help solve the chronic organ shortage, Lynch says. More than 109,000 Americans are waiting for an organ transplant, according to HRSA. About 12 die every day because of a chronic organ shortage.
Critics, however, say NRP is unethical because it violates the Dead Donor Rule, which is the most important rule protecting potential donors. The rule says transplant surgeons can only take organs from patients after they are dead because of brain death or circulatory death. But because NRP restarts circulation, critics say the procedure reverses the very condition upon which the person has just been declared dead.
"In order to be dead by circulatory criteria it means we're not going to attempt to reestablish circulation. But that's exactly what they do in NRP," says Dr. Lainie Friedman Ross, a University of Rochester bioethicist. "So, yes, I have a real problem with NRP. I think it violates the dead donor rule. It's taking organs from people who are no longer dead."
The other aspect of NRP that troubles critics is what surgeons do to try to make sure the donor is also brain dead, after circulation has been restarted by a mechanical pump. They clamp off blood vessels that supply the head. But alarm bells started going off for organ retrieval teams when blood appeared to get restored – or "reperfused" – to the brain during some NRP cases.
"We have seen signs of life in NRP when the brain has been reperfused," says Dr. Claire Morgan, a transplant surgeon who serves on the transplant network's Patient Affairs Committee and was the first to report such cases to HRSA. "It's extremely disturbing."
Those cases prompted HRSA to instruct the Organ Procurement & Transplantation Network (OPTN), which runs the organ system, to investigate and develop a response. On Nov. 6, the OPTN board of directors approved the first phase of the first uniform national guidelines for how to perform NRP.
The new guidelines, which will go into effect Dec. 6, call for surgeons to do more than just clamp the blood vessels to the brain. They should also cut holes in them, according to the new policy.
"Clamping the blood vessels should stop blood flowing to the brain," says Lynch. "Cutting or venting above the level of the clamping is a second safeguard to make sure that if the clamping is insufficient that it immediately drains out of the head and is not supplying warm oxygenated blood to the brain."
The new policy also includes other protections, including recommending against giving donors drugs that would paralyze them and mask any movements.
But critics say the new safeguards are insufficient. Most surgeons already both clamp and vent blood vessels to the brain, for example, they say.
"I honestly don't believe they have created a policy that creates much or any more protection than these donors already had," says Morgan, who also disagrees with the decision to implement the first phase of the new guidelines on an emergency basis before the public had a chance to weigh in.
Critics also say the new policy doesn't begin to address the bigger concerns that NRP donors are not technically dead when surgeons remove their organs. They worry the adoption of the policy could speed the use of NRP before the troubling questions have been fully aired.
"I really think the policy is the cart before the horse," says Dr. Matthew DeCamp, a University of Colorado bioethicist. "The fundamental issues around NRP still remain unresolved."
Lynch, however, argues the new guidelines will protect donors and that NRP is ethical.
"This is an important first step to make sure NRP care is available but that the safety of the family's loved one is always at the forefront," Lynch says. "This is life-saving care that will extend the supply and improve the quality of organs that patients can get in transplant. And if it is done properly, it is safe."

- According to experts, there is no evidence former British Prime Minister Winston Churchill said any variation of the quote, "Americans can always be trusted to do the right thing, once all other possibilities have been exhausted."
- Israeli politician Abba Eban, who died in 2002, appears to be the first to have said a version of this quote in the late 1960s, albeit with a reference to "nations," rather than "Americans."
- Historical records and reports indicate that people began attributing the quote to Churchill in the 1980s, long after his death in 1965.
For years, people have claimed that former U.K. Prime Minister Winston Churchill said, "Americans can always be trusted to do the right thing, once all other possibilities have been exhausted," or similar iterations of this quote.
One example of it was posted on Reddit as early as 2010 (archived).
The rumor recirculated on social media following the results of the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, seemingly in response to the Democratic Party winning control of both the House and the Senate.
Members of Congress, journalists and even a webpage of America's National Churchill Museum have also attributed this quote to Churchill.
(X user @fakedansavage)
There's just one problem: It has not been possible to find any evidence proving Churchill ever made such a statement.
A 2016 blog post by The Churchill Project of Hillsdale College, which is dedicated to accurately recording the politician's legacy, reads:
We have been unable to discover [the quote] in any transcript, memoir, or published or private writings, speech, or correspondence. This is not to say that Churchill didn't have that sentiment from time to time.
In 2013, NPR ran an audio story about how often U.S. members of Congress cite this unsubstantiated Churchill quote. Per the public broadcaster, Sen. Mark Warner, D-VA, used the line so regularly that "his staff decided to put it on a plaque or some other memento."
"But when they went to research the origins of the line, they came up empty, despite blood, toil, tears and sweat," NPR said.
Richard Langworth, editor of a 2008 book called, "Churchill by Himself: The Definitive Collection of Quotations," reportedly told NPR something similar:
"I wish I could substantiate that he said it. But so far, I cannot," says Richard Langworth, editor of the journal Finest Hour, published by WinstonChurchill.org.
Langworth has combed through millions of words written by and about Churchill and found no evidence that the former prime minister ever said that about America.
This phenomenon of attributing snappy quotes to Churchill and other notable figures of history is so common it has a name, "Churchillian Drift." Nigel Rees, former host of the BBC's now-defunct "Quote... Unquote" radio quiz show, first coined the term to describe "the process whereby the actual originator of a quotation is often elbowed to one side and replaced by someone more famous."
Where did the quote actually come from, then?
As fact-checking blog Quote Investigator reported in 2012, the earliest version of this saying appears to come from a comment made by Israeli politician and diplomat Abba Eban, per a 1967 New York Times article — though he did not mention "Americans":
Commenting that the passage of time offered the best hope of an end to the problems of Israel and her neighbors, he said: "Men and nations behave wisely when they have exhausted all other resources."
Eban also repeated this sentiment in a United Nations speech.
The first time this quote was used to reference Americans appears to be in a U.S. congressional hearing in 1970, when Bernard F. Hillenbrand — the first executive director of the National Association of Counties, a nonprofit that represents county governments across the U.S. — attributed the quote to an anonymous "Irishman" (see PDF Page 43):
And indeed, we often know how to do things by the philosophy that was expounded by another Irishman I know. He said that you can depend on Americans to do the right thing when they have exhausted every other possibility.
Quote Investigator reported that by 1980, people were crediting Churchill with the quote, according to the pages of an academic journal and a Harvard Business School bulletin that are not available online.
In 1985, U.S. Department of Agriculture then-Secretary John Block also attributed a variant of this quote to Churchill during a Senate hearing (see PDF Page 69):
Winston Churchill once said, "You can always count on Americans to do the right thing after they have tried everything else."
Churchill died in 1965, meaning historical records indicate the quote was only attributed to him after his death.

Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (H5N1) has been confirmed in chicken samples collected from a poultry farm at Kattiyankuppam village in Kurinjipadi taluk of Cuddalore district.
“The National Institute of High Security Animal Diseases (NIHSAD), Bhopal, had confirmed the H5N1 avian influenza virus in samples collected from a poultry carcass on November 5, 2026,” District Collector Sibi Adhithya Senthil Kumar told The Hindu.
The confirmation has triggered a full-scale containment operation, with the Animal Husbandry and Veterinary Services Department culling all birds in the affected farm and within a one-kilometre radius of the epicentre.
According to Mr. Senthil Kumar: “As many as 35,647 bird deaths were recorded in the affected belt till November 13, since the first case of sudden mortality was reported from a farm at Thamanampatti village in Thiyagavalli Panchayat on October 30.”
Samples sent to four laboratories
He added, “Veterinary teams that visited the farm on the day of the first report collected samples and sent them to the Poultry Disease Diagnostic Laboratory (PDDL) in Namakkal.”
As deaths mounted in neighbouring farms, further samples were routed to Poultry Disease Diagnosis and Surveillance Laboratory (PDDL) Erode and the Central University Laboratory (CUL) at Madhavaram in Chennai.
On November 5, a carcass sample was despatched to NIHSAD Bhopal, which confirmed H5N1 on November 13, he said.
Following the standard operating procedure under the National Action Plan, the district was divided into compartments to restrict the spread of the disease.
Culling and disposal
“Initially, we sent only one sample. But a total of 15 farms are affected, of which all the birds in 10 farms have already been wiped out. So only five farms remain, and we are going to cull all [the birds] anyway. As many as nine Rapid Response Teams have been deployed for this purpose,” the Collector said.
So far, 1,550 birds have been humanely culled, and the department is working to cull 100% of the birds in the epicentre farm and within the 1-km radius, in accordance with the Government of India guidelines, 2021.
The carcasses are being disposed of through deep burial in designated pits, with bleaching powder applied and biosecurity measures in place.
An official said that movement of birds to and from the affected farms has been strictly restricted.
All poultry farms in and around the affected area have been brought under intensive surveillance, and disinfection using VIRKON-S — administered orally to live birds and as a farm-level spray — has been carried out as a precautionary measure. Cleaning, disinfection, and fumigation of the affected premises are in progress.
The Cuddalore district administration has asked the public not to panic, stating that the outbreak has been confined to the Cuddalore compartment and that no confirmations have been reported from the other compartments so far.
Pamphlets have been circulated and residents have been advised to report any unusual bird mortality immediately to the nearest veterinary institution.
In the affected area, an advisory has been issued prohibiting restocking of poultry for three months. To monitor this, the Revenue Department and local bodies are involved at the village level, the official said.
Poultry farmers have been asked to strictly follow the prescribed protocols and cooperate with the containment efforts.
The situation is being continuously monitored by the Animal Husbandry Department under the supervision of the District Administration.

Few love stories have been as closely entwined with a nation’s history as that of Sonia and Rajiv Gandhi. The former’s much-awaited political memoir, Belonging, offers a strikingly candid account of her journey from a small town in Italy to the highest echelons of power in India – all for love, she says.
The veteran Congress party leader has been fiercely protective of her personal world. In Belonging, she opens up for the first time about the extraordinary twists and turns of a life that has largely unfolded in full public view. (The Guardian’s Hannah Ellis-Petersen has a rare in-person interview with Gandhi, and you can read an excerpt from the book here.)
Belonging, published today, contains moving glimpses of Gandhi’s private grief. She writes about the loss of her first child, who died shortly after birth, and the chilling discovery of grenades in a room of their house after Operation Blue Star, the 1984 military operation against Sikh separatists at the Golden Temple in Amritsar. She also provides a ringside view of several turbulent chapters in Indian politics, not least the violent assassinations of her mother-in-law, Indira Gandhi, in 1984 and her husband, Rajiv, in 1991.
Her book also revisits some of the darker episodes that have dogged the Gandhi family and the Congress party, including Indira’s imposition of the Emergency in June 1975, a 21-month period during which civil liberties were suspended, political opponents were jailed and the press was gagged, which caused fear and dismay across the country. In Gandhi’s account, it also caused a rift within the family.
Ultimately, Gandhi’s memoir is a vivid record of six decades of India’s political transformation from the Congress-dominated secular republic she moved to in 1968 until today, when Hindu nationalism has become the dominant political force under Narendra Modi.
Here are five key takeaways from her memoir and what they reveal about the state of Indian politics today.
Gandhi has had no real contact with Modi for the last 12 years
Gandhi’s account offers a glimpse of how deep the political polarisation runs in Indian politics today. In one revealing passage, Gandhi writes that she has had “practically no real contact” with Modi in the 12 years he has led the nation. In fact, at times when the two have been in the same rooms, such as the speaker’s small chamber, Modi “tends to look away, avoiding eye contact”, she says. On occasion, she adds, he has asked briefly about her health after a hospital stay.
For her, this breakdown is a departure from the past, when leaders on opposing sides of the aisle “would treat one another with cordiality”. After the 2001 terror attack on parliament, Gandhi immediately called then-BJP prime minister AB Vajpayee to enquire about his safety, a gesture he appreciated.
Gandhi sees an increasingly authoritarian style of politics, in which those in power seek to “belittle and torment” opponents. For years, Gandhi’s son, Rahul, has been the subject of BJP’s ridicule, which calls him Pappu, a derisive term intended to portray him as inexperienced and naive. She adds that similar things are happening elsewhere in the world, an observation that can be read in the context of US President Donald Trump’s use of personal insults and ridicule against opponents.
It’s lonely at the top for India’s female politicians
India has an illustrious history of women occupying top leadership positions, long before many other democracies. But their rise has often come at a cost – that of loneliness in navigating a male-dominated political world.
In the book, Gandhi describes a 2012 conversation with Hillary Clinton on the countrys’ female leaders and their backgrounds. In her recollections of Indira, she shares that, despite wielding authority, Indira could feel besieged and profoundly alone, and this was particularly acute, Gandhi writes, in the months leading up to the declaration of the Emergency by her mother-in-law.
Gandhi also writes of her own isolation, including when she decided to take on the leadership of the Congress out of a sense of duty to her family’s political legacy.
Those in power are increasingly stonewalling the press
Among the many ways in which Gandhi charts the erosion of India’s democratic conventions in Belonging, one particularly telling shift is the changed relationship between the media and those in power. She recalls a time when journalists had opportunities to question prime ministers directly.
In 12 years in power, Modi has not addressed a single press conference on his own. He has sat in on one press briefing at the conclusion of an election campaign, and appeared alongside US presidents at joint press encounters after bilateral meetings, where they took questions from the press. Modi has consistently avoided facing journalists in an open forum, and his media interactions have largely been one-on-one interviews with sympathetic, pro-government news anchors or in one much publicised exchange with a Bollywood actor who asked him how he liked to eat mangoes.
And it’s not just media …
The book’s publication has brought renewed attention to concerns about the space for free expression in contemporary India, and the extent to which apprehensions about repercussions may influence what can be said, written and published.
Penguin Random House India was to publish Gandhi’s memoir but withdrew from the project in August. Gandhi told the Guardian that it was “uneasy in general with the criticism of the government” and said it had dropped the book after she declined certain suggested edits. Penguin has disputed her account, saying that the suggestion it decided not to publish the book because of refused editorial changes “does not accurately reflect the circumstances”.
The book, released in the US by Alfred A Knopf, is being published in India by HarperCollins.
In June, Penguin had also pulled out of plans to distribute graphic journalist Joe Sacco’s The Once and Future Riot, about the 2013 Muzaffarnagar communal violence. The publisher cited an inaccurate map of India and unresolved citation issues. Sacco, however, blamed the decision on the “current political climate in India”.
She’s had quiet fallouts with the ‘thoroughly dishonest’
Western political memoirs, particularly by former heads of government or senior politicians, are often forthcoming in naming political adversaries, recounting private exchanges and offering candid assessments of colleagues. David Cameron’s 2019 memoir, For the Record, took aim at his former friend, Michael Gove, describing him as “mendacious” and a “foam-flecked Faragist”.
Gandhi, in contrast, is restrained. She writes warmly of the closeness between the Gandhi family and that of Bollywood superstar Amitabh Bachchan, whose parents she lived with when she first moved to India, but she makes no mention of the subsequent estrangement between the two families. In another instance, she does not name the political leader she describes as “thoroughly dishonest” and who she says she trusted in 1999, when Congress unsuccessfully attempted to form a coalition government.

Bahrain issues first threat alerts since September as Iran says it attacked US base
Bahrain urges people to stay calm and head to the nearest safe location after issuing two threat alerts as Iran claims a US base attack.
Bahrain issued two alerts of potential threats on Sunday (Nov 15), its first such warnings since September, as Iran said it had attacked a US base in the Gulf country amid uncertainty over a US-Iran deal aimed at ending the nearly nine-month-old war.
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said it had attacked a US military base in Bahrain in retaliation for "hostile US actions", Iran's Fars news agency reported.
The Revolutionary Guards said they had launched six drones targeting a US air-defence radar at the Al-Rifaa helicopter base in Bahrain, Iranian state-run Press TV reported. There was no immediate confirmation from US or Bahraini authorities.
Bahrain, home to the US Navy's Fifth Fleet, urged citizens and residents to remain calm and proceed to the nearest safe location, the interior ministry said. It did not provide further details on the threats.
Two days earlier the Revolutionary Guards said they had attacked a US early-warning radar in Bahrain. The US military denied this, saying it had intercepted two Iranian drones without any damage.
Diplomatic efforts to end the conflict have yet to produce a breakthrough, though Washington and Tehran have held off on direct attacks in the war that began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran on Feb 28 and then spread across the region, with Tehran launching missile and drone attacks on US bases in Gulf countries.
President Donald Trump has said in recent days that he might hold off on attacking Iran if the US faces no new provocations from Tehran or the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen, but that he would maintain a US naval blockade, Reuters reported on Saturday.
On another front, however, the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition fighting them have continued to exchange attacks, with the coalition saying on Sunday it had intercepted two Houthi ballistic missiles launched towards the Saudi capital Riyadh and three drones in the kingdom's oil-rich Eastern Province.

Hundreds take to water to protest coal exports at Newcastle port as Australia faces climate scrutiny
Protestors called for coal exports from Newcastle to end by 2030 and for workers to be supported in moving to other industries

More than 600 climate protesters have taken to the water at one of the world's biggest coal-export ports, after an Australian court rejected a police attempt to stop their demonstration.
Hundreds of kayakers and other small vessels gathered in Newcastle Harbour in New South Wales on Saturday, while hundreds more joined the protest from the shore. The hour-long demonstration, organised by climate campaign group Rising Tide, called for an end to coal exports and greater action on climate change.
No arrests were made, according to NSW Police and the organisers.
The protest went ahead after the Supreme Court of New South Wales rejected a police application to stop the gathering, with Justice Edward Muston ruling on Friday that the “public interest in the facilitation of political expression through assembly” outweighed the police objections, according to ABC News.
Police had argued that the demonstration could put participants at risk, particularly if kayaks collided or capsized. Rising Tide said it had made safety arrangements, including requiring mandatory life jackets and deploying a team to assist participants on the water.
Rising Tide organiser Anne Hodgson told the court the event would be family-friendly and that there would be no civil disobedience.
The court allowed the event to proceed, with a limit of 785 vessels. Shipping movements through the port were suspended between 10am and 2pm on Saturday.
Rising Tide spokesperson Joe Hallenstein used the demonstration to criticise Australian prime minister Anthony Albanese, who was attending the COP31 climate summit in Türkiye alongside climate change minister Chris Bowen.
“[Albanese] is over in Türkiye telling the world that Australia is a leader in climate action, when the opposite is true,” Hallenstein told ABC Newcastle. “Both Albanese’s federal Labor government, and Chris Minns’s state Labor government continue to approve new coal and gas projects, which is the opposite of action on climate change.”
Newcastle is home to the world’s largest coal export port, making it a focal point for Rising Tide’s campaign. The group wants coal exports from the port to end by 2030 and is calling for a transition to other jobs for workers currently employed in the industry.
On Tuesday, Newcastle City Council voted to ban Rising Tide and affiliated organisations from holding protests on council-owned land, after concerns surrounding previous demonstrations which resulted in clashes with police and mass arrests.
NSW premier Chris Minns had backed the council’s move, arguing that local authorities should not have to provide public land for protests that have involved illegal activity. Police minister Yasmin Catley had also criticised the group, describing its members as “bad faith actors”.
Rising Tide’s relationship with police has been strained by previous protests at the port. One hundred and seventy-three people were arrested during its 2024 demonstration; police later dropped charges against 125 protesters in August this year.
The group’s 2025 blockade also led to arrests after demonstrators entered the shipping channel and disrupted coal shipments.
The NSW government has been facing criticism over its support for the coal industry, particularly after a recent court ruling involving the Mount Pleasant coal mine in the Hunter Valley.
On 7 October, Australia’s High Court ruled that authorities must consider the global emissions produced when coal is burned overseas before approving certain mine expansions, in a decision seen as a significant victory for climate campaigners.
However, the Minns government announced legislation on 10 November to allow the Mount Pleasant mine to continue producing up to 16.5 million tonnes of coal a year until 2032. The government said the move was necessary to protect jobs and provide certainty for the industry.
NSW Greens MP Sue Higginson criticised the decision at Saturday’s protest, saying: “The government is literally carving laws that defy the High Court’s ruling because a coal company is threatening to lay off workers before Christmas.”
Rising Tide plans to return to Newcastle Harbour for a larger demonstration in February, with its annual six-day People's Blockade scheduled for 25 February to 2 March, shortly before the election.

The earliest example of the footage appeared on a Dearborn news agency’s social media account on June 28, 2026, months before the midterm elections. The video shows Shiite Muslims observing the holy day of Ashura.
On Nov. 3, Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed made history as the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate, resulting in numerous claims focusing on his religious identity. Footage spread online claiming to show Muslims in Dearborn, Michigan, demanding the implementation of Sharia, or Islamic law, in the United States.
The footage appeared on Facebook and X with captions calling it "an invasion" by Muslims. One post stated: "Thousands of Shia Muslims marched in Dearborn demanding Sharia in Michigan and rejecting American law. Now that they have a Muslim senator, they will become more emboldened than ever."
The footage in question was not taken after the Nov. 3 elections. A local Dearborn news agency shared it on Instagram on June 28 with a caption saying that it showed Shiite Muslims observing the holy day of Ashura, which has nothing to do with implementing Sharia. As such, we rate this claim miscaptioned.
Details indicated that the footage was not shot in November, including the facts that all the people marching are wearing T-shirts and the leaves on the trees are green. In November, Dearborn is cold and leaves have changed color and fallen.
Using Google's reverse image search tool, we found what appeared to be the original source of the footage. On June 28, the Instagram and TikTok account for local news organization dearborn.org, which focuses on immigrant Arab and Muslim news, posted the same footage in a reel (archived) with the caption, "From the Annual Ashura march in Dearborn."
A local newspaper, the Detroit Free Press, also covered the same march, posting photographs of the same men in black shirts, green vests and black-and-red vests.
As we have previously reported, Ashura is a holy day for Shiite Muslims. The reel shows a group of men participating in a religious ritual during Muharram, the first month of the Muslim calendar. The month is an important mourning period for Shiite Muslims in particular as it marks the anniversary of the seventh-century Battle of Karbala (in present-day Iraq) and the martyrdom of the Prophet Muhammad's grandson Imam Hussein.
It is common practice for Shiite Muslims to observe the period by wearing black, crying and beating their chests, particularly on Ashura, the 10th day of Muharram.
Similar footage of another procession went viral after Zohran Mamdani, who is a Shiite Muslim, became the Democratic nominee for New York City mayor in 2025. The footage spread with miscaptioned text claiming that the procession was taking place in New York City because of Mamdani, when it was actually from Azerbaijan.
For more reporting on El-Sayed, we have previously covered the claim that he would force Michigan students to learn Arabic numerals (they already do), the true claim that he called Michigan "the capital of Arab America" and a false rumor that he said it was acceptable for young girls to see male genitals in their locker rooms because "they are going to see them on the internet anyway."
