Bowen Yang made a surprise return to “Saturday Night Live” in the cold open, playing the disgraced tech mogul Jensen Huang as host John Mulaney led a group of tech billionaires through a CIA class on how to recognize female spies.
The cold open featured Mulaney as a CIA agent who gathered ultra-rich tech moguls at the agency’s headquarters for a crash course on how to recognize a classic espionage honeytrap, a nod to the Nvidia scandal that has rocked the business world. In the closing moments of the sketch, former “SNL” trouper Yang walked in delivering a pitch-perfect spoof of Huang, who was forced under pressure to resign on Nov. 12 from the Silicon Valley giant that he built for more than 30 years amid a growing sex scandal.
Yang introduced himself “Jensen Hide-Your-Wife Huang.” Yang as Huang lamented that “women don’t like guys like us. That’s how we became guys like us,” after Mulaney’s CIA agent flashes him Venn diagram charts that show no overlap between beautiful women and tech billionaires. Yang also quipped that when Huang comes into the room, “You know what’s about to go down — the S&P 500.” And in a nod to Nvidia’s heft in the stock market, he added: “That’s right — I’m in to BDSM: Breaking the stock market.”
The sketch featured “SNL regulars playing the tech billionaires who have flexed so much power over politics and culture in recent years. James Austin Johnson played Peter Thiel, Andrew Dismukes limned Mark Zuckerberg, Jane Wickline played Anthropic chief Dario Amodei, Jeremy Culhane inhabited Elon Musk and Ben Marshall spoofed OpenAI chief Sam Altman.
In a CIA conference room setting, Mulaney’s CIA agent used a pointer and monitor to flash Venn diagram graphics to school the billionaires in the difference between “Woman who would actualy want to have sex with you” and “A woman who is clearly a spy.” The sketch turned on the story that has made global headlines as Huang admitted to have a romantic relationship with a woman who is believed to be a spy for China. In the days since the scandal broke, allegations surfaced that Huang, who is married, had relationships with two employees at Nvidia.
“Never date a human woman,” Dismukes as Zuckerberg said of the lesson to draw from the Nvidia scandal. “Never date anyone lest they become the antichrist,” Johnson as Thiel offered.
Thiel defended the contributions of tech billionaires to the greater good and asked Mulaney to “name one time when technology has let us down?” Mulaney cited this week’s one-two punch of the massive disruptions that exposed the vulnerabilities of our wired world: The five-hour national ground stop on air travel on Friday and Microsoft’s widely used email platform Outlook experiencing a global outage for nearly 24 hours.
“Like yesterday when every plane was grounded? Or the day before when Microsoft Outlook went dark? Mulaney said.
Altman questioned whether he and Thiel, who are gay, needed the training to detect female spies. Johnson as Thiel added “and we are both bears in the sense that we’ve killed a lot of hikers.”
Mulaney is notching his seventh time as host of “SNL,” after working on the show as a writer from 2008 to He’s in the midst of a push for Amazon Prime Video’s John Madden biopic “Madden,” which bows on the streamer and in limited theatrical release on Nov. 18. He’s also touring at present on his “Mister Whatever” stand-up tour. Mulaney most recently took the helm in November 2024.
Phoebe Bridgers will perform as “SNL” musical guest for the second time. She’s currently on tour with her newest album “Lost Weekend.”

The World
For more than 30 years, the paper covered an increasingly repressive state under Vladimir Putin.
Novaya Gazeta was a newspaper of near-legendary status in Russia. It was the home of the investigative journalist Anna Politkovskaya, whose books in the early 2000s offered a searing account of human rights abuses, wartime propaganda and corruption in Vladimir Putin’s Russia. In 2006, on Putin’s birthday, Politkovskaya was shot and killed in the elevator of her apartment building. Twenty years later, Russia is back at war and Novaya Gazeta has shut down.
On Monday, the paper held its last editorial meeting. One final issue will come out in the next few weeks. I spoke to my colleague Valerie Hopkins, who was there to witness the journalists packing up their offices.
Sadness, defiance and pride
Valerie, Novaya Gazeta, the last big independent Russian media organization, closed its newsroom this week. The paper and its journalists have been under intense pressure from President Vladimir Putin for decades. Why now?
The real miracle is that they lasted this long. We’ve watched the Russian government systematically dismantle any media organization that is critical of the Kremlin and critical of the war in Ukraine. This didn’t happen overnight.
First their website was blocked, so you needed a VPN to read them. Then they lost their media license. Then Putin signed a decree nationalizing their printing presses. Then this spring, authorities raided the newsroom and one of their journalists was detained and put on trial. The paper was added to the list of so-called foreign agents — this kind of Stalin-era term that comes with many limitations on what you’re allowed to do.

Pakistan stunned host Bangladesh 1-0 to set up a blockbuster final against arch-rival India in the SAFF Championship in Dhaka on Saturday.
An 86th-minute strike from Abdul Samad Shahzad Arshad was enough to silence the home supporters.
Led by Hamza Choudhary, Bangladesh dominated the game in terms of possession (62 per cent), but it was Pakistan who had more shots on target and eventually found the back of the net in the dying moments of the match.
The first half of the match was filled with lacklustre attacks as both teams seemed devoid of creativity once they reached the attacking third. Bangladesh found more joy through its sustained possession, but couldn’t find an opening.
At the same time, Pakistan’s attacks were not fruitful until the second half. The side didn’t create many chances; however, they did hit the post after some exquisite work from its striker to control and hold the ball inside the box, but the Bangladeshi goalkeeper did enough to stop it from going in.
In the second half, the pattern followed, however, as the players tired there were more openings for both sides. This is when Abdul Arshad pounced on a chance that he created himself. He found some space in the box to cut onto his stronger left foot and took a chance by shooting at the Bangladesh goal on the near side. The goalkeeper, on this occasion, was unable to stop the ball from squirming under him as Pakistan scored a late winner.
This win means that Pakistan now go to the SAFF Championship final, on November 14, for the first time in its history. Pakistan will meet India in the final, who beat Bhutan 2-1 in the first semifinal.
The summit clash between India and Pakistan will take place on Tuesday.

Villagers in 25 districts of Rajasthan cast their votes for the fourth and final phase of polling on Saturday to elect the Zila Parishad and Panchayat Samiti members at a total of 2,524 seats. An estimated 72% turnout of voters at 11,905 polling stations was recorded by the end of the day.
The polling for first, second and third phases of Panchayati Raj elections was held on October 22, October 28 and November 3, respectively. Counting of votes for Zila Parishad and Panchayat Samiti elections across all four phases will be held on November 20, followed by elections for Zila Pramukhs and Panchayat Samiti Pradhans.
There were delays in polling at several places due to glitches in electronic voting machines (EVMs), while the voters at some villages in Baran and Jaisalmer districts boycotted the polling to press for their demands.
The villagers at Mundakya and Mundki in Baran boycotted the voting in protest against an irrigation project adversely affecting their lands. They have been demanding fair compensation for land acquisition for the project. The villagers at Bhojraj Ki Dhani in Jaisalmer did not cast their votes in protest against alleged anomalies in the reservation for Other Backward Classes.
Police took two persons into custody at a polling station in Sikar district’s Hapas village when they created a commotion while insisting on carrying their mobile phones inside the booth. The situation escalated when they began arguing with the polling officials and the policemen, leading to their detention on charges of disturbing peace.
The highest polling at 77% was reported at Baseri in Dholpur district. So, you think you’re an Elder Scrolls superfan? You say you’ve been there since The Elder Scrolls Arena on MS-DOS and have logged hundreds of hours in The Elder Scrolls Online? You say you’ve bought all of the roughly 5,000 re-releases and remasters of Skyrim that have been made available in the last 15 years?
Tell me, then: What do you think of The Elder Scrolls Travels: Shadowkey?
What’s that? You’ve never played Shadowkey? You weren’t there day one back in 2004, Nokia N-Gage in hand, ready to experience the game’s 176 x 208 resolution mobile hack-and-slash RPG combat for yourself? And you call yourself a real Elder Scrolls fan?
Well, don’t worry. Now you can fill in this crucial gap in your history without even having to track down functional, decades-old N-Gage hardware. That’s thanks to Shadowkey: Reforged, a free fan-made PC port that pairs updated art with the original game files and scripts for an upscaled, 4K experience that runs natively on PC, no N-Gage or emulator needed.
A few decades of upgrades
Moving from a pre-iPhone mobile game to a modern PC obviously comes with major graphical upgrades, powered by a completely rewritten PC graphics engine. What was once a cramped portrait orientation on the N-Gage has now been expanded for a 16:9 monitor standard that displays at up to 120 fps (though the game’s logic still matches the original game’s 25 fps). In addition to newly retextured character and environmental models, the new port also sports small touches like bloom lighting, rippling water, and an upgraded interface with sharper text rendering than was possible on an ancient mobile phone.

Most of my Steam collection won't run on my Mac. It's not (entirely) my fault.
I will be the first to admit that my collection is mostly old indie games, all of which work fine on Windows. Less so on the Mac. Apple stopped supporting 32-bit games back in 2019 when it released macOS Catalina. A good chunk of my Steam library has a "No" symbol next to it because of that restriction. And next year it will get even worse: macOS will drop support for running Intel Mac applications, which could leave even more games unplayable (though Apple claims that certain older games will keep working).
But there's another way. A free, open source app called FX Steam Launcher boots the ARM version of SteamOS—the operating system that powers Valve's Steam Deck gaming handheld—right on your Mac, using a combination of a virtual machine and compatibility layers. You will need a Mac with an Apple Silicon processor, as Intel Macs aren't supported, running macOS 15 or later. I set this up recently, connected a controller, and I've been playing all kinds of games that are otherwise unplayable on my MacBook Air.
It wasn't even hard to set up. To get started, download the application, mount the DMG file, and drag the app to your Applications folder. The first time you launch the application, a pop-up will offer to download and install SteamOS for you in a virtual machine.
Click Create New Disk, and you'll be asked a few questions. The most important step is the hard drive size—the default is 64 GB, which is plenty, but consider allocating more space if you plan on installing multiple large games. You can also choose the drive location, if you like, and set a password for opening SteamOS.
Click Create, and the application will download SteamOS and install it in a virtual machine. I recommend using this time to pair a game controller with your Mac in System Settings under Bluetooth. FX Steam Launcher works with most current gamepads, including Xbox, DualSense, DualShock, and Made for iPhone. I used a Nintendo Pro Controller.
Eventually, you will see the login screen, where you can enter your Steam credentials. Once you're in, you'll see your Steam library. The virtual machine operates like an actual Steam Deck, which takes some getting used to if you've never used one. It divides your library into games known to work in SteamOS and those that might work, which is helpful. A lot of my games started running immediately, with full gamepad support.
This isn't a drop-in solution for every game. SteamOS itself is quite fiddly, and you're now running it in a virtual machine. In some cases, I needed to tweak the graphics settings for games to run correctly. For Psychonauts, specifically, I had to download a user-made patch to get the controller working properly—but I'd have needed that fix for an actual Steam Deck too. When a game ran poorly, I frequently found the solution by Googling and finding actual Steam Deck owners who ran into similar problems.
There is a limit to the processing power you get out of a Mac, especially if you (like me) are using a MacBook Air. And a virtual machine, by definition, doesn't have access to all of your machine's capabilities. But the list of compatible games, compiled from other users, shows which devices have successfully played various titles. Check that page for your favorite games before you dive in.
If nothing else, this is a lot easier than my previous method for running Windows games on a Mac, which involved setting up a version of Wine that's no longer supported. I even got a few non-Steam games installed. Sideloading on SteamOS means booting into Desktop Mode, which you can find in the SteamOS sidebar under Power. You'll end up in a Linux-based desktop, complete with a web browser. You can download games, put them in the folder of your choice, and point Steam to them. I couldn't add custom art, but I got multiple games up and running this way.
Honestly, Valve should update the official Steam Mac client with similar compatibility tech so it can run Windows games natively. It would be a huge hit with Mac users.
If you're a power user, I recommend checking out the settings for FX Steam Launcher, which you can open from the menu bar or with the keyboard shortcut Command-comma. You can change the resolution for your virtual Steam Deck, configure the sound to your liking, and submit game statistics.
It's remarkable software. And, with an HDMI cable and a gamepad, you can plug your MacBook into your TV and game from your couch. That's what I plan on doing when I'm done writing this article (which I guess is right now).

It was July of 2024, and Jensen Huang was punchy.
I had agreed to travel to Denver, Colorado, to interview the Nvidia CEO at SIGGRAPH, the annual confab of computer graphics PhDs and practitioners. Early that year I’d conducted a lengthy sit-down interview with Huang for a WIRED magazine feature, which apparently went well enough—both for WIRED and for Nvidia’s executive communications team—that I had been asked to interview Huang again at this conference. Another opportunity to grill the CEO of the modern world’s most consequential company? Yes, of course. I began preparing.
What ensued was, in a word, bizarre. During the first prep call for the conference, the type of call-in which PR handlers typically try to coax specific questions out of journalists to prevent an ambush, a youngish, vaguely familiar woman took the lead. This was Madison Huang, Jensen’s daughter. She was clearly intelligent, commanding respect. She told me about the slides Jensen would be presenting on stage at SIGGRAPH and offered suggestions for key moments when I might tee him up to talk about the slides.
Slides? Tee up Jensen? What kind of “interview” was this?
I raised my concerns with both my editors and Nvidia. We agreed that I would ask the questions I intended to ask him, which included questions about the environmental impact of data centers, and that Huang would also be referring to slides. Let’s just say the interview didn’t go smoothly. (It’s on YouTube.) To this day, former and current Nvidia workers sometimes tell me that I “handled” the whole thing well. Huang was domineering, evaded some of my questions, and, immediately after our session concluded, did an impromptu Q&A session with a much more adoring crowd than me. Then I was guided offstage, and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg hopped on, where he and Huang had a lovey-dovey fireside chat.
As a longtime journalist I’m used to occasional adversarial interactions; I really don’t lose sleep over them. This was just a CEO being a CEO. Huang later agreed to meet with me again, in December 2024. But that interview in Denver had underscored for me how much Jensen Huang wanted to control the narrative. Not just wanted to; he assumed he would. And to a large extent he did. Until this week.
Narrative has always been a critical part of Huang’s success. He was not just your average electrical engineering nerd who toiled away on something that would eventually find a product-market fit. By Huang’s own telling, he was an immigrant founder, an underdog, a wife guy who chased (and eventually married) his college sweetheart, a scrappy startup guy who dined at Denny’s in the early days. A visionary who worked Sundays and who didn’t sleep well because he always heard the hoof steps of competitors. A parent who brought his kids into the corporate fold. A man who loved Nvidia so much he tattooed an abstract version of the company logo on his arm.
Huang built the highest-valued publicly traded company in history. That part’s not just fairy tale. It’s true. Now, it’s starting to read more like a Greek tragedy.
Back in January 2024, when I sat down with him for our first-ever in-person meeting, Huang right off the bat talked about the importance of storytelling. Here’s an excerpt:
Jensen Huang: Somebody who I really admire, as a leader and a person, is Shantanu Narayen, the CEO of Adobe. He said he always wanted to be a journalist because he loved telling stories.
WIRED: It seems like an important part of building a business, being able to tell its story effectively.
Yes. Strategy setting is storytelling. Culture building is storytelling.
You’ve said many times you didn’t sell the idea of Nvidia based on a pitch deck.
That’s right. It was really about telling the story.
Of course, even then, Huang was caught up in the crosshairs of the US–China AI war and at the mercy of regulators, as I wrote at the time. After Donald Trump’s reelection that year, Huang once again deployed his storytelling skills and lobbied the Trump administration to loosen export controls, so he could sell some of his company’s chips to China.
Another crucial part of the Huang lore is that he ran a “flat” organization, with a few dozen top executives reporting to him. (This is sometimes reported as being “60” people; insiders have told me at times it’s closer to 35.) Huang once said the structure allowed Nvidia “to adapt a lot more quickly, which we need because our technology is moving so quickly.” Huang was also known to be controlling of all aspects of the business—participating in every significant meeting, seemingly aware of every moving part, and staying in the loop on sourcing, supply chains, and the company’s allocation of chips.
This is where Huang’s cult of leadership, and his Nvidia storytelling, may have come to a stupidly disappointing final chapter. As one former employee put it, Huang can’t simultaneously have had knowledge of every element of Nvidia’s business and then potentially feign ignorance about where the chips may have fallen, both figuratively and literally. His apparent lapses in judgment have now led him to resign from the very company he coaxed into existence and have shattered the mythos of its ever-prescient founder.
It’s certainly not the narrative ending Huang would have chosen, were he still in control.

Unlike a bulky and almost always noisy treadmill, the best walking pad is a slim (ideally portable) machine that can slide under your standing desk or fit anywhere in your home. You can rack up steps while working, binge-watching reality TV, or just avoiding the looming winter. Sitting at your desk all day is literally a pain. It’s terrible for your posture and takes a toll on your physical and mental health; I know this because I'm currently typing this as a hunched-over keyboard gargoyle. Theoretically, you could take walking breaks away from your screen, but even then, you’re still spending a lot of the day on your tush.
I’m also convinced that walking pads make me more productive. Not only do you crush your daily steps before 5 pm, but daily use can boost your energy levels, mood, and cardiovascular health. Walking on an incline also strengthens and tones your lower-body muscles, so you can even get a decent workout in. There are tons on the market, offering varying speed capabilities, extra features like built-in desk platforms and wheels, and durability. Our remote testers clocked serious hours walking, working, and sometimes jogging to find the best walking pads worth the space and money.
For more WFH gear recommendations, check out Best Standing Desks, Best Laptop Stands, and Best Office Chairs.
Featured in this article
Updated November 2026: I’ve added the FlexiSpot MotionX Ultra Auto Incline Walking Treadmill, Merach UltraWalk W60, and the Umay U20F Folding 3-in-1 Walking Pad. I've also added more walking pads to avoid. Product information, prices, and links were also updated.
What Features Should I Look for in a Walking Pad?
Size and storage: Walking pads are typically much smaller than traditional treadmills, but check the product dimensions and make sure the footprint will work for you. If you’re working with an especially small space, consider a foldable or under-desk walking pad. If you’re planning to store it under furniture or in a closet when not in use, shop for slimmer models with wheels for portability.
Belt size and track length: The deck size is dependent on the product’s dimensions, and you should take into consideration how much space you have to work with. But, generally, I prefer wider and lengthier belts that feel more stable to walk on, especially if you’re on the taller side or have a longer stride.
Weight capacity: Walking pads aren’t as durable as treadmills and tend to have a lower weight capacity. Check the machine’s limit, and make sure it will work for you and anyone else in the household who will be using it. Per the online reviews we’ve read, walking pads are notorious for falling apart after only a few years or even a few months of use, so it might be worth getting something that’s a little more heavy-duty.
Speed range: Choose a walking pad that offers a speed range that best fits your lifestyle and goals. Most models will generally offer speeds up to 4 mph, which should cover everything from gentle strolls and brisk walks, and is ideal for home office use. There are walking pad-treadmill hybrids that offer faster paces if you’re also looking for a jog.
Adjustable inclines: Some models remain flat, but I prefer the walking pads that feature adjustable levels so that you can customize your cardio intensity as you see fit. Walking at an incline can also strengthen your lower body muscles and reduce anterior knee loading.
Metrics and display: Most walking pads have an LED display that tracks your steps, distance, time, and calories. Some models also include a remote control and/or app, which can sometimes sync your metrics from the machine, so you can check your workout data on your phone. This may not matter to you if you prefer to use your Apple Watch or fitness tracker.
Price: You can snag a solid, no-frills walking pad for under $300, but if you’re looking for a higher-end model with a surplus of features, it can cost $500+.
How I Test Walking Pads
Our remote team members evaluated each walking pad from their own home offices, using the pads during real workdays. Testers of different heights, stride lengths, and lifestyles walked for hour-plus stretches while answering emails, taking meetings, and performing other work-related tasks; we noted how each pad felt over time and whether any annoyances surfaced with prolonged use. We evaluated every model for at least two weeks across the following criteria:
- Design: We assessed how intuitive and painless each pad was to set up out of the box, transport, and store. We noted whether its footprint actually worked under a range of standing desks, in cramped apartments, and in garages.
- Speed and incline ranges: We recorded speed ranges and incline options, paying special attention to how smoothly speed adjustments happened mid-use and whether the controls were responsive or lagged. For models with wireless remotes, we also tested how intuitive the controls were in daily use and whether Bluetooth connectivity stayed stable.
- Noise: Pads were run during normal work hours to see how much sound got picked up in the background of Zoom calls. Beyond workdays, we also made a note of whether the noise levels were generally a distraction.
- Extra features: For models with companion apps, we tested the software separately to determine whether it meaningfully improved the user experience with additional controls or insights, or if the walking pad worked just as well (sometimes better) without it.
What Am I Testing Next?
I’ll be testing the DeerRun Q2 Urban Smart Walking Pad and the Urevo Strol 2E. I’m also reevaluating Urevo CyberPad for Home.
Best Walking Pad Overall
Most walking pads have similar capabilities, but the Urevo CyberPad stands out. It offers a 14-percent incline, which is one of the highest inclines on the market. WIRED contributing reviewer Kristin Canning loved that she could tackle steeper walks to get in a real workout without sacrificing her work productivity. She’s confident in the product’s durability, thanks to its solid feel underfoot and comfortable belt. It was ready to use right out of the box and painless to set up. It weighs about 71 pounds, so moving it around isn’t fun, but the wheels help.
You can control the CyberPad (and the colorful lights along the side rails) with its Bluetooth remote and app. As long as you open the app at some point during your walk, it’ll log your workout data from the machine, so you can keep track of daily step counts over time. You can also view your current workout metrics on a screen at the front of the machine.
The speed tops out at 4 mph, and the incline stops at level nine, which can be either a 9- or 14-percent incline, depending on how you position the machine’s feet. Unfortunately, the incline capability does make it difficult to store under furniture. Here’s the full review.

Connecting it to your TV is simple and features a display overlay that tracks your steps and elapsed time without distracting from your show. While it includes several preprogrammed workout routines, the lack of clear guidance makes speed and incline adjustments feel somewhat sudden. It also lacks handlebars, which is a drawback for anyone seeking extra support. Lastly, the paint began chipping after just two weeks of use.
Toputure TP6 Treadmill with Adjustable Handle for $299: This is a foldable, screenless walking pad that is ideal for small apartments and spaces. It takes only a few minutes to set up and compact, but it weighs 56 pounds, so it’s not the most portable treadmill. During my second day of testing, the pad began making a high-pitched scraping noise, which likely indicated a misaligned belt. This unbearable noise would come and go throughout my two weeks of testing. The handlebars are height-adjustable, ranging from 32 to 45 inches, and they are also tilt-adjustable. Be aware of the handlebar locks while walking by, as they can catch on clothing. It's a decent budget pick.
Umay U20F Folding 3-in-1 Walking Pad for $350: I always appreciate a walking pad that can pull double duty as a treadmill, and this sturdy, 44-pound model fits the bill: There’s a handlebar with tablet holder that can fold up if you want to run, with the walking surface adjustable to a 15 percent incline. However, due to the adjustable incline mechanism underneath, this pad is not able to sit all the way flat, which means it’s permanently at a 5-percent incline. This made it too tall for some standing desks, too tiring to walk on for long periods during the workday, and challenging to store compared with other walking pads. —Kat Merck
Urevo SpaceWalk 5L Smart Walking Pad for $400: The SpaceWalk 5L is decent and cheaper than the CyberPad, but I still prefer the latter for its 14 percent incline and the Strol 2S Pro for its speed and ability to double as a treadmill. The SpaceWalk 5L has a larger weight capacity, maxing out at 300 pounds, with the same incline as the Strol 2S Pro (9 percent) and max speed as the CyberPad (4 mph). Its track length is a solid 39 inches, and WIRED contributor Michael Venutolo-Mantovani said it’s compact enough to stash underneath a couch or loveseat.
Egofit Walker Pro M1 for $399: This is one of the first walking pads we tested, and it has a fixed 5 percent incline that might pose some storage issues (you won’t be able to just slide it under the couch). It can be controlled via an app or a remote, but it doesn’t automatically sync if you use the remote. But it’s lightweight and easy to move around your home.
GoYouth 2-in-1 Under Desk Treadmill for $265: This is an Amazon top pick, but it’s very bare-bones for this price. There’s no app, and the remote and controls are unintuitive. The built-in Bluetooth speaker sounds unsurprisingly crappy. But it does feel great underfoot, is very quiet, and has a higher weight capacity (300 pounds) and a slightly longer belt than the Sperax. If you’re a larger person looking for a simple, affordable walking pad, this will work for you. —Adrienne So
Lifesmart TM2202 3-in-1 Treadmill for $699: The 3-in-1 Treadmill gets its name from its ability to serve as a walking pad (with the rail down, the speed tops out at 3.7 mph), a treadmill (with the rail up, you can run up to 7.5 mph), and a workstation (with the rail up and desk attachment on) for multitasking. It’s easy to set up, and switching between modes is quick and simple (you just need to use a small tool to adjust the rail; the tool is magnetized, so it can live on the rail and never get lost in a junk drawer). The desk’s height won’t accommodate everyone; it was lower than I’d like, and I’m 5'4". But for basic tasks like answering emails or sitting in on a meeting, it was just fine. It also doesn’t have any incline options, though. —Kristin Canning
NordicTrack Commercial 1750 Treadmill for $2,500: With a top speed of 12 mph, incline and decline options, a springy running deck, fans, a 16-inch pivoting touchscreen, and two water bottle holders, this is the best treadmill tester Kristin Canning has used. Although it is a foldable treadmill and suitable for walking and hiking workouts, it’s still bulky and relatively expensive if you’re only looking for a space-saving walking pad. If you’re searching for a running treadmill, check out Kristin’s guide to the Best Home Treadmills.
Skip These Walking Pads
Sperax Walking Pad: The US Consumer Product Safety Commission has warned consumers to stop using several Sperax walking pad and treadmill models due to the fall and fire hazards they pose. According to the CPSC, the machines can unexpectedly change speeds or come to a sudden stop, and there have also been reports of overheating and fires. The warning applies to the Pro, Q1, RM-01, and RM-02 models, but I’d avoid this brand altogether.
GoPlus 2-in-1 Folding Treadmill for $170: There were just too many detractors for us to recommend this budget-friendly walking pad, although we hope to test some newer versions from the same company. The 3-foot power cord made it difficult to find a good spot for the pad since it needed to be so close to the wall. It was too bulky to transport around the house or store under furniture. The included remote was small and easy to lose, and the included battery died quickly. And there were no on-board buttons to control the treadmill, so if you lose the remote, you'll have an expensive paperweight until you can replace it. I also found the phone holder too small and the shipping box poorly designed. While the low price is appealing, and I liked the folding handles and general feel of the belt, you’d be better off investing in one of our picks. —Louryn Strampe

New Delhi: Describing the India-US relations as an essential element of the 21st century, former US secretary of state Antony Blinken said on Saturday that technological cooperation will drive the next phase of bilateral relations between the two countries.
Speaking at the Hindustan Times Leadership Summit 2026, he described the India-US partnership is a global relationship dealing with global issues. He noted that the two countries can collaborate on semiconductors, AI and space, among other sectors.
"The relationship, partnership or the strategic convergence between the US and India is an essential element of this new century and one that we continue to pursue and to deepen," he said.
Referring to the improvement in bilateral ties in the past 25 years and the signing of the civil nuclear deal in 2008, he added, “What really flipped the switch was our ability to do nuclear cooperation. Now going forward it's technological cooperation. That should be the driving force..our ability to work together on producing semiconductors together, our ability to secure AI supply chains, our ability to work together on space, work together on quantum. All of these things are a kind of glue that continues to get stronger.”
The statement comes at a time when India and the US are working on a bilateral trade deal. They are currently in talks to finalize the first tranche of a proposed trade agreement.
Blinken called the ongoing US war against Iran an "unnecessary war" and a "war of choice," adding that he expects the status quo to continue, with a 20–25% chance of further escalation in West Asia.
Calling for an off-ramp from the current conflict, the former secretary of state said, "The problem with the off-ramp..the acknowledgment of the off-ramp, is not sustainable, because that off-ramp requires some kind of accommodation with Iran, and that's what needs to be done to acknowledge it. If the off-ramp remains, I think it would be very possible to get an agreement and diplomatic resolution. But in that resolution, exactly what Iran does on its nuclear program may not look any different, or certainly not better, than the agreement that President Trump tore up. That's very hard for me to acknowledge."
The US launched the war against Iran on 28 February this year amid allegations of an imminent Iranian attack and after bilateral talks failed to contain Tehran’s nuclear programme. The two sides signed a preliminary memorandum of understanding, or ceasefire agreement, in June, though the truce proved fragile and the conflict has continued on a smaller scale.
Iranian foreign minister Syed Abbas Araghchi has urged the United Nations and its nuclear watchdog to condemn a US reward of up to $20 million for information on Tehran’s nuclear programme. The complaint follows a US State Department announcement offering the bounty, along with “possible relocation”, for specific details on Iran’s nuclear facilities and equipment, as well as the identities and movements of personnel linked to the programme, including scientists.
President Donald Trump has raised the prospect of bombing Tehran’s nuclear facilities again, citing his determination to prevent the Islamic Republic from ever developing nuclear weapons as justification for the conflict. The US and Israel had previously carried out airstrikes on Iran’s nuclear programme in June 2025.
But earlier this week, Trump indicated that further military strikes against Iran were not immediately necessary. While Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has been urging the US leadership to resume strikes and pursue regime change in Tehran, Trump has signalled reluctance to launch fresh military campaigns, favouring continued economic pressure and diplomacy instead.
The launch of the attacks on Iran and the killing of its Supreme Leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, in a joint US-Israeli military strike on his residential compound in Tehran on 28 February 2026, prompted Iran to close the Strait of Hormuz, triggering a surge in global oil prices. The strait is a vital chokepoint carrying 20% of the world's oil and gas trade.
Blinken further said that Washington’s bilateral ties with India and Pakistan must be de-hyphenated, noting that the US-India relationship is a global partnership focused on global challenges, whereas ties with Pakistan remain a regional partnership centred on regional issues.
Rituraj Baruah is a special correspondent covering energy, housing, urban affairs, heavy industries and small businesses at Mint. He has reported on diverse sectors over the last eight years including, commodities and stocks market, insolvency and real estate; with previous stints at Cogencis Information Services, Indo-Asian News Service (IANS) and Inc42.

The search for Nvidia's new CEO is officially underway.
The company's board of directors announced that CEO and founder Jensen Huang resigned "effective immediately" in a statement on Wednesday. The board tapped Colette Kress, executive vice president and chief financial officer, as interim CEO until a permanent successor is found.
Huang resigned three days after he admitted to having an affair, and Nvidia's board opened an investigation into whether he was the "target of a foreign intelligence effort."
As the fallout around Nvidia continues, analysts, investors, and prediction market bettors have begun to wonder who could helm the company next. Here's who they're pitching.
Rene Haas
The CEO of Arm Holdings, a semiconductor manufacturing company, is one name that's been bandied about. On Wednesday, The Financial Times reported that Nvidia has approached Rene Haas as it searches for a successor. Sources told the outlet that it's not guaranteed Haas will be offered the role or accept it.
Haas previously served as vice president and general manager of Nvidia's computing products business unit for 7 years.
Ian Buck
Reuters reported that analysts and investors view Ian Buck, Nvidia's vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing, as a possible candidate for the top job.
"The permanent job is a different story, though, because Nvidia's edge comes from its technology, and the board would likely want an engineer in the chair, Josh Gilbert, a lead analyst at eToro, told Reuters. "Someone like Ian Buck, who led the software platform that keeps developers tied to Nvidia's chips, is the sort of internal name you'd expect to come up."
Prediction market users are also banking on Buck. He's at the top of the list on both Kalshi and Polymarket.
Colette Kress
Reuters reported that analysts and investors also view interim CEO Colette Kress as someone who could do the job long-term. Armina Rosenberg, a cofounder at Minotaur Capital, which owns Nvidia stock, told Reuters that finding a new permanent CEO won't be quick.
"The more realistic route is an interim leader from the long-serving inner circle, possibly as a co-CEO structure: one leader to steady the business and the finances, such as Colette Kress, alongside a product and technology leader, such as Ian Buck," Rosenberg told the outlet.
Tim Cook
President Donald Trump also weighed in on the search for Nvidia's new CEO, recommending former Apple CEO Tim Cook. Cook stepped down as CEO in September, but remains executive chairman.
"NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place - TIM COOK of Apple. A Legend replaces a Legend!" Trump wrote in a Truth Social post on Thursday.
Thomas Kurian
Dan Ives, a partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., had a few ideas of his own. During an interview with Fortune, Ives named Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian as a promising candidate.
Kurian joined Google in 2019 after working at Oracle and McKinsey.
Nikesh Arora
Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora is getting swept up in the speculation, too. An Nvidia shareholder told The Economic Times that Arora is among his top picks to replace Huang. Ives also said Arora is on his list.
Johny Srouji
Johny Srouji, the senior vice president of hardware technology at Apple, is another name popping up in conversations. A person familiar with the matter told Semafor that Srouji is being considered for the CEO role.

The Best Digital Notebooks and Smart Pens
Featured in this article
Do you take a lot of notes? Whether it's daily to-do lists, notes for class, or just jotting down thoughts, I've found the best digital notebooks to keep them organized. Sure, you could just open your Notes app, but physically writing something down helps you remember and learn more. Plus, I just love to write things down, and these digital notebooks keep me from burning through paper or losing a great idea I wrote down.
Most of these tablets use E Ink technology to give you a more paperlike experience to write your ideas and notes on. It's easy on the eyes and helps keep you distraction-free as you take your notes as a classic notebook would. As our team's resident obsessive notetaker, I've tried almost every digital notebook on the market to find the best ones worth buying. Whether you want to be able to take detailed notes and access them on your laptop, annotate a book, or have near-never-ending battery life, I've found a digital notebook for you. They're especially great for students who need to do a lot of note-taking and stay engaged without getting distracted by notifications and other apps.
If your notes need an upgrade, I highly recommend giving these a try. If you're looking for more organizational tools and e-paper gadgets, don't miss my guides to the Best Paper Planners, Best Digital Wall Calendars, and Best E-Readers That Aren't a Kindle.
Updated November 2026: The Supernote Manta is now our runner-up pick, and the Supernote Nomad is now our budget pick.
Comparing Our Favorite Digital Notebooks
| Model | Display | Resolution | Color? | Storage | Weight | Battery life | 
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ReMarkable Paper Pro | 11.8 inches, adjustable front light | 229 pixels per inch | Yes | 64 GB | 1.16 pounds | Up to 2 weeks | 
| Supernote Manta | 10.7 inches | 300 pixels per inch | No | 32 GB, and can expand storage with a microSD card | 0.83 pounds | Under a week |

Our Favorite Smart Pens
Neo Smartpen M1+ for $129: If you don't want an entire tablet to write your digitized notes on, you can get a smart pen to use on regular paper that will log your notes into its companion app. The Neo Smartpen M1+ was the thinnest and lightest smart pen former WIRED reviewer Medea Giordiano tried, and she easily used it with notebooks and planners alike. You'll pair it with the Neo Studio app, which has a notebook system that's easy to navigate and organize your notes.
Neo Smartpen Dimo for $59: This is the cheapest smart pen option and uses replaceable batteries. It isn't compatible with Google Calendar, iCal, or Outlook like our other picks.
Honorable Mentions
Boox Note Air4 C for $470: If you're looking for something a little more powerful than just taking notes and annotating, but still want the E Ink screen experience, then a Boox device is what you need. The Boox Note Air4 C has an e-paper screen and is primarily described as an “e-paper notebook,” but runs on Android 13 and has access to the Google Play Store, giving it more of a tablet feel that happens to have a colorful e-paper screen instead of your usual brightly lit iPad or Android tablet. You're able to easily access the web (called NeoBrowser) right from the Boox homepage, which usually takes several steps and is incredibly slow on a true digital notebook. You'll also access apps that look like a tablet, including an image gallery, calendar, music player, and tools like a clock, recorder, and calculator. It was a pick in this guide, but it's now out of stock for US warehouses (you can still order from the Hong Kong warehouse, but you might have to pay extra tariffs and fees), and there's a new version out, the Note Air5 ($530).
Kindle Scribe Colorsoft for $630 and Kindle Scribe (3rd Gen) for $500 and Kindle Scribe Without Front Light for $430: The new versions of the Kindle Scribe are still solid all-around devices that have a good mix of e-reader and digital notebook features, but I still prefer the older model's price point. While the new Scribe Colorsoft is a nice option if you want color, I think these are too expensive for what they are. The price comes from all the AI features packed into the device, plus connectivity to services like Google and Microsoft, but it still isn't as powerful as a ReMarkable or Supernote if you want better tools. My picks above are a better price for similar features, though the Scribe does have the most impressive battery life of any digital notebook device I've tried (and that's still true for the older model that I recommend above, too, so you don't need the newest model for the best battery life).
Moleskine Smart Writing Set for $225: Moleskine is already known for its notebooks, and the brand has a smart version now, too. Our team previously tested a version in 2018 that only cost $149, but the current version that's $224 is next on my list to test. The set comes with a notebook and pen that will pair with the Moleskine Notes app to show you your notes.
Montblanc Digital Paper for $950: Yes, that Montblanc, the one with the famous pens, now has a digital notebook of its own. It's no surprise that I'd call its digital pen one of the best. It's got a super-lightweight feel while sporting three different buttons, two of which you can customize. (There's no eraser, but I'll give it up for that end of the pen to instead be a home button). I really like this device overall, but it's pricey for what you get—aside from the customizable pen buttons, there's not much to differentiate it from my top picks.
ReMarkable Paper Pro Move for $449: The ReMarkable Paper Pro Move is similar in size to a reporter's notebook, which turns out to be a pretty great size for daily task and to-do lists. There's room for a multilevel to-do list and brainstorming, and it's a nice, small size with just a 7.3-inch screen. There are other small options on the market, but this is the only one designed like a long notebook rather than a square, e-reader-like design. I like this size to layer on top of a paper planner or slip into a bag. It can do everything the larger Paper Pro can, including packing a color screen, and honestly feels like you sliced off a bottom third of the device and kept using it.
ReMarkable Paper Pure for $399: This is another good budget option if you want something larger than the Supernote Nomad. It has the same price as the second-generation Kindle Scribe I adore, but with more powerful digital notebook tools instead of a focus on reading. If you're looking for a great digital notebook without spending the better part of a grand, ReMarkable's new Paper Pure is its new basic digital notebook with a black-and-white screen, a lightweight feel, and a great writing experience that is one of the closest things you'll get to writing on actual paper. It doesn't have a front light, though, so you need to use it in lit rooms only.
ReMarkable 2 for $419 (Refurbished): This is the older ReMarkable digital notebook from 2020, and it's still a great device with a great range of accessories—while they're still available, that is. This device is only available refurbished or secondhand after getting essentially replaced earlier this year with the ReMarkable Paper Pure.
Rocketbook Fusion Plus for $30: If you really prefer the paper experience and don't want something you need to charge, then Rocketbook is for you. Rocketbook makes several reusable notebooks, planners, and accessories like index cards and sticky notes. I like the Rocketbook Fusion Plus since it comes with a ton of different template styles, from your classic monthly and weekly pages to project management layouts and meeting notes, making it feel closer to the variety a digital notebook can offer you. Take notes with an erasable Pilot Frixion Pen (one comes with whichever item you buy), scan photos of the pages into the Rocketbook app, and erase the whole thing with the damp microfiber cloth (also included). The app is designed to keep everything organized and easily send things off to Google Drive, Slack, Trello, OneNote, and a handful of other options.
FAQs
Do You Need a Digital Note-Taking Device?
The short answer is no. These devices are expensive, usually costing several hundred dollars when a simple notebook and pen costs a few bucks. But if you like the physical act of writing but need to have digital copies, they're worth considering.
Pros:
- Digital notebooks are thin and light but hold hundreds of notes.
- You can transcribe your notes into text files, making them easier to read and manipulate.
- Depending on the device, you can export files as PDFs, Google Docs, Evernote files, and more.
- Instantly digitizes your art, too.
Cons:
- Expensive.
- Need to be charged.
- Have a learning curve.
- Most smart pens need to be paired with an accompanying notebook. The upcoming Nuwa Pen promises smart notes on any paper.
What About an iPad?
E Ink notebooks are easier on the eyes and feel closer to paper than a glass-screened tablet. But in some cases, you might spend less getting an iPad and an Apple Pencil (and a keyboard if you also want to type sometimes). You can also do more on them thanks to the thousands of apps in the App Store. An iPad is pretty intuitive if you're familiar with the Apple ecosystem (though both ReMarkable and Supernote's ecosystems are also very intuitive). Past WIRED reviewers liked using an iPad with the GoodNotes and Notability apps; check out our guide to the Best iPads for more advice on which to buy.
I also have an iPad, and I'll say the upside of a digital notebook is that the battery tends to last longer, especially if you're the type to use it for a day or two and then forget about it for a few days. My trusty Kindle Scribe usually manages to have plenty of battery available for whenever I feel the note-taking itch, even if it's been a week or two since I last touched it.
Why Are Digital Notebooks So Expensive?
Just because these devices look like paper doesn't mean they're as cheap to make as a sheet of paper. Like any tablet or smartphone, these devices are packed with features, a special ecosystem, and the E Ink technology is no small feat to perfect, along with a sensation similar to writing on paper. It's an impressive piece of technology.
Prices haven't gotten cheaper for this category in the wake of tariffs' causing technology prices to rise. ReMarkable recently raised the price of our top pick, the ReMarkable Paper Pro. Another favorite of ours from Supernote has gone up a little less than $50, and Kobo also slightly raised its prices, though the $10 increase is pretty minor compared to other increases we’ve seen. We'll continue to monitor prices and flag if more price changes are to come.

Get in, loser: Broadway's newest 'Mean Girls' are ready to insult (and enlighten) you
What would it mean to become Miss Ghana 1986? Fame, fortune, perhaps rubbing elbows with '80s superstar Bobby Brown? For a group of six teenage girls at the Aburi Girls Boarding School, the answer is: everything.
The battle for the crown is at the heart of School Girls; Or, The African Mean Girls Play, written by Tony Award-nominated playwright Jocelyn Bioh. The play is ending a Broadway run this week and celebrating with livestream broadcasts on The League of Live Stream Theater's website for a fee (but is free for high schoolers).
School Girls is set at a boarding school in Ghana in 1986. It follows Paulina, the school's queen bee and her crew, whom she frequently belittles and bullies over their looks.
"So, do you want to be fat-fat? Or fit? And popular." Paulina asks Nana, harassing her over eating porridge instead of an apple at lunch.
Ahead of a visit from a pageant recruiter to the school, Paulina's plans to win Miss Ghana go awry after a new transfer student arrives: Ericka from … Ohio!
Ericka exposes Paulina's toxic behavior and shows her up during a performance of Whitney Houston's Greatest Love of All. Ericka, being lighter-skinned than Paulina, sparks a clash between the school's headmistress and the pageant director over beauty and who would have the best chance of winning the Miss Global Universe pageant.
Paulina becomes the victim of circumstances that she cannot control.
School Girls explores the themes of girlhood and impossible societal beauty standards with humor and humanity.
Although its title references the Tina Fey-penned 2004 film, Mean Girls, famous for its pink-hued portrayal of the toxic side of high school girls, Bioh says she wasn't actively thinking about the movie when writing School Girls.
After completing the play and needing to settle on a subtitle, Bioh found herself reflecting on the themes: "I'm like we're dealing with things and ideas and feelings and emotions." She said that her friend, actress Danai Gurira, described it as feral teenage girls. "I'm like, that archetype is incredibly universal."
A perspective on colorism
Beyond the talk about tiaras, '80s fashion and praise for Judy Bloom, School Girls tackles the issue of colorism head-on.
Bioh says she knew it was a topic she always wanted to write about after her own long journey to own her beauty as a dark-skinned woman. "I just wanted to write something that felt like it could maybe shorten the journey for somebody else who maybe felt the same way I did. Especially as a young, impressionable girl."
While School Girls approaches the topic from the perspective of Ghanaian women and girls, Bioh says the play's message has resonated with people from different backgrounds, underscoring that colorism is a global issue.
"'Cause who has decided that this one standard of beauty is the standard of beauty for everybody? I think that's a problem," Bioh explains. "I don't have a solution other than to, you know, create a play that people can feel entertained by or perhaps be impacted by, and hopefully shift their implicit bias as they move through the world."
The cast of School Girls displays a vast array of talent: Denée Benton (Paulina), Lucia Aremu (Ama), Nia Otchere-Sarfo (Gifty), Jordan Rice (Mercy), Erin Morton (Nana) and Jasmine Amy Rogers (Ericka), just to name a few. While it is an all-Black female cast, the diversity of physical appearance is clear.
"The audience, even if they are not young Black girls who went to school in Ghana, they still see facets of themselves in these girls. I think that's where the heart and beauty of it lies." Bioh says.
Audience reaction
School Girls is now on Broadway nearly 10 years after its Off-Broadway premiere. She says it's been a moving experience to see how the show's message continues to stay with audiences long after they leave the theater.
"I had a DM from Jenna Fischer of all people, who went to see the play a few days ago, and literally messaged me again today to say she's still thinking about the play," she says. "You know, how cool that someone who I just absolutely adore and also think is, like, a comedic genius, but who likely has never had any sort of experience with colorism, is still thinking about what the play is saying and how much it moved her.
For those who get to experience School Girls, Bioh hopes you have a good time and walk away with a deep sense of empathy not only for the young girls but for the adult women too.
"I ask people to shift their ideas about things," Bioh says. "If you can just move it just a little teeny bit, then I guess, you know, I've done my job."
