I've lived in Fort Collins, Colorado, for the last four years, and it doesn't surprise me that this city is regularly included on lists of the best places to live in the United States.
What does surprise me is that it gets roughly a million visitors each year, which is far fewer than other destinations in Colorado.
The city has the tight-knit community of a small town but many of the amenities typically found in a larger city. Just 65 miles north of Denver, it has a population of roughly 170,000 people and is about an hour away from Rocky Mountain National Park.
With friendly people, a historic downtown, and nature all around, there's always something to see or do here.
Here's why I think Fort Collins is a must-see city that deserves more attention.
There's easy access to nature throughout the city.
Fort Collins is famous for its easy access to nature.
One of my favorite scenic spots is Horsetooth Reservoir, which is just west of the city and tucked against the foothills of the Rocky Mountains.
I've hiked in the surrounding Horsetooth Mountain Open Space and Lory State Park year-round, but I especially love paddling around the reservoir's hill-framed inlets in the summer.
Fort Collins is also home to Cache la Poudre, Colorado's only nationally designated "Wild and Scenic" River protected by the US Forest Service.
Whenever I have visitors, I love driving them up the winding Poudre Canyon for beautiful views of the river, and stopping to hike or picnic along the way.
The area is also a popular destination for fishing and whitewater rafting.
Community events are a highlight.
There's always something interesting going on in Fort Collins, from concerts and happy hours to Colorado State University football games.
Throughout the summer, I head to the weekly City Park Food Truck Rally to sample a wide variety of cuisines and listen to live music, all in a picturesque neighborhood park.
Another annual highlight is Tour de Fat, a bicycle parade each August where riders don costumes and pedal to New Belgium brewery for drinks, food, and live music.
Later in the year, I love attending the Downtown Holiday Lighting Ceremony, when the city's Old Town is illuminated with thousands of LED lights.
Old Town Fort Collins is full of local gems.
Old Town, a historic part of the city, is located in the heart of Downtown Fort Collins and features a variety of restaurants, shops, and bars.
I never get tired of strolling around this area, which is said to be one of the places that inspired Disneyland's Main Street USA.
That small-town charm is what makes Old Town feel especially memorable. Not only is it home to small businesses, cafés, independent bookstores, and quirky thrift shops, but it also hosts a year-round ghost tour that highlights local history and legends.
There are also lots of interesting dining options, from American comfort food at The Regional to the best housemade gluten-free pasta I've had outside Italy at Rare Italian.
In the warmer months, I love going to The Exchange, an open-air food court and gathering space featuring restaurants, bars, an ice-cream stand, and an indoor mini-golf course.
On the weekends, I'll meet up with friends at classy speakeasies like Ace Gillette or Social, both located in Old Town. We also usually stop by my all-time favorite dive bar, Trailhead Tavern, for pickle shots.
This city is known as the craft-beer capital of Colorado.
If you love beer, Fort Collins is the place to be, since it's known as the craft-beer capital of Colorado.
We have big-name breweries like New Belgium and Odell Brewing Company, as well as many smaller, locally owned alternatives with dog-friendly patios and regular community events.
To me, there's nothing better than spending a summer evening with friends in the beer garden of Stodgy Brewing Company, located in a building that looks straight out of a Western movie. I also love that many breweries offer gluten-free and non-alcoholic options.
Whether they're beer drinkers or not, I think visitors can find plenty to love about Fort Collins. No matter the time of year, I always recommend checking it out and discovering why I think it's Colorado's best-kept secret.

Beijing – Beijing’s ban on possessing drones came into force Sunday, a measure authorities said will help ensure the security of China’s capital city.
The ban applies to both urbanized and rural areas in the municipality of around 16,400 square kilometers — an area roughly half the size of Belgium.
The ban, which Beijing announced in September, outlaws owning and storing uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAVs) to “safeguard the security of the capital.”
Transporting drones or their components into the city was also forbidden.
Owners had been forced to get rid of their devices ahead of Sunday’s implementation, either by reselling them at approved buy-back points or online.
They could also have transported them outside the enforcement area.
Beijing, home to China’s central government, top leaders and the headquarters of the ruling Chinese Communist Party (CCP), has faced strict security measures.
The ban comes after airspace safety fears were raised in June when a small plane crashed into the city’s tallest skyscraper, killing the pilot and injuring 13 others.
Beijing had already banned drone sales in May 2026, with owners required to register their devices with authorities but permitted to keep them.
Now, anyone in possession of a drone could face a fine and the confiscation of their equipment.
Exemptions for drone flights may be granted for specific reasons such as counterterrorism, law enforcement, emergency relief, agriculture or scientific research.
Drones have become extremely popular in China in recent years, particularly for filming landscapes.

Shiv Sena (UBT) mouthpiece cautions Sharad Pawar against NCP merger, says it could damage his political legacy
The editorial came a day after Saamana editor and Shiv Sena (UBT) Rajya Sabha MP Sanjay Raut visited the Maharashtra Congress headquarters.
Amid speculations of merger talks between the two rival NCP factions that extended close to two weeks, Shiv Sena (UBT) mouthpiece 'Saamana' warned Sharad Pawar against compromising the principles he has upheld over decades by engaging with a faction that “grovels at the BJP’s feet”.
In an editorial titled 'Let's play the merger game', the newspaper questioned the political wisdom of the NCP (SP) engaging in merger discussions with the rival faction led by deputy chief minister Sunetra Pawar, particularly when Sharad Pawar's party is an alliance partner of the Shiv Sena (UBT) in the Maha Vikas Aghadi (MVA) and the INDIA bloc.
The editorial came a day after Saamana editor and Shiv Sena (UBT) Rajya Sabha MP Sanjay Raut visited the Maharashtra Congress headquarters and attended an event organised to mark the 137th birth anniversary of Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru, the country's first prime minister and former Congress president.
‘Credibility’ warning for Sharad Pawar
It argued that merger discussions could undermine Pawar's political credibility and ideological standing, given the rival faction's association with the BJP.
"At a time when Sharad Pawar's party is part of the Maha Vikas Aghadi and the INDIA bloc, entertaining such discussions is damaging to his political image," it stated.
The editorial said Pawar should not allow the merger exercise to damage the political legacy he had built over decades by upholding the ideals of Shahu Maharaj, Mahatma Phule, Dr Babasaheb Ambedkar and Yashwantrao Chavan.
"It does not befit Maharashtra's political traditions for Sharad Pawar to sit across the table with a faction that shamelessly grovels at the BJP's feet, thereby creating an atmosphere of confusion and suspicion in the state," it suggested.
NCP (SP) is the third MVA constituent, and Pawar was the architect of the three-party alliance in the state, formed in 2019 after the Maharashtra Assembly elections.
Cautions senior NCP (SP) leaders
It also cautioned senior NCP (SP) leaders, including Sule, former Maharashtra president Jayant Patil and current state chief Shashikant Shinde, against getting carried away by the merger discussions.
“There may be two or four people in Sharad Pawar's party who are desperately hankering after ministerial positions. But it would be wrong for Sharad Pawar to compromise the principles he has upheld throughout his long political career merely to accommodate such individuals,” the editorial said.
The newspaper further questioned the rationale behind the proposed merger, asking, “Who will merge with whom?” It said the NCP (SP), which is part of the opposition alliance, should be wary of entering into an arrangement with a faction that it accused of unquestioningly following the BJP's political line.
Swipe at Sunetra Pawar-led NCP faction
Turning its attention to the Sunetra Pawar-led NCP faction, the Saamana editorial accused senior party leaders Praful Patel and Sunil Tatkare of repeatedly changing their position on the merger.
It pointed out that while they had earlier maintained that Ajit Pawar and Sharad Pawar had never discussed a merger, they were now claiming that Ajit Pawar was keen on bringing the two factions together and that the merger would have happened had he been alive.
“Such remarks are nothing but sheer opportunism,” it said while referring to Tatkare's flip-flop over merger talks. The editorial alleged that after splitting Sharad Pawar's party, Ajit Pawar, Patel and Tatkare had joined hands with Amit Shah and entered the BJP-led government, abandoning their ideological commitments in the pursuit of power. It further claimed that Ajit Pawar had subsequently begun to feel suffocated within the BJP-led government and wanted to reconsider his political course, but Patel and Tatkare opposed the move and created hurdles in the merger process.
It also took a swipe at Patel and Tatkare over the emergence of Parth Pawar as an influential figure in the party following Sunetra Pawar's elevation as national president.
“Patel and Tatkare consider Amit Shah their leader, but Parth Pawar is now the leader of the NCP. What are they supposed to do?” it asked, indicating why both the NCP leaders are now in favour of a merger.
Dig at Maharashtra CM
The newspaper also took a dig at chief minister Devendra Fadnavis for saying that he would have to be consulted on the merger, with the editorial sarcastically referring to his claim that he was playing the role of a 'panch' (umpire). It said the number of players entering the merger game was increasing by the day, making the exercise increasingly chaotic.
While Sunetra Pawar had said that the outcome would be known at the appropriate time and Sule had declared that the merger episode was over, the editorial questioned why those involved were unwilling to accept Sule's position.
“The merger game is becoming increasingly farcical with each passing day,” it concluded.

The National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) has warned of penal action against those failing to comply with the revised prices of 137 non-scheduled anti-cancer drugs
The authority, which functions under the Department of Pharmaceuticals, has asked State drug controllers (SDCs) to strictly monitor the prices and submit their action taken reports by November 16, according to an official release on Friday (November 13, 2026).
The revised prices for the 137 anti-cancer drugs came into effect on November 9, 2026, following a gazette order issued on October 17, 2026. The order capped the trade margin on these medicines at 30%.
Based on submissions received from pharmaceutical companies up to November 11, the latest revised price lists have been uploaded on the NPPA website as well as the Pharma Sahi Daam app and portal, the Chemicals and Fertilizers Ministry said.
All manufacturers, stockists, dealers, retailers, hospitals, and medical institutions have been directed to comply with the revised prices and prominently display the updated price lists at their premises and on their websites.
The SDCs have been instructed to strictly monitor compliance across the supply chain and healthcare facilities to ensure that the benefits of the revised maximum retail prices (MRPs) are passed on to patients.
Any violation of the directive may attract overcharging proceedings under the provisions of the DPCO, 2013, the release noted.
Complaints regarding overcharging, shortage, or non-availability of medicines can be reported through the Pharma Sahi Daam app or portal, the NPPA helpline (1800-111-255), or via email at monitoring-nppa@gov.in, it added.

Ukraine’s Starshield Access Is Being Restricted Again, Zelensky Says
President Volodymyr Zelensky said the system, which Ukraine uses to guide drones, was being throttled over Russian-occupied territory. SpaceX, its developer, has denied the claim.
Ukrainian military operations were disrupted again this week along the front lines because of restrictions on Starshield, the satellite internet system developed by Elon Musk’s SpaceX and controlled by the U.S. government, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Friday.
Mr. Zelensky told reporters that speed limits of about 100 miles per hour were being enforced for Ukrainian devices connected to the system. The previous restrictions caused Ukrainian drones to lose their connection to the system if they flew above certain speeds.
Mr. Zelensky said that the latest speed limits took effect on Monday and were being enforced over Russian-occupied territories, not over all of Ukraine. That hurts Ukraine’s ability to strike Russian troops with drones in those territories.
Imposing restrictions on occupied territories is “very dangerous, because it already has political implications,” Mr. Zelensky said. “If you impose restrictions there, you are already partially recognizing the temporarily occupied territories as not ours,” he added.
Mr. Zelensky said separately in his nightly speech that the Starshield limits hurt Ukraine’s ability to use newly developed interceptors to protect its cities from Russia’s jet-powered drones. It is likely, however, that those limits would not affect interceptors in Kyiv, the capital, which is being battered by jet-powered drones but is far from the front lines.
Mr. Musk and SpaceX did not respond to requests for comment on Friday evening. SpaceX had earlier told Axios that the Ukrainian claim about throttled connectivity was false.

Judo champion shakes up French presidential race with surprise candidacy
- Published
Apart from an overwhelming urge to pin one's opponent to the floor of the house, there is no obvious connection between politics and the world of top-level judo.
That has not stopped France's much-garlanded world heavyweight champion Teddy Riner from throwing his hat into the ring for next April's presidential race.
The Guadeloupe-born 37-year-old may have no experience of public office, no party behind him, and as yet no manifesto. All so far is a slogan La France qu'on aime (The France we love), a declaration on social media, and a campaign visit to a hospital in the Seine-Saint-Denis suburb of northern Paris.
But it would be a foolhardy pundit who would totally write off his chances.
Riner is, after all, one of the most popular figures in modern-day France, regularly topping the polls for embodying the nation's "values". He is a proven winner, with five Olympic golds and 11 world championships under his belt, as well as a successful career in business.
More than 28 million people have watched his election broadcast on Instagram and X, shot with proper presidential decorum against a backdrop of books and a French flag. Some 22% told an Ifop poll within 24 hours they "could" vote for him.
Actors and television personalities have become presidents in other countries. The ex-leader of Liberia – George Weah – was formerly a professional footballer.
So why not a judoka in the Élysée Palace?
"Anyone who thinks that being out of the political in-crowd disqualifies Riner from running for the Élysée would be very wrong," says Guillaume Tabard of Le Figaro.
"But [Riner] too would be wrong if he thinks not belonging to the in-crowd is all it takes."
For now the whole of the French political world has decided to take the Riner candidacy seriously – or at least to pretend to. That is partly because he is such a popular personality that mocking his political hopes could easily rebound badly.
But it is also because the state of French politics – outside of the burgeoning forces of the hard left and hard right – is one of total disarray.
The centre-ground is floundering, with no candidate yet emerging who can inspire anything like the sense of mission of hard-right leader Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon on the hard left, who for now look set to face off in the final round of the presidential election in May.
So when a popular figure like Riner enters the race - proclaiming himself "neither left, nor right", wanting to "unite the country" and "put money back in people's pockets", railing equally against "racists" and "yobs who scare people off our streets" – politicians have to take note.
It is perfectly possible, probable even, that Riner's campaign will fizzle out after a brief period of hype, and that the judoka will after all be a joker in the pack. But it is also possible that it won't, in which case the pre-election arithmetic will need a hasty readjustment: and it won't be the centrists who are smiling.
Thus far, Riner has shown himself a master of the codes required for this kind of out-of-nowhere candidacy, the first of which is to press home the message: "Don't Worry! I'm NOT a Politician!"
In this day and age in France, anyone who smacks of the "system" is automatically downgraded in voters' eyes, so it is important to emphasise that you are only running for office because, one, you have experienced real life (unlike those loafers in Paris); and two, you have discovered that there are solutions out there for the country's many problems. Solutions that are invisible to those same blinkered apparatchiks.
All this Riner was able to express in last Monday's social media broadcast by using sophisticated rhetorical devices.
"People say I am a fool for wanting to run for the presidency," he said.
"Am I a fool? Well, if refusing to see France sink under the weight of debt; refusing to see mothers and fathers grit their teeth every time they do their weekly shop, and tremble with fear when their kids go out on the street… if all that means being a fool, then yes call me a fool."
It was a promising oratorial start for the sportsman, and certainly attracted the viewers.
- Riner equals French gold medal record 
  - Published3 August 2024
But if he is serious – and Riner says he never does anything half-heartedly - that's not how he became an Olympic champion – then the hard work begins now.
What does Riner actually want to do? Who will be on his team? Where does he position himself on the all-consuming matters of the day: pension-reform, investment in education, the cost of living, public debt, the rise of populism or Russia's war in Ukraine?
In short, how does he intend to transform his undeniable popularity as a sporting figure into a political mandate?
Broadly, Riner appears to be on the right on economic matters and law and order, but being black and of Caribbean background he is also very strong on racism. When he says he is anti-extremism, he is referring mainly to Marine Le Pen.
In other words his pitch is somewhere in the centre, and against the extremes.
The trouble is, this is already an extremely crowded area, with important figures like ex-prime ministers Edouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal signally failing to take off.
Currently there are a dozen or so candidates in the area between centre right and centre left, stretching from the Socialist-backed Raphaël Glucksman to the Republicans' Bruno Retailleau on the right.
The latest possible addition is Christine Lagarde, who steps down as head of the European Central Bank next February.
The addition of yet another contender will dilute their polling numbers even further, making a second-round qualification for Mélenchon more likely.
So no wonder the leader of France Unbowed (LFI) seemed so happy about Riner's decision to run. "We know how it goes: neither right nor left means not left," Mélenchon told reporters on Friday.
The only other politician who seems genuinely pleased, rather than putting on a fixed smile, is President Emmanuel Macron, who said Riner was a "great champion" and that politics "did not belong to the professionals".
That could be explained by the president's cool relations with his former prime ministers, Philippe and Attal, both of whom are doing all they can to distance themselves from their unpopular one-time boss.
Riner said he viewed Macron's praise as a "poisoned chalice", telling reporters on Saturday that he was "not the president's envoy, I'm not a Macronist".
Politics and judo have very little in common, but of the two, as Riner will soon discover, the more vicious is not the one that is fought out hand-to-hand after mutual acknowledgement on the tatami mat.
In Japanese, judo actually means "the gentle way".
If he starts looking like a serious candidate, Riner must know his life will be turned upside down, not just his physical form.
In politics you do not bow in respect to your opponent. You give him a metaphorical headbutt.

Hakusai, also known as napa or Chinese cabbage, is available year-round, but its peak season is late fall to winter when frost makes the leaves especially tender and sweet. It’s a must-have vegetable in hot pots, soups and stir-fries.
Hakusai actually has a surprisingly short history in Japan, only being introduced in the late 19th century around the time of the First Sino-Japanese War of 1894-95. It is said that Japanese troops on campaign ate the leafy vegetable and brought back plants and seeds with them to their villages.
However, the vegetables were pollinated in mainland China by bees and butterflies that did not exist in Japan, so the plants brought into Japan never propagated. This meant that they had to continue to be imported at high costs.
It wasn’t until the 1930s that Kichibei Numakura, a scientist from Miyagi Prefecture, was able to breed a stable species of hakusai that could be reliably pollinated by native Japanese insects. Even today, Numakura is remembered as the father of Japanese hakusai.
The recipe is for a refreshing pickled mix based on hakusai. Shio-kombu (salted shredded kombu) adds an umami boost while chili peppers add spice. It is far quicker to make than kimchi — and vegan to boot.
Use this as a side dish for a traditional Japanese meal.
Serves 3-4
Prep time: 30 minutes
Pickling time: Several hours or overnight
Ingredients:
- 400 grams hakusai
- 5 grams salt
- 2 grams shio-kombu
- 2 red chili peppers
- Toasted sesame seeds
Directions:
- Cut the root ends off the hakusai, separate the leaves and wash well. Pat completely dry very, then slice into 4-centimeter-long pieces. Sprinkle each piece on both sides with salt.
- Cut the shio-kombu into 3-centimeter pieces. Remove the seeds from the chili peppers and slice into small pieces with kitchen scissors.
- Layer the salted cabbage, shio-kombu and chili peppers in a ziplock plastic bag. Squeeze the air from the bag and seal it up. Put the bag on a baking sheet or a plate and weigh it down with another sheet or plate. Place another weight on top (a few books or a couple of cans of food do the trick).
- Several hours later (or overnight, if you have the time), take the contents out of the bag and drain any extra moisture. Arrange in a bowl, sprinkle with sesame seeds and serve.

Chiclayo, Pope Leo’s Other Home, Comes Out in Force to Welcome Father Robert
Leo XIV returned to the city in Peru where he served as bishop for eight years, drawing large crowds who remembered him before he was pope.
It was hard to believe that anyone who lived in Chiclayo, Peru, was not lining its streets on Friday.
As the motorcade of Pope Leo XIV, who has been in South America for over a week, made its way through the city that he calls one of his homes, an almost unbroken stream of people stood by the roadside, waving, holding signs and clutching white and yellow balloons, the colors of the Vatican flag.
The last time many of them saw him, he was “Padre Robert” — Father Robert — but now they jubilantly welcomed him back as Papa Leon.
A month after being diagnosed with cancer and undergoing surgery to remove a lobe of his right lung, Leo arrived at the destination that made this 12-day tour of Uruguay, Argentina and Peru a true homecoming.
For eight years, Leo — then known as Robert Prevost — served as bishop of Chiclayo, a coastal city where he is remembered for working side by side with the Red Cross during devastating floods or driving for hours to get to parishioners in the highlands.
When he stepped out on the balcony in St. Peter’s Square after being elected pope last year, the one community he mentioned was his “dear Chiclayo.” It was while serving here that he became a Peruvian citizen.

Measles strategy works – Now it must expand to more countries
Cape Town Measles Declaration pledges to cut measles deaths by half
At a landmark World Health Organization (WHO)/United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) meeting in Cape Town, leading players in the fight against measles spelled out what it will take to stop 2000 children dying every day from this preventable disease. Together with UNICEF special ambassador Angelique Kidjo, they issued a call for intensified efforts and the resources necessary to ensure all children are protected against measles.
“We can do it – we’ve done it before – in Afghanistan, Angola, in countries devastated by conflict and drought and every other form of disaster,” said Carol Bellamy, Executive Director, UNICEF. “In just three years, and against great odds, we’ve cut the number of children dying from measles by almost 25%. It’s one of the most dramatic declines in disease mortality in history. But the next 25% will be harder. With the political and financial support of donors and governments around the world, we can together save many more lives.”
The “Cape Town Measles Declaration” calls on governments to take strong action against one of the world’s most vicious and prolific vaccine-preventable childhood killers – a disease which kills 745,000 children every year. We must control this disease to meet the Millennium Development targets of a 67% reduction in under-five mortality by 2015. The world leaders are well aware of the urgency. Last year, the UN General Assembly Special Session on Children set a 2005 target date to reduce measles deaths from 1999 levels by 50%. This year, the World Health Assembly, which includes 192 member states, endorsed the WHO and UNICEF measles strategy to combat the disease.
“When 30 million children are affected and 745,000 children die every year, you have to think big,” said Dr. LEE Jong-wook, Director-General of WHO. “Since the launch of the WHO-UNICEF strategy to reduce measles deaths in 2000, we have delivered measles vaccine to more than 200 million children globally. We know the strategy works. An additional half a million children are alive today because of all the partners’ efforts. But if we’re to prevent more deaths, we must do more. And we’ll need help from governments and from the international community.”
The campaign against measles has been dramatic – hundreds of thousands of children saved, the virus almost banished from the Americas and transmission cut drastically in many African countries, where the Measles Initiative Partnership has been the driving force behind the campaign. WHO and UNICEF have identified 45 countries as the highest priority for mortality-reduction strategies, accounting for 95% of global deaths from measles.
“It has been astonishing to see the results of the immunization programme in Africa,“ said Dr Mark Grabowsky, Senior Technical Officer, American Red Cross. “Now we have proof that we can reduce measles mortality even in countries torn apart by conflict, if governments are committed, communities are engaged and we have the support of donors, NGOs and volunteers. What we have accomplished so far through the Measles Initiative Partnership gives great hope for the future, and the many thousands of children we can still save.” The foundation of the measles mortality-reduction strategy is the re-invigoration of national immunization systems. At the Cape Town meeting, delegates discussed strategies with governments and policy makers for strengthening routine immunization services and making the life-saving measles vaccine available to all children as a matter of course.
”It’s not just about reducing childhood deaths today. We need to be in this for the long haul and this means a sustainable reduction in childhood deaths, which only a strong national health system can guarantee,” said Dr Stephen L. Cochi, Deputy Director, National Immunization Program, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). ”This kind of international focus and commitment gives us the opportunity to build that strength – boosting safe routine immunization services, establishing international laboratory networks and increasing surveillance to detect and respond to outbreaks.”
“Today the call to action is clear,” said Mr Nick Farrell, Senior Programme Officer, International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies. “ We have to ensure every child receives a second opportunity for measles immunization in these 45 countries, no matter how remote or marginalized, regardless of barriers of conflict, culture and poverty.
“To date we have seen tens of thousands of health workers and volunteers trek across mountains and deserts in all kinds of conditions to find these children to ensure they receive the life-saving vaccine,” said Timothy E. Wirth, President of the United Nations Foundation. “We are witnessing incredible commitment from ordinary people. They need – they deserve to be backed up by the world’s political will and financial support.”
Ms Angelique Kidjo, Special UNICEF ambassador, believes that the Cape Town Measles Declaration indicates a clear path towards a giant achievement in children’s health.
”The world has committed, to drastically reducing the devastating, pointless waste of young life,” she said. “If we reach our targets for measles, we will have taken a huge step towards keeping that promise. I believe we can get there – but only if we make it a priority to turn this declaration into action. This goal deserves all we can give. We must do whatever is necessary.”
Further information:
- Of all the vaccine-preventable diseases, measles remains the leading childhood killer. Measles is an important cause of overall under 5 childhood mortality.
- Measles affects over 30 million children. More than 745,000 die each year from measles – more than half of them in Africa.
- A safe, effective and inexpensive measles vaccine has been available for over 40 years.
- Measles accounts for an estimated 50% of vaccine-preventable deaths among children.
- One million measles deaths are already being prevented each year with existing immunization efforts. With the successful implementation of the WHO-UNICEF measles strategy (including routine immunization and periodic supplementary immunization activities), an additional 500,000 measles deaths can be prevented each year.
- Measles is a highly contagious vaccine-preventable disease caused by the measles virus. It is one of the most readily transmitted communicable diseases and probably the best known and most deadly of all childhood illnesses. Measles causes a high fever, rash, cough and can kill. It affects mostly children, but also young adults. Children usually do not die directly of measles, but from its complications such as pneumonia and diarrhea which attack their weakened immune systems.
- It costs less than a dollar to immunize a child against measles.
- A critical goal is to reduce measles mortality by 50% by 2005 (compared to 875,000 deaths in 1999).
- The WHO-UNICEF strategy to reduce measles deaths includes: achieving and maintaining high routine measles immunization coverage – ‘the first opportunity’ to infants; Providing a ‘second opportunity’ for measles immunization for all children through periodic supplementary immunization campaigns; Ensuring high quality measles surveillance is in place to detect and respond to outbreaks; and improving management of complicated cases.
- Collaborating partners include: WHO, UNICEF, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the United Nations Foundation, humanitarian and non-governmental organizations, including the American Red Cross and the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, governments of countries affected by measles, development banks, donor governments (e.g. Canada, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States of America).
- The importance of developing long term immunization planning cannot be underestimated. This includes ensuring measles activities are fully integrated with other national health goals, establishing high quality surveillance, mobilizing necessary human and financial resources and planning for financial sustainability of measles mortality reduction activities.

A two-hour hearing in Spain’s high court Friday on the US extradition request of wealthy leftwing activist and philanthropist James “Fergie” Chambers turned out to be a study in contrasts.
Chambers’s defense took most of the session to query the US citizen and detail irregularities in the Trump administration’s extradition request – several of which the Guardian has reported on – as well as the figures of Spanish law that would lead the three-judge panel to deny the request; while the prosecutor sped through his case, head down, asking Chambers no questions at all.
Notably, neither the judges or the prosecutor asked Chambers to address the insinuation in the extradition request that the wealthy activist had supported Hamas. Chambers’s case is the first known instance of the US seeking to extradite a citizen over alleged support for Hamas, an accusation apparently tied to an international money laundering charge and donations to organizations helping Palestinians in Gaza.
But the defense’s queries did allow him to speak for the first time since his 10 July arrest in Ibiza about events at the center of the case: 2023 protests against Israeli weapons manufacturer Elbit in Massachusets and New Hampshire and 2024 transfers of $7.2m to Tunisia, where he lived at the time. The latter was buttressed with testimony from a financial expert.
On the whole, Chambers painted a picture different from the depiction contained in the extradition request, that of a violent backer of Hamas on the run from the US. At one point, he noted that his family’s next door neighbor in Tunis was the US ambassador.
The court will decide next week on extraditing Chambers. If the decision is affirmative, Spain’s council of ministers can reverse the court’s decision. This means Chambers’s extradition may be among the last decisions made under Pedro Sánchez, the socialist prime minister, before national elections on 29 November.
Friday’s hearing began with Chambers’s defense asking about his wealth. A self-described communist and anti-imperialist, Chambers sold stock back to his family’s business, Atlanta-based Cox Enterprises, worth about $250m in mid-2023.
Then he started a foundation, he told the court. He and the foundation’s three-member board decide on funding and ensure that no projects seeking support are under US sanctions, Chambers said. The foundation has funded an estimated 100 progressive and humanitarian projects in 20 countries, according to his partner, activist and actor Stella Schnabel – including, Chambers said Friday, organizations in Gaza working on issues such as “medical treatment for children, transportation out of dangerous areas and clean water and food”.
Two of the request’s three charges – riot and conspiracy to riot – are related to the late-2023 protests against Elbit.
Chambers detailed his participation in the protests: locking himself to a door, marching in the street and – in New Hampshire – standing in the road, speaking to the media and paying bail for four protesters who were eventually found guilty of misdemeanor charges and served 30 days in jail.
As for the $7.2m, the defense and a financial expert serving as a witness laid out how ten bank transfers from the US to Tunisia mostly went to sponsor the football club Club Africain – described by Chambers as “one of the largest football clubs in Africa” – and a sporting business Chambers launched while living in Tunisia.
“Is there any indication that the money went to support terrorist activities?” asked defense attorney Aitor Martínez. “None,” said financial expert Albert Deulofeu Schilt.
Then, in about 15 minutes of rapid-fire monotone, prosecutor Juan Hernández Villalba laid out a wholly different picture of Chambers as backing “an organized structure … aimed at repeatedly committing illegal acts … together with funds destined for terrorist organizations”.
He accused the defense of laying out the facts of the case “in a fragmented way … when what’s most relevant is an evaluation of the whole picture”.
“The extradition petition isn’t based on ideology or political statements, but on actions [Chambers] organized, financed and carried out, causing material damage,” Hernández Villalba asserted.
The actions against Elbit “were presented as a simple protest”, he said. “Nevertheless, the actions described by the US were planned for days … with objectively violent content.”
Given all this, the prosecutor said, “there are more than enough indications to consider … that [Chambers’s] funding was aimed at terrorism”.
Among the 100-plus people in varying time zones following Friday’s hearing on the court’s YouTube channel was Irish film-maker and journalist Sinéad O’Shea, whose documentary on Chambers called All About the Money makes its New York premiere this weekend. It covers the time period cited by the FBI affidavit underpinning the US request. O’Shea said that extradition case “builds a false narrative which begins with the protest in New Hampshire – a piece of vandalism at worst and for which people ended up serving 30 days. I saw myself the football club in which he invested in Tunisia and his donations to Palestinian and other charities are a matter of public record. It is impossible not to see this as a politically motivated case.”
Chambers’s views have been extensively profiled in US media. A week after the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks on Israel, he posted on X about Israel’s response: “Stop calling it ‘collective punishment’/There’s nothing to be ‘punished’ for/No faction of the Palestinian resistance, Hamas or other, has done *anything* wrong/It’s simply genocide/Like it has been.”
Dressed in dark jeans, a grey-blue shirt, a black jacket, with a close-cropped haircut and mustache, Chambers got the last word during the hearing.
“To this day I cannot understand why I have been in prison since July for what amounts to speaking emotionally and committing minor offenses of public disturbance,” he said.
“I’ve never had any contact with any terrorist organization. I’ve certainly never financed any terrorist organization … and for this my family has been torn apart. I missed my grandmother’s funeral last week. My five-year-old son asks where I am every day. And my wife will give birth, God willing, in March – and I don’t know if I will be by her side.”
“[All] because I have spoken my mind, and I had a lot more money than others who have spoken their mind, in my country. And that’s all it amounts to.”

“These are conditions which are going to be closest to what we might get during the World Cup. The bigger concern is not the runs. It’s how quickly we got bundled out, around 26 or 27 overs. That is something which is always a concern,” said Gambhir.
Captain Iyer said conditions changed drastically in favour of the bowlers in the second innings but there was a stark difference in the PowerPlay performance of pacers on either side.
While New Zealand reduced India to nine for four in the sixth over, the Indian pacers were not able to make inroads in the opening powerplay. Gurnoor Brar went for runs and so did Auqib Nabi, though they did take a couple of wickets each.
Playing his first game of the series, Kuldeep Yadav was taken to the cleaners by Will Young. Kuldeep, who has hardly got game time on the tour, would be desperate to make an impact if he gets to play again.
Released from the Test squad, the left-arm wrist spinner would love to leave New Zealand shores with a performance of repute.
New Zealand, on the other hand, finds itself in another must-win situation as it aims to draw the series.
Opener Tim Seifert may have resurrected his career with a fifty in the fourth ODI, while Young, who was dropped twice in the slip cordon, went on to make a fine hundred.
The Indian pacers will need to stop the openers from taking the game away from them in the first 10 overs.
It remains to be seen if uncapped Brett Randell gets a game at the Bay Oval.
New Zealand has not lost a series at home in seven years and therefore will have plenty to play for against a wounded yet formidable opponent.

NATO is scaling back its high-level meetings and will not hold a leaders’ summit in Albania next year as previously planned amid tension within the alliance over defense spending, Iran and the war in Ukraine.
Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama said Thursday that “there is not yet a common position on when the summit will happen, for sure not in 2027.” He said that “in 2028, if it will be a summit, it will be in Tirana,” Albania’s capital.
NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte played down the issue. “We are flexible with NATO summits,” he told The Associated Press in an interview. “We have summits when we need them,” he said, and will hold the next one “when a necessity is there.”
Until about a decade ago, NATO held summits every two years.
Ministerial meetings are being cut back too
It’s not just about gatherings between U.S. President Donald Trump and his counterparts.
NATO defense ministers usually meet in October, but no talks took place last month, and none are planned for October 2027. Foreign ministers only have one scheduled meeting next year, instead of two, under what NATO describes as a “reorganization package.”
U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio have each skipped a NATO meeting or left before talks ended since they came to office. Hegseth has used defense ministerial gatherings to berate or cajole European allies and Canada.
Questions about Albania's defense spending
The planned summit in Albania highlights the alliance’s challenges. Albania was appointed next year’s host in 2025, but its name was removed from a July summit declaration.
Some allies believe that Albania is not spending enough on defense and they were reluctant to reward the country with NATO’s big event. The government in Tirana is projected to spend 2.15% of its gross domestic product on defense this year.
NATO’s target is for the 32 allies to spend 3.5% of GDP on core defense by 2035, and 1.5% on defense-related infrastructure. Albania is not the worst offender among the 32 member countries. Spain, Belgium and Slovenia are faring much worse.
Summits drain resources and have political costs
But hosting a summit itself has tremendous financial and political costs. The Netherlands required a year of preparation ahead of the 2025 meeting in The Hague, and a roughly $100 million investment.
Officials said NATO would have needed to decide on Albania by October for it to have enough time to organize a summit next year.
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, who hosted this year’s gala in his sprawling palace complex in Ankara, refurbished a military airport for leaders to arrive at, and mobilized tens of thousands of security personnel — virtually shutting down parts of the capital. Non-essential public workers were given a week off.
“There’s always a lot of security involved,” Rutte told AP. “It is a costly event to organize a meeting with 32 allies and then partner countries and the Indo-Pacific partners we have, like Japan and Korea, Australia, New Zealand.”
Asked whether it was all worth it, Rutte said: “It is.”
The challenge of keeping leaders focused
The summit in Turkey was also a political spectacle. It threatened to go off the rails even before Trump and his counterparts sat down to work.
Trump revived old talk about taking control of Greenland, a self-governing part of NATO ally Denmark, striking at the heart of the reason that the organization was formed in 1949: mutual defense.
He also demanded “loyalty,” accusing NATO of failing to back his war on Iran.
Summits are usually a sober show of resolve and unity of purpose by the member countries to dissuade any adversary that might be tempted to test NATO. European allies suspect that Russia wants to do just that.
In Ankara, Rutte led a “big reveal” defense industry splash to try to convince the American leader that allies are spending big.
Experts say a summit might not be needed
Besides the price tag, and the costs of keeping Trump on side, experts say that perhaps enough has been achieved for now. New spending goals and military capability targets have been set, and force planning was discussed in Ankara.
“There’s a strong argument to be made that if there aren’t things that merit bringing 32 leaders together, well then maybe you don’t have the meeting,” said David Cattler, Senior Fellow at the Center for European Policy Analysis think tank.
“You could go two, maybe three years,” said Cattler, a former top NATO intelligence official.
In any case, other options are available in an emergency. NATO held its first-ever virtual summit in February 2022, after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

We tested 6 popular apps to see what data they collect and share. Here’s what we found
Marketplace tested the Tim Hortons, PC Optimum, Weather Network, Facebook, Amazon and YouTube apps
Whether you are buying a coffee, groceries, checking the weather or unwinding with an online video, there’s a free mobile app for just about everything.
But a Marketplace investigation shows the cost of this convenience is your privacy – and the data you’re sharing goes far beyond what you might realize.
Marketplace tested six of the most popular Android and iOS apps in Canada — Tim Hortons, PC Optimum, the Weather Network, Facebook, Amazon and YouTube — to find out what data they collect and where it goes.
To do so, Joel Reardon, an associate professor in the department of computer science, and his team at the University of Calgary scanned the network traffic of the apps on an Android device. Privo, an organization that evaluates apps to ensure they comply with U.S. child privacy laws, also did a scan of the apps on iOS, Apple’s operating system.
While doing scans to see the network traffic of mobile apps on Android, some apps appeared to be sending information to outside companies around the world. The network scan above shows the activity from all the apps on someone’s phone, not necessarily the apps Marketplace tested. (CBC)
In their user policies, the apps we tested explicitly disclose that they collect or share certain data and that when you use the app, you accept their terms.
But Reardon and Celeste Rollason, an independent analyst who used to work with Privo, are concerned some apps collect more than they need and are sharing what they learn with others around the world.
That data ranges from your name and email address to your exact whereabouts.
“To me, this is not the internet we wanted. This is not the internet we deserve. It's turned into a monstrous data collection surveillance system,” Reardon said.
Here’s what we learned about each app we tested, and what you can do to protect your data.
Tim Hortons
(CBC)
The scan showed that the Tim Hortons app appeared to be sending data to third-party companies as soon as you launch it.
Reardon said one overseas third-party company built into the app appeared to be receiving enough information to create the equivalent of a digital fingerprint for each device, so it can be identified in the future.
“This was beyond the pale,” he said.
Some of those details include:
- The name given to the device (for example, Bob’s iPhone).
- An identifier unique to the device.
- A list of many of the sensors on the device.
- The details of the device’s camera (for example, the size of your lens).
- The names of the ringtones and alarm sounds used.
- The names of Wi-Fi routers near you, which Reardon said can be used to determine your location.
Rollason said the third party brands itself as a fraud protection service. She noted the amount of data collected “seems quite excessive” to validate the purchase of a cup of coffee.
Marketplace isn’t identifying any of the third-party companies or their locations because accountability rests with the app developer.
In a statement, Tim Hortons’ director of communications Michael Oliveira said this third party only collects this information for “fraud prevention, account protection, and payment abuse prevention, not for marketing or advertising … or to work around guests’ choices regarding those activities.”
Oliveira said the information collected can help detect if a never-before-seen device is being used on a customer’s account or if a “threat actor” is pretending to be a customer.
He also said the third party is not allowed to sell the data and that Tim Hortons does not sell users’ personal information to third-party companies or data brokers.
PC Optimum
(CBC)
The test showed the PC Optimum app appeared to be sending 10 outside companies information about which products users are searching for — even if the product was sensitive like a search for prenatal vitamins.
One third-party company appeared to be receiving a user’s latitude and longitude and an identifier unique to the device.
The scan also showed the app sending different details to an overseas third-party including:
- The first name of the user.
- Their unredacted email address.
- Their PC Optimum member number.
- An identifier unique to the device.
- How the user interacts with the app, like when they open the app and what they do in the app.
Reardon and Rollason said the data collection seemed to be more than what was necessary for the app to work properly. Based on their experience, they say they didn’t understand why the app needed 10 outside companies to know what users were searching for.
In a statement, Loblaw, the company behind PC Optimum, said the company has never sold personal information and continually reviews and strengthens its systems to protect people.
It said the information collected through Loblaw apps supports everyday features for customers such as shopping online and finding nearby stores.
The Weather Network
(CBC)
The scan showed that when users allowed the Weather Network app access to their location, it appeared to be sending a third-party company those details for targeted advertising, including:
- A user's precise latitude and longitude.
- The user’s local weather conditions.
- The device’s advertising ID (unique to each device).
Reardon said it could allow the app to send you advertisements based on where you are or “so you could get ads for a rainy day.”
He also noted it creates a “location history, because all of [the data sent] are bridged by this one thing that doesn't change — this device identifier.”
Rollason said understanding a user’s behaviours is key to advertisers.
“Are you using your phone more when it's raining or you're in the house, perhaps, versus going out on a nice day?” she said.
Pelmorex, the parent company of the Weather Network, said in a statement that the Weather Network does not sell any user data to third parties and data brokers. It said the app only uses location data when a user allows it and uses that data to provide the local weather and show relevant ads. It also said users can access the weather without giving the app their location.
(CBC)
The scan showed when users give the Facebook app access to their camera roll to post one image, the app appeared to collect the metadata of other images and videos on the device that were not uploaded.
Metadata contains details like the name of the file, the date and time it was taken and the camera settings.
For whatever image or video is actually posted to Facebook, the scan appeared to show the app also collected the latitude and longitude of where the image was taken.
The app also tracked what users do while using Facebook, including every scroll and how long you linger on something.
Reardon and Rollason noted Facebook didn’t appear to share any data with third-party companies during the scan.
Meta, the parent company of Facebook, had no comment on Marketplace’s findings; however, its privacy policy does state it collects this data. The policy also says “we don't sell any of your information to anyone.”
Amazon
(CBC)
The scan showed Amazon appeared to be collecting what users searched for, even if the product was sensitive, along with the device’s advertising ID.
It didn’t show Amazon sending data to any third-party companies during the scan.
“This is to be expected with these very large companies because they have the resources to have their own ad network,” Reardon said.
Amazon said in a statement it never sells customers’ personal data. It also said it designs products and services to “protect their privacy and to put them in control of their experience."
YouTube
(CBC)
The scan didn’t show YouTube sending data to any third-party companies at the time of the test. The data appeared to only be going to the U.S.
Marketplace also tested if YouTube would follow the rules of its parent company, Google, and not play targeted advertising while a user was watching children’s content.
The test found no targeted ads while watching a children’s video.
Google said in a statement it doesn’t sell personal information.
‘You lack total control’
Ann Cavoukian, the former privacy commissioner of Ontario, said Canada’s current privacy laws aren’t strong enough, and the country's privacy commissioners also need to step up.
Speaking generally, she also said companies should be prioritizing people’s privacy by only collecting what they need and deleting data when they don’t need it anymore.
“You lack total control,” Cavoukian said. “It can be used in a variety of unorganized ways. It can come back to haunt you.”
Ann Cavoukian served as the privacy commissioner of Ontario from 1997 to 2014. (CBC)
The Office of the Federal Privacy Commissioner of Canada declined an interview, but a spokesperson said Marketplace’s findings raise “a number of concerns.”
Speaking generally, the office of Canada’s AI Minister Evan Solomon said in a statement that Canadians need privacy protections that “keep pace with changing technology and the ways companies collect, use and share their data.”
His office also noted the government introduced Bill C-36 to give people more control over their information and to force companies to be more transparent and accountable about how they handle people's data. The bill is still before the House of Commons and has received praise and criticism from privacy experts.
How can you protect your data?
Cavoukian said people should ask companies what data is being collected, why it’s being collected and ask that it be deleted as soon as the company doesn’t need it anymore.
Reardon and Rollason said there’s little you can do to stop the transmission of data because apps on your device, and the third parties in those apps, may be sending or collecting information even when your device is out of reach.
They said deleting apps if you’re not using them and only keeping what you need is the best protection.

Welcome to Kernel Panic, a weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here.
With so much going on all the time, you may not have thought about ransomware and data extortion attacks in a minute, even though they’ve been among the the biggest cybersecurity threats to institutions—and, by extension, people—over the past decade. But in the new era of AI-powered and automated cyberattacks, the danger posed by ransomware is only increasing as cybercriminals profit by combining established methods with new techniques made possible or more accessible by AI.
It is difficult to determine exact numbers of ransomware attacks, given that victims don’t always disclose incidents and attackers wildly inflate their claims. But researchers who specialize in tracking and attempting to de-duplicate the field agree that claimed incidents have spiked over the last few months. Some put the number of alleged ransomware attacks on leak sites—where groups post alleged victims—at nearly 3,000 attacks over the summer. This would mean a 20 to 40 percent increase since the spring by some estimates. And, crucially, researchers emphasize that while volume always fluctuates somewhat, ransomware attacks overall have been consistently and concerningly elevated in recent years.
“What we see is most of the recent increase was fueled by international attacks; the United States was a little more steady, but still high, still a lot of attacks,” says Cynthia Kaiser, former FBI cyber deputy director who now leads research for the anti-ransomware platform Halcyon. “Internationally we’re seeing a lot more attacks. That to me is the really new part, and I do think it is in part fueled by AI.”
Fully AI-powered ransomware attacks have yet to emerge, perhaps because the criminal business model already works so effectively. But cybercriminals do appear to be using LLMs for some of the more mundane aspects of their attacks.
“We are seeing AI relied on more heavily in certain aspects of the ransomware attack chain, such as creating better phishing emails and in the negotiation process, but the ‘successful’ ransomware groups are still largely human operated,” says Allan Liska, a longtime ransomware researcher and threat intelligence analyst at Recorded Future. “But the fact that these groups are experimenting heavily with AI means that this could change going forward, and change quickly.”
Kaiser notes that broader trends in scamming are always relevant to ransomware, because attackers often use the same types of phishing and social engineering techniques to gain initial access to targeted systems. In Japan, for example, successful scamming has spiked drastically in recent months as AI enables foreign attackers to generate consistently convincing content in Japanese for the first time.
A few ransomware groups—namely, the Gentlemen, Qilin, and Akira—have emerged as some of the most prominent and stable operations in recent months. However, in their shadow is a range of smaller groups, emerging actors, and fragmentation of the ransomware ecosystem. In recent weeks, multiple new ransomware groups have appeared and quickly claimed to have attacked dozens of businesses. Halycon’s analysis says around 111 ransomware groups made claims of attacks between July and September this year.
One new group calling itself Global Secret Group claimed attacks on 48 victims, with more than half of these being listed on the same day, according to security firm ReliaQuest’s analysis. Another, called Storm, listed 71 victims in just 20 days. Not all of the attacks may be legitimate, but they still cause uncertainty for businesses.
“That growth has all happened because, in my eyes, this acceleration that AI has provided to these threat actors, essentially allowing for them to go out and start their own groups,” says Brandon Tirado, the director of threat research at ReliaQuest.
Instead of being beholden to traditional “ransomware-as-a-service” providers, all of the researchers Kernel Panic spoke to say they have seen more lone-wolf operators branching out. Tirado says his team recently managed to identify who is behind one new group and found that it is being run by an inexperienced teenager who has made more than $800,000 in under two weeks. He declined to name the teen publicly.
Halcyon’s Kaiser agrees that more actors are using AI to attempt to strike out on their own with expanded capabilities to trick targets, exploit vulnerabilities, check their code, and even compromise other groups’ remote-access tools to gain redundant access to a victim in case one avenue gets blocked. But she adds that it’s still not clear how successful these upstarts will be long-term. She suspects that many of them may surge initially and then burn out, because they don’t have the institutional knowledge and expanded resources of an established group.
While established attackers typically conduct “double extortion” attacks in which they deploy traditional ransomware that encrypts a victim’s systems while also exfiltrating a target’s data and then threatening to publish it online, those operating independently may be more likely to focus solely on data extortion to simplify their operations.
“The number of attacks that Recorded Future has seen this year already dwarfs the total number for 2025,” Liska says, “but the number of attacks involving encryption may actually decrease year over year.”

SpaceX Starship re-enters Earth, lands at same spot from which it launched a day ago
Company hopes accomplishment will further efforts to create fully reusable rocket
SpaceX's Starship spacecraft on Saturday returned from its longest flight in orbit yet to the Texas launch tower it was launched from a day prior, demonstrating the first key recovery of the rocket system's centerpiece vessel in the company's decade-long effort to develop a fully reusable rocket.
The towering two-stage rocket's Super Heavy booster — the rocket's bottom half — carried Starship to space on Friday, lifting off from SpaceX's Starbase, Texas, facilities. That booster had failed to return to the launch pad some 10 minutes after liftoff because of an onboard navigation issue, nixing SpaceX's plan to recover both parts of the rocket for the first time.
But the Starship upper stage's successful return after orbiting Earth 14 times for over 22 hours marked a key engineering milestone in the whirlwind, multibillion-dollar development of Starship, which billionaire Elon Musk sees as the future workhorse for SpaceX's satellite business and ambitions to put humans on the moon and eventually Mars.
After deploying 26 Starlink satellites in orbit Friday night while cruising some 260 kilometres in altitude, Starship on Saturday fired one of its engines to begin an atmospheric plunge. It faced blistering heat as its orbital speed of some 27,000 kilometres per hour slowed to a supersonic free-fall in the skies above SpaceX's Starbase facilities on the Gulf coast of south Texas.
The spacecraft then reignited three engines to flip itself in a vertical position and steer itself toward the launch tower, where two mechanical "chopstick" arms clasped onto the spacecraft as it hovered in place.
SpaceX's dominance in the global launch industry has been centred on its workhorse Falcon 9 rocket, which has launched more than 700 times since 2010. That rocket's first stage is reusable, but its second stage — the part that delivers payloads into orbit — is discarded into the ocean after each flight.
With Starship, Musk wants a rocket system that can fly to space and back in a manner and tempo akin to commercial airplanes.
Though Saturday's Starship recovery is a key milestone in that effort, SpaceX has yet to recover both Starship stages in a single mission. And Starship's heat-shield, composed of black hexagonal tiles that protect it from the blazing heat of atmospheric re-entry, is itself not yet fully reusable.
SpaceX is trying to engineer new tile designs that will require little to no refurbishment after each mission.
NASA's Space Shuttle system that ferried astronauts to the International Space Station before its 2011 retirement was partially reusable; its booster stages that got it off Earth were discarded after each flight. The reusable spacecraft itself had to go through extensive refurbishment before re-flying.

Real Madrid's Vinícius Jr sends surprise message to boy who lost his legs in Sudan's war
- Published
In a dark room in Cairo, a 13-year-old boy looks up at a television screen, barely blinking.
The screen flickers and Real Madrid's superstar winger Vinícius Júnior appears addressing the young boy directly, in Arabic: "Zaher, mahaba" - Hello Zaher.
Zaher barely moves, his eyes wide, locked on his favourite footballer.
We first met Zaher a year ago in the ruins of Sudan's capital, Khartoum. He was a small quiet child, scarred by war - one of millions of children whose lives have been upended since the country's army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) started fighting in 2023.
More than 17 million children are now in need of humanitarian assistance in Sudan, according to the UN children's charity, Unicef. It says it has been able to verify that at least 4,300 have been killed or maimed, although it believes the true figure is far higher.
Zaher had lost both his legs in a drone strike. With little access to specialist treatment, he dreamed of the day he might walk and play football again.
More than a year later, as we walk into an apartment in the Egyptian capital, Zaher greets us with an enormous hug. His mother, Habibah, embraces us too.
The boy we remember as shy and withdrawn is almost unrecognisable. He is confident, cheeky and full of smiles. And he is standing tall on two new prosthetic legs.
For almost a year, Cairo has been his home. Here, he has undergone surgery and months of rehabilitation, and is now able to walk and kick a ball again.
When we met in 2025, he had told us his favourite footballer was Vinícius Júnior. We were able to pass this on to the Real Madrid star, who said he wanted to send a personal video message of support. Reunited in Cairo, we gather round to watch it together.
"I was made aware of your story. I know how difficult the last few months must have been for you," the Brazilian footballer begins.
Vinícius has become a leading voice challenging racism in football and supporting black people, and a smile spreads across Zaher's face as the player tells him: "You are a hard-working black man. I really hope you will make good use of your new prosthetic legs, that you return to playing football and that you find happiness. You deserve it."
Then comes an invitation: "I would like to invite you to attend a Madrid match. We can spend the day together."
Overwhelmed, Zaher gets up and leaves the room. A few moments later, he returns wearing his new Vinícius Jr football shirt. He hopes that one day he will be able to get a visa and accept the offer.
"Tell Vinícius, I love him," he says. "His message has really uplifted me." His mother Habibah says she feels "like the whole world is cheering Zaher on, wanting him to succeed".
Zaher lost his legs in 2024, when he and his mother had been trapped in Khartoum. Much of the city had become a battleground as it was torn apart by fighting between Sudan's army and the RSF.
Food and basic supplies were running short and the family did not have enough money to flee. To survive, they sold lentils on the streets.
Then one morning, as Zaher and his mother worked side by side, a drone struck.
"I looked at him and he was bleeding. There was blood everywhere," Habibah explained last year.
She was devastated. "He would wake up and ask: 'Why did you let them cut off my legs?' I couldn't answer."
Back then, Zaher was wheeling himself through the rubble of his neighbourhood in a wheelchair, past burnt-out cars, abandoned tanks and shattered homes.
Before the war, Zaher had loved football. After the drone strike, he could only play on his knees, a painful process that put him at risk of serious infection.
"I wish I could have prosthetic legs so I can play football with my friends like I used to," he said at the time.
There seemed little prospect of that happening, but his story resonated far beyond Sudan, prompting an outpouring of support from people around the world.
Among them was Dena Latif, a UK-based lawyer of Sudanese origin. After seeing the BBC report, she helped spearhead an online campaign raising £45,000 ($60,000) for his medical care.
Unable to get the treatment he needed in Sudan, Zaher had to leave the country, which was far from straightforward. He and his mother had no passports and their birth certificates had been destroyed during the war.
After months of planning, he and his mother were able to fly to Cairo where an apartment had been prepared for them, with food in the fridge and medical appointments arranged.
For the first time in years, their immediate concern was no longer simply how to survive.

  - Published13 November 2025
Zaher underwent further surgery, followed by months of physiotherapy and training to learn to use his prosthetic legs. He also received psychological support to help him process the trauma he had been through.
"He was shy, a little bit depressed, sad," says Dr Bintelmuna Eltayeb , one of the doctors involved in his care. "To get a smile out of him was almost impossible, but now you can see he's laughing. He has great confidence in himself."
His transformation has been as much psychological as physical, say those close to him, and Dena says Zaher now approaches life with a determination that has surprised them.
As we spend time with Zaher, he laughs and jokes, making up for some of the childhood that war has taken from him.
He is eager to try new things, from horse riding to cycling, and wants to become an airline pilot. He hasn't had a game of football yet but is looking forward to playing with his friends back home.
For Habibah, watching her son regain his confidence has brought enormous relief. But she worries about his future, his education and how he will be received in Sudan, a country still locked in civil war.
The state of emergency has been lifted in their home city, Khartoum, with the Sudanese army back in control there. But throughout the capital, buildings have been left destroyed - burned, blackened and looted.
Concerns over security remain and 41% of Sudan's population are experiencing high levels of food insecurity, according to a recent statement released by the US and 30 other Western states. The group also warned of "potential famine".
"I hope that Zaher's story doesn't end with him," says Dena. She hopes his recovery will attract more attention and funds for the thousands of other Sudanese children who have suffered life-altering injuries.
Zaher and his mother are now back in Khartoum. They hope that as the city is more stable at the moment, he will be able to get his prosthetic legs checked and adjusted there as he grows.
Despite the safety they found in Cairo, they missed their home, family and friends. And while Zaher has been given a chance to reclaim his childhood, millions of other Sudanese children are still waiting for theirs.

The Federal Aviation Administration grounded all US flights Friday afternoon, due to “extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety,” the agency said in a statement. Flights already in the air will be allowed to land, the agency said, but no new ones are permitted to take off.
In a post on X, US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said that the ground stop was related to a communication issue affecting Air Traffic Control Centers.
The ground stop came after widespread reports of radio frequency outages among several of the nation’s most critical Air Traffic Control Centers, including in Boston, Chicago, and New York.
The FAA has not provided any additional details, and the agency did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Nationwide ground stops are rare. The FAA halted all air traffic on September 11, 2001. In January of 2023, a ground stop was issued after an outage to a critical system that the FAA used to distribute real-time data and warnings to pilots, known as NOTAM (Notice to Air Mission).
At San Francisco International Airport on Friday, hoards of confused travelers lined up to speak with airline staff. A number flights at the airport had already been delayed because of high winds, and the FAA ground stop was now compounding the issue.
“The FAA has issued a nationwide ground stop,” a United Airlines employee said over the intercom at Terminal 3 near the E departure gates. “This is a nationwide event.”
This is a developing story. Please check back for updates. Louise Matsakis contributed reporting.

5th soldier dies from CFB Wainwright fire: DND
Pte. William Douglas Dal Bianco died in hospital Friday from his injuries
A fifth soldier has died as a result of the fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta, the Department of National Defence says.
Pte. William Douglas Dal Bianco, of the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry (3 PPCLI), died in an Ontario hospital Friday from injuries he sustained in the fire on Oct. 17, the department said in a news release on Saturday.
National Defence Minister David McGuinty and military officials, including Gen. Jennie Carignan, the country's top soldier, were quoted in the release, offering condolences to loved ones and troops who knew him.
"We will honour his dedicated service and continue to stand with all those affected by this tragedy along the difficult road ahead," Carignan said.
The tragedy at CFB Wainwright, located roughly 200 kilometres southeast of Edmonton, occurred during afternoon live-fire training.
Military officials have previously said a grass fire was burning in a permanent danger area within the base, preventing base firefighters from accessing it. Sudden strong winds in the region — Environment and Climate Change Canada issued weather warnings that day for various parts of Alberta — rapidly spread the flames.
The fire initially killed four service members and injured 39 others.
Saturday's news release says 24 soldiers are still in hospital.

In early November, an image spread online claiming to show U.S. President Donald Trump posing for a photograph with comedian Russell Brand, social media influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate, mixed martial artist Conor McGregor, former boxer Mike Tyson and former football player Lawrence Taylor.
The alleged photograph showed (archived) Trump with his thumbs up, surrounded by a group of men convicted or accused of committing sexual offenses. An X post listed the names of the men at the alleged gathering:
Every MAGAt in this picture has been accused, indicted, convicted of, or found civilly liable for sex crimes. Three are currently in jail.
Andrew Tate @Cobratate - Indicted/Charged with multiple counts or rape and human trafficking
Russell Brand @rustyrockets - Convicted of Rape
Donald Trump @DonaldTrump - Civilly Liable / A federal Judge stated he raped E. Jean Caroll
Mike Tyson @MikeTyson - Convicted of Rape
Conor McGregor @TheNotoriousMMA - Civilly liable for Sexual Assault
Lawrence Taylor @LT_56 - Registered Sex Offender. Arrest for sex with a minor.
Tristan Tate @TateTheTalisman - Indicted/Charged with multiple counts or rape and human trafficking
(X user @MAGAts_Exposed)
The above image is fake and was created by artificial intelligence. There is no authentic photograph from a reputable media outlet showing these men together, let alone any evidence or reporting that they had all met even without cameras present. Google Gemini detected a watermark showing that the image was created or edited using Google AI.
Snopes ran the image through Google Gemini's SynthID check, a tool that scans for watermarks embedded by artificial intelligence software. That scan detected a SynthID watermark and concluded, "this image was generated or edited with Google AI, and a SynthID watermark was detected."
To confirm whether an image contains a SynthID watermark, readers can upload a photo to Google Gemini and ask, "Does this image have a SynthID watermark?" We should note, the absence of a SynthID watermark doesn't automatically mean an image is authentic, as it could have been created using other AI tools.
There are numerous signs that the image is AI-generated, namely that all the men's faces are blurred and it is of very poor quality. A video camera behind Brand is flashing light toward the photographer, creating an unnatural glow.
Using Google's reverse image search tool, we also found no reputable media outlets reporting on such an image. If such a photograph was real, it would be more widely disseminated.
The individuals in the above image have cultivated both distant and close ties to the Trump administration. The Tate brothers, who have been charged with rape and trafficking, among other criminal offenses, are connected to Trump allies, with Andrew participating in a Twitter Spaces livestream with Donald Trump Jr. As of this writing the Tates are being held at a Miami detention center without bail. Tyson, convicted of rape, has made public appearances with Trump.
Brand, who was convicted of rape and sexual assault, has appeared at numerous high-profile events led by Trump allies, including a Turning Point USA event and a Make America Healthy Again event. In November he was sentenced to more than 10 years in prison. McGregor, who was found liable of sexual assault in a civil case, has visited Trump at the White House and praised the president. In 2025, Taylor, a registered sex offender, was appointed a member of Trump's Council on Sports, Fitness, and Nutrition.
Snopes has covered numerous fake images of Trump, including one of Trump and sex offender Jeffrey Epstein on a private jet, and another one of them on a boat.
