Brainbees Solutions, the parent entity of baby and kids' products retailer FirstCry, managed to narrow its net loss by 75.1% to ₹12.6 Cr in the second quarter (Q2) of fiscal year 2026-27 (FY27) as against ₹50.5 Cr in the year-ago quarter. On a sequential basis, net loss narrowed 71.4% from ₹43.9 Cr in Q1 FY27. The listed company inched closer to profitability as operating revenue rose 14.1% to ₹2,395.8 Cr during the quarter under review from ₹2,099.1 Cr in Q2 FY26. On a quarter-on-quarter (QoQ) basis, FirstCry’s top line grew 13.7% from ₹2,106.2 Cr in Q1 FY27. Including other income of ₹41.8 Cr, the listed company’s total income stood at ₹2,437.6 Cr in the quarter under review. Meanwhile, total expenses rose 13.1% to ₹2,303.2 Cr in Q2 FY27 as against ₹2,036.9 Cr in the year-ago period. On the operational front, adjusted EBITDA declined 2.3% to ₹117.5 Cr in the quarter under review compared to ₹120.8 Cr in Q2 FY26. Adjusted EBITDA margin also rationalised to 4.9% from 5.8% in the year-ago quarter. “Our priorities remain clear – higher sustained growth, continue improving the customer experience, increase purchase frequency and strengthen profitability,” said FirstCry cofounder and CEO Supam Maheshwari in a statement. He added that the company’s consolidated business had seen its strongest revenue growth in the last six quarters while the India business had seen its best revenue growth in the last eight quarters. Giving a geographical breakdown of its top line, FirstCry said that the revenue of its India business rose 18.6% YoY to ₹1,637.9 Cr, while its international business grew 5.8% YoY to ₹249.3 Cr. However, its India business’ adjusted EBITDA dipped 10.5% to ₹112.2 Cr from ₹125.4 Cr in the year-ago quarter as raw material cost inflation, driven by rising crude oil prices, impacted its manufacturing margins. On the other hand, the international business’ adjusted EBITDA loss narrowed 15.6% YoY to ₹15.9 Cr, as the company attributed margin improvement to increased operating efficiency despite softer revenue growth. It also noted that the Middle East business grew revenue 6% YoY amid geopolitical volatility, hinting at higher growth in a more stable environment. Meanwhile, its house of brands vertical, GlobalBees, saw a 7.7% jump in operating revenue to ₹530.6 Cr from ₹492.8 Cr in Q2 FY26. Its adjusted EBITDA, too, improved to ₹19.2 Cr in Q2 FY27 from ₹10.4 Cr in the year-ago period as margins doubled. “Our Q2 growth would have been stronger had the annual sales by 3P (third-party) platforms not advanced to Q3 and had festivals like Dussehra not fallen three weeks later this year, shifting some festive sales from Sep 26 to Oct 26,” noted the management. The company’s ‘other’ business segment drove an additional ₹13.3 Cr in revenue and ₹5.3 Cr in adjusted EBITDA. In terms of operational metrics, the platform’s gross merchandise value (GMV) grew 9.2% YoY to ₹30,77.5 Cr in the quarter under review. Going ahead, FirstCry said its priorities will be to expand the service coverage and improve delivery experience of its logistics service RocketBees. It also plans to further scale its quick commerce service FirstCry Qwik, undertake assortment changes and resume store expansion. Shares of FirstCry ended today’s trading session 1.84% lower at ₹160.40.

Fuel crisis and protests pressure Chile's far-right president
SANTIAGO, Chile — Chile's ultraconservative president finds himself on the back foot after just eight months in power.
José Antonio Kast, a politician who spent a career railing against progressive issues, reproductive rights and welfare policies from the extreme fringes of right-wing politics, now finds himself with just 24% approval in the polls.
It is less than a year since Kast stormed to the presidency in December 2025 by avoiding all mention of his hardline stances on social matters, focusing instead on two hot-button issues whipped up in the national media: illegal immigration and public security.
But rather than pressing ahead with those at the top of his agenda, he has floundered. And as elsewhere around the Americas and worldwide, rising costs of living have come to hit him hard.
"Our salaries are maybe 20% of a European income, but with a similar cost of living – it's terrible," said Simón Echavarría, a 30-year-old architect, at a march in Santiago on Friday evening.
"We want to protest against the measures that have set us back on environmental issues, on human rights, even reducing the sentences of pedophiles – they are implementing things that nobody asked for," he said.
Behind him, heavily armed police blocked the streets and fired water cannons at protesters chanting and waving flags in the square.
Much of the recent ire stems from the revelation last month that Kast's government had signed decrees to cut the sentences of 56 prisoners whose crimes range from the rape of children to dictatorship-era human rights violations.
Kast has since admitted that this was an "error", but came out in support of the undersecretary who signed the decrees nonetheless.
But beneath the more egregious moves Kast has made in his first year in power is simmering discontent over affordability.
In July, Kast's government chose not to apply an anti-inflation tool available to the Chilean state to ease the rise in fuel prices brought about by the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran.
Protests exploded as prices shot up overnight and motorists joined long queues at gas stations to fill their tanks before the rise came into effect.
This week, Chile's formidable truckers' unions blockaded two major highways in an effort to exert pressure on the government and address high fuel prices.
On Friday, the strike was broken after the government backed down, sending a bill to Chile's congress which will reverse planned fuel price rises.
It is expected to be approved this month, but public anger continues to grow over the cost of living.
Politicians across the Americas who have enthusiastically aligned themselves with President Donald Trump are facing challenges similar to those confronting the U.S. administration, as rising fuel prices and the cost of everyday goods fuel public discontent.
In Argentina, far-right libertarian Javier Milei faces reelection in less than a year, with 60% of the country disapproving of his leadership amid spiraling inflation. In Peru, President Keiko Fujimori is also facing growing discontent, with 53% disapproving of her government, according to a recent Ipsos poll.
At the march in Santiago on Friday, 30-year-old veterinarian Patricia Pereira said that she was concerned about cuts to science funding, but that her discontent ran deeper.
"Here in Chile, it was a hard-won victory for children to have free education, achieved through protests, and now even that's also being called into question," she said.
Protests are likely to grow in Santiago if the government fails to address the rising cost of living. President Kast has shown little sign of doing so.
To the contrary, his budget proposal is making its way through Congress, with the government seeking cuts to education, culture, science and a host of social programs.

Lewis Hamilton has visited Egypt’s Rafah border crossing with the Gaza Strip to meet organisations sending humanitarian aid to the territory.
The seven-time Formula One world champion has spoken out about conflict and humanitarian crises in the region, and has called for peace. He has frequently posted on social media about children killed in Israeli airstrikes in Gaza and called for a ceasefire.
“I think we need to make sure we’re pushing to free Congo, free Sudan, free Syria, free Palestine. I think there’s a lot of peace that I’m hoping we get to at some stage,” Hamilton said in October.
A ceasefire agreement reached last year has halted major combat operations in Gaza, but the amount of aid reaching the territory continues to fall far short of the agreed-upon minimum of 600 trucks a day.
Israeli forces have continued to advance, expanding their control from 53% of the territory to at least 60%, an independent commission of UN experts said last month.
Airstrikes also continue, and Israeli fire along the advancing front has killed at least 196 Palestinians, including 18 women, 32 boys and 11 girls, the commission said.
Hamilton toured Egypt’s Rafah border crossing with Gaza before visiting logistics warehouses operated by the Egyptian Red Crescent, which facilitates the entry of aid to Gaza.
At the crossing, Hamilton greeted aid workers with “Assalamu alaikum” a widely used Arabic greeting meaning “peace be upon you.” He shook hands and briefly spoke to workers and officials.
Khaled Megawer, the governor of North Sinai, where Rafah is located, said the visit was intended to help Hamilton learn about Egypt’s efforts to send aid to Gaza.
The visit comes after Hamilton made his 400th race start on Sunday at the São Paulo Grand Prix at Interlagos.
The first black F1 driver, he made his debut with McLaren in 2007. He is only the second F1 driver to start 400 races after his former teammate Fernando Alonso, who achieved the milestone in 2024.

Southeast Asian leaders will call for peaceful resolutions of conflicts. Trump will join final talks
Southeast Asian leaders will gather in the Philippine capital this weekend for the annual ASEAN summit that will focus on global conflicts
MANILA, Philippines -- Some of the world’s most intractable conflicts will be high on the agenda when Southeast Asian leaders gather in the Philippine capital for annual summit meetings this weekend. U.S. President Donald Trump is expected to join them for the final talks.
The three-day summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations and their Asian and Western counterparts starts Sunday in a heavily guarded convention center in Manila Bay.
According to drafts of prepared post-summit communiques seen by The Associated Press, no breakthroughs are expected in the discussions that will focus on calling for the peaceful resolution of the South China Sea disputes, the civil strife in Myanmar and the wars in the Middle East and Ukraine.
This year, the Philippines holds the rotating leadership of ASEAN, a conservative regional bloc of 11 democratic and authoritarian states, including police states. The bloc has managed to keep together such a diverse grouping since its founding in 1967 largely because of its bedrock policy of non-interference in the members' domestic affairs.
In Manila, key rivals will again be face-to-face but no shake-ups are anticipated. ASEAN is known more for its photo-ops that project unity, cultural pomp and pageantry than for effectively dealing with the region's conflicts, including the civil war in Myanmar.
Trump will land in Manila with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday afternoon, after the main ASEAN summit meetings have concluded and the Philippines has turned over the regional bloc’s annual leadership to Singapore.
He will, however, be joining three key meetings on Tuesday night, including a special summit with ASEAN leaders over cocktails and a meeting of the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue consisting of the United States, Japan, Australia and India, according to Philippine officials.
China will be represented by its premier, Li Qiang, who will meet ASEAN leaders on Monday, but will leave before Trump arrives, the officials said.
The prepared communiques say ASEAN leaders and their major Asian and Western counterparts will exchange “views on regional and international issues of concern," before listing the conflicts that will be discussed.
“We reaffirmed our shared commitment to upholding international law, including the United Nations Charter,” the prepared statement says. It also underlines the "importance of the peaceful resolution of disputes, upholding freedom of navigation and overflight and other lawful uses of the sea, including the right of transit passage in straits used for international navigation.”
On Saturday, ASEAN foreign ministers met for pre-summit talks, linking hands and posing for a joint photo on stage, their national flags lined up behind them.
The talks, hosted by Philippine Foreign Secretary Theresa Lazaro, will include her report on a recent trip to Myanmar, where she pressed longstanding calls for the civil strife-plagued country to do more to comply with a five-point peace plan crafted by ASEAN leaders five years ago.
The leader and foreign minister of Myanmar, an ASEAN member, have been banned from attending the bloc’s annual meetings because of their government's failure to fully comply with the peace plan that calls for an immediate end to the deadly fighting that has gripped the country.
The prepared communiques also urged "all parties to commit to an immediate cessation of violence, safe and unhindered humanitarian access, inclusive dialogue with all stakeholders and the unconditional release of all those unjustly detained” in Myanmar.
On the South China Sea disputes that involve China, Taiwan and four ASEAN members — Brunei, Malaysia, the Philippines and Vietnam — substantial progress has been made in negotiations for a non-aggression pact called the “ code of conduct ” between Beijing and the regional bloc, according to three Southeast Asian diplomats who spoke to the AP earlier.
They said, however, that the pact — which has seen more than two decades of consultations and negotiations between China and ASEAN — will not be finalized this year. Negotiations about it will resume next year.
The pact aims to prevent on-and-off confrontation in the disputed waters from degenerating into a full-blown conflict that can endanger Asia’s economies.

Europe Agrees on a Team to Represent It in Talks With Russia
After coveting a seat in the Ukraine war discussions, Europe is poised to get one. The continent wants to fill it with a six-member team.
European leaders have waited on the margins of negotiations to end Russia’s war in Ukraine for months, eyeing a seat at the table. They learned this week that they would get one, and simply needed to decide which official should sit in that chair.
Instead, they decided on six.
European Union leaders concluded in Dublin on Friday that they will tap a group of major nations — Britain, France, Germany, Poland, and Italy — along with a representative from the E.U’s leadership arms, the European Council and European Commission.
In some ways, the choice of a crowd plays into jibes Americans have made about the continent’s indecisiveness: “If Europe could identify one person to speak on their behalf, that would be a bigger achievement than getting the Russians to include them in the negotiation,” Jared Kushner, President Trump’s son-in-law and a U.S. envoy, said earlier this week.
Europe’s failure to pick one negotiator leaves open the possibility that its fragmentation will diminish its influence. Even so, Europeans have underscored that they are a democracy of many nations, though, and that many voices must be represented.
“We decide on who represents us, and that is what we have done today,” said Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission.
“We need to work as a team,” António Costa, president of the European Union’s political leadership arm, said at a news conference on Friday, noting that America itself has two envoys.

Cape Verde could elect first woman president since gaining independence in 1975
Cape Verde could elect its first woman president as former Justice Minister Joana Rosa challenges incumbent José Maria Neves
Cape Verde could elect its first woman president Sunday as former Justice Minister Joana Rosa challenges incumbent José Maria Neves, who is seeking a second term.
Six candidates are competing, with a runoff scheduled for Nov. 29 if no candidate receives more than half the votes.
Rosa, backed by the opposition Movement for Democracy, is the first woman to run for president since independence from Portugal in 1975. Women have held senior cabinet posts, but Cape Verde has never had a female prime minister or president.
In Cape Verde’s parliamentary system, the prime minister directs government policy and holds most executive authority. The president’s role is largely symbolic, although the directly elected head of state can veto legislation.
The Atlantic island nation off West Africa, home to about half a million people, has a record of peaceful transfers of power and competitive elections in a region where that is rare. Nearly 77,000 Cape Verdeans abroad are registered to vote, almost a fifth of the total electorate.
Many voters feel distant from their leaders and want a president who understands their daily difficulties, while limited economic prospects were driving young people to seek opportunities abroad, said Roselma Évora, a professor of political science and gender studies at the University of Cabo Verde.
Neves, who won in 2021 with about 52% of the vote, has pledged to build cross-party support to improve housing, healthcare and education, create jobs and raise wages.
Incumbency gives Neves greater visibility, including among overseas voters, Évora said.
Rosa’s candidacy challenges traditional expectations of women’s roles in a society that remains “very patriarchal,” Évora said.
Rosa has centered her campaign on maintaining a balance of power, arguing that the country needs a counterweight to the African Party for the Independence of Cape Verde, which backs Neves and controls the government and most municipalities.
Known as PAICV, the party won a parliamentary majority in May, ending a decade of government led by the Movement for Democracy. A Rosa victory would again put the presidency and government in rival political camps.
Rosário Luz, a Cape Verde-based writer, said party loyalties mattered more than Rosa’s gender.
“We have a lot of women in politics, but we don’t have the policies for women that we should have,” she said.
Women carry much of the financial responsibility for their households in Cape Verde, but government policies have failed to address that burden, Luz said.

After the world’s hottest summer since records began in 1850, the death toll from extreme weather in 2026 is already in the high tens of thousands. That is a conservative estimate and is certain to rise much higher.
As Cop31 continues and scientists warn that climate breakdown may be accelerating, the Guardian looks back at a year of droughts, fires and floods as a reminder that, unless the world takes urgent action to cut emissions, this disastrous year will be one of the best of the rest of our lives.
January 
  
Fourth-hottest January on record
Extreme heat fuels wildfires in Australia 
  
As temperatures jump nearly 20C (68F) above average, Victoria and other southern states register new heat records, including 50C in Port Augusta and the tiny opal mining town of Andamooka. Melbourne hospitals report a 25% increase in heat-related illnesses, while authorities in many areas struggle with wildfires. Scientists say the supercharged climate has made the heatwave five times more likely. Heatwaves already cause more deaths in Australia than all other natural hazards combined.
February 
  
Fourth-hottest February on record
Mudslides kill 72 in Brazil after record rain 
  
The city of Juiz de Fora in Minas Gerais records its wettest ever month, triggering landslides that sweep away hundreds of homes in poor communities on unstable hillsides. Floods also disrupt Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo. More than 10,000 people are displaced.
March 
  
Fourth-hottest March on record
Devastating floods across much of the world 
  
In Ethiopia, at least 131 people are killed in floods and mudslides that bury entire villages. Eighty die in Kenya and 18 in Tanzania. The Arabian peninsula is battered by fierce winds and heavy downpours that flood the streets of the desert kingdom. Hailstones the size of tennis balls fall in Oman and lightning storms leave cities in the UAE inundated with water. Many areas report record rainfall. At least 30 die in Afghanistan as heavy rains trigger landslides. Hong Kong is soaked in twice the usual monthly precipitation. Flood waters in southern Russia submerge homes and leave more than 300,000 without electricity. Huge tracts of farmland are left underwater in Argentina and Chile.
World’s energy imbalance accelerates rapidly 
  
The World Meteorological Organization reveals an alarming buildup of energy in Earth’s system. More than 90% is stored in the oceans, where warming has more than doubled over the past two decades compared with the average over the previous 45 years. This makes weather more extreme and threatens health and food supplies. António Guterres, the UN secretary general, says: “The global climate is in a state of emergency. Planet Earth is being pushed beyond its limits. Every key climate indicator is flashing red.” Guterres urges the world to cut fossil fuel emissions as rapidly as possible to minimise future risks. However, CO2 in the atmosphere continues to rise.
April 
  
Second-hottest April on record
Super typhoon tears through Micronesia, Guam and Saipan 
  
At peak intensity on 12 April, Sinlaku registers a wind speed of 295km/h (183mph) – roughly the same as a Shinkansen bullet train and the joint highest recorded by a storm in the western Pacific basin so early in the year. It is also the deadliest in decades, killing 12, leaving 43,000 without power, forcing mass evacuation and causing $1.5bn (£1.1bn) in damages. This will remain one of the most powerful storms of 2026, superseded only by Super Typhoon Champi that will strike Taiwan and Japan in October.
May 
  
Second-hottest May on record
Hundreds of millions endure deadly heat in south Asia 
  
At least 47 heat-related deaths are reported in southern Asia as temperatures soar above 45C in several Indian and Bangladeshi cities, and hit a peak of 52C in Pakistan’s southern province of Sindh. Scientists warn that the climate crisis is exposing hundreds of millions of people in south Asia to longer, deadlier pre-monsoon heat.
June
  
Second-hottest June on record
Ocean heat enters uncharted territory 
  
Sea surface temperature graphs begin to jag upwards and away from all previous highs on 21 June, starting a trend that will worsen over the rest of the year. This alarms scientists because oceans absorb more than 90% of the excess energy in Earth’s system. If the seas start to release that heat then the land and air will get warmer more quickly. This coincides with the emergence of the latest El Niño, which is confirmed on 2 June.
Arctic and Antarctic swelter in unprecedented warmth 
  
Instead of the usual winter snow and ice, scientists at the Esperanza base on the Trinity peninsula of Antarctica are astonished to see rain and dirt outside their windows after an eight-day heatwave that peaked with a record temperature of 15C on 6 June. At the other end of the planet, the Arctic experiences its warmest ever June. Beliy Island, Siberia, registers 28.3C on 25 June, the highest temperature ever recorded that far north in the Eurasian Arctic.
West African deluge takes heavy toll 
  
Relentless rains claim almost 100 lives in west Africa from May to June. Record downpours of up to 140mm (5.5in) in a single day are made five times more likely and 23% more intense by the human-caused climate crisis. Floods and mudslides kill 59 in Côte d’Ivoire, 35 in Ghana and five in Togo.
July
  
Joint-hottest July on record
Fires choke Canada and Europe 
  
Almost 1,000 wildfires sweep across Canada, charring 3m hectares (7.4m acres) and sending a haze of smoke as far as New York. On 15 July Toronto registers the world’s worst air quality as a result of the haze. Smoke kills 4,000 people in Canada each year, almost four times as many as at the start of the century. Meanwhile, in Europe, prolonged droughts create tinderbox conditions for wildfires in Greece, Portugal, Italy, Norway, Germany, Spain and France. They burn 686,000 hectares in Europe, twice the average of the past 20 years.
Extreme weather disrupts US 250th birthday festivities and the World Cup 
  
Half of the US population is under a heat alert before 4 July independence celebrations, disrupting Donald Trump’s Great American State Fair on the National Mall in Washington and other events. Dozens of heat-related deaths are reported and thousands experience power cuts.
At least nine World Cup games are played in potentially dangerous heat and humidity, while fierce storms delay three matches by more than an hour, including Mexico v England.
August 
  
Hottest August on record
Nepal glacier collapse kills at least 1,300 
  
Lhende Khola river valley communities are swept away after a 2 sq km (0.8 sq miles) slab of rock and glacier ice falls 1,400 metres (4,600ft) in the Himalayas, triggering a flood of water and debris. More than 5,000 people are missing and 8,600 need medical attention. Scientists say unusually warm temperatures and long-term permafrost degradation owing to the climate crisis were among the likely causes of the catastrophe.
Europe’s murderous heat forces reactor shutdown
 
The UK and France are among a host of nations that swelter through the warmest summer (June to August) in European history. The heat kills an estimated 50,000 people in cities across the continent. Two-thirds of those excess deaths are attributable to the climate crisis. Many more are likely to have died in rural areas. As droughts spread, Romania is forced to shut down its only nuclear power station because the cooling system could not be replenished by low water levels in the Danube River.
September
  
Second-hottest September on record
Record heat and deadly storms lash Asia 
  
Hundreds are killed and millions evacuated as the world’s most populous continent experiences its hottest September and severe storms. Typhoon Dujuan kills at least 10 people in Japan, with violent winds of 144km/h and 832mm of rain in only 48 hours on the island of Izu Oshima. Three die in a mudslide in eastern China during Typhoon Saudel. At least 102 are killed in India and Nepal amid rain that is nine times the norm in some places. Eight die and half a million are affected by flooding in Bangkok, Thailand.
October
  
Hottest October on record
Governments warned to brace for peak El Niño 
  
The UN disaster relief agency urges countries to prepare for an unprecedented “wrecking ball” El Niño that is forecast to peak around the end of the year. UK authorities advise households to stockpile a few days of basic supplies. Climate scientists project more than 450,000 people globally will die by February as a result of the additional heat brought by the super El Niño.
Protests in Indonesia after deadly fires 
  
Demonstrators in Jakarta protest against Indonesia’s worst fire season in a decade, which has scorched almost 2m hectares of forest – more than twice as big an area as last year. The choking haze is estimated to have killed 3,560 people in one month alone.
Roads turn to rivers in Chile 
  
After the heaviest October rainfall in 76 years, the Chilean government declares the Santiago district of Las Condes a “disaster zone”, with more than 1,000 people evacuated from their homes, some by helicopter.
Drought and fire in the Amazon rainforest 
  
Months of drought leave some of the world’s mightiest rivers, including the Rio Negro, Madeira and Tapajós, close to record low levels, curtailing the water transport of essential goods. This coincides with a sharp rise in fire activity in the central and eastern Amazon region, releasing so much smoke that the city of Manaus registers the second-worst air quality in the world on 12 October.
November
2026 is forecast to be one of the hottest years in history
Global temperatures tie an all-time record of 2.04C above preindustrial levels, which was set in 2023. This year is forecast to be one of the four warmest years in history, along with 2023, 2024 and 2025. Sea surface temperatures are so high that the climate scientist Eliot Jacobson calculates the odds of being this far above the norm at 33tn to one. Meanwhile, the amount of CO2 in the atmosphere reaches a peak not seen in 2m years. On the plus side, global fossil fuel emissions are likely to fall this year thanks to a shift away from oil and gas owing to high prices after the US-Israeli attack on Iran, and ever cheaper renewable alternatives.

French-speaking nations hold a summit in Cambodia but an African conflict threatens a rift
France's President Emmanuel Macron and other leaders are attending a biennial meeting of French-speaking countries and territories in Cambodia
PHNOM PENH, Cambodia -- PHNOM PENH, Cambodia (AP) — Emmanuel Macron is set to attend a biennial meeting of French-speaking territories beginning Saturday in Cambodia, where the French president contending with public unrest at home will face international political challenges as an African conflict hangs over the proceedings.
The Organisation internationale de la Francophonie is holding the three-day meeting through Monday in the Cambodian capital Phnom Penh. Macron is expected to engage in bilateral discussions and join the summit meeting of the loose confederation of 90 member states and governments comprising 53 full members, five associate members and 32 observers where French is spoken.
Cambodia will take over the summit's chairmanship from Macron, who served as chair in 2024 when France was the host nation.
Before departing for Malaysia on Monday, Macron is scheduled to visit the Angkor World Heritage Site near the city of Siem Reap, where he and King Norodom Sihamoni will mark the completion of a French-supported restoration of the West Mebon temple.
The French leader's trip comes at a time of widespread domestic protests. France’s Interior Ministry said more than 600,000 people took to the streets earlier this month in a demonstration to demand higher wages and support the country’s student protest movement, which has resulted in thousands of arrests, hundreds of injuries and schools set on fire.
The summit's sticky diplomacy for Macron and other leaders will take place when participants decide on Monday who will serve for the next four years as the group’s leader and chief executive in the role of secretary-general.
The choices include candidates from two bitterly feuding African members, Rwanda's Louise Mushikiwabo, who is seeking reelection to a third four-year term, and the Democratic Republic of Congo's Juliana Lumumba, the 71-year-old daughter of the country’s martyred independence hero, Patrice Lumumba.
Congo, the United States and experts from the United Nations accuse Rwanda of backing the M23, one of about 100 armed groups that have been vying for a foothold in mineral-rich eastern Congo, along the border with Rwanda. Rwanda’s government consistently denies backing armed groups in Congo.
Congo has threatened to leave the OIF if Mushikiwabo is reelected. With a population exceeding 110 million people, over 40 million more than France, Congo is the most populous nation where French is the official language and its withdrawal would mark a significant blow to the Francophonie organization.
Two other candidates, from Romania and Mauritania, are poised to serve as compromise picks.
France is influential in the decision as the largest contributor to the OIF 2026 budget of €71.7 million ($79 million).
The outcome also could be delicate because the challenge comes on the heels of the withdrawals of Mali, Niger and Burkina Faso from the OIF announced in March 2025, following their membership suspensions over military coups.
Mali said the suspensions infringed on sovereignty, but the withdrawals also came in the context of Francophone African countries in recent decades shedding French political, military and cultural influence that they regarded as overbearing.
The summit's slogan, “Reinvest in Peace for Shared Prosperity and Lasting Stability,” is seen as a reflection of Cambodia’s recovery from years of war and unrest in the last quarter of the 20th century.
About 20 government leaders, including Canada’s Mark Carney, Vietnam’s To Lam, Rwanda’s Paul Kagame and the Democratic Republic of the Congo’s Félix Tshisekedi, are expected to attend the summit and likely will meet with Cambodia's king as well as Prime Minister Hun Manet.
Most of the summit’s agenda is uncontroversial. Documents set to be approved concern political commitment to peaceful coexistence, social, cultural and economic cooperation, resolution of crisis situations and peace-building, and the protection of cultural heritage and the promotion of cultural diversity.
Host Cambodia, which has an opportunity to showcase tourism potential and business opportunities, is holding side events highlighting commercial partnerships, cultural exchanges, science and technology.
Local political activists see the meeting as an occasion to press for more democratic freedoms in a de facto one-party state. U.N. Special Rapporteur Tom Andrews issued a statement pleading with summit delegates to uphold OIF values and pressure the Cambodian government for the release of detained rights activists.
“No one should be detained for defending human rights, reporting on matters of public concern, or voicing critical opinions,” he said.
Cambodia can lay claim to helping birth the OIF, as its late king and mercurial independence leader, Norodom Sihanouk, was one of four founders in 1970 of the Agency for Cultural and Technical Cooperation. Sihanouk was overthrown and his immediate successors did not join, as Cambodia subsequently endured civil war and the brutal rule of the communist Khmer Rouge from 1975 to 1979. Cambodia joined the Francophonie as an observer in 1991 and became a full member in 1993.

World leaders are coming to Shenzhen. What is China’s APEC message?
Analysts say the city’s transformation into a global tech hub makes it a fitting stage for next week’s APEC summit - showcasing China’s economic ambitions and push for deeper regional cooperation.
SHENZHEN: Once a little-known border town comprising fishing villages and rural settlements on China’s southern coast, Shenzhen is now preparing to take centre stage as host of one of the year’s most closely watched diplomatic gatherings.
As leaders from the 21 Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) economies prepare to gather in the Chinese megacity next week, Beijing hopes to showcase Shenzhen as a symbol of China's economic transformation - and a model of what it can now offer the region, analysts told CNA.
China has made openness, innovation and cooperation the priorities of its APEC host year, which will culminate in the Economic Leaders’ Meeting on Nov 18 and 19.
Analysts said Shenzhen’s evolution, from a magnet for foreign investment into a global technology powerhouse, makes it a fitting stage for that message.
For businesses, the test will be whether this year’s APEC summit produces practical measures that companies can actually adhere to and use, said Han Yonghui, a professor at Guangdong University of Foreign Studies (GDUFS).
“What matters more is which entities the measures apply to, when they take effect, whether transaction costs are reduced, and what channels of redress are available when disputes arise,” Han added.
FROM FACTORY FLOOR TO TECH POWERHOUSE: SHENZHEN’S RISE
With a population of more than 18 million, Shenzhen is now home to tech giants Huawei, Tencent, drone maker DJI and electric vehicle manufacturer BYD.
The city’s stunning rise from manufacturing base to global tech hub is central to why it was chosen to host this year’s APEC summit, said Xu Liping, an Asia-Pacific affairs expert at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences (CASS).
“Shenzhen has progressed from a policy-based special zone to a model of institutional opening up, and made an industrial leap from the world's factory to an innovation engine,” Xu said. 
Its transformation began in 1980, when it was designated one of China's first special economic zones - becoming a testing ground for market-oriented policies aimed at attracting foreign investment, technology and management expertise.
Late Chinese leader Deng Xiaoping’s landmark southern tour in 1992, which included a stop in Shenzhen, gave fresh momentum to China’s economic reforms.
Under President Xi Jinping, ambitions widened beyond the city. Shenzhen is now one of four core engines of the Greater Bay Area - a grand initiative to connect Hong Kong, Macau and nine Guangdong cities more closely through finance, research, manufacturing and trade.
Han from GDUFS said the city’s role had evolved and taken on more importance - from bringing in foreign capital and expertise to helping Chinese companies develop technology and expand into overseas markets.
“China’s deepening opening up is reflected in its greater capacity to jointly organise research and development, production and services with external partners while continuing to absorb global resources,” Han said.
Shenzhen-based cybersecurity and cloud computing firm Sangfor Technologies is just one example.
Founded in 2000, it began expanding overseas in 2008 and now serves more than 100,000 customers in over 100 countries and regions, according to the company.
Keith Lee, Sangfor's cloud business director, said the challenge had shifted from convincing overseas customers of its products and value to better understanding their needs.
"The challenge is no longer about proving the value of technology made in Shenzhen. It is about understanding what each customer needs as the landscape continues to evolve," Lee said.
When Window of the World, a local Shenzhen theme park, first opened in 1994, its miniature replicas of global landmarks like the Eiffel Tower and Mount Rushmore drew crowds of curious visitors - eager for a glimpse of places they might never see in person.
Decades on, the landmarks remain but the park has evolved. Robots, digital services and drone displays from Shenzhen companies now feature prominently.
Employee Wang Chao, a 44-year-old marketing executive from Hubei who joined the park in 2006, has witnessed that transformation firsthand.
“In the past, it was inconvenient for Chinese people to travel abroad, so they could come to Window of the World and see things from other countries,” Wang told CNA.
"Now, when foreign visitors come, they can also see things from Shenzhen and China through Window of the World," he said.
CHINA’S APEC JOURNEY
China has hosted APEC twice before - with this year’s summit in Shenzhen marking its third turn as host.
The first was in Shanghai in 2001, when China was also preparing to join the World Trade Organization. The central question then, said Xu from CASS, was how the country would integrate into the global economy.
By the time Beijing hosted the summit in 2014, China was the world’s second-largest economy and seeking a greater role in shaping regional cooperation.
That summit produced a roadmap towards a proposed Asia-Pacific free trade area and a plan to improve connectivity.
“This marked China’s shift from participant to agenda-setter,” Xu said.
This year's Shenzhen summit marks another shift, he added - from how China joins the global economy to what it believes it can contribute to the region.
OPEN FOR BUSINESS?
But how far does Shenzhen’s reputation for openness translate into real opportunities for foreign firms and businesses?
Singaporean entrepreneur Juana Lee, also the founder and CEO of Far Vision Consultancy, has experienced first hand both opportunities and challenges of operating in the city.
Lee first came to China in 2002 - helping relatives manage factories that produced scarves, sunglasses and umbrellas.
Work took her to the Longgang district, where she recalled ageing factories, pollution, poor transportation links and difficulty finding reliable information in English.
“It was a manufacturing world (then),” she said.
After leaving the family business around 2013, Lee set up a consultancy helping foreign companies navigate the Chinese market.
Shenzhen’s relatively low operating costs, compared with cities like Hong Kong and Singapore, made it easier for entrepreneurs to recover from financial setbacks while starting businesses, Lee said.
The city’s close proximity to Hong Kong was another draw. A direct high-speed train ride from Futian station to Hong Kong’s West Kowloon takes around 15 minutes.
But Lee has also seen newcomers struggle with unrealistic expectations - failing to understand local rules and encountering difficulties obtaining reliable information.
Some underestimate the responsibilities of running a company in the city, she said.
The businesses that do last are the ones led by owners willing to persist and learn from setbacks, she said.
Despite Shenzhen’s reputation for openness, foreign companies still encounter various barriers such as local protectionism, preferences for domestic firms and requirements to buy Chinese products, said Allan von Mehren, chief China analyst at Danske Bank.
“You can argue that Shenzhen as a symbol of openness often contrasts with the reality many foreign businesses meet when they enter the Chinese market,” he added.
THE SHENZHEN ADVANTAGE
Yet for foreign businesses to navigate and overcome those barriers, Shenzhen offers an advantage over other Chinese cities - the ability to develop ideas quickly and turn them into products.
When Singaporean entrepreneur Amit Kumar arrived at Shenzhen's Chaihuo Makerspace in June, he brought two bare circuit boards and a 3D-printed casing, according to its general manager, Ye Yu.
Kumar, founder of Singapore-based robotics and edtech firm Farm2Future Innovations, was developing an AI-powered tutor designed to answer school questions in multiple Indian languages.
Despite having no previous soldering experience, Kumar managed to assemble two working prototypes, Ye said - also developing firmware for an animated interface and launching a pre-order page within 48 hours.
He planned to return to Shenzhen to develop production moulds, build a supply chain and finalise the product, Ye added.
When Ye joined Chaihuo in 2013, its members were mainly enthusiasts experimenting with open-source hardware and robots.
Today, the community has expanded - now attracting people working in sectors like agriculture, education and environmental work - who want to turn their ideas into physical products.
Developers are able to draw on Shenzhen’s vast network, she said. They can source materials like chips, circuit boards, as well as casings and moulds - and also find factories able to produce small test batches while adjusting them as designs evolve.
“What makes Shenzhen special is that it greatly shortens the distance between an idea and a product,” Ye said.
BEYOND APEC
Speaking at a briefing on Saturday (Nov 14), Shenzhen Mayor Li Yun said measures introduced to make the city more convenient for overseas visitors - covering entry, transport, payments, education and healthcare - would be made permanent if they proved effective.
“We will do everything possible to turn the outcomes of hosting APEC into development gains that better benefit all residents,” he said.
Whether APEC can turn Shenzhen’s economic strengths into broader regional cooperation - while also easing concerns over market access and competition - remains to be seen, analysts said.
Analysts said much would depend on what APEC economies agree in Shenzhen, as US-China competition continues to reshape trade, technology and global supply chains.
This week, China extended its trade truce with the US ahead of the APEC summit, where Trump is expected to meet Xi.
But wider disputes over tech and market access remain unresolved.
“China needs to respond to external uncertainty with the certainty of cooperation,” said Han from GDUFS.
Xu from CASS noted that Singapore and other Southeast Asian economies could benefit from closer links in digital payments, services trade and green development - but would also be concerned about access to China’s market, dependence on Chinese suppliers and competition from larger Chinese companies.
Businesses would want clearer rules on fair competition and cross-border data flows, said Han - and would also want to know how investment could improve local skills and industrial capacity.
“What the Shenzhen summit promises is to translate cooperative consensus into institutional arrangements that enterprises can actually use,” he added.
Paperless trade offers one practical test.
If customs and other trade systems across APEC economies can recognise the same electronic documents, companies could spend less time submitting paperwork repeatedly when moving goods across borders.
APEC research estimates that paperless trade could cut transaction costs by almost 6 per cent.
Han said progress could include connecting electronic documents directly with customs systems, alongside clearer rules covering cross-border data, AI and product standards.
The two-day APEC CEO Summit, which will begin on Nov 17, is expected to produce a “Shenzhen Initiative” - outlining commitments from the regional business community.
Organisers have announced broad priorities including openness, inclusion, innovation and connectivity - but have yet to release detailed measures.
For businesses, observers say the value of any pledge will depend on when it takes effect - which companies can use it and whether it reduces the cost and uncertainty of operating across borders.

Memorial opens honoring victims of the 2015 Charleston church massacre
Eleven years after a white gunman killed nine Black parishioners inside the South’s oldest African Methodist Episcopal Church, a long planned memorial is opening to honor their lives

It took Alana Grant years to find the strength to set foot in the basement of Mother Emanuel AME Church in Charleston, where her grandfather, the Rev. Daniel Lee Simmons, attended his final Bible study.
Her fears have been replaced by gratitude and hope now that there is a completed memorial in a courtyard by the front door for the “Emanuel Nine,” the Black churchgoers killed by an avowed white supremacist in 2015.
The memorial provides a public space where “people can go and remember really what happened here,” Alana Grant said as she and her husband, state Rep. Hamilton Grant, got their first look.
On Saturday, the long-planned memorial at the South's oldest African Methodist Episcopal Church opens to the public.
Emphasizing remembrance and reflection, the marble memorial is anchored by a Fountain of Grace, symbolizing God's eternal love and mercy. Water flows from a shallow basin etched with the names of the six women and three men slain. Two Fellowship Benches with curved backs, sheltering anyone seated, flank the fountain. There is also a Cross of Hope, signifying redemption in the wake of suffering. A garden honoring the five survivors will come next.
The Rev. Eric Manning, co-chair of the Mother Emanuel Memorial Foundation board, hopes it will mean something to everyone.
“I was actually standing out there the other day,” said Manning, who took over after pastor and state Sen. Clementa Pinckney was among those killed. “Just for a moment, a peace came over me.”
How the memorial is helping victims' families
Grant sees the memorial as a place to inspire conversations with her three small children about their great-grandfather. Because the facts of the shooting have been so public, she doesn't want them to hear more from someone else.
“I spent a lot of time thinking about it and praying about it,” she said. “I do want them to go so that they can kind of see what even brought me to South Carolina.”
Former North Carolina state senator and Charlotte City Councilman Malcolm Graham, whose sister Cynthia Graham Hurd died huddled under a desk in the fellowship hall, attended the 2023 groundbreaking. He has anticipated visiting the memorial to reflect on “all the good times Cindy and I had as kids growing up, and being at the church and going to Sunday school.”
A library, scholarship and other awards now carry the name of the accomplished librarian. Now she'll live on in the memorial, too.
“She said before she died that I was the most famous person in the family,” Graham said. “She is the most famous person in our family and I still look up to her.”
As for the survivors to be honored with a garden, Grant says their living with memories of the shooting is “nothing short of heroism.”
“There are not a lot of spaces where you get to see the survivors. We as Black people have survived so much,” Grant said.
A church memorial that can be something for everyone
When a committee sought an architect in 2017, they heard from designers all over the world, said John Darby, another memorial foundation co-chair who runs a Charleston real estate development firm. The final candidates were not asked to submit design proposals, but instead give written responses to deep questions on topics like forgiveness.
That unconventional request was very prescient, said Michael Arad, an architect on the 9/11 Memorial whose design was ultimately chosen. He wrote about his admiration for the victims' families who offered forgiveness to the shooter.
A white, Jewish New Yorker who had never visited South Carolina, Arad did a deep-dive into the community for more than a year after he was selected. Having lengthy conversations with members of the congregation and researching the church's 200-year history was essential, he said, and while the 9/11 memorial was a bigger endeavor, this design wasn't any less complex.
“My job as a designer was to allow people who visit the site to see and hear what was here all along,” he said. “We understand who we are as Americans through stories like this, through our response.”
Arad said he embraces emotionally weighted projects as “a tremendous privilege” and he “could not imagine turning down a project like this.”
The foundation has raised around $25 million over the last decade for the memorial, garden and other costs, much of it from foundations, endowments and corporations, Darby said.
“It was one of those things that people wanted to be a part of,” Darby said. “We don't want it to be an expense to the church.”
Memorial stirs hope to learn from hate and tragedy
Established in 1818, Mother Emanuel was built by free and enslaved people. In the 20th century, the church became a place of resistance where the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. and other civil rights figures spoke.
The Emanuel Nine's families applauded in 2015 when Gov. Nikki Haley removed the Confederate battle flag from state buildings. But with Republicans stirring an angry backlash against diversity and equity efforts, Graham said “racism, hatred and discrimination continue to be this country's Achilles' heel.”
Alana Grant has tried over the years to gather support for a hate crimes statute, and her husband is among the lawmakers who pushed legislation named for Pinckney that would add enhanced penalties for hate crimes to South Carolina's criminal code. It failed to pass, even though a senator was among the Emanuel Nine.
She sees this memorial as an opportunity to raise “generational awareness” so younger people will campaign against hate. Tourists still come to the church daily out of curiosity or sympathy, and could leave the memorial feeling inspired.
“We want more than your thoughts and prayers. We want your advocacy,” she said.

In November, right around Veteran's Day, posts online claimed to show former U.S. President Bill Clinton personally helping a homeless veteran outside The John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts in 1997.
According to the tale, Clinton offered the man, Marcus Williams, his coat, before asking him questions about his service. He then supposedly ordered a Secret Service agent to get Williams food, and personally contacted the Department of Veterans Affairs to help Williams get back on his feet.
The posts began:
"On a freezing December night in 1997, President Bill Clinton was leaving a holiday concert at the Kennedy Center when he noticed a homeless veteran sitting near the entrance. The man wore a thin jacket and was shivering in the cold. In his hands, he held a piece of cardboard with a simple message written on it: "Marine. Desert Storm. Hungry." What happened next caught the attention of people in the presidential motorcade. Clinton stopped, took off his own coat, placed it around the veteran's shoulders, and sat beside him on the icy concrete.
The veteran, 42 year old Marcus Williams, later told reporters that the President never questioned how he had ended up on the street or lectured him about his choices. Instead, Clinton asked about his military service, the battles he had experienced, and whether anyone had ever properly thanked him for what he had done. According to Secret Service agent Larry Cockell, who later wrote about the encounter, Clinton stayed with Marcus for nearly 25 minutes despite the freezing temperatures. When Marcus admitted that he had not eaten in two days, Clinton sent an agent to a nearby restaurant to get him food. He refused to leave until Marcus had finished his meal.
The posts were accompanied by images supposedly showing the two meeting as well as Williams holding a cardboard sign reading "Marine. Desert Storm. Hungry." Snopes readers contacted us to ask whether the story and images were real or fake.
We first uploaded the images into Google Lens to perform a reverse image search. Next, we used search engines such as DuckDuckGo, Google and Yahoo with phrases such as "Bill Clinton Marcus Williams Homeless Veteran" to see whether any reputable news outlets had documented the events. If the scene had occurred and the images were real, we would find evidence in newspapers and media archives like Getty Images. That was not the case. We did not locate any examples of credible outlets publishing the images, nor reporting on the alleged meeting.
We found that neither the story nor the images were real, and that they were generated using artificial intelligence tools. Therefore, we've labeled the claim false.
We uploaded the images accompanying the story into several tools that screen visual media for signs of AI: Sightengine, Hive Moderation, and Google's integrated SynthID detector. The first two found a high likelihood that the images were AI-generated, and the SynthID detector found the invisible watermark indicating Google's AI tools generated the images. We also ran the story through the AI text detection tool Pangram, which also determined that all of the text was written using a large language model such as ChatGPT.
Let us note here: These types of AI detection tools are fallible. Snopes cautions people against using them for definitive answers on media's authenticity without supporting evidence.
Detecting that the image was fake without using those tools was more difficult, given it was grayscale and grainy, but not impossible. We noticed that the writing on the cardboard sign looked too perfect, the cardboard itself looked unusually bright and the supposedly parallel sidewalk cracks didn't form straight lines or meet at a single vanishing point.
Our searches also uncovered a January article written by the fact-checking organization Lead Stories debunking the exact same story, though featuring a real archival image of Clinton instead of an AI-generated one. That fact-check also noted some factual errors in the text, most prominently that one of Clinton's Secret Service agents wrote about the encounter in a memoir. (No such memoir existed.) Because the exact claim was also previously been fact-checked almost a year ago, we concluded that users posting the claim in October and November were doing so in an attempt to make money.
The fictional story is an example of glurge, which Dictionary.com defines as "stories, often sent by email, that are supposed to be true and uplifting, but which are often fabricated and sentimental." These types of low-quality posts often use standard or template language, making small tweaks in an attempt to game the social media algorithms. They rely on social media users' willingness to believe and share the made-up stories and hope to generate a profit from advertising revenue if the posts go viral.
Snopes previously explained the ongoing trend of politically motivated, AI-generated slop content similar to the claim debunked in this article.

'No racism in Spain' – De la Fuente message for Tuchel
- Published
Luis de la Fuente has dismissed concerns over racism in Spanish football before the national team's Uefa Nations League meeting with England in Madrid on Sunday.
Three Lions boss Thomas Tuchel had earlier confirmed he would remind his players of Uefa's anti-racism protocol before the fixture, which will determine who finishes top of League A Group 3.
While he has stressed he didn't expect there to be any incidents, the visit will be England's first to the Spanish capital since a notorious 2004 encounter at the Bernabeu was overshadowed by racist chanting directed at their players.
Spain head coach De la Fuente was asked whether Tuchel's message to his players showed there was still work needed to tackle racism in Spain.
But he responded: "What I'd tell you, and you can tell Thomas, is that in Spain, there's no racism.
"Just like that, crystal clear. Just like in England, there's no racism in Spain. We aren't racist, any of us."
The Spanish Football Federation was fined last month and ordered to partially close a stadium after supporters directed Islamophobic and xenophobic chants towards Muslims during a match against Egypt in Barcelona.
In the domestic game, Real Madrid's Brazilian forward Vinicius Jr has been a vocal anti-racism campaigner after frequently being on the end of racist chanting - and worse. In 2024 three Valencia fans were sentenced to eight months in prison for abusing him at a match.
Uefa operates a three-step protocol, allowing referees to stop matches, take players off the pitch temporarily and, ultimately, abandon a game if discriminatory behaviour continues.
Tuchel said on Friday: "Maybe we take our five minutes to inform the players about the protocol if there is a precedent [in Madrid]. And then, yeah, we will give our answers if stuff like this happens. Best answers are on the pitch."
However, when asked again about his views at a pre-match news conference on Saturday, Tuchel added: "I never talk about racism in Spain.
"I answered politely a question about what happens, I never expect racism. I got asked, 'what will happen if and if and if?'. And I said, 'if it happens, there's a protocol in place'. That's it.
"But my trust is that we have a friendly atmosphere, that we have an atmosphere who is clearly in favour of the Spanish team, and that football does what it does best: brings people together and not divide people."
Midfielder Declan Rice said: "In the past, I've experienced that in Montenegro and Bulgaria and there was a protocol in place that we followed - we came off the pitch. We know exactly where we are as a group on that.
"The times we are in now, 2026, there should never be racism in football. It's shocking we still have it in the game today.
"I don't want to think about if one of our players or their players is racially abused because that would be a horrible mark on football."
'England cannot play like Spain'
Focusing on the match itself, De la Fuente believed both teams are currently at the pinnacle of world football, although he rejected the suggestion one could simply replicate the other's playing style.
Spain were crowned World Cup winners in the summer, while England finished third after losing to Argentina in the semi-finals.
"I prefer the Spanish model. It's very recognisable, the players are perfectly adapted," said De la Fuente. "The English model is very good, but you have to have that type of player. Neither England can play like Spain, nor Spain like England."
He suggested Spain had faced increasingly aggressive opposition as their recent success had raised expectations.
"It's our best moment in a long time," added De la Fuente, whose side also lifted the Euro 2024 title by beating England. "They are all much more aggressive to beat us now than in other times."
He also defended the value of Spanish players, arguing their performances often outweighed their transfer-market prices compared with those in the Premier League.
"Spanish footballers surprise me that, compared to what is paid in England, they are very cheap," he explained. "I see them as better, in my opinion. Everyone in their market can set the prices."
On the fitness of forward Lamine Yamal, he remained cautious over whether the Barcelona teenager would start or how long he could manage.
"We will see if he is a starter, but if he comes out, it's because he's fit to play," said De la Fuente.

The Telangana State Women’s Commission (TGSCW) has initiated an inquiry into an alleged illegal oocyte donation racket in Hyderabad, issuing notices to eight Assisted Reproductive Technology (ART) centres and egg banks over suspected irregularities in their donor records and procurement practices.
The Commission examined representatives of the eight institutions on Friday, November 13, after directing their managements to appear before it. However, TGSCW Chairperson Nerella Sharada expressed dissatisfaction after some centres sent staff members and other representatives instead of senior management, despite being specifically instructed to attend in person. The inquiry was subsequently adjourned after the institutions assured the Commission that their management would appear at the next hearing.
During Friday’s proceedings, the Commission scrutinised reports, records and details of egg donors submitted by the ART centres and egg banks. “Several irregularities and suspicious elements have emerged from the records examined so far,” said Ms. Sharada.
She also questioned claims made by the institutions that nearly 90% of their egg donors came from other States and donated their eggs voluntarily without receiving any remuneration or financial compensation. She said the claims raised several questions and warranted further investigation.
Health Department’s investigation
Commissioner of Health and Family Welfare, Sangeetha Satyanarayana, also attended the inquiry, during which Ms. Sharada sought details about the progress of the department’s investigation into the alleged illegal egg procurement practices. The discussions also covered shortcomings in the existing Assisted Reproductive Technology Act and its implementation, particularly the challenges in regulating and monitoring ART centres and egg banks.
Ms. Sharada said she would soon meet Health Minister C. Damodar Raja Narasimha and Chief Minister A. Revanth Reddy to inform them of the findings and discuss corrective measures, including possible legislative amendments to strengthen regulation of the sector.
More ART centres likely to come under scanner
Ms. Sharada further said that the Commission has also received information indicating the possible involvement of several other ART centres and egg banks in the alleged racket. It plans to issue notices to their management and summon them for questioning as part of the ongoing inquiry.
“The Commission will not tolerate illegal practices that compromise women’s health, dignity and rights. We will continue the investigation in coordination with the concerned government departments to identify those responsible and ensure appropriate legal action,” she added.

On 11 November 2026, terrorists opened fire on a CRPF checkpoint near Mir Bazar in Kulgam district of Jammu and Kashmir, injuring three personnel. The attackers fled after the firing, and security forces launched a search operation to track them down (here, here, and here).
Amid the Kulgam attack on CRPF personnel, a video is being shared on social media (here, here) with the claim that it shows defence expert Wing Commander (Wg Cdr) Praful Bakshi (Retd) alleging that the attack was a false flag operation orchestrated to divert public attention from mounting political pressure on the Narendra Modi government, including Congress protests demanding the Chief Election Commissioner’s resignation and the Arunachal Pradesh controversy. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows Wing Commander Praful Bakshi (Retd) stating that the Kulgam attack on CRPF personnel was a false flag operation.
Fact: The video is digitally manipulated. Wing Commander Praful Bakshi (Retd) did not describe the Kulgam attack on CRPF personnel as a false flag operation. In the original ANI video, he discussed the security situation in Kulgam, the presence of terrorist sleeper cells, and the need for better intelligence coordination and proactive security measures. The Indian Army’s fact-check wing also confirmed on 12 November 2026 that the viral video was digitally altered and falsely attributed remarks to him. AI detection tools, Hive and Hiya, also indicated that the audio was likely AI-generated or manipulated. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
To verify whether Wing Commander Praful Bakshi (Retd) made any such statement, we searched Google using relevant keywords but found no credible news reports or official statements corroborating it.
We noticed the viral video carries an ANI watermark. A keyword search led us to an ANI post on X (archived), dated 11 November 2026, featuring the same footage of Wing Commander Praful Bakshi (Retd), wearing the same attire and speaking against an identical background. However, in the original video, he does not describe the Kulgam attack as a false flag operation or link it to the political developments mentioned in the viral clip. Instead, he expresses concern over the incident, noting that Kulgam has witnessed several such attacks in the past. He emphasises the need for a more proactive security approach, better intelligence coordination, and improved intelligence gathering in areas where terrorists operate and maintain sleeper cells. He also highlights the need to investigate how these groups receive logistical support, including accommodation, ammunition, and water.
We then analysed the viral video using multiple AI voice detection tools, including Hive and Hiya. The analysis indicated the audio was likely AI-generated or manipulated, suggesting fabricated audio was added to the original footage to make it appear that Wing Commander Praful Bakshi (Retd) was describing the Kulgam attack as a false-flag operation.
The Indian Army’s fact-check wing also debunked the claim in an X post dated 12 November 2026, stating that the video was digitally manipulated and falsely attributed remarks to Wing Commander Praful Bakshi (Retd). It clarified that he did not make any such comments in the original video and had instead spoken about terrorist organisations and the need for offensive action and better coordination to prevent such attacks.
To sum up, this video of Wg Cdr Praful Bakshi (Retd) alleging that the Kulgam attack on CRPF personnel was a false flag operation is digitally manipulated.

Mexican Prosecutor Who Helped C.I.A. Secretly Operate in His State Flees to the U.S.
The prosecutor, who faces arrest in Mexico after allowing C.I.A. officers into Chihuahua state, is under the protection of the U.S. government, according to U.S. and Mexican officials.
A Mexican former prosecutor facing arrest after allowing Central Intelligence Agency officers to operate in his state has fled to the United States and is now under the U.S. government’s protection, according to U.S. and Mexican officials.
The former prosecutor, Guillermo Zuany Portillo, shepherded C.I.A. officers for more than six months beginning last year as they trained forces in his state, Chihuahua, joined those forces on counter-cartel missions and provided expertise during ground operations, a New York Times investigation revealed this week.

Tamara Carrasco was in the dining room of the American Heritage cruise ship, docked in the Port of New Orleans, when she spotted a tanker heading straight toward them.
Carrasco, a retired elementary school teacher from Atlanta, was seated at a table by the windows so she could look out at the Mississippi River. She saw the tanker crossing under the bridge nearby and noticed it was lowering its anchor.
"I thought, 'Why would they be anchoring here?'" she said. Her friend turned to her: "It's not stopping. It's going to hit us."
Carrasco was skeptical, until she saw the crew running across the tanker's deck "like ants."
"What was going through my mind was: We're going to die," she said.
The tanker, Atlantic Asphalt, crashed directly into the American Cruise Lines riverboat on Friday, causing the ship to topple over and sink as passengers rushed to evacuate. Several people ended up in the river and had to be pulled out by first responders. Of the nearly 200 people on board, 32 were transported to hospitals. None were critically injured, officials said.
"We have zero people unaccounted for, which truly is a miracle on the Mississippi," New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno said at a press conference.
Carrasco, 65, said when the tanker approached the riverboat, she ran to the opposite end to get as far away from the glass windows as possible. She found a nook on the other end of the ship where she braced herself.
"It hit so hard I flew to the ground," she said.
After the collision, she ran to the stairwell in the middle of the boat and could see into the dining room. The tanker, she said, had broken through the glass windows and water was pouring in.
"Seen the movie 'Titanic'? There was a big gash and water is flying in, and I said, 'Oh, this is going down,'" she said.
She ran up to the next floor and exited the cruise ship usinga gangplank. The crowd gathering on dry land was in shock. Carrasco said it was like after 9/11.
"We're all just kind of wandering in a daze," she said.
They were checked for injuries. Carrasco said she has back issues and her friend has neck issues, so they both wanted to get checked out to be safe.
She was in the waiting area in the emergency room at University Medical Center in New Orleans, fielding calls from friends and family, with a blanket wrapped around her. It was "patriotic day" on the boat, so she was wearing a red, white, and navy blue Ralph Lauren shirt.
"This is the most memorable Friday the 13th I've ever had," she told her older sister over the phone.

Abdul El-Sayed will soon become the first epidemiologist in the Senate at a moment that would keep anyone with a public health background up at night. More than 5,000 Americans have been sickened by the measles this year and the United States is expected to lose its formal measles elimination status by the end of the month. Dengue fever is spreading in Florida, respiratory virus season is underway, and the United States just weathered a foodborne illness outbreak that sickened more than 20,000.
In a wide-ranging interview with STAT, the Michigan Democrat emphasized that he is hopeful the United States can fix its growing trust-in-science problem, but he expressed frustration — at Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., at drug and insurance companies, and at the field of public health — for leading America down this path.
“We’ve created the space for a few grifters to come in and in effect lie to the public,” El-Sayed said. “To create a level of distrust in science and in public health that has had disastrous consequences.”
Below, El-Sayed speaks about his plan to rebuild trust in science and public health, his intentions toward Kennedy, and how gatekeeping has kept scientific discoveries from the public. The interview has been edited for length and clarity.
As the senator-elect from Michigan, how can you help restore trust in health and science? What can you do from Washington to improve these issues?
Well, No. 1, I think you can start taking on greed. Which is why I support “Medicare for All,” because it gets the greed of the insurance industry and the greed of the pharmaceutical industry and the greed of the hospital corporations out of the way so folks can benefit from the incredible things that science creates.
No. 2, I think you have to show the grifters for who they are and how they are, the ways that they use big words that they don’t understand to trick the public, the ways that there’s always a catch at the end where they’re making money off of their grift.
And No. 3, I want to reinvigorate a movement for public health that is willing to stand up to the power of big corporations. … I think we need to be willing to pick a righteous fight in service of the public health.
You’ve mentioned your eagerness to investigate RFK Jr. Are you concerned at all that grilling RFK could serve to further polarize the people that do believe in him?
Well, depending upon how you grill him.
What do you mean?
You can grill a steak and get it to perfect medium rare, or you can grill a steak and it’s well done and inedible, the way the president likes it.
The mistake would be to focus on areas that are polarizing. I wanna understand why he DOGE’d away or he allowed the DOGE’ing away of the CDC [Centers for Disease Control and Prevention] and the FDA [Food and Drug Administration] in ways that left us eating crap lettuce. I want to understand why he hasn’t led the effort to take on the pesticides that are in our food or the additives in our food, why he’s kowtowing to the same corporations he said he was going to stand up to. I want to understand that. Let’s start there.
Why Kennedy supporters should trust him
I’m curious if you have a message to the people that do support Kennedy on why they should trust someone like you on issues of public health.
Well, he told you he’s gonna stand up to the corporations. He hasn’t. I have.
There’s no candidate who’s taken more spending against them in a primary election in their own party than I have, not in history. So at least you know I’m gonna stand up.
I’ve spent my whole career trying to make people healthier, trying to address the greed in our health care system.
There’s all this talk of back and forth: Should RFK Jr. be investigated? Should he be removed? What’s your latest thinking on this?
I think we focus too much on him. I think the bigger question is how do we build the CDC and FDA and NIH [National Institutes of Health] that are worthy of the people that they serve, and that’s gonna always be my focus.
So any investigation that we’re doing is about trying to correct the problems and address the flaws and the faults rather than trying to achieve any sort of retribution.
The people are struggling. They are suffering. They can barely afford groceries, can barely afford gas, can barely see a doctor, are worried about the air they’re breathing, the water they’re drinking, the quality of groceries they’re even buying for an exorbitant price.
My job is to serve them. The personalities involved are secondary to me. My job is to go in and figure out what went wrong, how do we fix it, and how do we hold accountable the people who — if they knowingly broke something — how we do we hold them accountable for it. It’s that simple. It’s less about the personalities. I think we focus too much on that.
Working with RFK Jr.
There’s been this desire among folks within your party to find common ground with RFK on issues. Are there issues that you think you could work with RFK and his team on, or are we kind of past that?
If he actually wants to show up and start doing the things he said he was going to do on pollutants, on additives, sure. I’ll work with anyone. He could be wrong on 95 things, but if he’s right on five, I’ll work with him on those five and hold him accountable for the 95.
Obviously Democrats can’t fix all of these issues. Trust issues started before RFK and I’m sure they’ll go on past RFK. How do you think about how we should judge Democrats’ progress on these issues?
Are we achieving goals that keep people healthy, reduce their costs, empower them. … If we’re doing that, then we’re winning and we’re succeeding. If not, then we’re not. I want people to be able to be their healthiest and their wealthiest. That’s really the bottom line.
It seems like a foregone conclusion, the U.S. will lose its measles elimination status. Do you have thoughts on that?
It’s a travesty. We didn’t have to get here. In a lot of ways, obviously, I blame mis- and dis-information mongers like RFK Jr. for that, but I also blame our collective scientific and health care apparatus for creating the circumstances where somebody like him could step in, and he would have a willing audience willing to listen.
Where did we go wrong in making health care so untrustworthy that somebody with such limited cognitive ability and who is so obviously a grifter, where he could step in and change so many minds? That’s on us.
Science is ‘a beautiful, incredible gift’
The belief that the measles vaccine causes autism is going up over time, and it’s been debunked for 20 years. … How do we break through here?
It starts with basic science education. … Too often the way that scientists speak is about speaking to other scientists to make themselves sound smarter rather than speaking to the public, to help the public feel as smart as they really are. By making sure that everybody understands how and why these things work. Science for the public good … that ethos is something that we’ve forgotten. And I really, desperately want us to remember it.
Science is a gift. It’s a beautiful, incredible gift, and we missed the opportunity to communicate it in all of its elegance because too often it is this thing that is sort of held among the scientific community for consumption by the scientific community. And then we allow a lot of our best science to sit behind paywalls people can’t hop over. So there’s a resentment that happens in publicly funded science for the most part, and we’re keeping [it] out of the hands of people who need it most.
These are big structural questions that ought to animate the way we do science for the rest of the 21st century, and I’m hoping that I can use my role as a doctor and a scientist in the Senate to start driving that conversation among the folks in science.
You can focus on RFK Jr. all you want, but he identified a set of weaknesses that those of us who have committed our lives to science and the public’s health that we allowed to exist in the first place.
How hopeful are you that we can solve these trust issues?
I wouldn’t be doing this if I didn’t believe we could. Science always wins. I just hope that it wins quickly. But the beautiful thing about science is that in the end it always finds the right answer.
