Lucknow:
 As an alliance partner of 
Samajwadi Party
 in the INDIA bloc, the 
Congress
 wants to contest on 181 seats in UP. This was formally confirmed for the first time by SP president 
Akhilesh Yadav
 on Saturday. The confirmation came moments after Akhilesh said that INDIA bloc will defeat BJP in UP polls and ruled out any change in alliance’s constituents in the future and added that SP has decided how many seats SP will contest.
Until now, Congress leadership has been throwing numbers in media interviews -- demanding equal partner status in UP polls and suggesting that it wants to contest on half of the 403 Assembly seats. The SP leadership, however, has been clear on its stance that winnability of candidates will remain the sole criterion for fielding candidates rather than count of seats. It has insisted that the priority id to defeat the BJP.
As INDIA bloc members, SP and Congress had outperformed the BJP in 2024 Lok Sabha polls by winning 43 of the 80 seats in UP and getting 43.52% of the votes. Congress had bagged six of the 17 seats it contested with a vote share of 9.46%, while SP had its best-ever winning tally of 37 seats. The BJP’s seats fell from 62 in 2019 to 33 and lowered its overall tally below the majority mark in the Lok Sabha for the first time since 2014.
The Congress contested the 2022 UP polls on its own but won just two seats, down by five seats from its tally of 7 in 2017 polls. Of the 399 seats that Congress contested in 2022, it secured a vote share of 2.33% (21.51 lakh votes). Not surprisingly, of the 399 seats, Congress candidates lost their deposits on 387 seats. On 46 seats the party got 10,000 plus votes. Of these 46 seats, 10 of them have sitting SP MLAs. The SP had won 111 seats in 2022.
On Saturday, Akhilesh was responding to questions at HT Leadership Summit in Delhi when he emphasised that SP enjoys “very good” relationship with the Congress. Asked that Congress was seeking to contest 100 seats in UP polls, he said: “The number of seats they have asked for is higher than what you are suggesting.” Asked whether the Congress has demanded 200 seats, Akhilesh said the count was slightly less. “Add one to 180,” the SP chief said when asked if the Congress had sought 180 seats.
Talking of his experiences with the alliances that he had entered in the past and if he had explored possibilities of reviving 2019 Lok Sabha poll alliance with Bahujan Samaj Party, Akhilesh said he had had good experiences with the alliances. He said his present alliance (with the Cong) stood on the movement and principles of Baba Saheb Ambedkar that was initiated by the BSP.
“The INDIA bloc alliance with the Congress that we have had in the past (2024 Lok Sabha polls), is the same alliance that we have today. I don’t see any change in that,” Akhilesh said. On the issue of delay in finalising seat sharing with the Congress, Akhilesh said Samajwadi Party and he has decided on how many seats they will contest. This time SP is going to defeat BJP. INDIA bloc together will defeat BJP,’ Akhilesh said, confirming that Congress has sought 181 seats.

Here is a thoroughly engaging, rousing and spectacular Indian epic melodrama from director Nitesh Tiwari, with music by Hans Zimmer and AR Rahman, based on the ancient classical poem about Rama, the avatar of the Hindu god Vishnu. It has often been adapted for live-action and animated movies in the past, though surely not on this scale, the current three-hour blockbuster being only the first half. (There are no musical numbers though.) The idea of aristocrats submitting stoically and yet playfully to exile in the forest has something Shakespearean about it, and if you are suffering from Homer-withdrawal after Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, a story about the noble Prince Rama finally vowing to wage war on a distant city where his wife has been abducted might just fit the bill.
Ranbir Kapoor plays the mythical Rama, a noble warrior and statesman who has been brought into being in the city state of Ayodhya as a bodily representative of Vishnu, and from the first his sense of destiny is overwhelming. But what exactly is that destiny? In broad terms, his fate is to face off with Ravana (Naveen “Yash” Kumar), king of far-off Lanka, a figure whose former slave status once triggered in him such a cosmically intense prayer for justice that Lord Brahma offered him the superpower of athletic strength and indifference to pain.
In Ayodhya, Rama marries the sweetly devoted Sita (Sai Pallavi), he enjoys an intense bond of comradeship with his brother Lakshmana (Ravi Dubey), and is the apple of his father’s eye; this is King Dasharatha (Arun Govil) who, careworn by affairs of state, is about cede the throne to Rama. But Rama’s stepmother Kaikeyi (Lara Dutta) furiously reminds Dasharatha that he promised the crown to Bharata (Adinath Kothare), the son they had together. Rama, Sita and Lakshmana are banished to the forest.
Over in Lanka, a toxic stew of plotting against Ravana is being stirred by his slippery, smirking brother-in-law Vidyutjihva (played by Bollywood veteran Vivek Oberoi), whom Ravana ruthlessly slays in single combat; this man’s widow Shurpanakha (Rakul Preet Singh), who is Ravana’s sister, is banished to the same forest where Rama is humbly eking out his civilian existence. She falls in love with Rama, using her witchy wiles to trick and bamboozle the happily married man, and this is to lead to a cataclysmic confrontation between Rama and Ravana.
With its giant canvas and some truly beautiful sunset skyscapes, this very enjoyable film has a little of Peter Jackson’s Lord of the Rings and even Disney’s The Lion King (the latter surely influenced the animal-kingdom tableaux). The bizarre flying machine piloted by Ravana (who does not have the ability to fly as such) has something engagingly Gilliamesque about it. As so often with Indian cinema, this movie reminds you of the forthright, unselfconscious storytelling energy that popular Hollywood films had in the 1950s and 60s, the era of sword-and-sandal. It’s a rather amazing adventure.

Last week, Elon Musk announced on X that Tesla would halt production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas “around the middle of next year,” supposedly to allow for increased production of self-driving Cybercabs.
Automotive industry observers were quick to surmise that the vehicle’s weak sales, delayed deliveries, inflated pricing, numerous recalls, and connection to Musk’s far-right MAGA politics may also have factored into the decision. Longtime detractors of the polarizing steel-paneled truck, originally positioned as an electric rival to classic gas-powered pickups, jeered Musk and Tesla fans over its demise, noting with some pleasure that the Cybertruck would exit the market within four years of its November 2023 rollout.
And, in Cybertruck fan communities across the web, owners began to mourn.
“Worst possible news,” a member of the Cybertruck Owners Club forum wrote in a response to Musk’s post. “No chance to buy another in future years for a newer model or after a car accident. No more aftermarket mods. No more service or parts.” Another remarked that they had waited for their truck “longer than the truck line was around.”
“So everybody in my group, they are not happy,” Michael Goldman, a contractor in Palm Springs, California, tells WIRED. As the administrator of the Facebook group Cybertruck Owners Only, which has more than 82,000 members, he’s been swamped with frantic messages. “I've had people reaching out to me through the group, asking me, like, ‘What are you going to do?’” Goldman says. “And I'm like, ‘Dude, I don't know.’”
Since hearing the news about the discontinuation of the truck, many owners have expressed feelings of betrayal and disappointment. Some are wondering if their pending orders will be fulfilled, as Musk has claimed that Tesla “will have to return deposits for a lot of people” due to demand outpacing production. Others have looked for a silver lining, speculating that the Cybertruck could become a valued collector’s item.
But Goldman doesn’t want to turn his truck into a “garage princess,” since he enjoys driving it and finds it useful in his construction business. “I don't want to ever drive another truck,” he says, and he considered buying a backup Cybertruck for when his first one reaches the end of its life. “I'll be honest with you, I was going pull the trigger on a [Cyberbeast] about two days ago, and I have a reservation already in my phone,” Goldman says, but when he was ready to complete the purchase, “the price increased like another $8,000 or something, and that was my sign to not do it.”
That Musk, against all odds, actually brought his vision of the Cybertruck to life makes it all the more painful for Goldman to see it scrapped. “That it actually happened and only happened for such a short period of time kind of blows me away,” he says. “That's why I want to call him out on it, you know?”
Troy Meekhof, a Tesla aficionado in Grand Rapids, Michigan, known as “the Cybertruck Guy” on social media, has not been shy about expressing his own displeasure. “I can’t help but think this is Tesla’s own unwillingness (or incompetence) to make Cybertruck a success,” he posted in reply to Musk’s announcement of the wind-down last week. “Where was the price cuts? Where were the advertisements? Where is range extender?”
“I absolutely do think this is the wrong move for the Tesla brand, and it’s not necessarily because of the removal of an under-performing product, but it’s a clear symbol of Tesla’s aggression towards transitioning to autonomous vehicles only,” such as the two-seater Cybercab, Meekhof tells WIRED in an email. “If you ask me, it is far too aggressive, and I have a growing conviction that, at least in America, the population and legislators are not ready nor interested in autonomous vehicles today en masse.”
In another X post, Meekhof warned that “Tesla has lost the plot” by going all-in on autonomous driving as the US enters “a governance era that opposes” the company’s efforts on that front.
Musk has repeatedly declared that Tesla’s future is as an AI and robotics firm rather than as an automaker. It’s a strategy that has increasingly alienated Tesla owners like Meekhof, who despite their excitement over self-driving technology, feel that the company is spurning its core supporters as it pursues breakthroughs in that field. Earlier this year, Tesla axed its Model S and Model X, and the end of the Cybertruck narrows its lineup to just the Model 3 and Model Y.
“Tesla, as a company, has made itself massively successful by making vehicles that appeal to enthusiasts, in either tech or automotive, and in many cases, both,” Meekhof says. “With their transition to autonomous-only vehicles, they leave those customers behind. I am one of them.” Meekhof has launched what he describes as a mostly “symbolic” petition urging Tesla to reconsider the plan to eliminate the Cybertruck from its slate. The letter has gathered more than 5,000 signatures.
Drew Million, an active member of the Cybertruck Owners Only group on Facebook, recently shared on the page that he was concerned about the transition to another vehicle once his beloved Cybertruck has run its course. “I’ve lost a lot of love for Tesla over this,” Million tells WIRED, adding that his interest in the brand is waning due to the “very stale consumer options” left on the table.
Million had ordered a second Cybertruck in February to replace a work van, and he’s hoping that it comes through before production halts completely in June or July 2027, per Musk’s estimate. But he’s dismayed, he says, that Tesla leadership isn’t paying attention to what customers actually want.
“After Cybertruck is gone, there isn’t a flagship vehicle,” Million says, nor one that meets his needs. His household went from owning no electric cars to four in less than a year. “The Cybertruck started that,” he says, and it can’t be replaced by rideshares in autonomous taxis.
It’s a point that comes up again and again from Tesla boosters protesting the sunset of the Cybertruck: They don’t want to give up their own independence in favor of robot chauffeurs. An owner wrote on X, for example, that they didn’t understand Tesla’s push “to delete the steering wheel, the pedals, the ownership, the freedom of having a vehicle” with the Cybercab, which cannot accommodate an entire family. They lamented that the company “doesn't seem to want to continue innovating in the customer car segment.”
Meekhof predicts that Americans won’t soon give up personally controlled trucks and SUVs capable of transporting several people and cargo in favor of smaller autonomous sedans. He worries that Tesla is headed for a “Google Glass scenario on steroids, where the technology came before the people.” Goldman is on the same page. “I think a Cybercab is cool for certain things, but I'm not going to take a Cybercab to a construction site, you know what I mean?” he says. “In rural towns, people want to drive their car to work.”
The overall consternation in Tesla world over the fate of Cybertruck has been somewhat compounded by Musk’s typically muddled messaging. According to the CEO, the truck is profitable and, indeed, so popular that the Gigafactory can’t make them fast enough to fulfill existing reservations—so why, owners ask, does it have to be suspended?
Would-be customers have also been disgruntled to learn that Tesla continues to accept Cybertruck orders, though only for the premium Cyberbeast model, priced at $109,990. “So they can't fill current orders, but will still take orders on the most expensive version ... yeah that's not scummy at all,” a redditor griped this week on r/cybertruck.
And there is a percolating sense of resentment among some Cybertruck devotees that they were taken for a ride, so to speak, with Tesla exploiting their passion for the novel vehicle and its driver-assistance tech to advance its agenda of autonomy at all costs.
“They're a data company,” Goldman says. “What they're doing is collecting data for the robots and for the self-driving cars and for the Cybercab. We were basically beta testers in the Cybertruck for the Cybercab.”
That’s part of the reason that Goldman and others feel they are owed a better explanation of Tesla’s latest move. “We want to know why,” Goldman says. “Is it because we were really just beta for the cabs, or is it really because you guys don't have enough space in the Gigafactory, or is it just because the sales are terrible?”
“Most of the people that have Cybertrucks have been following this truck for the past 10 years,” Goldman says. “We finally got literally the best truck made on this planet, and now they're taking it away from us, and we're bummed.”

A boxer and political prisoner on death row in Iran said he will “never surrender” as he accepted a prestigious human rights prize on behalf of “the generation that is paying the price of freedom with their lives”.
Mohammad Javad Vafaei Sani, an Iranian boxing champion, coach and political prisoner, has been sentenced to death three times and is one of seven athletes at risk of execution in Iran. He was given the Magnitsky award for outstanding human rights activist at a ceremony in London on Thursday night.
In a written message from Vakilabad prison in north-eastern Iran, he said: “I accept this award in the name of all those who, for the ‘crime’ of aspiring to a free Iran, have been imprisoned, tortured, threatened, or sentenced to death; in the name of my comrades in the resistance units and the generation that is paying the price of freedom with their lives.”
He added: “The regime demands repentance, televised confessions and surrender from us. But our answer is clear: ‘We will never surrender; we will never submit to humiliation.’”
Vafaei Sani, 31, was arrested in 2020 for taking part in nationwide democracy protests in 2019 and accused of supporting an opposition group, the People’s Mojahedin Organization of Iran (MEK).
He was convicted of “corruption on Earth” and sentenced to death for a third time in September 2024 after “a grossly unfair trial”, according to Amnesty International. The supreme court upheld his death sentence on 4 October 2025. Since his arrest he has been tortured and held in solitary confinement for extended periods.
His continued imprisonment has drawn widespread international condemnation from prominent sportspeople, human rights organisations and legal experts who have called for his immediate release and the annulment of his death sentence.
The Magnitsky awards are named after the Russian lawyer, Sergei Magnitsky, who died in Russian police custody after exposing government corruption. They began in 2015 as a way to recognise journalists, politicians and activists in the field of human rights.
Sir William Browder, head of the Magnitsky Justice Foundation and the chair of the awards committee, said Vafaei Sani’s case was emblematic of the plight of many Iranians who face execution for standing against the regime. “Most important, Mohammad Javad is still alive,” he said. “That is why this award matters. Every time the world pays attention, it becomes harder to kill him quietly.”
According to the Hengaw Organisation for Human Rights, at least 710 people have been executed in Iran since the beginning of 2026, including 79 political and religious prisoners.
In an October report, the organisation documented at least 106 death sentences against January protest detainees, 35 of whom had already been executed. In Vakilabad prison, where Vafaei Sani is detained, five people have been executed linked to the protests and 15 others are facing death sentences.
Vafaei Sani’s award comes at a time when there are growing fears for imprisoned Iranian athletes, who are considered role models in the country. Zohreh Abdollahkhani, founder of Human Rights for Sport, said: “The situation is really dire … We have seven athletes at risk of execution now, including Vafaei Sani.”
Ali-Sina Mostafavi, a mountaineer, was executed on 14 October after the anti-government protests. His death followed the killing of Siavash Jamshidi Kheirabadi, a taekwondo athlete, earlier that month, and the mixed martial arts fighter Gholamreza Khani Shakarab, who was hanged in May.
Abdollahkhani said people had been celebrating Vafaei Sani’s award. “Even people who don’t support his political view are supporting him to be heard,” she said. “I find it very inspiring that different political groups are coming together to say no to execution.”
In his message, Vafaei Sani said he wanted “a free and democratic Iran … where the people vote freely, women and men are equal, there is no discrimination on the basis of ethnicity, religion or belief, and no one is imprisoned or executed for political opposition”.
He added: “I remain steadfast in my pledge, and I will not bow before oppression until the people of Iran are free.”

I watched Hailey’s chest without pause, searching for the slightest movement, a tiny intake of breath, any sign of life.
Hailey (not her real name) was 22 years old, a college student who had suffered a catastrophic brain injury in a traffic accident. She lay before me in our neuroscience intensive care unit, her heart beating steadily, her skin warm, a ventilator breathing for her. I was performing an apnea test, the final step in determining whether she had died by neurological criteria. It’s part of my job as a neurointensivist at Oregon Health & Science University. The longest 10 minutes of my life are those I spend watching for any small chest movement as we remove a patient from a breathing machine. I can’t let my eyes wander. I can’t blink. Hailey never took a breath; she was brain dead.
Her parents sat vigil for two days, waiting for her sister to arrive from overseas so she could say goodbye. When they finally accepted that their daughter had died, the organ donation team took over.
Six months later, our ICU received a letter describing the four lives Hailey had saved. Her kidneys went to two grandparents, each now playing with their grandchildren. Her liver saved a young woman dying of hepatitis who was now snorkeling in a tropical ocean. And her heart was beating inside a young man with a fatal congenital heart condition who was now hiking along the coast.
I’ve never forgotten Hailey or the lives she saved, and I believe deeply in organ donation. But starting Nov. 18, new rules from the Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network will change how the organ donation process works, allowing organ procurement organizations to approach families about donation before they’ve decided whether to withdraw life-sustaining treatment.
The goal is to get more viable organs to the more than 100,000 people in the U.S. waiting for life-saving transplants. But I worry this approach blurs the line between the physicians fighting to save a patient’s life and the teams responsible for organ procurement.
That isn’t fair to families, who expect that our sole concern is their loved one’s well-being. Proposing potential organ donation early opens the door to distrust in their ICU care. We should keep that door shut.
Why it’s so hard to determine death
In 2025, the Department of Health and Human Services reported 73 cases in which organ donation had been authorized, but not completed, where donors showed “neurological signs incompatible with organ donation.” The New York Times reported that some patients may not have been dead at the time organ procurement was initiated, often in rural or small hospitals.
These findings raised troubling questions about whether the motivation for higher transplant numbers had taken precedence over careful assessment of the neurological condition of potential donors.
The Uniform Determination of Death Act, accepted by most states, establishes two definitions of death: irreversible cessation of circulatory and respiratory function, or irreversible loss of function of the entire brain, known as brain death.
To patients’ families, brain death is often harder to grasp than circulatory death. Their loved one appears alive: breathing on a mechanical ventilator, heart still beating steadily on the monitor, skin warm and pink. Yet without mechanical support, if their brain no longer functions, their body will no longer function.
Donation after circulatory death (DCD) involves patients with grave prognoses for whom a decision has been made to withdraw life-sustaining treatment. Many have catastrophic brain injuries, although they do not meet the criteria for brain death. Determining whether a patient is an appropriate candidate for DCD requires a physician’s judgment about the patient’s prognosis, a process that is difficult to standardize.
In contrast, medical standards for determining brain death are uniform and widely practiced in the United States. A diagnosis requires three criteria, as we did for Hailey, rigorously assessed: coma with a known cause, loss of brainstem reflexes, and loss of the ability to breathe spontaneously, tested by a strict protocol known as the apnea test.
No one who has been correctly diagnosed with brain death under these criteria has ever recovered. Not one person.
I’m careful to teach our medical students never to say that we “withdraw care” because even when we stop life-sustaining treatment, we continue to care for our patients. Care for the dying is as critical as care for the living.
These decisions require our full attention and the trust of patients’ families, so it’s imperative that a separate organ donation team work alongside us, remaining independent of the physicians treating the patient.
A safer path to more organ donations
Physicians should be working to increase organ donation while enhancing patient safety.
First, we need to better educate people about what it means to be an organ donor. When someone checks “organ donation” on their driver’s license, they should understand how we define death and what that check mark really means.
Second, we can expand access to neurological expertise in underserved areas, particularly small and rural hospitals that don’t have immediate access to neurologists or neurointensivists. A video consultation with a neurologist or intensive care physician at an academic or comprehensive health care institution can aid in assessing the level of consciousness of patients being considered for DCD, before they’re taken to the operating room for organ recovery.
Another way to increase organ donation is to focus on patients who have been declared brain dead. After brain death, families and health care teams have more time to obtain organs in an orderly fashion, facilitating the best outcome for both donors and recipients.
The ICU clinicians taking care of a patient nearing death are often deep in discussions of the differences (and similarities) between DCD and brain death as they apply to their loved one. The discussions are often confusing and cause conflicted emotions in families facing tragedy.
The new organ procurement organization policy allows donation teams to break into this discussion, often long before family and friends have fully grasped the gravity of the patient’s injury. This interruption can subtly blur the distinction between our caring for the patient and obtaining organs for someone else.
Our first priority must always be the patient before us, and ensuring that the family members making decisions on their behalf understand and trust the care we’re providing.
In the ICU we walk the path of brain death and cardiac death carefully, always remembering that organ donation offers a small piece of biological immortality. Our patients are not yet forever gone.
Tarvez Tucker, M.D., is professor of neurology and neurocritical care at Oregon Health & Science University. Her forthcoming book, “The Brain at Twilight: The Neuroscience of Our Last Words and Moments,” will be published in December 2026 by Columbia University Press.

Every year in Delhi, the arrival of the winter months also signals the beginning of what residents widely call “pollution season”. A thick toxic smog shrouds the city, home to 30 million people who have no choice but to breathe the poisonous air as they go about their daily lives, often while suffering from wheezy coughs, nausea and itchy eyes. While successive state governments have brought in measures intended to improve air quality, the situation has remained the same for more than a decade. Delhi is widely regarded as the world’s most polluted city. Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
Pollution season usually begins around the same time as Diwali, the Hindu festival of light. Amidst the plummeting air quality, people still gather in the markets for festival shopping and at festivities outside. Diwali is also known to cause a surge in the pollution levels, due to the tens of millions of cars that hit the roads and the use of firecrackers for the celebration. In previous years, firecrackers were banned, but this year the state government has allowed “green” firecrackers”. However environmentalists argue that these are still highly polluting.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
The causes of Delhi’s apocalyptic pollution are multi-faceted. In recent years, one of the biggest causes has been vehicle emissions, from the almost 10m cars, rickshaws, motorcycles and trucks on the city’s roads. It is also the season where farmers in the neighbouring states of Haryana and Punjab often burn their fields to ready them for the next crop. These fires are illegal but still occur. Factory emissions, dust from construction and rubbish burning also contribute to the toxic air quality levels.Photograph: Yanni Rawat/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock
So far, the air quality index (AQI) has already soared above 650, more than 30 times the limit the World Health Organization (WHO) deems to be safe. Air pollution is linked to numerous serious diseases, particularly respiratory, and hospitals have already reported a surge in patients suffering from breathing difficulties.The pollution season is expected to last until January, when the weather warms up.Photograph: Yanni Rawat/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock
Millions of Delhi’s residents are poor families or migrant workers, who have no choice but to go out to work in the toxic air, often suffering long term impacts on their health. Doctors and campaigners have described the pollution as a “health emergency”. According to a study last year, at least 15% of deaths in the capital are linked to air pollution. Pollution now kills more people in Delhi than obesity of diabetes.Photograph: Yanni Rawat/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock
As in previous years, the state government has introduced various restrictions to try and bring air quality levels under control. Coal and firewood have been banned as fuel. Construction has also been halted and so have older diesel and petrol cars. Offices have been instructed to get people to work from home to limit traffic on the roads. Trucks can often be seen spraying water on the roads. However, it is widely acknowledged that, so far, these restrictions have had little impact on the pollution levels. Photograph: Sajjad Hussain/AFP/Getty Images
The pollution has been a problem for so long in Delhi that it has become normalised and people carry on with their daily lives in the toxic smog.Residents rarely wear masks outside and the parks will still be full of families and children and people exercising outside.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
While rich and middle class families will buy air purifiers for their homes, they are unaffordable for most poorer families who often live in makeshift tents or informal homes. As a result, breathing clean air during pollution season has become a luxury privilege in Delhi.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
The pollution is not restricted to Delhi alone. All across north India, in states such as Punjab and Haryana, the air is also toxic due to coal-powered plants, vehicles and farm fires. Cities such as Amritsar in Punjab, on the border with Pakistan, also suffer from extremely dangerous air quality levels during the winter months. Photograph: Narinder Nanu/AFP/Getty Images
Campaigners say more money needs to be invested into proper public transport and better vehicle emission regulation in Delhi to tackle the root causes of pollution. Every year, the number of cars on Delhi’s roads keeps rising, releasing more harmful pollutants, and yet few the percentage of electric vehicles remains very low.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
Delhi has an extensive bus and metro network, but it is not sufficient to cope with the huge daily demand and still has poor connectivity in many areas. Most people still rely on polluting rickshaws, cars and motorcycles to get them to the bus stops or metro stations. Photograph: Raj K Raj/Hindustan Times/Getty Images
Delhi’s topography – a city built in a bowl-like valley, which has little breeze or rain in the winter months – means most of the emissions get trapped over the city as the cold weather hits and cloak the city in brown smog. Some call it Delhi’s “death shroud”.Photograph: Sajjad Hussain/AFP/Getty Images
In past years, the state and national government has been accused of manipulating the data to disguise how bad pollution levels are in the capital. Last year, it was found that water was being sprayed around the air quality monitors, allegedly to bring down the readings. Campaigners and opposition politicians have alleged that a lot of data from the air quality measuring stations has gone “missing”.
Environmental campaigners have argued that much more extreme measures are needed to bring pollution under control, similar to how Beijing successfully cleaned up its air in recent years. However, others have argued this would have an economic cost that India, as a developing country, can not afford.Photograph: Raj K Raj/Hindustan Times/Getty Images
One of the plans being prepared by the government this year is to experiment with “cloud-seeding”, to create rain which would clear the skies. But many residents and campaigners say that until the root causes are tackled, these plans are nothing more than a “gimmick”.Photograph: Sajjad Hussain/AFP/Getty Images

Arrested generals and a threatened VP: President's son fuels Ugandan succession fever
- Published
In Uganda's military, even senior generals are finding that their rank offers little protection from the wrath of the country's powerful army chief.
Over the past 15 months, at least a dozen generals and senior officers have been arrested under Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, who is also the son of President Yoweri Museveni, in a crackdown that has unsettled the military's top ranks.
The arrests come amid growing political tensions over who will succeed Museveni, who has ruled Uganda for four decades.
Gen Kainerugaba, 52, is widely seen as a potential successor, although his ambitions appear to be facing resistance within the ruling party.
This week, he threatened Vice-President Jessica Alupo with dismissal and possible arrest, while suggesting he should take her position.
The ruling National Resistance Movement (NRM) has, however, rejected reports that its senior leadership had rejected a proposal to back Gen Kainerugaba as the next president, describing the claims as "completely false".
This has all fuelled speculation that the arrests are part of an effort to sideline military officers opposed to the general's presidential ambitions.
Others see the arrests as evidence of an anti-corruption drive in which senior commanders are held to account.
At the centre of the tension are two powerful powerful institutions: the military, where Gen Kainerugaba wields considerable influence, and the NRM, where questions about his political ambitions appear to be dividing senior figures.
A recent meeting of NRM's top leadership ended without agreement on a proposal to position Gen Kainerugaba as Museveni's successor, according to the AFP news agency.
Five party sources who attended the closed-door meeting told AFP that a vote was abandoned after several members spoke against the proposal.
Uganda's news website ChimpReports, however, said that most members who spoke backed the general's potential presidency, although some questioned his readiness for civilian leadership.
In a statement on Thursday, NRM Secretary General Richard Todwong Awany confirmed that the party had met on 10 November to discuss "political, social and economic issues".
He dismissed reports that the meeting had rejected a proposal to position Gen Kainerugaba as Uganda's next president, saying the party would communicate any decisions "through the right channel, at the right time".
Dr Gerald Bareebe, a Ugandan-born political scientist at Canada's York University, sees a connection between the arrests and political manoeuvring over Museveni's succession, often referred to as the "Muhoozi Project".
"Senior officers believed not to support the project have been arrested, detained or charged with corruption and treason," he tells the BBC.
He says the allegations against some officers were widely viewed as politically motivated, reflecting growing divisions within the military over the succession question.
Some of those detained have since been released, apparently after securing the general's forgiveness.
The detention of one of the country's most prominent former commanders, Lt Gen Peter Elwelu, has brought the crackdown into sharper focus.
The former deputy army chief was detained on 2 November over allegations that he had plotted to destabilise the eastern Teso region.
His fall from grace followed a series of social media posts by Kainerugaba, who accused him of treachery and announced that he had been stripped of his three-star rank and demoted.
"The traitor Peter Elwelu is hereby stripped of his ranks. He is demoted to Private," Kainerugaba wrote on X.
He also claimed that more than 20 soldiers linked to Elwelu had been arrested.
The announcement raised legal questions, with Ugandan media reporting that military regulations do not allow a senior officer to be stripped of his rank through a social media post.
The army later confirmed Elwelu's detention, saying they had recovered 15 guns, military uniforms and two pickup trucks linked to him. His family has rejected the allegations.
Elwelu is among at least a dozen generals and senior officers detained since April 2025, according to an investigation by Uganda's Daily Monitor newspaper.
They include three former military intelligence chiefs who once oversaw some of Uganda's most sensitive security operations.

Maj Gen James Birungi, a former head of defence intelligence and security, was arrested in August 2025, on allegations including treason, terrorism and corruption.
He was charged before a military court but later released after Gen Kainerugaba announced that he had "forgiven" him.
Another former intelligence chief, Maj Gen Abel Kandiho, was detained in September this year over allegations of providing false intelligence and treachery. He remains in detention, according to the Daily Monitor.
His predecessor, Brig-Gen Charles Bakahumura, was also arrested in September over similar allegations, but was later released after the army chief announced that he had forgiven him.
Other officers have faced accusations ranging from stealing military fuel to taking money to spy on military communications.
The military has defended the arrests as part of efforts to tackle corruption and criminality within the armed forces.
Ugandan security analyst Freddie David Egesa says the arrests reflect investigations involving different security agencies, rather than an army-led purge.
He argues that detaining senior officers helps protect witnesses and demonstrates the seriousness of the anti-corruption drive.
"Gen Muhoozi has the overall duty to permit the investigation team to arrest these high-profile people, in consultation with the commander-in-chief," Egesa says, adding: "The arrests are not summarily done."
But Bareebe sees a wider political motive, arguing that officers suspected of opposing to Gen Kainerugaba's presidential ambitions are being targeted.
"The result is a broad purge that has affected both serving and retired officers perceived to be anti-Muhoozi," he says.
He points to divisions between the elite Special Forces Command (SFC), which he says is largely loyal to the president's son, and army commanders who remain unconvinced about his succession.
The allegations against the officers are at different stages, with some facing charges, others in detention without publicly announced charges, and several having been released.
Bareebe also questions whether military trials can deliver independent proceedings.
"Many Ugandans regard the charges as politically motivated and therefore expect little justice," he adds.
He alleges that some officers have had charges dropped after closed-door negotiations with the president and his son, during which they were pressured to declare support for Gen Kainerugaba.
Government spokesperson Allan Kasujja dismissed the claims of a succession fallout as "hogwash".
Unlike his predecessors, who communicated through official military channels, Gen Kainerugaba frequently uses X to announce arrests, criticise public officials and comment on domestic and international affairs. Some have sparked diplomatic controversy.
On the night of 9 November, he turned his attention to Vice-President Jessica Alupo, demanding to take her job.
"Whoever is in that office should prepare to hand it over soon," he wrote, in posts that he later deleted.
He also questioned Alupo's loyalty and threatened her dismissal, adding that the government would operate "on military terms", if he became his father's deputy.
The following day, his X account, which had nearly 1.4 million followers, became inaccessible.
It was unclear whether he deactivated it himself, which he has done before, or the platform had suspended it.
Alupo remains in office and has yet to respond publicly.
Egesa says Gen Kainerugaba's controversial posts reflect his preferred style of communicating, but adds that security analysts are assessing their implications for Uganda's political and military stability.
Bareebe, however, sees them as part of a broader effort by the army chief to extend his influence into civilian politics.
He says the public confrontation with senior political figures illustrates how the succession debate was spilling beyond the army and into the ruling party.
Gen Kainerugaba was appointed army chief in March 2024, after previously commanding the SFC, which is responsible for protecting the president and strategic installations.
Under Uganda's military structure, he reports directly to Museveni, giving him considerable influence over the army.
Bareebe argues that the SFC's loyalty to the president and his son could prove crucial in any future transfer of power.
"The regular army remains important but has been sidelined by the SFC, which now functions as a personal army for Museveni and his son," he adds.
At the heart of the tension is the question of who will succeed Museveni, 82, who has ruled Uganda since 1986, when his rebel National Resistance Army seized power after a five-year guerrilla war.
He was sworn in for a seventh elected presidential term earlier this year, extending his rule into a fifth decade.
Gen Kainerugaba has been regarded as a possible successor and has indicated that he intends to seek the presidency in 2031, when his father's current term is due to end.
He also leads the Patriotic League of Uganda, a political movement that has mobilised support around his leadership.
But recent developments suggest that a transfer of power from father to son may be more complicated than his supporters anticipated.
At the recent meeting of the NRM leadership, one official reportedly urged Museveni to retire his son from the military and give him a civilian role to gain administrative experience, AFP reported.
Local media reported that some party officials consider Gen Salim Saleh, Museveni's younger brother, better suited for civilian leadership.
There is, however, no indication that he is interested in becoming president.
Others reportedly defended Gen Kainerugaba, pointing to his military leadership, anti-corruption campaign and grassroots political mobilisation.
Bareebe says opposition to the proposed succession has grown within the NRM, with both veteran figures and younger members concerned about what they see as an attempt to secure power through coercion.
He suggests Museveni's reluctance to move his son out of the military could reflect the importance of retaining control of the army during any transition.
"The underlying calculation appears to be that, so long as Muhoozi controls the SFC, he can use it to capture power even in an event of a contested transition," he says.
The military has been central to Museveni's hold on power, making the loyalties of senior commanders particularly important as succession questions intensify.
The family's military influence has also drawn attention to the possibility of a political dynasty spanning generations, with Gen Kainerugaba's son, Ruhamya, recently graduating from Britain's Sandhurst military academy.
The succession debate is unfolding against a backdrop of sustained pressure on the opposition.
Veteran opposition politician Kizza Besigye remains in detention on treason charges, which he denies.
Bobi Wine, who came second to Museveni in this year's presidential election, has gone into exile in the US, after being threatened by Gen Kainerugaba.
The government has consistently defended its security operations as lawful and necessary to maintain stability.
For now, Museveni remains in power.
But the arrests, his son's threats and competing accounts of divisions within the ruling party have intensified questions about how Uganda's next political transition might unfold, and what role his family may play.

A video (here & here) of a man stabbing a girl is being shared on social media with the claim that a Hindu schoolgirl was stabbed in Dhaka, Bangladesh, by a local Jamaat youth leader for rejecting his advances. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Video showing a Hindu schoolgirl getting stabbed by a Muslim Youth in Dhaka, Bangladesh.
Fact: The incident took place in Kushtia city, Bangladesh, on 09 November 2026. Both the victim and the attacker involved in this incident belong to the Muslim community. The victim is identified as Zakia Sultana, daughter of Zakaria and Sumi Akter. The attacker is identified as Imon, son of Abbas Uddin Ali. Hence, the claim made in the post is False.
A reverse image search of keyframes extracted from the viral video led us to Bangladeshi news reports (here & here) covering the incident. According to these reports, the attack took place in Kushtia city on 9 November 2026, when Zakia (Jakia) Sultana, a Class X student, was stabbed by a youth named Imon outside her house.
Further searches led to more media reports (here, here & here) identifying the victim as Zakia Sultana, daughter of Zakaria Hossain and Sumi Akter. Zakia was reportedly returning home after an examination and waiting at her house’s gate when Imon approached and stabbed her repeatedly. She was subsequently taken to the hospital for treatment and is now out of danger.
According to Zakia’s mother, Imon had allegedly been harassing her daughter for a while at the coaching centre where they both studied. After Zakia’s family informed Imon’s guardians about the harassment, he reportedly stopped. The family suspects the attack was carried out in retaliation for their complaint. The police arrested Imon and identified him as the son of Abbas Uddin. We found no credible news reports linking Imon to Jamaat-e-Islami. The evidence clearly indicates that the victim is a Muslim, not a Hindu.
To sum it up, a video of a personal dispute and stabbing involving two individuals from the Muslim community in Kushtia is being falsely shared online with a communal angle.

Here's when a dedicated graphics card is worth it
Modern iGPUs are surprisingly capable, but they aren’t without limitations.
A discrete graphics card is often the most expensive component in desktop computers, especially in gaming-focused builds. Besides driving a display, dedicated graphics cards also accelerate productivity-focused tasks like high resolution video editing, loading and running local LLMs or playing high-fidelity video games. While discrete graphics cards provide big performance uplifts to desktop computers, they aren't necessarily devoid of drawbacks.
If all you do on your computer is browse the web, stream media and play casual games, investing in a dedicated GPU might be unnecessary, and that doesn't even count buying a compatible PSU to power the card itself. Instead, you can look toward integrated graphics, as modern iGPUs are quite competent at offering a solid desktop experience, including light productivity, seamless media encoding and decoding and even casual gaming. As the name suggests, an integrated GPU is built into the same processor package and shares memory bandwidth with the CPU, unlike dedicated GPUs that have their own VRAM.
If you're on the fence deciding between getting a dedicated GPU or an iGPU, ask yourself if the additional power is something you actually need. If your current computing needs don't involve demanding workloads, a modern iGPU, like the AMD Radeon 780M, should easily fulfill your daily computing demands.
Not all integrated graphics are created equal
You might be surprised to learn how capable modern iGPUs have become, as they were once a bit of a drag on a system. However, it's worth noting that not all CPUs come equipped with equally capable iGPUs. Some only support display output, while others can comfortably drive high-resolution displays at higher refresh rate displays (not to confuse with pushing high frame rates in games), play casual games and handle light GPU-intensive workloads.
Take the AMD Ryzen 7 8700G and Ryzen 7 9800X3D processors, for example. The former features the AMD Radeon 780M graphics with 12 compute units, while the latter comes with basic Radeon Graphics, consisting of only two compute units. Interestingly, despite the Ryzen 7 9800X3D being significantly faster at CPU-related workloads, it's considerably weaker than the Ryzen 7 8700G in GPU-intensive scenarios.
If you're putting together a desktop computer with an iGPU, both Intel and AMD offer options across different budgets. However, AMD is currently leading the desktop iGPU space with its iGPU offerings providing substantial graphics-processing horsepower over Intel's conventional integrated graphics solutions.
When is a dedicated graphics card worth buying?
If you increasingly find your workloads shifting towards high-resolution video and photo editing or high-fidelity gaming, buying a dedicated graphics card over an iGPU makes the most sense. Not only is a discrete graphics card considerably more powerful than an iGPU, its dedicated VRAM provides a separate and much higher bandwidth memory pool that graphics workloads can take advantage of, alleviating memory-related bottlenecks that iGPUs are commonly susceptible to.
Unlike a dedicated graphics cards, an iGPU's performance depends on more than just its clock speeds or core counts. Since iGPUs share system memory, RAM speeds, configuration and capacity can all contribute to memory-related bottlenecks. For instance, TechSpot found that switching from DDR5-6400 to DDR5-5200 saw significant performance drops on the Ryzen 7 8700G, across several games.
On the bright side, owning a desktop computer means the freedom to upgrade your machine based on your needs. Just because you built a computer with an iGPU, it doesn't mean you're stuck with it forever. If you find your computing demands shifting from light workloads to running demanding games, loading heavy LLMs, rendering 3D graphics or high-resolution video editing, popping in a powerful graphics card into you PC can give it the additional horsepower needed to meet those demands. However, don't forget to verify your power supply capacity, PCIe compatibility and case clearance to accommodate a discrete graphics card into your build.

Trump, Putin and Xi plan historic joint meeting in China next week, White House says
- Published
Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are planning to meet on the sidelines of a summit in China next week, the White House has said.
The historic meeting between the leaders of the US, Russia and China will take place as Trump attends the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in the southern city of Shenzhen, spokeswoman Olivia Wales told reporters.
"The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous," she said.
It is understood Iran may also be discussed during the meeting of the world's biggest nuclear powers, but not Ukraine. Moscow and Beijing are yet to comment.
No agreement was expected to follow the talks, an unnamed, senior American official said, according to news agencies AP and Reuters.
Trump will arrive in Shenzhen late on Wednesday for the two-day summit between the 21 member states. He will also take part in bilateral talks with Xi on Thursday - their fourth meeting since the US president returned to office in 2025.
"President Trump will conclude his visit to China with a trilateral meeting between the president of the United States, the president of the People's Republic of China, and the president of the Russian Federation," Wales said.
She said Trump's trip, which will also include attending an Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) summit in the Philippines on Tuesday, would "secure historic wins to the American people and advance America's interests in the Indo Pacific".
A nuclear weapons control treaty between the US and Russia expired in February, leaving the world's biggest nuclear arsenals without major guardrails and effectively marking an end to the arms control co-operation which helped to resolve the Cold War.
The UN has urged both sides to agree a new framework without delay. Trump however said he could replace the deal with a better agreement which included China, which has been building up its arsenal.
Former senior US officials and analysts told the BBC at the time that seeking Beijing and Moscow's co-operation could turn up major hurdles and take years.
Xi separately hosted both Putin and Trump in Beijing just days apart earlier this year, while the US president welcomed his Chinese counterpart to Washington in September.
Beijing has become a crucial trading partner for Moscow since it launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, which has isolated Russia and left it subject to Western sanctions.
But a controversial US deal to import Russian diesel and the suspension of sanctions targeting the biggest buyers of Moscow's oil and gas - including China - heightened European concern about the Trump administration's softening towards the Kremlin last month.
Trump and Xi have meanwhile sought to project warmer ties at summits in Beijing and Washington this year - though little significant progress appeared to have been made on key issues such as trade, their race for AI dominance, and Taiwan. The war in Iran has also been a sticking point, with Beijing the largest buyer of Tehran's oil and its biggest trade partner.
Chinese state media reported on Friday that Xi would take part in "bilateral" talks on the sidelines of the Apec summit, citing a foreign ministry spokesman, but has not reported on the trilateral meeting.
Earlier this month, Russian state news agency Tass reported that Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov had said there were "signals confirming readiness" for such talks at the summit.

What's Trump's strategy now with Iran? To keep things as they are
DUBAI, United Arab Emirates — President Donald Trump is confronting new realities nine months into the war with Iran that leave him with dwindling options to ending the conflict.
On Thursday, he waved away the need for a deal with Iran, saying the U.S. has billions of Iran's dollars frozen in overseas accounts.
"We don't need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed. We've got their money," he wrote in a Truth Social post.
Negotiations with Iran are stuck with mediator Qatar working to bridge the divide. Trump met Qatar's prime minister at the White House this week, and said afterward that Gulf Arab allies prefer "the status quo" of continued economic pressure on Iran. He wrote that while the U.S. remains "locked and loaded", an attack at this point "seems to be quite unlikely."
That's a pivot from his threats to carry out quick, intense strikes on Iran in the days before he had to contend with two election setbacks.
Trump's wartime ally, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whom he'd thrown his support behind, is on the cusp of being ousted from power after elections there.
Meanwhile, at home, Trump's party lost its majority in Congress in midterm elections. Vice President JD Vance blamed Republican losses on the unpopular war with Iran and the nature of U.S. relations with Israel.
With less room to room maneuver and Iran still defiant, Trump's strategy appears to be to keep things as they are, for now. That means the possibility of escalation still looms.
Senior UAE diplomat, Anwar Gargash, told an audience in Abu Dhabi this week the region must "prepare for a prolonged period of uncertainty, in which neither a decisive resolution nor a stable regional order can be taken for granted."
Here's what keeping the status quo looks like.
Iran's chokehold on the Strait of Hormuz persists
Official Iranian social media accounts frequently post videos of attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz for violating Iran's new rules requiring permission to navigate the waterway, which was open and free to ships before the war.
The U.S., meanwhile, is assisting oil tankers through the Strait of Hormuz using a route that's close to Oman's coastline. While this has helped Arab states export their oil, it does not solve the bigger problem of how to bring back the pre-war production levels of other vital products like liquified natural gas, fertilizer and aluminum. Nor does a status quo allow countries like Kuwait, Qatar and Bahrain to import goods to their ports.
The International Monetary Fund says Gulf Arab states are in economic recession as a result of the war, despite higher oil prices. It says Kuwait, Qatar and Iraq's economies are contracting approximately 16% this year. Bahrain's is down 11%.
More limited strikes that could rapidly escalate
The U.S. is sending a third aircraft carrier with thousands of troops to the region, leaving open the possibility of another planned military escalation.
This week, Iran unveiled what it says is a new underground missile production site.
The U.S. and Iran are also still occasionally carrying out tit-for-tat for strikes.
On Friday, Iranian media said the U.S. struck one of its islands in the Strait of Hormuz. It's an area where Iran has radars and drone launch sites. Iran's Revolutionary Guard said it hit back, targeting an early warning U.S. radar in Bahrain.
Iran remains economically battered, starved of oil revenue
Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters this week there's no need for military action against Iran at this stage because economic sanctions are doing the job.
"The pain that they're feeling is, eventually you have to eat. Eventually you have to be able to pay your own fighters and your own security forces," Rubio said.
There's also a U.S. naval blockade at sea barring Iranian ships from transporting oil to countries like China. This blockade, according to the U.S. military, has cut Iran off from at least $25 billion in revenue so far.
One of the biggest economic blows, though, has come from the United Arab Emirates. The UAE announced over the summer it was severing all economic and trade ties with Iran. The UAE had been among Iran's biggest trade partners and local bank accounts were allegedly used by Iran's supreme leader and Revolutionary Guard to move money around.
Meanwhile, the U.S. military's Central Command announced a new operation, dubbed "Iron Gate", with other U.S. government agencies, aimed at preventing Iran from using land routes to transport advanced weapons across its borders and the Caspian Sea.
War in Yemen intensifies, draws in more countries
Another consequence of the conflict with Iran is the resumption of all-out war between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis in Yemen.
The Houthis, who are not a direct proxy of Iran but are supported by it, say Saudi airstrikes across Yemen have killed scores of people in past months, including nearly 60 this past weekend, many of them women and children in a village near the capital Sana'a.
Saudi Arabia, meanwhile, faces daily missile and drone attacks by Houthis, including some this week that hit its key East-West pipeline carrying crude oil to bypass the Strait of Hormuz. Another Houthi attack hit Saudi oil company Aramco's skyscraper headquarters in Riyadh's financial district.
Deadly Houthi attacks on Saudi airports have led to flights and high-profile events being cancelled. https://www.npr.org/2026/11/02/nx-s1-6007693/wars-in-iran-and-yemen-dent-saudi-modernization-mega-projects
As the Yemen war drags on, Pakistan, Turkey and Egypt are among the countries entering the fray with defensive support to Saudi Arabia. The U.S. is assisting with intelligence on the Houthis.
The United Nations says some 330,000 Yemenis have been displaced by the renewed fighting between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government, exacerbating an already dire humanitarian crisis.
Efforts by mediators continue, neither side budges
Iran says it's prepared for a short-term pause on attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz, but insists that seven demands be met before entering into direct talks over its nuclear program.
"The message has been only one thing. These seven items are on the table. Take it or leave it," Hamidreza Gholamzade, Tehran municipality spokesperson, told NPR.
These demands include lifting sanctions, ending the naval blockade, unfreezing Iran's dollars in overseas accounts and enforcing a ceasefire across all fronts, which includes halting Israeli attacks in Lebanon and Gaza.
Rubio has described the conditions as "absurd".
There's also discussion on diluting and moving Iran's enriched uranium abroad. However, the head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, told Iran's state broadcaster Wednesday: "We will not remove even a shred of enriched nuclear material from Iran."
It's another indication of the gridlock.
NPR's Hadeel al-Shalchi in Antalya, Turkey, and Ahmed Abu Hamada in Cairo contributed reporting.

Meta Platforms said on Monday it would expand its AI age-estimation technology globally to move millions more teens on Instagram into Teen Account protections, even if they have given birth dates showing they are adults, as the company faces lawsuits alleging its platforms harm young users.
Teen Accounts, available on Instagram, Facebook and Messenger, include built-in protections that automatically limit who can contact teens, the content they see and their time on the apps.
Parents in the US will begin receiving Instagram notifications this month explaining how teens are placed in age-appropriate protections, Meta said.
In Australia, Meta has begun using Apple’s age-range signal as an additional method to help determine users’ ages.
Meta said it is continuing to roll out the technology on Facebook and will begin launching similar technology globally on Threads later this year.
Meta faces multiple lawsuits over allegations that its platforms harm teens.
In August, Meta struck settlements worth up to $18 billion with nearly every US state and territory to resolve lawsuits brought by attorneys general over the platforms’ harm to teens.
Under the settlements, Meta agreed to improve how it identifies teens and children under 13.
Meta settled with a teen plaintiff last month in a Los Angeles trial testing claims that Instagram and Facebook were designed to be addictive, causing mental health problems and an eating disorder.

How the Jensen Huang scandal created a headache for business-friendly Singapore
- Published
A major scandal involving Nvidia founder Jensen Huang and a suspected Chinese spy based in Singapore has cast a spotlight on the city-state's success as a global chip hub - and a location for alleged illicit trade.
On Thursday, Huang stepped down from the US chip giant after admitting he had an affair. He was reportedly involved with a woman named Alice Huang, who ran Singaporean data centre company Megaspeed, a major buyer of Nvidia's chips.
For decades, Singapore has painstakingly cultivated a reputation as an open, business-friendly economy offering easy access to both the US and Chinese markets.
With the AI boom, it has become a major hub for the trade of high-end semiconductor chips in recent years.
Singapore was the second-largest billing centre globally last year for Nvidia, accounting for nearly a fifth of what the US chip giant earns.
But notably, less than 1% of its earnings were for chips that actually entered Singapore, as the island acts as a hub for many Asian companies to place orders and send them elsewhere.
Since 2022, when the US restricted advanced American semiconductors from being exported to China or acquired by Chinese companies, US officials have been concerned that other countries such as Singapore could be used by Chinese companies to gain access to the chips.
Megaspeed is a case in point.
It became the biggest buyer of Nvidia's chips in South East Asia and is suspected of giving backdoor access to these chips to Chinese companies via its data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.
While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.
Singapore has said that while it does not enforce "unilateral export controls imposed by other countries" it expects all companies in its jurisdiction to respect such regulations.
The city-state has had some success in policing this.
It has charged four companies and five individuals - including Chinese nationals - for various offences including fraud, following US concerns that Chinese AI company DeepSeek had been buying Nvidia chips from third parties in Singapore, among other places.
They also tried to probe Megaspeed, but were faced with a number of difficulties.
In a statement released on Thursday, the government said that since February 2025, they had been looking into whether Megaspeed and other firms had made false declarations about data servers which were purchased and exported through Singapore.
The companies stated the equipment would end up in neighbouring Malaysia, but Singapore authorities suspect the equipment's final destinations were elsewhere.
Singapore said it sought assistance from US authorities several times to get more information from one of the investigated companies - Supermicro, a US-based company which the BBC understands was supplying computer servers to Megaspeed.
But "despite these repeated requests, Singapore has to date received limited information or assistance", it said in its statement. The BBC has sought comment from the US State Department.
Singapore authorities said they had also investigated Alice Huang - not for espionage, but for any possible role in Megaspeed's suspected fraud.
In the end, they found "insufficient evidence" of crime and let her leave Singapore in February this year, after holding her passport for several months.
Since launching their probe nearly two years ago, Singapore has yet to bring any charges against Megaspeed or any of the companies and individuals linked to the case.
Singapore and US investigations into Megaspeed are still ongoing.
In 2024, US officials had paid a visit to a Malaysian data centre owned by Megaspeed and saw Nvidia technology still in their boxes, raising concerns that Megaspeed was shipping high-end chips out elsewhere, according to a report by the New York Times.
Last year, Megaspeed appeared to have imported 50,000 more chips than Nvidia could account for, according to a Bloomberg report. Nvidia later adjusted its own figures after visiting more warehouses.
Megaspeed has maintained it has always acted lawfully and that previous inspections by authorities found no evidence of illegal activity.
On Thursday, the company said it "welcomes appropriate government scrutiny" and that it is "committed to working constructively and transparently with the US government".
China has also long refuted accusations that its companies and institutions are illegally obtaining high-end US chips.
How Megaspeed and Alice Huang came to Singapore highlights other vulnerabilities stemming from the city-state's openness.
In recent years, the city-state has become a prime destination for Chinese companies, with tech firms such as TikTok and Manus making it their global headquarters. Besides Singapore's ease of doing business, it has a population that is mostly ethnically Chinese and largely views China positively.
For a Chinese firm, Singapore offers a base near the mainland and a "neutral address" that global customers and investors accept, said Winston Ma, adjunct professor at New York University's School of Law.
But critics say this has given rise to "Singapore-washing", where Chinese companies use the city-state's clean image to obscure their origins, reduce suspicions and even cover up dubious activities.
Washington-based security analysis group C4ADS told the BBC they had assessed Alice Huang's setup of Megaspeed to be such a case.
BBC checks of corporate records in China, Hong Kong and Singapore found that in 2019, Huang sold a gaming company and its subsidiaries to Chinese gaming firm 7Road.
In March 2023, a 7Road subsidiary in Singapore named Huang as its executive director. The next day it changed its name - to Megaspeed.
Huang was in charge for eight months before she transferred the company to a Singaporean man.
During this period, Megaspeed went through "a critical period of corporate restructuring and regional expansion", and her corporate relationships raised questions about whether "Megaspeed's Singaporean identity is genuine or effectively Chinese-controlled", according to C4ADS.
Even after she transferred Megaspeed, C4ADS assessed that she was still "practically in control" of the company, based on her links to Megaspeed via another company as well as LinkedIn posts where she continued to identify herself as Megaspeed's "chairwoman" at conferences.
Megaspeed has not answered BBC queries regarding the company's and Alice Huang's links to China and the Chinese government.
All this reinforces the dilemma faced by Singapore.
"For the longest time, Singapore has managed to enjoy the best of both worlds with excellent relations with US and China," Nanyang Technological University politics and international studies lecturer Dylan Loh said.
Singapore has long positioned itself as a neutral party between the two superpowers. Its prime minister Lawrence Wong has insisted that his country is neither pro-China nor pro-America, but "pro-Singapore".
But Loh says this balancing act "has now fast become very difficult to manage and sometimes quite fraught too" with the US-China dispute over chips.
With the Megaspeed case, the tightrope Singapore has walked is set to get even narrower, according to analysts.
Beijing may ask why Singapore is investigating issues pertaining to US restrictions and whether they are siding with the US' interests, says Chong Ja Ian, a Singaporean political scientist and non-resident scholar with Carnegie China.
Washington, in turn, might read Singapore's latest statement as "pushing blame" on the US, which could lead to backlash from the White House, he said.
"Singapore has made a policy position not to take sides. But by not choosing a side, they run the risk of being seen as complicit" in either side's agenda, he said.
But Benjamin Ho, an assistant professor and China expert at Singapore's S Rajaratnam School of International Studies, noted that this was "not the first or last time Singapore will be caught between the US and China".
"This is the price that an open economy has to grapple with - you get caught in the middle when things turn sour."
Additional reporting by Jack Lau of the BBC's Global China Unit.
