I return to my room as my mother-in-law leaves for her office in the building adjacent to our home. I am about to start my bath when I hear a series of explosions, as of firecrackers, but different. I freeze. Someone comes pounding frantically on my bathroom door. It is Ongmu, the children’s nanny, crying hysterically. I fling open the door, my heart thumping. She is gesticulating wildly, speechlessly, towards the garden.
I run along the path leading to Akbar Road. I see the white Ambassador car slowly moving towards the same path. I hesitate. I stop, heart in my mouth. Dread, panic, fear. I feel suffocated. I can’t breathe. I am about to collapse. No, no, I can’t. I have to walk to the car. I see her being carried into it. I understand; I scream.
I’m in the car now, crouching on the floor, facing her … Blood – blood on her sari, blood on her chest. Her large eyes are wide open; her face wears a surprised expression. She doesn’t move. I attempt to speak to her, to call out, “Mummy, Mummy”, but no word comes out. I try again; she doesn’t reply.
Her aides are in the front of the car, screaming. Heavy, slow traffic, the car barely moves, it has no siren. One red light, then another. Then the hospital. The gate isn’t opening. Chaos. We are stopped; someone looks through the window in a questioning attitude. They let us in.
We reach the emergency department, teeming with people. We are stopped again, not allowed in, we have to wait for our turn. Someone calls out to the driver, signals him to move forward. They identify us; she is placed on a trolley. We are led somewhere – an operation theatre? They ask me to follow. I’m taken to a room nearby. No, no, I want to stay by her, I insist. I want to know. I have to see. They don’t reply; they are immersed in their emergency procedures.
I feel confused, lost … I don’t recognise anyone there. I’m shivering under my dressing gown. I feel scared, my mind is racing. Where is Rajiv? I try to remember. I can’t, I can’t. The children, yes, they’re in school; they must be brought home. Oh God, no, no. Let them be safe, let Rajiv be safe … Whom do I tell, whom do I speak to? I sense someone in the room. I don’t know who it is. I try to speak, to put some words together; nothing comes out. “There’s blood all over her clothes,” someone says. Some clothes are brought in for me. I am helped into them in a nearby closet.
Hours go by, agonising hours. More people come in and crowd around. I signal a question to the doctor; he shakes his head. I understand, yes, I understand. I break into sobs, uncontrollably. Someone tries to calm me. I feel numb, cold.
At two in the afternoon of 31 October 1984, Indira Gandhi was declared dead. I was driven home to collect some clothes for her body to be changed into. On the way, a group of men tried to stop our car, banging on its windows. They were angry, shouting something I couldn’t understand.
At home, the children, Rahul and Priyanka, rushed to my arms in tears. When they had been abruptly picked up from school by black-uniformed commandos, they sensed a catastrophe. Once home, they saw some of the staff sobbing. They asked question after question. “Where’s Mama?” “Why have we been brought home?” “Where’s Papa?” “What’s happened?” “Where’s Dadi?” “You aren’t telling us the truth!” My friends Nina and Sterre had been with them, trying to calm them down, not knowing what to say to them. I wanted to sit with them and hug them, to break the news to them gently, but I was unable to – I had to go back; Rajiv was coming to the hospital.
Rajiv had been in West Bengal at a political rally when his cavalcade was stopped by a police patrol. He was told there was a message from Delhi to say he should rush back – a serious accident had taken place. He was driven to the helipad, from where he flew to Calcutta and then to Delhi. He’d heard on a BBC bulletin that Mrs Gandhi was wounded and in a grave condition. Nobody told him directly that his mother was no more, but he understood.
He landed at 3.30pm and was driven straight to the hospital. He walked in with other people, and I remember longing to be left alone with him for a moment at least. We held each other, and as he spoke to me, it sunk in that he was saying something I didn’t want to hear. “I have been asked … They want me to be sworn in as prime minister.”
I felt as if a knife had been plunged right into my heart. I felt a pounding in my chest, a rage welling up deep inside me. I was about to explode. I attempted to hold it in. “You have been asked to? How dare they ask? How dare they? Who are they? Why you, why does it have to be you? Why did you allow them to ask you? No, it cannot be; this time it’s not going to be!” Seized by utter pain and anguish, soaked in perspiration, I felt like throwing up. I wanted to scream, to ask for help. “Someone please help me put an end to this.”
I burst out crying, pleading, begging him with folded hands, “No, no, you can’t think of it. You have to stop them, you must refuse, you must say no – for the children’s sake, for yourself. You can’t do this to us. They will kill you; they will kill you, too!” I cried out. He replied, “They will kill me anyway.”
We brought my mother-in-law home. The dining room had been emptied out, and we laid her body down on the floor, her feet pointing south as Hindu custom decrees. The same evening at around 6.30pm, Rajiv was sworn in as prime minister of India. I was too broken to even register what was happening around me. His mother lay there, her body pierced with more than 30 bullet holes. I knew, I knew it then in my heart: Rajiv’s path would lead to the same end.

IndiaIndia could secure a tariff advantage over competing economies in the US market under the proposed bilateral trade agreement with Washington, potentially giving Indian exporters a stronger footing against rivals such as Vietnam, Bangladesh and China. The United States has assured India of a comparative tariff advantage over its competitors under the proposed trade pact, news agency ANI reported, quoting a senior government official. However, the actual extent of this advantage will depend on the final tariff structure and the outcome of ongoing trade investigations. "The US has assured India of a comparative tariff advantage over its competitors in the trade deal. We will have to see how the tariff framework unfolds," the official said, as per ANI. The assurance comes as New Delhi and Washington continue negotiations on the first tranche of their bilateral trade agreement (BTA), alongside discussions on the broader pact. India is aiming to conclude the initial tranche by the end of the current financial year. A more favourable tariff arrangement could improve the competitiveness of Indian products in the US, particularly in sectors where exporters compete directly with manufacturers from Vietnam, Bangladesh and other Asian economies. The tariff differential could become an important factor in determining sourcing decisions by American buyers. If Indian goods face lower import duties than comparable products from competing countries, exporters could gain an advantage in pricing, attract fresh orders and potentially expand their market share. Vietnam and Bangladesh are among the economies competing with India for a larger share of the American market. Vietnam currently faces a reported 12.5% general duty on its exports to the US under Section 301, while Bangladesh faces a 10% duty. India and the US have been negotiating the bilateral trade agreement since its announcement in February 2026. Both sides are pursuing discussions on the initial tranche and the broader agreement simultaneously, with the first phase expected to deliver early outcomes. Services-related issues will not be included in the first tranche and will instead be taken up during the second phase of negotiations as part of the larger agreement. The final pact is expected to be structured as a legal text accompanied by annexures, with a dedicated chapter on customs and trade facilitation, the government official said. As part of the negotiations, a two-member US delegation visited India on November 2 and 3 to discuss customs procedures and trade facilitation. The discussions followed engagements between the two countries on reducing procedural barriers and improving the movement of goods across borders. Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal has also expressed confidence in the negotiations, saying India would secure one of the best trade agreements with the US. "And in every respect, India will have one of the best deals with the US," Goyal told reporters on Thursday. He said India had negotiated a strong set of outcomes with Washington under the proposed agreement. Despite the positive signals, uncertainty remains over the final tariff framework. The US imposed an additional 10% import duty on several countries, including India, effective July 24, 2026. The additional levy followed a US investigation into forced labour-related issues under Section 301 of the US Trade Act of 1974 and applies over and above existing Most Favoured Nation (MFN) tariff rates. Section 301 empowers the Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR) to investigate and take retaliatory action against foreign government policies and practices considered discriminatory or harmful to US commerce, including those that violate trade agreements. India is awaiting the outcome of a second investigation initiated by the USTR against the country. Its findings could have implications for the final tariff arrangements and the extent of the advantage New Delhi secures under the trade pact. A favourable tariff differential could strengthen India's position as American companies look to diversify their sourcing and reduce dependence on particular manufacturing hubs. Indian exporters in sectors competing with suppliers from Vietnam and Bangladesh could potentially benefit from improved price competitiveness. A lower tariff burden could also make India a more attractive destination for sourcing and encourage businesses to expand production and supply-chain investments. However, a tariff advantage alone may not be enough to help Indian exporters overtake established competitors. Manufacturing costs, production capacity, delivery timelines, infrastructure, product quality and the ability to meet large-volume orders will remain crucial. The broader question, therefore, is whether India can convert a potentially favourable trade arrangement into sustained export growth. Much will depend on the final agreement, the sectors covered and how effectively Indian manufacturers use the opportunity to gain a larger foothold in the US market. About 65 million light-years from Earth, three galaxies don’t look quite right. They aren’t whirlpools bursting with light, but pallid objects dimly illuminated by a smattering of stars. “They have this ghostly appearance,” said Michael Keim, an astrophysicist at Yale University. And this isn’t even the weirdest thing about them.
Dark matter is the invisible glue that keeps the largest structures in the cosmos together. It draws ordinary, visible matter toward it, allowing stars to form and keeping the stelliferous limbs of galaxies from flying off. “Almost all galaxies are dominated by dark matter,” said Shyam Balaji, a theoretical physicist at King’s College London.
But these three diffuse galaxies, known as DF2, DF4, and DF9, have left astronomers stunned. After using a suite of telescopes to estimate their masses—using the motions of their stars as a proxy—the researchers found that all three have little dark matter. Instead, a pittance of ordinary matter alone must have forged their small selection of stars. How could these rule-breaking galaxies have formed?
A paper published in June 2026 in The Astrophysical Journal offers a potential solution. Once upon a time, two regular galaxies collided. Their ordinary matter—their gas and dust—swirled about and got clumped up. But the dark matter passed right through and continued on, like a specter passing through a wall. The cosmic pileup left behind three new galaxies, each bereft of dark matter, each left to struggle to form a new batch of stars.
It’s a convincing explanation for many experts—one that, crucially, may tell us something about the mystery of dark matter.
Some scientists have suggested that dark matter, which has yet to be directly detected, may not exist. Instead, they propose that a tweak to our understanding of the gravitational force might explain various features of the universe.
These bizarre galaxies pour cold water on that idea. “What this is showing is that dark matter is … not just a modification of gravity,” said Keim, who is an author of the new study. If you segregate ordinary matter from dark matter, you’d expect that the dark-matter-lacking galaxies would struggle to form stars—and that’s what DF2, DF4, and DF9 show.
That suggests, as many have suspected for some time, that dark matter is a physical thing. “The absence of dark matter is, in a way, some evidence of dark matter, which is ironic,” Balaji said.
What, exactly, is dark matter? Ever since it was formally proposed by the astronomer Fritz Zwicky in the 1930s—and built upon in the 1970s by the astronomer Vera Rubin—cosmologists and astrophysicists have been putting forward their best candidates. Could it be a stealthy type of neutrino? Might it be so-called weakly interacting massive particles, or WIMPs? Some have even opined that it could be primordial black holes as small as individual atoms and as old as the universe itself.
“We don’t know which dark matter candidate is the right one,” said Daniel Whiteson, a particle physicist at the University of California, Irvine. Whatever it is, it has yet to be detected. But “there’s a lot of independent lines of evidence that dark matter is matter.”
Dark matter, which makes up 27 percent of the universe—and 85 percent of all matter—interacts with gravity. If it were down to the gravitational pull of ordinary matter alone, stars on the edges of rapidly spinning galaxies would escape into space. Ordinary matter alone would struggle to clump together tightly enough to form stars. Dark matter also seems to warp space itself, bending light around objects in a process known as gravitational lensing.
“You wouldn’t get galaxies without dark matter,” said Chamkaur Ghag, a physicist at University College London. “Is there a way of evolving the galaxies without dark matter in the first place? Our understanding says no.”
So when DF2 was discovered in 2018, astronomers didn’t quite know what to make of it. The galaxy is roughly the same size as the Milky Way, but with 200 times fewer stars, it’s considerably dimmer. Suspicious, scientists used the Keck Observatory in Hawaii to track the motions of those stars to estimate the galaxy's total mass. They discovered that, even for such a star-deficient galaxy, it was lightweight: It seemed to contain, at most, 400 times less dark matter than they would expect, making DF2 the first dark-matter-deficient galaxy ever spotted.
In 2019, they observed DF4, another phantom galaxy with a dearth of dark matter. And in 2026, scientists announced that a third, DF9, had joined the club. It contains the mass of roughly 100 million suns, which is consistent with having only ordinary matter. If it were also packed with dark matter, it would be 100 times more massive.
That all three gossamer galaxies existed along a line, as neighbors, didn’t escape the attention of astrophysicists, who began to coalesce around an origin story.
Dark matter is only known to act with the gravitational force; there’s no compelling evidence yet that it interacts with other fundamental forces, like electromagnetism. If two typical galaxies met in a head-on collision, the dark matter would experience very little friction, or drag, and would keep on rocketing by. But ordinary matter, which interacts using all four fundamental forces, would get all tangled up.
“An analogy would be two knights jousting, where the knights and their lances collide and may be thrown to the ground in a heap, while their horses keep on running at full speed,” said Aaron Romanowsky, an astronomer at San Jose State University.
Several independent experts buy the tale spun by Keim and his colleagues. “It’s very convincing,” Whiteson said.
It’s reminiscent of the Bullet Cluster, two massive collections of galaxies 3.8 billion light-years away that also collided eons ago. This destruction derby, which was recently observed by the James Webb Space Telescope, has a messy distribution of mass that only makes sense if dark matter and ordinary matter got torn asunder during the collision.
Although this kind of segregation can be seen with greater clarity in DF2, DF4, and DF9, not everyone agrees on how the separation took place.
Kinwah Wu, a theoretical astrophysicist at University College London, noted that the triplet does not exhibit any of the fluid, wispy features that one would expect to see after a galactic collision. He suggests that, in this case, DF2, DF4, and DF9 were passing through a large group of massive galaxies. This outsize rabble then stripped the triplet of all their dark matter during their ill-fated voyage.
Stacy McGaugh, an astronomer at Case Western Reserve University and a longtime proponent of modified-gravity theories, is more skeptical. “It’s not clear to me what the formation mechanism is,” he said. An ancient collision “is a plausible origin story, albeit an exceptional one. If that’s what’s happened, then the rest follows.” In other words: If these galaxies were created when their dark matter was stolen away, then it makes sense that dark matter is a physical substance.
“But the question is: Is that what happened?” he continued. “And I’m not convinced that that’s the only way that can happen.” Without definitively knowing their origin story, McGaugh doesn’t think it’s possible to say anything about the nature of dark matter itself.
Most experts, though, cannot see how DF2, DF4, and DF9 could exist without dark matter being a physical thing, even if the trio’s genesis can be debated. “It’s hard to explain how you’d get something like this evolving by itself without something like dark matter,” Ghag said.
That makes this galactic trio bad news for MOND, or modified Newtonian dynamics, an alternative to dark matter proposed in 1983 by the physicist Mordehai Milgrom. “MOND says: What if there’s only visible matter, but its gravity works differently than we thought?” Whiteson explained.
MOND implies that, when objects are experiencing a very weak gravitational pull—for example, when two stars are separated by extreme distances—the gravitational force doesn’t dwindle as much as scientists think. That could explain why spinning galaxies can be held together without needing an extra source of gravity from dark matter, its proponents have argued.
Dark matter has long been the favored theory for cosmologists, as MOND “could never really explain everything,” Ghag said. He explained that MOND suffered a significant blow in 2015 when the US-based Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory, or LIGO, detected gravitational waves—ripples in the fabric of the universe—for the first time. Scientists found that these waves move at the speed of light in all directions over huge distances, which implies that gravity works in a consistent, unmodified way throughout the cosmos.
DF2, DF4, and DF9 are also more elegantly explained by dark matter than by attempts to adjust the mechanics of gravity. “It’s easier to remove matter, cold dark matter, through something like a collision, than it is to turn off a law of nature,” Balaji said.
“I think it’s fine and healthy to have alternative theories and open debate,” Whiteson said. “But let’s also be frank about whether the theory fits the data. MOND does not.”
The identity of dark matter still eludes us. But these galaxies are arguably another nail in the coffin of its increasingly unpopular competitor.

The Pentagon's research arm tested how ground drones could be sent out in groups to look for and hunt down targets while keeping a human operator in the loop to make decisions.
The Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, or DARPA, program examined how uncrewed ground vehicles, or UGVs, could quickly drive, map out terrain, and gather information on their own in contested environments. Lessons will inform ongoing developments in uncrewed technologies across the US military, officials said.
Last month, DARPA experimented with four autonomous UGVs at an exercise at Fort Knox, Kentucky, as part of its Robotic Autonomy in Complex Environments with Resiliency, or RACER, program. During the exercise, the ground robots conducted surveillance of the surrounding area, independently searching for enemy forces for an operator located away from the action.
Jason Gregory, technical advisor at DARPA, told Business Insider that "we're moving sensors and effectors forward to the tactical edge while keeping the operator in safety out of harm's way," but humans still "maintained control and custody and situational awareness at all times."
Once launched, the UGVs went off on their missions. Gregory said they could work together or independently depending on the scenario. Meanwhile, the human operator supervised the UGVs, assigned them tasks, checked their findings, and then decided how best to engage enemy targets.
At the Fort Knox demonstration, the operator used satellite imagery to task the robots. One UGV stopped in place once it spotted a potential target — a closed box holding a drone inside — and then the human operator decided to launch a simulated rocket at the target.
An important part of the recent RACER robotic testing program was ensuring that the UGVs could perform their tasks without GPS. Instead, the robots built the map as they moved. The US military has said it needs to be prepared to fight through contested or denied environments where GPS isn't readily available, and is looking into alternative precision navigation and timing solutions, as well as more traditional tactics.
The military is also considering other possible disruptions, such as terrain interference or loss of signal.
"We developed this new software so that ground vehicles could use only their onboard sensors to make decisions to move as fast as possible," Gregory said. The software was tested on four-wheel, all-terrain UGVs as well as tracked UGVs to ensure it could be deployed on different hardware.
While teams worked to build systems using commercial technologies, the RACER program also involved five years of research to better understand the scientific and technical challenges of autonomy, artificial intelligence algorithms, and ground mobility.
DARPA's work also relied on observations from Russia's war in Ukraine on the distinct role of ground robots and how operators employ them in different situations.
Autonomous UGVs face distinct challenges depending on the terrain, environment, and climate. In the desert, for example, robots might need to navigate sand, rocks, and other obstacles, while extreme heat might strain the batteries and communications systems. Swamplands, forests, muddy fields, and snow can also make operations more difficult, requiring robots to be able to adapt to very different conditions.
RACER's demonstration offers lessons for the broader US military. While some are specific to autonomous ground robots, others — including operating without GPS, teaming humans with machines, and maintaining human oversight in robotic operations — could apply to uncrewed systems across the military. It's also sharing the lessons with industry.

The Italianization of Europe
Over more than a quarter-century, I’ve watched Europe’s politics become more like Italy’s, with all the resulting instability, as the far right came in from the cold.
When I first moved to Rome, I spent my time living in the past.
At the turn of the century, I drifted through a vintage postcard of postwar Italy: old women sitting around tables they had dragged into the street, old men playing cards in caps, cats arching their backs on the hoods of snub-nosed Fiats.
As newspapers filled with talk of Silvio Berlusconi, a media mogul with ambitions and appetites worthy of a Roman emperor, my meanderings inevitably took me toward Tiber Island, a sliver of land in the middle of the river that divides Rome.
An ancient bridge on the island’s left bank had a strange statue of weather-beaten faces positioned back-to-back as if they couldn’t stand one another. The heads rose out of the shared torso of a square pillar and represented Janus, Rome’s god of the past and future, the deity of transitions and change.
Back then, I didn’t see the change around me, but now, more than a quarter-century later, after spending decades reporting on Italian politics and changes across Europe, I have come to understand that I was living in the future.
In the time since, I have seen an Italianization of politics all around the continent, with coalitions of small parties resulting in instability, with fed-up voters desperate for new saviors. But more than anything, I have seen — in Britain, France, Germany — countries following the Italian model by allowing the far right into the political mainstream.

Happy World Kindness Day! Check out our kind photos of kindness to humans — and cats
Editor's note: Today, November 13, is World Kindness Day!
Kind-minded organizations from various countries came up with the idea and announced it on November 13, 1998. (And the date stuck.) The goal is kinda obvious — do something kind!
It doesn't matter if it's a modest action. One of the founding groups is the Small Kindness Movement of Japan. And no kind deed is too small to acknowledge. One year, the Japanese movement gave an award to a cabbie who pulled over to clear trash bags off the road lest they cause an accident. According to a report in the Christian Science Monitor, the cab driver humbly said it was "no big deal."
So on Friday, November 13, 2026, try a little kindness. To inspire you, we've talked to folks whose lives were changed by kindness — and asked the photojournalists of The Everyday Projects, a global network, to submit pictures that capture a kind moment. Animal lovers will be happy to see photos of kindness toward animals as well as an image of a support donkey — a reminder that animals can be kind to us humans, too.
Let's start with a simple yet profound story about a snack.
Back in 2004, Maymunah Yusuf Kadiri, a neuro-psychiatrist and mental health advocate in Nigeria, was a young doctor working in the emergency room at the Lagos State University Teaching hospital. One night sticks in her mind. It was chaos. There were accident victims everywhere. She recalls the blood, the cries and her own exhaustion.
"I hadn't eaten for over 12 hours, and my hands were shaking," says Kadiri, who was 28 at the time. "Then an elderly cleaner, one of those invisible heroes in hospitals, walked up to me with a small nylon bag." Inside was a biscuit and a sachet of water.
"Doctor," she said, "you need small strength to save people."
"It sounds simple, but I'll never forget it. That biscuit tasted like hope. Her kindness reminded me that healing isn't only about medicine, it's about humanity," says Kadiri. "As a psychiatrist, I've seen it over and over: People don't just heal in hospitals, they heal in human connections."
And while one isolated act of kindness may seem random, it can lead to much more.
Huguette Diakabana remembers when she had to drop out of school at age 10 — until a mysterious donor came to her rescue. Her family was planning to emigrate to the U.S. from Zaire (now the Democratic Republic of Congo) and couldn't afford school fees. They figured she'd make up the year later. She had a different idea: "I put on my previous year's uniform and sat outside under the street window of my would-be classroom." One day, the director invited her inside. Diakabana realized someone must have paid her school fees, but who?
Returning to the school years later, Diakabana discovered it was a school guard. She wanted to repay him. "He told me to help others when I could, so I launched a scholarship program," says Diakabana, who now lives in Switzerland and is co-founder of The Luminous Agency, which focuses on digital literacy.
Dr. Junaid Nabi, a physician-scientist who conducts research in health care technology at the RAND School in Washington, D.C. and is a senior fellow at the Aspen Institute, says he's come to realize that kindness isn't actually a trickle in the ocean. An act of kindness is more like dropping a stone that creates expanding ripples, he says.
"There are studies that illustrate how kindness spreads through social networks in measurable ways. When we are kind to someone, they don't just feel better — they become 25% more likely to help others."
One such investigation described how kindness can be contagious. It was sparked by reports of an outbreak of kindness on a cold December morning in 2012. A stranger picked up the tab for the coffee order of the next customer in the drive-through line at a Tim Hortons coffeehouse in Winnipeg, Canada. And that customer picked up the tab of the person behind him. In the end, 226 customers passed on this act of kindness.
The study authors, citing other examples of "pay it forward" kindness at fast food restaurants and their own experiments encouraging subjects to help others, write: "Why, in the absence of external sanctions and opportunities for reciprocation, do people help strangers? One possible explanation is that helping is driven by receiving or observing help. In other words, generosity towards strangers may be socially contagious."
Don't talk yourself out of it
It might sound contradictory, but researchers studying the psychology of altruism, kindness and giving have uncovered this curious paradox: Sometimes, people can be kind-hearted, have a genuine desire to help someone, but in spite of that, not give at all.
Marta Serra-Garcia, a professor of economics and strategy at the Rady School of Management in the University of California, San Diego, is one of the authors of the study Give Enough or Not at all.
"There's a growing body of work in economics and psychology trying to understand altruism. Altruism is a result of a feeling of empathy and the emotion of feeling warm and well when you help others. We know people are altruistic, but we're trying to understand when, why and how," she says.
The study, published in the September Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization, revealed that people may prefer to give nothing rather than donate an amount they consider too small — even when those on the receiving end would welcome whatever they can get.
"It seems like an odd thing," Serra-Garcia says in an interview over a video call with NPR. "You're generous, but because you want to do the right thing, you might end up not giving at all, out of concern that your gift would be viewed as inappropriate or might even offend the other person."
In one experiment in the study, givers tended to overestimate the minimum amount recipients would consider acceptable.
"We tend to think there are givers and non-givers," says Serra-Garcia. "The people who give are the generous and kind ones, the non-givers are just not generous." But the study indicates otherwise.
"That perception of appropriateness makes them think, "I'd rather not give at all, although I'm a generous person," says Serra-Garcia.
Nature or nurture?
And where does kindness come from? Are you born with it? Or can you learn to be compassionate and empathetic?
Jeff R. Temple, a professor and psychologist with UTHealth Houston, says kindness is a central thread running through his studies on healthy relationships among adolescents and young adults.
"In our intervention work — including with the Fourth R program and other school-based curricula — we teach adolescents to practice perspective-taking, to express care even during disagreement and recognize the impact of their words and actions. These are essentially the behavioral expressions of kindness."
Such kids are less likely to bully others because they know what healthy relationships are like, he says.
A ripple effect
And let's not forget that kindness can change not only the life of the recipient of the kind deed but of the kind person, says Nabi, who offers this anecdote.
In the 2013 Savar building collapse in Bangladesh, more than 1,000 garment workers died and thousands were injured. Nabi arrived at the disaster site as a Red Cross volunteer, expecting to gain experience in trauma care. Instead, he says, the experience changed his psyche, teaching him about the nature of true kindness.
"In the midst of chaos, with bodies awaiting identification, kindness came down to being present during others' darkest moments," says Nabi. "I performed CPR on workers I knew wouldn't survive and when I couldn't save someone, I stayed by their side, holding their hand."
"Before Savar, I was mechanistic, rushing through clinical work like tasks," he recalls. "The image of workers who had embraced each other as concrete crushed them — that final act of human kindness in the face of death — shattered my callousness completely."
When he returned to the hospital, he listened to patients differently, giving them more of his time. He also urges doctors to volunteer for humanitarian causes to practice compassion.
"Kindness, I learned, is about showing up completely for another person's suffering," Navi reflects, "and letting that experience fundamentally change who you are."
So if you began reading this story with the thought that World Kindness Day is … a gimmick … it is a gimmick imbued with heart and hope.
It's a good reminder to practice kindness more, Dr. Kadiri says. "And here's the beautiful part: When someone receives kindness, they don't just feel better, they become better." They may be inspired to perform their own act of kindness. And that, she says, makes the world a kinder, better place too.

Do the Dems need new leadership?
A Schumer challenger has entered the ring.
Hi readers, happy Friday! Today, we’re saying farewell — for now — to “Democrats in array.” Not quite two weeks after winning the 2026 midterms by a historic margin, the party has a leadership fight on its hands.
On Thursday evening, Sen. Chris Van Hollen, a Democrat from Maryland, made it official: He’s challenging current Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer for the title of majority leader next year, promising a bolder and more aggressive agenda for the party.
“It is about answering the call of the American people,” Van Hollen told MS NOW host Jen Psaki when he announced his candidacy on her show. “The call was really to reject the status quo and to reject business as usual. And to do that, I think we need new leadership.”
Newly elected Democrats Abdul El-Sayed (D-MI) and Peggy Flanagan (D-MN), each of whom defeated more leadership-aligned Democrats in their Senate primaries, are backing his bid. But Van Hollen will have an uphill climb to win the job, which is set to be decided in a closed-door vote early next month. Schumer, 75, has led Senate Democrats for nearly a decade, starting in 2017, and says he’s confident he will have the votes to be reelected in December.
Searching for “fighters”
The Senate is the only chamber currently dealing with an active leadership fight, but it’s not the only one with some leadership angst. In the House, current Democratic minority leader Hakeem Jeffries is the overwhelming favorite to become the new speaker in January (he currently lacks any Democratic challengers). But not everyone is happy about it, as my colleague Astead Herndon reported on Thursday.
The divide, he argues — both in the Schumer-Van Hollen showdown and frustrations with Jeffries — is not really about progressive versus moderate. Instead, he says, it’s about an energized, angry Democratic base looking for fighters to lead the party into what’s almost certain to be a combative final two years of the Trump administration, and a sense that neither Schumer nor Jeffries are ready to meet the moment.
It’s not just a problem for this cycle, either: Democrats won so widely last week that they’re very likely to hang onto their majorities at least through the 2028 election, Eric Levitz points out.
There’s nothing to say that Democrats will have the same leaders in two years (particularly Schumer, who’s up for reelection in 2028 but may either retire or face a serious primary challenge).
But the intra-party debate that we’re watching play out right now is effectively a preview of the higher-stakes fight to come in 2028, when Democrats could also have control of the presidency — and their freest legislative hand since the 2008 election.
As Eric writes, that will come with some real challenges, not least that Democrats currently appear to be facing an impossible trio of economic promises, one of which they’ll likely need to break. But it will also be a moment of opportunity — if the party’s leaders are ready for it.

Bompastor's risks pay off as Chelsea go top of WSL
- Published
In any big encounter you will often hear managers say it is the "fine margins" that decide a game of football.
Sometimes it is luck. Sometimes it is individual brilliance. But on Saturday it was Sonia Bompastor's bold decisions that helped Chelsea beat Manchester City 1-0.
The top-of-the-table Women's Super League clash was as intriguing as you would hope it to be and both managers needed to be on their toes.
Chelsea boss Bompastor "took responsibility" and brought off struggling defender Kadeisha Buchanan 12 minutes in, and it had the desired effect.
City striker Khadija Shaw was not able to get in behind like she had done in the early stages, and Buchanan's replacement Veerle Buurman shone.
Was it a tactical substitution or was Buchanan injured?
When the fourth official's board went up showing the number of the player Buurman would replace, there was confusion from Chelsea players.
It was clearly not planned, nor had Buchanan asked to come off. There was no apparent injury as she jogged off and she was clearly upset, heading straight down the tunnel.
Asked to clarify the situation, Bompastor said: "Yesterday in training she got a knock to her head in contact with a team-mate but she was fine.
"She was fine in the evening and we assessed her again this morning and everything was fine. I had that information before the game.
"But I felt from watching her at the beginning of the game that she was not herself. I took the responsibility to make the substitution.
"I felt I was almost forced to do that. I know my player and she was not in the game."
Surprise switch led to tactical battle
Whether Buchanan's shaky start was down to that knock is unclear, but Bompastor knew her decision was a risk and was willing to act immediately.
Buurman instantly marshalled Shaw, and City's early threat was quietened as Chelsea regained control and ended the half a goal up thanks to Sandy Baltimore.
Shaw did not record a shot on target and in-form England international Lauren Hemp was quiet as Buurman performed well in a stubborn Chelsea backline.
City manager Andree Jeglertz said he did not think the switch "changed the picture", but he was outsmarted by Bompastor during the 90 minutes.
Bompastor admitted she had not spoken properly with Buchanan at full-time but promised to "explain myself to her".
"I just told her a few words. My assistant coach Camille Abily will have done that already probably and I think everything will be fine," said the Frenchwoman.
"I always have good relationships with the players, bring them clarity, and I'm always direct and honest so they have the information. It won't be any different."
The risky substitution was compounded by an injury to striker Melvine Malard 23 minutes later, meaning Chelsea's XI was tweaked twice before half-time.
Not normally one to bring on players at the break, Bompastor was smart and hooked goalscorer Baltimore, who was likely still buzzing from her impact.
She was replaced by Maika Hamano, who went on to play the ball through to Alyssa Thompson when she was brought down by City goalkeeper Ayaka Yamashita, and she was shown a straight red card as a result, ending the visitors' comeback hopes.
"We knew going into the second half we only had one substitution slot and we knew Sandy has been playing lots of minutes," said Bompastor.
"I knew she probably didn't have the legs to go more than maybe 60 minutes and I knew I didn't have more slots after that. I was forced into this one as well.
"It paid off and that's good. Sandy was doing well but she knows the reason why we made that decision.
"That's the first time I experienced that kind of substitution in the first half. It's good for my own experience."
Risks 'paid off' in crucial game
Bompastor's bravery was rewarded and, while City certainly had their chances, Chelsea defended resiliently to see out the narrow win.
Jeglertz could not find a solution to Chelsea's attacking threats, which came largely from wide areas via Ellie Carpenter and Thompson.
Vivianne Miedema returned from injury and looked sharp when she came on for City in the second half, but it was not enough to change the result.
In contrast, Bompastor's risks proved the difference, and they were made with former Chelsea boss Emma Hayes, who mastered the art of bullish decisions, watching on in the stands alongside Sarina Wiegman at Stamford Bridge.
Chelsea's victory bumped them back up to the WSL summit, a point above City, while Buurman picked up the player-of-the-match award.
"It paid off today. You have to be brave to make that decision in that moment because you know bringing in a player in the game is a risk," said Bompastor.
"We had a good conversation with Veerle and she was clear on why she wasn't starting the game. That clarity was important for when she came in.
"She had a really good performance against a top player. Sometimes when it doesn't work, it's not so positive, but today it was.
"You have to react and be the one that analyses the situation and make decisions. I'm used to it, even if you don't see lots of substitutions in the first half most of the time in football."

A 27-year-old Indian-origin former student has been sentenced to 30 years in prison in the United Kingdom for grooming and sexually exploiting dozens of underage girls through social media and online gaming platforms. Bilal Kazi, who was described by UK authorities as a serial online groomer, was sentenced at Chester Crown Court on Friday, November 13, after pleading guilty to a series of child sexual abuse offences, according to a BBC News report. He will also serve an additional eight years on extended licence. The investigation uncovered the extent of his online offending, with police identifying 70 victims across 28 of the UK's 45 police forces. Investigators initially identified 180 potential victims, suggesting that the actual scale of the abuse could be considerably wider. Cheshire Constabulary and the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) detailed the investigation following his sentencing. Bilal Kazi is a 27-year-old Indian national from Mumbai, Maharashtra, who moved to the UK for higher education. According to Sky News, Kazi initially pursued a PhD in Chester before moving to Birmingham, where he studied chemistry at the University of Birmingham. He was living in Birmingham when he was sentenced at Chester Crown Court. Kazi was found guilty of a series of online child sexual abuse offences after admitting to charges involving the exploitation of minors, blackmail and the making of indecent images of children. The CPS said he was already a registered sex offender and was subject to a Sexual Risk Order when he committed some of the offences. He received a 30-year prison sentence, followed by an additional eight years on extended licence. The court also imposed a Sexual Harm Prevention Order and a restraining order, as per Sky News. Investigators found that Kazi followed a consistent pattern to approach and manipulate his victims. He reportedly used social media and gaming platforms, including Snapchat, Roblox and Wink, to contact girls, presenting himself as a white British teenage boy named 'Reece'. He reportedly used photographs of an unidentified teenage boy to make the false identity appear genuine. By pretending to be a teenager, Kazi gained the confidence of girls, some of whom believed they were communicating with someone their own age and eventually thought they were in a genuine romantic relationship. Once he had established trust, he began asking them to share sexually explicit photographs and videos. His demands subsequently escalated, with victims being pressured into recording themselves performing sexual acts. According to the CPS, Kazi manipulated the girls into believing that sharing such material was a normal part of being in a relationship. When some refused to comply with his further demands, he resorted to blackmail, threatening to circulate the images and videos they had already shared with him among their friends and other people. The threats left several victims frightened and intimidated, forcing some to continue sending explicit material. In certain cases, he maintained contact with victims for more than a year, as per CPS. The investigation began after a 13-year-old girl reported her experience to Derbyshire Police in November 2021. She had started communicating with Kazi on Snapchat, believing he was a boy of her own age. Their conversations soon turned sexual, with Kazi asking inappropriate questions and pressuring her to share explicit images. In July 2021, the girl told him she wanted to remain friends and no longer wished to send him photographs. Kazi responded abusively, calling her names and claiming that she belonged to him. He also threatened to distribute the images and videos she had previously shared unless she continued complying with his demands. Fearing that the material would be exposed, the girl continued sending him explicit content. Her Snapchat account was subsequently hacked, and the material she had shared with Kazi reached her friends. She then approached the police. The investigation was transferred to Cheshire Constabulary's Online Child Abuse Investigation Team (OCAIT) in May 2022 after enquiries established that Kazi's last known address was in Chester. However, investigators discovered that he had left the country. He was arrested at Heathrow Airport in July 2023 when he returned to the UK and questioned over the allegations. His mobile phone was seized and examined by the police's Digital Forensics Unit. The examination uncovered evidence of a much wider pattern of online offending, prompting investigators to expand the inquiry. The scale of the investigation emerged after specialist victim identification officers examined usernames, digital records and other information recovered from Kazi's devices. Police initially identified 180 potential victims. Further enquiries helped officers establish the identities of 70 girls who had been targeted across 28 of the UK's 45 police forces. The identified victims were aged between 11 and 17 at the time of the offending, although the CPS said Kazi had targeted girls as young as 10. Officers visited all 70 identified victims and offered them an opportunity to disclose their experiences. The investigation also uncovered hundreds of indecent images and videos on Kazi's devices. The CPS said more than 400 indecent images and videos were recovered from his phone during the Cheshire investigation, while more than 500 additional images and videos were found on devices examined in Birmingham. The inquiry involved investigators from Cheshire Constabulary and West Midlands Police, with the CPS's Organised Child Sexual Abuse Unit presenting the evidence in court. Detective Constable Georgia Hughes of Cheshire Constabulary's Online Child Abuse Investigation Team described the investigation as a "truly mammoth" operation that required significant resources and cooperation across the force, according to CPS. Kazi was sentenced to 30 years in prison at Chester Crown Court on November 13, 2026, after pleading guilty to a series of child sexual abuse offences. The sentence includes an additional eight-year extended licence period, during which he will remain subject to supervision following his release from prison. The offences included causing children to engage in sexual activity, blackmail and making indecent images of children. The court also imposed a Sexual Harm Prevention Order and a restraining order to restrict his future conduct. The CPS said its Organised Child Sexual Abuse Unit had presented extensive evidence gathered by police investigators in Cheshire and the West Midlands. Violent attacks on critics of China in Taiwan raise concern over transnational repression
Comedian Huang Yi-hao was involved in a car accident in September, but it turned out to be a deliberate attack
TAIPEI, Taiwan -- In September, comedian Huang Yi-hao was involved in a car accident, something that could happen to anyone. But one thing stood out: the men in the other car were unusually polite, and even offered to cover his medical bills and the damage to his car.
Huang later received a call from Taiwanese police telling him it wasn't an ordinary accident.
Taipei prosecutors in October charged five men for deliberately attempting to injure Huang in a case that has drawn attention across Taiwan. Authorities say it is part of a growing trend where operatives paid by China harass or attack people on the self-ruled island who are seen as critical of the government in Beijing.
“In the beginning, it was verbal harassment, then it morphed to pouring paint and property damage ... to the level of causing a fake car accident," Chiu Shao-Chou, the commissioner of Taiwan's Criminal investigation Bureau, said. "There's a trend of increasing severity, and that's something we have to take seriously.”
Taiwan is a democratic island claimed by Beijing, which hasn't ruled out using force to annex it. Taiwanese authorities have long worried about Chinese infiltration attempts, including spy plots targeting senior military officials and the president's bodyguards, disinformation schemes during elections or the use of cultural exchanges as a way to spread Communist Party ideology.
China's tactics to harass, spy on or even harm dissidents abroad have come to light in recent years. In 2023, authorities in New York made arrests in connection with secret police stations set up on behalf of the Chinese government to surveil Chinese dissidents.
Huang said the car attack might have been linked to his performance at the end of last year, in which he criticized Chinese President Xi Jinping and compared him to Winnie the Pooh. Huang is a comedian trained in the xiangsheng tradition, a form of Chinese comedic dialogue that relies heavily on wordplay and rhymes.
Prosecutors say the five men accepted about 450,000 New Taiwan dollars ($13,900) from someone from China who went by the alias “K” and wanted them to injure Huang seriously enough that he could no longer perform.
Huang said he had stopped collaborating with other comedians and believes his criticism of Xi is the reason. He said he knows of other comedians who had performances canceled in China and Taiwan because they had collaborated with him. He has no plans of taking his shows to China.
His solo shows, however, have sold out since the attack.
“The Communist Party is very childish. Your country’s leader was criticized by a comedian and as a result, you give such an aggressive response?” Huang said.
Hong Kong gangsters have been accused of plotting to assault Japanese political commentator Akio Yaita in what Taiwanese prosecutors called another instance of “transnational repression."
According to an October statement from prosecutors, five Hong Kong triad members, paid by a fellow gangster, entered Taiwan in early July and inspected the area around the hotel where Yaita was expected to give a speech. But before the attack, two withdrew, and the pair, alongside another member, left Taiwan, the statement said.
One of the men was offered 100,000 Hong Kong dollars ($12,750) to assault Yaita, the prosecutors said. He punched the commentator in the face and was later arrested, while another, who acted as a lookout, fled Taiwan.
Yaita, a former reporter in Beijing who now leads a think tank in Taiwan, believes the assault was linked to his remarks, including his criticism of the Chinese government’s policies.
“By violently attacking me, they hope to silence others who criticize China, including myself,” he said, adding that he wouldn't change his views.
Popular Reads
The man who was arrested pleaded guilty on Tuesday and will be sentenced later, Taiwan's Central News Agency reported.
Matt Brazil, a fellow at The Jamestown Foundation in Washington, D.C., said the recent attacks represented a “big step beyond" sending navy ships and warplanes around the island. He said anyone in Taiwan who speaks out against Xi and the Chinese Communist Party could be a target.
“(It) shows that Beijing may be turning toward a more militant stance in acting against its critics (in Taiwan). If successful, the party may expand such tactics elsewhere,” he said.
Taiwan's police say the threat of transnational repression isn't limited to Taiwan. They said they are in close coordination with U.S. authorities about similar cases that involve Taiwanese nationals overseas.
In October, U.S. authorities arrested a woman in Los Angeles for allegedly conducting surveillance on the son of Taiwan's President Lai Ching-te on behalf of the Chinese government.
“Taiwan is a democratic and pluralistic society, but with these types of actions which harm our national security, the investigation of this is of the highest importance,” Chiu, the police commissioner, said. He added that police treat the cases as national-level threats and coordinate with immigration authorities, the coast guard and other government agencies.
Catching the criminals before they leave Taiwan is a top priority, he said, adding that police would also investigate Taiwanese collaborators.
The island's Mainland Affairs Council, which handles relations with China, said it would seek to strengthen the Anti-Infiltration Act — a law designed to punish such acts.
In response to the attack on Yaita, China’s Taiwan Affairs Office said in July that the Hong Kong man who punched Yaita had acted out of “righteous indignation” and that it was an ordinary public security incident.
China denied any involvement in the attack on Huang. The Taiwan Affairs Office said Wednesday that “transnational repression” was a lie by Taiwan’s ruling Democratic Progressive Party. It said that the party had created the Anti-Infiltration Act to suppress political dissidents and restrict cross-strait exchanges.
But for Huang, who now travels with a police escort to every performance, the intended message was clear.
“They want to tell everyone that there's a cost to criticizing the Chinese government and its leader. They want to tell people, clearly, ‘If you do something abroad, we will come deal with you, so shut your mouth and accept reunification.'”

Hundreds of men lead protest to urge other men to help reduce violence against women
Hundreds of men have led a demonstration in the Swiss capital to denounce violence against women
BERN, Switzerland -- Hundreds of men led a demonstration in the Swiss capital on Saturday to denounce misogyny and a plague of violence against women, insisting men need to take a bigger and more vocal role in fighting both.
The “Men against Violence against Women” rally outside parliament follows high and persistent concerns that expressions of misogyny are too present online among teenage boys and young men — and that other men need to build a stronger counter-narrative.
It comes as some influencers on the fringe of the right-wing “manosphere” were emboldened after President Donald Trump'spresidential win in 2024 to justify and amplify misogynistic derision and threats online.
Academics and advocacy groups, for the first time, have tried to map the extent of the movement in Switzerland.
A survey released in June by the University of Zurich and mencare, an umbrella group of Swiss men's and fathers' organizations, found half of male respondents aged 18 to 24 had expressed concerns that “real men are increasingly marginalized in society" and had a “restrictive and dominance-based view of masculinity.”
The study pointed to the need for “a systematic and society-wide debate about ideals of masculinity that promote violence. The debate should start in schools.”
The Swiss government has been taking note: Justice Minister Beat Jans earlier this month attended a conference designed to raise awareness about the hazards of violent invective online against women.
In a speech on the issue on Nov. 2, Jans cited statistics that four-fifths of violent crimes were committed by men, and in cases of rape “it is as high as 99%.”
“It is not all men. But we must also admit: It is almost always men,” Jans said. “Violence by men does not begin with the first blow; it begins with a disparaging remark. We men all have a duty.”
In the movement, the idea is to open the eyes of young men who are caught up in the "manosphere" and the “patriarchy” more broadly.
“We men are part of the problem — the problem being violence against women and queer people,” said Christoph Gosteli, a 42-year-old social worker and co-organizer of the “Men against Violence against Women” demonstration with the group Maenner.
“That is why it is important for us to take a stand and say: We no longer want to be part of the problem; we want to be part of the solution,” he said.

On Nov. 10, the U.S. House of Representatives voted on articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who has been the face of the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran that began in February.
The impeachment effort failed in a 211-204 vote, which many Democrats blamed on 11 of their fellow party members who were absent from the voting chamber.
The 11 absent Democrats were Reps. Julia Brownley, Melanie Stansbury, Brittany Pettersen, Laura Gillen, Nancy Pelosi, Haley Stevens, Marilyn Strickland, Frederica Wilson, Jonathan Jackson, Steven Horsford and J. Luis Correa.
Social media users claimed some of those 11 missed the vote because they were attending an event related to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee — a powerful pro-Israel lobbying group.
The event in question was reportedly hosted by Elect Democrat Women. According to the nonprofit OpenSecrets, the top donor to the Elect Democrat Women-affiliated super PAC, EDW Action Fund, was the United Democracy Project — a super PAC affiliate of AIPAC.
Drop Site News, a nonprofit investigative news outlet, reportedly obtained an RSVP list of the event showing that three of the 11 Democrats who missed the vote were present at the event: Brownley, of California, Stansbury, of New Mexico, and Pettersen, of Colorado. As of this writing, the reported RSVP list was not publicly available and Drop Site News did not reveal how it sourced the list.
Two of the representatives, Brownley and Pettersen, reportedly acknowledged attending the Elect Democratic Women event. However, none of them had responded to our requests for comment by the time of publication. Until we hear directly from the representatives' offices or primary evidence confirming their attendance emerges, we've left this claim unrated.
On Nov. 11, USA Today reporter Zach Schermele posted that Brownley told him she "left last night's Elect Democratic Women event for the Hegseth vote with plenty of time to spare" and that "when the traffic jam made it clear she might not make it in time, she and other lawmakers started texting each other." He reported that Brownley, 74, then got out of her car and started running, missing the vote by "seconds" (archived).
According to Denver NBC affiliate KUSA, Pettersen acknowledged she attended the event, saying in a statement, "Last night, I was late to the floor and there is no excuse for that. I was at an Electing Democratic Women event."
Stansbury posted a video on Nov. 11 apologizing for her absence, saying, "I know I should've been there at that moment." She blamed rush-hour traffic on Independence Avenue for her absence. She did not mention the EDW event, though her comments were flooded with users accusing her of attending it.
Because the reported RSVP list was not publicly available and Drop Site News did not reveal where it sourced the list, we are unable to rate this claim. We can, however, break down Drop Site News' findings and any other publicly available information.
The document Drop Site News reportedly obtained also included a "Run of Show" listing the event's schedule, which read:
Run of Show:
- 4:30 pm: Event begins.
  - Mix and mingle
- 5:00 pm: EDW Chairwoman Lois Frankel to give opening remarks.
  - Thank everyone for attending, supporting EDW, and our historic wins.
- 5:10 pm: Acknowledge all new members in attendance and have them answer questions.
- 5:30 pm: Guests resume mingling.
- 6:00 pm: Event ends.
Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., publicly posted the voting schedule on Nov. 10, which indicated the vote on the impeachment articles he introduced would take place at 5:30 p.m. (archived).
According to Drop Site's reporting, the event took place at Goldfinch Social, a venue in Washington, D.C., about 2 miles from the Capitol.

I'm not a conspiracy theorist. But sometimes new information emerges that makes a wild theory worth considering.
That's where I find myself with the extraordinary downfall of Jensen Huang, the cofounder and longtime CEO of Nvidia, America's most important AI company.
Huang resigned this week after revelations that he had an extramarital affair with a Chinese businesswoman suspected of spying for Beijing.
The woman, Alice Huang, was also an executive at a company that bought billions of dollars worth of Nvidia's powerful AI chips and has been investigated over concerns that some of those products may have been illegally diverted to China.
The allegations were explosive. Nvidia's board moved surprisingly quickly; Huang was out, and the company's stock plunged, wiping about $300 billion off its market value.
But now some of America's most respected news organizations are publishing well-sourced reports that raise serious questions about the central allegation in this scandal.
And those reports point toward another possible explanation for Huang's abrupt departure. What if the spy allegations were exaggerated to achieve a political goal?
That might sound like a conspiracy theory. Until a few days ago, I would have been reluctant to give it much consideration. Now I'm not so sure.
The intelligence isn't conclusive
On Thursday, CNN reported that US intelligence agencies have not established that Alice Huang was actually spying for China.
There is disagreement among officials about whether she was recruited by China's intelligence services. Some CIA officials are unconvinced that intercepted communications prove she knowingly passed information to Beijing.
The lead reporter on this explosive piece is Natasha Bertrand, an accomplished national security reporter whose investigations have scrutinized both Republican and Democratic administrations, and whose reporting on Russia's invasion of Ukraine helped earn her team an Emmy.
The possibility that Alice Huang was a Chinese intelligence agent was likely the key reason Nvidia's board ousted Jensen Huang so quickly. (Business Insider has not confirmed whether Alice Huang was or is a Chinese spy).
Now, there's an open letter calling for the board to reinstate him as CEO until this is cleared up. It has over 100,000 signatures, including top executives and current Nvidia employees.
"We have not been shown evidence substantiating the allegation that the woman at the center of this controversy was a spy," the letter reads. "Suspicion or association alone is not a sufficient basis for ending Jensen's leadership."
There's more.
On Friday, The Washington Post reported that Secretary of State Marco Rubio, a prominent China hawk, took a less conclusive CIA intelligence report and used it to write his own memo warning President Donald Trump about Huang's relationship with an alleged Chinese spy.
According to a person familiar with the matter, Rubio recast the CIA's findings in more assertive language. The memo's findings eventually leaked, setting off the chain of events that ended Huang's 33-year reign at Nvidia, according to the Washington Post.
The Post's reporting doesn't prove Rubio deliberately misrepresented the intelligence or set out to remove Huang. But it raises a question I think deserves serious attention: Was intelligence about a possible Chinese spy amplified to help remove a powerful obstacle to tougher restrictions on China?
We've seen intelligence go wrong before
There's an uncomfortable historical precedent here.
In 2003, the US invaded Iraq after the Bush administration repeatedly warned that Saddam Hussein possessed weapons of mass destruction. Secretary of State Colin Powell famously presented intelligence to the United Nations to support that case.
After the invasion, investigators found that Iraq did not possess the stockpiles of weapons that had been alleged. The intelligence was badly wrong.
There has been extensive debate ever since about how much of that failure reflected flawed intelligence, political pressure, selective use of evidence, or deliberate exaggeration.
But the broader lesson is clear: Intelligence assessments can be presented with more certainty than the underlying evidence supports, particularly when powerful people have a policy goal they want to achieve.
The Bush administration wanted to invade Iraq. Claims about weapons of mass destruction helped build support for that decision.
Follow the chips
So, if intelligence about Alice Huang was exaggerated, who stood to benefit?
To understand the possible motive, you need to understand a bitter fight inside Washington over China's access to Nvidia technology.
For years, the US government has tried to stop China from obtaining Nvidia's most powerful AI chips, which are used to develop advanced artificial intelligence. The concern is that China could use this technology to strengthen its military and challenge America's technological leadership.
But enforcing these restrictions has proved surprisingly difficult. One reason is cloud computing. Here's how it works.
An American company sells AI chips to a data center operator. Those chips stay physically outside mainland China. The operator then rents that computing power to customers over the internet, including Chinese companies.
This kind of remote access can be legal under existing US rules, depending on the circumstances. It's also one of the main benefits of cloud computing: You don't need to own a powerful computer or even be in the same country as one to use it.
But some Washington officials see this as a loophole that undermines the whole point of restricting chip sales to China. And they want to close it.
Jensen Huang was one of the most powerful voices arguing against completely cutting China off. He argued that America is better off if Chinese AI companies continue using American technology. That gives US companies revenue, keeps China dependent on American products, and potentially gives Washington more visibility and influence over Chinese AI development.
Cut China off completely, Huang argued, and Chinese companies will simply accelerate efforts to build their own technology.
Of course, Huang also had an obvious financial interest. Nvidia makes money selling chips, and China is an enormous potential market. And he had direct access to Trump and had repeatedly pushed the administration toward a more accommodating approach.
Now he's gone. And the people who wanted tougher restrictions have shed their biggest opponent.
The timing is extraordinary
There's another detail about all this that bothers me. Aspects of this relationship and the concerns about Alice Huang are not new.
On October 9, 2025, more than a year ago, The New York Times published a detailed investigation into Megaspeed, the Singapore-based company where she was an executive.
The Times reported that the company had purchased nearly $2 billion of Nvidia technology and was under investigation over possible violations of US export restrictions.
It also described Alice Huang's close access to Jensen Huang, including photographs of them together.
US officials had been investigating the company since 2024. The FBI has also been investigating the relationship for at least a year, according to CNN.
So why did all this suddenly become an existential crisis for Nvidia's CEO in November 2026?
One possible answer is that the political environment changed.
Axios reported this week on tensions inside the administration over efforts to tighten restrictions on China's access to Nvidia technology.
Meanwhile, lawmakers are pushing legislation that could restrict Chinese companies from remotely accessing powerful American chips located in other countries. The Remote Access Security Act has already passed the House and is awaiting action in the Senate.
Nvidia has opposed efforts to impose sweeping restrictions on this kind of access.
A provocative assessment
On Thursday, SemiAnalysis, a respected AI research firm, published a provocative assessment of Huang's departure.
"We aren't ones for conspiracy theories, but a few events around the same time seem to create a narrative that is hard to ignore," they wrote.
"The US intelligence community is a large part of the push to get Jensen out of Nvidia," the firm added. "AI and chip restrictions on China are going to ramp now much faster with the biggest defender Jensen, gone."
SemiAnalysis offered this as a theory, not proof. But it deserves examination, especially after CNN's reporting and the Washington Post's article about Rubio's memo.
I'm not here to tell readers whether China should have access to America's most advanced AI chips. There are serious arguments on both sides. And I do not condone Huang's other behavior, including CEOs having relationships with subordinates at work.
What concerns me is the possibility that US intelligence was overstated to help bring down the leader of one of America's most important companies.
If that's what happened, officials may have damaged America's lead in AI in the name of protecting it.
A week ago, the idea that Washington's China hawks helped bring down Huang sounded like a conspiracy theory. Today, it's a possibility worth considering.
And given America's history of intelligence failures, I don't think we should simply take the government's word for it.

The Leader of the Opposition in the Jharkhand Legislative Assembly Babulal Marandi on Saturday (November 14, 2026), cornered the State Government over a series of criminal incidents.
He cited the incidents of including the sexual assault of a youth in Hotwar Jail, the alleged rape of a minor girl by a Congress MLA from Simdega, and the alleged rape of a woman who had gone to the Gamharia police station seeking justice.
Fifteen police officers were suspended in connection with the alleged rape of a 20-year-old woman on the premises of the Gamharia police station in Jharkhand, Saraikela-Kharsawan district, on November 1, 2026.
Launching a sharp attack on Sorens’ government, Mr. Marandi said law and order in Jharkhand has collapsed and it raises serious questions on the functioning of the government.
Addressing a press conference at the state Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) office in Ranchi, Mr. Marandi said that such incidents are continuously coming to light, and they are deeply disturbing.
“Today, in Jharkhand, neither jails nor police stations nor the residences of legislators are safe. What has happened to Jharkhand? How have conditions in the state deteriorated to such an extent that ordinary citizens no longer feel safe anywhere?” Mr. Marandi said.
‘Prisoners are not safe even in jail’
Expressing concern over the incident at Hotwar Jail, Mr. Marandi asserted that while a jail is considered the most secure place, even there, prisoners are not safe.
A man has recently filed a police complaint against 19 people, including Birsa Munda Central Jail officials, alleging severe abuse of his 20-year-old son inside the jail.
The father had accused jail inmates and staff of sexual assault of his son and forced him to consume narcotics while he stayed there as an undertrial prisoner.
“A 20-year-old youth was allegedly subjected to gang sexual assault. This incident is truly chilling. When the victim filed a written complaint, it was torn, and he was not even provided with proper medical treatment,” Mr. Marandi said.
He added that he had previously written to the government regarding incidents involving women at Hotwar Jail as well. Mr. Marandi further mentioned that even the court took cognisance of the matter, but instead of taking action and ensuring accountability, the government attempted to cover it up.
Senior Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) leader demanded the immediate removal of all responsible jail officials and the transfer of the accused inmates to another prison.
Reacting to the allegations against a Congress MLA, Bhushan Bara from Simdega, Mr. Marandi said that since the case involves an MLA from the Congress party, which is part of the ruling coalition, the government is under pressure.
Mr. Marandi mentioned that he had met with the victim, who shared her ordeal with him. He alleged that the MLA’s wife and sister also physically assaulted the girl. Mr. Marandi demanded an impartial investigation and strict action against those found guilty.
Hours after an FIR was registered against Mr. Bara on the charge of raping his minor domestic help, police said on Saturday (November 14, 2026) that they booked two persons for allegedly abducting and coercing the girl into making a “false” statement against the legislator.
427 deaths in police custody
Raising the issue of deaths occurring in police and judicial custody, Mr. Marandi said that, according to a report submitted by the state government to the Jharkhand High Court, 427 individuals died in police or judicial custody by 2026.
“Notably, 262 of these cases were not subjected to a judicial inquiry; instead, they were investigated by an executive magistrate. On May 14, 2026, the High Court had expressed deep displeasure and had directed that 262 cases be investigated afresh within six months,” Mr. Marandi said.
He added that despite the expiry of the deadline, no clear information regarding the progress of these investigations has emerged.
