When the retailer’s doors slide open, shoppers are greeted by rows of slashed price tags, frantic discounting, and all the other hallmarks of a department store closing down.
Except, this isn’t David Jones, the embattled upmarket retailer that is shutting half its 38 stores.
This is its longtime rival, Myer, where entire floors are seemingly permanently on sale.
With Myer’s profitability battered and share price languishing near all-time lows, DJs’ slide into administration raises an uncomfortable question: is Myer next?
‘Sustained erosion of relevance’
At first glance, Myer’s headline numbers seem to defy the retail gloom, with double-digit sales growth to $4.1bn last financial year.
That lift, however, was not driven by surging demand, but by adding sales from the newly acquired apparel chains, Just Jeans, Jay Jays, Portmans, Dotti and Jacqui E, bought from billionaire businessman Solomon Lew’s Premier Investments.
Meanwhile, to keep registers ringing, Myer employed “higher than planned promotional activity to stimulate demand”, according to its annual report, which reduced its profitability.
The department store has also slashed the value of its brands, down more than $200m in one year alone, in an admission that its labels are worth far less than they once were.
Department stores have faced a “sustained erosion of relevance over the past five years”, according to IBISWorld market researchers, as online platforms win over bargain-hunters and specialists like beauty retailer Mecca prove more nimble in capturing shifting tastes.
DJs and Myer, on the other hand, have been weighed down by long-running physical property leases tied to underperforming stores in their sprawling networks.
The era of Australian families being fiercely loyal to either David Jones or Myer is long gone, replaced by a grim battle for both chains to stay relevant.
The stress on big department store profitability has been exacerbated by a period of cost of living pressures that have “entrenched deal-hunting behaviour, reshaping how and when consumers engage with department stores”, according to IBISWorld.
Myer was contacted for comment.
Survival tactic or slow-motion bankruptcy
Myer, however, has a critical advantage over David Jones: time.
While DJs fell into administration under mounting debts, Myer finished last financial year with a $100m net cash buffer, buying management breathing space to fix the business.
It has been reducing store numbers and with it lease liabilities – down to 56 stores from 60 before the pandemic – which is something David Jones is only doing now that it has collapsed into administration.
For the moment, Myer is leaning into the discounts demanded by shoppers, in the hope that more profitable trading conditions will emerge.
Richard Hemming, the editor at Under The Radar Report, says in retail “volume is everything”.
“If you get the volumes through, that customer base will eventually be in a position to pay more, and when volumes and margins both improve, you get that double effect,” Hemming says.
While analysts have mixed views on whether permanent discounting is a smart survival tactic or a slow-motion way to go bankrupt, department stores do need to move huge volumes of stock to keep cash flowing and clear seasonal goods.
They can use those discounts to get more people signed up to their loyalty programs – such as the successful Myer One program – in the hope they will become long term customers.
Hemming sees the upside in Myer’s current pain, noting the retailer is “cleaning house earlier than rivals” precisely because investors have long priced it “like it’s going to go broke”.
Myer is revamping the business to aggressively pursue online sales.
Advantage over old rival
Myer shares have been heavily sold down over the years, and now hover around the 24c mark, representing a fraction of its $4.10 float price from 2009.
It did, however, receive a price bump on the day DJs fell into administration.
With roughly two in five Myer stores sharing a shopping centre with a David Jones outlet, investors are betting the coming closure of 19 DJs sites will hand Myer an easy market-share boost, even as its own long-term turnaround demands further store cuts.
In the short term, the pain is likely to intensify for Myer as the David Jones stores marked for closure are under orders to clear stock with widespread promotions, luring customers.
Broader retail sentiment is also souring, as a string of interest rate rises and escalating cost-of-living pressures force cash-strapped shoppers to pare their discretionary spend.
The Retail Doctor Group’s chief executive, Brian Walker, says the main long-term advantage Myer has over its old rival is financial flexibility.
“Whereas David Jones was incredibly encumbered, Myer doesn’t have that issue right now,” Walker says.
“As we sit here today, Myer is financially stronger, but strategically still pretty vulnerable.”

IPL founder Lalit Modi announces British citizenship, says UK is now his home
Reflecting on his life across different cultures and experiences, Modi said he looked forward to making positive contributions to the country he now proudly calls home.
Indian Premier League (IPL) founder Lalit Modi has announced that he officially became a British citizen on September 15, 2026, describing the development as a proud and deeply personal milestone.
Modi made the announcement on Saturday while addressing the Oxford Union, where he spoke about his journey towards acquiring British citizenship and his longstanding association with the United Kingdom.
In a post on X, Modi said he celebrated becoming a British citizen at a special ceremony on September 15, surrounded by family and friends. He described the UK as his home for many years, adding that he had developed a deep appreciation for its people, institutions, traditions and values.
"Becoming British is a privilege and a responsibility that I embrace with pride, gratitude and a genuine sense of belonging," he wrote.
Reflecting on his life across different cultures and experiences, Modi said he looked forward to making positive contributions to the country he now proudly calls home.
He also thanked his family, friends and the Oxford Union for providing him with an opportunity to share the news on what he described as a memorable occasion.
Modi said the announcement was particularly special as it coincided with the birthday of King Charles III. He ended his post with the words, "God Save the King!"
The former cricket administrator's announcement comes years after he left India in 2010 amid investigations into alleged financial irregularities linked to the IPL. He has been living in the UK since then.

Australia considers criminal penalties for rogue AI in wake of OpenAI hack
- Published
Australia plans to create a new AI safety regulator and has flagged criminal penalties for tech companies who do not comply, months after an OpenAI hack.
In September, Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese revealed that a rogue OpenAI agent had "infiltrated" a government health website and other systems, and criticised the company for taking months to tell them about the hack.
On Tuesday, he released the 18 recommendations made after a "rapid review" into the breaches including new safety and security standards for AI companies such as mandatory reporting of hacks.
AI brings opportunities, he said, but Australia must prepare for the "new risks" from this "rapidly advancing technology".
"The law needs to get ahead of and, in some cases, make sure that it catches up with, what is a very fast changing world," Albanese said.
One of the recommendations suggests changes to criminal law to have a standalone "failure to prevent" offence .
This would criminalise instances where a company develops "an AI model that engages in harmful conduct" and "fails to take reasonable steps to prevent that harm".
The review also recommended "mandatory, time-bound AI safety reporting" of hacks.
This point addresses what Albanese had earlier called his "disappointment" in the months-long delay for OpenAI to tell his government about the breach.
In June, a statistics portal containing "non-sensitive" data from Australia's universal healthcare scheme Medicare was hacked by a rogue OpenAI agent.
OpenAI said it only learnt of the breach in August while reviewing "misaligned model activity" and emailed a general inbox of an Australian government agency on 10 September.
It took several more days before the email was escalated to Australia's cybersecurity centre, with a message then sent to a government minister ahead of the prime minister being told.
Albanese said he spoke to OpenAI boss Sam Altman and raised "Australia's extreme concern about this incident", with Altman acknowledging there were "issues with protocols" at OpenAI.
Days after the hacks were revealed, OpenAI delayed its rollout of a new AI model, citing safety concerns.

I spend a huge portion of my life on airplanes as a frequent traveler and journalist, so I'm used to the usual delays, missed connections, and last-minute flight changes that come with commercial air travel.
But I have never experienced anything like the crippling air traffic control outage on Friday, November 13, that displaced thousands of passengers and crews and canceled over 12,500 flights.
I had been at cruising altitude, flying back from a vacation in the Caribbean island of Curaçao toward my home in Salt Lake City, when the Federal Aviation Administration halted departing flights across the entire US.
Before Friday, the FAA had only ordered a nationwide ground stop twice in modern history: once in January 2023, following a failure of a key pilot-alert system, and after the September 11 terrorist attacks.
Given the rare track record, I wasn't thrilled to find myself midair when I heard the news.
What should have been a quick two-hour layover in Miami unraveled into a chaotic overnight delay, with hours spent on a gridlocked tarmac as passengers raced for vanishing hotel rooms and flight inventory.
We learned about the nationwide shutdown at 35,000 feet
Before boarding in Curaçao, my flight had already been delayed by about 30 minutes, and I jokingly texted a friend that it better not be delayed any further because I refused to spend the night in Miami.
I should have knocked on wood, because about 40 minutes out from landing, the cabin speakers crackled to life.
The captain said he was sure some of us had WiFi and had seen messages about a nationwide ground stop, then confirmed it was true.
Hushed conversations throughout the cabin ensued, and I looked to my neighbor to check the news since I didn't have WiFi myself. This was the first time in a long time I was nervous on a plane.
I read that officials said a telecommunications issue was affecting Air Route Traffic Control Centers, the regional facilities responsible for directing and guiding aircraft at higher altitudes between airports.
I also read that officials did not believe the disruption was the result of AI or a cyberattack — something that I'd been wondering about. For some reason, that scared me even more. What was it, then?
My next thought: If air traffic control has a communications failure, how are we going to land?
I was relieved when the captain informed us that planes already in the sky, including mine, were cleared to land at their destinations, and that the order had frozen departures.
Although I didn't know it at the time, officials later said that pilots, air traffic controllers, and dispatchers have various backup methods and digital tools for communication, and pilots are trained to navigate and land without comms.
Still, the timing of the halt was unnerving, coming after the widespread Microsoft cloud disruptions the day before and the National Weather Service data hiccups earlier Friday.
Landing in Miami was only the beginning of the chaos
When our wheels finally touched down at Miami International Airport, I checked my phone and saw that the captain had kept us informed to the best of his knowledge; no further news had been released, but at least we had been able to land.
But now we were stuck on the plane. Because inbound flights were still arriving while outbound planes sat at their gates, the airport's ramp space was gridlocked.
With nowhere to park and unload passengers, our plane sat idling on the tarmac for the next two hours.
Around 7:30 p.m., about an hour after landing, passengers around me began murmuring that rebooking options were finally appearing in the American Airlines app.
When I refreshed my screen, every option required flying out the following evening on grueling 12- to 14-hour itineraries with multiple layovers.
Unwilling to spend a half-day hopping around the US from Florida to Utah, I accepted that I would spend the full weekend in Miami. But before I booked something for Sunday or Monday, I refreshed the list one more time.
Buried at the very bottom was a single direct flight departing at 7:45 p.m. on Saturday night. I booked it immediately, snagging one of the final three open seats — and crossed my fingers that the snowball effect would slow by then and my flight would actually take off.
Hotel rooms disappeared almost as quickly as flights were canceled
Still trapped on the tarmac, another problem emerged: finding a place to sleep.
Around me, passengers were frantically refreshing booking apps as airport hotels sold out in real time. I barely managed to book a room at the Hyde Hotel in Midtown Miami, about 15 minutes away.
It wasn't cheap — $621 for the night, to be exact.
The airline wasn't required to help me out in the uncontrollable flight disruption, and I'm not sure my travel insurance will reimburse me, so I've accepted I may eat that money.
When I finally deplaned around 8 p.m., cleared customs, and arrived at the lobby, the front desk agent told me the hotel had surged from about 40% full at 5 p.m. local time to sold out by 9 p.m. — filled to capacity by displaced flyers in under four hours.
Even in a major hospitality hub like Miami, inventory evaporates quickly when thousands of stranded travelers are competing for the same beds. Despite the pain in my wallet, knowing I wasn't spending the night on an airport terminal floor felt like I had won the lottery.
I was reminded that no matter how much I prepare, I'm at the whim of the air system
Once I reached my hotel, I refreshed my news app to see that the FAA had lifted the nationwide ground stop, allowing departures to slowly resume, but the effects had already disrupted the whole country.
Air travel is notorious for its snowball effect: a single thunderstorm in Dallas or Atlanta can trigger cascading delays thousands of miles away as planes and crews get displaced. A simultaneous shutdown of the entire US airspace system was a whole other beast.
A friend scheduled to fly to Las Vegas had his trip canceled before he had even left for the airport. But another friend flying from Panama to Denver ended up stranded in Houston — her second overnight stall in 48 hours after weather disruptions the day before.
For someone who flies regularly, the unexpected chaos was a reality check. I can build buffer time into my schedule, book early-morning departures and pack carry-on only, but none of that will protect me when a backbone of the national airspace system goes offline.
Lying in my hotel room in Miami, I'll admit I felt a flicker of hesitation about stepping back onto a plane Saturday evening. The thought of pilots losing clear communication with the ground is terrifying.
But that fear is merely one of the trade-offs we accept every time we board a flight to see the world — and I know the pilots are highly trained to deal with emergencies like lost comms.

Pope Leo speaks of community 'suffering' on visit to remote Andes town
- Published
On a visit to an isolated Andean village in his former diocese, Pope Leo XIV has spoken about the "suffering of those who are forced to leave their homeland in search of a better future", which he said had left communities under threat.
About 6,000 people live in Santa Cruz de Succhabamba, which is located in a remote part of the Andes mountains in northern Peru, but the Pope's visit drew a crowd of about 20,000, according to the Vatican.
At an outdoor Mass, Pope Leo spoke of "declining birth rates that are emptying villages," and the unequal distribution of the land's resources.
Over 40% of the population in the Cajamarca region, where the town is located, live in poverty - the highest figure in Peru, according to official data.
Cajamarca has lost the highest number of people to internal migration, with 729,000 people born there now living elsewhere in Peru.
In his sermon, Pope Leo thanked those who had made the journey to him and emphasised the importance of never losing heart, despite life's difficulties.
Santa Cruz is within the Diocese of Chiclayo, where Pope Leo served as bishop from 2015 to 2023. During his tenure, he visited Santa Cruz several times a year to minister to the town's rural population.
On Saturday he returned by helicopter, where he was greeted by singing and cheering. He later did a tour in a popemobile, where he waved to people who had travelled from across the region to see him.
Speaking at a local parish on Saturday, the Pope said he felt "joy" at being able to visit the small town once again.
"It is like a very big dream that the Lord has allowed this servant to come here," he said.
Rev. Kevin Noriega, who was ordained in 2018 by the then-bishop, told Reuters the visit had brought "enormous hope and emotion" to Santa Cruz.
He said: "People are eager to experience this Holy Mass ... because after so much time they will be able to see their bishop - 'Father Robert,' as they used to call him - now as the Holy Father."
Peru is the longest stop on the first tour of Latin America by the leader of the Catholic church, who was elected in May 2025.
The 12-day trip has included stops in Argentina and Uruguay, but his time in Peru carries personal significance.
The US-born pope not only lived in Peru for long periods between 1985 and 2023 but also became a citizen of the country in 2015, forging close ties with local communities.
The pontiff is set to leave Chiclayo on Sunday, when he will head to Cusco, and then on to a Peruvian sector of the Amazon rainforest. His tour of the region will conclude on Monday, at which point Pope Leo will return to Rome.

A video is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that it shows Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) chief Mohan Bhagwat saying that those who call India a Hindu nation should be sent to a mental hospital. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat saying that those who call India a Hindu nation should be sent to a mental hospital.
Fact: The video is clipped out of context. RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat was recounting an incident from the 1930s where a person named Ibrahim defended the RSS against an attempt to ban it. While making this argument, Ibrahim had said that those who call India a Hindu nation should be sent to a mental asylum. Bhagwat was quoting Ibrahim’s statement, not remarking himself. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to a Facebook post (archived) by The Economic Times, dated 09 November 2026, featuring a longer version of the same video. Upon reviewing the video, we found that Mohan Bhagwat was not making the statement himself but was quoting a person named Ibrahim. Referring to an incident from the 1930s, Bhagwat said that when the Central Provinces Assembly first attempted to ban the RSS, there were no volunteers or supporters of the RSS’s ideology to defend it. In this context, he recounted that a person named Ibrahim defended the RSS by saying that those who call India a Hindu nation should be sent to a mental asylum. Ibrahim further stated that he knew Dr Hedgewar, that he was not insane but a good man, and therefore, the RSS could not be communal.
We also found multiple media reports (here, here, and here) covering the statement made by Mohan Bhagwat on 09 November 2026, while inaugurating the newly constructed auditorium at the renovated headquarters of Nagpur Nagarik Sahakari Bank Limited in Nagpur.
We also found a video of the event, which was livestreamed on 09 November 2026 on the Facebook account of Nagpur Nagarik Sahakari Bank Ltd. In the approximately 1-hour-and-36-minute-long video, we found the segment corresponding to the viral clip at around 1:16:00.
During this segment, Mohan Bhagwat said, “The RSS, which was formed 100 years ago, is being discussed everywhere. That’s why so many books are being published now. I held an intellectual class here in Nagpur, where I explained that when the first attempt to ban the RSS was made in the Central Provinces Assembly in the 1930s, none of the RSS volunteers came forward to defend the RSS or support its ideology.”
He further said, “There was a Mr Ibrahim who spoke in favour of the RSS. He said that the RSS should not be banned and that it was not communal. But how did he make this argument? He said that those who say India is a Hindu nation should be sent to a mental asylum. This is my opinion, and I know Dr Hedgewar. He is not insane; he is a good man, and therefore, the RSS cannot be communal. So, that was in the 1930s. Five or seven years had passed since the RSS was founded. Everyone knew about the RSS, but Dr Hedgewar knew“
We also found that Jagran reported that a book on the lives of former RSS pracharaks was released during the event. Bhagwat discussed the lives of former RSS pracharaks and recounted an incident from the 1930s in this context. This confirms that the viral clip presents Bhagwat’s statement without the necessary context. In the original video, Bhagwat was quoting a person named Ibrahim, who had said that those who call India a Hindu nation should be sent to a mental asylum. The remark was made by Ibrahim, not Bhagwat.
To sum up, this video shows Mohan Bhagwat quoting Ibrahim’s remark about sending those who call India a Hindu nation to a mental asylum.

Tata Trusts Chairman Noel Tata has introduced a two-part plan for the country’s oldest and largest charity group: continue giving, but measure it by the results, and keep supporting Tata Sons’ investments in important national projects. Speaking at the Hindustan Times Leadership Summit in New Delhi on Saturday, the 70-year-old Tata Trusts chairman said the charitable institutions would have two distinct but complementary roles. “One part is the direct philanthropy, which we do. So building institutions, giving grants to other NGOs, or alleviating hardships directly with beneficiaries. The second is through Tata Sons, to invest and nurture projects of national importance,” said Noel. “We are, from a trust perspective, we stand 100% behind Tata Sons’ efforts to build these projects and invest in projects of national importance,” he said, noting that this is part of the institution. “And while continuing the philanthropy work, and basically we end up with a balance between some direct philanthropy, which happens every year, and some money going towards investment in national projects.” Noel said these investments were not necessarily detached from commercial considerations. “They are projects which have a longer gestation period. They might have a little more risk than a normal project,” he said. He added that the expectation was that such ventures, once incubated, would eventually become public companies and prosper in the marketplace. Tata Group’s approach is not new. The Group's founder, Jamsetji Tata, donated half his wealth to educational charities and backed pioneering ventures that helped build India’s industrial and infrastructure capabilities in steel, hydroelectric power, textiles and truck manufacturing. “I had to see what the founders' intentions were. What did they leave? Because they were really pioneers in philanthropy, let’s say, 130 years ago,” Noel said. “They could have left their money to the salary, to their cousins. Instead, they decided, no, we leave our shares and our money to these two trusts… This is embedded in the DNA of the group. And I think this will continue,” he added. Their instructions, according to Noel, were clear: “We want you to create institutions,” “We want you to provide relief to people in need, communities in need” and “We want you to advance knowledge.” These principles, Tata said, would remain his guiding light in setting the Trusts’ priorities and future programmes. Noel said direct charity work will focus more on clear results than on how much money is spent. Reviewing current programmes after he became chairman in October 2024 helped him see the importance of measuring the real impact of efforts, Tata said. “I began to see that possibly impact was more important than expenditure,” he added. The comments echo his message in the Tata Trusts’ 2025-26 annual report, which signalled that philanthropy will now be judged by results, not cheque size. “It is no longer enough to ask how much we have contributed,” Noel wrote in his letter. “We must ask what difference that contribution has made, and whether that difference will endure.” He added a line that appeared aimed at the country’s wealthy donors: “Trying to become the biggest before becoming the best rarely ends well.” The letter sets out three changes. The Trusts will create new institutions that can last as public resources, rather than only supporting existing ones. They plan a network of 40 to 50 non-profit general hospitals, where patients who can pay help cover the cost of care for those who cannot. They are also open to partnering with other philanthropies on big projects, a notable shift for a group behind landmark institutions such as IISc, TIFR and Tata Memorial. The Trusts paid out ₹1,556 crore (about $167 million) during the year. Institutions and programmes received ₹1,353 crore, while individuals in need received ₹203 crore, mostly for cancer treatment and student scholarships. Rural livelihoods took the largest share at ₹458 crore, followed by education ( ₹270 crore), cancer care ( ₹178 crore) and long-term support to institutions ( ₹169 crore). Taken together, health is the biggest theme: cancer care, healthcare and medical grants to individuals add up to about ₹428 crore, or 27% of the total. Spain test will reveal if Tuchel and England have learned World Cup lessons
- Published
England's proof of progress and the lessons learned by head coach Thomas Tuchel since the disappointment of World Cup semi-final defeat by Argentina will be put to the sternest test when they face holders Spain in Madrid.
Spain present the toughest assignment England could face, with the world champions' unbeaten run – in which they claimed the sport's biggest prize by beating Argentina in New Jersey in the summer – now stretching to 43 games.
Luis de la Fuente's side last lost - to Colombia - in March 2024, winning 34 games and drawing nine in the intervening period, during which they also became European champions, beating England in the Euro 2024 final in Berlin.
Little wonder, then, that England captain and Ballon d'Or winner Harry Kane describes Sunday night's visit to the Metropolitano Stadium as: "The perfect opportunity to try and prove ourselves."
Tuchel, who revealed Leeds United's James Trafford will get another opportunity in goal as he continues to alternate with Jordan Pickford, clearly feels the same as he added: "This will be proof of concept on the highest level. It's the biggest test in world football. Spain are unbelievable on an incredible run.
"Spain won the last big titles. We are trying to take it away from them. We are up for it. We are in a good moment to push our limits. We are up for something spectacular."
It was a message echoed here in Madrid by England midfielder Declan Rice, who said: "It's a massive game.
"I don't think you can get much bigger than a Champions League final with Arsenal or a World Cup semi-final against Argentina, which I've played in, but when you are playing against the world champions in Spain there is no greater incentive.
"It's the sort of game that brings out the best in us. We want to play against the best teams and the best players. It will show where we are as a group. We're going to see where England are at."
Spain are particularly formidable on home soil, unbeaten in 20 games - winning 15 and drawing five - since a 2-1 defeat by Switzerland in September 2022.
England's most recent win in Spain was a 3-2 triumph in a Nations League encounter in Sevilla in October 2018, their first away victory against them for 31 years.
Yet England came closer than most to piercing Spain's air of invincibility, even though they lost 3-2 at Wembley in September, when a rare Kane blemish from the penalty spot prevented them taking a potentially decisive 3-1 lead.
Spain subsequently punished England and Kane, who will be hoping for better fortunes when the countries meet again in the latest Nations League encounter.
England arrived in Madrid on Saturday evening having reeled off four successive victories since that Wembley loss, the latest of which was a 2-1 win against Croatia at Wembley on Thursday.
Spain will present an altogether different opposition, but also a barometer of whether England have moved forward since the World Cup, when Tuchel was heavily criticised for what was perceived to be a negative approach in the 2-1 loss to Argentina in Atlanta, especially after Anthony Gordon put England ahead.
Former England defender Matthew Upson, who will be in Madrid for BBC Radio 5 Live, told BBC Sport: "Harry Kane saying this is the perfect opportunity for England to prove themselves is a great way to build this challenge up.
"I wouldn't expect anything less from him considering where he is at now, where his belief level is and what he wants to achieve.
"Harry is achieving incredible personal accolades like the Ballon d'Or, but he won't rest there. He will want a team honour with England, and if you play against the best in the world there is no better barometer of where you're at as a group.
"It's going to be a very interesting test. It's fair to say we didn't see England at full flow against Croatia, so now we will see if they adjust, improve and produce something of their best, which they will have to do if you are going to get any sort of result against Spain in Spain.
"If England get a point, or even better a win, against Spain with their record, at home and away, we will come away thinking they are at a high level.
"If you get a result, you will have had to play really well because you won't do that with anything else.
"By that, I don't mean a blistering game. I just mean doing things well and showing the level you are at."
In the aftermath of that World Cup loss to Argentina, the post-tournament process embarked upon by the Football Asssociation included canvassing the opinions of the whole squad, where it emerged it took place at a "full and frank" meeting with Tuchel at the start of the September international break.
Kane and Jude Bellingham were understood to have given forthright views, where the approach in the devastating loss to Argentina was a key theme.
There is now believed to be a feeling in the squad that Tuchel has taken on the lessons of Atlanta and is focusing on a more positive approach.
Upson said: "England are still a bit of a work in progress. We have two or maybe three players who are playing some of the best football across Europe and the world at the moment. I am thinking of Kane, Bellingham and, at times, Anthony Gordon.
"The key is utilising that, then getting the rest of the team to a place where it can support that and deliver its own world-class support. This is the challenge for Thomas Tuchel."
"England are adopting a more positive approach, but look a little vulnerable defensively, which is maybe the compromise.
"Yes, England could have been 3-1 up against Spain had Harry Kane scored his penalty, but don't forget we could easily have been 3-0 down before we scored."
The intense environment of facing the World Cup holders on their own turf will also be a forensic examination of England's mental progress as well as footballing prowess.
Upson said: "The biggest thing to fix after the World Cup was player reaction and player belief when we're in certain situations, especially if we go ahead and all of a sudden the game is difficult, as it was against Argentina. What is our mindset going to be?
"Since then England have tried to play much more freely, openly and confidently. That's how I see it. That's how we played when we won 7-0 in Croatia. We were free, open, positive. Belief was through the roof.
"This is why this test against Spain is great because you will get tested to the maximum there. If England go ahead, let's see how they do and what they do. If they go behind, let's see what we do.
"Against Spain at Wembley, I saw a reaction at half-time from England, which was fantastic. We should have gone 3-1 up with Harry's penalty, and in that 15 minutes after half-time we were super positive, aggressive in our decision-making.
"This was another ideal situation to test that. They came through that really positively. It would be great if we get another test like that on Sunday.
"It it all plays into what Harry Kane said. This is something which will test people. It's a really significant game for England on a lot of levels."

From postcards to texts, the different ways a manager gets the sack - Pulis
- Published
When you hear about a manager parting company with a club, he has usually either been sacked or has resigned, but there are actually lots of different ways you can leave.
Over the years I spent working at every level of the game in England, from the bottom to the top, I have witnessed and been involved in many break-ups.
Some are smooth but others are far more fractious and don't happen face-to-face. I've witnessed managers being sacked over the phone or by text, or hearing they are losing their job by word of mouth.
One of the most soul-destroying times for a manager is when speculation is rife regarding not only your imminent sacking, but also about who is going to replace you.
During my career, I've known certain individuals who actually put their names forward for jobs before a manager is even sacked. Some go to the club involved through agents, some directly to the owners themselves.
Many managers are sounded out before eventually being appointed and another policy which has become popular with clubs is to drop names out to the press about possible replacements, to see the supporters' reactions to the names in the frame.
For the manager who is still in place, and whose stress levels are through the roof, it is devastating... but it is just another part of the job that you have to handle.
I've experienced that situation myself, in a scenario which went on for many months. Your confidence, not only in yourself but also in the club's hierarchy, takes another massive knock.
When it happened to me, I'd heard about the club's intentions from people in the media at quite an early stage and also worked out where the new manager would be coming from, but I had to bite my lip - myself and my staff were under contract, so we had to just carry on.
We kept pulling results out of the bag which delayed the inevitable, but eventually I knew my time was up.
Sacked on the drive up for pre-season
When they are getting treated this way, you can hardly blame managers for sometimes wanting to stick two fingers up to the people in charge.
One story comes to mind of a manager I know who was relieved of his duties by being placed on gardening leave while the club found a way to release him permanently.
During that time, and while he was still getting paid, the manager decided to go on holiday somewhere hot with his family. After watching his old team lose on TV in the sunshine, he sent a postcard to his chairman, which simply said 'wish you were here!'.
When he got home, he was sacked - but I bet he was still glad he did it!
Sadly, most managers don't get that kind of satisfaction - and often you don't even get a chance to say a proper goodbye to the players and staff you have worked closely with for many months or years.
My first spell at Stoke ended when I was driving up the motorway from my home in Bournemouth for the first day of pre-season in the summer of 2005.
I'd had a pretty good idea of what might happen since the end of the previous season but, over the next few weeks, the club's Icelandic owners did not say a word - until then.
I didn't have a problem with the decision, by the way. They were nice people and my view has always been 'if you don't want me, you don't want me'.
Anyway, I'd already been driving for four hours and, just as I got to the junction that would take me to the ground, my phone rang. It was the chairman, who told me he'd been meaning to call.
I was told I was no longer the manager, but also that I could not enter the stadium at any cost - I soon understood the urgency of the situation because it turned out the new manager had already arrived there. I had to just turn the car around, and head back home.
That kind of thing can happen to any manager, and you learn to be ready for it.
'Every manager needs to think about their cardboard box'
I always remember playing at Swansea in one of my early games in my first job with Bournemouth, and their manager Frank Burrows inviting me into his office afterwards.
Frank, who sadly passed away in 2021, was a wonderful man and also a superb old-school manager who was always happy to offer advice to younger coaches and share his experiences.
We were having a drink and I noticed he had this big empty cardboard box next to his desk. I asked him what it was for, and he said it was to hold all his belongings - from his files on players to his family photographs - that were in his office.
"All the important stuff I'd like to keep is on the top of my desk," Frank said. "And every time I lose my job, because that time always comes, I can just sweep it into the box and off I go again. That box has travelled around the football world with me."
That always stuck with me. Management is such a precarious occupation that every manager has to think about that box, even if they don't have it sitting next to their desk every day!
It was not long afterwards that I found out what it was like to be sacked for the first time.
I still had a year left on my contract with Bournemouth but the chairmanship of the club changed and, in the summer of 1994, I was out.
It was hard enough to go from doing almost everything at the club to doing nothing, not even going in for pre-season training - but, because it was my hometown club, I also had to come to terms with listening to stories of my children being teased about my exit at school.
I also had my mortgage and my family to look after and unfortunately Bournemouth were not very helpful with the money they owed me.
It's a lot to think about, when you have just been thrown out into the real world, especially when it's a world you have no experience in or any other qualifications to fall back on. I was lucky enough to get another chance in management, but not every young manager does.
Fortunately, I've not always left clubs on bad terms, either. I've already mentioned a few difficult separations, but I've had some happier endings too.
Finishing as friends
I've talked a lot in these columns about my affection for Peter Coates and his wonderful family. As well as owning Stoke City, they are a special group of people who have been unbelievably successful in their own ways, but they have never lost that human touch.
When the time came for me to part company with the club in 2013, they did so in a proper manner - Peter and John, his son and now chairman, were dead straight with me about wanting to go in a different direction, and made a difficult situation into a respectful parting of the ways.
I spent almost 10 years at Stoke over two spells but, while I was only at Middlesbrough for 18 months, it was a similar story with their owner and chairman Steve Gibson.
Steve has spent his entire life looking out for Boro but his commitment to his club goes far beyond being a lifetime supporter. He cares deeply for the people of that area and has devoted so much of his hard-earned cash towards making Boro a success.
I loved my time there because of the warmth of Steve and his family, and beyond. The area reminded me so much of south Wales, where the community was cherished and people, especially at the club, could not do enough for you.
After the last game of the 2018-19 season I was completely shot, and frustrated that we had not reached the Championship play-offs. My drive home that night was long and lonely but I felt worn out.
Once the dust had settled on that season, Steve and I met up in London. Our discussions were honest and open but my contract was up and we both agreed it was a good time for me to leave - I wanted it to end on good terms, and we certainly did that.
After dinner we had a fair few drinks and it ended up being a very, very late night. We arranged to have breakfast the following morning but I told him I have always been an early riser so, by 6am, I was up and on my way to the station to get back home.
My wife had just picked me up in Bournemouth at just after 8am when Steve rang to ask if I was down for breakfast yet - and he didn't believe me when I said no, I am back home.
I missed breakfast, but we remained good friends. Steve is a class act and I always hold Boro up as a club that deserves to be successful because of the attitude, commitment and honesty of everyone we came across.
My family still talk about how much they loved going there, and were genuinely disappointed when I left - something that doesn't apply to all my former clubs, obviously!
Tony Pulis was speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan.

Copper wire upgrade caused nationwide flight suspension, US transport secretary says
- Published
A nationwide US ground stop that caused thousands of flight cancellations was caused by an issue following a copper wire upgrade, Transport Secretary Sean Duffy said.
Duffy told a news conference that the government was trying to find out whether the problem was caused by "incompetence" on the part of the company doing the upgrades, or faulty equipment.
The US government does not believe it was as a result of a cyber-attack, although an investigation is still under way, Duffy said.
Friday's suspension was the longest such incident since the 11 September 2001 attacks on the US and the disruption is expected to last for days.
- What we know about the US ground stop and what to do if you're affected 
  - Published3 hours ago
Maintenance was being carried out to switch from copper wire to fibre by a contractor called L3Harris, a technology provider company, Duffy said.
The US has "an incredibly old telecommunications system", he added.
"It was such an old wire that it was being discontinued," he said.
The transport secretary explained that a router that was being worked on had started flooding other air traffic control systems and created communication issues with planes which led the government to shut down the airspace for safety reasons.
Bryan Bedford, who heads the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), told the same news conference: "We see zero evidence of anything nefarious, and zero evidence of anything AI related."
No flights were allowed to take off from the continental US for more than four hours from 15:54 EST (19:54 GMT) on Friday.
More than 3,500 flights were cancelled and more than 2,000 delayed in the US on Saturday, according to tracking website Flight Aware, as knock-on disruption continues.
In some cases, passengers were left stuck inside planes on the tarmac, unable to take off or to return to the gates. Some international flights were allowed to depart US airports, in an apparent effort to clear space.
Duffy warned that a similar issue could arise again unless the US Congress approved upgrades to air traffic control infrastructure.
US President Donald Trump has requested $30.1bn for the upgrades. Both chambers of Congress are currently controlled by the Republican Party.
Former TSA Administrator John Pistole told the BBC that "the fact that they were able to get it restarted in four-and-a-half hours is good news - it shows a resilience in the system - but what's to say it's not going to happen tomorrow?"
A nationwide ground stop has only been ordered one other time since all flights were banned from take-off for several days following the 11 September 2001 attacks.

At St. Joseph’s Church in Kuriachira, Thrissur, Keralam, faith and fitness go hand in hand. An open gym on the church premises is drawing parishioners of all ages to stretch, sweat and stay fit. The unusual initiative is adding a healthy new dimension to church life.
Set up in a corner of the church campus, the facility has quickly become a meeting point for fitness enthusiasts. With no fixed timings, parishioners can drop in at their convenience, with many heading to the gym after attending Holy Mass. The altar boys, numbering around 60, are among its regular users. Parents also bring their young children, while senior citizens use the basic equipment to stay active.
Roots in fitness routine of vicar
The initiative has its roots in the personal fitness routine of the church’s vicar, Fr. Frederick Eluvathingal, 69. A footballer and basketball player during his student days, he has never allowed age or a demanding schedule to come in the way of exercise.
“I have been working out for the past 51 years, ever since my days at the Papal Seminary in Pune,” he says. His fitness routine continued during his higher studies in Rome and Jerusalem and his church assignments in Australia.
When he arrived at Kuriachira more than a year ago, he began looking for a suitable space to continue his regular exercises, including push-ups and pull-ups. Parallel bars were installed first, followed by a basketball hoop. The idea gradually grew into a community gym.
“I wanted to create a space where people could develop the habit of working out. We generally do not have a strong workout culture. If people can fit in some basic exercise when they come to church, they may gradually make fitness part of their lives,” he says.
The need is particularly pressing at a time when lifestyle diseases and obesity are on the rise. The initiative also seeks to draw more youngsters into church activities and channel their energy into constructive pursuits.
The parish welcomed the proposal, and a space around a well on the church premises was chosen for the facility. The limited space available in Kuriachira meant that the gym had to be modest, but the response has been encouraging.
“Within a week of starting the gym, quite a few people began coming here. If the demand grows, we will have to think about expanding the facility,” says P.R. Wilson, one of the church trustees.
For regular user John Vazhappilly, a real estate broker who lives nearby, the gym has come as a timely help. “I have been coming here every evening for the past week. After an accident and surgery, the muscles in my leg became weak. I want to strengthen them. This is a comfortable place to exercise, with fresh air and an open campus,” he says.
‘A form of spiritual service’
The church sees the initiative as more than a fitness facility. “We want to groom a healthy generation. Many people suffer from lifestyle diseases, while youngsters often turn to private fitness centres. We felt that providing basic facilities here would benefit the community. Spirituality is also about nurturing a healthy mind and body. We consider this a form of spiritual service,” says assistant vicar Fr. Jees Akkara.
For Fr. Eluvathingal, there is another purpose. “Youngsters rarely come to church or participate in its activities these days. This is also an opportunity to bring more of them into the church community,” he says.

On Friday afternoon, the Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop, halting departures from all US airports. Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy announced the ground stop on X, citing a “communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers.” Duffy promised updates as more information is known and said FAA staff were troubleshooting the problem.
Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said that the ground stop was not prompted by a security threat. “This is a telecommunications outage out of the FAA. Out of an abundance of caution, we have grounded all of the flights,” Mullin said. “There’s no indication as of yet that this is a nefarious attack against us.”
Mullin said the FAA would handle incoming international flights on a case-by-case basis.
This is only the third nationwide ground stop issued by the FAA. The first, and most memorable, came during the attacks of September 11, 2001, when the FAA stopped all civilian departures nationwide and subsequently ordered all airborne aircraft to land. Commercial flights did not take off again until September 13. Flights were also grounded for less than two hours the morning of January 11, 2023, after its Notice to Air Missions system suffered an outage.
Unfortunately for travelers, based on what is known so far, this is likely to be a lengthy ground stop. Airlines have already canceled flights scheduled to leave later Friday, and American Airlines warned that disruptions are expected for the rest of the day. “This is going to take some time,” Mullin said. “Flights are accounted for, and there should be no fear to the public at all.”

Two Celebrity Cases Put a Spotlight on British Courts’ Gag Orders
Russell Brand and the TV personality David Walliams both persuaded courts to suppress misconduct allegations against them. Some say the libel laws need to change.
Two recent cases have brought new attention to the ways that British laws can allow the wealthy and powerful to silence their critics.
The first was the rape and sexual assault trial of the comedian Russell Brand. Before his conviction last week, Mr. Brand had obtained an injunction prohibiting another accuser from telling almost anyone — including the police, her family and most doctors — about her claims that he assaulted her. (Mr. Brand has denied her allegations.) That injunction, first revealed by Dan Neidle, a tax lawyer and free-expression activist, apparently remains in force.
In the second instance, two British news organizations were temporarily blocked from reporting allegations of sexual misconduct against David Walliams, a television personality and author of children’s books, before a judge declined to make the injunction permanent. The Guardian newspaper and ITV News, a British broadcaster, published investigations last week into the allegations, which Mr. Walliams denies.
Though both men now face public scrutiny, the revelations of how they used court injunctions — essentially gag orders — to protect their reputations have provoked no shortage of public and political outrage. Judges in other cases have issued “super injunctions,” which prohibit publishing any information even about the injunction itself.
“What will the government do to prevent these abuses of process, and stop the abusive injunctions and super injunctions which stop scrutiny, accountability and the work of the free press?” Nick Timothy, the shadow justice minister, asked in Parliament on Tuesday.
The British government is now “looking at what we can do,” Alex Davies-Jones, the government minister responsible for victims of crime and violence against women and girls, said in response.

Fiji 'did Ireland a favour' before South Africa game
- Published
Former South Africa head coach Jake White said his Fiji side "did Ireland a favour" in Saturday's Nations Championship contest before the Irish face the Springboks in Dublin next week.
Fiji lost 43-15 to Ireland at Aviva Stadium having frustrated Andy Farrell's side during a closely contested first half.
While Ireland scored 26 unanswered points in the second half, White - who led South Africa to World Cup glory in 2007 - said Andy Farrell's team cannot afford similarly sluggish spells against the back-to-back world champions.
"Well, I think we probably did Ireland a favour today," the 62-year-old said.
"Let me put it that way, because I think Ireland deep down know that if they play like that against South Africa, they're gonna be up against it."
- Ireland shake off sluggish start to brush aside Fiji 
  - Published2 hours ago
White, who was appointed Fiji boss last month, was frustrated that his side opted to take a tap penalty instead of a scrum when the game was in the balance.
"I know how South Africa operate and they would've taken that scrum there, they would have backed the fact that they wanted to get [Ireland] a yellow card," said White.
"They would have taken another scrum and another scrum and another scrum, and they wouldn't have worried about the ref making a call about collapsing or early engaging.
"If I'm coaching South Africa and Malcolm Marx is standing there [as captain], there's no way he is going to say, 'we'll take the tap'. There's no way that happens.
"Marx will say, 'let's take the scrum,' or 'we'll kick it out into the corner and we'll take the line-out'. And that's because they back themselves in those situations."
White added: "The five-metre line-outs that we didn't take opportunities in, and the five-metre scrum and tap penalties, South Africa will turn those into points and I'm sure that Andy [Farrell] and the players will be aware of that.
"They [Ireland] have been around a long time, and they know what's coming, and that's probably why he picked the team that he did because he wanted to make sure that they get a little bit more gun-ready for next weekend, because the easiest thing would have been to change the team and then they're probably one game shy of playing South Africa next week."
When White's comments were put to Farrell, the Ireland boss said: "We were just saying in the changing rooms that we learned some good lessons and use them in the right manner for next week."
Farrell also admitted the scoreline flattered his side after they pulled clear having only led 17-15 at the break.
"Pleased to get the win, especially the scoreline, it flattered us a little bit but having said that you've got to work for those points and after 25 minutes you're down by five points against a side that's playing pretty well.
"As far as the physical nature of the game, I thought they were winning collisions, they were good in the air and on the floor, running really physically through the line and the breakdown was pretty good.
"All in all, we need to understand that wins here when you're under a bit of pressure, they're all pretty precious."
While Ireland struggled to shine at times, Farrell was impressed by James McNabney's shorter-than-expected debut.
The Ulster back row came off the bench and made two huge carries before being forced off with a head injury which rules the 23-year-old out of featuring against South Africa.
"He's joking in the changing rooms - he's delighted with himself for the shortest cameo of a first cap," he said of McNabney.
"I reckon it's the best cameo of three-and-a-half minutes or whatever it was on a debut in Irish history really.
"He remembers the two breaks that he made, so he seems in good spirits."

On Wednesday, Mississippi’s Senate race was officially called for Democrat Scott Colom, who will become the first Black person to represent the state in the US Senate since Reconstruction, more than 140 years ago. Colom’s win is a stunning, historic upset — and for many Black Democrats, like Rep. Bennie Thompson, it’s been a long time coming.
“A rich message, but a poor campaign”: How Scott Colom beat the odds in Mississippi
Rep. Bennie Thompson on his 50-year fight to see a Black senator from Mississippi.
Thompson, who also won his race last week, has represented Mississippi’s majority-Black Second Congressional District since 1993. Over the years, the 78-year-old lawmaker has frequently invoked the story of his father, who was never able to cast a vote because of racist Jim Crow laws that enforced segregation until the mid-1960s.
I sat down with Thompson for Today, Explained to talk about Colom’s run for Senate, how he won, what it means for Thompson personally.
Below is an excerpt of our conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts, Pandora, and Spotify.
Your dad was never able to cast a vote during his lifetime because of Jim Crow laws. And I wonder, growing up in Mississippi, what did you learn about who was allowed to participate in democracy?
You were a second-class citizen. That means you could go to school, but you couldn’t go to school with the white kids. Or the one swimming pool in town was for white kids, and the Black kids had to swim in the creeks or the ponds around the community. No lifeguard, no anything. My mama and daddy paid taxes, but they weren’t allowed to vote. My uncle fought in World War II; defended democracy all over the world, but when he came back home, he had to ride a segregated train behind the white German prisoners.
Jesus.
So you had the white soldiers, the white German prisoners, and the Black soldiers. And that was the order of the day. It was something that we grew up with.
When you were young, I wonder, did you associate the right to vote with the ability to change things? Like, if we get to cast a ballot, then we get to fix this mess?
The best thing that I can say is I went to Tougaloo College [near Jackson, Mississippi]. And on that college campus, I met Martin Luther King Jr., I met Stokely Carmichael, I met Harry Belafonte, I met Sammy Davis Jr. — all of the major civil rights icons of the day.
That was how we cut our teeth into civil rights and voting rights. The first campaign I worked on was Mrs. Hamer’s campaign for Congress.
Fannie Lou Hamer, the civil rights icon.
And I now represent that district.
But I remember telling my mother that, oh, I had gone to Ruleville, Mississippi, to help register Black people to vote for Congress. And my mama said, “Well, I don’t know why you way up there.” Said, “Black people don’t vote here in Bolton.” And so it hit me. And Lord have mercy. In my own hometown, you know, I was in the same situation. And we did voter registration. We did all kind of things.
“For me, having gone through those life experiences and now to see a Scott come along, you know, it not only brings tears to your eye, but it also says that there’s hope.”
We brought Head Start to the community, and started understanding that real freedom comes with political freedom. And so we started holding meetings about what we wanted to do. We decided to run three people for the board and the three African Americans won.
But it really wasn’t a good four years on that term because the current mayor didn’t want any progress. So we ran an all-Black slate: mayor, clerk, alderman. We won every position.
We’re talking about 50 years ago, and all these challenges that you faced, all these challenges to being able to vote, being able to assume office, being able to function as a mayor in a town that is so segregated. Fifty years later, Scott Colom is winning in Mississippi.
I want to ask you to reflect on when you became aware of his candidacy and what you thought about the potential there.
One of the challenges that I’ve had to deal with is that every time I run for public office, I’ve always been the first. But I wanted to create some kind of vehicle to get other people engaged. So we formed the Mississippi Black Leadership Institute. Well, Scott Colom was in the first class. And he really said, “I want to run for something. I don’t know what it is.” He said, “But there’s a district attorney’s position that’s available. It’s three counties.”
We helped Scott put his campaign together. We hooked him up with various people, and he beat a 28-year incumbent as district attorney.
Why do you think he won?
Well, because he had the fire in the belly. And he never met a stranger. And so we prepared him, and he’s one of our star pupils of that class. And look, uh, when the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee would not support him, they—
They would not support him.
They would not support him. But this was my — Bennie Thompson’s position is that Northeasterners were still looking down on Southerners.
Well, did you call them up and scream at Chuck Schumer or somebody and say, “Guys, I am telling you, we got one here who can win?”
Look, we did everything that the system says you should do. We gave the demographics. That district [Colom] represented was not a majority-African American district. He beat that sitting district attorney in a majority-white district because he had a plan and he had a message. We had a rich message, but a poor campaign. Because we couldn’t get our DSCC to help.
Have you called any of those people in national leadership and said, “I told you so?”
Oh yeah. All of a sudden, the week before the election, they’re going to say, “Well, we’re going to be able to do this, but we’re going to shoot the spot and we’ll send it to you.” So you really didn’t give us the money. You know what I’m saying?
So that’s all right. We’re going to keep doing our low budget, social media-attractive thing. And so it took off.
You are 78 years old? Do I have that right?
Yep.
This has been most of your life. The fight for this has been most of your life.
Yep.
You sit here today, we sit here today. Where is your head at in all of this? Did you lock yourself in the bathroom and cry for 10 minutes?
No question. I’m happy for Scott personally. His trajectory is tremendous. But you know, it’s been a tough journey. We had a poll tax put on us that we had to pay money to be a registered voter. We had to interpret sections of the Constitution. In many instances when my mama registered — my mama had a college degree, she was a teacher — but the person who asked her to interpret the Constitution was an elementary school graduate. You see what I’m saying?
I sure do.
And so for me, having gone through those life experiences and now to see a Scott come along, you know, it not only brings tears to your eye, but it also says that there’s hope. There’s hope for young African Americans that at some point, the choice will be, do I stay or leave? It won’t be, “Well, when I get an education, I have to go somewhere else to seek a career.”
And so that’s the exciting part. I’m just really happy. And for a guy who’s been in it over 50 years and been called everything but a child of God, because I’m trying to elevate people who look like me to where I know if they have it, they’ll do a great job. So for Bennie Thompson, Scott’s victory is a dream come true.

Canadian judge decries U.S. sanctions of International Criminal Court as 'attack in favour of impunity'
Winnipeg-born Kimberly Prost and other ICC officials sanctioned last August
Kimberly Prost began to feel the effects of the U.S. sanctions immediately.
"These economic sanctions are not symbolic in any way," said Prost, a Canadian judge at the International Criminal Court (ICC), who was sanctioned by the Trump administration last year.
Prost's credit cards were cancelled and her access to banking services hindered, she said, because of the U.S.'s wide-reaching impact on the global banking system.
"Every time literally I go to make a bank transfer, I hold my breath because I don't know if it's going to work," Prost said in an interview with CBC News.
"To order an Uber, book a hotel, buy a theatre ticket — everything requires some form of credit card, and so you're sort of struggling to adjust."
Based in The Hague, Netherlands, the ICC investigates and tries individuals charged with genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity when courts in its 125 member states, including Canada, are unwilling or unable to do so.
The sanctions on Prost are part of a larger U.S. campaign to discredit and dismantle the ICC, which began in earnest after a February 2025 executive order imposed sanctions for investigating American personnel and issuing arrest warrants against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his former defence minister Yoav Gallant.
U.S. President Donald Trump has since sustained his attack on the international court, calling on member states to immediately "resign from this rogue institution" in a September UN General Assembly speech. Just last month, Secretary of State Marco Rubio threatened to dismantle the ICC "brick by brick" if allies do not "rein in" the court.
In a Sept. 22, 2026, speech at the United Nations General Assembly, U.S. President Donald Trump urged member nations of the International Criminal Court to 'officially resign from this rogue institution immediately.' (Yuki Iwamura/The Associated Press)
Prost says these actions are an attack against the international system of criminal justice and rule of law that has been built since the Second World War.
"It is an attack that foresees a world where victims of atrocity crimes are forgotten. And it is an attack in favour of impunity and ending accountability for these crimes. That's the only way it can be framed."
Rubio warns ICC endangers Americans
Prost was singled out for her role in judicially authorizing a March 2020 preliminary investigation into alleged war crimes in Afghanistan since 2003, including by U.S. service members.
Since 2021, however, the investigation has deprioritized the role of the U.S., focusing instead on the Afghan government and Taliban forces.
"To my knowledge, there's no active investigation of the Americans in that case, but I'm sanctioned."
The United States has never been a member of the ICC, and has long expressed concerns that its citizens could be prosecuted.
"As the United States works to bring peace around the world, our diplomats or our soldiers could be drawn into this court," President George W. Bush said the day after the court was inaugurated in 2002. "It's very troubling to me."
Twenty-four years later, Rubio echoed the same rhetoric about the "dangers" of the global court, warning that American border patrol agents, marines and prosecutors would "be at the mercy of foreign judges," risking imprisonment for defending their own country.
However, Prost says Rubio's arguments are misleading, as the ICC would have "no jurisdiction" if the U.S. asserted its sovereignty and conducted its own genuine investigations or prosecutions when allegations arise.
Member states 'have to protect' ICC
Prost and two other ICC judges sued the Trump administration in June, opposing the sanctions that they say are "designed to exert extra-judicial pressure" and coerce them into "prioritizing their private interests over deciding cases on the basis of the law and facts."
"We decided that it was so significant and such an impediment to our work — and to the work of the court — to challenge it before the courts of the United States," said Prost.
In July, four former U.S. ambassadors and prosecutors of international criminal tribunals submitted a brief in support of the ICC judges, arguing that the sanctions "penalize independent judicial decision-making."
Canadian officials have not intervened in Prost's lawsuit. But in a September interview with CBC News, Foreign Minister Anita Anand said Canada "remains committed to the ICC process."
"As a sovereign country, we determine our foreign policy, and that includes the principles on which our foreign policy is based," Anand said. "One of those fundamental principles is respect for international law."
Prost said the efforts to intimidate her and other judges are ultimately "futile."
"We continue to judge our cases on the facts and the law and the evidence before us objectively and independently, and that will never change," she said.
In October, the U.S. allowed the ICC to access certain information technology and banking services for six months. The State Department said that time would allow member states to demonstrate "meaningful progress" on U.S. concerns.

Prost says losing access to those systems could have a "very crippling effect" on the court's operations.
Though some member states have signaled support, she says the moment remains "critically important" to safeguard the ICC, which has taken steps to prepare in case sanctions come into full force.
"It's their court. It's not the prosecutors' court, not the judges' court. It's the states' court, and they have to protect it."

Journalist’s Arrest Adds to Fears Israeli Security Agency Is Being Politicized
Abed Abu Shehadeh, a Palestinian citizen of Israel, was detained without being charged with a crime, raising concerns that the domestic security service is overstepping its authority.
Abed Abu Shehadeh, a 38-year-old journalist and a Palestinian citizen of Israel, said he was putting on his pajamas on the evening of Nov. 3 when police officers and intelligence agents burst into his family’s third-floor apartment in Jaffa.
They strip-searched him, confiscated his phone, allowed him to dress and then whisked him away, he said in an interview at a restaurant in the city.
Five days later, after interrogations by Israel’s domestic security agency, the Shin Bet, Mr. Abu Shehadeh, who lives with his wife and two young children, was let go.
A former elected member of the Tel Aviv-Jaffa City Council, Mr. Abu Shehadeh has not been charged with a crime. The Israeli authorities have not publicly offered a reason for his arrest, though court records reviewed by The New York Times show that he was accused of being in contact with an unnamed “foreign agent.”
His highly publicized arrest — a week after Israel’s national elections — came as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his allies have claimed that foreign actors illegally funneled large amounts of money to bribe Arab citizens to vote for Arab political parties.
Critics say that Mr. Netanyahu and his allies are seeking to undermine the legitimacy of the record gains by Arab parties in the Parliament, or the Knesset, by contending without basis that Arab voters stole the election.

Florida city cancels St. Patrick's Day parade, citing new anti-DEI law
One of the first casualties of a new Florida law that prohibits taxpayer dollars from going toward diversity initiatives is a St. Patrick's Day parade in a beach town that has been celebrating its Irish American community for nearly 60 years.
The city of Delray Beach announced this week that it was canceling its popular St. Patrick's Day festivities in compliance with a new law that takes effect on Jan. 1. The city will also withdraw its sponsorship of LGBTQ Pride celebrations in June, officials said.
The law, backed by Republican Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis is part of the state's ongoing crackdown on diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) initiatives that the governor has called discriminatory and said have "no place" in public institutions.
The city lawyer for Delray Beach, a community in southeast Florida with picturesque beaches and a historic downtown, told the mayor that any government-sponsored celebrations of culture, ethnicity or heritage that are not a national holiday (for example: Independence Day) could run afoul of the new anti-DEI law. So, Mayor Tom Carney said, he made the difficult decision to cancel one of the city's biggest events of the year.
In past years, the parade, an annual event since 1970, wound its way through the downtown core of Delray Beach with spectators lined up several-people deep along the route. Local businesses and organizations sponsored floats and giveaways. School bands played as they marched through the streets. Participants included members of the Ancient Order of Hibernians, the largest and oldest Irish Catholic organization in the country.
"I've said it's engrained in the DNA of Delray and I do mean that. It's one of our signature events," Carney, a Republican, told NPR.
The mayor said he's hopeful that the city can find a path forward — and a way to preserve the event.
If a private sponsor were to volunteer to take over the St. Patrick's Day parade, or the June Pride celebrations, Carney said, the city would gladly hand over the reins and support the continuation of these festivities.
"These types of events we should be celebrating because in this country, people can have these events. In other countries, you can't do this. We have great freedoms here," he said. "And if the community wants something and it's not against public policy then I would support them to do it if they're using private dollars. If we can do it, we should do it."
Carney, who is of Irish descent, said the parade was privately run until about eight years ago — so returning to a private-sponsorship model would be a callback to the parade's origins. His own family, he said, was involved in keeping the parade going during the 1980s and 1990s.
Delray Beach officials said they have been inundated with emails, calls and social media messages from constituents who are angry that the community's decades-long celebration had been axed.
"It was kind of a call to action to me," Carney said. "The community really wants to have it, so we should go ahead and have it, we just need to get it privately funded."
The governor, meanwhile, has accused Delray Beach of weaponizing the new anti-DEI measure to make a political point. DeSantis said the city was "engaging in "malicious compliance" in a message he posted on X following the city's cancellation announcement.
"What they are doing is not mandated by Florida law," the governor wrote. "It's just an attempt to make a political point — a point that legacy media will no doubt try to amplify. We've seen these stunts throughout the years. Rinse and repeat."
The mayor said the city is merely trying to stay out of trouble with the law. The measure, SB1134, asserts that any official that violates the provision could face civil or legal consequences.
"The legislation has unintended consequences. The governor may genuinely believe what he believes and I take him at his word; our city attorney came up with a different conclusion," Carney said. "I'm going to leave it at that."

Are you a young professional living in a metro city who struggles to find time to cook? Between office deadlines, long commutes, social commitments, and managing expenses, looking after one's health can sometimes take a back seat. Even something as basic as eating a balanced meal can become a challenge. For many, planning meals, tracking protein intake and counting calories can feel like additional responsibilities in an already busy routine. A Bengaluru couple decided to address this very problem. According to a report by Startup Pedia, Diya Krishnakumar and Adithya Natarajan, both IT professionals, launched their venture, Wellfed, in September 2024. The idea emerged from their own experiences of trying to balance demanding work schedules with healthy eating. They wanted meals that were convenient, nutritious, and satisfying, while retaining the familiarity of home-cooked food. However, the meal subscription services available at the time did not quite meet their expectations. The couple eventually identified an opportunity to bridge this gap and decided to build their own food business. Stepping away from their IT careers, the duo launched Wellfed, a healthy meal subscription startup in Bengaluru, with an initial investment of ₹15 lakh, largely from their personal savings. The venture has since generated ₹56 lakh in revenue between January and September 2026. It has also served more than 1,500 customers and delivered over 55,000 meals so far. Speaking to Startup Pedia, Diya Krishnakumar said, "We are trying to change this exact trade-off that young professionals get caught up in. Healthy, comforting meals should come with the convenience of not worrying about your pantry stock or your busy mornings and afternoons. Fifty-five thousand meals later, we are still unwaveringly true to this vision." Bengaluru-based Diya and Adithya, both 28, are computer science engineers who began their careers at the same company. After spending more than three years working in the IT sector, they decided to leave their jobs and pursue an MBA. During their time in the IT industry, the couple realised how difficult it was to maintain regular eating habits alongside demanding work schedules. Their busy routines often left little time for cooking. On some days, they would return home with takeaway food, while on others, one of them would barely manage to prepare dinner. Diya also realised that preparing everyday meals could take considerably longer than most people anticipate. She explained that recipes advertised as taking just 20 minutes often require much more time in a regular kitchen. Expecting people to cook after a long and demanding workday, therefore, was not always practical. The couple began exploring meal subscription services that could provide both lunch and dinner. However, they found that most available options focused on offering multiple cuisines and elaborate preparations rather than simple, everyday Indian food. They wanted healthy meals without making customers feel as though they were following a restrictive diet. Their preference was for familiar dishes featuring dal, vegetables, roti, and protein-rich preparations. Unable to find an affordable service that matched their expectations, they decided to create one themselves. When Wellfed first started, the team consisted of six members, including the two founders, a nutritionist, a cook, a steward, and a delivery person. The nutritionist helped plan the meals and calculate their nutritional composition, while the rest of the team handled food preparation and deliveries. During the initial phase, the couple shared their meals with friends and family to understand how people would respond to the concept. The encouraging feedback gave them the confidence to continue. Diya believed that the familiarity and comfort of home-style food offered something that elaborate restaurant dishes could not always replicate. Wellfed's menu includes everyday preparations such as dal, aloo gobhi, jowar roti, adraki chicken and chole chaat. It also incorporates protein-rich ingredients such as paneer, tofu, soya and chicken. For customers looking for more variety, the menu features wraps, biryanis and popular Indo-Chinese dishes. The venture received an early boost when a Bengaluru-based nutritionist shared a reel about Wellfed on social media. This collaboration helped the startup attract its first 100 customers.
