Controversial change to 'safer-supply' opioid prescriptions abruptly paused due to legal challenge
Change was set to start Monday; prescription recipient Aaron Simkin calls pause 'good news'
A controversial change to "safer-supply" opioid prescriptions that would force recipients to take them in front of a pharmacist, rather than on their own schedule at home, has been abruptly paused due to a legal challenge.
The College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario (CPSO) announced the pause Friday, days before the changes were to come into effect on Monday.
The medical regulator, which governs prescription policy for doctors, said it was served with a legal challenge Friday that included a motion for an injunction to halt the changes. An injunction is a court order that forces an entity to do something specific ordered by the court. CPSO says it agreed to pause the changes to allow time to respond to the injunction.
"We recognize that physicians may already have been working with patients and other members of their care teams in preparation for November 16," the release said. "During the pause, physicians should continue to practise in accordance with their professional obligations and exercise clinical judgment based on the individual circumstances and needs of their patients."
CPSO did not respond to a request for more information ahead of publication.
The CPSO announced Oct. 13 that its board had voted for the proposed changes. In addition to eliminating take-home doses of opioids, the changes would require physicians to assess patients receiving the drugs at least once a month in person, and that people on the drugs should also be prescribed a long-acting opioid, such as methadone or suboxone, widely used therapies for opioid addiction.
The college said the proposed changes would "strengthen expectations for physicians who prescribe safer supply medications" and help prevent the drugs from being used by people for whom they aren't prescribed.
"The diversion of safer supply medication raises serious concerns for patient and public safety," said Dr. Nancy Whitmore, registrar and CEO, in a release. "These amendments… represent meaningful regulatory action within CPSO's mandate to serve in the public interest."
Hamilton prescription opioid recipient says pause brings relief
Hamilton resident Aaron Simkin, who says prescription opioids helped stabilize his life after many years of homelessness and drug use, called the pause "good news."
Simkin lived at the Hamilton YMCA for four years, and spent most of his time looking for drugs to fuel his addictions. Now, he has an apartment, five cats and four part-time jobs, and credits prescription opioids for helping turn his life around.
"It just stabilized my life because I didn't need to score any drugs," said Simkin, 47. "You don't have to run around looking for people to buy from and… worrying [about getting] fake drugs or fentanyl.
"There's no chaos."
Simkin picks up his prescription, which includes Dilaudid to treat opioid dependence, once a day. He takes the medication every four to five hours, a routine that staves off the physical symptoms of withdrawal. "I'm not getting high. It's just maintaining," he said.
Simkin said the proposed changes would drastically affect his daily routine and lead to long stints where he can't access the drugs, during the hours the pharmacy is closed. He's scared he won't be able to continue to hold down work while in withdrawal, and worries he could return to the black market to make it through.
"It's so hypocritical," he told CBC Hamilton in a Friday interview in a coffee shop near his apartment. "They talk like taking drugs off the street is 'community safety,' but they create a vacuum. They create a black market. It's not safe. The drugs aren't safe."
CPSO says changes will prevent diversion of drugs
In devising the proposed new regime, CPSO says it consulted with "physicians with expertise in addiction medicine and health system partners, including the Office of the Chief Medical Officer of Health."
Rami Safi, a Hamilton pharmacist with several clients who receive these medications, does not believe adequate consultation occurred.
Safi, manager of Wellness Wave pharmacy near Ottawa and Barton streets, said that in addition to impacting patients, the changes also affect pharmacies, social workers and others who provide care for drug users, groups that do not appear to have been consulted.
Rami Safi stands in front of his pharmacy, Wellness Wave, on Barton Street East in Hamilton on Friday, Nov. 13, 2026. (Saira Peesker/CBC)
He said he often sees complaints on social media about drug users loitering around pharmacies, and said the proposed change was bound to increase tension between pharmacies, their customers and others in their neighbourhoods.
"It's going to make it worse because people will just hang out around the pharmacy" between their doses, he said. "This has created so [many] problems for me and for my colleagues across the city. It's an extra pressure that we don't need in these situations."
'Do we ditch them and just say, "Let them die"?'
Safi, who is also a psychotherapist, believes stricter rules — such as the proposed change to safe-supply prescriptions — come from a place of moral judgement of people who use drugs, rather than an approach that would best address the crisis.
"We see it as morality because the consequences of using drugs might lead to crime," he said. "When you see it in your own personal life, you know that it's actually way deeper than that. It's biological factors, it's social factors and it's psychological factors."
After safer-supply prescriptions allowed many drug users to function better within mainstream society, Safi worries the new changes will push them back to the margins.
He'd like to see the health care system redirect its efforts toward better treating the mental-health conditions of people who use drugs, and better-integrated health care where a patient's various practitioners — including doctors, social workers, pharmacists and mental health experts — could work as a team with a shared approach.
Safi pointed to the shocking number of people who have died from opioid toxicity in Canada — 57,509 between January 2016 and March 2026, according to Statistics Canada.
"If you have an army fighting somewhere, you will not lose this number," he said. "Do we ditch them and just say, 'Let them die'? That's what we're kind of doing in a way. Or do we have to find real proper solutions and access to care?"

On September 27, US transportation secretary Sean Duffy posted a video on X with the words “GAME CHANGER.” “Introducing ‘SMART’—the new air traffic management tool that saves YOU time, cuts back DELAYS, and makes your flying experience BETTER,” he wrote. This was a new AI-infused air traffic control system. Almost three weeks later, that post would get a new life, as a nervous joke, as the FAA issued a national groundstop on Friday the 13th that instantly threw the world’s airline schedules into chaos. The administration quickly announced that there was no evidence of a cyberattack, and no sign that SMART had anything to do with the communications failure at the heart of the government’s decision to suspend flights. But when asked on Friday night whether he could definitively rule out AI failure, Homeland Security secretary Markwayne Mullin could only say, “There’s nothing certain right now.”
New systems like SMART are only the tip of the iceberg when it comes to the AI aviation revolution currently underway. Take, for instance, the Cessna Caravan that took off from Buchanan Field Airport in Concord, California, and flew south to Phoenix on a calm September morning. The plane, a single-engine turboprop, then turned east to Fort Worth, stopped at Shaw Air Force Base in South Carolina, and finally arrived at Dare County Regional Airport off the coast of North Carolina. The zigzag, coast-to-coast trip covered 3,200 miles; along the way, the aircraft navigated busy airspace and maneuvered to avoid storms.
None of this would be remarkable, save for one fact: The entire journey took place without a single human hand touching the plane’s controls.
According to Joby Aviation, the company that carried out the project, a safety pilot was aboard the Cessna at all times—but never needed to intervene. The pilotless trip marked a major milestone in aviation. The air travel industry has long been technologically conservative, and with good reason: When human lives are at stake, it’s better to be time-tested and a little dated than cutting-edge and unpredictable. But AI is making inroads into aviation with unprecedented speed. The effects now are hard to see, but the changes in the offing are huge, promising to remake the economics of air travel and transform how people and things move around in the sky. A big question remains, though: Can we trust this technology to be reliable and safe?
Depends who you ask. “We're introducing all this new technology to improve the system, and it's going to be a disaster,” says a recently retired FAA employee. “This is literally a Pandora's box that we are going to regret.”
Aviation’s embrace of AI traces back to the early 2000s, when advances in batteries and microelectronics suddenly made drones much more capable and inexpensive. The surge convinced officials that robots and humans would eventually need to share the airways, and that new infrastructure would be necessary to allow that. At the time, virtually all aircraft were human-piloted, and there was no way for drones to avoid human-flown planes or each other.
In 2007, the federal government rolled out a sweeping project called Next Generation Air Transportation System—NextGen, for short—that mandated broad changes to the air travel system over the decades to come. Among its provisions was the requirement that, by 2020, aircraft in the United States be equipped with ADS-B, a system that constantly sends radio signals telling everyone in the vicinity where you are and where you’re headed.
With a road map to robot-friendly skies in place, big players like Amazon and Walmart began working on ambitious plans for drone delivery services. In 2014, Google unveiled Project Wing, a drone delivery offering that by 2018 was ferrying food, coffee, and medication to 164 homes near Canberra, Australia. The next year, the pilot program was expanded to Christiansburg, Virginia. Costs were high and service slow, but those early programs weren’t meant to become viable businesses. Instead, they were providing Google with operational experience for the years to come.
Around the same time, a host of startups began working on a related kind of vehicle: electric vertical takeoff and landing aircraft, or eVTOLs, also known as electric air taxis. These are, essentially, oversized drones (with room for pilots, for now) designed to carry a small number of people a short distance. By 2022 there were 600 different models under development. Soon, their manufacturers promised, cheap, short aerial hops would be commonplace. Joby was among those leading the charge: In 2020, the company unveiled the design of its S4 model, which it said would be able to carry a pilot and four passengers 100 miles or more at speeds of up to 200 mph. The S4’s maiden flight took place last year.
A commercial launch seemed just around the corner. But deadlines kept getting pushed back. As it turned out, engineering a flying autonomous robot was just part of the overall problem. You also needed to design an airspace that they could operate in, train humans to pilot or supervise them, develop an economic framework within which they could earn money, and so on. “It's a very important, safe, careful dance,” says Greg Bowles, Chief Policy Officer at Joby Aviation.
Silicon Valley’s speed has long been in conflict with air travel norms. “Aviation regulation has been conservative and prioritizes reliability, because the consequences of failure are severe,” says Mary Schiavo, an aviation lawyer and former inspector general in the Department of Transportation. “Certification standards and airworthiness require proof and demonstrated safety, and that usually means incremental rather than radical change.” The FAA was in no rush to let unproven robots go careening around the national airspace.
AI faced another kind of resistance in Europe. In 2017, aircraft manufacturers Airbus and Dassault asked the EASA, the European Union’s version of the FAA, to consider allowing airliners to operate with a single pilot in the cockpit. Traditionally, airliners require multiple pilots to divide the considerable workload of flying a plane and to ensure that if one pilot becomes incapacitated, the other can carry on. In Airbus’ vision, automated systems would shoulder the copilot’s workload and even take over entirely if needed.
That idea horrified pilots. The European Cockpit Association, a union of airline pilots, lodged a strong protest. Such a move “would remove an independent safety professional from the flight deck and give operators greater influence over the safety judgments that a pilot would otherwise make,” the union explained to me in an email. Last year, EASA shelved the plan.
Nevertheless, AI pressed onward. In 2023, the FAA began issuing waivers to allow delivery-drone flights beyond the visual range of operators; by the end of this year it could make the rule change permanent. Some of the biggest players are already pushing ahead aggressively. This past August, Amazon announced that it planned to expand its drone delivery service to 500 locations across the country by the end of the year. Walmart is planning drone delivery from 270 store locations by the end of 2027.
The ultimate goal is far larger. Industry insiders say that in a maximal vision of the technology’s build-out, hundreds of thousands of drones will be servicing most or all of the US population. “In five to 10 years, it’s going to be completely ubiquitous,” Anthony Vittone, chief operating officer of the drone technology company DroneUp, told me in a story for Sherwood News last year. “People are going to be, like, ‘I don’t know how I lived without it.’”
Joby and other eVTOL companies haven’t progressed quite as fast, but they, too, are moving ahead. In April, Joby flew the first-ever point-to-point eVTOL flight within New York City, from John F. Kennedy Airport to three heliports in Manhattan. The company has carried out similar flights in California and Texas, all under the auspices of the eVTOL Integration Pilot Program (eIPP), a federal initiative rolled out by the Trump administration this past March to demonstrate the capabilities of modern drones and eVTOLs.
These demo flights, Bowles says, are just the “front edge” of the Joby S4’s operational rollout. Next will come demonstration flights with nonpaying passengers, demonstration flights with paying passengers, and finally flights that will take passengers from A to B. “All of that is permitted under eIPP, with increasing levels of oversight,” he says.
To start, these flights will have human pilots, but it’s very expensive to pay one human to fly around a handful of paying passengers; for the model to make any economic sense, the aircraft will have to fly themselves. And if self-driving is a tough challenge for cars, it’s all the more so for aircraft, where an unexpected control system failure isn’t just dangerous but likely deadly.
Given the scale of the challenge, the entry point of AI into human passenger flight won’t be as flashy as piloting eVTOLs; it’ll occupy a more modest, behind-the-scenes role. Already, data companies like Palantir and aviation industry stalwarts like Jeppesen and Thales are selling AI-enabled software that lets regulators, airlines, and flight dispatchers sift through masses of data to identify risks and plan aircraft and crew scheduling.
In September, the FAA announced that it deployed software built by the Boston-based data company Air Space Intelligence. The new AI-powered tool is called “Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories,” or SMART, and it’s aimed at “fundamentally reshaping how we manage our airspace.” The program isn’t intended to replace controllers, the government says, but to make doing their jobs easier by using predictive AI to head off scheduling snags. “Combining SMART with our ongoing hardware upgrades gives us the tools to cut flight delays, optimize traffic, and keep airspace capacity across the country open—all while maintaining our gold standard of safety,” FAA administrator Bryan Bedford said in a press release.
The system is supposed to help controllers make decisions, not make those decisions for them. But if the program feeds nonsensical information into the system, will human operators be able to catch the mistake? “This is the Trump/DOGE/Musk effect,” says the recently retired FAA employee, who asked to remain anonymous. “They’re pushing through all this new technology without any understanding of the complexity of the national airspace system.”
Some lawmakers are also concerned about SMART. On October 13, almost two dozen Democratic lawmakers reportedly sent a letter to the Government Accountability Office asking it to review the program, citing fears that it might “hallucinate safety-critical information.”
Then there’s the question of whether SMART could worsen the chronic shortage of air traffic controllers. The FAA hopes that the technology lessens the shortage by requiring fewer workers; other industries, though, have yet to see AI-generated efficiencies actually materialize. Even if the software doesn’t directly replace humans, the efficiency could be used to justify a workforce reduction. In May, the FAA reduced its staffing target for active air traffic controllers from the 2024 goal of 14,633 down to 12,563, citing “modern staffing models and scheduling tools.”
Some are more optimistic than others. “I think the SMART program is an important improvement,” Schiavo says. “No one wants the current aviation environment with midairs, runway incursions, myriad near misses, delays, groundings, loss of separation, and long taxi or clearance wait times.”
Michael McCormick, a professor of air traffic management at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University, also sees advantages to a predictive tool. “When you have the computing capability to look at the entire trajectory of the aircraft, you can see where the conflicts are going to be,” he says. “And the general axiom in air traffic control is that the sooner you know about a potential conflict, the less effort is required to resolve it.”
That sounds great, but building machines that do a good job most of the time is one thing; machines that can function at the level of reliability required by aviation is another. At present, researchers are focusing on so-called deterministic neural networks—models trained offline whose weights are frozen before being deployed in the real world. These can’t hallucinate, but they may harbor other risky failure modes. In a 2021 paper, Darren Cofer, a researcher at Collins Aerospace, pointed out that when such systems find themselves in situations they haven’t encountered before in training, they can generate “unexpected (and potentially dangerous) outputs.”
The stakes will be even higher when AI software starts making real-time air traffic control decisions, which will start in airspace devoted to autonomous aircraft. According to McCormick, that’ll most likely be select corridors near drone hubs and eVTOL vertiports. With swarms of robot aircraft zipping back and forth, things will be too hairy for human pilots and controllers. “The objective is not to use traditional air traffic control,” he says, “because it would overwhelm the national airspace system if it tried to handle that volume and complexity of airframes moving around.”
With two systems working side by side—one with human decisionmakers, the other with AI—we’ll have a real-time basis to compare the performance of both approaches. Any computer-based system can potentially be hacked; any AI system creative enough to ideate novel solutions could also hallucinate crucial details. Without a human in the loop, seemingly obvious mistakes might go unnoticed until it’s too late.

After Democrats in Texas flipped a U.S. Senate seat, won 14 U.S. House seats and the governor's office in the 2026 midterm elections, a claim (archived) circulated that the wins happened only because the party fraudulently "found" 20 million new voters who all voted blue.
For example, an X user wrote, "There's no chance Texas found 20 million new voters who voted exclusively 100% for Democrats. It's fraud!"
The same text also circulated on Facebook (archived) and other social media platforms.
We found no proof that the Democratic Party in Texas fraudulently "found" and registered 20 million new voters to skew races in their favor in the Nov. 3 elections. The claim appeared to conflate a separate, unproven claim about the number of new voters nationwide with the number of new voters in Texas alone.
Therefore, we rate this claim false.
Texas had just over 19 million registered voters by mid-October, according to its secretary of state. Figures from that office showed the number of registered voters had risen by about 2% since the presidential election in 2024. The number of registered voters rose about 5.4% between the 2022 and 2024 elections. An additional 20 million voters would have created a 107.4% increase in registered voters since 2024 or a 113.2% increase since 2022.
The state's unofficial voter turnout figures showed that 9,850,031 people voted in person or by mail in the state's 2026 midterm elections — a little more than half of Texas' registered voters.
Given the figures from the Texas secretary of state, it wasn't possible for Democrats to have fraudulently "found" 20 million people to tip the state's elections, because fewer than half that number voted in the elections at all. A sudden doubling of the number of registered voters would have raised alarm bells with officials. This did not occur.
The origin of the "20 million" figure was unclear, but it may have come from a bar chart that claimed to show that House Democrats gained 20 million voters across the entire U.S. between 2022 and 2026. The fact-checking organization Lead Stories reported on this graph and found no credible source for its projected 2026 voter numbers.
Rather, Lead Stories pointed to the University of Florida's General Election turnout tables, which showed 123,540,000 ballots counted nationwide in the 2026 midterms by Nov. 6. The same source showed 112,030,874 ballots counted in the 2022 midterms, the most recent equivalent race. The bar chart claimed 126 million people had voted in House races in 2026, around 2.5 million more than the University of Florida's estimate.
The university's figures suggested an increase of 11,509,126 ballots counted between the 2022 and 2026 elections, around half of the 20 million figure the unsourced bar chart suggested.
It wasn't possible to determine how many more individual voters had voted for House Democrats in 2026 vs. in 2022 because state officials had not yet certified their election results at the time of this writing and when the graph circulated.
Regardless of the accuracy of the graph or claim, it was true that Democrats picked up a sizable number of votes in their House and Senate races to secure control of both chambers nationwide. Pollsters credited young voters, male voters and Hispanic voters with securing Democratic wins.
At the time of this writing, there were no credible allegations of widespread fraud.
The false claim played into election fraud theories about bad actors "finding" votes in elections. Snopes has previously reported on variations of this claim in the form of noncitizen voting (which rarely happens), duplicate ballots (which are extremely difficult to produce) and vote spikes (which are a natural part of vote counts).

Lupus patients struggling with the debilitating disease are lining up to try experimental CAR-T therapies even after the recent deaths of four patients in clinical trials for a variety of autoimmune diseases, according to doctors who treat the life-threatening condition.
The trials remain halted and full details of the deaths — three linked to Novartis and one to Bristol Myers Squibb — have not been released.
Still, patients are willing to take the risk, compelled by accounts of people with advanced disease who were able to stop all medications and reclaim normal lives.
“I have patients that are literally waiting to get in,” said Dr. Anca Askanase, chief of rheumatology at the Hospital for Special Surgery in New York, who has enrolled patients in the Bristol Myers CAR-T trials.
Systemic lupus erythematosus, or SLE, the most common and severe form of lupus, causes agonising joint pain and raises the risk of stroke, heart attack and kidney disease. Current treatments, which range from steroids to immunosuppressants and targeted biologics, often fail to control the disease. Some 10% to 15% of people with lupus die prematurely.
Brittan Kopittke, 27, who works for the University of North Carolina helping to counsel patients considering CAR-T, was diagnosed with lupus at age 22. SLE, which affects about 300,000 people in the US, typically develops between the ages of 15 and 44.
What began as a rash on her chest rapidly progressed to crippling joint pain, mouth sores and crushing fatigue. Steroids to reduce inflammation and the antimalarial drug hydroxychloroquine to tamp down antibodies attacking her healthy cells and tissues failed.
“My mouth sores were rampant. I was struggling to eat. I was struggling to drink. I was just very, very miserable,” she said.
Despite trying a cocktail of medicines, her disease advanced, attacking her kidneys, heart and lungs.
“I had reached the end of the line with treatments,” she said.
In June 2024, Kopittke went to UNC-Chapel Hill for a trial testing CAR-T, a personalised immunotherapy successfully used to treat blood cancers. It involves removing blood cells called T cells, genetically reengineering them to attack rogue immune cells, and reinfusing them with the aim of growing new, healthy immune cells.
Kopittke developed two dangerous reactions: cytokine release syndrome, which causes systemic inflammation, and a life-threatening, high-grade neurological complication called ICANS that left her unresponsive for three days.
Now, some two years into remission, Kopittke said she does not “sugarcoat” the risks when advising patients. “But I do say that I would do this again.”
150 trials underway
Novartis, Bristol Myers, and other companies with approved CAR-T cancer therapies, such as Johnson & Johnson and Gilead, are currently testing the technology against other hard-to-treat diseases.
There are about 150 trials underway pursuing CAR-T for lupus, as well as many others for myasthenia gravis, scleroderma, myositis, multiple sclerosis and stiff-person syndrome.
“There’s billions and billions of dollars pouring into this space,” said P.J. Utz, a Stanford Medicine autoimmunity researcher.
The risks became clear when Novartis in late August said it halted eight trials of its experimental rap-cel CAR-T therapy in autoimmune and neurological disorders after three patients died from a rare but known hyperinflammatory complication called IEC-HS.
Novartis, in an emailed statement, said it is working with multiple investigators and external academic experts to understand the root cause of the deaths and will share its findings “once the analysis is completed and the results can contribute to furthering patient care.”
Bristol also paused enrollment in its CAR-T autoimmune trials, citing temporary inflammatory events in patients. On October 23, it announced the death of a multiple sclerosis patient in one of the trials but said it had identified the cause of the safety issue and hopes to resume testing in 2027.
Piecing together what happened
The revelation of deaths in the Novartis trials surprised doctors eager to try CAR-T, buoyed by the success of Georg Schett of the University of Erlangen-Nuremberg. In 2022, Schett published a paper in the New England Journal of Medicine showing five lupus patients achieved remission with CAR-T. Subsequent studies showed lasting remission.
The Novartis deaths have left doctors in the dark, Schett said. The company needs to disclose what diseases the patients had, how well controlled their diseases were and what emergency treatments they received, Schett added.
Without those details, he said, doctors enrolling patients in other trials are left to speculate. “This is very sad for the community.”
Schett said he and CAR-T inventor Carl June of the University of Pennsylvania have tried to piece together what happened in the Novartis trials for an article they have submitted to NEJM.
He attributes the rare hyperinflammatory events in part to Novartis’ compressed manufacturing process, which reduces the time it takes to produce the cells from more than 10 days to fewer than two.
With this process, patients receive cells in an immature form, which Schett suggests is triggering a severe inflammatory response as cells expand in patients’ bodies. “We don’t see that in other programs,” he said.
He and others were less concerned about the more familiar side effects reported by Bristol Myers.
“We have treated high-grade inflammatory events that have been reversible with treatment,” said Kopittke’s doctor, Saira Sheikh, of the University of North Carolina, who chairs a network of nearly 70 lupus clinical trial centres.
Dr. Cuoghi Edens, a rheumatologist at the University of Chicago Medicine, which treats more than 100 paediatric lupus patients, said her hospital has had great success with a CAR-T therapy from Cabaletta Bio, which uses a more traditional manufacturing process.
Cabaletta has started testing its treatment in patients as young as 12. Edens said she walked through the informed consent process with a 15-year-old late last month.
“When the potential long-term impact of your diagnosis is death,” Edens said, “I don’t know if (treatment risks are) going to make that big of a difference to these patients.

A post is being widely circulated on social media (here, here) claiming that Members of Parliament (MPs) in India are exempt from GST on purchases of cars, air conditioners, and flight tickets. It also claims that MPs are entitled to toll tax exemptions and free train travel. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Indian MPs are exempt from GST on purchases of cars, air conditioners, and flight tickets. They are also entitled to toll tax exemption and free train travel.
Fact: MPs are entitled to free train and air travel, as well as toll fees exemption. However, they are not exempt from paying GST on purchases of cars and air conditioners. Hence, the claim made in the post is MISLEADING.
First, according to the details of benefits available to MPs on the official Parliament website (here and here), each MP is entitled to 34 free single air journeys per year anywhere within India. They can use these tickets to travel with their spouse, relatives, or friends.
Additionally, MPs are entitled to free first-class AC or executive-class train travel anywhere in the country. Their spouse or another accompanying person can also avail of this facility. An accompanying assistant is entitled to a free AC two-tier (2-Tier) train pass.
According to the National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) regulations (here and here), vehicles used by MPs are exempt from paying toll fees on national highways. MPs are also entitled to toll-exempt FASTags for two vehicles during their tenure.
However, there is no evidence to suggest that MPs are exempt from paying GST on cars, air conditioners, or other items they purchase. Neither the Salary, Allowances and Pension of Members of Parliament Act, 1954, which outlines the benefits and entitlements of MPs, nor any official government notification mentions such a GST exemption.
To sum up, while MPs are entitled to certain travel benefits, they do not receive any GST exemption on the cars, air conditioners, or other items they purchase.

Seven days of chaos in the ER: How this country's healthcare system is unraveling
In northern Ethiopia, conflict pushes a strained healthcare system to the brink
"It was a mess, it was chaos, and that continued for almost seven, eight days. Without (cell) network, without electricity," recalls a surgeon in Ethiopia.
On September 24, a two-year ceasefire between rebels and the Ethiopian government began to collapse. As injured people streamed in from the countryside, this surgeon and his colleagues treated as many as they could at a hospital in Mekele, the capital city of Ethiopia's northern Tigray region. Fearing repercussions for treating rebel fighters, the surgeon asked NPR not to publish his name.
"The whole emergency (room) was flooded with war trauma patients," he recalls. "The floors were all filled up, there was no place to step."
For the past several weeks, the violence has continued at a steady pace, raising concerns that Ethiopia could again face a civil war. The Ethiopian military has accused Sudan, Egypt and Eritrea of backing Tigrayan militants, who have aligned themselves with seven rebel groups in Ethiopia with the goal of ousting Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed.
After drone strikes in late October killed at least 15 people, including children, the director-general of the World Health Organization, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, posted on X that the violence in northern Ethiopia "is pushing an already fragile health system closer to collapse."
During the initial outbreak of violence in September, the surgeon in Tigray says he spent days operating on victims of gunfire, drone attacks, and mortar shells. Some were clearly civilians, but others were fighters in uniform. Complicating matters, he recalls, there was no way to know how many patients were coming because cell service and the internet were cut.
"We don't know where they're from — you just go ahead and do whatever you can, you know?" he told NPR.
There had been signs that the war between Ethiopia's federal government and rebel groups could reopen. In May, Tigrayan rebels ousted regional leaders and installed their own. In response, Ethiopia's federal government cut funds to Tigray — including to hospitals run by the regional administration. Doctors, he says, haven't been paid in months.
"It's an open wound, which was never closed, you know. Left for healing and never healed," he says. "I guess now it's infected."
For Tedros of WHO, the situation is deeply personal. He is Tigrayan and previously served as Ethiopia's minister of health. In his social media post, he wrote that hospitals are facing shortages of workers, medicine and ambulances, and that WHO and the U.N. are working to deliver medical supplies to the affected regions.
"As fighting continues, more people are likely to lose access to essential healthcare … civilians must be protected," Tedros wrote. "The most courageous choose peace."
A worldwide worry
Public health experts say targeted attacks on healthcare —– generally considered a war crime —– have become a growing concern in conflict zones around the world.
So far in 2026, attacks on health care facilities and workers in 19 countries led to more than 960 deaths, according to data collected by WHO. While the largest mass casualty event occurred in a Pakistani airstrike on a drug rehabilitation center in Afghanistan, hundreds of people have died in attacks on healthcare settings in Sudan, Lebanon, and Ukraine.
Complicating matters are funding cuts to global health initiatives, including the dismantling of USAID shortly after Donald Trump took office in 2025.
"The continual attack against healthcare is eroding the norm of healthcare being a protected part of conflict," says Lindsey Green, a researcher focused on Ethiopia for the U.S. nonprofit Physicians for Human Rights.
The Tigray war lasted two years, killing an estimated 600,000 people. The majority of Tigray's health facilities were only partially functional, as the Ethiopian government imposed an aid blockade on the region — home to more than 7 million people.
Attacks continued, despite a peace agreement
The government struck a peace agreement with Tigrayan rebels in 2022, ending most hostilities, but attacks on healthcare continued. In August of this year, Physicians for Human Rights worked with the Organization for Justice and Accountability in the Horn of Africa to publish a report detailing these attacks.
Of more than 600 health workers surveyed across three regions of northern Ethiopia, 63% reported attacks on ambulances, some as they tried to reach injured patients, and 57% reported witnessing an armed takeover of their clinic or hospital between 2020 and 2024. One health worker in Mekele recalled Ethiopian forces occupying a hospital and placing the uniforms of Tigrayan rebels on the floor and forcing staff to step on them. "Nonsense stuff," he said.
"Armed groups were occupying facilities to take resources or to destroy resources, to destroy machines and equipment, really with the goal of making healthcare harder to access," Green says.
In the report, researchers confirmed targeted attacks on health care workers perpetrated by both rebels and government forces – often as retribution for a community's perceived alliances or against doctors who treated an enemy. But there has been no way for victims to seek justice from either party.
"It's very clear that this ongoing pattern of attacks on healthcare links back to impunity for these violations," Green says.
NPR reached out to Ethiopia's Foreign Ministry and Office of the Prime Minister, but did not receive a response.
Doctors in northern Ethiopia say the one-two punch of a war that specifically targeted healthcare, followed by foreign aid cuts, have left the region without a chance to recover.
A health worker in Tigray counted more than 100 women who died in childbirth over the past year. He attributed their deaths to the dire state of the health system. He spoke to NPR on condition of anonymity, due to fear of being targeted for speaking out.
"They died during delivery because of a lack of medicine, lack of health care providers, a lack of fuel. So the ambulances are not functional," he said.
An independent review of birth data during the Tigray war from 2020 - 2022 showed that the maternal mortality rate per 100,000 live births increased fivefold, compared to prewar data. Researchers in 2022 found that 83% of clinics and hospitals were no longer able to serve pregnant women. Additionally, systemic rape and sexual violence were regularly used as a weapon of war.
"They told us, the people should be punished, because we are supporters of the TPLF (Tigrayan rebels)," the health worker says.
Ayoda Werede, a California-based physician with the nonprofit, Health Professionals for Tigray, says that since the latest outbreak of violence, the Ethiopian military has not targeted health centers. But other unidentified groups have stolen supplies, "including medication, equipment, even mattresses off of patient's beds," Werede says. "This was just the opportunistic vacuum space that was created because of this conflict."
Her fear is that Ethiopia's healthcare system is already stretched beyond its capacity — and as the conflict reignites, injured people will have nowhere to go. The surgeon in Mekele has similar concerns. Many of Tigray's doctors, he says, have already left the country.
"We've lost our sense of being secure," he says. "It's a repeat of what's happened in the past."

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps says it has targeted and destroyed a US early-warning radar in Bahrain in response to a US airstrike on a communications tower in Sirik overlooking the strait of Hormuz. It is Iran’s first direct attack on US military installations for months.
“This is a serious warning to the aggressor enemy to end its aerial mischief and oil smuggling in the strait of Hormuz,” the IRGC said. “In the event of repeated violations and aggression, the IRGC aerospace force is on full alert to confront the enemy without constraint.”
US Central Command denied that the radar system had been destroyed and said US forces had intercepted two Iranian drones headed for Bahrain.
Donald Trump has said in a series of media interviews over the past 24 hours that he will attack Iran only if necessary, claiming that Gulf countries, such as Saudi Arabia, have urged him to hold back from planned large-scale military strikes.
Trump said he had asked the vice-president, JD Vance, to end his interest in negotiating a new deal with Iran and instead focus on corruption and fraud in Democrat-run cities and states.
Vance had been seen by the Iranians as the most trustworthy figure close to Trump, but they had rejected his request for a personal meeting with their negotiators to discuss the terms of a peace deal.
Vance has been at the forefront of Republicans saying the war was the cause of the widespread Republican losses in the midterms. Trump said he had been disappointed in the American public because higher diesel prices were a small price to pay for preventing Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon.
An opinion poll in the UK showed 65% of the British public would oppose the US resuming the war in Iran, and only 14% would back it. The poll was conducted by YouGov for the Council for Arab-British Understanding (Caabu).
It also found 54% oppose UK bases being used by the US to mount attacks on Iran, with 29% in favour. Support for additional UK sanctions against Iran was 45%, with 22% opposed.
The poll was conducted on Tuesday and Wednesday this week, before two Iranians were found guilty on Thursday of spying and planning attacks on journalists in the UK. The Iranian embassy has rejected the court judgment as an attempt to advance a political agenda.
Chris Doyle, the director of Caabu, said: “The British public are sceptical about any war on Iran and what it might achieve. What might make the Burnham government take note is the very high level of opposition to any further war amongst 2024 Labour voters, at 79%.”
Iran’s Assembly of Experts, a body of elected Islamic jurists responsible for choosing the supreme leader, has become the first governing institution in Iran to call for a review of the country’s defence doctrine, potentially leading to religious permission for Iran to try to acquire a nuclear weapon.
In a statement released on Thursday, the assembly called for a review of Iran’s membership of the nuclear non-proliferation treaty, describing the move as an “unavoidable necessity” and a “public and national demand”.
The intervention carries a religious as much as political significance because the 88-strong assembly comprises senior clerics, most of whom are supposed to be qualified to exercise independent Islamic legal reasoning.
Iran has had a longstanding prohibition on nuclear weapons, based on a fatwa issued by the late supreme leader Ali Khamenei, but the relevance of the fatwa in the wake of the US attacks on Iran has been questioned widely in political and security circles.
Whether Iran has the stockpiles of uranium or technology to build a nuclear weapon is contested.
The UN nuclear inspectorate has expressed alarm about a continued lack of information from Iran about its nuclear sites. It said: “Our concerns are growing over Iran’s refusal to allow access to design information or inspections of the Isfahan facility. We do not know the exact location of the Isfahan uranium enrichment facility or whether it contains nuclear materials. It is imperative that we carry out our verification activities in Iran without further delay.”

FAA ground stop disrupts college football
The Federal Aviation Administration's ground stop on Friday has led not only to travel headaches, but also schedule changes and delays in college sports.
Many college football teams were in airports Friday on their way to upcoming games when the nationwide ground stop was issued and thousands of flights were canceled. The FAA on Saturday said airports were returning to normal operations, but that delays and cancellations would continue through the day.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy acknowledged the ground stop's impact on college football. Several games on Saturday were delayed for hours.
"If you look at the cost of what happened yesterday, we're talking if you like football — I know we've had some disruptions to the college football schedule. Some games are being moved," Duffy said during a news conference Saturday. "That's not the most important thing, but we do want to move teams around the country so we can have playoffs happen."
Utah, ranked No. 2 in the College Football Playoff Rankings, will kick off against Arizona in Tucson at 8:30 p.m. local time — a three-hour delay. The Auburn vs. Mississippi State game was pushed back more than four hours to start at 3:15 p.m. local time in Mississippi because of the ground stop. The Florida Atlantic Owls were also unable to fly to Oklahoma on Friday ahead of their game against the Tulsa Golden Hurricane. Saturday's game, which was supposed to begin at 2:30 p.m. local time, was moved to 6:15 p.m. local time.
While other college teams were able to arrive at their destinations and proceed with games on Saturday, the University of Mississippi did not.
Ole Miss, ranked No. 19, was not able to fly to Oklahoma as planned on Friday for its matchup with the University of Oklahoma Sooners. The game between the two teams, which was scheduled to occur Saturday, will now take place on Sunday at 1 p.m. ET, according to the Southeastern Conference. The game will compete with several NFL games that will be televised at the same time. NFL teams were largely unaffected by the ground stop.
In order to help alleviate fans' frustration, the Sooners on Saturday announced "fan appreciation" promotions for the rescheduled game. Oklahoma students can go to the game for free with their student ID and there will be reduced prices on concession items such as $2 for popcorn or a 16-ounce beer.

U.S. Visa Restrictions Threaten African Contestants in Miss Universe
A crackdown on entry by some citizens of African countries by the U.S. immigration officials means that some contestants might not get visas in time to attend the pageant in Puerto Rico this month.
At least two African contestants for Miss Universe said they were in danger of missing the pageant in Puerto Rico this month because they had not secured U.S. visas amid a crackdown by the Trump administration.
One contestant, Miss Zambia, Mubanga Pamela Hatyoka, said she would not travel to the annual event on Nov. 24 because she had not received her visa, according to Arm Model Management, which said it was the franchise holder of Miss Zambia 2026.
Her nonattendance is “linked to the United States presidential travel restrictions affecting Zambia and other African nations,” the agency said in a statement on social media. “She earned her crown, she earned her title, and she deserves the opportunity to represent the nation she proudly serves.”
The contestant from Zimbabwe, Roseanna Hall, said on social media that she, too, had not received a U.S. visa. “I will not give up,” she said. Contestants from South Sudan and the Republic of Congo also faced delays, according to news reports.
The Miss Universe organization did not immediately reply to a request for comment. The Department of Homeland Security also did not respond to a similar request. It was unclear why the contestants had not received visas.
The social media page of the Miss Universe organization listed 20 African countries among its contestants for the pageant to held in the U.S. territory.
The Trump administration has curtailed several avenues to legal migration to the United States as part of a crackdown, including visa bans and restrictions that have hit African countries hard. The administration in January imposed full or partial travel bans and visa restrictions on 36 countries, and 29 of those are in Africa.
In December, the Trump administration widened travel restrictions to additional countries, including Zambia and Zimbabwe, while keeping in place full restrictions for citizens of the Republic of Congo and adding them for South Sudan.
Homeland Security has said it was “slamming the door shut on the foreign invaders who have undermined our national security.”
Citizens of African countries have for decades complained of draconian visa rules imposed by the governments of the United States and European countries. Governments say the restrictions aim to control migration and prevent fraud, but many Africans say they impede legitimate professional, business and study opportunities and stop family members from attending occasions such as births, weddings and funerals.
Those restrictions have become more severe since public attitudes in many Western countries have turned against immigration over the past decade.
Matthew Mpoke Bigg is the East Africa bureau chief for The New York Times, based in Nairobi, Kenya.

The government will make a one-off contribution of $600 million to the project after it's delivered, and hand the development rights for the former Gabba site to the consortium to build about 4,000 new homes.
What's next?
Construction of the new arena and precinct is expected to begin in January.
Construction of Brisbane's new entertainment and housing precinct is set to begin in January, with the state government selecting a private sector building partner.
Deputy premier Jarrod Bleijie announced this morning construction consortium Gather Brisbane had been chosen as the successful tenderer for the $1.4 billion Brisbane Arena in Woolloongabba.
The consortium includes Live Nation, Oak View Group, Plenary and Webuild, and beat out the Brisbane Entertainment Alliance consortium for the deal.
The Brisbane Arena is planned to have a 17,000-seat capacity, increasing to 18,700 for concerts.
The arena is intended to replace the Brisbane Entertainment Centre at Boondall in Brisbane's north and will be adjacent to the new Woolloongabba Cross River Rail station.
Mr Bleijie said the Gabba stadium nearby would be decommissioned following the 2032 Brisbane Olympic and Paralympic Games, giving way to "open public space" and almost 4,000 new homes.
He said the government had committed a one-off $600 million contribution to the project's projected cost of $1.4 billion, to be delivered following its completion, which is expected in 2031.
"To get the acts to come to Queensland, to get the sporting events, to get the music events, the concerts to come to Queensland, you need a venue that rivals the rest of the venues around the world," he said.
"Entertainment lovers will love it, public transport users will be able to access the Cross River Rail here once it opens and I can say confidently … we look to be on-site in January."
He said the state would continue to own the land in a long-term commercial arrangement with the arena operator.
"This is a 40-year deal and the maintenance [and] the obligations to maintain the arena will be [on] the consortia and the operator,"Mr Bleijie said.
"There will be a commercial arrangement going forward with the operators, but as I said, it's over 40 years.
"That will be locked in before the end of the year, before construction starts on the new arena in January."
Brisbane live music stalwarts Lisa and Jess Origliasso — also known as The Veronicas — backed the new arena and said it would be an "incredible opportunity".
"We look around Brisbane and, you know, we have so many memories here — every part of our career has a sentimental attachment to different parts of Brisbane," Jess Origliasso said.
"That is why this is so fantastic — I think this is a dream coming true," Lisa Origliasso said.
Developers to be handed Gabba land
Mr Bleijie insisted the government was "not giving away the land" on which the Gabba stands.
"This is a very complicated commercial transaction," he said.
"Part of the process for getting the consortia to design, finance, and operate [the arena] without any government contribution until at least 2031, is to obviously have the ability that they know the investment [is] going forward.
"We're not giving away the land, it's a commercial transaction and the commercial transaction that we've entered into is over a 40-year period."
He said the state government would be responsible for tearing down the Gabba after the 2032 Games, before handing the land to the consortium.
"The previous government had no plans to unlock this site," he said.
"In contrast, this government does, and we are very happy to partner with the private sector to get things done."

More than 500 vineyards are scattered across the slopes and valleys of South Africa’s Western Cape, one of the world’s most biologically diverse landscapes. The region produces about 90 percent of South Africa’s wine, but winemakers there are increasingly struggling with drought, excessive heat and erratic rainfall.
Temperatures in the region have risen 1.5 to 2 times faster than the global average over the past five decades. And extreme storms have become more intense as climate variability increases. The late 2010s brought a significant challenge for winemakers, as three years of severe drought placed vineyards under intense stress and reduced grape production.
As climate variability places increasing pressure on grape production, many wine producers are building on sustainability measures that have long been part of vineyard management.
We are a team of geographers and sustainability scientists who study environmental change, environmental health, conservation, agriculture and land management. Our team wanted to better understand how farmers in South Africa’s wine-producing regions are responding as a range of environmental and economic pressures rise. We talked with growers, conservation practitioners and wine industry experts in the Western Cape and analyzed how 107 vineyards, about 20% of the total, were using sustainable land stewardship practices to adapt.
In many agricultural landscapes, production and conservation goals are frequently viewed as competing priorities. But our research found that many vineyard operators in the Western Cape see long-term stewardship and conservation of soil and wildlife habitat as essential strategies for business success.
Conservation as an investment, not a constraint
The Western Cape is home to the Cape Floral Region, a global biodiversity hot spot. It includes fynbos, a unique biome containing thousands of endemic plant species, including types of proteas, ericas and restios that are found nowhere else on Earth.

The Kerala State Human Rights Commission has sought a report from the Kozhikode Municipal Corporation Secretary within 10 days on the lack of parking facilities for city buses operating on the Mananchira-Medical College route.
Commission judicial member K. Baijunath directed authorities to address a complaint alleging that more than 100 city buses operating on the route had no designated parking facility on the Medical College premises. The Commission directed authorities to investigate the issue and submit a report within 10 days.
The complaint alleged that traffic police and the Motor Vehicles Department were imposing hefty fines on buses for parking on the Medical College premises, while private vehicles were allowed to park there. It also pointed out that bus employees had no facilities to attend to their basic needs, leaving them under considerable mental stress.
Despite several complaints being submitted to the authorities, no effective action had been taken, the complainant alleged. The Commission will consider the case at its sitting at the Government Guest House in Kozhikode on November 25.

A Pakistan link has surfaced in connection with the November 3 railway track blast near Sri Ganganagar. A joint operation by the Rajasthan Anti-Terrorism Squad and Punjab Police led to the arrest of two accused from Punjab's Gurdaspur, identified as Mehakdeep Kaur and Devinder Singh. Initial interrogation revealed that the accused received explosives dropped via drone from Pakistan and planted them on the railway track following instructions from a Pakistan-based handler. Security agencies recovered weapons, 46 live cartridges, and 30,000 rupees in blast-related funds from their possession. An investigation remains underway to trace the cross-border handlers and uncover the entire terror network.

A.I. Weapons Need Data for Their Training. Ukraine Has a Lot to Offer.
The Ukrainian government has opened up a trove of five million battlefield videos to defense companies at home and abroad.
The forest, seen from a drone, appeared as a vast, monotonous landscape of black tree trunks, shadows and patches of snow.
To the human eye, it appeared deserted. But to an artificial intelligence system looking for people, it did not. The system put a red box around a tiny human form, probably a soldier lurking in the trees.
Behind this feat lay vast volumes of data. Just as ChatGPT and other A.I. chatbots must be exposed to how humans write, military A.I. systems must be exposed to how humans fight. In Ukraine, this happens through a huge trove of battlefield videos, audio and text data collected over nearly five years.
The war database is being used by about 30 Ukrainian defense companies to develop A.I. weapons. Ukraine is now opening this repository, which it calls Avenger Labs, to firms in allied countries, hoping to deepen security partnerships.
Ukraine is providing the data at no charge, but companies must give the Ukrainian military licenses to any software they develop. Under the first agreement to be reached, 12 British defense companies will gain access. Ukraine is in talks with other countries.
While there is no shortage of Western companies developing autonomous weapons, there is a shortage of the data needed to train them. Ukraine can offer more of it than any other potential partner.

A dramatic Microsoft 365 outage impacting widely used services like Outlook, Teams, and Copilot dragged into a second day on Friday after the company failed overnight to resolve an issue that left institutions and individuals around the world without crucial communication tools. The services did seem to be on a slow path to recovery by midmorning on Friday.
“We’re observing sustained improvements in service availability,” Microsoft said in a statement posted to its status dashboard on Friday morning. The company had said on Thursday evening that its initial attempts to fix the problem were “not taking as expected.”
The outages have caused widespread disruption to schools, courts, governments, and law enforcement agencies—plus countless businesses and millions of employees—around the globe, highlighting how many of the world’s most crucial systems rely upon technologies from a small number of tech companies. And when they fail, the ramifications can be huge.
Microsoft has not said yet what caused the outage but has hinted that it was related to cascading server failures inside multiple data centers around the world that shifted too much load onto remaining operational machines.
“We determined the elevated load isn't driven by an increase in traffic, but by a number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable; straining the remaining infrastructure,” the company wrote in Microsoft 365 Status update on Thursday afternoon. “We’re testing a configuration change to address a problem that's causing servers to fail automated health checks and become unavailable,” the company added a few minutes later.
An additional update a few minutes after that noted, “We've not identified any recent change correlated with the start of impact; however, our investigation indicates the failed health checks may originate from a specific component that's responsible for processing server health.”
Microsoft emphasized repeatedly in statements that there was no indication of the outage being caused by a cyberattack.
“This is absolutely going to go down as one of the big ones, up there with the Facebook outage of October 2021,” says Doug Madory, director of internet analysis at monitoring firm Kentik. “We don't know the root cause yet, but it is interesting to break down the traffic by source data center. The recovery came in fits and starts and varied greatly by source, probably due to Microsoft's efforts to bring the service back online.”
A prolonged outage of such a critical underlying digital service is not unprecedented, but Microsoft has a special position among cloud providers as an older company that was already ubiquitous in global computing from the PC era. Many organizations integrate Microsoft productivity services at the core of their operations, simply because they have used Windows computers for decades and have longstanding relationships with Microsoft.
“What makes this particularly significant is the criticality of the services affected, especially email and communication systems relied upon by government and other essential organisations,” says Swapneel Patnekar, the CEO of Indian web security firm Shreshta IT Technologies. “The impact goes well beyond the inconvenience of a typical service disruption.”
Many observers pointed out on Thursday and Friday that Microsoft has recently shed staff through attrition, layoffs, and buyout offers. The company’s annual filings say it had 223,000 full-time employees on June 30, down from 228,000 at the same time in 2025. Then in July, the company eliminated 9,000 jobs globally, of which 3,200 were cuts related to an overhaul of its Xbox teams. In October, the company reportedly made buyout offers to 60,000 employees, though apparently this was intended to speed attrition, not cull all of those roles.
Then there’s the AI factor. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said in April that as much as 30 percent of the code the company is generating is now written using AI in automated tools.
“Satya's recent comments have a much different look today than they did even a week ago,” says Jake Williams, a faculty member at IANS, an intelligence and security consultancy. “I don't think we'll ever be able to say that the staff reductions caused this outage, but you'll never convince me that all the tribal knowledge that walked out the door wouldn't have been invaluable in resolving it.”
Microsoft did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Reports of widespread disruption from the Microsoft outage started appearing during the working day on Friday in countries in Asia and Australasia, spreading across the world as more people logged on.
Schools, retail stores, courts, and medical organizations across Australia said everything from exams to health care appointments were disrupted. “Medical scans have been cancelled due to both myself and the clinic not being able to access referrals via email or fax,” one person told Australian media. Officials in Japan’s government said its own platforms had been disrupted, and staff were using phones and chat tools as they couldn’t access Outlook.
In the UK, multiple police forces have said they are unable to accept online crime reports due to the outages of Microsoft services, though phone lines for emergency and nonemergency reports remained available. Parts of the National Health Service, including doctor surgeries and hospital services, also reported that some services were impacted by the outages. “Those who work in 111 and 999 services are unable to refer patients in the normal way—creating a massive backlog,” the GMB trade union posted on X, referring to nonemergency and emergency health services.
Meanwhile, Deutsche Bahn, the provider of train services across Germany, updated its alerts page saying the email outages “severely restricts the sending of timetables.” Courts, local government agencies, and media organizations in the Netherlands reported issues with their communications services, according to local press. In France, some health agencies and local governments also reported similar issues. One winemaker in South Africa told the BBC his company had been brought to a standstill by the outages.
Unsurprisingly, these disruptions continued to be echoed across Canada and the US as millions of people have attempted to sign on. Canadian rail service Via Rail posted online that customers may not receive details of their booked trips via email, with with York’s Department of Investigation posting on X that housing evictions planned for Friday had been canceled and Arapahoe County Sheriff’s Office, in Colorado, also posting on X that a lack of email notifications means bond payments being made online were not being processed.
“It's literally named 365. That implies a specific duty,” says longtime security and compliance consultant Davi Ottenheimer. “Can’t sell an empty bottle called ‘Bottle of Water.’”
During the outage, multiple officials around the world called for countries to rely less on giant tech firms or reevaluate their relationships. “The global Microsoft outage only serves to highlight once again the lack of resilience in the UK’s digital infrastructure, and the dangers that this dependency can pose to our security, economy and public services,” Chi Onwurah, the chair of the UK parliament’s Science and Technology Committee, said in a statement.
Since the start of the second Trump administration—with its chaos, unpredictability, and threats changing the nature of international relationships—countries across Europe and other parts of the world have been starting to change their attitudes and reliance on some US-based big technology firms, such as Google, Microsoft, and Amazon Web Services. Officials in France have been developing local, open source alternatives to Zoom, Teams, and other productivity software, while WIRED has documented dozens of other European efforts to ditch US big tech services.
Patnekar, from Indian security firm Shreshta, says that while much tech infrastructure has been provided by centralized services in recent years, email seems particularly challenging to create resiliency. “Ultimately, the lesson isn't necessarily that organisations should stop relying on large technology providers,” Patnekar says. “Rather, they need to identify which services are genuinely mission-critical and ensure they have an independent fallback when those providers become unavailable.”

The EU’s foreign policy chief has warned against “walking into the traps that Russia is setting” as she said Moscow was trying to start a debate about European security in order to divert attention from its aggression.
“We have one aggressor and one victim, and the aggressor does not have security concerns,” Kaja Kallas said on arrival at an EU leaders’ summit in Dublin. “Nobody has ever attacked them. They have attacked others. I mean, keep the focus, people.”
In talks on the Ukraine war, Russia has revived its hardline demands for a total overhaul of European security – demands that were rejected in 2021 because they were seen as an infringement of the sovereignty of central and eastern European countries. The latest round of talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US was held this week in Abu Dhabi.
Donald Trump’s envoy and son-in-law, Jared Kushner, said on Thursday night that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to expand the next round of peace negotiations to include the Europeans. However, Russia quickly contradicted that assurance.
European leaders have long said they will support Ukraine in any peace talks, but want to see a ceasefire before negotiations. They also stress the continent has an extensive web of security agreements that Russia has violated.
Friedrich Merz, the German chancellor, said: “Russia wants to talk about questions of a European security architecture. We do not need to discuss that; it already exists.” He added that it was a “given” that his country would be part of any European delegation.
The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said it was “self-explanatory that Europe is included in the peace talks to safeguard our interests, but also to support Ukraine”.
The Kremlin said on Friday: “Once we understand [Europe’s] real intentions and their willingness to contribute to the peace process, then we can make a decision on holding talks in an expanded format.” Russia’s lead negotiator in Abu Dhabi, Vladimir Medinsky, said it was “unclear what there is to discuss” with Europe.
The US call to involve Europe in talks has turned the spotlight on who would represent it.
Speaking after a summit of EU leaders in Dublin on Friday, the European Council president António Costa said leaders had agreed on a negotiating team: the EU institutions and E5 countries, namely Britain, France, Germany, Italy and Poland.
“Europe must speak with one clear and united voice in all discussions that shape the future of Ukraine and the security of our continent,” he said. “This is ultimately a team effort.”
The format had already emerged in recent months, but the need to formalise the grouping gained momentum after Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, this week urged his European allies to decide who will represent Europe in negotiations.
Kushner also mocked the absence of a single person to speak for the entire continent. “If Europe could identify one person to speak on their behalf, that would be a bigger achievement than getting the Russians to include them in the negotiations,” he said earlier this week.
But there was an increasingly settled view that Europe would not be represented by a single person, but by different interlocutors from the wider continent. Paris and Berlin had argued for a continued role for their own envoys in the E3 format of Britain, France and Germany, alongside EU representatives. Smaller member states put the emphasis more firmly on the EU representatives: Costa and Kallas, the EU’s high representative for foreign affairs and security policy.
Earlier in the day, Sweden’s prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, said the discussion on who should represent Europe was “slightly overstated” as it had differing interests.
Some of the issues in peace talks were “pure EU interests”, he said, citing financing Kyiv and Ukraine’s future membership in the bloc. He also supported other formats, such as the “pretty uncomplicated” E3 and the “very legitimate” E5, which includes Italy and Poland, as well as a role for EU representatives. He said: “I am quite flexible on that. I think what we actually say is more important than the exact configuration of the people in the room.”
Several at the summit, including Kallas, also pointed to the importance of including the UK, a founder member of the coalition of the willing, a broad group of countries committed to future peacekeeping in Ukraine.
Ireland’s taoiseach, Micheál Martin, said the UK and Norway each had a significant role and “that all has to be taken into consideration because it’s a European, continent-wide issue”.
The British prime minister, Andy Burnham, said it was for the EU to decide who would represent the bloc. He said there was a strong view among European leaders that it was for Europe – in the wider sense – “to decide its own arrangements” on security.

Zelenskyy says a new European security framework floated by US could benefit Putin
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says the U.S. has raised the idea of a new postwar security framework for Europe
KYIV, Ukraine -- Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the United States had raised the possibility of a new security framework for Europe as part of efforts to end Russia’s war in Ukraine, warning that Moscow could use such discussions to weaken NATO and reshape the continent’s borders.
Separately, Ukrainian forces struck a major Russian oil facility supporting Moscow’s war effort, Ukraine's General Staff said in a statement Saturday. Russian
“In my view, this can be dangerous,” Zelenskyy told reporters Friday, referring to the new security framework. “This should not be the main agenda.” His comments were embargoed until Saturday.
He said he believed Moscow was interested in reopening broader questions about European security rather than focusing exclusively on ending the 4 1/2-year war.
“(Russian President Vladimir) Putin’s desire to change borders in Europe is a fact. I am sure this is part of his concept of revising security guarantees in Europe,” he said. “This is dangerous because, in my view, it is precisely things like this that lead to wars or escalations.”
European leaders have stressed that decisions about the continent’s security must be made by Europeans themselves, warning against allowing Russia to dictate the terms of a new security order or negotiate NATO's future.
Zelenskyy said the U.S. had asked for the first time whether Ukraine would withdraw from parts of the Donbas region in eastern Ukraine that Russia does not control if Kyiv were admitted to NATO. He reiterated that Kyiv would not surrender its territory.
Ukraine is discussing a comprehensive security package with its partners that could include specific guarantees from NATO and the European Union, a strong Ukrainian military and financial support for a specified period, he said. It would also include a recovery plan, he said.
“If the American side confirms precisely this to us, together with other NATO partners, then I will ask our Ukrainian society what it thinks: do we accept it or not?” Zelenskyy said.
He stressed that any arrangement would not involve recognizing occupied territories as Russian.
Zelenskyy also rejected the possibility of Ukraine committing to neutrality, saying that would require changing the country’s constitution.
“If Putin expects Ukraine’s neutrality to be enshrined, that’s not going to happen,” he said. “We’re not in NATO right now anyway.”
Ukrainian strikes on the Samara oil pipeline station near the village of Prosvet in Russia’s Samara region Friday set several oil storage tanks on fire, Ukraine's General Staff said.
Moscow has not commented on the strike.
The facility is a key part of the network exporting Russian oil to global markets, the General Staff said. The military also said it struck the Lipetsk-2 airfield in Russia’s Lipetsk region.
Separately, 22 people, including three children, were injured in a Russian attack on the southeastern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia on Friday, Ukraine’s Emergency Service said. The injured include a 6-month-old baby, a 2-year-old girl and a 12-year-old boy.
Zelenskyy warned that broader discussions about Europe’s security could allow Putin to seek changes to NATO’s military presence, including the withdrawal of American troops.
He said Putin had raised similar ideas with then-President Joe Biden in 2021, seeking a redistribution of power in Europe and the world.
“I think Putin will bring up Finland and Sweden. I’m sure he will raise the issue of Hungary and the presence of American troops in the Baltic countries,” Zelenskyy said.
He said any changes to Europe’s security arrangements must be decided by European NATO members only after the war ends.
“The sequence should be as follows: a ceasefire, an end to the war in Ukraine, and security guarantees for Ukraine,” he said. “There can be no security guarantees in Europe, or for Europe, without Ukraine.”
Zelenskyy said Ukraine’s priorities in Abu Dhabi included an energy ceasefire, reopening the Black Sea, prisoner releases and preparations for a leaders’ meeting to end the war.
He said Russian negotiators lacked authority to decide on several issues and Moscow was unwilling to accept an energy ceasefire.
“At the meeting in Abu Dhabi, the Russian delegation said they didn’t have a mandate to decide this issue, but we can also see that they are unwilling,” he said. Negotiators were told to resolve ceasefire questions directly with Putin.
Zelenskyy said talks in Moscow with U.S. negotiators resulted in an agreement to exchange more than 1,000 POWs on each side. The exact number was still being determined, he said, estimating 1,200 to 1,300.
He said Washington supported Ukraine’s demand for European countries to participate directly in future negotiations, rather than remain outside the main negotiating room.
Britain, France, Germany and Italy attended the Abu Dhabi meetings, Zelenskyy said. He expected three to five European representatives at future discussions.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Moscow was open to European participation, adding that it would “help us understand how their stand could help the peace process.” He said Russia would accept any representatives European countries chose to send.
Zelenskyy accused SpaceX of imposing restrictions on its Starshield satellite system in Russian-occupied Ukrainian territory, saying the limitations were hampering efforts to intercept Russian drones.
He said the system’s speed had been restricted to a maximum of 161 kph (100 mph) in occupied areas and that the limitations had been in place for five days.
Zelenskyy questioned the explanation that the problem was technical, saying the restrictions appeared to have been imposed by SpaceX despite previous assurances from U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio that Starshield was more under the control of the U.S. government.
“The current Starshield restrictions suggest that SpaceX imposed them,” Zelenskyy said. “That’s what our team is telling me. So this doesn’t quite line up with what we heard earlier. That’s why we need to get to the bottom of all this.”
He said the restrictions prevented Ukrainian forces from intercepting Russian jet-powered Shahed drones over occupied territory as they approached from the east, forcing them to wait until the drones reached areas where the limitations did not apply.

Popular weight loss drugs including Ozempic and Wegovy will carry a new warning about a possible rare side effect that can sometimes lead to permanent vision loss, U.S. health regulators announced Monday, November 9, 2026.
The Food and Drug Administration said the risk will be added to the labelling of all GLP-1 drugs, the blockbuster medications used to treat obesity, diabetes and several other medical conditions. The class includes a dozen injectable or pill-based drugs, including widely used brands like Zepbound and Mounjaro.
The eye condition, known as non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, can cause significant vision loss. The problem, which has been reported with all GLP-1 drugs, is caused by decreased blood flow to the optic nerve, although the underlying cause isn't understood, the FDA said.
FDA scientists began looking into the problem after the publication of a 2024 medical paper tying the condition to certain patients taking semaglutide, the active drug in Eli Lilly's Ozempic.
An FDA analysis of more than 125 clinical trials found that the problem occurred in roughly 6 of every 100,000 patients who took a GLP-1 for at least one year. The comparable rate for people taking a placebo or other types of glucose-lowering medications was less than 4 per 100,000, the FDA said.
The agency also found reports of the problem in its electronic reporting system for drug injuries and side effects.
Symptoms of the problem include blurred vision, blind spots, distorted colors and other visual disturbances, according to the FDA. Patients experiencing such problems should contact a health care professional immediately, the agency said.
