They Left Iran, but Now the Regime Is Seizing Their Assets to Silence Them
The Iranian authorities are pursuing diaspora dissidents and journalists, extending the government’s repressive apparatus far beyond its borders.
The retired couple in Iran first realized that something was wrong when their bank cards stopped working in early May. After inquiring with the authorities, they discovered that their assets had been frozen by order of the country’s intelligence ministry.
The couple learned, eventually, that they were being punished for the actions of their daughter Noushin Najafiragheb, who lived in Europe — specifically, for her social media posts opposing the Iranian government, according to another daughter, Mehrnoush Najafiragheb.
Across Iran, the government has used asset seizures as punishment for actions taken abroad. Homes and businesses have been seized, life savings raided, family heirlooms taken. When those targeted had little inside Iran themselves, the authorities went after their family members back home, interviews show.
As the Najafiragheb family pressed their case with the authorities, Mehrnoush said, they encountered dozens of other people facing the specter of losing their life’s savings as punishment for the actions of their relatives abroad.
“We realized we weren’t alone,” Ms. Najafiragheb recalled her mother telling her. She said her sister Noushin had declined to be interviewed to avoid further government pressure on her family.

A communication glitch in the network connecting US air traffic control centres brought flights nationwide to a standstill for more than four hours on Friday. Although the grounding order was lifted late in the day, airlines still need a few days to get back on track, with several flights having been diverted during the disruption.
What made the disruption particularly significant was that it was not confined to one airport or a single flight route. The trouble lay in the communication network linking regional air traffic control centres, allowing a problem at one end to ripple across the country.
Michael McCormick, a former airspace manager with the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), described the network as “one of the largest telecommunications systems in the country”.
And when a system of that scale runs into trouble, the impact can travel far beyond the point where the glitch first occurs.
So, what exactly went wrong? How do these regional centres keep aircraft on course across thousands of miles, and how can a glitch in ground-based equipment bring flights in the air to a halt?
Old equipment, too many attempts: What went wrong
Trump administration officials said on Saturday that outdated equipment in the US air traffic control system caused intermittent communication and radar disruptions. 
The resulting ground stop lasted more than four hours on Friday.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said a contractor was replacing a section of old, discontinued copper wiring with new fibre-optic cables at a remote location on Friday afternoon. Similar replacement work has been taking place across the country and across industries for decades.
However, the work coincided with a surge in connection attempts, putting pressure on the system.
“Specifically, we had over 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds,” Duffy said, as cited by AP. “And what that did was gave us issues with our communication with airplanes, and it also caused some disruption with our radar feeds. And when we see that, your safety is paramount, we shut down the airspace.”
With communication and radar feeds facing interruptions, officials decided to ground flights. Aircraft that were already flying when the order came into effect were able to land safely by following established procedures, Duffy said on Friday.
The incident has also brought attention to the ongoing modernisation of the country's air traffic control infrastructure. Congress approved $12.5 billion for the overhaul last year. The work includes replacing miles of old copper wires with fibre-optic lines and gradually upgrading radio systems at airports.
However, the exercise is still incomplete. Duffy urged Congress to allocate more funds for the upgrade during during news conferences on Friday and Saturday.
How US air traffic control works
The FAA operates 22 regional air traffic control centres across the US, AP reported. These centres manage aircraft travelling between departure and arrival airports, particularly those flying at higher altitudes.
According to McCormick, associate professor and programme coordinator in the Department of Applied Aviation Sciences at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University, regional centres generally take control of flights once they cross altitudes of 10,000 feet.
Centres located in places such as Anchorage, Alaska, Houston and Indianapolis form one of three layers involved in guiding aircraft.
The process begins with airport control towers, which direct pilots during take-offs and manage aircraft at more than 500 airports that have towers. As planes move further away, Terminal Radar Approach Control centres take over and guide them. Once aircraft reach higher altitudes, regional air traffic control centres assume responsibility.
The process is reversed when planes descend towards their destinations.
At these regional centres, controllers monitor radar screens and manage aircraft within their assigned airspace. Control is passed from one controller to another as a flight moves between different areas.
Stephen Creamer, president and CEO of the Air Traffic Control Association, a trade group for equipment manufacturers involved with air traffic control, explained how this transfer takes place.
“As you fly, your flight is handed off from one controller to another controller,” he said. “That handoff process is like taking the screen and the aircraft on one screen and making sure it’s on someone else’s screen before you send the communications over to that next controller and have the pilot start talking to them.”
What helps pilots stay connected 
Regional air traffic control centres cannot communicate with aircraft on their own. They need to be connected to remote radio transmitter and receiver sites, which provide radio frequency coverage for communication with pilots.
These sites, in turn, are linked to the control centres through telecommunications networks. Parts of this infrastructure are now being upgraded, with old copper wires being replaced by fibre-optic cables.
The communication works both ways and plays an important role in keeping aircraft at safe distances from one another.
However, the system can face unpredictable disruptions. McCormick said Friday's incident was particularly difficult because it involved what is known as a rolling outage, where the problem can move between different centres rather than remain confined to one location.
“What is especially problematic in this case is that it’s what’s known as a rolling outage,” McCormick said. “In other words, it's unpredictable and it may impact one air traffic control center now and then it gets better and then impacts another air traffic control center.”
The FAA is also moving towards a digital communication system known as controller pilot data link. It allows pilots and controllers to exchange routine clearances, instructions and requests through text-based messages instead of relying only on voice radio.
How one failure disrupts flights miles away
A disruption at one location does not necessarily mean its impact will remain limited to that area. Friday's incident affected the wider communication network, allowing the problem to spread across several regional control centres.
FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford told reporters on Saturday that intermittent frequency instability had affected as many as 17 of the 22 regional air traffic control centres in the US.
R. John Hansman, an aeronautics professor at MIT whose research includes information technology in aviation, said the failure was different from a localised problem because it involved the communication network itself.
“The thing that was unique about this is that it was a type of failure that wasn’t local because it was part of the communication system,” he said. “It propagated around the country.”
A similar disruption occurred in September at Newark Liberty International Airport, where radar communication with aircraft was temporarily lost after railroad construction workers accidentally cut a backup fibre-optic line. The FAA had to cancel hundreds of flights travelling to and from the airport.
However, aviation experts said the Newark incident was different from Friday's nationwide disruption.
The impact of a communication failure can also continue even after the immediate problem is resolved because aircraft operate across multiple routes. A plane scheduled to travel between two cities may have several other journeys lined up afterwards. A delay or diversion on one route can therefore affect its subsequent operations.
Aviation consultant Andrew Charlton said this chain reaction can be particularly significant for long-haul and international flights.
“The aircraft doesn’t just fly from A to B and back to B and then stop,” he said. “It then moves on to C and then over to E and around and around and around. It is, of course, exacerbated if you’re talking about long-haul flights, international flights over the Atlantic or over the Pacific.”
McCormick said the disruption could take days to fully work its way through airline operations, even after the FAA lifted the grounding order late Friday.
How pilots can communicate
Even when regular communication systems face disruptions, pilots have other ways to stay in touch and maintain awareness of aircraft around them.
Aviation experts said many aircraft are equipped with satellite phone systems that can be used for communication. Pilots can also speak directly to other pilots in nearby aircraft through radio.
Hansman said aircraft also carry equipment that helps pilots identify other planes in their vicinity.
There are alternatives for airport control towers as well. If a tower loses its radio communication capabilities, controllers can use high-intensity light beams to send signals to pilots. These signals help alert them about whether it is safe to descend.
Hansman said several backup arrangements are available to help aircraft continue flying safely during communication disruptions.
“We have a number of backup systems that allow the airplanes to fly safely to the extent that air traffic control can still communicate directly with the radio,” he said.

A university that Viktor Orbán tried to chase out of Hungary is open to expanding its presence in Budapest, in a mark of confidence in the country’s democratic future.
Carsten Q Schneider, the interim president and rector of Central European University (CEU), said it was interested in increasing its programmes in Budapest, as long as this did not damage the student experience.
So far the CEU has not held formal talks with Hungary’s new government, which has promised to restore academic freedom, “but our hand is reaching out, their hand is reaching out – it is just that they have many things to do”, the academic told the Guardian.
The CEU relocated its main activities to Vienna from Budapest in 2019, after pressure from the previous government led by Orbán. But the outlook changed when Péter Magyar won a landslide victory in April pledging to root out corruption and reform the state.
The CEU, founded by Hungarian-American financier and philanthropist George Soros in 1991 to entrench democratic change in the region, was forced to cease awarding degrees in Budapest in response to a law widely seen as targeting the institution.
The EU’s highest court struck down Hungary’s “Lex CEU” in 2020, finding that it violated the EU charter of fundamental rights, but the verdict came too late for the university. The CEU retains 312 staff in Budapest, mostly administrative, but the majority, 476, and all its teaching, are in Vienna.
Schneider said upgrading the status of the CEU, which is privately funded, in Budapest would be “a symbol for academic freedom [and] of resilience” but depended on goodwill and funding independent of the Hungarian government. He said a decision on its future in Hungary would be taken by the CEU’s 13-member board, whose members include Soros and his son, Alexander Soros.
“We don’t want special treatment,” Schneider said. ‘“We are a great asset, so let’s work out something.”
But the CEU, which he said was “thriving tremendously” in Vienna, does not plan a wholesale return to Budapest. Any change would have to ensure the quality of the student experience, for instance, assuring that students would be able to combine courses, say in economics and history, without having to travel the 200km-plus distance between the two cities.
Focused on social sciences, law and humanities, the CEU has more than 1,400 students from 103 countries, mostly doing master’s and PhD programmes.
According to Schneider, for the first time in the CEU’s 25-year history, students from the US now make up the largest cohort of master’s students (10%). The CEU has seen an increase in US applicants since Donald Trump returned to the White House and launched a sweeping campaign against elite universities, including slashing federal funding and seeking to exert control over internal policies.
The CEU rector has had informal talks with US academics on how to maintain academic freedom under pressure from rightwing populists. He described his message as: “Don’t be naive for a second. These people have a plan, so it’s not by accident that they attack universities. They want to have cultural hegemony.” He added, however, that Trump and allied movements, such as Germany’s Alternative für Deutschland, have identified “real problems”, such as in the US how universities have entrenched “a reproduction of elites”
When coming under political pressure, he said universities needed “to look for allies”, among other academic institutions, students, alumni and parents. Institutions also had to stand up for disciplines under attack, such as gender studies, Schneider added.
He recalled the outpouring of support for CEU – when tens of thousands of people protested in Budapest in defence of the university – as “one of the most humbling experiences I have had”.
Schneider, a German political scientist who specialises in the study of democracies and regime transition, said Magyar had successfully used Orbán’s political machine against him.
“Nobody has a better idea than [Magyar] how to defeat the most potent and the most skilled illiberal populist [Orbán]. So he knows something.” He added: “The people and skills that you need to bring a non-democratic regime down are not the same and sometimes the opposite of what it takes to establish a democracy. So the question now is whether he [Magyar] has the skills to basically reinvent liberal democracy for the 21st century.”
Schneider said Hungary could be the world’s first “post-illiberal democracy” – a model for democratic restoration, just as Orbán inspired rightwing populists around the world. But he also raised doubts about this thesis, saying there were questions about how Magyar and his Tisza party might develop in the context of Hungary’s “very difficult economic situation”.
The test would be, he suggested, when Magyar faces losing support and, eventually, defeat at the ballot box. “So what happens when he loses support and then cracks in his movement appear? Will he be the visionary leader who manages … to establish a three, four, five-party system, where people compete? That is to be seen.”

Mirra Andreeva defeated Jessica Pegula 6-3, 6-4 to reach the title match of the WTA Finals on Saturday, becoming the first teenager to do so since 2004.
The 19-year-old Russian will meet Elina Svitolina of Ukraine in Sunday’s final. Svitolina raced past Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova 6-2, 6-1 in the other semifinal. Andreeva has a 2-1 career record against Svitolina.
Andreeva has yet to drop a set at the $10 million, season-ending event. She lost just 11 games while going 3-0 in her round-robin matches, the fewest of any player since 2003.
Andreeva improved to 4-5 against Top 10 players this year, including wins over No. 2 Aryna Sabalenka, No. 6 Svitolina and No. 5 Pegula in the Southern California desert. She beat Svitolina 6-4, 6-0 in round-robin play earlier in the week.
Pegula broke Andreeva to take a 3-1 lead in the second set, but dropped five of the final six games to end her fifth consecutive Finals appearance. She lost in the 2023 final and was a losing semifinalist last year, too.
It was the first career meeting between Andreeva and Pegula, who was caught on a hot mic during a practice session at Indian Wells Tennis Garden referring to the teenager as a “diva” who “needs to be humbled.”
“The storyline writes itself,” Pegula said before the match. “I guess we had to play each other.”
Pegula said she later apologised to Andreeva.
“I think we’ve all seen that Mirra has a pretty good sense of humour with everything,” Pegula said. “She said she embraces it, so it was kind of funny. I was like, maybe I need a little bit more of that in myself on the court. We’re all good.”
Andreeva, who won her first Grand Slam title at the French Open in May, ensured she’ll clinch a career-high, year-end No. 2 world ranking with the win, keeping Pegula from doing so.
Fellow Russian Maria Sharapova was 17 when she reached the championship match of the 2004 Finals and beat Serena Williams in three sets.

The US government has expanded the use of an AI tool for advising air traffic controllers to assist in managing air traffic across the entire national airspace system. Airline executives have voiced support for the rollout, but the US labor union representing air traffic controllers has said it was not involved in designing or testing the AI-driven system.
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) says the $875 million SMART system has helped reroute 180 flights since being implemented in airspace over Washington, DC, on September 21. The agency claims that this saved an average of 10 minutes per flight and almost 80 gallons of fuel per flight—and it is apparently hoping such results can be replicated nationwide through the expanded deployment.
“After a successful initial rollout to the National Capital Region in September, the FAA will now use SMART in the airspace of all 22 centers across the country to reduce delays, reduce fuel consumption and improve the travel experience for the flying public,” according to the agency statement posted on November 10.
The FAA fact sheet describes SMART as a cloud-based system that combines information about “weather patterns, flight paths, traffic flow and controller staffing metrics” to predict air traffic patterns. It is designed to make scheduling recommendations, identify optimal flight routes, and determine the best order of arrivals for aircraft.
However, a human team of FAA specialists based in DC is ultimately responsible for validating the SMART system recommendations before passing them along to air traffic control facilities across the country, according to the agency.

WHO, the United Nations Foundation and Illumination have partnered to launch a Public Service Announcement (PSA) that reinforces safe and healthy practices during these challenging times, featuring Illumination’s globally beloved Gru and the Minions. The PSA focuses on lifesaving behaviors to help mitigate the impacts of COVID-19, including physical distancing, being active at home and remaining kind to each other —all aimed at making sure people of all ages stay safe and healthy during this pandemic.
“At this challenging time, we must find all ways possible to provide hope to people while sharing advice that can protect our health,” said Dr. Tedros Adhanom, Director-General of the World Health Organization. “WHO is excited to be working with Illumination and Steve Carell and the joys of the Minions and Gru to promote the importance of physical distancing, keeping active and connected, and being kind and compassionate to overcome COVID-19.”
The PSA is voiced by Academy Award® and Emmy Award® nominee Steve Carrell, who voices the character Gru in the Despicable Me franchise. The PSA will be localized into multiple languages including Spanish, French, Portuguese and Arabic, among others.
“Storytelling is a powerful tool to accelerate positive social change in the world. It is an honor to partner with the WHO and UN Foundation to remind people around the globe to protect themselves, each other and our communities during this pandemic. I am also appreciative to Participant for helping to organize the collaboration and to my partners at Comcast/NBCU for helping to amplify this important message,” said Illumination Founder and CEO Chris Meledandri.
Illumination is the first Hollywood Studio to partner with WHO, the UN Foundation and the COVID-19 Solidarity Response Fund to create an entertaining and educational PSA for global audiences. Participant helped facilitate the collaboration between Illumination to the United Nations Foundation and the World Health Organization.
"As the world continues to grapple with the challenges of COVID-19, one of our most powerful weapons is kindness," said Elizabeth Cousens, President & CEO of the United Nations Foundation. "We are delighted that the Despicable Me characters are letting their love show and showing ways to keep themselves and their communities safe during this unprecedented time."

The ringing bell had the same effect as a break horn blowing in an industrial factory. Doors would slowly open along the corridor, and disheveled bodies stumbled out. At our house, 6:30 p.m. was dinner time. I can't remember when the bell was introduced, but it proved the most effective way to call five young teenagers down to the kitchen to eat.
Despite regularly being called the Brady Bunch when out in public (particularly when in a line on moving escalators), five kids is actually quite a convenient number. Five weekdays were perfect for each person to have an allocated day for duties: to cook, to walk the dog, even to sit in the front seat of the car (an honor every teenager in the early 00s fought for).
I'm the youngest, and so my day was Friday, which was a clear injustice because I was convinced I had to wait longer than everyone else.
We all had a job to do
Five children and two adults meant eating dinner was "feeding time at the zoo," according to my dad. Yes, there was a one-serving-only policy in place, and messy plates were inevitable, but once we finished eating, we became a well-oiled machine. Someone collected the dirty dishes, someone washed up, someone dried, someone put items away, and someone cleaned the table.
I remember an adult family friend joining us for dinner one evening, their eyes widening as we all stood in sync to start our jobs, rolled up our sleeves, and discussed the unfair compensation.
We'd mumble that one day we'd form a union.
Birthdays had a similar efficiency. In the morning, the person celebrating would have breakfast, then wait patiently in the lounge while we all mysteriously disappeared upstairs. In hushed tones, resentful about the gifts we weren't getting, a parent would hand each of us a present to carry. We'd then queue up in age order and slowly descend the stairs singing happy birthday in different pitches, the person in the lounge overacting their surprise as we finally came into view.
Christmas was another meticulous affair. We'd watch as a parent burrowed through piles of presents, handing each of us one and instructing us not to open it until everyone had theirs. We'd then unwrap our assigned gifts one by one in front of the family, acknowledging who they were from and muttering well-rehearsed "thank yous". The rounds were strategically ordered so the "main" gift would be handed over last, and so, throughout the event, we kids would keep one eye on the remaining presents, processing by elimination to see if what was left could be what we'd asked for.
There were processes and workflows
We were a family, but we were also an organization. The sheer mass of us turned basic processes into workflows. If I'd been born today, I think my parents may have developed data-tracking tools and KPIs to report to board members (my grandparents) to optimize family dynamics and returns.
My dad once told me a story about when he took us five children for a dog walk with his friend. Two of us were in the stroller, one was walking beside him, and each adult had a child strapped to their front. A golden retriever and cocker spaniel floated through the crowd of bodies. Two people passed them in the street and my dad overheard one whisper to the other "They even had dogs".
I loved the comedy our family attracted; it was like starring in a sitcom. Things that seemed mundanely routine to us always amused outsiders. The ordeal of buying clothes got particular interest. We'd be taken into town, given a budget, a time limit, and pen and paper, and we'd be set free to go to the shops. When we found an item we liked, we'd have to write down what it was and how much it cost. When our time was up, we'd rush back to the meeting spot and have to present our cases to the bank of Dad.
Having such a big family felt like being both anonymous and constantly noticed. Our internal structures made the busyness of life smoother, if you complied with them. Being out in public felt exposing: we suddenly weren't a well-oiled machine but a large, disruptive force interrupting paths and restaurants. Our chaos was more real when we were off shift in the real world.
It took a while to appreciate the ways our big family moved — I assumed other families were more fun and had more space. But as an adult, I miss the proximity those systems gave us. We were colleagues, teammates, and citizens of a (not-so-little) island nation, constantly striving for a decent GDP and a sense of peace.
I definitely had my protests and times of exile, but ultimately, I learned to share; I developed an idea of fairness; I had to be patient; and I got really good at drying the china.

Japanese police arrested a U.S. Air Force captain Saturday on suspicion of drunk driving in Okinawa, a police spokesman said, in the latest twist to strains between the Pacific allies.
The arrest comes just a week after Tokyo and Washington agreed to measures aimed at preventing crimes by U.S. service members on the island of Okinawa after a murder allegedly involving an American marine triggered outrage.
The U.S. military has around 54,000 personnel stationed in Japan, mostly on Okinawa. Crimes committed by its members have been a thorn in relations between the close security allies.
U.S. officials also said last week they would extend a curfew to lower-ranking service members through Dec. 7, while banning all service members from drinking alcohol outside their homes between midnight and 5 am.
Police arrested the 27-year-old as he “was driving on a road in Okinawa City at around 3:09 am Saturday,” a spokesman for Okinawa prefectural police said.
“It is not clear if he violated the curfew” imposed by U.S. officials, he said.
The arrested captain was assigned to Kadena Air Base on Okinawa, Kyodo News reported.
Officials at the base were not immediately available for comment.

Srinagar- Families of the two Special Police Officers (SPOs) killed by terrorists in Jammu and Kashmir’s Kishtwar district have demanded a Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) probe into the killings, alleging security lapses and seeking immediate strengthening of security arrangements in the remote Kiyar village.
The killings have reopened old wounds in Kiyar, where at least 10 residents were killed in terrorist attacks between 2000 and 2004. The latest incident has revived memories of the August 2000 massacre, in which eight villagers were gunned down, followed by two more killings in 2004.
SPOs Babi Chand (57) and Rashpal Kumar (45), both residents of Kiyar, were found dead in the Dachhan forest early Thursday, a day after they went missing while travelling towards a security post at Basnand in adjoining Marwah tehsil.
The two were allegedly killed between Deharna and Kiyar villages at an altitude of nearly 8,860 feet. Their service weapons, an INSAS rifle and a .303 rifle, along with magazines and ammunition, were missing and are suspected to have been taken by the attackers.
Empty cartridges of Pakistan-origin armour-piercing ammunition were also recovered from the scene.
For the bereaved families, the killings are not isolated incidents but part of a history of violence that they allege was never properly investigated.
“One (of the victims) was my brother, the other was my nephew. We have lost loved ones, but nobody is listening to us. Two of our people were assigned duty in a far-flung area. We believe something is amiss. Why were they assigned duty outside their jurisdiction when security posts already exist in that area?” Ramesh Kumar, brother of slain SPO Babi Chand, told Hindustan Times.
He demanded a CBI investigation into the latest killings as well as previous attacks, alleging that the security infrastructure in the region had weakened over the years.
Kumar claimed that around 45 security posts had been established in the region following the August 2000 massacre, but only four personnel were presently guarding their hamlet, leaving residents vulnerable.
Pawan Kumar, grandson of Ramesh Kumar, also called for an urgent review of security deployment in Dachhan and adjoining areas.
“Why were our men sent away from here when security posts already exist in Marwah? This is Dachhan, and the security of our villages should have been the priority. We want Lt Governor Manoj Sinha to intervene and order a CBI probe into the killings. A thorough investigation is necessary to establish what happened and why,” he said.
The families also expressed dissatisfaction over what they described as negligence by senior police officials following the killings. They alleged that no senior officer had visited them and that the deceased had not been accorded due honour.
They urged the Lieutenant Governor to intervene and ensure restoration of security infrastructure, adequate deployment of personnel, effective intelligence gathering and regular security reviews to prevent further attacks on vulnerable villages.
Kiyar, a predominantly Hindu hamlet located in remote Dachhan tehsil, lies at an average elevation of around 9,460 feet and has poor mobile network connectivity. The region also lacks direct all-weather road connectivity, making access difficult, particularly during adverse weather conditions.
Deharna, where the killings are believed to have taken place, is situated around 14 km from the Marwah tehsil headquarters and 30 to 50 km from Kishtwar town.
Meanwhile, Kishtwar Deputy Commissioner Pankaj Kumar Sharma, who camped in the village, attended the last rites of the deceased on Friday evening along with senior BJP leaders, including Leader of Opposition in the Jammu and Kashmir Assembly Sunil Sharma and Kishtwar MLA Shagun Parihar.
The Deputy Commissioner assured the bereaved families of all possible assistance. He said cases for compassionate appointment of eligible dependent family members under the Jammu and Kashmir Rehabilitation Assistance Scheme, along with compensation admissible under applicable rules, would be taken up and processed on the recommendations of police and competent authorities.
He also assured villagers that issues concerning road connectivity, mobile network coverage and other developmental requirements of Kiyar would be assessed by the concerned departments and taken up on priority.
BJP MLA Shagun Parihar also raised concerns over the security situation, claiming that threats had been issued to the deceased. She questioned the pattern of selective killings and called for a thorough investigation into the incident, besides action against those providing support to terrorists.

'We can't let them down' — After midterm wins, Democrats turn to charting path ahead
DENVER — Democrats descended on Denver for a two-day conference that was half victory party, half sober look at the road ahead on delivering for the voters who elected them.
The "What's Next" conference, hosted by the group Majority Democrats, was scheduled long before Democrats outperformed expectations with their best electoral performance since Watergate. It brought together rising stars — like incoming Gov. Rob Sand in Iowa and Sen.-elect James Talarico in Texas — along with strategists, organizers, state and federal lawmakers and potential presidential contenders.
Held at a concert hall, with colorful artwork of party heavy hitters dotting the venue, Democrats attended sessions like "What Voters Want" and "What Needs To Change." The overwhelming emphasis from speakers was that Democrats have to earn back trust.
"We won races in places where we haven't won in a long time, even in some places where we've never won. And the message shouldn't be that [voters] are fully embracing the Democratic Party," said Colorado Rep. Jason Crow in an interview.
"It took us decades to dig ourselves in a hole and to push people away from us, and it's going to take us more than one cycle to earn that trust," said Crow, who is one of the party's recruitment co-chairs.
A party on probation
Anderson Clayton, chair of the North Carolina Democratic Party, took the party to task for not investing more in the South and in Black voters.
"When we say that Black voters are the base of our party, then I ask why are we not investing in a region of the country that on Tuesday night just proved everybody wrong of what is possible," said Clayton to much applause. "Rural America deserves the investment from the Democratic Party and we must run towards communities that our party has run away from."
Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg said Democrats shouldn't rest on their laurels.
"I think we are adequately politically traumatized by the last few cycles, so that we will not draw the wrong lessons from all of this," Buttigieg said. "Because here's the thing: it is yet to be written whether what we just experienced is one more oscillation from one side to the other and back, or whether it is the beginning of a tectonic movement changing American politics."
He said Democrats can learn from the current White House on two fronts, by having: "a bias towards action and a readiness to get things done coming out of the gate and at the very same time a readiness to plan for the long-term," adding Democrats should come out of the gate strong, with a rapid-fire series of bills to lower the cost of living.
Presumptive next Speaker of the House Hakeem Jeffries told the audience he has plans to do just that, with a robust agenda that includes reversing Medicaid cuts, banning congressional stock trading and mid-decade redistricting, establishing a statutory right to abortion, and overturning the Supreme Court's Citizens United decision that did away with limits on political spending by corporations and unions.
The conference itself was peppered with potential presidential contenders, including Buttigieg, New Jersey Sen. Cory Booker, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, Arizona Sen. Ruben Gallego, and California Rep. Ro Khanna, one of the few progressive speakers.
No one announced an official run, but many gave previews of their theory of the case.
"I do think it's important that whoever we hire to be the chief executive of this country knows how to run something, knows how to get stuff done, knows how to not just have a vision but knows how to deliver on it," Shapiro told reporters.
Someone who was previously kicking the tires for a possible White House bid — Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen — told reporters he's no longer considering it, as he instead pursues the top leadership post in the Senate.
Should Democrats work with Trump?
Throughout the conference, Democrats debated whether and how to work with the Trump administration in order to deliver meaningful change for voters.
"If slapping Trump's name on it and putting it in gold letters would get it through — hell yes, I would do that," said Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin.
Talarico agrees.
"The American people cannot wait two years for change, so we must work with President Trump," Talarico said. "We should make the final two years of his presidency the most productive of any American presidency."
But New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill added a note of caution, describing the president as a bad faith actor.
"The art of the deal to Trump is he figures out what you want, he leverages the you know what out of you, and keeps taking, taking, taking, and never delivers," Sherrill said. "My advice to Sen. Talarico is if Trump wants to work with us, we will lay out the agenda, and he can sign it."

The Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) on Tuesday (November 10, 2026) indicated that it was considering steps to capture peak levels of particulate matter (PM), a major pollutant, that exceed the existing monitoring range, after air quality data from several government monitoring stations in Delhi went missing for hours during the pollution spike following Deepavali on Sunday.
The Hindu reported on Monday (November 9, 2026) that the data gaps had led to an artificially lower official air quality index (AQI), making air quality appear better than it actually was, according to experts.
In a statement on Tuesday (November 10, 2026) , the CPCB said PM levels were measured only up to 1,000 micrograms per cubic metre (µg/m³) for AQI calculations, which explained the missing data on Deepavali night, when actual concentrations exceeded this limit.
“The PM analysers deployed at the time of introduction of the NAQI (National Air Quality Index) [in 2015] were calibrated for a measurement range of 0-1,000 µg/m³. Accordingly, consistent with this, the designed system of automated data validation treats hourly readings beyond the calibrated range as outside range, and such readings are not used in the computation,” the CPCB statement read.
“During extreme episodes, which are occasional, like Diwali firecracker bursting, this may appear as a data gap at the particular station concerned, and those hours do not contribute to the 24-hour average of the relevant pollutant for the concerned station,” the statement added.
Deliberations under way
The CPCB said internal deliberations and consultations on processing data “beyond system design range” were under way.
The CPCB also said spikes in ambient pollutant concentrations, such as those caused by firecrackers bursting, are episodic and short-lived. “The NAQI recognises that prolonged exposure, rather than a momentary reading, is a more relevant indicator of ill effects on human health,” the statement read.
Under the AQI calculation methodology adopted by the CPCB in 2015, the overall index is based on eight parameters and is calculated only if data are available for a minimum of three pollutants, out of which one should necessarily be either PM2.5 or PM10.
“The methodology was formed in 2015 and at that time it was decided that the accuracy was good only up to 1,000 µg/m³ and both PM2.5 and PM10 were capped at it for calculation of AQI. But the equipment got better with time and Delhi’s air quality analysers and instruments were also updated, but the methodology was never updated after that,” an official told The Hindu.
“But now there are discussions of raising this cap so that peak values above 1,000 µg/m³ could be measured,” the official added.
Of the 59 air quality monitoring stations in Delhi, 46 are operated by the Delhi government’s Delhi Pollution Control Committee (DPCC), which does not calculate the AQI. The DPCC had recorded PM2.5 and PM10 levels exceeding 1,000 µg/m³ on Deepavali night, though several readings were initially missing.
The CPCB uses data from these 46 stations, along with readings from other monitoring stations, to calculate the AQI.
Air quality improves
Meanwhile, Delhi’s air quality improved to the ‘poor’ category on Tuesday (November 10, 2026), with the 24-hour average AQI recorded at 299, just below the ‘very poor’ threshold of 300.
Experts attributed the improvement to increased wind speeds and said air quality was likely to improve further over the next few days.

Indonesia's VP resigns as his eligibility and academic credentials are questioned
JAKARTA, Indonesia — Indonesia's vice president resigned on Thursday as questions grew over his eligibility for the office after recent court rulings disputed his educational credentials.
Gibran Rakabuming Raka, the 39-year-old son of former President Joko Widodo, submitted his resignation to the leadership of the People's Consultative Assembly, the country's highest legislative body, at the parliament building in the capital, Jakarta.
Raka didn't comment as he left the meeting.
"There will always be political dynamics in public office, that's normal," his father, Widodo, told reporters from his hometown in Solo, adding that he had reminded his son that political positions are temporary.
"We will continue to support President Prabowo's government, especially programs that serve the interests of the broader public," he said, referring to Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto.
The academic credentials investigation was apparently not related to investigations into allegations that top police officials had been involved in wiretapping targeting the president.
Prabowo accepts Raka's resignation
Raka had offered to resign Tuesday during a meeting with Prabowo, saying he wanted to avoid a prolonged political controversy. He personally delivered his resignation letter to the president on Wednesday.
Prabowo addressed the nation Thursday afternoon after holding a meeting with Raka and the parliamentary leadership at the presidential palace.
Flanked by Raka and top leaders of parliament, a grim-looking Prabowo said that he accepted Raka's resignation "with a heavy heart" and praised the vice president for showing "courage, responsibility and statesmanship" by stepping down.
"He chose to resign for the greater interest of the nation, the state and the Indonesian people," Prabowo said in a televised statement. "He has been a great help to me, from our election campaign through the past two years of government. Many of our achievements would not have been possible without his contribution."
Prabowo praised Raka's dedication and hard work, highlighting Raka's visits to 35 provinces and 149 regencies and cities to inspect 303 government projects during the past two years as examples of his commitment to public service.
"I will continue to support him, and I pray that he and his family are given strength during what is undoubtedly a difficult time," Prabowo said.
Under the Indonesian Constitution, a vice presidential vacancy doesn't trigger a new election. The office remains vacant until the People's Consultative Assembly elects a replacement from two candidates nominated by the president within 60 days.
Long-running allegations over candidacy lead to court disputes
The Constitutional Court and the Supreme Court ruled last month that the documents that Raka submitted regarding his overseas education didn't meet election requirements.
A subsequent petition, submitted Wednesday to the House leadership by 120 lawmakers from eight political parties, began a parliamentary process that could have led to his impeachment.
The push for his impeachment was driven largely by long-running allegations that Raka's candidacy was enabled by a Constitutional Court ruling that critics see as a conflict of interest and evidence of weak political accountability and dynastic privilege.
Before Prabowo chose him as his running mate for the 2024 election, Raka didn't meet the age requirement of 40 for vice presidential candidates. But the court's contentious ruling in October 2023 carved an exception allowing those who served or had been elected as regional leaders to run at a younger age.
Under Indonesian election law, a presidential or vice-presidential candidate must have completed senior high school or an equivalent level of education. Because Raka completed his secondary education overseas, he was required to provide documents showing that his qualifications were equivalent to an Indonesian high school diploma.
Raka was the first vice president of the country to resign before the end of a term since the fall of dictator Suharto and the start of Indonesia's democratic reforms in 1998.
Parliamentary leaders were due to convene immediately to begin the process of selecting a replacement, Speaker Ahmad Muzani said.
"We ask for the prayers and support of all Indonesians so that this democratic process can proceed smoothly and serve as a constructive new precedent in our constitutional system," Muzani told reporters.

For three months, Suraj Kumar’s job was to feed discarded clothes into shredding machines in Panipat, an industrial city in the north Indian state of Haryana. Clothes discarded in the US, Canada and Europe arrive in the city to be torn back into fibres and spun into yarn, feeding a textile recycling industry that supplies markets across the world.
Suraj, 19, had travelled from West Bengal state to work in Panipat’s factories, following his cousins and friends who had already found jobs there. He hoped to earn enough to send money home to his parents. But in late August, an electrical short circuit in the machine propelled him into the shredding mechanism. The accident crushed both arms.
“I wish I had died rather than lost both my arms,” Suraj says. An only child, he had hoped his job in Panipat would support his parents. Instead, he fears he has become a financial burden on them. The work he had taken up to help his family has left him dependent on others, with no certainty about what his future will look like.
By some estimates, Panipat processes more than 1m tons of used clothing from across the world every year, making it one of the world’s largest textile recycling hubs. In the city’s 20,000 factories, employing about 300,000 people, discarded clothes are shredded into yarn and made into finished products, including home furnishings for brands such as H&M Home, Ikea, Primark, Tesco and Walmart.
But the fast-fashion industry, built on buying more and more clothes and wearing them less, carries a devastating cost for workers tackling its waste. Ramesh Chaudhary, an environmental activist who has worked in Panipat’s labour department, has been tracking reports of injuries and amputations across the city for the past five years. He estimates that at least one worker a day loses a limb, rising to as many as five on some days.
“Every day, we come across cases of workers injured inside factories, sometimes losing a hand or a leg, and sometimes even dying,” Chaudhary says. He gathers his information through a network of labour contractors who supply workers to factories across Panipat. But not all news of injuries reaches him, he says, suggesting the scale of the problem could be greater.
Between 17 and 24 August this year, the Guardian monitored reports from 11 private hospitals and two government hospitals in Panipat. In that period, six cases of textile workers with severe limb injuries were reported: two had lost an arm, another man lost both, one lost a hand, one lost a leg and the sixth their fingers.
Such injuries are common in Panipat’s factories, says Chaudhary, because machinery often lacks the necessary safety mechanisms. If a worker gets caught in a spinning machine, he says, cutting the power may not stop it immediately. By the time the machine comes to a halt, a worker may already have catastrophic injuries.
During numerous visits to spinning units and factories, the Guardian did not see anyone wearing any kind of safety gear. None of the workers interviewed reported having safety training.
India’s 1948 Factories Act places a duty on factory owners to protect workers’ health and safety. It requires serious workplace accidents to be reported to the authorities. But the effectiveness of safety oversight remains a concern, says Sandeep Sachdeva, co-founder of the Safe in India Foundation, which works to reduce industrial injuries.
“Factories are often audited by buyers, especially where quality and critical components are involved, and inspected by government industrial safety and health departments. Buyer audits tend to focus more on commercial requirements and product quality than on workplace safety or working conditions,” he says.
“Government inspections are selected through a central software system, but inspectors are now required to inform factories before visiting. Their role is now that of a facilitator-cum-inspector – a shift that undermines the effectiveness of inspections, particularly in factories with unsafe working conditions.”
For workers, losing a limb means losing their livelihood. Ramashankar Singh, who is in his fifties, from Chapra in Bihar, spent 18 years in Panipat’s factories before an accident last year led to him having a leg amputated.
It happened when a hot ball bearing fell on his foot. Ramashankar’s injury was first just wrapped in discarded cloth, before the factory owner sent him to a pharmacy.
The wound worsened as the infection spread. When Ramashankar approached his employer again, the owner agreed to arrange treatment and admitted him to a private hospital. By then, the infection had progressed so far that doctors had to amputate his leg above the knee.
“The factory owner said he would give me another job, possibly as a cook or a security guard at the factory,” Ramashankar says. “But that never happened.” The owner also said he would help him secure a government disability pension, but he has received no pension since the accident and relies on a prosthetic leg provided by a charitable organisation.
After so much of his life spent in a factory, Ramashankar says: “I have almost forgotten how to live without work. Much of my day now passes lying on my bed, staring at the ceiling fan.”
He also struggles with guilt that he has become a burden on his family.
India’s textile industry is the country’s second-largest source of employment after agriculture, directly employing more than 45 million people. An estimated 92% of its workforce is informally employed. In Panipat, more than 90% of workers are employed informally, says Ina Bahuguna, programme manager at the Estonia-based Reverse Resources, which monitors the city’s textile waste.
“Formal employment contracts and the social security benefits that accompany them, including pensions, are largely limited to workers in management, clerical roles and some specialised jobs, such as tailoring,” says Bahuguna.
Most workers on the factory floor lack these protections, leaving those who suffer serious injuries particularly vulnerable. Without formal employment or adequate social security coverage, they are left without employer-backed compensation, rehabilitation support or a source of income.
The Guardian asked several factory owners why they hired workers on a contractual or piece-rate basis rather than in permanent positions, and most cited the workers’ seasonal migration, saying some did not return to Panipat after travelling home.
For workers who sustain life-changing injuries, getting employers to pay for medical treatment can be a struggle. Indrapal Singh, who lost his arm in 2017, had worked in Panipat for 15 years, two and a half of those at the factory where he was injured. His hand was caught in a Chinese-made carding machine, which tore away the skin. He was given a painkilling injection but, as the infection worsened, his arm had to be amputated. The factory owner refused to pay his hospital bills.
Indrapal spent six years fighting his case through the courts, but says he received no compensation. The police told him that he had signed documents withdrawing his complaint, something Indrapal, who says he cannot read or write, disputes.
“I lost my arm, fought for six years, and in the end, all I got was a government pension of 5,700 rupees [£45]. The factory owner has faced no consequences, and the factory continues to operate as before,” he says.
Chaudhary says: “Workers have very little bargaining power when they are up against factory owners who are not only financially powerful but sometimes politically influential too. For many workers, taking them on in a legal fight is simply not an option.”
Arvind Kumar, the officer in charge at one of Panipat’s 12 police stations, says three workplace injury cases have been registered at his station so far this year. One involved the death of a worker. “Fewer than 1% of workplace injury cases reach the police and are formally registered,” he says.
Most cases, the officer says, are settled outside the formal legal system. Workers may receive a one-time payment towards medical bills, but then are generally left to manage the long-term consequences of their injuries on their own. The police rarely get involved.
For now, Suraj Kumar’’s family are grateful that the factory owner covered his hospital bills. They are not sure whether to register a police complaint.
“He [the owner] is like God to us. He is paying for our boy’s treatment,” says his mother, Sita.
Suraj struggles to imagine what comes next. “I thought that if I worked hard for two years, I could buy myself a motorcycle. I had so many things I wanted to do with my life. I never thought I would have to start by figuring out how to live without my arms.”

South Africa's ANC records worst-ever results in local elections
- Published
South Africa's ANC has recorded its worst-ever showing in local elections since Nelson Mandela led the country out of apartheid and into democracy more than 30 years ago, a result the party has called "catastrophic".
While it won the most votes of all parties in the country, the African National Congress won 30.76% of the overall vote, one third down from the 46% it gained in 2021, and a far cry from the 64.82% 20 years ago.
The story of its decline is also clear in the provinces and cities. The party won a majority in just one of the country's nine provinces, Limpopo. In 2021 it won six. It also won the most votes in just two of the eight cities, compared with six at the last local elections.
The Democratic Alliance (DA) came second in the overall vote with 24.64%, retaining majority control of the city of Cape Town. Former president Jacob Zuma's MK party came third overall with 9.76%, unseating the ANC as winner in the city of Durban, while the Economic Freedom Fighters (EFF), led by Julius Malema, once seen as a serious challenge to the ANC, came fourth with 6.22%.
"This has been a very catastrophic outcome for the ANC," said secretary-general Fikile Mbalula on Saturday. "We knew this disaster is coming, we're staring at it. As we got into elections, the cost of living of our people was too high. The middle class have turned on the ANC in big numbers."
Entering the count centre tonight, South Africa's president and leader of the ANC Cyril Ramaphosa said: "We accept the will of the people however concerning it might be, we accept that this is how the people of South Africa in our towns, in our cities, in our metros have spoken - and this is their verdict, we accept it with humility. It is a decline that is concerning, that is how I characterise it."
It's a continuing decline for the ANC, which lost majority rule in the national elections in 2024 for the first time in its history. It then had to form a coalition government with a raft of other parties in what is now known as the GNU, or government of national unity.
While the Democratic Alliance made significant gains in the cities in these local elections, its overall vote share rose marginally from 21.83% in 2021, and was below the 26.9% it gained in 2016.
Voter turnout was 52.29%, an increase from 45.9% in 2021, when elections were held during the Covid pandemic.
"This election is delivering a devastating message to the ANC", said political analyst Susan Booysen. "It's an ANC in decline at local municipal level, at the metropolitan level, and when the results are reflected provincially and nationally, we see severe declines in ANC levels of support all around."
The reason for that decline in support is largely due to poor service delivery and infrastructure across the country, from water and power to sanitation. "These are huge problems," says Booysen, "and have really been affecting the lives of ordinary people, in the suburbs, in the townships, and in very dramatic ways."
The big picture looks even more bleak for the ANC. The party will elect a new leader next year as Cyril Ramaphosa comes to end of his term. He is due to stay on as president of the country until the next national elections in 2029, but there are few candidates lined up to succeed him in either role.
- ANC under pressure to reverse South Africa decline 
  - Published4 days ago
"It is sort of the end of the liberation movement era in South Africa," said political analyst William Gumede, "and the dominance of the liberation movement since the end of apartheid. So the ANC is going to be a party that by 2029 could be the second biggest rather than the biggest party. It may actually spiral into a long period of just total infighting. This is a new era for South Africa's politics and also the ANC."
The elections also saw a significant shift in voting patterns, with the DA, traditionally known as the "white party" for attracting a largely white vote, gaining more black votes. "We're moving towards a post-racial voting pattern in South Africa," added Gumede.
South Africa now faces days of local coalition building, with the three metropolitan municipalities in the province of Gauteng, the country's powerhouse, under particular scrutiny. The ANC may even find itself shut out in the cities of Johannesburg and Pretoria.
"We are now in a coalition country," said Gumede. "Essentially, what the voters are saying is, "Well, the ANC has dominated the last three decades, they didn't use their power to change the society for the good, so we don't want the dominant parties anymore, whether at national level, provincial level, or rather now at a local level. We actually want coalitions. We want people to work together."
Parties now have 14 days from the moment results were announced to negotiate coalitions.

On Veterans Day, a video (archived) circulated online that social media users claimed authentically showed a U.S. Army sentinel guarding the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier reprimanding U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth and his group after someone talked and laughed while taking photos at the monument.
One X user who shared the clip wrote, "Pete Hegseth and his group were loudly reprimanded for laughing while visiting the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier"
Pete Hegseth and his group were loudly reprimanded for laughing while visiting the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier https://t.co/mKZzmTQa0L https://t.co/DZUT7MpTRp
— philip lewis (@Phil_Lewis_) November 11, 2026
Claims about what the clip showed also circulated on Facebook and Instagram (archived, archived). Snopes readers also contacted us about the video.
The video was authentic and showed a real event on Nov. 11. CNN posted the video on its YouTube channel. There was no indication the footage had been created or edited using artificial intelligence. Therefore, we rate this claim true.
The Department of Defense's Assistant to the Secretary of War for Public Affairs and Senior Advisor Sean Parnell told Snopes in a written statement:
The Secretary and the entire Department have always honored—and will always honor—the sacrifices our military men and women have made to keep America safe. While commemorating this solemn day, a soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum.
In the video, Hegseth and four others posed on the steps in front of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, a monument in Arlington, Virginia, that marks the grave of the unidentified service members from the U.S. who died in wars since World War I.
As Hegseth's group walked up the stairs away from the monument (time code 00:41), someone could be heard talking and laughing. The U.S. Army Sentinel on guard shouted in response, "All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times."
It was not clear who in Hegseth's group talked and laughed, though one woman who posed with Hegseth could be seen gesturing with her hands as the group walked up the stairs before the sentinel's reprimand.
Newsweek reported that the group caught talking and laughing at the Tomb of the Unknown soldier consisted of Hegseth, his wife Jennifer Hegseth, his chief of staff Ricky Buria, his Deputy Chief of Staff Patrick Weaver and senior adviser Tami Radabaugh.
A photo from reputable photo repository Getty Images showed Hegseth's wife was present at the Veterans Day commemoration at Arlington Cemetery on Nov. 11 and wore a dark brown or burgundy dress that was also visible in CNN's coverage.
Because the other three people in the group stood with their backs to the camera, Snopes could not independently verify Newsweek's claim that they were Hegseth's senior staff.
Soldiers have guarded the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at Arlington since March 1926. The Arlington National Cemetery wrote on its website that the guards initially "discouraged visitors from climbing or stepping on the Tomb."
The 3rd U.S. Infantry Regiment, also known as "The Old Guard," has guarded the monument since April 6, 1948. Barbara Starr, CNN's former Pentagon correspondent, told (time code 11:24) the network on Nov. 11 that sentinels will correct any visitors who do not act with "respect and silence" at the tomb.
The incident at Arlington comes at a time when Hegseth is facing immense pressure over the war in Iran, which has been widely understood as a reason midterm voters moved away from the Republican Party in the November midterm elections.
On Nov. 10, the day before the incident at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, Republicans in the House blocked an attempt to impeach Hegseth. That same day, U.S. President Donald Trump signaled his continued support for Hegseth on Truth Social, calling the outgoing Republican congressman Thomas Massie, who led the push for Hegseth's impeachment, a "TOTAL LOSER."
For further reading, Snopes has previously investigated a number of rumors about Hegseth.

NEW DELHI: Nikhil Gupta, facing trial in an assassination attempt probe in US, has indicated that he was acting alone and apologised in a remorseful letter to US district judge Victor Marrero ahead of his Nov 20 sentencing. Gupta also opened up about his psychological turmoil following his initial arrest, admitting he did not recognise the person he had become in early 2023.
"I had lost my mind... wish I could turn back time to 2023 and undo my mistakes," Gupta wrote in the letter, describing how heavy drinking and personal struggles clouded his judgement. He revealed that he faced severe suicidal thoughts during his early days in custody, constantly worrying about the agonising pain he had caused his wife, children, mother, family and two cats.
Detailing his time in detention including solitary confinement in Czech Republic and subsequent placement at Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn, Gupta described turning toward meditation, yoga, and spiritual books to cope with isolation and the constant threats of violence from fellow inmates.
"The most serious challenge in front of me at that time was to contact my family and to let them know that I was alive and to make them aware of the situation, but I could not do so for several weeks due to many restrictions on me as an American law offender...," 
he wrote.
The upcoming sentencing on Nov 20 comes amid high-profile legal filings. Recently, federal prosecutors requested the target of the plot, Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, be granted 20 minutes to address the court directly.
Concluding his letter to the judge, Nikhil Gupta stated that he would accept whatever judgement the court handed down.

Stranded B.C. flyers out thousands amid flight cancellations due to FAA-ordered ground stop
Air Canada says it cancelled about 250 flights Friday, affecting roughly 27,000 passengers
Some frustrated Air Canada passengers say spotty communication and a lack of rebooking help have left them paying out of pocket amid widespread flight cancellations.
British Columbians Patricia Arndt, Corey Shack, Nancy Kristoff and Lisa Dolinski were in Cancun, Mexico, celebrating a 50th birthday but had to spend thousands of dollars to stay in Mexico after their return flight was cancelled.
"You just feel lost," said Arndt. "You’re going to have to figure it out yourself."
The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a ground stop on Friday afternoon due to communications problems at regional air traffic control centres, stemming from a maintenance issue, according to officials.
Air Canada says it cancelled roughly 250 flights Friday, affecting about 27,000 passengers following the FAA's order.
In an email, a spokesperson for Vancouver International Airport (YVR) said there were 54 flight cancellations Friday and another 23 related cancellations Saturday morning.
Unclear updates
Arndt said Air Canada didn’t communicate updated information in a timely manner. The airline told them they would receive an update about rebooking within 30 minutes, Arndt said, but no update came.
The four travellers said their return flight faced a two-hour delay and gate change before they received a text message saying it had been cancelled. They were forced to split up to find accommodations.
Between booking resorts and paying for trips to and from the airport, they estimated each of them spent roughly $2,000 to $3,000, with some families paying even more.
"That was the most frustrating part, because other airlines were communicating with their customers and we were getting zero communication," said Kristoff.
Dolinski woke up first thing Saturday to seek help at the Cancun International Airport, since she said Air Canada’s online platforms weren’t allowing them to book alternate flights home.
Dolinski said the Air Canada line only had one agent tending to it, and they waited three hours before eventually booking an alternate flight home on Wednesday.
Rerouting issues
She said some of her group members booked through Air Canada without extra charge but had to spend money on accommodations, while others paid out of pocket for their flights home but were able to secure a seat on Sunday flights.
McKenzie McMillan, managing partner at Travel Group in Vancouver, said Friday's mass cancellations were unlike anything seen in decades.
"This was a dramatic situation that unfolded yesterday for tens of thousands of passengers," he said.
McMillan says because these cancellations stem from an issue outside airlines’ control, airlines won’t be on the hook to cover those additional costs.
According to the Canadian Transportation Agency, if an airline delays or cancels a flight for reasons outside its control, it's not obligated to compensate affected passengers and the requirement to provide minimum assistance, like paying for food, drink or accommodation, does not apply.
McMillan said even though the FAA lifted its ground-stop order, it will likely take more than a week for airlines to get back to a normal schedule.
Air Canada says it has added flights where possible to help affected passengers, but further disruptions are expected as aircraft and crews remain out of position across its network.

Two attacks in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) have killed 4 workers responding to the Ebola outbreak and injured 5 others.
The attacks occurred overnight on a shared living camp in Biakato Mines and an Ebola response coordination office in Mangina.
“We are heartbroken that people have died in the line of duty as they worked to save others,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, World Health Organization Director-General. “The world has lost brave professionals.”
The dead include a member of a vaccination team, two drivers and a police officer. No WHO staff are among those killed, one staff member was injured.
“My heart goes out to the family and friends of the first responders killed in these attacks,” said Dr Matshidiso Moeti, WHO Regional Director for Africa. “We are doing everything possible to bring the injured and front-line workers in the impacted areas to safety. These constant attacks must stop. We will continue to work with the DRC Government, partners and MONUSCO to ensure the security of our staff and other health workers.”
In the last week, there were 7 cases of Ebola, down from a peak of over 120 per week in April 2019.
“Ebola was retreating. These attacks will give it force again, and more people will die as a consequence,” said Dr Tedros. “It will be tragic to see more unnecessary suffering in communities that have already suffered so much. We call on everyone who has a role to play to end this cycle of violence.”
The situation is still evolving. WHO will provide updates as new information comes in.

The Telangana Health Department has intensified its investigation into the alleged illegal oocyte (egg) collection racket, with inspections conducted at 27 of the 44 identified Assisted Reproductive Technology (ART) facilities across the State. Officials have detected 13 regulatory violations in seven hospitals and issued show-cause notices to their managements.
Health Minister C. Damodar Rajanarasimha has directed the department to conduct a comprehensive investigation into alleged illegal activities being carried out under the guise of oocyte collection and initiate stringent action against institutions and individuals found violating prescribed regulations.
Acting on the Minister’s directions, task force teams have been inspecting IVF centres across the State for the past four days. Inspections at the remaining facilities are continuing.
Aspects of investigation
The department said further action would be initiated after a detailed examination of records seized by the police and information obtained from the National ART and Surrogacy Registry. The investigation also includes examining the involvement of women identified in connection with the case, doctors, IVF centres and intermediaries allegedly facilitating the activities.
As part of the investigation, the Health department officials visited the National ART and Surrogacy Registry in New Delhi on November 6 and sought details of the data submitted by registered ART clinics and ART banks operating in Telangana.
The department has reiterated that oocyte collection must strictly comply with the provisions of the Assisted Reproductive Technology (Regulation) Act and Rules. All ART clinics and ART banks operating in the State are required to obtain mandatory statutory registration and adhere to the prescribed regulatory framework.
The Health Department also cautioned women against falling prey to misleading assurances and financial inducements offered by intermediaries, warning that such arrangements could expose them to unauthorised medical procedures.

FAA blames Friday's ground stop on 'equipment issue' during telecoms network upgrade
Friday's nationwide ground stop was declared after an error occurred while a contractor was updating an old Federal Aviation Administration telecommunication line, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Saturday.
L3Harris, a long time contractor for the Federal Aviation Administration, was doing routine maintenance in at least one of FAA's remote locations changing copper wire to fiber, he said. Duffy said the routers in these facilities were manufactured in 2001. These updates have been happening in American institutions for decades, Duffy said.
"Virtually every single institution in America has gone from copper to fiber, from analog to digital," Duffy said. "Just maybe the FAA is the last one to be doing this work because the investments haven't been made, but this is not complicated."
L3Harris did not immediately respond to NPR's request for comment.
Duffy said the FAA is still investigating the exact error that started flooding other routers in the air traffic control system.
"It's pretty straightforward work that we were doing yesterday at, again, a very remote location. So what we're working to determine was whether we had incompetence, meaning was it user error, installator error from L3Harris, or did they install a faulty router?"
Bryan Bedford, the FAA administrator, who joined Duffy at the briefing said there was no evidence of anything nefarious happening or AI-related issues.
Thousands of passengers miss flights
Tens of thousands of passengers across the U.S. are still stranded Saturday after a rare ground stop halted all flights.
The chaos is expected to linger for days.
The aviation system is back online and slowly returning to normal Saturday morning, but delays and cancellations will continue after yesterday's nationwide ground stop, Duffy said in the press briefing Saturday.
"Based on everything that we're hearing from our airline partners, they believe that they'll be able to have full schedule integrity by the close of business on Sunday," Bedford said.
Duffy told reporters Friday night: "I think we're going to be back up and operational as we come into the heat of travel during Thanksgiving."
For about four hours on Friday, thousands of flights at U.S. airports were grounded in one of the biggest disruptions of the nation's air travel system since the terrorist attacks on September 11, 2001.
Nearly 25,000 flights were delayed, and over 9,000 were cancelled on Friday, according to FlightAware, a flight tracking site. The disruption seeped into Saturday morning with more than 4,000 cancellations recorded. That's 14% of flights departing the U.S., according to data from Cirium, which tracks aviation analytics.
Duffy said Friday that air traffic control facilities had experienced "intermittent" outages of their radar and communications systems beginning earlier in the afternoon. Duffy blamed "old switches, old routers" for the failures. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin joined Duffy in the White House briefing room and said there was no evidence the issue was due to an attack.
Flight boards at airports across the country Saturday morning continued to be riddled with red cancelled marks. At Tampa International Airport in Florida, people in the main terminal area before security curled up in chairs to grab a wink of sleep.
On Friday night, a flight board at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport in D.C. showed dozens of flights delayed into the early morning hours or cancelled.
Passengers Erin and Jake Britt spent half the day at the airport in D.C. on Friday. Their plane to Fort Lauderdale, Fla. boarded at 3 p.m. By 5:30 p.m., they were getting off the plane — but they were still in D.C.
"Overall, our plane was definitely annoyed, but reasonable," Erin Britt said, as the couple left the airport at 8pm. "People being upset and asking like, 'Well, how are you not prepared for this?' And it was like, 'Well, no one was prepared.'"
She said neither the pilot nor flight attendants had any more information than passengers."They seem just as in the dark," she said.
The pair decided to cancel their weekend trip, but the night didn't end there. They spent over nine hours overnight waiting on the JetBlue customer service call line to be reimbursed. "I was setting alarms in 20 minute intervals in case I fell asleep," Erin Britt said.
For people who had events or plans over the weekend – the delay added an extra layer of stress. Joe Romano and Maddie Cabana had a cruise leaving Orlando, Fla. Saturday afternoon.
"It was a big eye roll. I mean, I travel a lot for work already, so I'm constantly dealing with flight delays," Romano said. "When this happened, I was just like, 'Of course, it always happens to me.'"
"Just rather inconvenient and frustrating," Cabana added, as the pair contemplated checking their bags or going home. "Hopefully, everything will be fine. It'll all work out. It always does."
And it did – eventually. After their JetBlue flight was ultimately cancelled, they quickly booked another one on Southwest Airlines and made it early Saturday morning.
Others, like Suze DiPietro decided flying wasn't worth it anymore. Her husband drove about four hours down from Ocean City, New Jersey to pick her up in D.C. Luckily, they had friends in the area where they spent the night.
"My husband, my hero, is driving down from New Jersey to come get me," DiPietro said.
Other alternatives included people switching to Amtrak trains as they struggled to get to their destination. Although, even Amtrak's system had a brief outage Friday night.
This was only the second nationwide ground stop since September 11, 2001. The U.S. last issued a ground stop of this scale in 2023, when all U.S. airports were shut down due to an outage in the NOTAM (Notice to Air Missions) system, which alerts pilots and airports of real-time hazards.
That outage prompted fears of a cyberattack, but the FAA later determined the issue was caused when contract workers inadvertently deleted critical files.
The FAA has recently begun rolling out an AI-enhanced software tool known as the SMART system as part of its ambitious overhaul of the nation's air traffic control system. But Air Space Intelligence, the company that makes the tool, quickly dismissed speculation that its product could be connected to the flight disruptions.
"The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC," the company said on social media.
