Former Indian cricketer Ajinkya Rahane has picked up an undisclosed stake in D2C cookware brand Ember. The startup did not disclose the financial terms of the investment. The investment comes as the Bengaluru-based brand plans to expand into new product categories, strengthen its distribution network and ramp up its market presence. “... The kitchen is at the heart of every household, and I believe there is significant potential for brands that bring together thoughtful design, quality and functionality. I am delighted to be associated with Ember and look forward to being part of its journey as it enters its next phase of growth,” said Rahane in a statement. “... Our priority is to build the scale, market presence and operational strength required to achieve it. Ajinkya's association comes at an exciting point in this journey as we prepare for the next stage of growth,” added cofounder and CEO Siddharth Gadodia. Founded in 2024 by Gadodia, Himanshi Tandon and Bret Recor, Ember is a D2C brand that sells a range of products including ceramic cookwares, stainless steel pans, cast iron pots, Dutch ovens, kitchen tools and other appliances. The startup claims to have developed its own proprietary ceramic coating called ‘Arcilla’, and claims to manufacture its products in Italy. It sells its offerings via its own website, ecommerce marketplaces and quick commerce platforms across Delhi NCR, Mumbai, Bengaluru and Hyderabad. The capital infusion from Rahane comes more than a year after the D2C cookware brand raised $3.2 Mn in its seed round in September last year. However, this is not Rahane’s first investment in an Indian startup. He has previously backed startups such as Chupps, Hudle, Proxgy and Oatey in the past. Notably, the infusion comes as a host of Indian cricketers make a beeline for the Indian startup ecosystem. Just a day ago, cricket icon Sachin Tendulkar joined the cap table of Hyderabad-based waste management startup Recykal. Earlier this month, Tendulkar also infused an undisclosed amount of capital in Metasports Interactive, the gaming startup behind mobile cricket strategy game Hitwicket. Sports retail startup PlayBlue also onboarded cricketer KL Rahul as an investor and brand ambassador earlier this week.

Indonesia’s Vice President Resigns as a Political Alliance Unravels
Gibran Rakabuming Raka, who is stepping down amid a scandal over his academic credentials, was a symbol of the partnership that elevated President Prabowo Subianto into office.
The vice president of Indonesia submitted his resignation to Parliament on Thursday, succumbing to a scandal about his academic credentials and injecting new political uncertainty in Southeast Asia’s largest economy.
Gibran Rakabuming Raka was elected as Indonesia’s youngest vice president in 2024, in a precipitous rise. He was a symbol of the partnership between his father, the outgoing president, Joko Widodo, and the incoming leader, Prabowo Subianto, that elevated Mr. Prabowo into office.
“The relationship has clearly fractured,” said Yoes C. Kenawas, a political analyst at the Indonesian Survey Institute. With Mr. Gibran’s departure, “Prabowo is attempting to demonstrate that he has stepped out from Jokowi’s shadow,” he added, referring to the former leader by his nickname.
Initially a political outsider, Mr. Joko came to be seen as a transformative leader of Indonesia. He helped rehabilitate the image of Mr. Prabowo, a former special forces commander who was discharged from the military for his involvement in the abduction and torture of pro-democracy activists under the dictator Suharto. To many, Mr. Prabowo was a reminder of the country’s authoritarian past. But Mr. Joko endorsed Mr. Prabowo as his successor, with Mr. Gibran running on the same ticket.
The alliance between Mr. Joko and Mr. Prabowo was cast as one of political continuity. Many voters had seen Mr. Gibran’s vice presidency as a way for Mr. Joko to continue his political influence.
“From the beginning, Gibran was brought on board solely to serve as a ‘vote-getter,’ rather than as an integral part of a unified leadership team intended to strengthen the performance of the Prabowo administration,” said Titi Anggraini, a lecturer of constitutional law at University of Indonesia.

The young Somali woman changing how the world sees Mogadishu
- Published
As the sun rises over the Indian Ocean, waves lap onto the golden sands while palm fronds rustle in the cool sea breeze. Welcome to... Mogadishu.
This is the image that one young Somali woman wants the world to have of her home city - in contrast to the one of suicide attacks and young men wielding AK-47s that many people currently associate with Somalia's capital.
Sucdi Abdul Fattah Abdul Khader is among a growing number of local guides taking visitors beyond the headlines to explore Mogadishu's beauty spots, historic sites and culture.
Her favourite spot is Jazeera beach, where visitors can enjoy the sea before heading to nearby sand dunes.
"It's one of the tourist attractions where we bring our guests. It's a nice place," says the 23-year-old.
The dunes, she adds, remind some visitors of the Sahara.
But her tours are about more than scenic views. She also takes visitors to the fish market, where they discover the variety of marine life available along Somalia's extensive coastline and to parts of the city that reflect its history as a busy Indian Ocean trading centre, with the influences of both its Ottoman and Italian former rulers.
Visitors can also sample Somali food, including camel meat, samosas and traditional tea.
Sucdi says many arrive in the city with expectations shaped by years of hearing about the insecurity.
"Mostly, they are surprised by how beautiful the country is and how welcoming people are," she says.
At the fish market, she says, visitors are particularly impressed by the variety of fish species.
Guiding tours runs in Sucdi's family. Her father worked in the profession for over three decades, taking journalists, photographers and visitors from different countries around Somalia.
He introduced her to the business nearly three years ago.
"I started this job as a hobby, but it has become something that I like and am passionate about," she says.
She now works alongside her father and a team of guides, building on his experience while using social media to reach a wider audience.
She shares videos of her tours on TikTok, offering people outside Somalia a glimpse of places they may never have imagined visiting.
She is also considering producing content in English to reach audiences who do not speak Somali.
Tourism remains a relatively new field in Somalia, she says, with only a handful working as guides in Mogadishu.
The business is seasonal, but Sucdi says this year has been particularly encouraging, although numbers are still fairly low. Having five tourists a week is considered a success but she is confident that numbers will grow.
However, she says many visitors are still concerned about security.
Since the collapse of Somalia's central government in 1991, Mogadishu has endured decades of civil war, destruction and displacement. Much of the city centre was reduced to rubble, and basic services and infrastructure largely broke down.
But following the withdrawal of the Islamist militant group al-Shabab from most of the city in 2011, and the establishment of the federal government in 2012, Mogadishu has undergone a gradual transformation.
Returning members of the Somali diaspora, local entrepreneurs and investors helped fuel a construction boom, with new hotels, restaurants, businesses and residential developments reshaping the capital.
Today, Mogadishu is a growing commercial hub, although insecurity and the legacy of conflict remain part of everyday life.
About 10,000 tourists visited Somalia in 2024, a 50% increase on the previous year, according to the country's tourism department.
Many visitors ask about their safety before travelling and often encounter security checkpoints around the city.
But she says their experience on the ground is generally positive.
"What they heard from the news and everywhere else is not the same as what they see in the country," she says.
Although some question whether Mogadishu is safe enough for a young woman to be working as a tour guide, Sucdi is determined to continue.
She wants visitors to experience a Somalia that is rarely seen.
"I would want them to see the beautiful, welcoming side of Mogadishu, and not the side that they heard from the media, which is explosions and bombs," she says.
Somalia has Africa's longest mainland coastline, stretching more than 3,000km (1,860 miles) along the Indian Ocean and Gulf of Aden.
Its beaches and sand dunes sit alongside historic coastal cities such as Mogadishu, whose culture reflects centuries of Indian Ocean trade.
For some tourists, that contrast between the country's reputation and what they experience can be striking.
American travel content creator Chris Reese, who goes by the name Authentic Travelling, has visited Mogadishu twice.
His first trip, almost a year ago, was a solo visit. He enjoyed it so much that he decided to return with a group of friends, who had seen videos of his visit on social media.
"I had such a positive experience - I really enjoyed seeing the country for the first time - that I opted to bring back a group of my friends," he says.
What stands out for Chris is the city's coastal setting, its food and atmosphere.
"It is such a beautiful tropical place. I love the vibe, the weather and the food," he says.
During the group's visit, they enjoy lunch overlooking the Indian Ocean before heading out to explore the beaches and sand dunes.
"The desert is beautiful and picturesque. It is also amazing that it's barely a 30-minute drive from Mogadishu," he says.
Before his first trip, Chris says, much of what he knew about Somalia came from international news coverage.
"If you only read the news reports about Somalia, you would be scared to visit. And honestly, that's what I saw in the media before I came, mostly negative headlines."
But visiting the country challenged those perceptions.
"Coming here, on my very first trip, showed me that there is so much more to this country than what is shown in the headlines," he says.
Mihaela Patap, from Romania, loves Somalia's natural beauty.
Although she has spent only a few hours in Mogadishu, she has already visited the sand dunes and taken in the Indian Ocean coastline.
"The desert was so beautiful to see. I have also enjoyed the beach, and the ocean. It is inspiring," she says.
Having travelled to Somalia from neighbouring Ethiopia, she says she has been struck by the people's friendliness.
"I don't see anything dangerous. I feel safe and the people are warm," she says.
An experienced traveller, Mihaela says she prefers to visit new countries without having preconceived ideas.
"I travel the world to see new places, to see countries, to see the differences. I don't take a picture in my mind to compare the reality with. I'm just expecting the new to come to me," she says.
She hopes to share her experience and encourage others to visit Somalia.
"I'm going to post my pictures and say good things about what I'm experiencing. I'm going to promote it," she says.
For Sucdi, that potential is personal.
She is continuing a family profession while building a business in an industry with few women and using digital platforms to reach audiences far beyond Mogadishu.
"Somalia still has a long way to go before tourism becomes a major industry," she says.
"Through my tours, I am giving visitors an opportunity to experience its landscapes, our culture and people beyond the familiar negative headlines."
For her, every visitor is another opportunity to tell a fuller story of Mogadishu.

Ebola tops 11,000 cases in Congo's deadliest outbreak
BUNIA, Congo — Congo's Ebola outbreak has topped 11,000 cases, the government said Wednesday, a stark figure that underscores the severity of the situation as the country grapples with the relentless spread of the disease.
According to the latest health ministry data, 11,042 people have been infected with the deadly virus that has now killed 5,387 — nearly half of those infected in what has been Congo's deadliest outbreak.
The outbreak was declared in mid-May, and since then, Congolese authorities have struggled to contain it due to several factors, including armed conflicts, a health system crisis, poor roads and violence from residents fueled by mistrust and misinformation.
The Bundibugyo virus responsible for this outbreak has no known vaccine or treatment and has spread to eight of the country's 26 provinces.
The resurgence of violence in the two major hotspots in Ituri and North Kivu provinces has sparked worry among health authorities who are calling for a halt to the fighting to allow health workers unhindered access to the sick.
Health facilities and medical professionals have also been targeted by many in communities skeptical of the virus, and there have been several attacks on health workers.
Experts have called for more efforts to slow and contain the disease in Congo, while it has spread to multiple African countries including Uganda, Kenya and Nigeria.
Dozens of Ebola outbreaks have been reported since the disease was first discovered in 1976. The largest and deadliest occurred in West Africa in 2014 to 2016, with 28,000 infections and more than 11,000 deaths.
The current outbreak already ranks second and has had at least three times the number of cases and deaths in the time since it was declared, compared with the West Africa outbreak.

STARBASE, Texas—The black and silver ship fell out of the sky, emerging from the cloud deck near the very end of its flight. Incongruously, the rocket flew horizontal until the last moment when three Raptor rocket engines ignited and it swooped into a vertical position.
Slowly, gently, haltingly, the Starship upper stage eased its way toward the waiting tower where two arms extended outward, awaiting expectantly. The margins are so incredibly narrow. Two nubs on either side of the rocket, each protruding only about one foot, were the only purchase the rocket would have on the arms.
Then, less than a minute after it came into view, the Starship upper stage was snagged by the launch tower, as snug as you like. And so it was all over. SpaceX, nearly a quarter of a century after its founding, had just taken a hugely significant step toward developing and optimizing a massive, rapidly reusable rocket.
We are dazzled
This was a breathtaking feat; a brilliant technical achievement that required the best engineering minds to think through a million different, difficult problems. And on Saturday evening, following a handful of practice runs into the Indian Ocean, they did it before the entire world.
Watching Starship launch from here a little less than a day earlier, and knowing it had orbited the planet multiple times, added to the sense of unreality in seeing this spaceship return to Earth under its own power, and be captured by the tower.
It felt like stepping into the future. SpaceX has dazzled us before, by landing rockets on barges and returning humans to space with Crew Dragon. But this flight took things to another level. Starships are huge. They carry a huge amount of energy coming back from orbit. And until a few years ago, it seemed beyond fantastical to think about capturing a rocket with what are essentially outsized chopsticks.
Nevertheless, it happened.
Rapid reuse is firmly on the horizon
Humans have built reusable spacecraft that flew into orbit before. In the 1970s, flush with confidence after the triumphant Moon landings, NASA designed and built several Space Shuttles. They had solid rocket boosters that were fished from the ocean and reused. The large orange external tank was not recovered after each flight, but the orbiters went to space for two weeks, or even longer, before returning to Earth and landing on a runway.

Washington, Nov 15: A temple pond near Houston, a California lake and the banks of the Potomac River in a Virginia suburb of Washington have become places where diaspora families keep a familiar tradition close: gathering at the water's edge to offer prayers to the sun.
Across the United States and Canada, Chhath is bringing together fasting devotees, children, relatives and volunteers. The settings are North American, but organisers' invitations carry a shared concern -- preserving the rituals of home and helping another generation make them their own.
Houston Families Gather For Chhath Celebrations
Near Houston, the pond at the Jagannath Hindu Temple of Rosenberg is the centre of a community effort involving families, donors and volunteers.
The organisers say six scientists are sponsoring, cooking and serving food for families attending the celebration. Other volunteers help with setup, parking, cleanup and welcoming people. The invitation reads: "Open to every family that celebrates."
The work behind the prayers is part of the gathering. Registration helps organisers plan food and space at the water, while families can sign up to help with the tasks that make a community celebration possible.
Potomac River Hosts Two-Decade-Old Tradition
In the national capital region, community members have celebrated Chhath on the banks of the Potomac River in Virginia for two decades. It all started in 2006 when Kripa Shankar Singh and his wife, Anita, sought a place to observe the festival.
"This is our attempt to keep our culture alive in a foreign land," Anita Singh told IANS in an interview, adding that what began as a family affair now attracts hundreds of community members from far and near every year.
New Jersey Community Preserves Cultural Roots
In New Jersey, the Bihar-Jharkhand Association of North America expresses a similar purpose in its invitation to families. It asks participants to "help us keep our traditions alive, far from home but never apart".
The invitation welcomes those observing the fast and those coming to support them. Relatives and friends have a place alongside the devotees, making the gathering a shared community occasion.
California Celebrations Bring Families Together
On the West Coast, the Bay Area celebration includes a gathering organised by Quarry Lakes Chhath in Fremont, near Silicon Valley. Its registration page pairs arrangements for the evening offering with the practical requirements of using a public recreation space, including advance parking passes.
Farther south, the Bihar Jharkhand Bandhu Association is bringing families to Oso Lake Scout Camp in Rancho Santa Margarita.
Children, friends and volunteers are invited alongside fasting devotees. The group describes the gathering beside the lake as an opportunity for families to observe the festival together in a natural setting. Its invitation emphasises strengthening cultural connections and passing the tradition to another generation.
Chhath Celebrations Extend Across North America
Celebrations also extend to Hindu Buddha Mandir in Maryland, in the Washington-Baltimore region, and the Shiv Mandir of Atlanta in Sugar Hill, Georgia. Near Seattle, the Hindu Temple and Cultural Center in Bothell is accepting registrations for collective Chhath worship.

In Canada, shared meals are central to preparations at the Vaishno Devi Temple in Oakville, Ontario. The Bihar and Jharkhand Association of Canada says donations and sponsorship will make meals, puja and prasad free throughout its three-day programme.
Its appeal connects the celebration to maintaining the traditions of Bihar and Jharkhand in Canada, with community contributions supporting the gathering.
The invitations reflect different community priorities: bringing family and friends together in New Jersey, involving children in California and sharing meals in Oakville.

For years, we at Inc42 have tracked the Indian tech startup ecosystem and seen it grow from a kid to an adult. Among the clearest signs of evolution and maturity of this ecosystem is the growing number of startups eyeing a public listing now. For Indian companies, achieving a public listing has for long symbolised operational progression, transparency, and long-term viability. For startups, it’s a relatively new but increasingly critical rite of passage, one that not only signals coming of age but also creates pathways for investor exits and wealth creation. Currently, a handful of startups, including the likes of Razorpay, PRISM, PhonePe, among others, are in various stages of their IPO journey. Meanwhile, over 70 Indian new-age tech companies have already crossed the milestone and are now listed on the bourses. The list also includes Indian companies like MakeMyTrip and Freshworks, which are listed on Nasdaq in the US. India’s startup IPO wave reached its peak in 2025, surpassing the previous year's momentum. While 18 startups listed in 2025, 18 startups have already reached that milestone in 2026. With companies like Cult.fit, OYO, others, eyeing to tap the public markets this year, the list is only expected to grow further this year. 18 new-age companies — Tonbo Imaging, Zetwerk, AceVector, Moneyview, Rentomojo, ESDS, Purple Style Labs, Turtlemint, Klassroom, Shiprocket, LEAP India, Kissht, Aye Finance, Fractal Analytics, Amagi, Shadowfax, Mobavenue and SEDEMAC — have made their public market debut in 2026. As of now, the total market capitalisation of the listed companies stands at over $194 Bn. To consolidate all the information about listed startups, Inc42 has launched the Indian Listed New-Age Tech Company Tracker. From the movement in the shares of the companies since their listing to the financial performance of these companies, the tracker is your one-stop resource to know everything you need about the listed tech companies. Table not loading? Open the tracker. Read our methodology here. Inside The Dalal Street Startup Ride Indian startups had gained a reputation for being “loss making” by prioritising growth at all costs and market share over immediate profitability. The trend of putting scale ahead of the bottom line was at its peak amid the funding boom of 2020-22. While prioritising growth is not wrong for startups, especially at early stages, the start of funding winter in 2022 gave a reality check to the Indian startup ecosystem. Subsequently, startups started pushing for profitability. Giving further wings to the aggressive profitability push was the ambition to list on the exchanges. While new-age tech companies look to turn profitable before filing their draft IPO papers, those that cross the line manage to stay in the green, data shows. Over 60 of the new-age tech companies are currently profitable. In terms of profits, Groww now leads the pack of new-age tech companies, posting a net profit of ₹2,083 Cr in FY26. Prominent internet companies Paytm and Eternal trail Groww in terms of profitability, raking in profits of ₹553 Cr and ₹366 Cr in FY26, respectively. It is pertinent to mention that these companies have been listed on the bourses for years now, with Info Edge making its public market debut in 2006. While these companies trace their origin back to the 90s, a large majority of the new-age tech stocks under Inc42's purview are about a decade old. From a broad perspective, Inc42 data reflects that the median time taken for a startup to get listed on the bourses is 11 years. While listing for 18-year-old ixigo and 19-year-old Fino Payments Bank came relatively much later, ArisInfra's IPO materialised within four years of its operations. Meanwhile, the new-age tech companies that have made their public market debuts this year generally turned profitable right before their public market debuts. For instance, eyewear major Lenskart reported a net profit of around ₹297 Cr , a significant turnaround from a ₹10 Cr loss in FY24. The company maintained profitability in FY26, raking in a PAT of ₹494 Cr in the fiscal. Urban Company also reported its first consolidated net profit of approximately ₹240 Cr for FY25, it returned to the red in FY26. For the full year FY26, the company reported a net loss of ₹234.8 Cr against a net profit of ₹239.8 Cr in previous year despite seeing a revenue growth of 36% YoY to ₹1,555.5 Cr Sectors Driving India’s Startup IPO Boom The startup sectors producing the most number of listed companies is proportional to the private funding trends witnessed in the Indian startup ecosystem. The three most funded sectors, fintech, ecommerce and enterprise tech, also house the highest number listed startups. While fintech and ecommerce house 14 names each, 13 enterprise tech startups have listed on the bourses so far. The dominance of the fintech and ecommerce sectors on the bourses is expected to continue as the likes of Tonbo Imaging, Zepto and OYO would soon be making their public market debuts. Delhi NCR Home To Highest Number Of Listed Startups While Bengaluru continues to be the startup capital of India, Delhi and its neighbouring cities Gurugram and Noida account for the most number of listed new-age tech companies. Overall, the Delhi NCR region is home to 27 listed new-age tech companies, ahead of Bengaluru's ninetineen and Mumbai's fifteen. While fifteen companies, including Eternal, Delhivery, and Lenskart, call Gurugram their home, Awfis, EaseMyTrip, MapmyIndia and E2E Networks are from Delhi. Noida on the other hand is home to six listed new-age tech companies, including Paytm and IndiQube. Delhi NCR contributes $105.2 Bn in the cumulative $194 Bn market cap of new-age tech companies. Ramayana – Part I, starring Ranbir Kapoor and Yash, continues its extraordinary run at the worldwide box office. The Nitesh Tiwari-directed mythological epic has achieved yet another massive milestone, crossing the coveted Rs. 1200 crore worldwide mark. With its latest global collections reaching a staggering Rs. 1215.40 crores gross, the film has also surpassed the lifetime worldwide collections of Shah Rukh Khan's Jawan (2023), climbing further in Bollywood's all-time box office rankings.
According to the latest figures, Ramayana has collected Rs. 667.98 crores nett in India, translating into domestic gross collections of Rs. 804.80 crores. Overseas territories have contributed another Rs. 410.60 crores gross, taking the worldwide total to Rs. 1215.40 crores. The film has thus crossed three major landmarks — Rs. 1200 crores worldwide, Rs. 800 crores gross in India and Rs. 400 crores gross overseas.
One of the biggest developments in Ramayana's worldwide box office journey is that it has overtaken the lifetime collections of Jawan. The Atlee-directed blockbuster, starring Shah Rukh Khan, had collected Rs. 1148.32 crores gross worldwide. The achievement is particularly significant because Ramayana has accomplished this feat within its second week of release, while Jawan's figure represents its entire theatrical run.
Earlier, Ramayana had also overtaken the lifetime worldwide collections of Pathaan (2023), which had grossed Rs. 1050.30 crores. With both Pathaan and Jawan now behind it, Ramayana has climbed to No. 3 among the highest-grossing Bollywood films worldwide excluding China

I love a good Zone 2 ride. There’s nothing like getting on the bike, settling into a groove, and letting the miles (and hours) flow by. But sometimes when I hopped on the Specialized Tarmac SL9 S-Level, Zone 2 would turn into a tempo ride. It was like having a little imp—the stereotype dressed in red with the pitchfork—on my left shoulder whispering into my ear: “Go fast. This bike was built to go fast. Speed is good. You can do a Zone 2 ride tomorrow.” Normally, I’d count on the good imp—the dude with the harp and wings—on my right shoulder to restrain these urges. But the Tarmac is so seductive that he would just shrug and say “he’s got a point.” And in a moment of weakness, I would drop the hammer and head into the red, just because the SL9 makes that so rewarding.
The Tarmac SL9 is Specialized’s aero road bike, with the S-Level sitting just below the S-Works in Specialized’s top tier of carbon, aero road bikes, where it replaced the Tarmac SL8 Pro. After it got an update this year, I spent several weeks riding it, putting nearly 1,000 miles on it
Specialized offers the Tarmac SL9 in four models, all available with SRAM and Shimano drivetrains (Ars tested the SRAM version). Notably, you don’t need to buy the top-of-the-line bike to get the top-of-the-line groupset. Here’s the breakdown of the Tarmac SL9 lineup (note that the Shimano versions of the Expert is 20 g lighter and Comp is 70 grams heavier than the SRAM versions):
|  | Drivetrain and price | Claimed weight (56 cm SRAM build) | Wheelset | Saddle | Cockpit | Frame and fork | 
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| S-Works | RED AXS: $13,999.99 Dura-Ace Di2: $13,499.99 | 6.60 kg | Roval Rapide CLX III carbon | S-Works Power with Mirror | Roval Rapide integrated bar/stem | FACT 12r / FACT 12r | 
| S-Level | RED AXS: $10,499.99 Dura-Ace Di2: $9,999.99 | 7.10 kg | Roval Rapide CL III carbon | Power Pro Mirror; hollow titanium rails | Roval Rapide integrated bar/stem | FACT 10r / FACT 12r | 
| Expert | Force AXS: $6,999.99 Ultegra Di2: $6,499.99 | 7.55 kg | Roval C38 carbon | Body Geometry Power Expert; hollow titanium rails | Specialized Expert Shallow Drop alloy bar; Roval Rapide alloy stem | FACT 10r / FACT 12r | 
| Comp | Rival AXS: $4,499.99 105 Di2: $4,199.99 | 8.14 kg | DT Swiss R470 alloy rims; Specialized hubs | Body Geometry Power Comp; chrome alloy rails | Specialized Shallow Drop 6061 alloy bar; Roval Rapide alloy stem | FACT 10r / FACT 12r | 
The $10,500 S-Level offers the top-of-the-line SRAM Red groupset and integrated cockpit, just like the $14,000 S-Works. But the frameset, wheelset, and saddle differ. The major difference is the frame: the S-Level gets the same carbon-fiber FACT 10r frame as the Expert and Comp. At 822 g for a 56 cm frame, the FACT 10r is 135 g heavier than the FACT 12r used on the S-Works. Despite the weight difference, Specialized says the FACT 10r offers the same stiffness and comfort characteristics as its lighter sibling. Along with the frame, different wheelsets and saddles make the S-Level 500 g heavier than the S-Works. With bottle cages, a Garmin mount, and my preferred Shimano XTR XC PD-M9200 MTB pedals, the S-Level I tested weighed in at 7.98 kg. By way of comparison, my own road bike—a Gen 8 Trek Madone—weighs in at 7.71 kg.

Why does Australia want Brits to swap Sydney for the outback?
- Published
In a Mexican restaurant in north-east Australia, the tacos are served by staff from France, Italy, Ireland and Argentina.
Cairns has long attracted a young and transient international crowd, who enjoy the tropical lifestyle while earning money for travel.
But one nationality is in shorter supply than it used to be.
"You get far fewer British backpackers looking for jobs here these days," says Mexicairns owner Peter McLeay.
It's a trend McLeay has noticed since mid-2023, when a free trade deal between the UK and Australia kicked in.
That agreement - as well as tariff-free trade in Tim Tams and Penguins - included special treatment for Brits on working holiday visas: exemption from having to find jobs in regional or remote places if they wanted to remain beyond a year.
That, along with an increase in the age limit from 30 to 35 saw backpacker visas issued to Brits surging from 47,200 in 2023-24 to just over 77,000 in 2025-26, according to the latest Australian government data.
Without the incentive to go regional, many are choosing to base themselves in the big cities, or, according to Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, "Bondi or Coogee" - two of Sydney's most famous beachside suburbs.
Now though, with Brits making up almost a quarter of all 323,000 backpacker visas issued last year, his government wants the free trade deal to be revisited.
A privilege not enjoyed by others
"Many Brits don't treat it as a working holiday anymore. It's more a three-year career break," says Dan McConnell, general manager of the Mad Monkey backpacker hostel chain.
He says Brits used to be the largest clientele at its Cairns accommodation but "now French outnumber British three to one".
"We see the Brits get to Sydney, decide it's the coolest place in the world, and stay there," he adds.
It's a privilege not enjoyed by working holidaymakers from other countries who must do at least 88 days of "specified regional work" in industries that need a seasonal or temporary workforce - including agriculture, fisheries, tourism and hospitality - if they want to qualify for a second year extension, and six months to stay a third year.
Barely a month ago, Albanese ruled out forcing British backpackers to do the same, accepting it as part of the trade deal.
But, under pressure from businesses here in Far North Queensland and other regional Australian communities, who are concerned about a lack of labour, the mood music has changed.
Last week Albanese met UK counterpart Andy Burnham at the meeting of Commonwealth leaders in the Caribbean.
And alongside AI, gender violence online and the AUKUS defence pact, backpackers were on the agenda.
Despite speculation in the Australian media, no immediate announcement was made. Albanese instead told reporters that he had pushed for a change in the rules on backpackers and that Burnham had been "very constructive about it".
"We'll work those issues through over coming weeks," he said adding that the free trade agreement was not set in stone and tweaks could be made "if there are good policy reasons".
Backpackers make up one in seven farm jobs across Australia, with about 52,000 people on working holiday visas doing jobs in horticulture each year, according to the National Farmers Federation.
It welcomed Albanese's discussions with Burnham, but said the issue of worker shortages in agriculture was far broader than the UK deal.
Of greater concern are wider proposals, announced in September, to cut net migration into Australia, under political pressure from the resurgent right wing populist One Nation party and the opposition coalition.
That includes an overhaul of the working holiday visa system, introducing a ballot for backpackers wanting to extend their stay – capped at 45,000 for people wanting a second year in Australia (down from 57,000 who qualified this year) and just 5,000 allowed to remain for a third year (compared with 31,000 this year).
This, the federation says, is "a low blow".
Those plans are still out for consultation, but immigration officials have slowed processing rates for some working holiday visa applications and paused them from several countries.
Tourism Tropical North Queensland chief executive Mark Olsen has also been among those lobbying Albanese in Canberra - telling him that backpackers brought both the spending power and the temporary labour needed to fill seasonal roles in a region famed as a gateway to the Great Barrier Reef and the Unesco world heritage listed Daintree rainforest.
Young Brits temporarily living and working in this region peaked at around 20,000 he says. Now it's closer to 11,000.
"Numbers have dropped significantly since the UK free trade agreement kicked in when border arrangements returned to normal [after the pandemic] in 2023 ," he said.
A two-way street
Cairns restaurateur Fintan Rafferty says that of about 180 staff on his payroll across four venues, only five are British. Prior to the visa rule change, that was closer to 25.
UK workers came with good skills in hospitality and "were willing to work, and to work flexible hours", he told the BBC.
And, he said, it was a two-way street. "The pay is very good, the conditions are very good. And one of the great things about the 88-days rule is that it forces people to travel. It's enriching their experience."
Bucking the trend, at the bar of Gilligan's backpackers, Paige Tomlinson serves vodka and soda with plenty of ice and a broad South Yorkshire accent.
The 27-year-old, from Barnsley, has been in Cairns for four months, attracted by the "chilled" lifestyle and local waterfalls.
"Most people prefer Sydney and they question me all the time why I'm here," she laughs. "But I got to Sydney and I just didn't like it. It was too busy, too much like London and I don't like London."
She says she'd like to see the regional work requirement brought in for all Brits, "getting them out their comfort zone".
"If every other country's got to do it, why should we not?"
About 200km north, at Red Valley Farm in Lakeland, general manger Peter Inderbitzen agrees.
Workers mainly from Tonga, hired on a Pacific labour scheme, pick bananas there year-round.
But Inderbitzen also relies heavily on backpackers, especially at peak avocado season, employing about 25 people for a couple of months each year.
"It's very short, sharp, get it done, get it out kind of work," he told the BBC. "But without those pickers, the avos stay on the tree."
While a few British backpackers were still applying for work, numbers had "completely dropped off" since the rule change, said Inderbitzen, who'd "love" to see British travellers having an incentive to head to the regions.
"As much as it wasn't perfect, [that programme] was working."
Back in Cairns, most of the young Brits the BBC tracks down are on tourist visas - but many want to return for a working holiday.
Among them is Ethan Phillips, 23, from Buckinghamshire who has been having way too much fun to keep up to date with what politicians have been discussing.
"It makes sense for them to want us to do [regional work] again," he says. "I mean I'd rather not do it, but if we have to, it's only three months … it can't be that bad."

Gajju Khan is smiling as he sits in an unfinished building in the northern Indian state of Punjab in the late afternoon. The 87-year-old is hopeful that before he dies he will hear the azaan, the Muslim call to prayer, echo across his village once again when the mosque is completed.
The last time he heard it here was when he was eight years old, living with his parents in Tira Maloya, a village in Chandigarh, not far from where he lives now.
He is also excited because the mosque has been funded almost entirely by the Sikhs and Hindus living in his village of Jakhiwal, in Fatehgarh Sahib district. Even though he fondly remembers how Sikh neighbours sheltered him and his brothers when brutal sectarian violence erupted during partition in 1947, he never expected a house of worship to be rebuilt for the 18 Muslim families who remain in the village.
“This was my maternal home. My parents sent my two brothers and me here to save us from the bloodshed – they were killed back in our village,” says Khan. “Sikhs hid us from the patrols of men with sticks and burning torches.”
Khan reserves his deepest gratitude for Bibi Rajinder Kaur, 77, a Sikh villager who persuaded her grandson to donate a parcel of their farmland to build a mosque. She did so, she says, because every other faith had a place to gather, while local Muslims had none.
“There is no deed better than giving someone a place to worship,” Kaur says. “Also, it felt like we needed to appease God for the blood this land had seen. The Muslims in our village had to travel 4km [2.5 miles] to another village just to pray.”
During the partition of British India, the border severed Punjab in two, unleashing catastrophic communal blood-letting and forced migrations that virtually emptied the eastern, Indian side of the region of its Muslim population. Hundreds of village mosques were abandoned, desecrated or turned into cattle sheds and storage units.
But over the past decade, several rural Sikh and Hindu communities have quietly stepped forward to restore these places of worship. Even in villages without a Muslim population, people have invited Muslim farmhands and clerics from nearby districts to pray in these newly revived mosques.
About 50 miles fromJakhiwal, in Sangrur district’s Punawal village, Jaspal Sharma, who comes from a family of Hindu priests, donated his land for the construction of a new mosque and hosted a feast for the entire village at its inauguration in February.
Sharma, 48, says the donation was about neighbourly duty. The village has 550 households, of which just a very small proportion are Muslim.
“It’s right opposite our house, so the sound of prayers five times a day creates a lively atmosphere. We like it,” says Sharma. “And it wasn’t just us; everyone in the village, Hindus and Sikhs together, contributed what they could. Some gave money; others donated bricks and cement.”
For Sukhjinder Singh Pandher and his brother, restoring a local shrine in Malerkotla’s Umarpura village was an act of filial reverence. Their grandfather fled west Punjab during partition to settle in India.
“Nobody is treated as different here,” says Pandher, sharing a cup of tea with his Muslim neighbours on the bare floor of the restored mosque. “Eid and Gurpurab [Sikhs’ most holy festival] are celebrated by both communities with the same fervour.
“We live as one and no matter what happens in the rest of the country, the mood here is that of love and unity. Punjab’s conscience cannot tolerate cruelty against a being, irrespective of caste and religion,” he says.
Pandher points to the syncretic traditions and blending of cultures that are deeply rooted in Punjabi history, noting the popular belief that the 16th-century Sufi saint Hazrat Mian Mir was invited to lay the foundation stone of Sikhism’s holiest site, the Harmandir Sahib, or Golden Temple, in Amritsar.
Inspired by the former shahi, or chief, imam of Punjab, Maulana Habib-ur-Rehman Sani Ludhianvi, non-Muslim villagers have contributed to more than 165 such mosques in the past nine years.
“Partition tore at the natural fabric of Punjab,” says the current shahi imam, Maulana Muhammad Usman Rehmani Ludhianvi, who succeeded his father in 2021. “This state itself is an inquilab [revolution]. Online, there is immense polarisation, but on the ground in our villages, ordinary people are still choosing to protect each other.”

Karnataka’s Health Department is developing a mobile application to track the collection, sale and reuse of used cooking oil, with the objective of preventing its re-entry into the food chain, Health Minister U.T. Khader said on Thursday (November 12).
The application, which is expected to be developed within three months, will create a digital trail from the point at which cooking oil is purchased by hotels and other food business operators to its eventual disposal or transfer to authorised agencies for industrial use, Mr. Khader said.
The initiative is aimed at addressing the illegal diversion of used cooking oil, which is sometimes collected for industrial purposes such as soap manufacturing and biodiesel production but allegedly finds its way back to small hotels and eateries for reuse in cooking.
Addressing presspersons in Bengaluru, Mr. Khader said the Food Safety and Drugs Administration Department would manage the application. All manufacturers and food business operators would be required to register on the platform. The department would initially conduct a trial run in Bengaluru, Mysuru, Mangaluru and Hubballi.
Proposed mechanism
Explaining the proposed mechanism, he said hotels and other establishments would have to enter details of the quantity of fresh cooking oil purchased, its source, and the quantity of used oil generated. They would have to record the identity of the person or agency to whom the used oil was handed over.
The collectors, in turn, would have to upload details of whom they sold the oil to, the quantity transferred, and the amount paid.
“If a hotel uses 500 litres of oil in a month, it must account for the 50 to 75 litres of used oil generated, assuming a 10% to 15% recovery. It must submit details of whom it handed over the used oil to. The person who collects it must record whom they sold it to. The entire chain has to be tracked,” he said.
No reliable data
The Minister said the system was necessary because the department currently lacked reliable data on the movement of used cooking oil and its eventual destination.
Under the proposed arrangement, used oil collected from food establishments would have to be channelled towards authorised industrial uses rather than being sold back to food businesses.
Illegal diversion
Mr. Khader said some agencies authorised to collect used cooking oil for industrial purposes were diverting a portion of it to small hotels.
Explaining the economics behind the diversion, he said collectors could receive around ₹80 for a litre of used oil intended for industrial purposes, while small hotels were willing to pay ₹120 to ₹125 a litre.
“Why would someone sell it for ₹80 when they can get ₹120 by supplying it to a small hotel?”
He pointed out that used cooking oil had several legitimate industrial applications, including the manufacture of soap, biodiesel and aviation fuel. However, the absence of an effective tracking mechanism made it difficult to ensure that oil collected for these purposes did not return to the food market.
The Minister said the Karnataka government would write to the Centre seeking greater flexibility in the regulations governing the reuse and export of used cooking oil, particularly given the demand for it in the aviation fuel sector.
He said the department would eventually explore a system to collect used cooking oil from households as well. “Just as we have a system to segregate and collect wet and dry waste from households, we can eventually establish a mechanism for households to store used cooking oil in cans and hand it over for collection. But this will be a step-by-step process,” he said.

WILL WEISSERT/JOSH FUNK
Washington- Airlines across the US worked to recover from the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years that cancelled thousands of flights Saturday, stranded hundreds of thousands of passengers, spread ripple effects around the world, and forced pro and college sports teams to scramble for alternate transportation.
New technology being added to the nation’s air traffic control system overloaded antiquated equipment and caused “intermittent” communications and radar gaps, leading to the flight shutdown of more than four hours, Trump administration officials said.
Airports were slowly returning to normal, Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said, with planes taking flight and landing. But the effects could be felt for days. Officials say the system will likely return to normal in time to handle the Thanksgiving travel rush.
The nationwide stop was the first since January 2023, when another key Federal Aviation Administration computer system that sends notices to pilots malfunctioned, and the second since September 11, 2001, attacks.
Andrew Charlton, an aviation consultant, said Friday’s stoppage affected about a quarter of the 45,000 flights in the US each day.
“The knock-on effect of that is incredible,” said Charlton, managing director of Aviation Advocacy. “The aircraft doesn’t just fly from A to B and back to B and then stop. It then moves onto C and then over to E and around and around and around. It is, of course, exacerbated if you’re talking about long-haul flights, international flights over the Atlantic or over the Pacific.”
Thousands of flights delayed and cancelled
At airports, passengers stared at screens showing delays or rushed to find buses or trains to their destinations.
Emily Brown and her 14-year-old daughter waited more than four hours Friday at the Dallas airport for their flight to Columbus, Ohio, before giving up. They were travelling to surprise her daughter’s best friend. Instead, she had to settle for phoning the friend through tears in the airport, Brown said.
“She saved up her money to buy her own ticket, and she’s planned this whole weekend,” Brown said. “Now we’re not sure when we’re gonna be able to go.”
A cheerful Southwest Airlines gate agent greeted passengers at Dallas Love Field at dawn Saturday with, “Good morning, good morning,” then repeatedly said all flights were full and asked passengers to have boarding passes ready to expedite the process and help keep flights moving.
Sports teams scheduled to play this weekend adjusted game start times, searched for hotel rooms, rescheduled flights and chartered buses.
Auburn University’s football team opted to take a bus to Mississippi State, and the Saturday start time was pushed back from noon ET to 4:15 pm. Other universities affected by the stoppage included Baylor, Washington, Kansas State, Minnesota and No. 19 Ole Miss, which did not plan to fly until Saturday morning for its game against Oklahoma.
FlightAware, a website that tracks flights, said more than 4,100 flights had been cancelled. Cirium, a similar site, put that number above 3,200 flights.
Corbyn Wascher’s flight was on the tarmac at the Charlotte, N.C., airport for four hours Friday on his way home to Moline, Illinois, from a conference in Miami. The 37-year-old high school teacher paid USD 100 to take an Uber to a hotel 25 minutes from the airport after he was unable to find a flight until Saturday afternoon to Chicago.
At London’s Heathrow Airport, several flights to and from the US were listed as delayed or cancelled Saturday.
“While US flights have resumed, there may be some follow-on disruption as airlines work to rebook affected passengers and get all services back to normal,” said Tim Johnson, consumer director at the UK Civil Aviation Authority.
Officials say no one was in danger during ground stop
Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin told reporters at the White House that no one was in any danger as more than 3,000 flights in the air at the time of the grounding order landed safely.
Duffy blamed Congress for failing to approve more funding for new technology, while downplaying the fact that trying to implement new fixes overtaxed the system. He suggested more disruptions might occur.
“We didn’t think we would have this kind of outage. We did,” he said. “We were able to review what went wrong, and then reboot the system and go. But, you will have more of these.”
Duffy said the failure involved old equipment and was not linked to the FAA’s new AI-powered system, which the agency is rolling out to help predict problems in the sky.
The problem was due to updating a system that can never shut down, Charlton said.
“What you’re watching here is trying to change the tires of your car when the car’s going at 80 miles an hour down the expressway, because nothing stops in aviation,” Charlton said. “It’s a 24/7 operation. And to make changes on the fly, if you’ll pardon that pun, is incredibly complex and dangerous.”
The FAA already replaced thousands of old copper wires with fibre optic lines and upgraded hundreds of radio systems as part of the overhaul that began last year after Congress approved USD 12.5 billion in funding. Duffy and the White House are pushing for USD 30 billion more to complete the work.
Past problems have been linked to equipment failures
The problem appeared similar to a regional air traffic control communication outage in September that snarled hundreds of flights across the Northeast, although that disruption was linked to a construction crew cutting a fibre optic line. Ageing equipment was also blamed for brief radar outages last year that disrupted Newark airport.
Aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said the difference this time was the nationwide scale of the disruption, which left controllers unable to reliably talk to pilots.
“If you don’t have that ability, whether it’s because the old wires that they have are just run down or for whatever reason, you’ve got to stop airplanes on the ground and not put them in the air, where you’re going to risk not being able to communicate with them,” said Arroyo, a former United Airlines pilot.
It differed from the one after 9/11 because planes were not being told to land immediately and pilots likely were able to communicate with ground controllers at airports, Arroyo said. (AP)

The Eurovision Song Contest crowned its first Asia champion in Bangkok on Saturday, in an event that tested whether a high-camp singing competition with an ardent fan base could appeal to audiences in a new market.
Carmelle of the Philippines was declared the winner of the inaugural Eurovision Song Contest Asia, beating out artists and original songs from 10 other countries: Bangladesh, Bhutan, Cambodia, Laos, Malaysia, Mongolia, Nepal, South Korea, Thailand and Vietnam. The show was live-streamed on YouTube and broadcast by television stations across the region.
Eurovision has been a fixture of the European cultural calendar since it began in 1956. Past winners include Sweden’s ABBA and the Canadian chanteuse Celine Dion, who represented Switzerland in 1988.
Asian artists have readily embraced the kitschy outfits and spectacular sets that are part of Eurovision tradition, with costumes that include traditional dress, as well as feathered capes and sequined corsets. Malaysia’s performer plans to enter the stage in a giant teardrop.
But the Eurovision format has not been tested in Asia. Fans and regional partners have expressed concern in recent weeks that budget constraints, production issues and weak audience demand could imperil the spinoff. Organizers say the contest could take time to build an audience.
“It would be profoundly arrogant to think that just because we have a heritage brand and a huge global audience for the European show, that we would walk in and demand it to be the same here,” said Martin Green, the European Broadcasting Union’s director of the Eurovision Song Contest. “Like any new thing, it needs to find its roots.”
Two previous attempts to take the competition to Asia were abandoned by the European Broadcasting Union, which owns Eurovision, and its partners in the region. A Eurovision spinoff in the United States, NBC’s American Song Contest, ran for one season in 2022.
The Asian edition kicking off on Saturday is far smaller than its European counterpart. Eurovision organizers said they were in talks with more countries to join future seasons. They include China, Japan and India, whose music industries have global reach.
“Bringing the world together through music is a fundamentally good idea,” Mr. Green said. “Europe shouldn’t keep it to itself.”
Here’s what we’re covering:
- Ballads: Nine of the competition’s 11 participating countries picked performers singing about love in a wide range of styles, from ballads to a cappella hip-hop. Their choices suggest that the bombastic music often associated with victors of the European edition might not be a winning formula for Asian viewers. Read more ›
- Fans: Our reporter spoke to some of the fans who traveled to Bangkok for Eurovision. Read more ›
- Politics: Geopolitics have long intruded on the European edition of the Eurovision Song Contest, but they were not really a factor as the event prepared to expand into Asia. Read more ›
- No shows: For a competition meant to introduce the diversity of Asian pop music to the world, the lineup for the first Eurovision Song Contest Asia has several notable absences, starting with China and India. Read more ›
As Thailand’s Mang and Daou waited to learn whether they had won, the 26-year-old Mang was shown onscreen crying as if she couldn’t take the tension. That’s the sort of emotion needed to make Eurovision’s expansion into Asia a success. Acts have to want the title. But the show will also need the big Asian nations -- India, Japan and China -- to buy in, and much could now depend on the reaction in the Philippines to Carmelle’s win. The event was far less spectacular than a typical Eurovision in Europe. It also featured far too many ballads for my taste, but it was a fun afternoon’s viewing.
The jury votes are all in, and it’s close. The Philippines is first with 93 points, Vietnam second with 83 points and Malaysia third with 82 points. We’re about to learn how many points each country’s act received from the public, starting with the current last place act, Bangladesh’s beatboxing-heavy crew Beatmosphere. It has 16 points.
One of the best parts of Eurovision is how the public’s choice is often completely diffferent from those of the juries, so don’t worry if your favorite act isn’t top of the ranking after the jury votes are all in. The Philippine’s jury, the first we’ve heard from, just gave its 12 points to Malaysia. That doesn’t mean it’ll win
The problem Eurovision has with interval acts like Jeff Satur is that their stagecraft, singing ability and melodies are often a million times better than the artists in competition. Satur, who has 1.4 million monthly listeners on Spotify and over five million Instagram fans, has dozens of camp dancers onstage and a statue of a dragon. He would have cruised to victory if he’d been in competition, especially because of his ability to hold high notes close to the range only dogs can hear.
Simon Robinson, one of the fans who traveled to Bangkok for the Eurovision Song Contest on Saturday, said that his history with the competition is nearly as long as its seven-decade run.
He was eight years old when he first watched it with his family in Yorkshire, England, when Britain's Mary Hopkin finished in second place behind Ireland’s Dana.
“I really liked the concept of bringing Europe together after the war,” said Mr. Robinson, 63, who now lives in Melbourne, Australia. He described the contest’s annual broadcast as a social activity for his family and neighbors.
“Eurovision helped to create the European identity,” he added.
Other fans had their own motivations for traveling to see the contest’s first Asian edition.
Some are Europeans living in Asia, on the hunt for nostalgia, while others are Americans who were eager to experience their first Eurovision.
Lee Hudson, an American television executive based in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, said that he gets emotional when he talks about Eurovision, which he has watched since 2012.
“The only reason I know any music from European countries is because I heard them on Eurovision,” he said. “Eurovision Asia makes sense because the musical cultures are distinct.”
Mr. Hudson said he still listens to Loreen’s “Euphoria,” which won the competition for Sweden in 2012.
It was also the first Eurovision that Drew Andrea watched from his home in Sydney. A year later, he got a passport to fly to Sweden for the 2013 edition, and has attended every final since. Coming to Bangkok for Eurovision Asia was much more affordable, he said.
“Asia understands the brief — the kitschy costumes, the dance music,” he said.
His top picks among the Asian performers were the Philippines’ Carmelle and Vietnam’s Toc Tien. “I think they hit the nail on the head with the song, staging, costume and traditional elements,” he said.
Luca Cian, a professor of marketing at the University of Virginia who grew up in Italy, said that Eurovision built a global fan base by offering a shared cultural experience.
“Millions of people across Europe watch it at the same moment,” he said. “Families have watch parties with food and drinks. There are public discussions. Rituals create community.”
Carmen Chung, a British accountant, said she hijacked her family’s holiday in Bangkok to attend Eurovision Asia with her brother Garry Chung, a banker who lives in Hong Kong. “We were raised on Eurovision,” she said of their childhood in Yorkshire.
European acts, she said, tend to copy whatever style of music won the previous year. “This year, because there are no expectations, everyone has just done their own thing,” she said. She and her brother said they were rooting for Bangladesh’s Beatmosphere, a beatboxing group that will perform an a cappella love song.
Martin Green, the director of the Eurovision Song Contest, said that about half of the tickets for Saturday’s final were purchased by “super fans” from outside Asia. Organizers have kept the inaugural show modest, with 11 participating countries and a 5,000-seat venue.
Mr. Andrea said he didn’t mind the small scale.
“I’m O.K. with humble beginnings as long as it keeps growing every year,” he said.
The presenters are talking to the artists in the green room and trying to get them to talk excitedly about Bulgaria, the country that will host the 2027 Eurovision Song Contest. The winner tonight might get to perform at that event. That seems to be making this show less about Asia itself than a spin-off of the main Eurovision event
Eurovision voting involves two parts. Juries representing music industry professionals from each country are allocated half the votes, and the viewing public decides the other half. To try to build tension, the show always announces the jury votes first by going live to representatives from each country who reveals their top acts. In the European edition of the contest, some of those spokespeople are celebrities, and often they try to give mini speeches or make jokes. This part of the show is always awful. You have been warned.
Reporting from Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia
Mohamad Iqbal Dzulqarnain, an Aina Abdul fan in Kuala Lumpur, said he felt her performance was better than the recording version.
“She left no crumbs,” he said. “She is going to win the contest.”
We’ll see.
For a competition meant to introduce the diversity of Asian pop music to the world, the lineup for the first Eurovision Song Contest Asia has several notable absences.
For starters, the continent’s four most populous nations — China, India, Pakistan and Indonesia — won’t be there. Even Japan, a country globally considered a cultural powerhouse, is absent.
That leaves some of the region’s best-known musical cultures out of the mix. India has Bollywood hits. China has produced both Mandopop and Cantopop, the genre associated with Hong Kong pop stars. JPop was once huge across Asia.
As a result, the only large pop powerhouse in this contest is South Korea.
China’s absence is relatively simple to explain. Performers are entered by local broadcasters, and Eurovision has long had a messy relationship with China’s, which are heavily regulated and try to reflect the government’s social and political values. Mango TV once had a deal to broadcast the high-camp Eurovision to Chinese viewers, but Eurovision abruptly canceled it in 2018 after Mango TV censored acts whose performances featured gay themes. It also blurred rainbow flags in the performance arena.
Frank-Dieter Freiling, a former Eurovision official, said in an interview that such censorship was against Eurovision’s values and that the show’s organizers had historically barred broadcasters from airing the competition with delays.
It’s less clear why broadcasters from India, Pakistan, Japan and Indonesia are not participating. Assaf Blecher, Eurovision Asia’s executive producer, said that conversations with Chinese, Japanese and Indian broadcasters had not concluded in time. But he insisted that they “are knocking on our door.”
Not participating saves those countries the potential embarrassment of being the regional power that comes in last.
Just look to Europe, where Britain and Germany often perform badly at Eurovision. In this year’s show, Britain’s Look Mum No Computer placed last, scoring only one point, while Germany finished third from last. Whenever that happens, political commentators give interviews suggesting that the results reflect those countries’ poor standing across Europe.
Here at the watch party in Kathmandu, Pratik’s relatives are happy with his performance.
“His voice was cracking during the selection round in Nepal,” said Sunita Rai, his sister-in-law. “Today’s performance was much more powerful.”
His relatives have been on social media all night, urging their friends who live overseas to vote for him. (You can’t vote for your own country’s performer.)
The presenters have just announced a technical issue! When Laos’s Thinla performed earlier, she had an earpiece problem and was unable to hear her own music. So that explains why she sang so out of tune. They’re now playing a recording of an earlier performance to everyone to try to ensure the event is fair
Reporting from Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia
Rizal Kamal, a senior adviser to the Arts, Live Festival and Events Association, an entertainment nonprofit based in Malaysia, said he felt that Aina Abdul was the right singer to represent the country at Eurovision.
“Aina is seasoned in major competitions and she knows how to wow both the judges and the audience,” he said. “I am filled with pride.”
Reporting from Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia
Aina Abdul’s inventive wardrobe and her powerful voice sets her apart from the Asian peers, said Adriana Syuhaidah, a fan in Kuala Lumpur.
“She is the Lady Gaga of Malaysia,” she said.
When they sat down to plan the final show of the inaugural Eurovision Song Contest in Asia, the organizers faced a challenge: How could they introduce variety when most of the entries were slow-paced love songs?
Nine of the competition’s 11 participating countries picked performers singing about love in a wide range of styles, from ballads to a cappella hip-hop. Their choices suggest that the bombastic music often associated with victors of the European edition might not be a winning formula for Asian viewers.
“Europeans tend to prefer songs with a crescendo, a hook and a grand ending, but also a strong social message,” said Dean Vuletic, a historian of contemporary Europe at the University of Luxembourg who is an authority on Eurovision.
“The audience doesn’t want to see an innocuous pop song,” he said.
Electro-pop and dance songs have featured heavily on the list of Eurovision winners over the past decade. In May, Bulgaria’s Dara won with “Bangaranga,” a dance-pop song inspired by her diagnosis with attention deficit hyperactive disorder. Nemo, from Switzerland, won in 2024 with an EDM opera about their nonbinary identity, while in 2018, Israel’s Netta won with “Toy,” a pop anthem about female independence.
Some countries hold a nationwide contest to select an artist and a song to represent them in Eurovision, while others leave the choice to Eurovision’s local broadcasting partner. Audiences in the Philippines voted for Carmelle in a televised competition, for example, while Vietnam Television chose Toc Tien.
The two are considered front-runners in the Asian edition, with their high-energy folk-pop songs about female empowerment.
Malaysia’s Aina Abdul, another early favorite, will showcase her powerful vocals in “Bluest Sky,” a ballad with an orchestral arrangement that is about a troubled relationship. The track is reminiscent of “Wasted Love,” an opera-techno song that won Austria the European title in 2025.
Pratik Himal Rai of Nepal, who got married this summer, said love was easy to sing about because it can be understood across borders and languages.
“It is love that holds the world together,” he said in an interview.
He will sing “Ananta Maya” in Nepali. Other Eurovision Asia artists blend English lyrics with their national languages.
In Europe, every winning song after 2022 has been in English. That year’s champion, Ukraine's Kalush Orchestra, sang in their own language on “Stefania,” a hip-hop track that interspersed a Ukrainian lullaby with rap verses and traditional woodwind instruments.
Winning songs tend to blend a country’s national instruments and musical motifs with internationally trendy pop, Mr. Vuletic said.
A traditional Bhutanese flute can be heard in “Lhayi Semo,” Nyendra’s love ballad. Monetrey’s “I Let You Go” uses a Cambodian bamboo xylophone and a tro, a string instrument played with a bow. A kulintang, a percussion instrument made of eight brass gongs, keeps the fast beat in Carmelle’s “Sobra-Sobra.”

Divers explore recently scuttled SS United States in new video
The ship, which was once the fastest in the world and longer than the Titanic, was intentionally sunk off the coast of Florida, in order to create the world's largest artificial ocean reef.
The SS United States spent nearly 30 years docked in Philadelphia before it was moved to Florida, where it will become a home for sea life and an underwater attraction for marine enthusiasts.
Activists unsuccessfully fought for the historic liner - which crossed the Atlantic Ocean hundreds of times - to be preserved as a museum.

- Mojang revealed the Minecraft Throwing Disc weapon during TwitchCon San Diego on November 14, 2026.
- The weapon will have five crafting tiers: Copper, Iron, Gold, Diamond, and Netherite.
- The Bedrock Edition will finally receive full off-hand support similar to the Java Edition as well.
During TwitchCon San Diego on November 14, Mojang Studios revealed the Throwing Disc, a brand-new ranged weapon coming to Minecraft’s first game drop in 2027. But that’s not all: the developers also confirmed that Bedrock Edition is finally getting full off-hand support, narrowing the gap with the Java Edition.
The new Minecraft Throwing Disc is a ranged weapon that works a lot like a boomerang. You can just equip it, throw it at the enemy mobs in Minecraft or at literally any surface, and watch it trace its path right back to your hands. Honestly, I can’t wait to grab one and start taking down creepers like I’m holding the Vibranium shield.
The best part of this new throwing disc weapon in Minecraft is not just that it can return without the need for an enchantment. Instead, it’s the Throwing Disc’s ricocheting mechanic.
Although the Disc doesn’t travel particularly far when thrown normally, it can bounce off hard surfaces, such as walls and the ground, to extend its trajectory. This opens up an opportunity for trick shots, especially in enclosed areas, such as when defeating waves of mobs inside the Trial Chambers in Minecraft.
Furthermore, the Throwing Disc in Minecraft can pass through multiple enemies in its path, allowing you to damage several mobs in a throw. With that said, the weapon comes in five crafting tiers as follows:
- Copper Throwing Disc
- Iron Throwing Disc
- Golden Throwing Disc
- Diamond Throwing Disc
- Netherite Throwing Disc
Alongside the new weapons, Mojang confirmed another long-requested feature, that now the Bedrock Edition players will be able to equip a wider variety of items in their off-hand, including tools, and pickaxes.
Java Edition has had this functionality since 2016, whereas Bedrock players have been limited to just a few compatible items. Although the exact release date or version hasn’t been announced, we can speculate that all these features will arrive for the Minecraft Spring Drop in March 2027.
