The investigation started with a tip from a British couple.
After trying to have a second child for several years, they had signed up with a U.S.-based company called International Fertility Group (IFG), paying tens of thousands of dollars for access abroad to an experimental fertility procedure illegal in the U.S. and tightly regulated in the U.K. The procedure, known as MRT — for mitochondrial replacement techniques — is sometimes called “three-parent IVF,” because it involves creating embryos that combine the genes of a mother and father with a bit of DNA from the mitochondria of a third person.
In the U.K., MRT is allowed at only one academic medical center, and only for the purposes of lowering the risk of passing on mitochondrial disease. But according to IFG, the procedure could also help older women overcome issues that make the odds of IVF go down significantly after the age of 40. Despite being a doctor herself, the woman in the couple had been taken in by the hope of a miracle.
Her husband reached out to me concerned the claims were unfounded, and hoping STAT could look into it.
Over the past eight months, my reporting took me inside an emerging international MRT tourism industry. It led me to IFG’s headquarters in an office park outside of Chicago and to one of its partners in Albania, an upscale fertility clinic where a Turkish embryologist living in Slovakia would fly in monthly to perform the procedure on IFG clients’ eggs or embryos. With the help of an Albanian journalist, Inva Hasanaliaj, we dug into corporate registration and medical licensing records. Freelance science reporter Edward Chen helped us to gather the stories of current and former IFG clients and interview scientists, including the world’s top MRT researchers.
All of this reporting was undertaken in an effort to understand what is driving demand for this unproven procedure, what risks women are taking to seek it out, and how commercial claims stack up against the science. Here’s what we found.
Evidence that MRT can effectively treat age-related infertility is lacking
Currently, there are no peer-reviewed studies in humans supporting the idea that MRT can overcome infertility issues caused by aging, especially in women 35 years and older. A pilot study from a fertility clinic in Greece, published in 2023, reported that MRT could improve live birth rates for women under the age of 40, but the biggest improvements occurred among the youngest patients. For the 12 patients who were 39 at the time of MRT, the live birth rate was less than 10%.
Researchers affiliated with IFG did present some data in a conference abstract for a 2025 European scientific meeting, claiming that among 66 patients with a mean age of 39, live birth rates following MRT reached rates of 40% or higher. But scientists told STAT the abstract lacked key information required to support that claim, and a conference organizer questioned whether it should have been accepted.
The most compelling evidence it might work in older women comes from a single lab study in mice. But even the underlying hypothesis that mitochondrial dysfunction contributes to age-related infertility is supported by very little direct evidence, experts told STAT.
And, in fact, data obtained by STAT shows MRT doesn’t work for patients of advanced maternal age
Before Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Kyiv was poised to become the MRT capital of the world. Women traveled from Europe, Israel, and the U.S. to at least three clinics there offering it as an infertility treatment. Unpublished data from the Nadiya Clinic — the most advanced operation in Kyiv — shows that a form of MRT called pronuclear transfer did not improve the odds of IVF for older women. Among 19 patients aged 36 to 44, only one gave birth to a baby following pronuclear transfer.
In contrast, among 10 infertile patients under the age of 35, MRT resulted in nine live births.
That hasn’t stopped reproductive tourism agencies and fertility clinics overseas from marketing MRT to older women
For the past few years, International Fertility Group has advertised its MRT program as “a groundbreaking fertility treatment that offers renewed hope to women with advanced maternal age or a history of failed cycles.” The company’s social media posts about MRT frequently targeted women over the age of 35, and its own internal data showed its clients were skewing older. According to an IFG webinar from February, the average age of a patient in the company’s MRT program was 39.2 years old in 2022; last year it was 45.6 years old.
After STAT contacted IFG about these materials, which several experts described as “misleading” and “unethical,” the company removed them. In a statement, IFG acknowledged that the evidence for MRT remains limited and emphasized that its role is to provide nonmedical support to patients. “IFG does not characterize innovative treatment as guaranteed, routine, or risk-free,” the statement said. “Patients are not promised a pregnancy, a live birth, or any particular outcome.”
The company’s MRT program is currently on pause. Last week, hours after STAT’s investigation was published, Birol Aydin, the Turkish embryologist who performed the procedure for IFG clients in Albania, announced on LinkedIn that he was stepping back from clinical work to focus on research.
Clinics unaffiliated with IFG operating in Mexico and the Bahamas are continuing to market MRT as a fertility treatment to women 40 and older as a way to combat age-related declines in egg quality. Neither has published any outcome data.
Bioethicists worry about patients being misled and possible health risks for resulting children
The concerns are twofold. First, that companies are profiting from selling false hope to people with a strong desire to try everything possible to have genetically related children. And second, that children born through commercial MRT won’t be monitored for any adverse health effects that might emerge later in their lives.
Scientists still see promise that it could work better than conventional IVF for some forms of infertility in younger women
Data from the Nadiya Clinic underscore similar results from that 2023 pilot study in Greece, showing that a different form of MRT, called maternal spindle transfer, could help women under the age of 35 with a history of severe infertility get pregnant and have children.
Researchers at Ghent University are currently launching a small study of MRT for addressing these types of fertility failures, which collectively are called OZEMA (for oocyte, zygote, and embryo maturation arrest). Initial results are expected sometime next year. Positive outcomes would add to the increasing pressure to ease restrictions on human trials of MRT for infertility in countries where such studies are currently banned, including the U.S., so that people don’t have to go abroad.

Rest assured this week that while Outlook, Teams, and other Microsoft services were flatlining, the company’s billing operations were still firing on all cylinders. Copilot can’t run on air alone, after all. It needs cash.
The silver lining to the week is that, in the light of our global recovery from one of the most debilitating tech outages in recent memory, Microsoft now owes you compensation. And depending on the size of your operation and the degree to which you rely on Microsoft products, the payout could be substantial.
If you have a business relationship with Microsoft—a subscription to a Microsoft 365 Business plan, email hosted on Microsoft Exchange, or perhaps a Teams Premium tier—that relationship is governed by reams of documentation, among them being a Service Level Agreement.
Service Level Agreements, or SLAs, are old hat to large enterprises who use them to hold accountable service providers like web hosts and email services, ensuring they stay online and operational—and they are often in the realm of demanding 99.99 percent reliability or higher, as is the default promise with Microsoft Azure. If a provider fails to hit the promised availability level, the customer is due a refund (or credit towards next month’s bill, at least).
But SLAs don’t only apply to the Fortune 500. If you have a business account with Microsoft, no matter how small it is, your service is also governed by these promises. And now, Microsoft owes you compensation.
“Business account” is the key phrase in the above, mind you. If you have a Microsoft 365 Family plan or any other individual or personal plan, you are basically out of luck. Outlook could go offline for a month, and you wouldn’t be entitled to anything aside from a series of pointed Facebook posts.
The consumer Microsoft Services Agreement states that individual users can get refunds or credits at Microsoft’s “sole discretion,” but it doesn’t even mention SLAs and promises nothing in the way of uptime. In other words, if your email system wasn’t working for you on November 12, you can ask for money back, but your odds of receiving anything are low.
The Fine Print Is in Your Favor for Once
Business users are in a much more advantageous position, though Microsoft doesn’t exactly go out of its way to guide you through the refund process. SLA refunds are not automatic. You have to request them for each incident, and the process is hardly straightforward.
To figure out what you’re owed, start by taking a look at the SLA for Microsoft’s Online Services. (This is different than the above consumer Microsoft Services Agreement.) It’s more than 53,000 words long, and quite repetitive, but I’ll digest the important facts for you here.
While many of the promised service levels are identical, start by double-checking the specific Microsoft products you use, as the SLA is broken down by product. A search for “Exchange Online” reveals everything you need to know, in surprisingly plain English.
Downtime is defined as “Any period of time when users are unable to send or receive email with Outlook Web Access.”
Uptime Percentage is calculated by a simple formula: Subtract the minutes of downtime from your total User Minutes, then divide the result by your total User Minutes. Take that result and multiply it by 100.
“Downtime is measured in user-minutes; that is, for each Applicable Period, Downtime is the sum of the length (in minutes) of each Incident that occurs during that Applicable Period multiplied by the number of users impacted by that Incident.”
User Minutes is the total number of minutes in the billing cycle; typically 30 days.
If the calculated Uptime Percentage falls below 99.9 percent, you are entitled to credit (not a cash refund) under the following terms:
| Uptime Percentage | Service Credit | 
|---|---|
| < 99.9% | 25% | 
| < 99.5% | 50% | 
| < 95% | 100% | 
If we assume the outage lasted about 18 hours for you, that equates to a 2.5 percent Downtime Percentage or a 97.5 percent Uptime Percentage for a 30-day billing cycle. And that puts you squarely in 50 percent Service Credit territory.
How to File for Compensation
While Microsoft is transparent about what you are owed, it has less to say about what you have to do to receive it.
The SLA simply states that “In order for Microsoft to consider a claim, you must submit the claim to customer support at Microsoft Corporation including all information necessary for Microsoft to validate the claim.” You are also directed to supply the following:
That’s a lot of information, but Microsoft likely does not need much in the way of (i) , (ii), or (v) to validate this global incident. You will need to supply the name or your “affected resource” and how many users were impacted. For the sake of completeness, include in your message the codes for outages for Exchange (EX1550543), Outlook (MO1550821), and Teams (TM1550488) as relevant to your business.
I also did the math on what my various Microsoft subscriptions cost. I only have two, Exchange Online and Microsoft 365 Business Standard, both of which were impacted by the outage. Total price of my last bill: $24.88. Thus, total credit due: $12.44. That may barely be beer money for me, but a company of 100 people will likely be owed over $1,000. If you don’t have these numbers handy, you’ll find them under Billing > Bills & Payments in the Microsoft 365 Admin Center.
With that information collected, then what? Microsoft simply directs you to file a claim with customer service, so that’s exactly what I did. In the same Admin Center, the method to file an email service request is a little tricky. It’s not in the left-hand navigation but rather can be found on the bottom right of the screen. Click the headset icon which expands to reveal “Help & support.” This will default you to Microsoft’s AI chatbot. Within this page, click the headset icon at the top of the screen, which will take you to a “Contact support” page. Choose Email from this screen, and fill in the form with the information you’ve collected.
Your submission should garner a quick response that includes a case number tracking ID. I filed for compensation on Friday and haven’t received any other response yet than a confirmation of receipt, but considering that 12 principal-filled dollars are on the line, you can bet I’ll be tracking it closely.
As a final note: Be aware that claims must be submitted by the end of the month following the outage. So you have until December 31, 2026 to file your claim for the November 12 incident.
I reached out to Microsoft for comment on this story and a PR rep said she would “let me know if the company has anything to share” while offering the same statement you have probably seen too many times already: “We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners. We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously.”
Now we’ll see how seriously it takes the refund process.

New world order will be more multipolar and transactional: Jaishankar at HT Leadership Summit
Jaishankar said this new order is taking shape at a time when the world is navigating “very stormy seas" amid multiple conflicts.
The new world order taking shape will be more multipolar and transactional, with more centres of autonomous decision-making, thereby making it more unstable and setting the stage for sharper competition, External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar said on Saturday.
Speaking at the 24th Hindustan Times Leadership Summit, Jaishankar said this new order is taking shape at a time when the world is navigating “very stormy seas” because of multiple conflicts, including those in Ukraine and West Asia, the grim situation in parts of Africa, and disruptions and volatility in food and fuel supplies.
“The general acceptance is that the new order would be more multipolar, that there’d be many more centres of autonomous decision-making. Countries overall would be much more national in their choices and in their decisions,” he said in a conversation with HT's Editor-In-Chief R Sukumar.
Deep Dive
“The alliances will be less cohesive because of national interests and more transactional, because they feed into each other — less cohesive, more transactional; more transactional, less cohesive.”
The new world order will also be one of “more variables”, and “much more complex [and] less predictable” because there are more players, who are also more self-centered. “That will be the culture or the ethos of the era that we are moving into. I don’t want you to get a sort of picture of an anarchy, but definitely sharper competition, more national assertions, and in that sense inherently more unstable,” Jaishankar said.
Jaishankar acknowledged that the world was “in a mess” and charting “very stormy seas”, with global headwinds having consequences for India. The changes underway have been exacerbated by the wars in Ukraine and West Asia, the grim situation in Sudan and Central Africa, the volatility of food and fuel prices, and the continuing fallout of the Covid-19 pandemic, he said.
“Five years ago, it would have been inconceivable in this day and age, when everything is so globalised and interdependent, that we could have a major war. We’ve actually had that war now into its fifth year,” he said, referring to the Russia-Ukraine conflict.
“What you see in the Gulf — the idea that countries would actually be firing missiles at each other, targeting bases, cities, forces, leaderships — would have been something which people would have rated its chances as pretty near zero,” he said, adding that the situation in West Asia had become “much more bitter and intractable” since the terror attacks by Hamas in October 2023.
Food exports from Ukraine and Russia were stuck in the Black Sea, impacting global food prices, including those in India, while fuel prices too were rising because of disruptions, he said.
Tackling these challenges requires strong, steady and experienced leadership that “knows how to get the country through this, because the compass for navigating it is our national interest”, Jaishankar said.
“When we look at all these challenges, when people ask us where do you stand on Ukraine or where do you stand on the Gulf or what is your view on a particular challenge, we will view it understandably through the lens of our national interest. That’s the compass which will guide us,” he said, adding this turbulence will show up in different ways till the end of the current decade.
The turbulence on the global stage is being driven by multiple causes, though US-China competition is a “big part of the overall…disturbance or volatility”, Jaishankar said. “One part of it is when countries get caught up in between, but it’s also led to the US itself changing the manner in which it approaches the world,” he said.
The changes underway have acquired a greater degree of sharpness amid the US-China competition and a marked change in Washington’s approach towards even its long-standing partners. The US’s focus on reindustrialising to ensure it isn’t excessively dependent on a particular country or geography has also led to vulnerability. “One part of it is to look at a US-China competition in a very orthodox way. But if you look at it more deeply…each one of these feeds into the other and a big part of it is really the changed approach of the US to the world, even to its friends and allies,” Jaishankar said.
The US was politically dominant in the world order put in place after World War II because it was willing to underwrite economic arrangements as they served American interests. But things changed, going back to the term of former president Joe Biden, as the US found that the rules “it was underwriting had been gamed to its disadvantage”, he pointed out.
“The US, which was a big energy importer from the Gulf, today is self-sufficient and an energy exporter. If it was an energy importer today, I’m not sure many of the events which are happening in the Gulf would still be happening,” Jaishankar said.
As the energy scenario has significantly changed, technology gaps have grown, and there has been a revolution in warfare, the political atmosphere has led to greater propensity to take risks. “It’s a more competitive word, it’s also a much more risk-taking word, and not limited to the US,” Jaishankar said. “Other players are also taking risks. Everybody is pushing the envelope [and] the more powerful are able to push the envelope much stronger and on many more issues.”
With the world in a transitional phase, there is an expectation that the new order will have a “much stronger role of India or much stronger influence by India”, Jaishankar said. This will require stronger domestic capacities, including through initiatives such as Atmanirbhar Bharat (Self-Reliant India), Make in India and Innovate in India, which are the building blocks of foreign policy.
At the same time, India will have to reforge relationships, diversify and de-risk. “In the last decade, we have laid a very solid foundation…with this very strong push for industrialisation because…we missed the manufacturing bus. That for us, [from] the 1960s to the end of the 1990s, we may have had reform, but these were really lost decades. Even the reform was only a correction and a partial correction of what were lost decades before 1992,” he said.
India has to build itself into a manufacturing power and acquire the technologies and capabilities needed for the contemporary era, including through schemes such as the Production-Linked Incentives (PLI) initiative. “We have to become economically competitive, which means much better infrastructure and logistics. We have to improve our talent, which means more educational institutions, more skilling. But we’ll also have to invest in semiconductors, We’ll have to invest in upgrading life sciences. We’ll have to look at preparing for the AI era,” he said. “We’ll have to address multiple levels in order to navigate those stormy seas.”

As of this morning, Microsoft is still scrambling to restore service following yesterday’s global outage, with millions of users unable to access Outlook and other vital tools. It’s not the end of the world, but it does seem fitting that this should happen on the day a physicist predicted would be the end of humanity: November 13, 2026. And it falls on a Friday, too. The physicist in question is Heinz von Foerster, who published a 1960 paper in the journal Science predicting that by today, overpopulation would reach the breaking point.
It’s not a new fear. English economist Thomas Malthus—one of the early pioneers in modeling population dynamics—made a similar prediction in 1798, claiming that a rapidly growing population would eventually exhaust the available food supply, and humanity would starve to death. His model rested on the assumption of exponential growth, but the equation is only applicable under specific conditions, such as scientists growing bacteria in a lab in a perfectly controlled environment. Even then, while growth occurs exponentially for a time, it does not continue forever.
Population dynamics are notoriously tricky to calculate because there are so many variables to consider and so much unpredictability in the system. In his 1960 analysis, Von Foerster accurately measured past trends in population growth, but like Malthus, he assumed those trends would carry into the future largely unchanged. So he projected that human population growth would march inexorably toward infinity. We wouldn’t starve to death; von Foerster thought we would be ingenious enough to solve the food supply problem. Instead, “they will be squeezed to death,” he wrote.
Plenty of scholars objected at the time, dismissing von Foerster’s conclusion as “ridiculous” and “manifestly absurd.” The global population did not keep accelerating at an exponential rate; the baby boom petered out just a few years after von Foerster published his paper.
“He got the picture right just as that picture ceased to be right,” mathematical biologist Joel Cohen of Rockefeller University and Columbia University recently told Popular Science. “The all-time peak happened in the early 1960s.” Nor did von Foerster foresee the impacts of longer life expectancy and the sharp decline in child mortality rates.

Jensen Huang’s midlife-crisis makeover hasn’t helped the Nvidia CEO’s image this week. In a matter of days, Huang’s questionable sartorial leanings have shifted wildly from wannabe cool Harley dad to low-down leather Lothario. Fashion moves fast, but even in the style world, this is a breakneck volte-face.
As Emma Childs wonderfully observed in The Cut, “a $9,000 leather moto is not the outerwear of a man faithfully going home to his wife and kids after a long day of architecting the AI revolution.” And since Huang’s tomfoolery has managed to spank more than $1 trillion in less than a month, something has to be done.
This is where WIRED comes to the rescue, aided by Vogue, GQ and a celebrity stylist, no less. We’ve charted the menacing glow-up of tech bros before, but merely observing the worrying trend back in 2025 is clearly no longer enough. It’s time to roll up our Armani sleeves and help.
“Tech bros were total nerds before," says Karen Clarkson, a professional stylist whose clients have included Nike, Google, Apple, Calvin Klein, and Vivienne Westwood. "Fashion didn’t touch their lives at all. They didn’t have style.” Pictures of Huang’s pre-biker fashion-vacuum days certainly bear this out. “Then, like [Jeff] Bezos, they all stepped up. And there’s a rivalry that’s come with that, whether it’s the fashion makeover, the grooming, the skin treatments, or gym regimen. Now we have Mark Zuckerberg in the front row at Prada.”
As a man clearly in dress distress, where better to start than with Murray Clark, head of editorial at British GQ. Controversially, Clark has a radical notion that Huang should keep clothing matters as they are. “I’d argue that Jensen Huang stays exactly how he is because this is who he is—a coiffed, leather-jacket wearing, mistake-making middle-aged man for all the world to see.”
Before publicly admitting on Sunday to having an affair with a businesswoman who US intelligence says is also a Chinese spy, in 2024, Huang confessed onstage that his wife, Lori, suggested and chose his biker outfits for him because he found most other fabrics “itchy.”
If Jensen keeps his jackets (he apparently owns 30 to 40), Clarkson thinks that Huang might even find himself on the catwalk. “If he wants to go down that route, then for sure Demna [Gucci’s creative director] would have him walking in his next show in Milan,” she says. “But he’s very Arnold Schwarzenegger and the Terminator with his black leathers, which is a bit close to the bone, really, with AI and that humanity is potentially doomed. I don’t know if he’s wise to lean into Arnie too heavily.”
Let’s get some sage advice, then, from Chioma Nnadi, head of editorial at British Vogue. “If I were styling Jensen Huang, I’d advise him to cleanse the palate entirely, ditch the rock and roll shrunken leather jackets for something more somber,” Nnadi says. “A collared Oxford shirt and a navy or gray crewneck jumper would do the trick and wouldn’t read as aggressively corporate as a traditional suit. The message needs to be ‘I’m a serious person, and I’m leaving that tragic try-hard boomer dad wardrobe behind along with my despicable behavior.’”
Clarkson agrees, saying that while the term “unapologetic” is often used in fashion, in this instance, Huang needs a more apologetic dress code, moving away from anything too flashy. So out go the overtly sexual Tom Ford leathers—which Jensen can handily sell off for $1 million a pop to his Huang-boys to offset any alimony outlays that may, or may not, be coming his way—and in come understated and neutral tones.
“He could take a leaf out of Harry Styles’ dress down codes and check The Row for minimal looks,” Clarkson says. “A Lemaire workwear jacket is also a good vibe. It shows he’s willing to put in the work to win back his family. Also, since he’s spoken about feeling itchy, maybe he should repent a bit and wear lambswool instead of cashmere.”
Asking Clarkson to step away from her celebrity clients for a moment to perform a hasty hypothetical make under (or glow down?) for Huang, she has very kindly put together three outfits that I think we can all agree give off considerably fewer bad-egg biker vibes with pieces from Paul Smith, The Row, Lemaire, Giorgio Armani, Brunello Cucinelli, and more. If you’re lucky enough to have a budget to match Huang's, we’ve added links to the individual pieces in the captions under each “look.”
“There’s been a lot of tight-fitted leather jackets that just about cover his biceps, which always feels like he’s looking to lure his next lover or like he’s just whizzed off on his Ducati to have a quick lunchtime visit with his mistress,” says Clarkson. “That’s not the vibe you want to go before Congress with.” For the Hill, she suggests Huang go for a Nehru collar that “feels a bit more buttoned up.”
However, because Huang’s existing look is so strong, Clarkson advises that changing it too quickly will not only draw an enormous amount of commentary but even more memes. “Little steps, not a full overnight makeover. That’s why he should perhaps keep the leather jacket, something like a suede blouson instead of the biker,” she says, adding that the black jeans should be ditched in favor of proper pants.
“He could do a tie as well—a bit more apologetic, a bit more formal, a bit more respectful. So a brown leather jacket with a tie and a shirt—so then it’s a segue into a new direction,” Clarkson says, citing Giorgio Armani’s June Milan collection as ideal inspiration.
However, Clarkson says credit must ultimately go to Lori Huang, Jensen’s wife of 41 years. “She did a brilliant job. If anyone comes out of this as a winner, it’s her. She could rebrand as a Hollywood stylist at this point because she’s done a great job of creating an identity for her husband. Almost too good because it’s attracted too many women. Still, she could step away with a really great divorce settlement and a whole new career.”

Why some USB ports are yellow (and less common than others)
Yellow USB-A ports usually mean Always On charging, but the particulars are up to the manufacturer.
A yellow USB port usually marks an "Always On" port, meaning it will continue to charge your device once you turn the computer off. It's one of several colors on USB-A ports, but none are an industry standard.
For example, the USB Implementers Forum (USB-IF) recommends one insert color, a specific blue, to help people tell the difference between USB 2.0 and USB 3.0 ports. However, this is just a suggestion, not a mandate. Every other color, yellow included, is a convention manufacturers can follow or not.
Lenovo, for example, jumps around with colors. The older IdeaPad Y400 and Y500 feature yellow USB-A ports that are specifically for Always On charging. Later Lenovo models dropped the yellow entirely and replaced it with battery icons.
Always On still needs power, and sometimes a setting
Yellow USB-A ports are not a common sight because they're a specialty feature that manufacturers only include on specific enterprise or business laptops. Manufacturers are also shifting toward symbols instead of a variety of colors.
A battery symbol next to a USB port indicates a port that's good for charging. A trident symbol also indicates the USB implementation, like USB 3.0 or USB4. On top of that, USB-C ports on many PCs and laptops are skipping the color coding entirely, since one connector shape tends to cover a wide range of capabilities.
If you come across a yellow port, don't assume it's ready to roll right out of the box. Depending on the PC or laptop, you may have to enable the Always On setting in the BIOS. Some laptops also ship with the "Charge in Battery Mode" disabled, so you can only charge devices when the laptop is plugged into AC power.
Which USB port color is faster?
Red is generally the fastest of the color-coded USB-A ports and is commonly used for 10 Gbps to 20 Gbps connections. Yellow doesn't really have a spot on the speed ladder, and color charts can't even agree on its place. Corsair lists yellow ports as either USB 2.0 or USB 3.0, and USB Memory Direct's color guide places yellow on a level playing field with red.
If you see a teal USB-A port, you're probably looking at a USB 3.1 Gen 2 or USB 3.2 Gen 2 connection, with speeds up to 10 Gbps. Black and white USB-A ports sit on the lower end, while blue is typically 5 Gbps USB 3.0. Everything you just read is subject to manufacturers' discretion.
Charts just aren't a safe bet for confirming data transfer speeds. If a yellow port turns out to be USB 2.0, it'll work fine for a keyboard, mouse or basic accessories. An external SSD, on the other hand, needs to be plugged into a port with a 5 Gbps rating or higher.
While yellow may indicate Always On charging, the only way to know for certain is to check for a label or icon, then confirm it in the user manual or on the manufacturer's spec page.

MILWAUKEE — Kat Zilka sat on the floor of her living room, beside a glowing Christmas tree and a pile of essays, and felt like weeping. It was late in 2022, and she had asked her 12th grade digital journalism students to reflect on their relationships to devices.
“The things they were writing were deeply disturbing,” she said.
Teenagers quietly enduring online abuse, using their phones all night without their parents’ knowledge, or trapped in a cycle of deleting and redownloading social media. Their words made real what Zilka had been observing for years — how the light in students’ eyes was dimmer, especially since Covid — and revealed the astonishing magnitude of the problem.
“It was like they were just waiting for someone to ask,” she said.
That semester would change the trajectory of Zilka’s career, and place her at the forefront of an emerging national conversation about kids’ degrading attention, and its effect on their health. At that time, there were no surgeon general advisories on the matter, nor were there dozens of state legislatures clamoring to crack down on phones. It was people like Zilka, on the ground, trying to beat back an encroaching mental health crisis with minimal guidance.
Over winter break, she sketched out an elective course called “Digital Detox.” Students loved the class, she said, in part because Digital Detox was unlike anything else they were doing in school. That began with the first 10 minutes of class, when students would just sit with their thoughts. “Halfway through the semester, they were, like, hankering for it,” Zilka said.
Despite the mostly positive feedback, she felt the course was bound by an unresolved tension: It was adding to the academic pressure, while trying to help students’ mental health.
The students didn’t want more coursework. They wanted a support group.
Zilka thought something spiritually connected to Alcoholics Anonymous, or even the church youth groups of her childhood, could fit the bill. “The opposite of addiction is connection,” she said. Elsewhere in the country, other grassroots experiments began to take shape — all molded by youth, and fueled by a sense of urgency that was absent from mainstream politics and the slow crawl of science.
“Young people are developing today. They don’t really have time for us to wait 10 years to find out how to help them,” Rachel Hanebutt, a Georgetown University researcher studying teens’ relationship to tech, said.
As regulators and researchers, already years behind on the problem, struggle to respond to ever-evolving platforms, homegrown efforts have a distinct advantage, she said: They are nimble.
Some projects teach young people to set hard boundaries with social media, and use rich experiences IRL to draw them away from digital isolation. Others are blatantly political, aiming to turn teenagers’ rebellious streaks on Big Tech itself.
Their collective mission is to give generations of American kids raised with an iPad and schooled with a Chromebook an escape hatch — out of the disorienting blue haze and into the rushing, cool air of the real world.
‘Not real’
Zilka was so convinced by what she saw in Digital Detox that she formed a nonprofit, called dis//connect, and quit her teaching job. The first meeting took place in May 2024.
She also raised a small pot of money, around $1,200. About a year ago, Zilka brought in clinical psychologist Thekla Ross, a leader in the emerging field of “digital harm reduction,” to measure how well the program is working and find ways to expand the model.
Now, on most Monday and Thursday nights, Zilka and Ross gather with about 8 high schoolers in their respective meetings. The hourlong sessions start by logging average daily screen time by hand and slipping silenced phones into a filing box. Then they celebrate the “slow media” they’re consuming, and sit quietly for 10 minutes.
Spread across the tables are a variety of fidget toys, coloring books, and word searches so the teens have something to do with their hands. They talk about what’s on their minds: Friend breakups, frustrating teachers, and toning themselves down in public because someone might be recording (a habit Zilka and Ross dub, in a forthcoming book, “flatlining”).
Caroline, an ambitious rower with a darting gaze and mouthful of braces, is nervous about not making the team for an upcoming tournament in Boston. By Thursday night, she’d made the boat, and was troubled by other ideas.
Tonight’s reading, from Anna Lembke’s “Dopamine Nation,” is about how the author became obsessed with romance novels — a parallel to how social media hijacks the brain’s reward system. Like Lembke, Caroline has recently struggled to read anything but love stories.
“I didn’t even think about it until now,” she said, noting how short she is of her goal of 150 books for the year.
A copy of “To Kill a Mockingbird” sat on her shelf for weeks, and went back to the library untouched, as she devoured romance stories instead. The harder something is for the brain, the more delayed the reward, Zilka acknowledged.
“It can be really hard in our world to convince ourselves to do the delayed gratification thing,” she says.
It all reminds Caroline of a recent discussion in her literature class, about how books have changed as fewer people read for pleasure. She and Tala, a curly-haired friend who’s new to the group, commiserate over the lack of fellow bookworms at school.
Their male counterparts are even less likely to read for fun — or, it seems, come to groups like these. Boys at school are gripped instead by the mind-altering influence of Clavicular and online gambling, the girls say.
“They act … not real,” Caroline says.
(Earlier in the night, a polite overachiever named Ethan said attending dis//connect eased his anxiety about feeling left out on apps like Snapchat. Now less self-conscious, he goes out of his way to wish classmates “happy birthday” to their face. Recently, a girl responded by saying he could’ve texted her instead.)
Boys and girls tend to use the internet about the same amount — four in 10 U.S. teens say they are online almost constantly, according to a 2025 Pew survey of 13-to-17-year-olds. However, boys face different pressures online, such as the meteoric rise of sports betting apps, which experts say build on the alluring design elements of other platforms.
“Convince me that Kalshi, predictive markets, FanDuel, and DraftKings are not social media companies,” said Hanebutt, the Georgetown researcher.
Betting apps could further obscure the nature of digital addiction, who is most vulnerable to harm, and why.
As it is, we don’t really know what phones are doing to us.
‘I guess it’s bad’
Type the words “phone addiction” into a search bar on social media, and you will find a long and seamless scroll of hundreds of videos on the topic.
It might be a surprise, then, to read credible researchers’ disagreements about whether the word “addiction” is the right term for what’s happening. Some, like the prominent Digital Mental Health Group at the University of Cambridge, question whether social media shares the same underlying neurocognitive mechanisms as addictive substances.
But other researchers say the “infinite scroll” and algorithmic feeds are addictive by design, and that heavy users can experience addiction-like symptoms: craving, withdrawal, quitting attempts, and relapse.
“It’s akin to each time you smoke a cigarette, the cigarette itself increasing in nicotine content to you in particular,” said Vikram Bhargava, an assistant professor at the George Washington University business school who studies the ethics of technological innovations.
(Meta, as part of its historic $17.1 billion settlement with dozens of states, agreed to interrupt endless scrolling and add time limits to teen Instagram accounts. The company has denied that its products are addictive.)
The questions don’t stop there. Over a decade after the birth of Instagram, researchers aren’t even sure about whether social media causes mental distress. It might just be feeding into vulnerable people’s underlying problems. Or, it could be doing both. Two people, given the same platform for 30 minutes, can have vastly different experiences.
“It might not be the dose of use — how many hours an adolescent uses social media — but actually the nature of that use,” Kelila Kahane, a psychiatrist and fellow in child and adolescent psychiatry at NewYork-Presbyterian, said.
This is the technological maze researchers find themselves in as they confront the fact that the kids are not alright. Kostadin Kushlev, leader of the Happy Tech Lab at Georgetown University, is one of the people grappling with these unknowns.
His lab received a grant from the National Institute of Mental Health to study how social media directly affects teens’ mental health. The study involves giving a group of 10-to-14-year-olds their first phone. For three months, half the group has as much access to social media as their parents allow, while the other half has none. All of the kids complete brief daily surveys, along with three longer surveys, over the course of six months.
The phones also track their movement, sleep, and online activity, such as most-used apps and what times of day participants are opening them.
“That sort of addresses a second critical issue in the literature: A lot of the evidence is based on these very basic, rudimentary, almost laughable measures of screen time,” Kushlev said. One common metric asks: On a spectrum of “not at all” to “several times per day,” how often did you use your phone in the past week?
Tech companies are still the keepers of the richest datasets, which could actually help researchers tease out differences between users. But in the U.S., the companies are not required to share that information with outside scientists. Most of what we know about the depths of data extraction has come from Silicon Valley whistleblowers, he said.
“It’s so stark when you think about it,” Kushlev said. Researchers spend years designing studies and applying for grants, only to spend bucketloads of money for data that’s less useful than what tech companies already have.
That lackluster data is then driving policy.
“All we have is these negative correlations, and it’s sort of like, ‘Oh, I guess it’s bad, so let’s ban it all,’” he said.
Dozens of states have enacted phone restrictions in recent years, and the Trump administration has encouraged others to pursue “bell-to-bell bans.” Congress too has floated screen time-related bills, including a recent bipartisan proposal that would limit social media use for those under 16.
Evidence is mixed on how well bans work. In Australia, where in 2024 lawmakers banned kids under 16 from making accounts on certain social media platforms, initial data suggest little changed about teens’ reported use.
In some cases, in-school restrictions have been shown to reduce phone usage in class, or marginally improve academic performance in certain subjects. But they can also lead to more disciplinary action or even declines in school performance at the start of the policies. Data are still unclear on whether they provide any long-term mental health benefits.
While it’s too soon to tell what really works, a recent review by the Cambridge group found promising evidence for things that add friction — think: a pause or prompt before opening a certain app — and programs that teach practical digital skills. Teacher- or peer-led sessions focused on attention and self-control also demonstrated some short-term benefit.
“The underlying mechanisms of change may be more important than the intervention level itself,” they wrote.
People leading attention projects intuit something else: Simply taking screens away won’t solve the nation’s problems. Teens need something new to be excited about.
‘Human fracking’
Consider a bright September day on Brooklyn’s picturesque Washington Street, where tourists are weaving around each other, necks craned, snapping pictures of the Manhattan Bridge, its enormous crown poking between historic buildings.
Here, all of a sudden, are a half-dozen teenagers bisecting the cobblestone street, arms lifted, hands assuming the claw shape of a smartphone holder, but grasping only air.
For five minutes, the small band of “attention scholars” does this: Pretends to take pictures of the bridge while surrounded by people trying to take actual pictures of the bridge. After a few minutes, their presence becomes a human barricade, then an attraction — cameras click at them, people stare and giggle. Others frown.
One woman, clad in a sunhat, tries to fill the claw-shaped void with her own cellphone, wordlessly requesting that one of the teens take a picture of her against the backdrop.
Then Jahony Germosen, who has been standing nearby with a timer, rings a bell and the teens file back into the lobby of their building, where they erupt into giddy laughter.
That was a “public intervention” done by “attention activists” training at the Strother School of Radical Attention.
SORA, as insiders call it, is perhaps the best-known group in the U.S. devoted to this kind of work. Started by academics and artists in 2023, it operates as a nexus for a movement that seeks to liberate people’s minds from Big Tech.
“You can think of this as a health problem. You can think of this as a productivity problem. We’re thinking of it as a systemic problem,” Peter Schmidt, SORA’s program director, told STAT. “You need collective action.”
Its weeklong summer camp, now in its third year, introduces young people to the idea of attention as political, and something worth defending. “Our attention is the precondition for our freedom,” Schmidt said.
Some of the campers have never been on social media. They feel that gives them a clearer vision of their peers’ dependence. (STAT agreed to identify participants only by age.)
One participant, a 14-year-old science fiction lover, wasn’t allowed to have a cellphone until seventh grade — later than most American kids — and felt routinely excluded from conversations because of it. SORA camp has been refreshing, she said. “It helps that other people are noticing the same thing.”
The 17-year-old sitting beside her, wearing thick eyeliner and armfuls of beaded bracelets, recently stumbled upon the New York City Luddites, an anti-smartphone group that hosts events around the city.
She found the idea of “human fracking” — SORA’s teaching that tech companies are forcibly breaking, capturing, and selling human attention — particularly compelling, since she already disliked the fossil fuel industry.
The 17-year-old started hating how she felt when she’d mindlessly scroll TikTok and Pinterest, so she deleted the apps. In her free time, she’s learning how to hand-code a website. And she tries to talk to her parents instead of scrolling before school. Sometimes, they are the problem.
“Screenagers,” she said.
Another 14-year-old, sporty and shy in a black hoodie, was forced by his dad to come to the camp, but has found some of the discussions thought-provoking. That may be as far as it goes.
When he called a friend to share what he’d been up to at the end of August — turning off his phone, staring at a sculpture with childlike wonder, talking about extractive profit models — his friend scoffed, “What the hell is that?”
There was more to it: Together, the teens identified the New York City subway as a site of human fracking, because so many people are scrolling during their commute. The students identified “questions to live with” — What would my life be like as a fish? How long would it take to swim to Manhattan from here? — instead of consulting artificial intelligence chatbots. They’ve also delved into “Attensity!” the movement’s manifesto, published this year.
Camper Consuelo “Leo” Burnett, 17, is well acquainted with this world because her father, the Princeton history professor D. Graham Burnett, is one of SORA’s founders. Nevertheless, she has grown personally invested in the subject of attention, and acts as an idea translator for younger students. (STAT obtained permission to use Burnett’s full name.)
During the Covid pandemic, Leo Burnett lived in an extended lockdown, barely leaving home for over a year as her family tried to protect two immunocompromised members. She got her first cellphone around the same time. “The internet was my one way of feeling connected with the world,” she said, her blue eyes wide.
But she was also prone to anxiety and panic attacks throughout childhood, and in her search for queer community, joined online groups where mental illness was seen as a “badge of honor,” Burnett said. Her mental health cratered, and she developed an eating disorder.
This complicated history with social media started to make more sense once Burnett went to SORA camp. Her reliance on TikTok for bursts of dopamine no longer felt like a personal failing.
“It’s a multibillion dollar industry trying to control young people’s attention,” she said.
‘My phone is fake’
There is a view of the attention crisis that deems it a runaway train.
But the other take — the one adopted by many who work with youth, and who must hold onto some optimism to get through the day — is that we have more control than we think.
“Attention spans have not, in some deep, permanent way, been hampered,” Michael Vazquez, associate director of UNC Chapel Hill’s Parr Center for Ethics, said.
Vazquez and his colleagues have undertaken one of the largest academic efforts so far to test that idea. Last year, they received an almost $800,000 grant to run a three-year experiment, “Educating for the Virtues of Attention,” or EVA.
Attention is a virtue because it’s “upstream of a lot of other things we care about,” such as learning, flourishing, and building relationships, Vazquez said.
As part of EVA, every freshman at Chapel Hill is exposed to curriculum about the demands on our attention, and how those pressures shape our well-being. Some students are finding courses gone totally analog: Instead of submitting assignments on a web portal, they are told to write them in a physical journal. Or, a professor might add extra hoops to jump through before a student can use technology in class.
The idea is to give all students a taste of EVA, “and then we have deep dive opportunities for those who want to continue,” he said. That could look like an oral reading of ancient poetry at a local bookshop, or it could be a phone-free picnic in the university’s arboretum.
This fall, a cohort of over two dozen undergraduates committed to restricting their social media use to a certain number of hours per week as part of a new program called “Carolina Unplugged.” They gather weekly for dinner to reflect on their progress and plan cultural events on campus.
Each student received a Brick, a physical device that disables select apps once a person taps their phone to it. Apps remain blocked until the phone is tapped again. The freebie was what initially drew in Natalie Easley, a 20-year-old junior from Bethesda, Md. She had tried all of the built-in tools for controlling screen time, but nothing worked.
Since middle school, Easley had deleted apps and then caved, redownloading them. How many times had she gone through that cycle? “This is not even exaggerating: Probably like 50-plus,” she said.
But within days of leaving home with her phone Brick’d — and not being able to undo it until the evening — she realized how much better she felt. “I didn’t even realize how much of a compulsion it was, just to pick up my phone,” said Easley, a math and philosophy double major. Then she started to notice how many people walked around with their heads down, scrolling between classes. Her evenings spent on X were no longer satisfying.
“Twitter is fake. My phone is fake. Why is something that is not tangible ruining my day or making me pissed off?” she said.
She deleted X and Instagram, and slashed her average daily screen time by one-third, down to four hours. Easley has found that, free from social media, she can use her phone for discrete tasks — to take photos, learn about things she’s interested in, or text her friends.
She also has more time to let her mind wander. On a recent day, it summoned Aristotle’s assertion: We are what we do.
If one-third of her waking hours were spent online, Easley realized, “then maybe I am, like, my phone.”
“When you’re not distracted, you’re actually able to think about it.”

Heavy rain and strong winds will continue to affect parts of south-eastern Europe and Turkey over the next few days, as an area of low pressure in the region has allowed for the formation of powerful thunderstorms. During a particularly intense thunderstorm in Antalya, a coastal city in the south-west of Turkey, the formation of a tornado resulted in the deaths of four construction workers on Tuesday. Authorities in Greece and Turkey have released severe rainfall and flooding warnings, as a further 100-150 mm (nearly 4-6in) of rain is expected this week in central Greece and western parts of Turkey, with locally higher totals possible.
Travelling eastwards towards South Asia, strong winds and heavy rainfall have swept across the Indian regions of Odisha and Andhra Pradesh as Cyclone Arnab made landfall. With wind gusts in excess of 85 mph (140 km/h) and rainfall totals in some regions exceeding 200mm, the severe storm has prompted mass evacuations of over 180,000 people, as well as widespread disruption to energy and transport infrastructure. The cyclone will weaken as it continues to traverse northwards over the coming days, though will continue to deliver heavy rain to parts of northern and central India as it does so.
Heading towards the western Pacific Ocean, Typhoon In-fa was upgraded on Wednesday to super typhoon status, with exceptionally strong sustained wind speeds of 150 mph (240 km/h), with winds gusting over 185 mph (296 km/h). Travelling north-westwards, it is expected to avoid Guam, which was hammered by Typhoon Champi earlier this month. However, In-fa is expected to affect the Mariana Islands, which have already been battered by four super typhoons this year alone.
Meanwhile, across the Pacific Ocean, Tropical Storm Vance has been affecting parts of western Mexico. Though it has recently weakened to a tropical depression, Vance brought heavy rain and dangerous coastal conditions, with the regions of Sinaloa, Durango and Nayarit recording 50-100 mm of rain, with some areas locally exceeding 150 mm. The high rainfall totals are expected to cause disruption due to flooding and landslides, with the storm swell resulting in dangerous surf and rip current conditions off the coast.

Nvidia’s ousted CEO Jensen Huang and Donald Trump’s commerce secretary are expected to testify before Congress in the coming weeks, as the fallout from Huang’s reported affair with an alleged Chinese spy reverberated across the US, sparking bipartisan concerns for national security and calls for a tougher stance against Beijing.
Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said Huang and Nvidia must answer as to whether America’s security had been jeopardised, adding that the Trump administration also must account for what it did once it learned about Huang’s reported relationship with Alice Huang, who is accused of spying for China.
Donald Trump’s close ties with Jensen Huang have also come under renewed scrutiny as a timeline of the saga started to emerge. The president called Jensen Huang two days before he stepped down and urged him to fight for his job, the New York Times has reported.
On Thursday, Schumer questioned what Donald Trump knew when he personally invited Jensen Huang aboard Air Force One on a state visit to Beijing earlier this year, adding: “Americans deserve to know that those at the highest levels of power are putting America first, not their bottom line or their personal friendships.”
House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said he had demanded a classified briefing for all members of Congress about Nvidia.
The scandal has also drawn in Trump’s commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, after criticism of his department’s oversight of Nvidia’s exports to China and its refusal to add dozens of Chinese companies to a key US trade blacklist.
“Secretary Lutnick has proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the banking committee to address their questions,” Kristen Eichamer, a spokesperson for Lutnick, told NBC News.
Republican Tim Scott, the Senate banking committee chair said he had sent letters asking Lutnick and Jensen Huang to appear before him because: “Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive US technology.”
Scott said he would consider subpoenaing Huang if he did not voluntarily appear. “The American people deserve answers,” Scott said.
Jensen Huang resigned from Nvidia on Thursday, and was replaced on an interim basis by chief financial officer Colette Kress after reports emerged of multiple affairs, key among them with Alice Huang, who is no relation but is suspected to be a Chinese spy.
The statement from Nvidia’s board of directors confirming Huang’s departure did not mention the spying scandal and personal conduct revelations, instead paying tribute to Huang’s “profound” contributions to the company he co-founded.
House foreign affairs chair Brian Mast, a Republican, said on Thursday that congressional staff had spoken to Nvidia on Wednesday night about a date and location for Jensen Huang’s testimony.
House Speaker Mike Johnson said on Thursday there was now growing consensus in Congress on limiting chip exports to China.
Nvidia’s advanced AI chips are widely used to develop cutting-edge AI models, making the company key to the US race against China to build superior AI systems. The US has sought for years to limit China’s access to Nvidia’s chips because it does not want the Chinese military to benefit from them.
“The export controls on chips to China has been a big issue around here,” Johnson told reporters at the US Capitol, adding he favoured limiting China’s access to the advanced technology. “I think there’s a developing consensus in Congress that is an important position to take.“
Chinese AI companies are now trying to secure Nvidia chip capacity outside China, amid growing concern that the gap in US export controls may now be closed after the scandal, people familiar with the matter told Reuters.
Beijing has also stepped up efforts to develop domestic alternatives, including through Huawei, although analysts say Chinese chips remain less efficient for training advanced AI models.
Lawmakers are pressing their colleagues to pass at least four bills on chip exports, according to statements issued since Monday.
On Chinese social media, many expressed surprise at what they see as the swift resignation, and mourned the sudden end of an era that lasted for over three decades.
News of his resignation attracted more than 400m posts overnight on Chinese microblogging platform Weibo.
Huang had enjoyed rock-star status in China, where his visits drew crowds seeking selfies and autographs and his casual outings became social-media sensations. During a January 2026 visit, opportunistic sellers advertised photographs with him for 25,000 yuan ($3,700), while a Beijing restaurant launched a special menu costing more than 400 yuan after he ate there.
Additional reporting by Yu-chen Li

John Mulaney‘s opening monologue on this week’s “Saturday Night Live” took an unexpected turn when he mocked controversial U.S. secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
The comic started by impersonating Kennedy, saying, “‘My father was a good man and I’m a lousy man but I have same name. Am I good if I have same name as father? No, please, let me be in charge of your bones and your tummy. Please allow me to control how your blood feels in your butt and everywhere. Stop the science … Robitussin when taken during menstruation will cause telekinesis. This is clear from the pamphlets in my rental car.’”
Mulaney then slammed Kennedy’s vaccine skepticism, saying, “No one likes him. You dumbass … your thing can’t be the measles!”
He then mocked Kennedy’s previous occupation as an environmental lawyer, saying, “He would just join cases late if they were about be successful. ‘Are you about to win? I’m part of this too.’”
Mulaney then described the times he interacted with the politician by doing comedy at benefits for Kennedy’s Riverkeepers organization.
“They were in charge of keeping the Hudson River in New York City clean,” Mulaney said. “That was his job. That’s how good he is at jobs. His old job was keeping the Hudson River, whose native fish is tied-off used condom, clean. Now he’s in charge of all of our tummies.”
The Nov. 14 episode was Mulaney’s seventh as host. His monologue also touched on family issues and children whose deep, scratchy voices remind him of Kennedy.
