South Sudan postpones first national elections again, to February 2027
South Sudan has again postponed its first national elections since independence in 2011, moving polling from December to February
JUBA, South Sudan -- South Sudan has again postponed its first national elections since independence in 2011, moving polling from December to February amid concerns about insecurity, funding shortages and the country’s readiness to vote.
A revised timetable published Saturday by the National Election Commission sets Feb. 11, 2027, as polling day, replacing Dec. 22. The document did not give a reason for the postponement.
The polls have been repeatedly delayed, including in 2022 and 2024. The latest announcement follows warnings that elections could further unravel the country’s fragile peace.
The commission published the timetable on social media on the day voter registration was scheduled to begin. It also sets dates for candidate nominations and campaigning.
A day earlier, commission chairperson Gabriel Bol Deng told journalists in Juba that registration would run from Nov. 14 to Nov. 28 at 3,161 registration centers across the country’s 10 states and three administrative areas.
Deng urged eligible citizens to register and called on political parties, civil society groups, community leaders and the media to help raise public awareness.
South Sudan became independent from Sudan in 2011 after decades of civil war. A new conflict broke out in 2013 between forces loyal to President Salva Kiir and followers of his rival, Riek Machar. A peace deal was signed in 2018 and a transitional government of national unity was formed in 2020.
Fighting between government and opposition forces escalated in early 2025, and Machar was placed under house arrest in Juba that March. He and seven co-defendants are on trial on charges including treason, murder and crimes against humanity linked to an attack on an army garrison in Nasir, in the northeast. They deny the charges.
The transitional unity government was dissolved in September and replaced by a caretaker administration.
Popular Reads
The South Sudan Civil Society Forum said in a statement issued in late October that conditions did not support fair, credible, peaceful and inclusive elections within the remaining time. It called for an inclusive dialogue on electoral preparations and the country’s transition.
Kiir’s ruling Sudan People’s Liberation Movement, or SPLM, has been holding primaries across the country. But there has been little electoral activity among other registered parties, Anita Kiki Gbeho, head of the United Nations Mission in South Sudan, told the U.N. Security Council on Nov. 10.
“Elections must be a milestone in the transition, not its conclusion. Elections cannot substitute for political dialogue, confidence-building and continued implementation of the Peace Agreement,” she said.
On Thursday, two SPLM delegates were killed in an attack in Miri Loko village, in Western Equatoria state, while returning from party primaries and congresses, officials said. It was the third security incident affecting the party’s primaries and congresses in the state, according to Deng Dau Deng, who chairs the SPLM’s high-level committee there.
One of those killed was Veronica Lucy Gordon, a former South Sudan Broadcasting Corporation journalist who had recently been nominated to contest a women’s seat in the National Legislative Assembly.
Edmund Yakani, director of the Community Empowerment for Progress Organization, condemned the attack, urging those opposed to the delegates’ political views to pursue dialogue rather than violence.
Following news of the postponement, Yakani called for transparency in the commission’s decisions. He also said the locations of registration centers remained unpublished on the day registration was scheduled to begin, leaving citizens without clear information about where to register.

President Donald Trump railed against the federal judge overseeing a lawsuit challenging his plans to overhaul a public golf course in Washington, D.C. while remaining publicly silent on a historic nationwide air travel shutdown.
In a lengthy Truth Social post Saturday afternoon, Trump criticized U.S. District Judge Ana C. Reyes for blocking his administration from moving ahead quickly with a renovation of East Potomac Golf Links, a nearly 400-acre public park and course along the Potomac River that the president repeatedly referred to as “Trash Island.”
The president also posted dozens of unflattering photos of the park, which he also did a few weeks prior.
“Trash Island is currently the Worst Golf Course anywhere in the World, but the Department of the Interior is going to make it into the Best Golf Course anywhere in the World,” Trump wrote, claiming the layout was “very dangerous” because the fairways were too close together.
Trump’s focus on his capital building plans comes as he has yet to make a public statement regarding Friday’s nationwide Federal Aviation Administration ground stop — a rare telecommunications failure that halted all U.S. airport departures for more than four hours and led to over 9,000 flight cancellations.
It was the second nationwide ground stop of all departures since the September 11, 2001 attacks.
“Several Truth Social posts from President Trump today, including many concerning East Potomac golf course, but nothing on yesterday’s nationwide ground stop or the fallout,” noted CNN’s Kit Maher.
“Trump still hasn’t said a word about the historic ground stop, but he is posting about golf courses,” added journalist Aaron Rupar.
The President is getting constant updates on the situation, a White House official said Friday.
In his Truth Social post, Trump argued the overhaul would attract major tournaments like the U.S. Open and Ryder Cup, and promised a 50 percent discount on rates for Washington-area residents.
The president also touted other federal maintenance work in the capital, including updates to 83 fountains, monuments and statues, as well as repairs to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, while claiming crime in the city had dropped by 91 percent.
Critics and political observers have pointed to Trump’s continued push for large-scale Washington construction projects as disconnected from voter priorities following the recent midterm elections, in which Democrats won control of Congress.
The legal dispute escalated during a contentious court hearing on Friday. Reyes warned that she would initiate contempt or sanctions proceedings within a “zeptosecond” — which she noted is the shortest measured unit of time — if she found credible evidence that administration officials destroyed documents tied to Trump’s Washington renovation projects.
Her warning followed whistleblower allegations reported to Democratic lawmakers claiming officials were deleting records related to the president’s building initiatives.
Preservation groups and local golfers sued the administration to block the closure of the park, arguing that officials were using safety concerns as an excuse to turn an affordable public space into an exclusive, high-end golf club. While Justice Department attorneys initially told the court there were no immediate plans to shutter the facility, filings later confirmed the administration intended to close the course on November 15 for a roughly 15-month rebuild.
The Justice Department pushed back in court filings Friday against Reyes’s recent decision to appoint a former federal prosecutor to investigate whether government lawyers lied or violated ethics rules over the shifting timeline, arguing there was "no reasonable basis" for an inquiry.
The administration has maintained that deteriorating infrastructure, including a failing seawall, requires closing the grounds, and the nonprofit that manages the course is set to end its operations after this weekend. However, Reyes questioned the urgency of shutting down the park, pointing out that thousands of runners recently passed through the area during the Marine Corps Marathon without safety warnings.
During Friday’s hearing, the judge also asked spectators in the courtroom to raise their hands if they opposed the renovation design — and then instructed a senior Justice Department official to turn around and look as a large majority of the more than 100 people in attendance raised their hands.

Congress leader Rahul Gandhi announced a series of social security measures for gig workers in Telangana, including accident insurance of ₹5 lakh, health insurance of ₹10 lakh, dedicated Wi-Fi-enabled rest zones and a mechanism to ensure that 1% of every transaction is credited towards their social security.
Addressing gig workers, Mr. Gandhi said the Congress government in Telangana was fulfilling its promise to protect workers engaged in the platform-based economy and ensure that they received their fair share of the benefits generated by their labour.
Describing the 21st century as the age of data, Mr. Gandhi pointed out that while companies such as Google, Facebook, WhatsApp, and Uber operated on data, gig workers had so far been denied access to information about their own work.
Under the proposed legislation, workers would be able to access complete details of their transactions, deliveries, working hours, and payments through their mobile phones. “The data belongs to you, the labour is yours, but you were not even allowed to see your own data,” he said.
He said the government would also establish dedicated, Wi-Fi-enabled rest zones in Hyderabad and other cities to enable delivery personnel and other gig workers to park their vehicles, rest and relax during working hours.
Announcing insurance benefits, Mr. Gandhi said every gig worker would receive ₹5 lakh in accident insurance and ₹10 lakh in health insurance. A social security contribution mechanism under which 1% of every transaction, including deliveries and cab rides, would be contributed towards the workers’ future security.
The amount would be collected from companies and routed through the Gig Workers’ Board before being transferred directly to the workers’ bank accounts, he said.
Drawing a political distinction between the Congress and the BJP-RSS, Mr. Gandhi alleged that the latter wanted to turn gig workers into bonded labourers while allowing large corporate houses and platform companies to reap the benefits. In contrast, the Congress believed that workers were the foundation of the country’s economy and should be treated as partners.
“Do not be afraid. The Telangana government, Rahul Gandhi, Revanth Reddy and the Congress team stand with you. We want to make you partners and ensure protection for you and your families,” he said.
Revanth recalls Bharat Jodo Yatra
Chief Minister A. Revanth Reddy said the Congress government had fulfilled the promise made by Mr. Rahul Gandhi to gig workers in Telangana by bringing in legislation to protect their rights and provide them with social security.
Speaking at an event in the presence of Mr. Rahul Gandhi, the Chief Minister recalled that during the Bharat Jodo Yatra from Kanyakumari to Kashmir in 2023, which covered nearly 4,000 km, Mr. Gandhi had understood the difficulties faced by people from different sections of society.
“The Gandhi family stands by its word. A promise made by Rahul Gandhi is as good as a commitment written in golden letters. For us, his word is an instruction,” the Chief Minister said.
Labour Minister Vivek Venkataswamy also spoke on the occasion. Deputy Chief Minister Mallu Bhatti Vikramarka, Ministers Ponnam Prabhakar, Komatireddy Venkata Reddy, Ponguleti Srinivasa Reddy and TPCC president Mahesh Kumar Goud were present.

Britain should not be permitted to act as a 17th-century colonial power treating the waters around the Falkland Islands as a Dominium maris Britannici, Argentina has told an international tribunal.
Marcelo Kohen, representing Argentina at a hearing in Hamburg, mocked Britain for apparently believing in the historic doctrine that the British crown has sovereignty over expansive parts of the oceans.
Argentina has applied to the international tribunal for the law of the sea (Itlos) for a ruling that would force Britain to suspend the drilling for oil in the North Basin of the Falkland Islands ahead of further arbitration.
The Sea Lion oilfield is about 130 miles north of the Falkland Islands, a British overseas territory over which Argentina has a longstanding sovereignty claim.
Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, reportedly shared among his cabinet a photograph of the Argentinian legal team in Hamburg, describing it as “tremendous”, adding that “we are working on the Falklands issue like no one else in history”.
Addressing the tribunal on the second day of hearings, Kohen said that the dispute over the archipelago of 700 islands in the south Atlantic – known in Argentina as the Malvinas – did not mean that the area was a “legal black hole” and that the UK could do as it wished with its natural resources.
“The fact that the parties dispute sovereignty does not turn the areas surrounding the Malvinas into some kind of Dominium maris Britannici,” he said. “We are not in the 17th century … We are in an era where we should put an end to the last vestiges of colonialism.”
Ellie Reeves, the attorney general for England and Wales, told the tribunal’s panel of judges on Tuesday that Argentina was seeking to further its sovereignty ambitions by applying for suspension of the drilling.
She claimed that such a move would kill the Sea Lion project, with “disastrous consequences” for the Falkland Islanders and the companies involved. The UK claimed that the tribunal, which adjudicates over maritime matters, does not have jurisdiction to wade into matters of sovereignty.
Kohen, switching from French to English, said the UK had failed to mention in its submissions the “elephant in the room” or the “whale in the bathtub”. The UN regarded the Falkland Islands as a non-self-governing territory, he said, and had called in 1976 for both sides to refrain from taking decisions that would unilaterally change the situation before the sovereignty dispute was settled.
The exploitation of hydrocarbons would put the islands among the “highest ranks of wealth just below the principality of Monaco” while depriving Argentina of its rights to those resources, Kohen told the tribunal.
Argentina’s legal team claimed that suspension of the drilling, which is due to start in March next year and which could double the GDP of the islands, was urgent given the irreparable damage to Argentina’s rights.
The UK has claimed there is no urgency as oil extraction would not take place until 2028, before which an Itlos arbitration panel would have come to a conclusion on the future of the oilfield.
In his closing remarks to the panel of 20 judges, Mario Oyarzábal, a legal adviser to Argentina’s ministry of foreign affairs, said they rejected the UK’s attempt to characterise the proceedings as an attempt to litigate the sovereignty dispute.
He said: “The question before this tribunal is a much narrower one: whether, while the underlying dispute remains unresolved, the UK may unilaterally authorise or carry out new drilling for the exploitation of hydrocarbons in the disputed maritime area.”
Milei described the reclaiming of the Falklands as a “national cause” during his recent speech at the UN general assembly. Argentina invaded the islands in 1982 on the orders of the dictator Gen Leopoldo Galtieri. The 74-day conflict ended with the surrender of the Argentinian forces and cost the lives of 649 of its military personnel, 255 British military personnel and three Falkland Islanders.
The UK will offer further submissions on Wednesday.

Formula One driver Lewis Hamilton said on Wednesday that Israel must allow aid trucks into Gaza, a day after he visited the Rafah border crossing in Egypt.
Hamilton, a seven-time world champion, arrived in El Arish on Tuesday, where he was briefed on how aid is prepared and coordinated before it is sent into Gaza, as he toured the Rafah crossing and the Egyptian Red Crescent’s aid warehouses.
He has frequently posted on social media about children killed in Israeli airstrikes in Gaza and called for a ceasefire. A ceasefire agreement reached last year has halted major combat operations in Gaza, but the amount of aid reaching the territory continues to fall far short of the agreed-upon minimum of 600 trucks a day.
“The past three years of Israel’s genocide in Gaza is appalling. It’s an injustice for people to be denied their freedom, their safety and their dignity. No human being should be treated as though their life matters less,” the Ferrari driver wrote on Instagram.
Israel strongly denies accusations of genocide and says its military campaign in Gaza targets Hamas militants.
Hamilton described seeing food trucks lined up and ready to go at the border that were regularly held up or faced major delays.
“I saw walls stretching for miles, built to keep them in. Standing there, outside what felt like an open-air prison, all I could think about was getting in to help,” he said in the post. “At the Rafah border, I saw food trucks lined up ready to go, but they’re regularly not allowed in or face major delays. The first driver in line that I spoke to had already been waiting over 12 hours. At the nearby logistics centre, I saw the hard work of the aid workers, but I also saw what gets rejected for crazy reasons. Sleeping bags, first aid kits, medical equipment, wheelchairs even footballs for kids.
“Israel needs to fulfil its obligations under the ceasefire and let the aid trucks in. I know so many people feel that same helplessness. That same need to do something rather than just watch. No excuse. I don’t want us to get used to their suffering. I don’t want us to look away.”
Hamilton, 41, is an advocate for humanitarian causes. In 2021 he founded Mission 44, a charity that supports young people and works to improve their access to education and employment.
“I think we need to make sure we’re pushing to free Congo, free Sudan, free Syria, free Palestine,” Hamilton said last month. “I think there’s a lot of peace that I’m hoping we get to at some stage.”
At the crossing on Tuesday, Hamilton greeted aid workers with “Assalamu alaikum” a widely used Arabic greeting meaning “peace be upon you”. He shook hands and briefly spoke to workers and officials.
Hamilton is fourth in the drivers’ championship. Mercedes’ Kimi Antonelli has won the title with three races to go. The Las Vegas Grand Prix is 21 November before the Qatar Grand Prix on 29 November and the season-ending Abu Dhabi Grand Prix on 6 December.

ANTALYA, Turkey—Amid upbeat green-tech pep talks and notices for happy hours at the annual United Nations COP31 climate change conference on Thursday, two new reports offered a stark reminder of how far the world remains from containing global warming.
Climate Action Tracker, a nonprofit group that analyzes climate policies, found that the planet is still on track to warm nearly 5° Fahrenheit by 2100, a rise that would devastate coral reefs, disrupt agriculture and forests and melt most of the world’s ice. In a separate bulletin, the European Union’s Copernicus climate change service reported that global warming has accelerated significantly since the 2015 Paris climate agreement.
When the Paris agreement was adopted, the average global temperature was projected to surpass the pact’s long-term threshold of 2.7° Fahrenheit above the preindustrial average around 2045. After another decade of global climate summits, warming is now projected to cross that benchmark as soon as 2029, according to Copernicus.
“This striking change suggests that global warming has accelerated in recent years,” the EU scientists wrote. Even without understanding every aspect of the recent rapid global temperature increase, “It is clear that the ever-growing concentrations of greenhouse gases emitted by human activity in the atmosphere remain the main driver of this trend.”
The current level of warming has already triggered deadly and destructive floods, wildfires and catastrophic glacier collapses, said Swedish activist Greta Thunberg, who is attending the UN “Conferences of the Parties” climate talks, for the first time since 2021.
“The climate crisis is a matter of life and death,” she said. “The actions from those in power here are completely detached from reality. As we speak, we are losing priceless lives, ecosystems and species that we will never get back.”
Sarah Heck, a climate policy analyst with Climate Analytics, an international climate science and policy institute, said governments have failed to meaningfully improve the outlook for end-of-century warming.

A team of scientists at the CSIR-Centre for Cellular and Molecular Biology (CCMB) has identified critical weaknesses in the bacterium that causes Tuberculosis (TB), a finding that could pave the way for the development of new treatments against one of the world’s deadliest infectious diseases.
The discovery is particularly significant for India, which accounts for nearly a quarter of global TB cases and about a third of drug-resistant infections, according to the World Health Organisation’s Global TB Report 2025. Drug-resistant TB remains a major public health challenge, as treatment requires a combination of antibiotics taken over several months and is becoming increasingly difficult due to the emergence of resistant strains.
Led by CCMB Director Vinay Kumar Nandicoori, the research team mapped the protein export machinery of Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), the bacterium responsible for TB. The study sheds light on how the pathogen transports proteins within and outside its cells, a process essential for its growth, survival and ability to cause disease.
The research was carried out by joint first authors Priyadarshini Sanyal and Jagadeeshwari Uppada in collaboration with scientists from the Institute of Mathematical Sciences, Chennai, led by Areejit Samal, and the Translational Health Science and Technology Institute, Faridabad.
Using a combination of computational modelling and laboratory experiments, the researchers identified 92 key components and nearly 200 molecular reactions involved in the bacterium’s protein transport network. These included the general Sec pathway, the Twin-Arginine Translocation (Tat) system and the specialised ESX secretion systems unique to this group of bacteria.
“Protein secretion acts like a delivery system inside the bacterium and is vital for its survival,” said Dr Uppada. The team focused on two major secretion pathways, SecA1 and Tat, employing CRISPR-based gene-silencing technology to reduce their activity. The results were striking: bacterial growth declined sharply both in laboratory cultures and inside immune cells, demonstrating that both pathways are essential for the pathogen’s survival.
Dr Priyadarshini Sanyal said further analysis revealed that disrupting these systems affected the export of more than 100 proteins in the SecA1 pathway and around 140 proteins linked to the Tat system. Researchers also observed structural damage to the bacterial cell membrane, making it unstable and more permeable. Proteins that normally remain inside the bacterium began leaking into the surrounding environment.
Dr Nandicoori said that these changes highlight the close connection between protein secretion and the maintenance of the bacterial cell envelope, a key factor behind TB’s persistence and resistance to treatment. The findings, published in the peer-reviewed journal Molecular & Cellular Proteomics, could help researchers identify new drug targets, although translating the discovery into effective medicines will require several more years of research.

‘Travesty to term it state-inflicted death’: India votes against UN death penalty moratorium
India objected to linking judicially mandated capital punishment with unlawful executions while speaking on the resolution concerning extrajudicial executions.
India on Saturday voted against a United Nations General Assembly draft resolution calling for a moratorium on the use of the death penalty, saying there was no international consensus against capital punishment and that every sovereign state had the right to determine its legal system and penalties.
During the same session, at the Third Committee's 43rd plenary meeting of the 81st UN General Assembly, India also weighed in on a separate draft resolution (A/C.3/81/L.37) concerning extrajudicial, summary or arbitrary executions, news agency ANI reported. While India supported the adoption of the resolution overall, it formally disassociated itself from a specific paragraph that equated lawful capital punishment with torture and arbitrary killings.
Bhavika Mangalanandan, an Indian Foreign Service (IFS) officer serving as first secretary at India's Permanent Mission to the United Nations, objected to linking judicially mandated capital punishment with unlawful executions while speaking on the resolution on extrajudicial executions.
"There is no international consensus against capital punishment, and article six of the ICCPR permits its use with restrictions. Capital punishment is meted out after rigorous and due legal process," she was quoted as saying.
"It is therefore a travesty to term it state-inflicted death," Mangalanandan added.
She further objected to the discussion of capital punishment under a resolution or report concerning extrajudicial and arbitrary executions, calling it "disingenuous and mischievous".
"To discuss this topic under a resolution or a report on extrajudicial and arbitrary execution is therefore disingenuous and mischievous, intended to portray personal ideological preferences as settled international law," she said.
At the outset of her remarks on resolution A/C.3/81/L.37, Mangalanandan emphasised that India opposed extrajudicial, summary or arbitrary executions and supported the broader resolution addressing such human rights violations.
"Extrajudicial, summary or arbitrary executions are unlawful and a clear violation of human rights. They deeply affect the families of victims and violate the most fundamental human right, the right to life," she said.
"India therefore supported the adoption of the resolution that calls upon states to eradicate instances of such grave human rights violations," she added.
She clarified that India's objection was specifically directed at Operational Paragraph 6 (OP 6) of the resolution, which refers to a report by the Special Rapporteur presented to the Human Rights Council at its 62nd session and calls on states to take its recommendations into account.
"We strongly disagree with the assertion conveyed in the report of the Special Rapporteur and thereby through the resolution. The death penalty inherently constitutes torture or ill-treatment," Mangalanandan said.
Explaining India's legal position, she noted that capital punishment is a statutory provision in the country and is imposed exclusively in the "rarest of rare" cases.
"In India, the death penalty is a statutory provision exercised exclusively in the rarest of rare cases; a legal framework guarantees multi-tier procedural safeguards, including the presumption of innocence, mandatory confirmation of death sentences by a higher court and extensive mitigation consideration," she said.
"In view of the above, my delegation is constrained to disassociate from OP six of the resolution," she added.
Meanwhile, India's vote against the separate biennial draft resolution on a moratorium on the death penalty (A/C.3/81/L.43) is consistent with its position in previous sessions, including those in 2016, 2018 and 2024.

Watch SpaceX attempt to catch the Starship upper stage for the first time
While the company has pulled off this trick a few times with Super Heavy boosters, it'll be a first for the Ship.
SpaceX launched Starship from Texas on Friday for its 15th test flight, in which it set out to achieve some of its most ambitious goals yet. The company planned to demonstrate its first double catch, which would see the Super Heavy V3 booster return to the launch site to be caught by the tower's chopstick arms before the upper stage, or the part known as the Ship, attempted the same landing maneuver a day later. SpaceX has caught and reflown V1 Super Heavy boosters a couple of times so far, but it hasn't yet tried to catch the Ship.
Starship has been circling Earth in orbit since the launch on Friday afternoon, and is expected to make its landing attempt shortly after 4PM ET Saturday. SpaceX has been live-streaming the flight on its website and on X.
While Flight 15 completed some of its main objectives successfully, including deploying 26 Starlink V3 satellites to orbit, the first stage booster experienced a problem on its way back down to Earth and aborted the catch attempt, instead changing course to splash down in the Gulf, where it exploded before hitting the water. The Ship, though, has continued on its journey in orbit for roughly 22 hours following launch before heading back down to the surface.

DEHRADUN: A Congress MLA allegedly vandalised a stage at the Jauljibi Fair in Uttarakhand after he was denied an opportunity to address the gathering in the presence of chief minister 
Pushkar Singh Dhami
, who inaugurated the event near the India-Tibet border.
Microphones and chairs were allegedly thrown around on the stage after the chief minister left the venue, triggering a political row between the 
Congress
 and BJP.
The BJP condemned the conduct of Dharchula MLA Harish Dhami, particularly the "abusive language" he allegedly used against the chief minister and demanded that an FIR be registered against him.
'I am the chairperson'
Harish Dhami later said he was the "chairperson" of the fair but was not allowed to speak or raise the concerns of local residents before the chief minister.
“I am the chairperson of this fair, yet I was not even given the chance to speak or present the demands of the local people to the chief minister,” he said.
“This government is corrupt and is afraid of the opposition. The chief minister lacks the courage to hear the truth about the rampant corruption in the state," Harish added further.
Shortly after the incident, Congress workers also staged a protest, questioning why another Congress MLA from the district, Mayukh Singh Mahar, had not been invited to the inauguration.
District Congress president Mukesh Pant said the government's decision to leave out an elected representative amounted to a disregard for democratic values.
“By failing to invite an elected representative from the district, the government has completely disregarded all values,” he said.
'Wanted to raise two issues'
In a subsequent social media post, Harish Dhami said he had wanted to raise two issues with the government: the death of an eight-year-old girl in the region two days earlier and concerns over road connectivity in Kanar.
"Was raising one’s voice on such serious matters constituted a crime?" he asked.
“Chief minister, a fair is not merely a platform to sing praises of the government. It is a democratic forum to voice the problems, suffering and rights of the people of this state. As an elected representative, it is my moral and constitutional duty to bring forth the concerns of the people of my constituency," Harish added further.
The BJP, however, criticised the MLA's behaviour and said the event had already been shortened because of the chief minister's time constraints.
BJP hits back
Senior BJP leader Mahendra Singh Budiyal condemned the language allegedly used by Harish Dhami against the chief minister while addressing the gathering.
“The abusive language used by the MLA against the chief minister is condemnable. The BJP views this as a sign of the MLA’s frustration, as the Congress party’s support base in the Dharchula assembly constituency is weakening," Budiyal said.
He said the BJP's district unit had decided that cultural programmes at the fair would not be allowed if an FIR was not registered against Harish Dhami by Sunday afternoon.
Earlier, Pushkar Dhami inaugurated the 10-day Jauljibi Fair, which showcases goods and cultural traditions from Tibet, India and Nepal.
The fair has historically reflected trade links between the three regions. This year's stalls feature woollen goods brought from Tibet through the India-Tibet trade route, alongside products sold by Indian and Nepalese traders.

FIFA has joined forces with the United Nations (UN) and the World Health Organization (WHO) in supporting the #BeActive campaign launched on the UN International Day of Sport for Development and Peace to encourage people to be #HealthyAtHome as the world comes together in the fight against COVID-19, today and every day.
WHO recommends all healthy adults do at least 30 minutes a day of physical activity and children at least 60 minutes per day. As part of this, #BeActive and remain #HealthyAtHome include the following suggestions along with any other form of recreation to stay healthy at home:
- Taking some online exercise classes,
- Dancing,
- Playing active video games,
- Jumping rope, and
- Practising muscle strength and balance training.
“We are delighted that football is strongly supporting the International Day of Sport for Development and Peace by asking everyone to #BeActive and to remain healthy at home during this difficult time,” said António Guterres Secretary-General of the United Nations. “FIFA has asked the football community, from member associations and clubs, to players and fans, to show their support, to put their rivalries aside and to show a new solidarity so we can overcome the coronavirus. This is an important lesson not only for today, but for every day.”
“More than ever, especially now, one thing must be clear to everyone, health comes first,” said FIFA President Gianni Infantino. “FIFA is delighted to support both the United Nations and the World Health Organization in amplifying the #BeActive campaign today, and we are encouraged that the football community is also playing an active role in ensuring the message understood globally. For the first time ever, we are all on the same team and together, with team spirit and positive energy, we will win.”
“WHO is proud to collaborate as part of the UN family with FIFA and football lovers worldwide to promote the importance of being active for both physical and mental health,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of the World Health Organization. “The #BeActive campaign supports WHO’s drive to help people be healthy at home.”
The campaign kicks off with Real Madrid CF, FC Barcelona, Liverpool FC and Manchester United FC asking football fans to set aside their rivalries and to come together to #BeActive in order to defeat the coronavirus. Other clubs, including Club América, CD Guadalajara, Beijing Guoan FC, Shanghai Shenhua FC, Mohun Bagan AC, East Bengal FC, Melbourne City FC, Sydney FC, Auckland City FC, Team Wellington FC, CA River Plate, Olympique de Marseille, TP Mazembe, CR Flamengo and SE Palmeiras will also join the initiative in the coming days.
As part of the campaign, world-famous players share the following message: “At this time, even rivals need to stick together. We have to keep our distance, but we do not lose our focus. We can show solidarity by being active, and active means following the guidelines from the WHO.”
The video campaign will be published on various FIFA digital channels, with regular subsequent updates from clubs and players across the world during subsequent days. #BeActive is also being supported with graphics toolkits for the 211 FIFA member associations and various media agencies to facilitate additional localisation and to further amplify the message.
WHO, the UN’s specialized health agency, and FIFA, football’s world governing body, collaborate closely to promote healthy lifestyles through football globally and launched the “ Pass the message to kick out coronavirus” campaign last month to share advice effective measures to protect people from COVID-19.

Nvidia's interim CEO inherits risky AI bets and a legal mess
Nvidia's CEO resigns after alleged spy scandal. What's next for the company?
A suspected intelligence scandal, reports of multiple extramarital affairs and the abrupt departure of one of Silicon Valley's most influential CEOs. It's been a dizzying week for Nvidia and the AI industry.
Jensen Huang helped bankroll the AI boom. Now, after 33 years at the helm of the leading company in AI, he's out, leaving questions about the future of an industry that has relied heavily on his company's financial backing. Longtime finance chief Colette Kress has stepped in as interim CEO.
"Nvidia has put itself basically in a position of being a bank, backstopping everything," Gary Marcus, a cognitive scientist and longtime AI researcher, told Morning Edition.
He was describing circular financing: Nvidia invests in AI companies that then use the money to buy Nvidia's chips. OpenAI, Anthropic and CoreWeave have relied on that funding, he said, even as many AI businesses struggle to turn a profit.
"Jensen was kind of a swashbuckler, willing to make bets of arbitrary size," Marcus said.
Unlike Huang, whose background is in engineering, Kress comes from finance and appears more cautious about making large financial bets, potentially changing how Nvidia backs the wider AI industry.
Kress will also have to contend with potential federal and congressional investigations into Nvidia's dealings involving China, leaving her to "clean up that mess," Marcus said.
He said lawmakers need answers about what information Huang may have shared with Alice Huang and why Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had not intervened earlier.
"Why didn't Lutnick shut some of this down when he was asked to?" Marcus said.

Jammu, Nov 15: Chief Minister Omar Abdullah on Saturday praised J&K Lieutenant Governor Manoj Sinha for his role in streamlining the academic system and strengthening institutional accountability in Jammu and Kashmir's higher education sector.
Addressing the maiden Convocation of Cluster University (CU) of Jammu at Abhinav Theatre, Omar, who was the special guest at the occasion said LG Sinha's personal commitment over the past several years to streamlining academic calendars, ensuring regular convocations and aligning higher education with national benchmarks brought much-needed discipline and momentum to campuses.
The Chief Minister, who was addressing the gathering in the presence of the Lieutenant Governor, acknowledged his contribution towards improving the functioning of higher education institutions across Jammu and Kashmir.
Referring to LG Sinha's academic background as an alumnus of IIT-BHU, CM Omar said J&K LG brought a keen appreciation of academic rigour, institutional accountability and the transformative potential of public universities.
He said these priorities were crucial for strengthening the higher education ecosystem and ensuring that universities remained aligned with national academic standards.
CM Omar said the elected government was aware that unemployment was the greatest anxiety facing the youth of Jammu and Kashmir.
"Whenever I travel across the region, from Kathua and Samba to Udhampur, Akhnoor, Baderwah, Rajouri and Mender young graduates hand me their resumes and ask me quite fairly, we have earned our degrees, where do we go from here," he said.
Omar further said that he will not offer "hollow slogans" or pretend government jobs alone can absorb every graduate.
"Across India and the world, public employment accounts for only 2-4 percent of the workforce," he added.
He said while J&K government was committed to expediting transparent, time-bound recruitment, true prosperity in Jammu and Kashmir will come when our youth transition from being solely job seekers to becoming value creators, innovators and entrepreneurs.
"My government is determined to back those of you who take this leap by strengthening start-ups, simplifying clearances and improving credit access," he said.
He asked the graduating students that financial security and professional recognition have their rightful place, but education without character was like a ship without a rudder.
"My government is committed to providing the autonomy, faculty strength and infrastructure our universities need to become genuine engines of knowledge and regional problem solving," he added.

Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond
- Published
The tech world has spent the day digesting the extraordinary news that Jensen Huang - the charismatic, leather-jacket wearing chief executive of the multi-trillion dollar firm Nvidia - is being investigated by his own company over an extramarital affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.
None of us had that on our bingo cards for 2026.
Huang's alleged romantic affair with Alice Huang (no relation), the former CEO of a Singapore-based data centre company, has cast ripples far beyond his immediate family - undoubtedly on an emotional rollercoaster of their own - taking us to a crossroads at which technology, geopolitics and national security intersect.
In a nutshell, this is about the bitter rivalry between the US and China, as well as whether Jensen Huang has betrayed the US as well as his wife.
The US is locked in a fierce race with China to develop the best AI models.
"Whoever wins AI, wins," as US President Donald Trump puts it. He thinks that the country with the more dominant AI technology will benefit the most from it and, ultimately, will be the most powerful in the world. He may well be right.
Nvidia happens to make the best chips in the business for AI – so much so that it has been overwhelmed with demand.
It sets its prices accordingly: a single unit of the firm's latest kit for data centres starts at £37,000 ($50,000). A medium or large site might have hundreds of them.
The US administration initially slapped an export ban on Nvidia's more recent devices to prevent China from taking advantage of their superior capabilities. It has since softened the rules a little.
But there are suggestions that Alice Huang's company, Megaspeed, may have been involved in sneaking them into the country while she was in charge. Bloomberg reported that the firm bought billions of dollars worth of Nvidia tech in November 2025. Megaspeed denies that it was used illegitimately.
For his part, Jensen Huang has lobbied heavily for the export rules between the two countries to be relaxed, arguing against the weight of general opinion that the AI race doesn't matter and that it would be no bad thing for China to become dependent on US tech.
"President Trump wants American to win and President Xi wants China to win, and it's possible for both of them to do so," he told the BBC last year.
I think it's safe to assume that neither country sees it that way.
- Could this be the end of 'Jensanity' 
  - Published1 day ago
The difficult questions Nvidia now has to try to answer include whether Alice gained special access to the firm's latest technology, either deliberately or not, via Jensen - and, if so, whether she shared it with Beijing or others.
We don't know when their affair began or ended, but there are numerous photos and videos of Jensen and Alice together at events. It is feasible that there were moments when they spent quite a lot of time together and Jensen has talked about always having an eye on his work.
China denies that she was engaged in espionage.
Interest in economic espionage is neither new nor unique to China. But many Western countries say that China does it on a grand scale, using a combination of technology tools and agents embedded in various organisations - including private companies.
China having access to significant enough numbers of Nvidia's chips to make use of them, or stripping them down and learning how to make its own versions, would infuriate the Trump administration, which is trying to keep its AI technology close to its chest.
Some models have even been withheld from the UK-based AI Safety Institute on the grounds that they are potentially too dangerous to be shared. The US does not want anyone having a headstart or misusing its innovations.
Another potential bombshell lies in the form of any national security information to which Jensen Huang may have been privy.
He is a man operating at the very top of the US elite - one of a handful of people who could probably walk into the White House unannounced and have tea with Trump. He has influence, he has access and he has powerful friends. It's quite possible that secrets were shared with him.
Nvidia says there's no evidence so far that he passed anything on and the firm has launched an internal investigation. Huang says he will co-operate and wants to keep his job - though if nothing else, he has broken Nvidia's own code of conduct, which states that company members should not have relationships with clients.
But can he survive?
At present, he has the backing of both the Nvidia board and Trump, who described him as "honourable" and speculated that there must have been a reason for what had transpired. In other words, he's not throwing his tech boss buddy under the bus.
Nvidia's share price has fallen but has not tanked spectacularly, suggesting shareholders are not abandoning the company under his stewardship in their droves either.
An AI industry with a weakened Nvidia would undoubtedly be a slower one.
And there isn't really a natural successor waiting in the wings to replace Jensen were he forced out.
Huang has run Nvidia for more than 30 years - to many, he is Nvidia. He has steered it through multiple crises and it was his decision for the firm to focus on AI before it was trendy.
He is known to be a demanding boss who expects staff to work long hours and to high standards. There are stories about him calling all-staff meetings to tell off individuals who had made mistakes. He has said this was to prevent others making the same errors – but you can only imagine how it felt for those on the receiving end.
While he awaits the conclusion of the investigation into his actions, Huang must hope that, despite not tolerating the mistakes of his colleagues in the past, they will be gracious about his own failings.
And he must also live with the irony that he was potentially caught out not by a sophisticated high-tech sting, but by the oldest trick in the book: a honey trap.

British government ministers were told not to engage formally with Vantara, the controversial mega-zoo run by the Indian billionaire Anant Ambani, after lobbying efforts by the private animal sanctuary in the run-up to a UK-chaired meeting on the trade in endangered species, according to documents.
This week, the UK heads a 32-country committee meeting in Geneva of Cites, the United Nations body that regulates trade in endangered species. The meeting will examine how India has responded to compliance concerns about imports of endangered animals.
Documents obtained by the Guardian and the news outlet Mongabay under the UK’s Freedom of Information Act reveal Vantara’s efforts to lobby British officials and ministers before the meeting.
Ambani, 31, is the heir to the oil and gas fortune of one of India’s richest men, Mukesh Ambani. He set up a 1,400-hectare (3,500-acre) private zoo near his family’s oil-refining facilities in Gujarat, where more than 150,000 animals have reportedly been amassed since 2022. Vantara boasts high welfare standards for animals in its care, including facilities such as an elephant hydrotherapy pool, where more than 260 elephants can also receive oil therapies and Ayurvedic massage.
But conservation groups have repeatedly questioned how such a vast number of species, many of which are endangered, were gathered so quickly. Last year, India’s supreme court cleared the zoo’s operators of any wrongdoing.
A subsequent Cites fact-finding mission looking into the zoo raised concerns about India’s compliance with international rules on animal imports in 2025. It recommended temporary restrictions on India, although the recommendation was later withdrawn.
Its November 2025 report said: “There is a need for caution to ensure that imports of large numbers of animals by these facilities are not inadvertently creating a demand for illegally sourced animals.”
In May, officials from the UK’s Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) met a representative from Vantara and the US lobbyist firm Checkmate Government Relations, founded by Ches McDowell, a hunting friend of Donald Trump Jr.
Before the meeting, internal briefing documents said Checkmate was “seeking to persuade the UK to take a more sympathetic view of India’s handling of imports to Vantara and of Checkmate’s argument that responsibility for verifying legality sits primarily with exporting or re-exporting parties rather than with India as importer”.
During the meeting, the Vantara representative invited UK officials to visit the zoo – an invitation that was subsequently declined to ensure the impartiality of the UK’s Cites chair role.
After the meeting, a representative from another lobbying firm, Atlas Strategy, working on behalf of Vantara, approached the then secretary of state, Emma Reynolds, and then nature minister, Mary Creagh, also raising the prospect of a visit to the zoo.
When a department official asked for advice, a note was issued recommending that ministers did not engage formally with Vantara.
The government documents also reveal concerns about an application by Vantara to import falcons and falcon hybrids, after an unnamed organisation made a £50,000 “donation” to a breeder in the UK, whose identity was also not disclosed. British Cites officials classified the transaction as commercial, according to the documents. The falcons were not exported to India.
A spokesperson for Vantara said it had not imported falcons from the UK, nor had the zoo hired or paid a lobbying firm. It is understood that Checkmate and Altas Strategy were working pro bono for Vantara and not required to register with the Office of the Registrar of Consultant Lobbyists.
After recent scrutiny, Vantara has sought to “reset” its activities by voluntarily suspending animal imports for a year and hiring John Scanlon, a former Cites chief, to oversee its operations. In an interview with the Sunday Times this year, Ambani said he only brought animals to Vantara legally to ensure their welfare, mentioning a group of hippos he had saved from a hunting lodge in South Africa and jackass penguins saved from a shopping centre in Qatar.
“I think since I was a baby I have been taking care of animals. It’s always been a passion,” he said.
Vantara was used to host Ambani’s lavish pre-wedding celebrations in 2024, which were attended by celebrity guests and politicians. In September, Newcastle University awarded the oil heir a professorship of practice for “his work in conservation, biodiversity protection, animal welfare and environmental stewardship”, sparking a backlash from conservationists.
A Defra spokesperson said: “The UK has strict rules in place to protect endangered species and ensuring international wildlife trade is legal and sustainable, with every application assessed individually against internationally agreed and domestic requirements.”

Which NVIDIA GPU is closest to the PS5? The answer isn't so simple
It's a bit like comparing apples and oranges, but this NVIDIA GPU will give you the closest results to a PS5
There's no getting around it: We're in an era where it's never been more financially-punishing to buy either a new console or PC hardware. Given that we're now dealing with a tech-savvy Sophie's Choice between a PS5 and the most affordable gaming PC you can put together for similar money, value has to be taken into consideration. Is mid-range PC gaming really that much better than what the current consoles can provide?
In an age where Sony and AMD are teasing the GPU tech they're building for the next PlayStation, it's understandable folks want to compare and contrast modern console and PC tech. If you're lucky enough to own a PS5 Pro before GTA VI launches, I say stick with the kit you have. Of course, there are also exceptions where high-end gamers might want to invest in PC hardware, so let's get into when those particular, pixel-counting scenarios make sense.
What GPU offers the same power as the PS5?
First of all, this is a bit of an awkward question, but we'll get to that. Are you happy with your PS5? Then keep being happy with your PS5. As someone who has been building PCs since 2004 — yes, I'm ancient — I can't recommend assembling a custom gaming rig in an era where RAMaggeddon has hideously skewed the prices of computer components. But if you really want to know what GPU most closely aligns to the PS5's graphics solution, I can point you in the right direction ... with caveats.
According to the frame-counting wizards at Digital Foundry, the graphics card that best matches the base PS5's APU is the NVIDIA RTX 2070 Super. Notice that I said "APU" rather than "GPU". That's because the PS5, like the Xbox Series X, uses a central chipset that handles both GPU and CPU tasks in a single processor.
As for the 2070 Super, this card is now three generations old, so it's hardly cutting edge by modern standards. Thanks to our current AI-obsessed timeline though, the cheapest model of this now seven-year-old card currently costs $280 on Amazon. That's around 53 percent of the $600 PS5 Digital Edition.
If you're wondering how to buy a GPU in 2026, you really should be looking at the second-hand market. The cost of new cards right now is utterly unhinged, so I'd never recommend dropping the thick end of $300 on a GPU that launched in 2019. Specs-wise, the 2070 Super has 8GB of GDDR6 memory, but that's not an apples to apples comparison with the PS5's system-wide 16GB of GDDR6 unified memory. The 2070 Super can produce PS5-level performance under the right conditions, but comparing the PS5's APU to Team Green's aging GPU isn't a straightforward prospect.
Is the RTX 5060 stronger than the PS5 Pro?
In September 2026, the fifth gen NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5060 was the second-most used card according to the Steam Hardware & Software Survey with 4.40 percent market share. This lower end Blackwell GPU supports the controversial DLSS 5 that has made the internet so upset. It also boasts 8GB of GDDR7 memory with a base clock of around 2280 MHz. Currently, you'll struggle to find this card retailing for less than $500.
Enter the PS5 Pro. Sony's supercharged system now costs an inflated $1,250 (it originally launched in late 2024 at $700). In the middle of a PS5 Pro shortage, GTA 6 is only making things worse. Talking specs, the big boy PS5 leans on a custom AMD Zen 2 8 core/16 thread "Trinity" APU. While this represents a major boost over the standard PS5 in terms of GPU performance, in reality the CPU bump is only around 10 percent. That's why, in spite of the best efforts of PSSR, many Pro titles continue to fall below the sort of mid-range PC performance results you'd hope from a $1,000 box.
From a horsepower perspective, the 16GB RTX 5060 TI model and AMD's Radeon RX 9060 XT provide the best comparable performance to the raw horsepower of the PS5 Pro. But again, it's not a like-for-like comparison. With the right settings tweaks and a capable gaming CPU, either of these cards can outgun Sony's prosumer console. Yet the simplicity of Sony's $900 machine undoubtedly makes it incredibly user-friendly, and thus appealing for folks who just want to experience GTA VI in the best fashion possible.
Why comparing a graphics card to a console GPU is complicated
There are a bunch of reasons why it's unfair to compare open-ended PC setups to closed-source console hardware. Talking about the base PS5, we're dealing with a custom AMD RDNA 2 GPU that acts alongside a CPU on a single chip. There's no directly comparable piece of hardware in the PC space. Developers have routinely hit 60 FPS/supersampling, near-4K results on PS5 and PS5 Pro through canny development.
Sure, the RTX 2070 Super can generally match PS5 performance in certain games, but that's only through the lens of what that particular GPU is capable of. It doesn't take into account the broader, component-wide setup of a modern gaming PC you'd need to assemble in order to match the performance of the most powerful console ever built.
The CPU and the amount and type of RAM you pair with a card that's roughly on the level of PS5's APU matters massively. Scrimp on the processor front and you'll quickly be CPU-bound, meaning even an RTX 5090 couldn't save your console-shaming bacon. Building or buying a gaming PC needs a lot of consideration, especially during our currently ruinous financial times. If you want 4K gaming without hassle for less than $1,000, a PS5 is absolutely the way to go. Wondering how long you can expect a PS5 to last? It should be years, so there's no reason to sweat over the longevity of Sony's massively successful console.
Both the standard PS5 and the amped up PS5 Pro are outstanding consoles. Using AMD APU solutions, they hit pleasing, 4K results with smooth frame rates. Mid-range graphics cards when paired with decent gaming CPUs are going to cost a lot more. For 60 FPS/4K results with reasonable ray tracing, a PS5 or PS5 Pro will do you just fine. That said, if you want cutting edge path tracing at 120 FPS, a gaming rig with a high-end GPU is where it's at.

In mid-November, people shared a rumor that the coffee-and-doughnuts chain Dunkin', formerly Dunkin' Donuts, stopped using the word "Christmas" but still celebrated Ramadan and Pride Month earlier in the year.
The claim served as the latest chapter in what has become known as the "war on Christmas," a long-running debate in which generally conservative-leaning politicians and commentators have alleged bad-faith actors aimed to remove Christmas from society, particularly in the United States. In the past, that "war" extended to Starbucks' holiday-themed coffee cups, with outraged voices failing to mention the company has for many years sold a special "Christmas Blend."
The Dunkin' claim first started circulating on Nov. 11 when conservative Instagram user Josh Seiter posted a video (archived) with the caption, "Dunkin' celebrates Ramadan and Pride but hates Christmas." His Instagram account, with 2.4 million followers and a bio identifying him as Christian and a political and cultural commentator, displayed videos promoting similar claims about other brands.
In the video, Seiter says Dunkin' has "some explaining to do," citing alleged examples from 2026 of the chain's Ramadan-themed specials, Pride Month-themed celebrations and no mention of Christmas or any "Christmas meals" on the company's website. He then alleges the company intentionally omits the word "Christmas" from corporate materials, citing purported authoritative and trusted sources.
Seiter addresses Dunkin', "I wanna know why you have no problem using the words 'Ramadan' and 'Pride' but you can't bring yourself to use the word 'Christmas.'"
Others reposted Seiter's video on Facebook (archived), X (archived) and other platforms, as well as made their own videos (archived) spreading the rumor. Snopes readers also searched this website and emailed us about the matter.
In sum, Seiter's claim was false. He failed to present the full context of the images he displayed in his video, whether they were misleading, outdated, of international origin or otherwise missing context.
For example, he showed Ramadan specials from the Dunkin' regional pages for Egypt and Singapore without making note of the countries, which have large Muslim populations. He also didn't mention both of those regional Facebook pages featured messages of "Merry Christmas" last year, nor did he highlight past posts displaying the word "Christmas" on the U.S.-based Dunkin' Instagram page.
Snopes emailed Seiter at an address listed on his Facebook page, which bounced back with a failure notice. We also messaged him via Messenger, asking if he researched the specific sources of the images and graphics shown in his video prior to making his content, if he could name examples of what he called "Christmas meals" that Dunkin' supposedly lacked and if he could tell us what inspired him to make the video. We also emailed Dunkin' to ask about the video and will update this article if we receive further details.
Breaking down the alleged controversy
In Seiter's video, he makes various claims about Dunkin' while displaying numerous examples of flyers and photos as his purported supporting evidence.
His first displayed example of a flyer promoting special Ramadan hours appeared to apply to a single store in 2024 in Cary, North Carolina — a town reportedly home to a large Muslim population. With a reverse image search, we located the apparent original post of the flyer on a Raleigh, North Carolina, Facebook page.
Seiter's second and third examples showed flyers for specials named "Eid-credible Delights" and "Happily Ever Iftar." Those two flyers appeared on the Singapore-based Dunkin' Facebook page (@dunkindonuts.sg), not the U.S.-based page.
The fourth example about a "Ramadan specialty drink" flavored with pistachio originated from the Egypt-based Dunkin' Instagram page (@dunkineg).
Regarding those two sources, the Singapore and Egypt Dunkin' regional pages both posted messages reading "Merry Christmas!" in December 2025.
Seiter's first Pride Month example originated from a 2024 post on a Facebook page named Taneja Restaurants for a single store based in Minnesota. In December 2025, that same page posted a message including the words "Happy Holidays" and "Merry Christmas."
His second and third Pride Month examples dated back to news releases from Dunkin' or its owner, Inspire Brands, in 2019 and 2021. We didn't locate any mentions of Pride Month, which takes place annually in June, on the Dunkin' website or the U.S.-based Instagram page during or surrounding the month in 2026.
Seiter continued, "With Christmas around the corner, I went to see what Christmas meals you had and noticed you don't even mention the word 'Christmas' anywhere on your website or anywhere in your stores." As noted before, we reached out to ask what he meant by "Christmas meals."
A search of the U.S.-based Dunkin' website for the word "Christmas" found more than 30 mentions, with most of them dating back several years. At the same time, the U.S.-based Dunkin' Instagram page has displayed mentions of the word "Christmas," or featured Christmas-themed posts, in recent years, for example at least twice in 2022 (including a post with a Christmas tree), numerous mentions in 2023, 2024 and a Christmas tree video from 2025 mentioning it's never too early to begin celebrating the Christian holiday.
Seiter ends his video by showing two images he says he "Googled" supposedly featuring authoritative and trusted sources that confirm Dunkin' intentionally omits the word "Christmas" as some sort of corporate policy. However, those images appeared to feature information generated with artificial intelligence, such as answers from Google's "AI Overview" or the Gemini tool website — tools Seiter previously said he was "exposing" as "evil" in another video (archived).
An exhaustive look back at hundreds of posts on the U.S.-based Dunkin' Instagram page found that the company usually announces its "holiday" cups and special offerings around the beginning of November, to account for all of the popular holidays during the season, including Thanksgiving, Hanukkah and Christmas, among others.
Also in 2026, ahead of the Fourth of July Dunkin' shared patriotic posts — including mentioning the Founding Fathers and promoting an eagle-shaped cup — and did not share Pride Month content. The company also offered free donuts to veterans and active military members for Veterans Day on Nov. 11.
For further reading, we previously covered a Starbucks cup controversy in which critics said the coffee chain removed all mentions of Christmas from its red holiday cups because "they hate Jesus."

Warning: this article contains discussion of eating disorders
"If you keep this up, you'll be in a wheelchair at 30."
That is what doctors told British long-distance runner Jake Smith four years ago.
From the outside looking in, his career was flying.
By the age of 23, he had signed a professional contract with Nike and represented Great Britain on the global stage.
But at the same time, his body was deteriorating - enduring a relentless pattern of race, illness, injury, repeat.
Balancing an intense training regime with disordered eating meant the 28-year-old returned from a running camp in Uganda weighing just eight stone (51kg) at 5ft 5in (1.7m). He had such brittle bones that he was told his career could be over.
After suffering two stress fractures in the space of four months, Smith sought professional help and was diagnosed with REDs – relative energy deficiency in sport.
It is a syndrome that can affect anyone and if left undiagnosed or untreated, can have an impact on performance and cause serious, long-lasting health problems.
The symptoms are slightly better documented in women - just last month, tennis player Emma Navarro revealed her diagnosis and subsequent decision to step away from competition until 2027.
But men are just as susceptible and due to stigma and lack of obvious warning signs, it can go undetected for longer and means many, like Smith, suffer in silence.
BBC Sport explains what the condition is, how it affects men and women and why, despite its prevalence and severity, REDs remains a relatively under-reported and overlooked area of sports science.
REDs can cause bone stress injuries, disrupted sleep, fatigue and low mood. Left untreated, the condition can lead to serious long-term health problems, including osteoporosis, cardiovascular disease and fertility issues.
Dr Nicky Keay, an expert in hormone health, says many of these symptoms stem from hormonal disruption caused by insufficient energy intake.
"Hormones go to every single bit in your body. So, if your hormones are not working well for you, you're going to feel it in all sorts of different areas," she says.
"In order to have healthy hormones, they need to be fed regularly. If you're not doing that and there's an energy deficit, often some of those hormone systems will slow down or shut down completely."
Women have a monthly barometer of their hormone health with the menstrual cycle, described by Keay as a "free monthly medical check".
Put simply, she says, a woman suffering from REDs has her periods "switched off".
For men, it is more subtle – testosterone levels will drop, resulting in a reduced libido and fatigue.
The impact on a woman's period is why the condition was first referred to in the early 1990s as the "female athlete triad".
But it was renamed by the International Olympic Committee in 2014 to acknowledge the broader range of symptoms of energy deficiency and that it also harms male athletes.
"We realised we were ignoring the other half of the population," Keay says.
"It's a strange situation because normally it's women's health that is the one being ignored but, in this situation, it's the men who weren't being recognised or represented."
Twelve years later that decision appears to be vindicated, with recent research highlighting the prevalence in men.
Meta-analysis published in Australian journal Sports Medicine last year, following a study involving thousands of elite and amateur athletes around the world, indicated 44.2% of female athletes and 49.4% of male athletes had low energy availability.
So why is REDs so common?
One of the answers lies in the phrase 'lighter is faster'.
For decades, it had been an accepted wisdom in sports like endurance running, cycling, climbing, horse riding, dancing and aesthetic sports like diving and gymnastics.
And for athletes like Smith, it is how his problems started.
"I believed it for years. I thought that was the way forward," he says.
"I started thinking 'how do I improve my half marathon by 10 seconds? Is it a drop in weight?'. And that's when my head completely went."
Initially, the strategy can work.
When it comes to choosing energy to cover training demand or energy to stay healthy, the body has learned through evolution and threat of predators to always prioritise movement.
It means that athletes can drop weight and still train and exercise and achieve good results.
But eventually, the luck runs out.
Described by Keay as "fool's gold", the body will adjust to the energy deficit and cause a drop in performance and high risk of injuries.
Olympic and world champion Jonny Brownlee acknowledges under-fuelling mistakes he made in his triathlon career contributed to serious injuries.
"I didn't see the importance of it. Training came first and I think we weren't educated enough in how important fuelling was," he tells BBC Sport.
"You were seen, culturally, as a bit weak if you were fuelling on the bike. And the impact of that was definitely injuries - probably not recovering from my training quite as well as I should have done, stress responses, stress fractures. So there's that side of it and probably underperformance in races as well."
Brownlee, who recently announced his retirement, believes the culture of not fuelling on the bike has now changed but a stigma lingers around REDs and the perception that it is a "female issue".
"In females, there are more obvious signs but in males it can go under the radar a little bit and then it hits you by a really serious injury," he says.
"I think there's a stigma attached in there, or it's not looked at as the obvious answer to some of your problems, it's found later down the line. Men also don't like to talk about under-fuelling because it's just seen as 'you probably should feel better and you should be on top of that'."
It is those attitudes among male athletes that prompted Keay to conduct an experiment in 2019.
Assessing 50 male competitive cyclists, Keay found in her initial screenings that nearly half had poor bone health and 25% were suffering from REDs.
The cyclists were then split into two groups and across a six-month period, one half continued their training and fuelling habits as before while the others were tutored by Keay and offered nutrition and training advice.
"The group that I left to their own devices unfortunately went on the default and they lost even more bone mineral density, similar to an astronaut in space… And they performed OK, but relative to their functional threshold power, they didn't get the race results that you would have expected.
"For the group I took under my wing, there was an improvement in their bone health and really good race results.
"So, I had evidence that REDs definitely does exist quite extensively in my group of the male cyclists and you're going to underperform if you don't fuel sufficiently. The good news is that REDs is reversible. But if you don't take action, it's a decline."
As the syndrome and its symptoms are still not commonly known, it is often difficult to know where to find help.
After former GB runner Pippa Woolven's struggles with the condition, she set up a website called Project REDs which offers information and practical resources for athletes, coaches, parents and healthcare professionals.
Keay also helps people competing at all levels to recover from REDs. Most of her patients are women, but she is starting to see more men reach out for help who, she says, are often in "bad shape".
"I think the men are maybe more reluctant than the women, or maybe they don't realise they've got it. Sometimes they might use a different word for it, they say burnout," Keay says.
"I don't mind that though because there is definitely a psychological aspect to REDs. Why are you doing this? Why are you not eating the carbohydrates?"
Sometimes, it's hard to answer those questions because the under-fuelling is unintentional, either from not understanding or underestimating energy requirements or failing to match an increase in the intensity or duration of exercise with higher calorie or carbohydrate intake.
For others, former British cycling champion Brian Smith among them, the answer comes from intention.
Competing in the road race for Great Britain at the 1996 Olympics should have been the highlight of his career but, behind the scenes of the success, Smith was suffering with an eating disorder and serious mental health condition called bulimia – something he believes he developed from his sport's obsession with weight.
"I always felt like I was overweight. Everybody was under pressure regarding weight, but nobody really spoke about it," he says.
"I'm just under six foot and I've got large glutes and thigh muscles. As a road cyclist, I used to race at 68kg and for my height and build, that's quite skinny. I even got down to about 66kg and when I got down to that, I felt underpowered, I felt bad."
Smith, now 59, only discovered he had been suffering from REDs during his career when he started running eight years ago and developed three severe stress fractures, including one in his femur.
Such has been the toll on his body that Smith says he would now never encourage anyone to pursue a career as a professional cyclist.
"It really is not healthy," he says. "If you want to go to the highest levels of the sport, you will suffer later on in life. You're destroying your body.
"Sporting teams don't care - all they're worried about is performance. So they will nurture a rider, they will feed a rider, they'll get a rider to be a certain weight. They don't care about what happens to them later in life.
"I'm suffering now and I've so many regrets. I just wish I'd known more about this."
While Smith believes his sport has a long way to go in changing attitudes, British Cycling says a lot of progress has been made through education that starts at academy level and annual physical and psychological screenings.
"One of the big things we've done in the past 10 years is try and turn this into a performance-related conversation," Dr Nigel Jones, British Cycling chief medical officer, tells BBC Sport.
"Now, we couch the conversation with an athlete around 'if you under-fuel, you will not be able to perform at your best', whereas previously, conversations in power-to-weight ratio sports might have been 'you need to be lighter'.
"I think it would be naive to say REDs is never going to be an issue. But I would like to believe that its prevalence will reduce with the work that we're doing," he adds.
British Cycling is not alone in this approach, with World Climbing taking things a step further two years ago with the introduction of mandatory health checks on athletes.
Using a combination of pre-season questionnaires and 'random and targeted' screenings at competitions - similar to the way doping tests are enforced – climbers at World Championship or World Cup-level competitions are monitored for any indicators of low energy availability or REDs and could be prevented from competing if they are not deemed to be healthy.
The policy was drawn up by expert Professor Naama Constantini, who says she is "proud" of the move by World Climbing and believes other federations should follow suit.
"We are trying to educate and prevent. I'm not a policeman and we're not looking for cheaters. I'm a medical doctor and we want to make sure our athletes are healthy," she says.
"Prevention is the best medicine you can give. We want athletes and coaches to understand that it's not about weight. It's about strength, it's about performance and fuelling the body and you pay a price if you lose weight in an unhealthy way."
With more awareness and education, it is hoped the tide can be turned on REDs.
But many still suffer in ignorance, as well as silence. That is what motivates Jake Smith to keep sharing his recovery on social media, with hundreds of men and women messaging him for advice and support.
Smith has managed to reverse his condition and is now racing better than ever, recently completing the Berlin marathon in a personal-best time of two hours, nine minutes and 24 seconds.
The big goal is the 2028 Olympics, but he is adamant that the priority is making sure he stands on every start line as healthy as possible.
"I'd never want to see an athlete go through the years I've had. I'm 10-15 kilos heavier than I've ever been and the biggest thing I can say is I've never been so happy. You need a healthy body to do everything else.
"I'm heavier, I'm faster, I'm happier."

An eight-year-old boy diagnosed with Type II achalasia – a rare disorder that affects the ability to swallow food and liquids – has undergone a Perora-l Endoscopic Myotomy (POEM) procedure at Rela Hospital.
Achalasia affects the nerves controlling the muscles of the oesophagus, causing the lower oesophageal sphincter – a muscular valve connecting the food pipe to the stomach – to remain abnormally tight. This prevents food and liquids from passing normally into the stomach. The condition is estimated to affect 0.1 to 0.18 children per 100,000 annually.
The child had progressively worsening difficulty swallowing both solids and liquids. Following the procedure, he was able to resume consuming clear liquids and subsequently, a soft diet, within 24 hours.
POEM involves passing an endoscope through the mouth and creating a small tunnel within the oesophageal wall to reach and divide the muscle fibres causing the obstruction. Unlike conventional surgery, the procedure does not require external incisions or stitches.
S.N.K. Chenduran, senior consultant and endoscopic surgeon, Department of Medical Gastroenterology, performed the procedure, which took about 50 minutes. He said performing POEM in children required particular precision because of the smaller dimensions of the oesophagus and the delicate tissues.
Dinesh Jothimani, director, Hepatology and Medical Gastroenterology, said persistent swallowing difficulties, regurgitation, vomiting, and unexplained weight loss in children warranted medical evaluation.
