US has lost measles elimination status, global health authorities say
The U.S. has lost its status as a country where measles is eliminated, a public health triumph secured a quarter century ago.
Researchers with direct knowledge of the deliberations on the country's status told KFF Health News that the Pan American Health Organization reached the conclusion this week: Measles has reestablished regular transmission in the country.
PAHO had planned a public announcement on Nov. 17.
In public health parlance, measles elimination depends on a country's sporadic outbreaks ending within a year. That's no longer happening in the United States.
"It's a very sad moment," said Anne Schuchat, an epidemiologist and a former deputy director at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention who was not involved in PAHO's decision.
"Measles causes so much unnecessary suffering, everything from a high fever and missed work and school to long-term complications like progressive degenerative nerve disease and death," Schuchat said.
Measles outbreaks are entirely preventable: Two doses of the measles-mumps-rubella vaccine prevent about 97% of infections, so when almost everyone in a community is fully vaccinated, the virus can't spread.
In the past two years, over 830 people have been hospitalized with measles in the U.S. More than 8,000 people have been sickened in outbreaks that have cost roughly $125 million in medical care, public health response, and productivity losses, Johns Hopkins University researchers estimate.
States have reported 13 measles-associated deaths, including a 7-month-old in New York and infants in Pennsylvania and Wisconsin in recent months. Babies typically aren't vaccinated before they're a year old.
PAHO, an international group that oversees health in the Americas and works with the World Health Organization, based its assessment on two analyses: one by the CDC and another by an independent group of measles experts.
Researchers anticipated this conclusion after an outbreak in Utah surpassed the one-year mark in June.
A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services, Emily Hilliard, attributed the resurgence of measles to vaccination gaps that opened years before this administration. Indeed, rates of childhood vaccination have steadily declined since the COVID pandemic started.
But many scientists also blame the Trump administration for spreading vaccine misinformation and stifling a swift, strong response to outbreaks.
For example, the administration cut millions of dollars from children's immunization programs run by state health departments and terminated funds for research on vaccine hesitancy.
After Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. sacked CDC director Susan Monarez in August 2025, she told Congress she was fired because she would not preapprove changes to vaccine recommendations "without reviewing the evidence."
Monarez added that "we already have seen the largest measles outbreak in more than 30 years" and that, "if vaccine protections are weakened, preventable diseases will return."
Spokespeople for HHS and the White House defended the administration, and Kennedy, who led a prominent anti-vaccine organization before he took the helm at HHS. "The President and the Secretary have repeatedly encouraged measles vaccination, coordinated with states, and facilitated the deployment of vaccine doses across the country," White House spokesperson Allison Schuster wrote in an email.
Past administrations sounded alarms
For more than three decades, the federal government treated measles as a preventable tragedy, with sizable outbreaks triggering national efforts to boost vaccination and stop the virus from spreading.
That's no longer the case, said Patsy Stinchfield, executive director of the Measles Collaborative, a new initiative that educates the public about vaccines and assists health workers responding to outbreaks.
Stinchfield was a pediatric nurse at a children's hospital in Minnesota during the nation's last surge of measles before elimination, from 1989 to 1991. She recalled an entire ward devoted to children with measles and the enormous effort required to prevent the virus from spreading to kids with cancer and weakened immune systems.
Two children at the hospital died of measles. "That changed my career forever," she said.
Back then, she said, the federal government "saw the urgency." Officials held press conferences, spoke on the news about vaccines, issued clinical guidelines, and published reports in the CDC's flagship journal — the Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report, or MMWR — that drove policies.
When data suggested that some children weren't mounting a strong response to a single dose of the measles-mumps-rubella vaccine, a CDC advisory committee recommended two doses of the shot.
When CDC analyses found that many children with measles hadn't been vaccinated due to cost, the government launched the Vaccines for Children program to make immunizations available free of charge to underinsured families.
Cases plummeted. By 2000, the CDC and PAHO determined that measles was no longer a national threat — measles transmission had been eliminated.
"Elimination" allows for occasional outbreaks, because measles is not eradicated worldwide and a small fraction of people, such as young infants, can't be protected by vaccines.
People infected abroad sparked occasional outbreaks after U.S. elimination, but — until now — those fizzled out because of herd immunity, when 95% of people within a community are immunized. In those situations, outbreaks peter out and vulnerable people are protected.
It would be 14 years before another significant outbreak in the U.S. Then in 2015, the virus took off among unvaccinated children at Disney parks in California, giving rise to outbreaks elsewhere. Congress saw some 125 cases as an emergency and summoned the CDC's Schuchat to testify on the situation.
"Vaccination wasn't a partisan issue," she recalled. "This was about problem-solving: What can we do about this?"
National television aired a video of then-U.S. Surgeon General Vivek Murthy talking with Sesame Street's Elmo about vaccination. HHS officials worked with vaccine experts on strategies to boost public confidence in vaccines. California and Vermont tightened vaccine requirements.
In 2019, House and Senate committees met again about measles, as a large outbreak took hold in Orthodox Jewish communities in New York and New Jersey took hold. Congress asked HHS leaders how the administration planned to curb the rise of vaccine misinformation online.
"Internet fraudsters who claim that vaccines are not safe are preying on the unfounded fears and daily struggles of parents, and they are creating a public health hazard that is entirely preventable," Lamar Alexander, then a Republican senator from Tennessee, said at the time.
Alex Azar, health secretary during the first Trump administration, and then-CDC Director Robert Redfield held a press conference stressing the "importance of on-time vaccination."
And during the 2014, 2015, and 2019 outbreaks, the CDC's MMWR published detailed articles within weeks of data collection. Timing matters since the reports guide emergency response. "The MMWR is the voice of the CDC," Schuchat said, "alerting the nation, the media, clinicians, and public health experts to events that require action."
'The dog didn't bark'
Just after President Donald Trump took office in 2025, a measles outbreak exploded in West Texas. Within seven months, it surpassed the size of any in the U.S. since 1992, spread to Mexico and at least three other states, sickened more than 4,500 people in the two countries, and killed at least 16.
Instead of broadcasting clear, repeated messages on the importance of measles vaccines, Kennedy falsely claimed on Fox News that they lead to "deaths every year."
Congress didn't call a hearing, and HHS didn't send funds until after the emergency in West Texas had subsided. Besides an annual measles update, the MMWR didn't publish a single report on the outbreaks that year.
"A lot of this is the dog didn't bark," said Dorit Reiss, a vaccine policy researcher at the University of California Law San Francisco. "Something that normally happens isn't happening."
Political appointees have delayed or blocked several MMWR articles, according to multiple CDC officials whom KFF Health News agreed not to identify because they feared retaliation for speaking with the press. "There's a deliberate effort to downplay vaccine-preventable diseases by the administration," one official said.
"Measles reports from West Texas and New Mexico were intentionally shelved," another scientist at the agency said. In April, The Washington Post reported that Jay Bhattacharya, who temporarily led the CDC this year and remains head of the National Institutes of Health, had blocked the publication of a study in the MMWR finding that COVID vaccines halved the likelihood of emergency department visits.
"The suggestion that HHS is deliberately suppressing information about measles or other vaccine-preventable diseases is false," Hilliard, the HHS spokesperson, said in an email to KFF Health News.
Hilliard said Kennedy and the CDC have provided approximately $100 million in additional funding to respond to outbreaks. The timing of MMWR reports, she added, varies due to factors such as data analysis and scientific review.
More than a year after data was collected from Texas, a few reports came out in the CDC's journal. One study on 60 people hospitalized for measles in West Texas revealed that two required intubation and mechanical ventilation and that a baby born to a mother with measles experienced dangerous brain swelling due to the virus.
The MMWR still hasn't published detailed reports on massive outbreaks in South Carolina, Utah, and Pennsylvania. The CDC's national measles update hasn't appeared in the MMWR this year either. Instead, the journal has featured less urgent articles on scientific techniques that may help characterize future outbreaks.
CDC scientists told KFF Health News that they continue to analyze data but no longer expect to publish their findings in the MMWR because the process has become slow, opaque, and unpredictable. An urgent CDC report on the risks of measles to pregnant women was withheld, The Washington Post reported recently.
"We have two CDCs now," an official at the agency said. "One is staffed by CDC scientists and civil servants who are committed to public health, and the other is political appointees who go in and change the website."
The CDC's measles dashboard counts four fewer measles deaths than state health departments have reported this year. Kennedy has disputed some deaths and made unsubstantiated claims that Pennsylvania health officials misrepresented data.
Kennedy personally instructed the CDC to alter language on a webpage that said vaccines do not cause autism, he told The New York Times last year.
The page now suggests a potential link between the two and no longer lists a slew of peer-reviewed studies that rigorously searched for an association and found none. These have been replaced with speculation about a correlation and unsubstantiated accusations that the scientific establishment has buried a potential link in order "to prevent vaccine hesitancy."
The Trump administration has muddied the message on vaccines in other ways, Reiss said. Trump incorrectly said in August that the measles-mumps-rubella vaccine could be "quite lethal," and he repeated the debunked idea that vaccines may cause autism.
Stephen Miller, now Trump's White House chief of staff, has falsely said doctors "pump your kids full of shots days after birth with no understanding of the long-term consequences." Recommended vaccines and the vaccine schedule have been thoroughly studied.
Kennedy has made such claims for two decades, including as health secretary. "Having top leadership disseminating rumors, disinformation and flat-out falsehoods has been unforgivable," Schuchat said.
When pressed by journalists and Congress, Kennedy and Trump have recommended measles vaccines. But they haven't repeated the message clearly and unprompted on social media or on the podcasts and videos that Kennedy regularly appears in.
Kennedy also replaced vaccine experts on a panel advising the CDC with fringe researchers holding anti-vaccine views. And under his leadership, the CDC has laid off or forced out many vaccine specialists, including all of those in a group that partners with community organizations and pharmacies, the Immunization Services Division partnership branch.
At the same time, Kennedy has devoted resources to searching for potential harms from vaccines, including through an attempted clinical trial considered unnecessary and unethical by medical societies and the WHO.
To regain measles elimination status, the current U.S. outbreaks must end — then, future outbreaks must stop spreading within a year, said Paul Rota, a microbiologist and former CDC official. With outbreaks expanding in several states, he said, that moment isn't on the horizon.
"Bigger fires create more embers, and any one of those embers can seed another fire," he said.

What to Know About Continued Flight Disruptions
After a nationwide ground stop Friday, travelers are still encountering snags, and it could take several days for flight schedules to return to normal.
Effects of a nationwide ground stop on air travel Friday evening, which stranded thousands of passengers and caused widespread delays, rippled into Saturday as airlines canceled thousands of flights and airports struggled to recover.
The air traffic control system, which faced a faulty upgrade that caused communications failures leading to the ground stop, is expected to be back to normal by Sunday night, said Bryan Bedford, who leads the Federal Aviation Administration. Flight schedules could take several days to return to normal.
Federal officials are still trying to determine who is at fault and have called for congressional funding to prevent similar failures. There is no evidence that the problem was caused by a cyberattack, officials have said.
Here’s what to know:
What caused the ground stop?
L3Harris, a contractor managing the F.A.A.’s telecoms network, made a standard upgrade at a remote air traffic location, federal officials said Saturday. L3Harris was conducting a routine task — replacing copper wire with more modern fiber optic cable — that was expected to pose no significant disruption to air traffic, said Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary.
But the switch from copper to fiber overwhelmed the system with levels of data it could not handle, prompting widespread communications failures across air traffic facilities that manage the national air space. Alarmed at the scope of the problems, officials issued a rare nationwide ground stop for hours.
Administration officials say it’s still unclear whether L3Harris or faulty equipment was to blame. L3Harris said in a statement on Saturday that it was supporting the F.A.A. investigation and that it “takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously.”

Around 86% of the spending on measures against tuberculosis (TB) in 2025 came from domestic sources, the recently released Global Tuberculosis Report 2026 by the World Health Organisation (WHO) said, even as the reduction in international donor funding to combat the infectious disease remains a cause of concern.
TB cases remain one of the leading causes of death from a single infectious agent, with a quarter of all cases concentrated in India in 2025. The report notes that $22 billion is needed annually for TB prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and care to achieve the global targets agreed on at the 2023 United Nations high-level TB meeting by 2027.
In absolute terms, Brazil, China, India, the Russian Federation, and South Africa accounted for $3.7 billion (65%) of the total of $5.63 billion provided from domestic sources in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs).
The report notes that international donor funding fell by 14%, from $1.1 billion in 2024 to $0.94 billion in 2025, having been relatively stable at about $1.1–1.3 billion per year between 2015 and 2024.
Financing for TB research and innovation, at $1.2 billion in 2023, also continued to fall far short of the global target of $5 billion per year. Progress to date has been constrained by the overall level of investment, said the report.
“TB mostly affects adults in their most productive years. However, all age groups are at risk. Over 80% of cases and deaths are in low- and middle-income countries. In 2025, the largest number of new TB cases occurred in the WHO South-East Asia Region (35%),’’ said the report.
South-East Asia Region
The WHO on Friday (November 13, 2026) called on countries in the South-East Asia Region to accelerate action to end TB. The latest TB estimates show the region accounts for 3.6 million people who developed TB in 2025 — 34% of the global total — and 4,00,000 TB-related deaths, or 35% of the global total. "These numbers are a stark reminder that TB remains one of the Region’s most pressing public health and development challenges,” said Nilesh Buddha, officer-in-charge, WHO South-East Asia Region.
A release issued by the regional office added that in 2025, $1.03 billion was available for TB prevention and care in the region, with 91% from domestic sources. Yet this represented only around 16% of global TB funding, despite the region accounting for 34% of global cases. "Closing this gap in resources is critical to sustaining progress," the WHO said.
“Ending TB is not simply a health sector responsibility. It requires leadership across government, sustained investment, strong health systems and communities at the centre of the response. We have tools to prevent, diagnose and treat TB. What is needed now is the commitment to ensure they reach everyone who needs them, without delay or financial hardship,” said Dr. Buddha, adding that ending TB by 2030 will depend on countries turning political commitments into measurable action, with greater urgency and scale.
Far from target
Meanwhile, the Global TB Report said that across the world, about 50% of people treated for TB and their households face total costs (direct medical expenditures, non-medical expenditures, and indirect costs such as income losses) that are catastrophic (more than 20% of total household income). This is far from the target of the WHO End TB Strategy of zero.
In 2025, globally there were an estimated 0.96 million new TB cases that were attributable to undernutrition, 0.92 million to diabetes, 0.73 million to alcohol use disorders, 0.69 million to smoking, and 0.55 million to HIV infection.

Kratom and 7-OH can feel like 'a miracle.' They can also be addictive
Tyler's opioid addiction began in his early 20s, and when he decided he wanted to quit, he used kratom leaf powders to help ease withdrawal symptoms.
Tyler, now 38, told NPR he thinks kratom helped him stop using opioids for a decade.
Tyler asked NPR to use only his first name because of the stigma attached to his history with drug use and addiction.
In early 2025, he saw a new product at a gas station called 7-OH. He hadn't heard of 7-OH, but said the tablets were advertised as "kratom products." He decided to try them, since the kratom powders he'd taken in the past "can be hard on your stomach," he said.
At first, 7-OH gave him a feeling of euphoria he described as similar to opioids, which "felt like a kind of a miracle," he said.
Nearly a year and a half later, he was in a rapid detox program in Michigan, where he was sedated to sleep through the withdrawals he experienced when he tried to stop taking it.
In the past few years, highly concentrated products with 7-OH — sometimes alongside other semi-synthetic opioids — have popped up online, and at many smoke shops, liquor stores and gas stations. They can come in the form of tablets, gummies, tonics and chocolate.
7-OH, or 7-hydroxymitragynine, is one of the major psychoactive ingredients in kratom, which comes from a tree in the coffee family. It's naturally found in kratom in very small amounts, and seems to act more like an opioid in the human brain than kratom leaf products. Kratom is used by some people with opioid addiction to maintain long-term recovery. Some people say it makes them feel energized or focused. Others describe the effects of kratom like those of opioids, and say it can relieve pain, feel calming or even create euphoria.
"More potent than I imagined"
Some users of 7-OH and kratom show classic signs of addiction, researchers and policy officials say. But the products are not always clearly labeled, so it's difficult or impossible for users to know what quantity of the substances they are consuming.
"I did not know at all what I was in for. It was much more potent than I had imagined," Tyler said.
Estimates of how many people use kratom and 7-OH in the U.S. are wide-ranging. Some suggest over 5 million people have used kratom in their lifetime. David Epstein, a senior investigator at the National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA) Intramural Research Program, says he's seen estimates of kratom use as high as 15 million. Those estimates don't usually distinguish between whole leaf kratom, 7-OH or other related products.
In the last decade, the U.S. government has attempted to restrict both kratom and 7-OH products, but strong opposition to those moves by the public and powerful advocacy groups backing the substances have kept them federally legal.
That's started to change in the last few months.
A federal crackdown is likely on the way
No federal actions have been taken against "traditional botanical kratom," but a new federal restriction on some 7-OH products could go into place as early as Friday, Nov. 13, 2026.
The path there has not been straightforward. In August, the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) restricted the making and sale of three semi-synthetic opioids derived from 7-OH and other related compounds: MGM-15, MGM-16 and mitragynine pseudoindoxyl (MGPI). Those compounds were listed under the Controlled Substances Act alongside the most highly restricted drugs, like heroin and LSD.
That caused backlash from kratom advocates who worried the rule would affect products with "trace amounts" of the semi-synthetic opioid, MGPI. One kratom advocacy organization, the American Kratom Association, filed a federal lawsuit on Aug. 26 against the DEA. It asked the DEA to ensure natural kratom products with traces of MGPI would remain legal.
The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) then issued a new recommendation on 7-OH and MGPI on Oct. 9, and the DEA changed its course. They now plan to restrict a narrower range of 7-OH and MGPI products: ones that contain higher concentrations of 7-OH and/or MGPI.
HHS and the DEA say they are not focusing on natural kratom products.
The research on kratom and 7-OH
Many people who oppose the restriction say kratom and 7-OH products have kept them away from traditional opioids, and helped them manage chronic pain, mood and mental health. Some also point to the fact that opioid deaths in the U.S. are decreasing. In 2023 alone, a KFF report found there were over 79,000 opioid deaths, and in 2024 there were 54,000.
A recent report of data from 53 U.S. poison control centers shows reports of calls related to kratom increased about 1,200% between 2015 and 2025. Chris Holstege, a physician and a professor of emergency medicine and pediatrics at the University of Virginia's School of Medicine, is one of the authors of that report. He said he and the other authors "were a bit stunned" by those findings, which do not distinguish between kratom or products like 7-OH.
The report included 233 deaths associated with kratom during 2015–2025, with 79% of those deaths involving multiple substances. The most severe outcomes were linked to people using multiple substances alongside kratom products, like opioids, stimulants and benzodiazepines.
But Holstege points out over half the reports of calls, 62%, involved people using kratom without other drugs.
The authors used data on kratom from the National Poison Data System (NPDS), which includes calls from the public, healthcare professionals or medical examiners, and medical records.
For some, a "life-changing" dose
Still, there are people who report benefits of using kratom or 7-OH, said Epstein, the NIDA investigator.
NPR spoke to one mom in Delaware, Angela Wilson, 44, who said 7-OH has helped her manage excruciating chronic pain related to endometriosis, and symptoms of depression she's had since she was a teenager.
She said she's been taking 32 to 40 milligrams of 7-OH a day, split into three doses, for the last year and a half.
Wilson said kratom powders made her feel anxious and shaky, and 7-OH seems to work for her without those side effects.
"It's been truly life-changing for my family situation, my personal life," she said.
Wilson doesn't have health insurance, and said losing access to 7-OH under new restrictions would be "devastating" for her and her family.
"We're not really sure, you know, what I'm gonna do when it's not available," she said.
"It was game over." Dangers of addiction
Epstein has also heard stories like Tyler's. He said people can become addicted or dependent — and some of his ongoing research suggests that risk is higher with 7-OH products than with whole leaf kratom.
He said for some people, their 7-OH use "seemed to go nicely for the first couple of days, but then they found that they had to keep using to avoid withdrawal," Epstein said. "And some of them, not all of them, but some of them, even said they had to, you know, they couldn't make it through the night. They had to get up in the middle of the night to take more."
He said other people were happy with the effects they got from taking 7-OH and didn't feel like it caused problems for them.
Tyler told NPR that 7-OH tablets gave him more energy at first. He works a job where he's on his feet a lot, and with 7-OH, he said, " I can go, go, go, go, go, you know?"
He began taking around 300 to 400 mg of 7-OH a day, about ten times the dose Angela Wilson takes. In the next year, he said he made a few attempts to stop, but the withdrawals were debilitating.
"The best way to put it, I think, is to imagine having the flu, the worst flu you've had, you know, multiply that by at least three times," he said. "And then just know that all you gotta do is take one pill, and it's gone in seconds."
Another former kratom and 7-OH consumer, Brian, 41, told NPR at the height of his use, he was using much more 7-OH than both Angela Wilson and Tyler. Brian also asked NPR to use only his first name because of the stigma associated with drug use.
Brian used 1,200 mg of 7-OH — and estimates he spent around $150 each day — on the substance. He'd quit using opioids in 2016, but found kratom at a gas station in 2022. He said it claimed to help with energy.
"And 'cause literally right next to the register, nothing taboo about it, looks like those 5-Hour Energy shot type things," he said.
Brian said within minutes of taking it, he realized he felt "exactly" like he did when he'd been taking opioids.
"I was like, 'What is this?,'" he said. "'Like, are you telling me I found a legal, you know, healthy opiate that f***s you up and, you know, you feel great and no consequences, like the legality of it and everything?"
"I was like, 'This is it,'" he said.
Brian tried to stop taking kratom multiple times, but couldn't. One day at a smoke shop, he said the clerk offered him a sample of 7-OH. The clerk described it as a "version of kratom" that Brian could take in lower doses to get the same effects.
"Once I found these little tiny tablets — that I had to take one and it felt like I had taken an Oxycontin — you know, that was it," Brian said. "It was game over."
An uncertain future
Researchers say more research should be done to understand the potential benefits of kratom and 7-OH products, including whether they can help treat addiction. On their website, NIDA says, "early studies suggest kratom and kratom compounds warrant further study as experimental treatments for substance use disorders, specifically opioid use disorder."
In the meantime, Holstege, at the University of Virginia's School of Medicine, says current marketing around kratom products seems to attract users for other reasons.
"I find it a little hard to believe that all the shops that are popping up around my campus right now are trying to advertise to people who are addicted to opioids," he said. "So the question is, what else are they advertising this product for?"
" I certainly have a growing list of patients in addiction clinics who are addicted to this, and in withdrawal, that we're having to manage," Holstege added.
Brian stopped taking 7-OH in April 2026, when he said he decided to "quit cold turkey." He said he experienced more debilitating withdrawals from 7-OH than he had from quitting opioids. He noted, though, he'd had a much easier time accessing 7-OH, and took it more frequently than he'd taken opioids.
When stopping 7-OH, he said he felt fearful, anxious, and had gastrointestinal issues. He lost the desire to leave his house.
"It was a nightmare," Brian said.
Tyler told NPR he hasn't used 7-OH or kratom since he traveled to the Michigan detox program in March. He said he doesn't think he would have been able to stop using 7-OH without that program.
"There's no chance," he said. "It's just too addictive and too accessible."
He said the road to feeling like himself again has been even longer than when he stopped using opioids. With opioids, he said, it took a few weeks to feel like he had energy again.
With 7-OH, he said the process has taken months.
"Kind of just this week I'm starting to feel kinda great," he said in October. "But it's been a long journey of getting my energy back."

Indonesia's vice president resigns amid signs ruling alliance is fraying
- Published
Indonesia's Vice-President Gibran Rakabuming Raka has submitted his resignation, an aide has told the BBC, in a move which could further strain the political alliance that helped propel President Prabowo Subianto to power.
It comes after Indonesia's Supreme Court ruled that a high-school document used during Gibran's 2024 election campaign was invalid.
The ruling prompted more than 100 lawmakers to support a parliamentary initiative that could have paved the way for proceedings to impeach Gibran.
The aide, Budi Arie, said Gibran's resignation letter was submitted directly to Prabowo on Wednesday. It remains unclear if it has been accepted.
Gibran has long faced controversy over whether his high school qualifications met legal requirements to run for office.
Having studied in Singapore and Australia, he had used an Indonesian equivalence certificate to demonstrate his educational credentials.
Indonesian law requires vice-presidents to have completed senior secondary school or its equivalent, but the Supreme Court found no evidence to prove Gibran had graduated.
"No evidence was found to show Gibran had a foreign diploma or certificate that could serve as the basis for equivalency with a senior high school or equivalent qualification," it said.
It also considered a Constitutional Court ruling from earlier in October which came to the same conclusion.
Gibran previously argued that undertaking university education was sufficient proof that he had completed senior high school.
On Tuesday, he asked for the chance to challenge the ruling and be given the opportunity to prove the legitimacy of his education credentials, State Secretary Prasetyo Hadi said.
Gibran's ascension to Prabowo's ticket in the 2024 election was part of an alliance formed between his father, outgoing president Joko Widodo - known as Jokowi - and Prabowo, his erstwhile bitter rival.
Gibran was 36 at the time, and only became eligible for candidacy after a controversial ruling by the Constitutional Court, which exempted him from the minimum age requirement of 40.
His resignation comes as tensions between Jokowi and Prabowo appear to have flared.
Since taking the presidency, Prabowo has shown little interest in pushing ahead with Jokowi's legacy project: the construction of Nusantara, a new capital. Instead, he has focused much of the state's resources on his own flagship programme to provide free school meals across the country.
In a series of personnel reshuffles over the past year, Prabowo has also shifted many Jokowi loyalists into new roles, including long-serving finance minister Sri Mulyani Indrawati.
Last week, authorities arrested presidential chief of staff Listyo Sigit Prabowo - no relation - on suspicions of wiretapping the president.
Prabowo sacked Listyo a day later, in what many pointed to as a sign of a crumbling alliance: Listyo, who formerly served as the national police chief, is widely considered a long-time ally of Jokowi.
Within the government, allegiances seem to be shifting. On Monday, three members of Prabowo's cabinet collectively resigned from the party led by Kaesang Pangarep, Jokowi's youngest son, citing their desire to focus on their duties in Prabowo's administration.
All this is unfolding at a particularly turbulent period in Prabowo's presidency. The free school meals programme is struggling for funding, parts of Indonesia have recently battled the country's worst wildfires in a decade, and the national stock market faces crisis amid allegations of widespread market manipulation.
On Tuesday, students across the country staged demonstrations to protest against the government's handling of a range of issues, including the environmental crisis and corruption.

The 'manager's dream' who has put NI one game from history
- Published
It was a moment that Northern Ireland needed.
When Terry Devlin picked the ball up on the edge of the area in the 68th minute against Ukraine there was only one thought in his mind.
And when the ball flew into the corner Windsor Park erupted at another highlight of a Nations League campaign that has been a real feel-good story so far.
Heading into Saturday's game they had yet to concede a goal, but the one thing they had lacked was a home win - or even a home goal - after drawing blanks in stalemates with Hungary and Georgia in Belfast.
They had already come close when Jamie Donley slotted home in the first half but the forward had strayed offside, leaving the moment the hosts had been waiting for to come through Devlin's superb winner.
It leaves Northern Ireland's Nations League fate in their own hands, and a draw or better in Hungary would secure promotion to League A for the first time.
For Northern Ireland boss Michael O'Neill, it was a huge moment from a player who he said is "a bit of a dream" to manage.
"Terry's a great lad. He deserves everything he'll get from the game and he's one of those lads that maximises what he has," O'Neill said about the 23-year-old Portsmouth defender.
Speaking about his versatility - Devlin can play in midfield as well as a full-back on either side - O'Neill added: "He does it with no fuss. He tries to do it to the best of his ability.
"He's a bit of a dream for a manager and he has the ability to contribute goals."
The average age of O'Neill's starting XI on Saturday was just 22.9 with eight players aged 23 or younger.
Devlin epitomises what this team are all about with his all-action display rewarded with a first international goal.
A versatile option, he broke through into senior football with his hometown club Dungannon Swifts in the Irish Premiership and impressive performances for Glentoran saw him earn a move to Portsmouth in 2023.
He has now become a cult hero at Fratton Park, and he is the club's top scorer in the Championship this season.
His winner in Belfast was a fitting moment for a player who continues to grow on the international stage.
"He's a very valuable player for Portsmouth and I think he's in the process of signing a new contract there, and I imagine a lot of teams in the Championship will be disappointed by that."
'We're in a great position'
While Devlin will get the headlines after his man-of-the-match performance, goalkeeper Pierce Charles came up with a big moment of his own with a superb reflex save to deny Danylo Sikan in the closing stages.
The 21-year-old has yet to concede in the Nations League campaign, and he has produced several big moments to make it 466 minutes and counting without shipping a goal for Northern Ireland.
"You don't keep five clean sheets because you're good with the ball at your feet. You keep five clean sheets because you make good decisions," said O'Neill.
"You make saves when it's needed. He kind of does it without any fuss as well, which I think is really good.
"He doesn't come and cause any issues with the back-three, which is very important for any goalkeeper, and he has a good decision-making process and a good understanding of the game."
Northern Ireland will now head to Hungary with their Nations League destiny in their own hands in what is essentially a Group B2 decider.
They are guaranteed a promotion play-off at the very least, but the goal will be to earn automatic elevation to League A for the first time.
Considering Northern Ireland had just one Nations League win in 16 League B matches before the campaign, back-to-back promotions would be a remarkable achievement.
One down side from the win over Ukraine was the two yellow cards accumulated, one for O'Neill and the other for key striker Jamie Donley.
Both were for reactions to a perceived lack of decisions from French referee Francois Letexier, and both manager and player will now watch the game in Budapest from the stands.
"The referee doesn't like my reaction and there's not much I can do about that," O'Neill said.
"I would assume that I'm going to have to watch the game from the stands, but I'll be able to influence it from there, I'm sure."
On Donley's booking, which came for protesting after Letexier failed to stop play when Trai Hume was bleeding from a cut on his head, O'Neill said it was a "poor yellow".
"I thought Jamie had a very good game for us. He'll be a blow for us," he said.
But the suspensions will do little to dampen what was another encouraging night at Windsor Park.
Hungary had piled the pressure on Northern Ireland by winning in Georgia earlier on Saturday, and Northern Ireland's response sets up a showdown to top the group on Tuesday.
"We were aware that Hungary had won the game earlier and we're in a great position," O'Neill added.
"It would be great to win the group. It will be a tough, tough game but this is a brilliant game for us. It's a great arena to play in."
Having kept five clean sheets in as many matches, O'Neill is targeting completing the campaign without conceding.
If they can do that, they would not only win promotion but secure a play-off for Euro 2028 as a back-up should their qualifying group not go to plan.
"For a nation of our size, with our players at this stage of their careers, to have a chance to win the group and also to be playing Nations League A is a big achievement.
"I think we would probably be one of the smaller nations to play at Nations League A level since the start of the competition.
"We want to try to achieve that and we have a chance to do that on Tuesday night."

Called 911? A drone may now be the first response
Police departments from New York to North Carolina are facing a shortage of cops - and drones have been made part of the solution. But the rapid rollout of the tech raises fresh questions about privacy and surveillance, Jasmine Fernández reports

Already a member? Log in
In a growing number of U.S. cities, the first responder on the scene of a 911 call is no longer a police car but rather a drone launched from a nearby precinct roof.
From departments in Chula Vista, California, to larger agencies like the Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department and the NYPD, law enforcement is increasingly turning to rooftop-launched aircraft to cut response times, give dispatchers live overhead video in minutes, and provide early intel before cruisers even roll out.
Proponents say the technology cuts response times and relieves pressure on depleted police forces but privacy advocates warn that airborne cameras are expanding public surveillance faster than state laws and local regulations can adapt.
Brandon Henderson, a criminal defense attorney at HMW Law in Cleveland, Ohio, whose practice involves challenging police technology used as evidence, told The Independent that drones offer clear benefits and can “puts eyes on a scene faster without putting help there.”
But he added: “It cannot make an arrest, secure a scene, or put hands on a patient.”
In St. Louis, Missouri — a city that has battled severe police staffing shortages and high violent crime rates — a new drone program was adopted earlier this month by city police.
The “Aerial Response Unit” of two drones, operated by department drone pilots, takes off from launch pads on the North and Central Patrol division’s roof to answer 911 calls and assist ground response. Within hours of the program’s approval, drone pilots made their first flights and helped officers in the search for a missing boy who was safely returned home.
“While officers searched on the ground, the drones checked several locations the boy was known to frequent or may have traveled to,” St. Louis Police Department said. “By covering those areas from the air, the drones freed ground officers to search other locations. An officer on the ground ultimately located the boy, and he was safely returned home.”
The department’s director of public affairs, Mitch McCoy, told KSDK that drones can be on scene within 70 seconds of a 911 call being dispatched.
McCoy added that the aerial units would assist with “calls in progress” and “calls for shots fired or shot spotter activations.”
“This truly will help us even potentially free up officers where a drone might be able to respond to a call instead of a police officer,” McCoy added.
Eyes in the sky
St. Louis is just one of many law enforcement agencies which has adopted drones after struggling to fill positions. From 2019 through 2024, officer resignations and retirements reduced police staffing nationwide, according to the Government Accountability Office.
In North Carolina, the Durham and Fayetteville police departments approved their drone programs earlier this year. The Raleigh Police Department is currently “gathering information” about the technology, WRAL reported.
In New York City, the NYPD operates a Drone as First Responder program across precincts in Brooklyn, the Bronx and Manhattan. Deployed remotely from station houses, the drones fly autonomously to select priority calls — including ShotSpotter alerts, robberies and missing person searches —to stream live video to responding officers’ smartphones.
And in Las Vegas, the Metropolitan Police Department formally launched a drone program after first using the aircraft to map the extensive crime scene of the 2017 Route 91 Harvest music festival mass shooting. Today, the department deploys a fleet of unmanned aircraft to cut emergency response times, inspect building interiors and assist ground personnel with search-and-rescue operations.
Chula Vista Police Department in California was the one of the first law enforcement agencies to launch a drone program in the U.S. in 2018 and has flown more than 25,000 missions.
The department reports its drones arrive in about 97 seconds, on average, resolving roughly one in five calls without patrol units.
“What a drone offers that a patrol car cannot is information before anyone commits,” Henderson, the defense attorney, told The Independent.
“Officers arriving at a chaotic scene normally know only what a frightened caller managed to say. A live overhead view tells them whether a reported weapon is real, which way a suspect ran, whether a crowd is forming, and whether the emergency is an emergency at all.”
Henderson added that resolving calls remotely can de-escalate situations before physical contact occurs. Yet the expansion of the cameras has raised significant privacy concerns.
“A drone answering a 911 call does not record only the caller or the suspect,” he said. “It records everyone underneath it: neighbors in their yards, people on the street, families who never asked the government to watch them, most of whom never learn they were filmed at all.”
Rapid response
Academic research is beginning to measure the operational impact of these drone systems. Scott Mourtgos, an assistant professor of criminology and criminal justice at the University of South Carolina, led what is believed to be the world’s first randomized control trial to gauge the effectiveness of using drones as first responders.
He studied the use of drones by departments in Montgomery County, Maryland, and Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, in trials that wrapped up earlier this year. His research was published in October.
“What we found across both of those agencies is that certain drones in first responder programs, at least as implemented in those two agencies, certainly seem to have a positive benefit when it comes to being able to handle and respond to calls for service, 911 calls, more quickly,” Mourtgos told WRAL.
Mourtgos noted that the drones proved most effective when responding to so-called “Priority 2” calls — such as a retail theft or vandalism in progress — arriving roughly two minutes faster than typical response times.
Yet the authors cautioned that the data could not determine whether faster arrival times outweighed the financial, organizational and privacy costs of the surveillance.
Taking flight
Despite concerns, it doesn’t seem like rollout of police drones will be slowing down any time soon.
“These programs will keep spreading because the economics work for stretched departments, and the FAA keeps making beyond-visual-line-of-sight flight easier to approve,” Henderson told The Independent.
“What communities should weigh before adopting one is who owns the footage, how long it lives, and what else it may be used for... because those terms are nearly impossible to tighten once a program is running."

New Delhi: The government’s attempt to recover value from its ageing office equipment has hit an e-waste hurdle, with the Department of Investment and Public Asset Management (Dipam) cancelling a tender to auction decades-old laptops, printers, air-conditioners and furniture, two government officials said.
Dipam has decided to segregate electronic waste from other obsolete assets and dispose of it through authorised recyclers, in line with existing rules.
It has informed bidders that no further action will be taken on bids submitted against the cancelled tender, the first official said.
Mint had in August reported about Dipam’s plan to auction a wide range of obsolete office assets through a single tender. The inventory included Apple MacBooks purchased in 2011, Dell and HP laptops bought between 2010 and 2013, and computers acquired as far back as 2005-06. Several electronic devices were listed as non-functional.
The list also covered printers and scanners from manufacturers such as HP, Samsung, Kyocera and Brother, along with fax machines and multifunction printers.
Air purifiers, air-conditioners, water dispensers, heaters, ovens, fans, televisions, batteries and telephone equipment were also listed for auction.
The items also included chairs, tables, plywood gates, suitcases, wall clocks, trolleys, treadmills and paper shredders.
Segregating items
Dipam had planned to sell the entire lot through sealed bids on an 'as is where is' basis, under which successful bidders would acquire the assets in their existing condition. The department had not estimated the proceeds, with the final amount expected to depend on bids received.
“Now, the department will segregate electronic waste from other obsolete office assets and follow the prescribed disposal process. Electronic waste is required to be handled through authorised dismantlers or recyclers under applicable rules,” said the second person.
Dipam manages the government's disinvestment and public asset monetisation programme. The proposed auction was a relatively small exercise within its broader mandate, but an attempt to recover some value from equipment that had remained unused for years.
Queries sent to the spokesperson of the finance ministry and Dipam secretary remained unanswered till press time.

Storm Charles has brought destructive weather to the Iberian peninusla this week, particularly in Portugal and the far south of Spain. Heavy rain and strong south-westerly winds arrived first in the Portuguese island of Madeira, before the system headed towards the mainland on 11 November. A wind gust of 84.5mph (136 km/h) was recorded at Funchal airport, alongside rainfall totals reaching 355mm in 12 hours. Lisbon saw 183 flights cancelled on Wednesday, around a third of its normal daily traffic, while Madrid Barajas airport had 155 cancellations.
After causing widespread flooding in Spain and Portugal, the system moved on a north-easterly track through southern France and then towards northern Italy. This resulted in significant flooding in parts of Cannes, some of which caused rock falls and led to the closure of roads along the French Riviera. The Italian weather service issued a red rainfall warning, its highest level, for the area extending from Tuscany to Venezia. Further heavy rain is expected to fall in Italy and the Balkans over the next few days, with the latest forecast models indicating an additional 100mm could accumulate widely, while totals close to 200mm are likely in more mountainous areas.
Successive rounds of heavy rain and strong winds have caused flooding, landslides and disruption across British Columbia, Canada through the last week or so.
Between Monday and Friday last week, severe rainfall and strong winds left more than 400,000 customers without power in British Columbia. These unsettled conditions continued into the weekend, with further heavy rain leaving 135,000 customers without power, alongside downed trees, flooded roads and landslides. Strong winds were also recorded on Sunday, with a gust of 72.1mph (116 km/h) on Herbert Island and a gust of 60mph (96 km/h) at Victoria international airport.
Heavy rain warnings were then issued on Wednesday for British Columbia’s Vancouver Island and southern coastal areas as multiple stations recorded rainfall totals in excess of 100mm. Additionally, the River Forecast Centre issued flood warnings on Wednesday across the south coast with heavy rain and high streamflow continuing to bring an increased risk of flash flooding and landslides.
A further area of low pressure is expected to bring torrential rain and strong winds across this same region over the weekend. More than 100mm is likely across central and southern parts of Vancouver Island on Saturday, with gusts in excess of 60mph likely too.

Hungarian authorities uncover $20m during probe of Orbán-era minister
- Published
Nearly $20m (£14.8m) in cash has been found hidden in farm buildings and buried in forests as part of an investigation into a former minister of Viktor Orbán, authorities have said.
Miklós Seszták, who served as minister of national development for four of the ex-prime minister's 16-year rule, is accused of accepting bribes as part of a scheme involving the state transport company. He has denied any wrongdoing.
Hungary's new Prime Minister Péter Magyar unseated Orbán in a landslide election in April on the promise of launching a sweeping anti-corruption drive.
On Friday, following the two-day search for the cash - found in secluded locations across the country - Magyar described it as the end of the "mafia".
Investigators found wads of banknotes in safes, buried in woodlands and hidden in agricultural and residential buildings and warehouses, as part of the probe into Seszták, the National Asset Recovery and Protection Office (NVVH) said in a statement.
The cash amounted to "5,071,632,000 forints, €2,658,350 and $1,257,100", it added, bringing the combined value to $19.5m. It has been deposited into the Hungarian State Treasury, the body said.
The NVVH was established to investigate allegations of corruption during the Orbán rule, which Magyar has dubbed "Operation Purgatory".
Magyar promised Hungarians "regime change" during the election earlier this year and has set about undoing many Orbán-era policies since entering office.
Allegations of corruption and cronyism have long dogged Orbán, who during the course of his tenure turned Hungary into what the EU characterised as an "electoral autocracy".
His government faced accusations of offering lucrative government projects to allies. Orbán has strongly denied the claims.
Two of his former ministers, including Seszták, and the former central bank chief Gyorgy Matolcsy have been under arrest since September over accusations of graft in separate investigations. They all deny wrongdoing.
On Monday, Hungarian authorities also detained Orbán's brother and three others as part of a people-smuggling case.
The former prime minister dismissed it as political revenge, saying: "In this dirty game, the aim is the elimination of the political opponent and the establishment of a one-party system.
"I am the target, my younger brother is just a tool."

Cacao is a 6-year-old Pomeranian surrendered to ARK this spring when his family, for no fault of his, could no longer keep him. Cacao was, to put it mildly, not happy with the decision, in which he had had no say. When he first arrived at ARK, he was an angry little fellow and even refused to have a lead put on him.
That was seven months ago and the transformation has been magical.
Cacao is affectionate and loves having his fur brushed. He also loves to run. He’ll race around full of energy and joy.
That said, Pomeranians are said to be spirited and confident, and those two traits can spell trouble if their wishes are not taken into full consideration. Simply said, Cacao wants to be heard. He wants to “participate” in decisions that affect him.
He’s independent and he’ll play all by himself, but he also likes your presence and expects you will be just as smitten by him as he is of you.
Cacao wants a family or a friend that, largely, wants to do what he does. He’s not at all difficult for the right person: Someone loyal, someone who will dote on him, someone whose life will revolve around him (only when he’s looking is fine). Does that sounds like someone you know? Then Cacao is your boy!

Nigeria cautions against travel via Ethiopia's main airport due to altitude
- Published
Nigeria's government has cautioned its citizens, in particular those with medical conditions, against travelling via Ethiopia's main airport due to its altitude.
The foreign ministry in Abuja said 16 Nigerians with underlying health problems had died this year while transiting through Addis Ababa.
The city sits at an altitude of 2,334m (7,657ft) above sea level, making it one of the highest capitals in the world. Bole International Airport is a major hub for travel between Africa, the Middle East and Asia, serving millions of passengers a year.
Nigeria said those with cardiovascular and respiratory conditions were at an increased risk.
The Nigerian foreign ministry did not disclose the identities of the travellers it said had died, nor the cause of death.
It urged anyone with a health condition exacerbated by high altitudes to "exercise caution" when planning a journey via Addis Ababa and "obtain appropriate medical guidance" before doing so.
The ministry stressed that it did not want to discourage Nigerians from travelling through the Ethiopian capital.
Visiting an area at a high altitude can be dangerous for people with heart and lung diseases, as the air is thinner and so less oxygen can get into the bloodstream, experts say.
This means the heart has to work harder to get enough oxygen to different parts of the body, which can sometimes lead to heart failure among those with existing conditions, according to the American Heart Association.
The lack of oxygen at high altitudes can cause adverse effects such as dizziness, fatigue and shortness of breath among healthy people - which can cause complications for people with lung disease, studies show.

Wider access to diabetes technology needs policy support, experts say
Continuous glucose monitors and automated insulin delivery systems drastically improve glycaemic control and cut hospitalisations, yet steep out-of-pocket costs and socioeconomic disparities leave a massive adoption gap
Technology can improve monitoring and support treatment decisions |Image used for representational purpose only
| Photo Credit: Wikimedia commons
Diabetes management is moving beyond periodic finger-prick tests and clinic visits, with technologies such as continuous glucose monitors (CGMs), insulin pumps and mobile applications providing more detailed information on glucose levels and helping patients make day-to-day decisions about their care.
CGMs use a sensor placed on the arm or abdomen to measure glucose levels at regular intervals, offering a picture of fluctuations through the day and night. Insulin pumps deliver insulin continuously, while automated insulin delivery systems combine CGM readings with algorithms to adjust insulin delivery. Mobile applications can bring together information on glucose levels, food intake, physical activity and medication.

Revanth Reddy assured the Public Health Foundation of India (PHFI) of the State government’s full support for establishing its Institute of Public Health Sciences (IPHS) Deemed-to-be University in Hyderabad, setting June 2, 2028, as the deadline for completing the proposed campus and promising assistance with land, funds, permissions and other requirements.

By Dr Syed Riyaz Ahmed
When someone develops Type 2 diabetes, doctors usually look at their diet, body weight, physical activity and family history. These are well-established factors that help explain why the disease develops.
Genetics, ageing, excess body fat, an inactive lifestyle, diet and social conditions remain the main risk factors. However, scientists are now looking at another possible influence: the chemicals people breathe, drink, eat and come into contact with at work may also affect their chances of developing diabetes.
This takes the discussion beyond the doctor’s consulting room, towards polluted streets, agricultural fields, industrial areas and even household kitchens. It raises an important public health question: how much does environmental pollution contribute to the growing number of diabetes cases?
Research is beginning to provide some answers, although the strength of the evidence differs from one pollutant to another.
Scientists studying endocrine-disrupting chemicals have found reasons for concern. These substances interfere with the body’s hormone system, which helps control metabolism.
Laboratory experiments suggest that some chemicals may encourage the development of fat cells, interfere with insulin production and function, and trigger inflammation and oxidative stress.
These findings help explain how chemical exposure could potentially increase diabetes risk.
However, laboratory findings need careful interpretation.
Some experiments use chemical concentrations much higher than those people normally encounter. A reaction observed in an animal or an isolated cell also does not prove that the same effect occurs in humans. Scientists need stronger human evidence before drawing firm conclusions.
Studies involving people provide more convincing reasons to examine this connection, particularly in the case of air pollution and arsenic.
A 2018 study by Bowe and colleagues, published in The Lancet Planetary Health, examined 1.7 million US veterans. It found that people exposed to higher levels of fine particulate matter, known as PM2.5, faced a greater risk of developing diabetes.
The researchers estimated that air pollution contributed to around 3.2 million new diabetes cases worldwide in 2016.
This finding gives polluted air significance beyond its well-known effects on the lungs. Traffic emissions, industrial activity and the burning of solid fuels release tiny particles that people breathe during ordinary daily activities. When exposure continues over long periods, polluted air can become a serious public health concern.
The study found a strong association, although this does not mean that air pollution alone causes diabetes in everyone exposed to it.
Arsenic is another concern, particularly in areas where groundwater contains high concentrations of the substance. Research reviewed by Maull and colleagues in 2012 linked high levels of arsenic exposure to diabetes.
Parts of eastern India and Bangladesh face this problem, making contaminated groundwater an important environmental health issue. Families using unsafe water may therefore face health risks beyond the immediate effects of arsenic poisoning.
The evidence involving other chemicals is less clear.
Persistent organic pollutants, which can enter the food chain through fatty foods and remain in the environment for many years, have shown possible links with diabetes.
Research on PFAS, often called forever chemicals, has also attracted attention. These substances are found in drinking water, food packaging and treated fabrics.
A 2022 US study by Park and colleagues, published in Diabetologia, found that middle-aged women with the highest combined exposure to PFAS were more likely to develop diabetes. Earlier studies, however, reported mixed results.
This suggests a possible connection, but scientists need more research to understand how strong it is.
The evidence surrounding BPA and phthalates is even less certain. These chemicals are commonly associated with food packaging, plastics and personal-care products. However, the body removes them within hours or days.
A single urine sample, therefore, cannot reliably show how much a person has been exposed to over several years. Pesticides are another concern, particularly for agricultural workers, although research has yet to establish a clear connection with diabetes.
These differences are important because finding a link between chemical exposure and a disease does not automatically prove that one causes the other.
Body weight and changes in the way the body stores chemicals can influence exposure measurements. Diet, income, occupation and body fat can also affect both chemical exposure and diabetes risk, making it difficult to identify the effect of an individual substance.
The challenge becomes greater when people encounter several chemicals at the same time.
Research focusing on one substance may miss the combined effects of different exposures. Limited exposure measurements and publication bias, which makes studies reporting positive findings more likely to appear in scientific journals, create further difficulties.
There is also a question of who faces the greatest risk.
Agricultural and industrial workers, people living near contaminated sites, residents of heavily polluted cities and households using solid fuels for cooking often experience greater environmental exposure.
These communities may also have fewer resources to protect themselves.
A worker handling pesticides may have little control over workplace safety, while a family dependent on contaminated groundwater may have no easy alternative source.
Public discussion can sometimes make the science harder to understand.
Headlines often report relative risk without explaining what the numbers mean. If six out of 1,000 people develop diabetes in a year, a 50 per cent increase would raise that figure to nine.
The increase becomes significant when millions of people are exposed, although age and family history may still be stronger predictors of an individual’s risk.
Governments have an important responsibility in addressing these concerns.
Public health agencies should monitor environmental exposure, enforce safety standards and update regulations as scientific evidence improves.
Uncertainty about the link with diabetes should not delay action against chemicals already known to cause other health problems. Several persistent pollutants have faced restrictions, while regulations on BPA and some PFAS have also been tightened.
Employers who handle pesticides and industrial chemicals should provide safe working conditions, proper ventilation and protective equipment. Workers also need access to occupational health services where they can report concerns about exposure.
Individuals can take some practical precautions without becoming fearful of everyday life.
Household and garden chemicals should be used according to their instructions. Food should be stored in suitable containers, and unsuitable plastics should be kept away from heat.
People living in areas with known arsenic contamination should use water that has been tested and found safe. During periods of heavy air pollution, exercising indoors can help people remain physically active.
There is also a need to be careful about commercial claims that exploit public anxiety.
Detox kits, cleanses and restrictive programmes often promise to remove unspecified toxins and prevent diabetes. However, such products rarely identify the chemicals involved or provide reliable evidence that their methods work.
People living with diabetes should never replace prescribed treatment with detox products. Blood glucose management, blood pressure control and cholesterol treatment remain essential parts of diabetes care.
Environmental chemicals may contribute to the development of diabetes, but the evidence suggests that their influence varies, with stronger findings involving air pollution and high-level arsenic exposure.
The challenge is to understand the extent of this contribution while reducing exposure wherever possible.
A family should not need to understand complex medical science to know that its drinking water is safe or that pesticides are handled responsibly at a workplace.
Protecting public health must begin long before someone walks into a doctor’s clinic and receives a diagnosis of diabetes.

What we know about the longest US nationwide flight ground stop since 9/11
- Published
The US Federal Aviation Administration has lifted the longest nationwide ground stop of flights since the 11 September 2001 terrorist attacks.
The FAA said Friday's stoppage, which lasted more than four hours, was "due to extraordinary circumstances" from a communication issue affecting all air traffic control centres.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication of an attack and that everybody was safe.
Here's what we know.
How many flights were affected?
The ground stop led to more than 8,500 delayed and nearly 8,000 cancelled flights on Friday, according to FlightAware.
The FAA's initial announcement at 15:54 EST (20:54 GMT) said all flights departing within the US would be grounded until further notice.
More than 3,500 airplanes were in the air at the time. Some were diverted to other airports and others flew on to their destinations.
Hours later, some flights were allowed to take off from San Francisco International airport.
The Federal Aviation Administration opened skies again at until 20:15 EST.
What about international flights?
All US-bound air traffic from Eurocontrol member states was suspended "on request of the FAA due to technical issues", according to Eurocontrol's website.
There are 42 Eurocontrol member states, including dozens of EU nations, the UK, Ukraine, and Turkey, as well as Israel and Morocco.
Australia's largest international airport, Sydney, grounded all US-bound flights until further notice.
Air Canada cancelled flights between the US and Canada.
When will normal service resume?
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in a news conference on Friday night that the outage would cause a ripple effect for a few days.
"It's going to take us some time to unwind what's happened this afternoon," Duffy said.
Tens of thousands of people were stranded in airports around the country, many of them "without any knowledge of where they're going to sleep tonight", Duffy said.
Delta Air Lines and United Airlines said they were resuming operations.
American Airlines said it was "focused on operating as many remaining flights as possible this evening". JetBlue said it would resume flights on Saturday morning.
What caused the ground stop?
Duffy said a legacy air traffic control communications system became overloaded.
"So this is analogue telecom. Our switches, our routers actually got overloaded with data and they went down," Duffy said.
He said this had affected communications and radar. The system needs a complete overhaul, he said, estimating a $50 billion price tag.
"It's going to continue to fail," he said.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told the news conference said they had seen "zero evidence" it was a cyber-attack.
He also ruled out any link to the global Microsoft outage that began on Thursday.
Mullin said the introduction of some new technology into an old air traffic control system had overwhelmed it.
Both cabinet secretaries insisted the public was never in danger during the stoppage.
When was the last ground stop?
It was only the second such nationwide stoppage since the immediate aftermath of the al-Qaeda plane hijackings of 11 September 2001.
"This looks like the worst since 9/11, but clearly not on that scale," Dr Guy Gratton, an associate professor of aviation at Cranfield University, told BBC Verify.
Dr Gratton pointed to a US grounding in 2023 due to a failure in the Notice to Air Missions (Notam) system.
"That lasted 1 hour and 52 minutes, delayed about 9,500 flights and cancelled about 1,300," he said.
The 2023 outage meant air traffic safety notices could no longer be published, and flights were grounded until that system was restored.
But Friday's incident lasted longer than the 2023 event.

Starbase, Texas – Elon Musk’s SpaceX on Saturday carried out the first-ever recovery of a spaceship, pulling off a successful “catch” of its Starship vessel as it returned to its launch site after a day in orbit.
The spaceship emerged from a cloudy sky after withstanding the extreme heat of re-entering the Earth’s atmosphere, and descended slowly over Starbase before slipping smoothly between mechanical “chopstick arms” above Launch Pad 2.
The feat marked a milestone in the space industry’s decadeslong pursuit of fully reusable rocket systems — a goal that can drastically reduce mission costs and make more frequent launches possible.

Premier says Quebec ready to vote independently from Canada for Francophonie leadership
Quebec, Canada and New Brunswick all have right to vote in election for new secretary-general
Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon is further distancing himself from the Canadian government in his first international outing since winning last month's provincial election.
He suggested Saturday that he was prepared to vote differently from Canada in the election for secretary-general of the Francophonie.
St-Pierre Plamondon is in Phnom Penh, the capital of Cambodia, to attend a summit of the international body of French-speaking states and governments.
Quebec, Canada and New Brunswick all have the right to vote in Monday's election to choose a new secretary-general.
Louise Mushikiwabo of Rwanda is seeking a third term as head of the organization, and is running against Juliana Amato Lumumba of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Dacian Ciolos of Romania, and Coumba Bâ of Mauritania.
St-Pierre Plamondon hasn't said who he'll support, but said he won't necessarily align with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and New Brunswick Premier Susan Holt.
“We’re not bound by another candidate’s vote,” he said, adding that discussions are ongoing among member states.
Mushikiwabo has expressed her desire for support from Quebec, saying she maintains “very good relations" with the province.
“I would very much like to have Quebec’s support,” she said alongside her deputy, Quebec native Caroline St-Hilaire, whose position is also at stake.
Carney, Quebec premier to have 1st in-person meeting
The topic may be on the agenda as St-Pierre Plamondon and Carney have their first in-person meeting on Sunday.
St-Pierre Plamondon said Saturday that he's optimistic about the discussions, despite his outspoken criticism of Ottawa.
“We’re preparing an (economic) update, so there will be important discussions on that,” he said.
Speaking in the Philippines, Carney also expressed confidence that he and St-Pierre Plamondon will be able to work together.
“I work with all the other premiers in Canada and leaders from countries around the world, so I’m sure we’ll find common priorities,” he said.
St-Pierre Plamondon began his day in Cambodia by addressing a roundtable of Quebec entrepreneurs, and encouraging them to use the Francophonie to pursue trade opportunities.
He then gave a speech at another entrepreneurs' gathering, where he reminded the attendees that Quebec has been a full member of the Francophonie for over 50 years.
"The (organization) is an example of how we can exercise our sovereignty at the international level," he said.
While Quebec's international relations minister has said the province wouldn't be raising the issue of independence in Cambodia, the premier said his sovereigntist government is sparking interest from other states.
“I won’t hide the fact that we’ve had ... several hallway conversations in which people are curious because we are the Parti Québécois,” he said.
“So, we discuss the topic of independence, but informally.”
St-Pierre Plamondon has promised his government will hold a referendum on sovereignty towards the end of his term, once U.S. President Donald Trump leaves the White House.
On Saturday, however, the Quebec premier's appearance on stage drew laughs as he was mistakenly introduced as the prime minister of Canada.

Israeli prime ministerial hopeful Gadi Eisenkot accused caretaker premier Benjamin Netanyahu on Friday of fuelling a “racist” campaign against the country’s Arab minority, after he sought to delegitimise the community’s lawmakers by linking them to Hamas.
Eisenkot’s statement was a rare instance of a prominent Jewish political leader taking a strong stand in defence of Arab Israelis, who make up more than 20% of the population.
Two Arab-majority parties, Ra’am and the Joint List, secured a combined 19 seats in last month’s election, winning nearly a sixth of the 120-seat parliament and potentially emerging as kingmakers in efforts by Eisenkot to form a government.
“Arab citizens of Israel are an integral part of the Israeli story,” Eisenkot wrote on X on Friday.
“They have been subjected to a racist and aggressive campaign of delegitimisation, fuelled by the outgoing prime minister and those around him for political purposes,” he added.
“The attempt to marginalise them and vilify them collectively is a profound violation of the principles of civic responsibility.”
Netanyahu and his allies have repeatedly criticised leaders of Arab parties for refusing to describe Hamas as a “terror group” after its unprecedented 7 October 2023 attack on Israel.
All leaders of Arab parties have condemned the attack, in which Arab Israelis – descendants of Palestinians who remained in what became Israel in 1948 – were also among those killed.
Netanyahu has also repeatedly alleged electoral fraud by Arab-majority parties, but electoral authorities have rejected the claims.
In a speech, Netanyahu lamented that the two Arab lists refused to recognise Israel as a Jewish state, although Ra’am’s leader, Mansour Abbas, has done so in the past.
He further claimed that they sought to establish either an “Islamic state” or a “nationalist Palestinian state”.
During the same ceremony, the national security minister, Itamar Ben Gvir, heckled Joint List’s leader, Yousef Jabareen, during his oath of allegiance, accusing him of having “pledged allegiance to Hamas”.
“It is entirely legitimate to disagree with representatives of the Arab parties, even to strongly disapprove of some of them. But it is neither legitimate nor acceptable to malign an entire community, and I will not allow it,” Eisenkot said.
President Isaac Herzog tasked Eisenkot with forming a new government on Sunday after consultations in which a majority of political parties, including the two Arab lists, recommended him for the role.
But one of Eisenkot’s rightwing allies, Avigdor Lieberman, has said he will back out of the coalition if Arab Israelis are part of it.
If Eisenkot fails to form a government within 28 days, he may request a 14-day extension. Should he still fall short, the mandate would pass to another lawmaker, most likely Netanyahu.

Nations Championship - England 78-15 Japan: Will Joseph scores five tries in first cap since 2022 as hosts score 13
Will Joseph (five), Freddie Steward, Ellis Genge, Cadan Murley, Ben Earl, George Martin, Ben Curry, Marcus Smith, Greg Fisilau score tries as England post huge Nations Championship victory, with Eddie Jones' Japan alarmingly inferior in contest; Joseph on first appearance since July 2022
By Michael Cantillon at Allianz Stadium Twickenham
Last Updated: 14/11/26 6:34pm
Will Joseph scored five tries on his first England appearance since 2022 as Steve Borthwick's side destroyed Japan 78-15 in Saturday's Nations Championship.
Joseph (five), Freddie Steward, Ellis Genge, Cadan Murley, Ben Earl, George Martin, Ben Curry, Marcus Smith and Greg Fisilau each scored tries on a day when Japan appeared alarmingly inferior to the hosts, copping a 20-minute red card to lock Harry Hockings after just a minute of play.
Indeed, England's points total would even have been 16 greater had eight conversions not been missed off the kicking tee - George Ford missing six, Henry Slade two.
Japan scored tries through lock Warner Dearns and replacement prop Opeti Helu, but it was a rather sombre return for former England head coach Eddie Jones to Twickenham, with his side falling well short of professional standards.
What's next?
For England, they next face New Zealand in their third Nations Championship Test of the autumn at Allianz Stadium Twickenham on Saturday, November 21 (2.10pm kick-off).
Japan travel to face Scotland at Murrayfield in Edinburgh for their next Test, also on Saturday November 21 (2.10pm kick-off).
