Nightmare Eclipse, the pseudonym of a researcher with an ongoing, very public beef with Microsoft, has dropped yet another Windows zero-day.
On Tuesday, Nightmare Eclipse disclosed SignDrop, a vulnerability that gives local users full System rights on some versions of Windows. The vulnerability resides in the Common Log File System, which Microsoft describes as a “general-purpose logging service used by software clients running in user-mode or kernel-mode.” By forcing a privileged process such as Windows Defender to open a crafted CLFS container, an attacker with ordinary user rights can abuse the privileged file creation to elevate privileges to System.
Turning a Windows defense against itself
The attack exploits the interaction of CLFS, Windows Defender, and Windows file permissions. The exploit uses Windows Defender to open a log file created by a standard user by calling ServerMpUpdateEngineSignature, a legitimate Defender function for processing antivirus signature updates.
By manipulating Windows Object Manager symbolic links, the attacker causes Defender to open the CLFS container in the security context of the antimalware engine. If an associated authentication file is missing, CLFS creates it using Defender’s System privileges. Because CLFS assigns the newly created file the Discretionary Access Control List of the original file, the attacker may gain access to a file created with System privileges, allowing the file-creation operation to be abused as part of a privilege-escalation attack.
Ironically, the vulnerability stems from a security measure Microsoft introduced in October 2025 to prevent attackers from exploiting other vulnerabilities in CLFS.
“If everything is chained correctly, funnily this legit security mitigation can be used against itself and allow an elevation [of] privileges,” Nightmare Eclipse wrote. “Everything is done properly by Microsoft here but the logic allows abuse.”

Common reasons your Roku TV can turn on by itself and how to fix it
Some people have been experiencing random power-ons recently.
You're sound asleep in the middle of the night when, all of a sudden, your TV turns on. You know you turned off the TV before you went to bed, no one else is awake, and there's nothing near your remote to accidentally push the power button. What — or who — could have turned on the TV? A bored spirit haunting your home? A burglar looking to take a quick break?
Those scenarios are highly unlikely. But, unfortunately, some Roku TVs and Roku streaming device owners have been jolted out of their slumber by those products inexplicably powering on randomly over the past few months. And no one really knows why it's happening. There may be a few explanations, however, and a couple of potential fixes to try if your Roku device has gone rogue during the wee hours.
A bug in Roku OS 15.3
When Roku OS version 15.3 went live in August 2026, owners of Roku TVs and Roku streaming devices began reporting these middle-of-the-night disturbances. Not every Roku TV or streaming player has been impacted by this supposed 15.3 bug, but the timing of the reports with the software update seems more than coincidental.
What's odd about that, though, is that there was nothing in the 15.3 update that involved autoplay features or even power management. So, in theory, the changes that were made to the Roku OS shouldn't have spurred these instances of people's Roku TVs "waking up" without being powered on by anyone (or anything) and playing a TV show or movie. But we all know that software updates often introduce bugs with no real rhyme or reason, and that feels like the most logical explanation for these strange occurrences.
A glitchy HDMI-CEC connection
Having your Roku TV's HDMI-CEC feature enabled is another very plausible reason the TV powers on randomly. If you're not familiar with HDMI-CEC, it's basically a chain that links all your A/V components with built-in HDMI switching (like soundbars, gaming consoles, receivers and speakers) since they're all connected via HDMI cables. And this allows all of those devices to be controlled with one remote.
So, when you power on your Roku TV, for example, HDMI-CEC essentially notifies all the other connected components to turn on. All it takes is one glitchy signal to confuse the whole chain, which could lead to a random power-up. And there is a history of HDMI-CEC causing strange switching between inputs and components, as well as phantom power-ons. Samsung Anynet+, Sony BRAVIA Sync, LG SimpLink and Roku 1-Touch Play are all just different names for the same HDMI-CEC standard, but each has its own custom software added to it to create the proprietary HDMI-CEC feature for each brand of smart TV.
Unfortunately, compatibility sometimes becomes an issue unless all of your connected devices are made by the same company (though even that doesn't guarantee incident-free performance). This can cause signal miscommunication that results in the random behavior of your Roku TV or streaming device.
Fast TV Start
There are other possible explanations for your Roku TV turning on by itself. For example, the Fast TV Start feature is a proprietary power-management setting that keeps your Roku TV's OS on in the background even when you shut off the TV.
This allows the TV to turn on instantly without any boot time, and it keeps the TV on alert for voice commands to turn the TV back on. Fast TV Start has also seemingly caused phantom power-on problems in conjunction with the Roku OS 15.3 update, as the always-on network connection kept open the door for overnight glitches.
How to prevent your Roku TV from turning on by itself
You may try all of these suggestions and still not have much luck because the root of the issue has not been "officially" identified by Roku, or anyone else, for that matter. And without the root cause, there remains no guaranteed fix. But these possible solutions are certainly worth trying and just might do the trick.
The first thing to try, if you haven't already, is updating your Roku TV's OS to version 16, which was released in October. Fixing the 15.3 bug wasn't part of the update, and no reports have surfaced that OS 16 patched the automatic power-on problem, but it's definitely worth trying. The worst-case scenario is that your Roku TV's OS is fully updated.
Next, disable 1-Touch Play (HDMI-CEC) not just on your Roku TV but on all the other components connected to the TV, regardless of brand. This includes your A/V equipment and gaming consoles. To do so on your Roku TV, go to Settings > System > Control other devices and uncheck 1-Touch Play. Also disable Fast TV Start, which you can find under Settings > System > Power > Fast TV Start, then either clear the Enable Fast TV Start option or check Off to disable it.
If these don't work, try unplugging the TV when you're done watching it each night (no, not ideal), using a smart plug to automatically cut the power for you or consulting Roku's tech support portal at support.roku.com for further assistance.

Kashmir’s land reforms are usually remembered for one historic idea: those who cultivated the land should own it.
But there was another group whose lives were closely tied to the land, even though they did not own the fields or the ground beneath their homes.
These were agricultural labourers and other rural families who spent generations living on property belonging to landlords or employers.
Their houses were part of the village, but their legal claim to the land beneath them remained uncertain.
Section 6 of the Jammu and Kashmir Agrarian Reforms Act, 1976, sought to address this problem.
It recognised that the history of land reforms was also about protecting the homes of certain people whose lives and livelihoods had long been connected with agriculture.
Nearly five decades later, this provision remains important for families with old residential claims and for the revenue authorities responsible for examining them.
The roots of this legislation go back to the political changes of 1947.
At the time, land ownership was concentrated in the hands of powerful proprietors, while much of the rural population depended on tenancy, agricultural labour and cultivation for a living.
A cultivator could spend a lifetime working another person’s fields without having secure rights over the land.
The first major changes came in April 1948, when the government abolished feudal arrangements such as Jagirdari, Muafi and Mukarrari.
Measures introduced in October that year gave tenants-at-will greater security of tenure.
The Big Landed Estates Abolition Act, 1950, took the reforms further by setting limits on landholdings and transferring surplus land to those who cultivated it.
Further tenancy reforms followed in 1955, 1960, 1965 and 1970.
Together, these measures changed the relationship between landowners and cultivators.
A historical account published in the Government of India’s Yojana magazine in May 1973 also traced this reform process to the measures introduced in 1948.
The 1976 Act addressed another problem that had received less attention.
In village society, agricultural workers and economically weaker families often lived in houses built on land owned by proprietors or employers. Some had spent years serving the landowner while raising families in these homes. Their residence depended heavily on the owner’s willingness to let them stay.
Section 6 sought to give legal protection to certain people in this position.
Its scope was specific: it applied to a dwelling house occupied on September 1, 1971, by a person belonging to one of the categories listed in the Act.
These included tillers, members of Scheduled Castes, landless agricultural labourers, Gujjars, Bakarwals, Gaddis and landless labourers engaged in occupations connected with agriculture.
Where these conditions were met and the occupant did not own the site, the owner’s rights, title and interest in the dwelling house, its site and the land attached to it were deemed extinguished and vested in the Government with effect from May 1, 1973.
The retrospective date gave legal effect to the provision from a time before the Act itself came into force.
The legislature also recognised that different families could have different claims.
The first proviso protected a dwelling house constructed at the expense of the occupant or a predecessor-in-interest. Such a house would not vest in the Government under this provision.
The second proviso dealt with long-standing occupation. A person who had remained in continuous occupation of the house for ten years by the commencement of the Act was deemed to have acquired ownership of the dwelling house in return for services rendered to the owner of the land beneath and adjoining it.
This was an important recognition of the relationship between residence and labour.
A family that had spent years living in a house connected with its work could establish a claim under the conditions laid down by the law.
However, occupation alone did not create an automatic right to ownership. The prescribed categories, dates and other statutory conditions had to be established.
The Act also placed a ceiling on the land covered by Section 6.
Under subsection (2), the aggregate qualifying area beneath and attached to the dwelling house, when considered with the specified areas beneath other buildings and exempted lands under Section 3, could not exceed four kanals for the individual and the family collectively.
Revenue authorities must therefore examine the total qualifying area rather than look at the house site in isolation.
Section 6 also needs to be read alongside Section 8(3).
The former provides for the vesting of the relevant property in the Government, while the latter sets out how ownership rights can subsequently vest in a qualifying occupant.
This remains subject to the conditions under Section 6(2) and payment of the prescribed levy under Schedule III.
Establishing occupation, therefore, is only one part of the legal process.
The responsibility of the Revenue Department is considerable. In many villages, houses have remained within families for generations, while old revenue records may continue to show another person’s name as the owner. Such cases call for careful examination of Jamabandies, village maps, field records and other available documents.
Officials must establish whether the house existed and was occupied on September 1, 1971, whether the occupant belonged to a qualifying category and whether the site was owned by that person.
They must also examine who paid for the construction, whether the ten-year occupation condition was fulfilled, whether the total area falls within the four-kanal ceiling and whether ownership was subsequently granted under Section 8(3), subject to the prescribed levy.
A present-day revenue entry cannot replace this examination. Equally, a genuine claim should not be dismissed simply because the relevant records are old or incomplete. Decisions must rest on evidence and the conditions laid down in the Act.
Kashmir’s land reforms changed the lives of cultivators by recognising their rights over agricultural land. Section 6 addressed a different but closely related concern: the position of families whose homes stood on land they did not own.
A house was where children grew up, families worked and generations established their lives. Its legal status could influence the future of an entire household.
The provision was an attempt to bring these long-standing residential relationships within the protection of the law. Its proper implementation now depends on revenue officials examining old claims with care, while respecting the rights of all parties.
A village house may appear as a small structure on a revenue map, but its history can go back several generations.
The law must look beyond the name recorded against the land and establish whether the people who lived there qualify for the rights that Section 6 was written to recognise.

Cristiano Ronaldo retired from international football earlier this month, and now the Portuguese national team has found a unique way to honour him.
Ronaldo wore the number seven and popularised the term CR7 through his jersey number, which he wore at every club he went to. He wore that number as he won numerous titles in his career and went on to become the men’s all-time leading scorer.
“Time to debut a new 7. Because there’s one that will be eternal,” said the Portuguese national team.
The announcement video by the national team shows a cross through the number 7, indicating how the number will be a cross to bear for anyone who follows Ronaldo. This is meant in terms of the pressure of following in his footsteps, but also as a way to honour him after his retirement.

It was, says Ido Rakovsky, like reporting on "science fiction", rather than sport.
Israel, whose senior team have qualified for the World Cup just once, had beaten global powerhouses Brazil in the quarter-finals of the under-20 version of the tournament.
At the final whistle, the commentator covering the match for Israeli television vowed "you will tell of this night to your children, and they will tell it to your grandchildren".
Plenty heard him.
Five days later, the team's semi-final against Uruguay was the most-watched thing of the evening on Israeli television, drawing a 23% viewing share.
Politicians clamoured to congratulate the team.
It was June 2023.
"That summer, everybody was watching under-20 football, everybody knew the players," says Rakovsky, who was covering the team for Israeli media outlet Haaretz.
"Everybody in Israel fell in love with these kids."
It wasn't just their deeds on the pitch that felt otherworldly, though.
After scoring a stoppage-time winner against Uzbekistan in the last 16, Anan Khalaili had given an interview to Israeli television.
In it Khalaili, an Israeli Arab, thanked the viewers back home for staying up late to watch his team win in Argentina.
To do so, he used the words 'Am Yisrael' - a Hebrew phrase that means 'People of Israel' and is bound up in Jewish religion, community, culture and history.
"That an Arab player used that figure of speech said something about the identity of that team," says Rakovsky.
"That team made real the claim that football can really bring people together - that Muslim players are part of the national team of the Jewish state, representing Israel and creating something better, both for the present and future."
But a little over four months after Khalaili's interview and the win over Brazil, Hamas attacked Israel.
The armed Palestinian group killed about 1,200 people and took 251 hostages. In response, Israel launched a massive military offensive in Gaza. The United Nations believes the retaliation has killed more than 70,000 Palestinians., external
As the war goes on, can the potential of a golden generation of Israel's footballers, in sport and society, be realised?
Beaten 1-0 by eventual champions Uruguay, Israel finished third at that Under-20 World Cup in 2023.
Their run was no fluke.
The same set of players, with a few additions and omissions, had already impressed at continental level.
They were runners-up at 2022's Under-19 Euros, beaten by England in extra-time in the final, and would go on to make the semi-finals of 2023's Under-20 Euros.
Israel has produced outstanding players in the past. Eyal Berkovic and Yossi Benayoun were technical, gifted attackers with long Premier League careers.
But a depth of talent, emerging together, sets the current cohort apart.
Khalaili has been one of the most sought-after young prospects in Europe this summer.
After his £21.5m move to Inter Milan fell through, Crystal Palace saw off competition from Nottingham Forest to pick him up for a similar fee from Belgian side Union Saint-Gilloise.
Playmaker Oscar Gloukh, 22, wears Ajax's number 10 shirt after his form earned a move from Red Bull Salzburg.
Left-back Roy Revivo signed for Spanish club Elche on transfer deadline day this month from Maccabi Tel Aviv, while Twente defender Stav Lemkin, also 23, is also highly rated.
Dor Turgeman, Ilay Feingold and Idan Toklomati are impressing in Major League Soccer in the United States.
All have now won full caps, but were moulded into a collective, cohesive unit - something that has often been beyond the senior side - by Israel's age-grade coach Ofir Haim.
"It isn't an issue at all here," Haim said, external of the different backgrounds in his squad during the 2023 Under-20 World Cup.
"We don't have any problem with religion. Not at all. We have players here who put on tefillin [Jewish ceremonial wear, containing verses from the Torah] - and Anan [Khalaili], Hamza [Shibli] and Ahmed [Salman] perform the Muslim prayers.
"We don't even talk about this. We unite everybody, and I wish the country were as united as this team."
Football has long been the part of Israeli society where communities mix together who may not otherwise meet.
"The majority of the Jewish people who arrived in the mandate period [a spell between 1923 and 1948 where the region was run by Britain] emigrated from Europe," says Dr Omer Einav, a historian and author of Defending the Goal, a book on Israel's football history.
"They were Europeans and when you think about cinema, music, theatre, dance, they had nothing in common with Middle Eastern culture. Nothing, except football. That was the only common language, the only thing they both love in the same way."
Encouraged by the British administrators who ran the region, teams from different communities, and some made up of elements of each, would play against each other.
When the modern state of Israel was formed in 1948, much of the Arab population that remained inside its borders continued to identify as or with Palestinians. Most still do.
They are also an intrinsic part of Israeli football.
While they make up 20% of Israel's population, they represent about 35% of those involved in the sport at elite level nationally.
The first Arab player to represent Israel's national team was Rifaat Turk in 1976. In 2018, Bibars Natcho became the first Muslim to captain the team.
Neither was without controversy.
Turk was roundly abused. Natcho's decision not to sing Israel's national anthem, the lyrics of which relate to the Jewish search for a homeland, was condemned by some., external
For a short time in the summer of 2023, it seemed as if Haim's under-20 side might offer a watershed moment of unity and co-existence.
But football, like everything in Israel, changed on 7 October.
Matan Segal directed Kick It Out Israel, an anti-discrimination initiative with similar aims but no link to the English organisation of the same name, for almost four years before stepping down a few months ago.
Racism has long been present in Israeli club football. Beitar Jerusalem's fans are among the most notorious.
In 2013, ultras burned down their own club's offices in protest at the signing of two Chechen Muslims.
The most extreme Beitar fans have long taunted Israeli Arabs with chants of "may your village burn", while declaring themselves "forever pure".
However during his time at Kick It Out Israel, Segal saw racism against Arab players become more virulent and widespread.
Covid, during which fans radicalised online during lockdown, was one cause.
The election of Israel's far-right government at the end of 2022, legitimising views towards Palestinians that were previously seen as extreme, was a second.
The war was undoubtedly another.
"Before 7 October, people generally respected the Arab players," Segal said.
"Even though they had difficulties with them not singing the Israeli anthem, they respected them and they could talk about it.
"After 7 October though, we saw an increase in racist remarks.
"It was happening at small clubs where we hadn't seen it before. There were terrible songs - 'Let's kill all Arabs', 'There are no schools in Gaza because there are no children left'."
Football, inevitably, has become a focal point for emotion generated by the conflict.
Clubs which are usually bitter rivals came together to remember those killed by Hamas. Scarves were part of the commemoration at the site of the Nova music festival, where hundreds were killed.
Hapoel Jerusalem's club badge now features a silhouette of Hersh Goldberg-Polin, who was abducted and killed in captivity and whose parents have campaigned for peace through their grief.
Meanwhile, Israeli Defence Force (IDF) soldiers have posed with club flags and banners while on operation in Gaza, dedicating their actions to the clubs and ultras back home., external
In such a heightened atmosphere, young footballers – closely connected to the conflict through Israel's programme of national service and a barrage of online commentary and images – are under constant scrutiny and pressure.
Gloukh's lifelong friend Afik Tery was killed by a Hamas explosive while serving in the IDF.
After his death, Gloukh posted a poignant set of pictures, external of the pair arm-in-arm over time - as young boys at birthday parties, as young men at a wedding - with the final slide showing Tery's funeral.
Among the online replies were the taunts of pro-Palestinians.
For Israel players with Palestinian heritage, the stakes are especially and dangerously high.
Dia Saba plays in a similar playmaking role to Gloukh. The 33-year-old has scored three goals in 13 appearances for Israel.
He is unlikely ever to add to that tally.
Saba was one of Maccabi Haifa's most high-profile stars when, at the start of the conflict, his wife Narmin posted a message to Instagram.
"There are children in Gaza, too," she wrote.
Saba apologised for the outrage caused, but could not save his career in Israel. He left Maccabi Haifa in 2025 and now plays for Turkish side Amedspor.
"My dream was to play for Maccabi Haifa, the club that I support, the team that I grew up with," Saba said at the time.
"I wanted to continue. But sometimes there are reasons that are stronger than us that don't allow it."
Saba and others are used to having their loyalty questioned. From all sides.
Many in the Arab world would like more Palestinian prospects within Israel to follow the example of Ataa Jaber.
Jaber captained Israel's Under-21 side but switched nationalities, external to represent Palestine in June 2023, saying he could no longer separate sport and politics after seeing police evict Palestinian families from their homes in Israeli-occupied East Jerusalem.
Switching away from a high level of international football damaged his prospects of a move to Europe. At home, there were calls for his Israeli citizenship to be revoked. But, for Jaber, it was preferable to representing a country whose actions he deplored.
Those footballers who voice an opinion on the conflict choose their words carefully.
Beram Kayal, the former Brighton, Celtic and Israel player, knows the dilemmas and reality well.
"To be Arabic in Israel, it's sometimes hard," he says. "Sometimes it is tough.
"Opportunities-wise, sometimes we are not on the same level."
However, he believes in a pluralistic future for Israel and football as a tool to achieve it.
His friendship with Tomer Hemed - whom he first met as a young teenager at Maccabi Haifa's academy and later played alongside at Brighton and Charlton, as well as international level - sums up his approach.
"When I played with Tomer, he prayed like this," he says, touching his hand to his back of his head to indicate a kippah, the small skullcap worn as a sign of Jewish faith.
"And I was praying for Allah," he adds, raising his arms above his shoulders in worship.
"He was my team-mate and he is my brother.
"In football, on the pitch, you never look at colour, culture or religion. You just want the best people around you to win the game."
The 38-year-old is now employed by Israel's Football Association to work with young talents from Palestinian areas.
In doing so he works alongside former Israel goalkeeper Boni Ginzburg, who played across Glasgow at Rangers and is now the IFA's technical director.
After Arabic was relegated behind Hebrew as Israel's official language by a controversial 2018 law promoted by prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the IFA put on Hebrew language lessons for Arabic-speaking coaches to ensure they could still obtain their qualifications.
"Not in our building," says Kayal when asked about the precedence given to Hebrew.
"I'm in this place [the IFA] to bring the culture of the Arabic people to the table.
"I say to the Arabic players when they come into the national team: Speak in your language, don't be afraid, don't be shy to speak, don't just afraid to show yourself.
"Israel is a young country. We need to learn from our DNA, to see the different between the Jewish, the Circassians, the Arabic, the Muslim, the Christian, the Druze – all the colours – put that together and learn what we could do better."
Israel's aim is to go better than their national team has managed in more than 50 years.
Ran Ben-Shimon was appointed as the senior side's head coach in 2024. He was given the goal of converting youthful promise into qualification for Euro 2028, which will be staged in England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland.
Success would place more stress on Israel's players and, potentially, squad unity.
Large-scale protests are planned for Republic of Ireland's forthcoming Nations League matches with Israel. Dublin will host seven games at the tournament.
Villa Park in Birmingham, from which Maccabi Tel Aviv fans were banned from attending a Europa League match in November, will stage four matches.
Hampden Park, two miles across Glasgow from where Celtic fans have held vociferous pro-Palestine protests, has six.
Wherever Israel play, players will be confronted with criticism of their country's treatment of Palestinians, both at home and in Gaza, that is rarely voiced at home.
"Israelis are very sensitive to anyone showing any kind of sympathy for what happened on 7 October," says Dr Sophia Solomon, part of Ben-Gurion University's Center for Sports Diplomacy.
"It is like denying the Holocaust, that is the proportion of it. A war is a special situation, it wasn't like this before, but to express your agony became more encouraged as we saw the European arena become more anti-Israeli.
"One reaction ignited another and there is more obligation to identify yourself with the victims of 7 October."
She believes that it will take time for Israeli society, footballers included, to understand the past three years and speak openly about the conflict.
"Until the ongoing war ends, no-one can say what he thinks," she said. "Even after the Middle East returns to its 'normal' craziness, maybe it will take a decade to pass before people can start talking about their experiences and expectations.
"Time has to pass until you can touch certain areas, and at the moment you can see a lot of avoidance about talking about it, even mentioning it."
The time for this stellar generation to fulfil their potential may come before that.
It may not. Translating youth-level promise to senior-level product is never simple.
But, whatever the future holds, for a few months, in the summer of 2023, Haim and his team gave Israel something special.
"We saw Anan Khalaili and Hamza Shibli scoring against Brazil and that was our hope, that was the future. That was our future," says Einav.
"I'm not so optimistic, but people thought maybe it's really a magical thing that can help Israeli society in general.
"There was something there, something new, something where people said 'OK, if we co-operate, if we work together, we can also succeed in sport.'
"That's what we all care about, right? We want to be good at sports. We are sick of watching the World Cup from our living room.
"I think football is in some isolated, sterilised dimension - some kind of bubble - inside Israeli society. It is not hermetic. A lot of dirt comes in - racism, violence - but I do believe that football can reflect good things that can happen. The equality of chances, the tolerance and solidarity of all people living here.
"It can't heal anything but it can help us see one another in a more human way.
"So, yeah there was definitely a moment, but it was before our world changed and collapsed."
Only time will tell what remains of that moment and whether it can be revived.

Perhaps the Rumors of Democracy’s Demise Were Premature
Did the midterm election save it?
Before the midterms this month, experts who measure the health of democracies saw the United States experiencing “the most dramatic decline in American history,” in the words of one global index.
Warnings also came from judges ruling on election-related cases. In late October, Judge David O. Carter blocked the Justice Department from ordering California officials to segregate the ballots of 20,000 voters who were on a list of suspected noncitizens that Carter found to be unreliable. “If the executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger,” he wrote.
Against the backdrop of such fears, the November election became not just a referendum on President Trump, but also a crucial test of American democracy. In the end, the country passed. Turnout was the second highest for a midterm in more than a century, and Republicans, including Trump, have accepted the results. Even this week, when Democrat Scott Colom was declared the winner of the tight race for Senate in Mississippi, there were no challenges or protests in the historically Republican state.
Does one free and fair election mean the concerns that preceded it were overblown? There’s little question that Trump’s hyperaggressive use of presidential power and his family’s self-enrichment have served as a shock to the county’s democratic traditions. But the election suggests that American democracy has the resources to heal. The point is not that Democrats were the victors. It’s that the popular will won and reflected a wholesale turn against the administration in power.
Leading up to the midterms, scholars debated whether the country was sliding into a soft form of authoritarianism in Trump’s second term, akin to Hungary under former Prime Minister Viktor Orban. The answer was yes, the political scientists Steven Levitsky and Lucan A. Way argued in an article published in October. They cited Trump’s leveraging of federal power to cow law firms, prosecute political opponents, pressure news media outlets to alter their coverage, and steer political donations toward his own super PACs. It was all an effort to entrench himself and his party in power, Levitsky and Way wrote, as was Trump’s mid-decade gerrymandering push.
On the other side of the debate, Kurt Weyland, a professor of government at the University of Texas at Austin, said that while Trump was transgressive, he was not transforming the U.S. government into an authoritarian regime. For the most part, the laws and traditions protecting free expression and civil society blocked his undemocratic initiatives. The United States was not turning into Hungary under Orban or Turkey under President Recep Tayyip Erdogan. “The mayor of Istanbul is sitting in prison” for opposing Erdogan, Weyland said. “James Talarico isn’t in prison.” In fact, he is headed to the Senate.

Cartier and Van Cleef & Arpels help Richemont buck the luxury downturn
The Swiss luxury group reported stronger-than-expected profits as its jewellery maisons continued to grow and its specialist watchmakers showed signs of recovery.
Richemont said strong demand for its jewellery and a recovery in watch sales helped profits jump more than a third as the Swiss luxury group continued to defy a prolonged downturn in the sector.
The owner of Cartier and Van Cleef & Arpels said net profit for the six months to the end of September rose 39 per cent to €2.5 billion (US$2.76 billion; S$3.55 billion), beating expectations. Sales rose 17 per cent organically to €12.3 billion.
The results underscore how Richemont, along with a handful of luxury rivals including Burberry, has managed to outperform in a sector that has been hit by weaker Chinese demand and instability in the Middle East, with a pullback in spending by aspirational shoppers.
Jewellery has been particularly resilient, as wealthy consumers continue to spend on high-end pieces even as demand for luxury handbags and fashion has faltered.
Richemont’s jewellery businesses, including Cartier, Van Cleef & Arpels and Buccellati, remained the main engine of growth, with sales rising 19 per cent organically to €9.1 billion.
“We see an overall very positive trend for jewellery brands,” said Richemont’s chair Johann Rupert.
Analysts at RBC said the results were “reassuring in a difficult luxury operating environment”, but noted that jewellery sales growth in the second quarter was slightly below expectations.
“Solid margin delivery was tempered by early signs of jewellery growth normalisation,” said Thomas Chauvet, an analyst at Citi.
Shares in Richemont fell 7 per cent in early morning trading on Friday (Nov 13).
Richemont’s specialist watchmakers, including Vacheron Constantin and Jaeger-LeCoultre, also showed signs of recovery, with second-quarter sales rising 12 per cent organically, well ahead of analysts’ expectations of 4 per cent.
Japan was the strongest-performing market in the quarter, with organic sales growth of 23 per cent, followed by the Americas at 19 per cent and Europe at 15 per cent.
However, demand in mainland China remained subdued, while sales in the Middle East and Africa fell 7 per cent as the regional conflict weighed on tourist spending.
Rupert declined to comment on Richemont’s potential involvement in the management of De Beers. The luxury group has considered joining a consortium bidding for the diamond producer, which is being sold by mining group Anglo American, according to reports.
Richemont announced earlier on Friday that its results would be delayed following an outage at Microsoft, which has disrupted services to businesses around the world.

At least four people were killed and almost 90 others were injured when two trains collided on Sunday south of Cairo, authorities have said.
The crash occurred in al-Ayyat district in Giza province, about 30 miles (5okm) south of the capital, when a train travelling to the south-western Fayoum province crashed into the rear of a train heading to the southern province of Aswan, according to the transport ministry. It said one of the trains had derailed.
The health ministry said at least four people had been killed and 88 injured. The injured were taken to nearby hospitals for treatment, it said.
The president, Abdel Fatah al-Sisi, said in a social media post that he had ordered a prompt investigation into the crash to hold those responsible accountable.
Emergency teams and cranes were dispatched to the scene to clear the wreckage and restore services to their normal schedule as soon as possible, the Egyptian railway authority said.
A train driver and his assistant were injured in September last year when two freight trains collided in the same district.
